The Mysterious Island

Five castaways, one engineer, and an island that keeps its secret — translated fresh and complete from Verne's French

by Jules Verne

1874-1875 2026

This is an AI modernization of The Mysterious Island into contemporary English. The original is available from Wikisource (the Hetzel 1875 text). Also available as an epub.

Editor's Introduction

Jules Verne (1828–1905) published The Mysterious Island in three parts in 1874 and 1875, first in instalments in the family magazine run by his publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel and then as a book. It opens in March 1865, in the last weeks of the American Civil War. Five Northerners trapped in besieged Richmond, Virginia, two of them prisoners of war, steal a Confederate balloon during a hurricane and escape in it, along with a dog. The storm carries them for days and drops them on an unknown island in the South Pacific, more than a thousand miles from any other land, with almost nothing in their pockets.

The leader of the five is Cyrus Smith, an engineer, and the book is really about what an engineer knows. Starting from one match, then from none, the castaways make fire, bricks, pottery, iron, steel, glass, soap, candles, explosives and in the end a telegraph. Verne gives every step. The long chapters of chemistry and metalwork are the heart of the book's argument, which is that knowledge is the one thing a shipwreck cannot take from you, and they are kept here in full.

From the start, though, things happen on the island that nobody can explain. The answer, when it comes, ties this book to two earlier ones. Captain Grant's Children (1867–68) left a criminal marooned on a nearby island, and Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1870) ended with Captain Nemo's submarine vanishing into a whirlpool. Verne could not make the dates of the three books agree, and his publisher printed notes admitting as much. Those notes are left out here.

In the earlier book Nemo hides where he comes from. Verne had wanted him to be a Polish nobleman at war with Russia, and Hetzel talked him out of it. Here Verne tells the story at last: Nemo was an Indian prince who fought the British in the rising of 1857 and lost his whole family to it. W. H. G. Kingston's English translation of 1875, the one most English readers have known, cut and softened that history. This edition is translated complete from Verne's French and gives it in full.

Some things in this edition differ from the original. The heroes are American, so Verne measured in feet, miles and degrees Fahrenheit and added metric conversions for French readers. The American units are kept and the conversions dropped. Nab, Smith's servant, is a freed slave who chose to stay with him. Verne's narrator often calls him by a racial term rather than his name, and this edition uses his name. Two asides that mock his race have been cut, and so has a comparison between an ape and named human peoples. What Nab says and does is unchanged.

Part One: Shipwrecked in the Air

Chapter 1: The Hurricane of 1865

The hurricane of 1865 — Cries in the air — A balloon carried off by a waterspout — The torn envelope — Nothing but sea in sight — Five passengers — What happens in the basket — A coast on the horizon — How the drama ends

"Are we going up again?"

"No! Just the opposite! We're going down!"

"Worse than that, Mr. Cyrus! We're falling!"

"For God's sake, throw out ballast!"

"That was the last sack!"

"Is the balloon rising?"

"No!"

"I can hear something like waves splashing!"

"The sea's right under the basket!"

"It can't be five hundred feet below us!"

Then a powerful voice tore through the air, and these words rang out:

"Throw out everything that has any weight! Everything! And God help us!"

Those were the words that burst out in the sky above the vast watery desert of the Pacific at about four o'clock in the afternoon on March 23, 1865.

No doubt nobody has forgotten the terrible northeasterly gale that broke loose at the height of that year's spring equinox, when the barometer fell to seven hundred and ten millimeters. It was a hurricane, without a single lull, and it lasted from March 18 to March 26. The damage it did was immense, in America, in Europe, and in Asia, across a band eighteen hundred miles wide that ran slantwise to the equator from the thirty-fifth parallel north to the fortieth parallel south. Cities flattened, forests torn up by the roots, shores laid waste by mountains of water that came rushing in like tidal bores, ships flung up on the coast — the shipping registers of the Bureau Veritas counted them by the hundreds — whole districts leveled by waterspouts that ground up everything in their path, several thousand people crushed on land or swallowed at sea: that was the evidence of its fury that this tremendous hurricane left behind it. In the scale of its disasters it outdid even the two that had devastated Havana and Guadeloupe so horribly, the one on October 25, 1810, the other on July 26, 1825.

Now, at the very moment when so many catastrophes were taking place on land and sea, a drama no less gripping was being played out in the churning air.

A balloon, carried like a ball on the top of a waterspout and caught in the whirling motion of that column of air, was racing through space at ninety miles an hour, spinning round and round as though some aerial Maelström had seized it.

Beneath the neck at the bottom of the balloon swung a basket holding five passengers, barely visible in the thick vapors, mixed with spray, that trailed down to the surface of the ocean.

Where had this balloon come from, this plaything of the frightful storm? From what point on the globe had it set out? It obviously could not have taken off during the hurricane. But the hurricane had been raging for five days already, and its first signs had shown themselves on the 18th. So one would have been justified in thinking that the balloon had come from very far away, since it could not have covered less than two thousand miles in every twenty-four hours.

In any case, the passengers could have had no way of estimating how far they had come since setting out, because they had nothing at all to take their bearings by. In fact, a curious thing must have happened: carried along in the midst of the storm's violence, they did not feel it. They were moving, they were spinning, without sensing anything of the rotation or of their headlong travel sideways through the air. Their eyes could not pierce the thick fog that heaped up beneath the basket. All around them was mist. The clouds were so dense that they could not have said whether it was day or night. No glint of light, no sound from inhabited lands, no roar of the ocean could have reached them in that dark immensity as long as they stayed in the upper heights. Only their rapid descent could have told them of the danger they were in above the waves.

Meanwhile the balloon, lightened of heavy things — ammunition, weapons, provisions — had risen again into the upper layers of the atmosphere, to a height of four thousand five hundred feet. Once they realized that the sea lay beneath the basket, the passengers decided that the dangers above were less fearsome than the dangers below. They had not hesitated to throw even their most useful possessions overboard, and they were trying not to lose another breath of the gas — the very soul of their machine — that held them up over the abyss.

The night passed in an anxiety that would have killed less determined spirits. Then day returned, and with the day the hurricane began to slacken. From the very start of that day, March 24, there were signs of calm. At dawn the clouds, thinner and more vaporous, had climbed back into the heights of the sky. Within a few hours the waterspout spread out at the top and broke apart. The wind dropped from a hurricane to what sailors call "a strong gale" — that is, the speed at which the layers of air were rushing along was cut in half. It was still what sailors call "a three-reef breeze," a wind that makes them shorten sail three times over, but the improvement in the turmoil of the elements was considerable all the same.

Toward eleven o'clock the lower air had noticeably cleared. The atmosphere had that damp clarity which you can see, and even feel, after the passage of great storms. The hurricane did not seem to have gone any farther west. It seemed to have killed itself. Perhaps, after the waterspout broke, it had drained away in sheets of electricity, as sometimes happens with the typhoons of the Indian Ocean.

But at about that same hour, anyone watching could have seen once more that the balloon was slowly sinking, in one continuous movement, into the lower layers of the air. It even seemed to be deflating little by little, its envelope stretching and sagging, changing from the shape of a sphere to the shape of an egg.

By noon the balloon was floating only two thousand feet above the sea. It held fifty thousand cubic feet of gas, and thanks to that great capacity it had clearly been able to stay aloft for a long time, whether by climbing to great altitudes or by traveling horizontally.

Now the passengers threw out the last things still weighing the basket down: the little food they had kept back, everything, down to the small odds and ends in their pockets. And one of them, hoisting himself up onto the ring where the cords of the net came together, tried to tie the neck of the balloon shut as tightly as he could.

It was plain that the passengers could no longer keep the balloon in the upper air. They were running out of gas!

So they were lost!

For it was neither a continent nor even an island that stretched out below them. The whole expanse offered not a single place to land, not one solid surface for their anchor to bite into.

It was the immense sea, its waves still smashing together with incomparable violence! It was the ocean with no limits in sight, even for them, high above it, their gaze sweeping a circle forty miles in radius! It was that liquid plain, beaten without mercy and lashed by the hurricane, which must have looked to them like a stampede of wild-maned waves with a vast net of white crests flung over them! Not a scrap of land in sight, not a ship!

So they had to stop the descent at any cost, to keep the balloon from being swallowed up by the waves. And that urgent task was clearly what the passengers in the basket were working at. But in spite of their efforts the balloon kept sinking, while at the same time it was driven along with tremendous speed in the direction of the wind — that is, from northeast to southwest.

A terrible situation for these unfortunate men! They had obviously lost all control of the balloon. Nothing they tried could work. The envelope was deflating more and more. The gas was escaping, and there was no possible way to hold it in. Their descent was visibly speeding up, and at one o'clock in the afternoon the basket was hanging no more than six hundred feet above the ocean.

The truth was that nothing could stop the gas from leaking, because it was pouring freely out through a tear in the envelope.

By lightening the basket of everything it held, the passengers had been able to keep themselves in the air a few hours longer. But the inevitable catastrophe could only be put off, and if no land appeared before nightfall, passengers, basket, and balloon would vanish for good beneath the waves.

The only maneuver left to try was tried at this point. The balloon's passengers were clearly people of great energy, people who knew how to look death in the face. Not a single complaint could be heard from their lips. They were resolved to fight to the last second and to do everything they could to delay their fall. The basket was nothing but a kind of wicker box, useless as a boat, and if it fell into the sea there would be no way at all to keep it afloat.

At two o'clock the balloon was barely four hundred feet above the waves.

At that moment a manly voice — the voice of a man whose heart fear could not reach — made itself heard. Other voices, no less determined, answered it.

"Has everything been thrown out?"

"No! There's still ten thousand francs in gold!"

A heavy bag dropped into the sea at once.

"Is the balloon rising?"

"A little, but it won't be long before it falls again!"

"What's left to throw out?"

"Nothing!"

"Yes there is! The basket!"

"Grab hold of the net! Overboard with the basket!"

That was in fact the one last way left to lighten the balloon. The ropes that tied the basket to the ring were cut, and the balloon, after its fall, shot back up two thousand feet.

The five passengers had hauled themselves up into the net above the ring and were clinging there in the mesh, staring down into the abyss.

Everyone knows how sensitive balloons are to any change of weight. Throw out the lightest object and the balloon moves up or down. Floating in the air, it behaves like a scale of mathematical precision. So it is easy to understand that when it is relieved of a relatively large weight, it moves a long way, and suddenly. That is what happened now.

But after hanging in balance for a moment up in the higher air, the balloon began to sink again. The gas was escaping through the tear, and there was no way to mend it.

The passengers had done everything they could do. No human means could save them now. They had nothing left to count on but the help of God.

At four o'clock the balloon was only five hundred feet above the surface of the water.

A loud bark rang out. A dog was traveling with the passengers, hanging on in the mesh of the net beside his master.

"Top's seen something!" cried one of the passengers.

And at once a strong voice rang out:

"Land! Land!"

Driven steadily southwest by the wind, the balloon had covered a considerable distance since dawn — hundreds of miles — and a fairly high piece of land had in fact just appeared in that direction.

But that land was still thirty miles away to leeward. It would take a good hour to reach it, and that only if they did not drift off course. An hour! Wouldn't the balloon lose all the gas it had left before then?

That was the terrible question! The passengers could clearly see that solid spot, which they had to reach at any cost. They did not know what it was, island or continent, since they barely knew what part of the world the hurricane had carried them to! But that land, whether inhabited or not, whether it would welcome them or not — they had to get there!

By four o'clock, though, it was plain that the balloon could not hold itself up any longer. It was skimming the surface of the sea. The crests of the enormous waves had already licked the bottom of the net several times, making it heavier still, and the balloon now lifted only halfway, like a bird with lead shot in its wing.

Half an hour later the land was only a mile off, but the balloon, exhausted, limp, stretched out of shape and crumpled into great folds, kept gas only in its upper part. The passengers clinging to the net were still too heavy for it, and soon, half plunged in the sea, they were being battered by the furious waves. Then the envelope bellied out like a pocket, and the wind, rushing into it, drove it along like a ship running before the wind. Perhaps it would reach the coast that way!

It was only two cable lengths from shore when terrible cries burst from four throats at once. The balloon, which had seemed as if it would never rise again, had just made one more unexpected leap after being struck by a tremendous wave. As though suddenly relieved of yet another part of its weight, it climbed to a height of fifteen hundred feet, and there it met a kind of eddy in the wind which, instead of carrying it straight to the coast, sent it along a course almost parallel to the shore. At last, two minutes later, it slanted back in toward the land and came down for good on the sand of the beach, out of reach of the waves.

Helping one another, the passengers managed to free themselves from the mesh of the net. Relieved of their weight, the balloon was caught up again by the wind, and like a wounded bird that finds one last moment of life, it vanished into the sky.

The basket had carried five passengers, plus a dog, and the balloon had thrown only four onto the shore.

The missing passenger had obviously been swept away by the wave that had just struck the net, and that was what had let the lightened balloon climb one last time and then, a few moments later, reach land.

The four castaways — for that is what we can call them now — had barely set foot on solid ground when all of them, thinking of the one who was gone, cried out:

"Maybe he's trying to swim ashore! Let's save him! Let's save him!"

Chapter 2: An Episode of the Civil War

An episode of the Civil War — The engineer Cyrus Smith — Gédéon Spilett — Nab — The sailor Pencroff — Young Harbert — An unexpected proposal — A meeting at ten o'clock at night — Departure in the storm

The men the hurricane had just thrown onto this coast were neither professional balloonists nor amateurs who liked to go adventuring in the air. They were prisoners of war, whose daring had driven them to escape under extraordinary circumstances. A hundred times they should have died! A hundred times their torn balloon should have flung them into the abyss! But heaven was saving them for a strange destiny. On March 24, after fleeing Richmond, which General Ulysses Grant's troops had under siege, they found themselves seven thousand miles from the capital of Virginia, the chief stronghold of the secessionists during the terrible Civil War. Their voyage through the air had lasted five days.

Here, then, are the curious circumstances in which the prisoners had escaped — an escape that was to end in the catastrophe we already know.

That same year, in February 1865, during one of the surprise attacks General Grant launched, without success, to take Richmond, several of his officers fell into enemy hands and were held in the city. One of the most distinguished of those captured belonged to the Federal general staff, and his name was Cyrus Smith.

Cyrus Smith, a native of Massachusetts, was an engineer and a scientist of the first rank, to whom the government of the Union had entrusted, during the war, the running of the railroads, whose strategic role was so enormous. He was a true Northerner: thin, bony, lanky, about forty-five years old, his close-cropped hair already going gray, and his beard too, of which he kept only a thick mustache. He had one of those fine heads that look as if they were made to be stamped on a coin or a medal — burning eyes, a serious mouth, the face of a scientist of the fighting kind. He was one of those engineers who chose to begin by handling the hammer and the pick, the way some generals choose to start out as common soldiers. So along with an ingenious mind he had supremely skillful hands. His muscles were remarkably firm and strong. Truly a man of action as much as a man of thought, he acted without effort, driven by a great overflow of vitality, with the kind of stubborn persistence that defies every stroke of bad luck. Very learned, very practical, and "très débrouillard," to borrow a phrase from French army slang — a man who could always find a way out of a fix — he had a superb temperament. He stayed master of himself whatever the circumstances, and he met to the highest degree the three conditions that together make up human energy: activity of mind and body, intensity of desire, and power of will. His motto could have been that of William of Orange in the seventeenth century: "I need no hope to undertake, nor success to persevere."

Cyrus Smith was also courage itself. He had been in every battle of the Civil War. He had started out under Ulysses Grant with the Illinois volunteers, and he had fought at Paducah, at Belmont, at Pittsburg Landing, at the siege of Corinth, at Port Gibson, at the Black River, at Chattanooga, in the Wilderness, on the Potomac — everywhere, and bravely, a soldier worthy of the general who once answered, "I never count my dead!" A hundred times Cyrus Smith should have been among those dead that the terrible Grant did not count. But in those battles, where he hardly spared himself, luck was always on his side, until the moment he was wounded and taken prisoner on the battlefield at Richmond.

On the same day as Cyrus Smith, another important figure fell into Southern hands. It was none other than the Honorable Gédéon Spilett, "reporter" for the New York Herald, who had been assigned to follow the ups and downs of the war with the armies of the North.

Gédéon Spilett belonged to that astonishing breed of English and American correspondents, men like Stanley, who will stop at nothing to get accurate news and send it to their papers as fast as it can possibly go. The newspapers of the Union, such as the New York Herald, are true powers in the land, and their envoys are representatives that have to be reckoned with. Gédéon Spilett stood in the front rank of those envoys.

He was a man of great merit — energetic, quick, ready for anything, full of ideas. He had traveled the whole world. He was a soldier and an artist, fiery in council, decisive in action, counting neither trouble nor fatigue nor danger when it came to finding out everything, for himself first and for his paper second. A true hero of curiosity, of news, of the never-before-told, of the unknown, of the impossible, he was one of those fearless observers who write under a hail of bullets, file their stories under cannon fire, and count every danger as a stroke of good luck.

He too had been in every battle, in the front line, a revolver in one hand and a notebook in the other, and grapeshot never made his pencil shake. He did not clog the wires with endless telegrams, like people who talk when they have nothing to say; but every one of his dispatches, short, sharp and clear, threw light on some important point. And he did not lack a sense of humor. It was he who, after the fight at the Black River, determined at any cost to keep his place at the telegraph office window so that he could report the result of the battle to his paper, wired the first chapters of the Bible for two solid hours. It cost the New York Herald two thousand dollars, but the New York Herald had the news first.

Gédéon Spilett was tall, forty at most. Reddish-blond side-whiskers framed his face. His eye was calm and sharp, quick to move from one thing to the next — the eye of a man used to taking in every detail of a landscape at a glance. Solidly built, he had been hardened in every climate, the way a bar of steel is tempered in cold water.

For ten years Gédéon Spilett had been the New York Herald's staff reporter, enriching its pages with his articles and his drawings, since he handled a pencil as well as a pen. When he was captured, he was in the middle of describing and sketching the battle. The last words found in his notebook were these: "A Southerner is aiming at me, and..." And the Southerner missed Gédéon Spilett, for, as was his unfailing habit, he came out of the affair without a scratch.

Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett, who knew each other only by reputation, had both been taken to Richmond. The engineer's wound healed quickly, and it was while he was recovering that he met the reporter. The two men liked each other and came to value each other. Soon the life they shared had only one aim: to escape, to rejoin Grant's army, and to fight in its ranks again for the unity of the Union.

So the two Americans had made up their minds to seize any chance that came. But although they had been left free to move about the city, Richmond was so strictly guarded that escape had to be considered impossible.

Meanwhile Cyrus Smith had been joined by a servant who was devoted to him in life and in death. This fearless man was a Black man, born on the engineer's estate to a father and mother who were slaves. But Cyrus Smith, an abolitionist by reason and by heart, had freed him long ago. The slave who had become a free man had not wanted to leave his master. He loved him enough to die for him. He was thirty years old, strong, nimble, skillful, intelligent, gentle and calm, sometimes naive, always smiling, helpful and kind. His name was Nebuchadnezzar, but he answered only to the short, familiar name of Nab.

When Nab learned that his master had been taken prisoner, he left Massachusetts without a moment's hesitation and made his way to Richmond. By cunning and skill, after risking his life twenty times over, he managed to get inside the besieged city. There are no words for Cyrus Smith's pleasure at seeing his servant again, or for Nab's joy at finding his master.

But if Nab had managed to get into Richmond, getting out was another matter entirely, because the Federal prisoners were watched very closely. It would take an extraordinary opportunity to attempt an escape with any chance of success, and not only did that opportunity fail to come, it was very hard to see how to create one.

Meanwhile Grant was pressing on with his operations, hard. His victory at Petersburg had been bitterly contested and very dearly bought. His forces, joined to Butler's, were still getting nowhere in front of Richmond, and nothing suggested that the prisoners would be set free any time soon. The reporter, whose tedious captivity no longer gave him a single interesting detail to write down, could not stand it any longer. He had only one idea: to get out of Richmond, at any cost. Several times he even tried it, and was stopped by obstacles he could not get past.

Meanwhile the siege went on. And if the prisoners were in a hurry to escape and rejoin Grant's army, some of the besieged were in just as much of a hurry to get away and rejoin the secessionist army — among them a certain Jonathan Forster, a fanatical Southerner. For in fact, if the Federal prisoners could not leave the city, neither could the Confederates, because the Northern army had them surrounded. The governor of Richmond had been cut off from General Lee for a long time already, and it was of the greatest importance to let Lee know the city's situation, so as to hurry the relief army along. This Jonathan Forster then had the idea of rising into the air in a balloon, crossing over the besieging lines, and reaching the secessionist camp that way.

The governor authorized the attempt. A balloon was built and put at Jonathan Forster's disposal, and five of his companions were to go up with him. They were supplied with weapons, in case they had to defend themselves when they landed, and with food, in case their voyage through the air went on longer than planned.

The balloon's departure had been set for March 18. It was to take place at night, and with a moderate northwest wind the balloonists expected to reach Lee's headquarters within a few hours. But that northwest wind turned out to be no mere breeze. As early as the 18th, anyone could see it was turning into a hurricane. Soon the storm was so violent that Forster's departure had to be put off, because there was no way to risk the balloon and the men it would carry in the middle of the raging elements.

So the balloon, inflated in the great square of Richmond, stood there ready to leave at the first lull in the wind, and in the city people grew very impatient to see that the weather did not change.

March 18 and 19 went by without any change in the storm. In fact, they had great trouble protecting the balloon, which was tied to the ground and which the gusts kept knocking flat against it.

The night of the 19th to the 20th passed, but in the morning the hurricane was blowing even harder. Departure was impossible.

That day the engineer Cyrus Smith was approached in one of the streets of Richmond by a man he did not know. It was a sailor named Pencroff, somewhere between thirty-five and forty years old, powerfully built, deeply tanned, with bright, blinking eyes but a good, kindly face. This Pencroff was a Northerner who had sailed every sea on the globe, and when it came to adventures, everything extraordinary that can happen to a two-legged creature without feathers had already happened to him. It goes without saying that he had an enterprising nature, ready to dare anything, and that nothing could surprise him. At the start of that year Pencroff had come to Richmond on business with a boy of fifteen, Harbert Brown of New Jersey, the son of his captain — an orphan whom he loved as if he were his own child. Not having managed to leave the city before the first operations of the siege, he found himself trapped there, very much to his displeasure, and he too had only one idea left: to get away by any means possible. He knew the engineer Cyrus Smith by reputation. He knew how impatiently that determined man was chafing at the bit. So that day he did not hesitate to come up to him and say, without any more preamble:

"Mr. Smith, have you had enough of Richmond?"

The engineer stared at the man who had spoken to him like this, and who added in a low voice:

"Mr. Smith, do you want to escape?"

"When?" the engineer answered quickly — and it is safe to say the answer slipped out of him, since he had not yet taken a good look at the stranger speaking to him.

But after studying the sailor's honest face with a penetrating eye, he could not doubt that the man in front of him was a decent one.

"Who are you?" he asked curtly.

Pencroff told him.

"Good," answered Cyrus Smith. "And how do you propose we escape?"

"In that lazy good-for-nothing of a balloon they've left sitting there doing nothing. It looks to me like it's waiting just for us!"

The sailor did not need to finish his sentence. The engineer had understood at a word. He took Pencroff by the arm and led him off to his lodgings.

There the sailor laid out his plan, which was very simple, really. All they risked by carrying it out was their lives. The hurricane was at its most violent, true, but a skillful, daring engineer like Cyrus Smith would surely know how to handle a balloon. If he, Pencroff, had known how to work one, he wouldn't have hesitated to take off — with Harbert, of course. He had seen plenty worse, and he wasn't going to start worrying about a storm at this point!

Cyrus Smith had listened to the sailor without a word, but his eyes were shining. The opportunity was right there, and he was not a man to let it slip. The plan was merely very dangerous — and therefore it could be done. At night, despite the guards, they could get to the balloon, slip into the basket, and cut the ropes that held it down! Of course they might be killed, but on the other hand they might succeed. And without this storm... But without this storm the balloon would have left already, and the opportunity they had looked for so long would not be there now!

"I'm not alone!" Cyrus Smith said at last.

"How many people do you want to bring, then?" asked the sailor.

"Two: my friend Spilett and my servant Nab."

"So that makes three," answered Pencroff, "and with Harbert and me, five. The balloon was supposed to carry six..."

"That's enough. We'll go!" said Cyrus Smith.

That "we" committed the reporter, but the reporter was not a man to back out, and when the plan was explained to him he approved it without reservation. What surprised him was that such a simple idea had not already occurred to him. As for Nab, he followed his master wherever his master wanted to go.

"Tonight, then," said Pencroff. "The five of us will just wander over that way, like people out for a look!"

"Tonight, at ten o'clock," answered Cyrus Smith, "and heaven grant that this storm doesn't die down before we go!"

Pencroff took his leave of the engineer and went back to his lodgings, where young Harbert Brown had stayed behind. The brave boy knew the sailor's plan, and it was with some anxiety that he was waiting to hear how the approach to the engineer had gone. So, as you can see, it was five determined men who were about to throw themselves into the storm, in the teeth of a hurricane!

No! The hurricane did not die down, and neither Jonathan Forster nor his companions could dream of facing it in that flimsy basket! The day was terrible. The engineer feared only one thing: that the balloon, held to the ground and blown over flat by the wind, would be torn into a thousand pieces. For hours he prowled around the nearly deserted square, keeping an eye on it. Pencroff did the same on his side, hands in his pockets, yawning when the occasion called for it, like a man who has no idea how to kill time — but he too was dreading that the balloon would tear, or even break its ropes and fly off into the sky.

Evening came. The night was very dark. Thick mists drifted like clouds along the ground. Rain mixed with snow was falling. It was cold. A kind of fog hung heavy over Richmond. It seemed as if the violent storm had brought about a sort of truce between besiegers and besieged, as if the cannon had decided to fall silent before the tremendous blasts of the hurricane. The streets of the city were empty. In such horrible weather it had not even seemed necessary to guard the square where the balloon lay struggling. Everything was clearly in the prisoners' favor. But a voyage through those raging gusts!

"Nasty tide!" Pencroff muttered to himself, jamming his hat down with his fist as the wind tried to tear it off his head. "But bah! We'll come through all the same!"

At half past nine Cyrus Smith and his companions slipped into the square from different directions. The gas lamps had been blown out by the wind, and the square lay in deep darkness. They could not even see the enormous balloon, which was lying almost completely flattened on the ground. Besides the ballast bags that weighted the cords of the net, the basket was held by a strong cable passed through a ring set into the paving stones, with both ends brought back up on board.

The five prisoners met beside the basket. No one had seen them, and it was so dark that they could not even see each other.

Without a word, Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Nab and Harbert took their places in the basket, while Pencroff, on the engineer's orders, unhooked the bundles of ballast one after another. It took only a few moments, and then the sailor joined his companions.

The balloon was now held only by the doubled cable, and all Cyrus Smith had left to do was give the order to go.

At that moment a dog leaped up into the basket in a single bound. It was Top, the engineer's dog, who had broken his chain and followed his master. Afraid of too much weight, Cyrus Smith wanted to send the poor animal back.

"Bah! One more!" said Pencroff, and he heaved two bags of sand out of the basket.

Then he let go one end of the doubled cable, and the balloon shot off at a slant and vanished — after knocking its basket against two chimneys and bringing them down in the fury of its departure.

The hurricane was now raging with appalling violence. During the night the engineer could not even think of trying to come down, and when day came, the mists hid every sight of land. It was only five days later that a break in the clouds revealed the immense sea beneath the balloon, which the wind was sweeping along at a terrifying speed!

We know how, of those five men who had left on March 20, four were thrown on March 24 onto a deserted coast more than six thousand miles from their country — while at home, on April 5, Richmond fell to Grant, the secessionists' revolt was crushed, Lee withdrew to the west, and the cause of American unity triumphed!

And the one who was missing, the one the four survivors of the balloon had rushed off to rescue first of all, was their natural leader — the engineer Cyrus Smith!

Chapter 3: The One Who Is Missing

Five in the evening — The one who is missing — Nab's despair — Searching to the north — The islet — A long night of anguish — The morning fog — Nab swims for it — A view of the land — Wading the channel

The engineer had been carried off by a wave through the mesh of the net, which had given way. His dog had vanished too. The faithful animal had thrown himself into the sea of his own accord, to help his master.

"Come on!" cried the reporter.

And all four of them — Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Pencroff and Nab — forgot how worn out and exhausted they were, and began to search.

Poor Nab was weeping with rage and despair at once, at the thought that he had lost everything he loved in the world.

Not two minutes had passed between the moment Cyrus Smith disappeared and the moment his companions reached land. So they could hope to get there in time to save him.

"Let's look for him! Let's look for him!" cried Nab.

"Yes, Nab," answered Gédéon Spilett, "and we'll find him!"

"Alive?"

"Alive!"

"Can he swim?" asked Pencroff.

"Yes!" answered Nab. "And besides, Top is with him!"

The sailor heard the roar of the sea and shook his head.

The engineer had vanished off the north part of the coast, about half a mile from the spot where the castaways had just come ashore. If he had managed to reach the nearest point of the shore, then that point had to lie half a mile away at most.

It was nearly six o'clock by then. The mist had just come down, and it made the night very dark. The castaways walked north along the east coast of this land onto which chance had thrown them — an unknown land, whose place on the globe they could not even guess. Underfoot was sandy ground, mixed with stones, that seemed to have no plant life of any kind. The ground was very uneven and rough, and in some places it seemed riddled with little potholes that made walking very hard. Every moment, big, heavy-winged birds burst out of these holes and fled in all directions, unseen in the dark. Others, quicker, rose in flocks and swept past like clouds. The sailor thought he recognized gulls and sea mews, whose shrill whistling competed with the roaring of the sea.

Now and then the castaways stopped, shouted at the top of their lungs, and listened for any answering call from the direction of the ocean. They reasoned, in fact, that if they had come anywhere near the place where the engineer might have come ashore, then the barking of the dog Top would have reached them, even if Cyrus Smith himself was in no condition to give a sign that he was alive. But no cry stood out above the rumble of the breakers and the rattle of the surf. Then the little band would set off again and search every least nook and cranny of the shore.

After twenty minutes of this, the four castaways were brought up short by a foaming fringe of waves. There was no more solid ground. They were standing at the tip of a sharp point, and the sea was breaking furiously against it.

"It's a headland," said the sailor. "We'll have to go back the way we came, keeping to the right, and that way we'll reach the mainland."

"But what if he's out there!" answered Nab, pointing to the ocean, where the enormous waves showed white in the darkness.

"Well then, let's call him!"

And all of them, joining their voices, gave a mighty shout, but nothing answered. They waited for a lull. They tried again. Still nothing.

So the castaways turned back, following the other side of the headland, over ground just as sandy and rocky as before. Pencroff noticed, though, that the shore here was steeper and that the ground was rising, and he guessed that it must join up, by a fairly long slope, with a high coast whose mass he could make out dimly in the dark. There were fewer birds on this part of the shore. The sea, too, was less rough and less noisy here, and it was striking how much the tossing of the waves had died down. They could barely hear the surf. No doubt this side of the headland formed a half-moon cove, sheltered by the sharp point from the swells rolling in from the open sea.

But following this direction meant walking south, away from the stretch of coast where Cyrus Smith might have landed. After a mile and a half the shoreline still showed no bend that would let them turn back north. Yet this headland, whose point they had rounded, surely had to be joined to the mainland somewhere. The castaways were at the end of their strength, but they kept on walking bravely, hoping at every moment to find some sharp turn that would put them back on their first heading.

Imagine their disappointment, then, when after walking about two miles they found themselves stopped once more by the sea, on a fairly high point made of slippery rocks.

"We're on an islet!" said Pencroff. "And we've walked it from one end to the other!"

The sailor was right. The castaways had been thrown, not onto a continent, not even onto an island, but onto an islet no more than two miles long, and obviously not very wide.

Was this barren islet, strewn with stones, without plants, the bleak refuge of a few seabirds, part of some larger archipelago? There was no telling. When the balloon's passengers had glimpsed land through the mist from their basket, they had not been able to make out how big it was. Even so, Pencroff, whose sailor's eyes were used to piercing the dark, thought he could just now make out some dim masses to the west that suggested a high coast.

But in this darkness there was no way to work out what sort of land the islet belonged to, a single island or a whole group of them. Nor could they get off it, since the sea surrounded it. So the search for the engineer had to wait until the next day — and he, alas, had not given a single cry to show where he was.

"Cyrus's silence doesn't prove anything," said the reporter. "He may have fainted, he may be hurt, he may just be unable to answer for the moment. But let's not give up hope."

Then the reporter suggested lighting a fire somewhere on the islet, as a signal to the engineer. But they searched in vain for wood or dry brush. Sand and stones — there was nothing else.

It is easy to understand how Nab must have grieved, and his companions too, for they had grown deeply attached to the fearless Cyrus Smith. It was all too clear that for now they were powerless to help him. They had to wait for daylight. Either the engineer had managed to save himself on his own and had already found shelter somewhere on the coast, or he was lost forever!

Those were long and painful hours to get through. The cold was sharp. The castaways suffered cruelly, but they hardly noticed it. They did not even think of resting for a moment. Forgetting themselves for the sake of their leader, hoping, determined to go on hoping, they walked back and forth across the barren islet, returning again and again to its northern tip, where they had to be nearest to the scene of the disaster. They listened, they shouted, they strained to catch some last call for help. Their voices must have carried a long way, because the air had grown fairly calm by then, and the noise of the sea was beginning to fall with the swell.

At one point one of Nab's cries even seemed to come back as an echo. Harbert pointed it out to Pencroff, adding:

"That would prove there's a coast fairly close to the west."

The sailor nodded. Besides, his eyes could not be deceiving him. If he had seen land, even a little, then land was there.

But that distant echo was the only answer Nab's cries drew, and all along the east side of the islet the vast emptiness stayed silent.

Meanwhile the sky was clearing little by little. Toward midnight a few stars came out, and if the engineer had been there beside his companions, he could have noticed that these were no longer the stars of the Northern Hemisphere. The North Star was nowhere to be seen on this new horizon. The constellations overhead were not the ones he was used to watching in the northern part of the New World, and the Southern Cross was blazing near the south pole of the sky.

The night went by. At about five in the morning on March 25, the upper sky took on a faint tinge of color. The horizon was still dark, but with the first light of day a thick fog rose from the sea, so that no one could see more than twenty paces or so. The fog unrolled in great heavy coils that drifted slowly along.

This was a setback. The castaways could make out nothing around them. While Nab and the reporter peered out over the ocean, the sailor and Harbert looked for the coast to the west. But not a scrap of land could be seen.

"Doesn't matter," said Pencroff. "If I can't see the coast, I can feel it. It's there... right there... as sure as we're not in Richmond anymore!"

But the fog would not last long. It was only the light haze of fair weather. A good strong sun was warming its upper layers, and the heat was filtering down to the surface of the islet.

Sure enough, at about half past six, three quarters of an hour after sunrise, the mist was growing thinner. It thickened up above but melted away below. Soon the whole islet came into view, as though it had just come down out of a cloud. Then the sea appeared, spreading out in a circle, endless to the east but bounded to the west by a high, steep coast.

Yes! The land was there. And there was safety — for the time being, at least. Between the islet and the coast lay a channel half a mile wide, and through it an extremely fast current was running noisily.

At once, though, one of the castaways, listening to nothing but his heart, plunged into the current without asking his companions' advice, without saying a single word. It was Nab. He was in a hurry to reach that coast and work his way north along it. No one could have held him back. Pencroff called after him, but it was no use. The reporter was getting ready to follow Nab.

Then Pencroff went up to him.

"You mean to cross this channel?" he asked.

"Yes," answered Gédéon Spilett.

"Well, wait, take my word for it," said the sailor. "Nab can manage to help his master on his own. If we went into that channel, we'd risk getting swept out to sea by the current — it's running hard as anything. Now, unless I'm mistaken, it's an ebb current. Look, the tide's going out over the sand. So let's be patient, and at low water we may find a place where we can wade across..."

"You're right," answered the reporter. "Let's split up as little as we can..."

Meanwhile Nab was fighting the current with all his strength. He was crossing it at a slant. They could see his dark shoulders come out of the water at every stroke. He was being carried sideways at tremendous speed, but he was gaining on the coast too. It took him more than half an hour to cross that half mile between the islet and the land, and he came ashore several thousand feet from the spot directly opposite the place he had started from. Nab climbed out at the foot of a high granite wall and gave himself a good shake. Then, running hard, he soon disappeared behind a point of rock that jutted out into the sea at about the level of the islet's northern tip.

Nab's companions had followed his daring attempt in anguish, and when he was out of sight they turned their eyes to the land where they were going to ask for refuge, eating a few of the shellfish that lay scattered across the sand as they looked. It was a meager meal, but at least it was a meal.

The coast opposite formed a broad bay. To the south it ended in a very sharp point, bare of any plants and very wild-looking. This point joined the shore in a rather fanciful curve and was braced against tall granite rocks. To the north, on the other hand, the bay widened out into a more rounded coastline that ran from southwest to northeast and ended in a slender cape. Between these two end points, which held the arc of the bay between them, the distance might have been eight miles. Half a mile from the shore, the islet took up a narrow strip of sea. It looked like an enormous whale — like a whale's carcass, greatly enlarged. At its widest it was no more than a quarter of a mile across.

Facing the islet, the shoreline began, in front, with a sandy beach strewn with blackish rocks, which were now coming back into view little by little as the tide went down. Behind it rose a sort of granite rampart, sheer as a wall and topped by an irregular ridge at least three hundred feet high. It ran on like this for three miles and ended suddenly on the right in a flat-cut face that looked as if it had been carved by human hands. On the left, by contrast, above the headland, this ragged sort of cliff broke up into prism-shaped fragments, made of jumbled rocks and fallen rubble, and sloped down in a long ramp that gradually blended into the rocks of the southern point.

On the high plateau along the top of the coast there was not a single tree. It was a bare tabletop, like Table Mountain above Cape Town at the Cape of Good Hope, only smaller. At least, that was how it looked from the islet. But there was no lack of green to the right, behind the flat-cut face. They could easily make out the dim mass of tall trees, crowded together and stretching on beyond the limits of sight. That greenery cheered the eye, which the harsh lines of the granite face had made so gloomy.

Finally, far in the background and above the plateau, to the northwest and at least seven miles off, a white summit was gleaming in the sunlight. It was a cap of snow, crowning some distant mountain.

So there was no saying yet whether this land was an island or part of a continent. But at the sight of the twisted, heaped-up rocks on the left, a geologist would not have hesitated to call them volcanic, for they were beyond question the work of underground fire.

Gédéon Spilett, Pencroff and Harbert studied this land closely. Perhaps they were going to live on it for many long years. Perhaps they would even die on it, if it did not lie on the route of passing ships!

"Well," asked Harbert, "what do you say, Pencroff?"

"Well," answered the sailor, "there's good and bad, like in everything. We'll see. But the ebb is starting to tell. In three hours we'll try the crossing, and once we're over there, we'll do our best to get ourselves out of this mess and find Mr. Smith!"

Pencroff had not been wrong in his forecast. Three hours later, at low tide, most of the sand that formed the bed of the channel had come uncovered. Between the islet and the coast there was nothing left but a narrow passage of water, which would surely be easy to get across.

And in fact, at about ten o'clock, Gédéon Spilett and his two companions stripped off their clothes, bundled them on their heads, and ventured into the channel, which was no more than five feet deep. Harbert, for whom the water would have been too deep, swam like a fish and came through splendidly. All three reached the opposite shore without trouble. There the sun quickly dried them, and they put back on the clothes they had kept out of the water, and they held a council.

Chapter 4: The Chimneys

The lithodomes — The river at its mouth — The "Chimneys" — The search goes on — The forest of evergreens — The supply of firewood — Waiting for the ebb — From the top of the cliff — The timber raft — Back to the shore

First of all, the reporter told the sailor to wait for him right where he was, and that he would come back and join him there. Then, without losing a moment, he set off up the shore in the direction Nab had taken a few hours before. He quickly disappeared around a bend in the coast, so impatient was he for news of the engineer.

Harbert had wanted to go with him.

"Stay here, my boy," the sailor had told him. "We've got a camp to set up, and we need to see whether we can find something more solid to sink our teeth into than shellfish. Our friends will need to get their strength back when they return. Everybody has his job."

"I'm ready, Pencroff," Harbert answered.

"Good!" the sailor went on. "That'll do. Let's be methodical about this. We're tired, we're cold, we're hungry. So what we need is shelter, fire, and food. The forest has wood, the nests have eggs. All that's left is to find the house."

"All right," said Harbert. "I'll look for a cave in these rocks. I'm bound to find some hole we can squeeze ourselves into!"

"That's the idea," said Pencroff. "Let's go, my boy."

So off the two of them went, walking along the foot of the enormous wall, on the beach that the falling tide had left wide and bare. But instead of heading north, they went south. A few hundred paces below the spot where they had landed, Pencroff had noticed a narrow break in the coast, which, he thought, must be the outlet of a river or a stream. Now, on the one hand, it was important to settle near a supply of drinking water. And on the other, it was not impossible that the current had carried Cyrus Smith in that direction.

The high wall, as we have said, rose to a height of three hundred feet. But it was solid rock from end to end, and even at its base, which the sea barely licked, it did not offer the slightest crack that could serve as a temporary home. It was a sheer wall of very hard granite that the waves had never worn away. Around its top fluttered a whole world of seabirds, especially various species of the web-footed order, with long, narrow, pointed beaks — very noisy birds, and not much frightened by the presence of man, who was no doubt disturbing their solitude for the first time. Among these web-footed birds Pencroff recognized several skuas, a kind of gull sometimes called jaegers, and also some small, greedy sea gulls that nested in the crevices of the granite. One gunshot fired into that swarm of birds would have brought down a great many of them. But to fire a gunshot you need a gun, and neither Pencroff nor Harbert had one. Besides, these gulls and skuas are hardly fit to eat, and even their eggs taste dreadful.

Meanwhile Harbert, who had moved off a little to the left, soon pointed out some rocks carpeted with seaweed, which the high tide would cover again a few hours later. On these rocks, in among the slippery wrack, swarmed two-shelled mollusks of a kind that starving people could hardly turn up their noses at. So Harbert called Pencroff, who came running.

"Hey! Mussels!" cried the sailor. "That'll make up for the eggs we haven't got!"

"They're not mussels," answered young Harbert, who was carefully examining the shellfish clinging to the rocks. "They're lithodomes."

"Can you eat them?" asked Pencroff.

"Absolutely."

"Then let's eat lithodomes."

The sailor could rely on Harbert. The boy was very good at natural history and had always had a real passion for that science. His father had encouraged him in it, sending him to the lectures of the best teachers in Boston, who were fond of this intelligent, hardworking boy. His naturalist's instincts would prove useful more than once in the days to come, and on this first occasion he was not mistaken.

These lithodomes were oblong shellfish that hung in clusters and clung tightly to the rocks. They belonged to that species of boring mollusk that drills holes into the very hardest stone, and their shells were rounded at both ends — a shape you do not see in the ordinary mussel.

Pencroff and Harbert ate a good many of these lithodomes, which were half open in the sun just then. They ate them like oysters and found that they had a strong, peppery taste, which left them with no regret at all that they had neither pepper nor seasoning of any kind.

So their hunger was satisfied for the moment, but not their thirst, which only grew after eating these naturally spicy shellfish. Now they had to find fresh water, and it seemed unlikely that there would be none in a country so wildly broken up. Pencroff and Harbert took the precaution of laying in a large supply of lithodomes, filling their pockets and their handkerchiefs with them, and then made their way back to the foot of the high ground.

Two hundred paces farther on they reached the break in the cliff through which, just as Pencroff had guessed, a little river was flowing brimful. At this spot the wall looked as if it had been split apart by some violent volcanic upheaval. At its foot a small cove cut into the shore, and the inner end of it made a fairly sharp angle. The stream here was a hundred feet wide, and its banks on either side were barely twenty feet across. The river ran almost straight in between the two walls of granite, which grew lower as they went upstream from the mouth. Then it turned sharply and disappeared under a thicket half a mile away.

"Water here! Wood over there!" said Pencroff. "Well, Harbert, now all we need is the house!"

The river water was clear. The sailor made sure that at this stage of the tide — that is, at low water, when the rising sea did not push into it — it was fresh. With that important point settled, Harbert hunted for some hollow that could serve as a shelter, but it was no use. Everywhere the wall was smooth, flat, and sheer.

At the very mouth of the stream, however, above the high-water line, fallen rock had formed — not a cave, but a heap of enormous boulders, of the kind you often come across in granite country, and which go by the name of "Chimneys."

Pencroff and Harbert made their way fairly deep in among the rocks, along sandy passages that were not short of light, since it came in through the gaps the blocks of granite left between them — some of those blocks staying up only by a miracle of balance. But with the light came the wind too — a real hallway draft — and with the wind, the sharp cold from outside. Still, the sailor thought that by closing off certain parts of these passages, and stopping up some of the openings with a mixture of stones and sand, they could make the Chimneys livable. Their ground plan looked like the printer's sign &, the one used to abbreviate et cetera. Now, by walling off the upper loop of the sign, where the south and west winds came rushing in, they could no doubt make use of its lower part.

"This is just the thing," said Pencroff. "And if we ever see Mr. Smith again, he'll know how to make something of this maze."

"We will see him again, Pencroff!" cried Harbert. "And when he comes back he has to find a home here that's more or less bearable. It will be, if we can set up a fireplace in the left-hand passage and keep an opening there for the smoke."

"We can do that, my boy," the sailor answered, "and these Chimneys" — that was the name Pencroff kept for this temporary home — "will do just fine for us. But first, let's go and lay in a supply of fuel. I've a notion the wood will come in handy for blocking up these holes the devil's blowing his trumpet through!"

Harbert and Pencroff left the Chimneys, rounded the corner, and started up the left bank of the river. The current was fairly swift and was carrying along some dead wood. The rising tide — and it could already be felt at this point — must push the river back hard for quite a long way upstream. So the sailor thought they might be able to use this flow and ebb to carry heavy loads.

After walking for a quarter of an hour, the sailor and the boy reached the sharp bend the river made as it swung away to the left. From there on, its course ran through a forest of magnificent trees. These trees had kept their green, late in the season though it was, because they belonged to the conifer family, which is found in every region of the globe, from the northern climates to the tropics. The young naturalist recognized deodars in particular, a kind of cedar very common in the Himalayas, which gave off a pleasant fragrance. Between these fine trees grew clumps of pines, spreading their dense umbrellas wide. In the tall grass, Pencroff felt dry branches snap under his feet, crackling like fireworks.

"Well, my boy," he said to Harbert, "I may not know the names of these trees, but I do at least know how to file them under 'firewood,' and right now that's the only kind that's any use to us!"

"Let's gather our supply!" answered Harbert, and he set to work at once.

The harvest was easy. They did not even need to strip branches off the trees, since huge quantities of dead wood lay on the ground at their feet. But if there was no shortage of fuel, the means of carrying it left a good deal to be desired. Since the wood was very dry, it would burn quickly. So they would need to bring a large amount of it back to the Chimneys, and what two men could carry would not be enough. Harbert pointed this out.

"Ah, my boy," answered the sailor, "there's got to be some way of moving this wood. There's always a way to do anything! If we had a cart or a boat, it would be too easy."

"But we've got the river!" said Harbert.

"Right," said Pencroff. "The river will be a road that travels all by itself, and timber rafts weren't invented for nothing."

"Only," Harbert pointed out, "our road is traveling the wrong way just now, since the tide's coming in!"

"Then we'll just have to wait for it to go out," answered the sailor, "and it'll be the sea that delivers our fuel to the Chimneys. Let's get our raft ready anyway."

The sailor, with Harbert behind him, headed for the corner where the edge of the forest met the river. Each of them carried as heavy a load of wood as his strength allowed, tied up in bundles. On the bank, too, there was a great deal of dead branches, lying in grass where very likely no human foot had ever stepped. Pencroff set to work on his raft at once.

In a sort of eddy, made by a point of the bank that broke the current, the sailor and the boy laid down some fairly thick pieces of wood, which they had tied together with dry creepers. This made a kind of raft, and on it they piled the whole harvest, layer after layer — at least twenty men's worth of carrying. In an hour the work was done, and the raft, moored to the bank, had to wait for the tide to turn.

That left a few hours to fill, and Pencroff and Harbert agreed to climb up to the plateau above, to get a look at the country over a wider area.

As it happened, two hundred paces back from the bend in the river, the wall ended in a slide of fallen rocks that sloped gently down to the edge of the forest. It was like a natural staircase. So Harbert and the sailor began to climb. Thanks to their strong legs they reached the top in no time, and took up a position at the corner where the crest overlooked the mouth of the river.

When they got there, their first look was for the ocean they had just crossed under such terrible conditions! They gazed with deep emotion over all that northern stretch of the coast where the disaster had happened. That was where Cyrus Smith had vanished. They searched with their eyes to see whether some piece of wreckage from their balloon, something a man might have clung to, was still floating. Nothing! The sea was nothing but a vast desert of water. As for the coast, it was deserted too. Neither the reporter nor Nab was anywhere to be seen. But it was possible that at that moment they were both so far away that no one could have made them out.

"Something tells me," cried Harbert, "that a man with as much energy as Mr. Cyrus couldn't just let himself drown like anybody else. He must have reached the shore somewhere. Don't you think so, Pencroff?"

The sailor shook his head sadly. He had little hope left of ever seeing Cyrus Smith again. But since he wanted to leave Harbert some hope, he said:

"Of course, of course. Our engineer's the kind of man who gets himself out of a fix where anybody else would go under!..."

All the same, he was studying the coast with the closest attention. Below him spread the sandy beach, bounded on the right of the river mouth by lines of breakers. Those rocks, still out of the water, looked like herds of seals lying in the surf. Beyond the band of reefs the sea glittered in the sunlight. To the south a sharp point closed off the horizon, and it was impossible to tell whether the land went on in that direction or whether it turned southeast and southwest, which would have made this coast a kind of very long peninsula. At the northern end of the bay the outline of the shore went on for a great distance, in a more rounded curve. There the shore was low and flat, with no cliff, and with broad sandbanks that the ebb tide left uncovered.

Then Pencroff and Harbert turned around to face west. Their eyes were caught at once by the snow-capped mountain that rose six or seven miles away. From its lowest slopes to within two miles of the coast stretched vast wooded masses, set off by great patches of green where the trees kept their leaves all year. Then, from the edge of this forest to the coast itself, there spread a broad green plateau dotted with clumps of trees scattered about at random. To the left they could catch a glint, now and then, of the little river's waters through a few clearings, and its fairly winding course seemed to lead back toward the buttresses of the mountain, among which it must have its source. At the point where the sailor had left his timber raft, it began to flow between the two high walls of granite. But while on its left bank the walls stayed clean and steep, on the right bank, on the contrary, they sank little by little — the great masses turning into lone boulders, the boulders into stones, the stones into pebbles, all the way to the tip of the point.

"Are we on an island?" the sailor murmured.

"If we are, it seems pretty big!" the boy answered.

"An island, however big it is, is still only an island!" said Pencroff.

But that important question could not be settled yet. Its answer would have to wait for another time. As for the land itself, island or continent, it seemed fertile, pleasant to look at, and varied in what it produced.

"That's a piece of luck," Pencroff remarked, "and in all our misfortune we ought to thank Providence for it."

"Then God be praised!" answered Harbert, whose devout heart was full of gratitude to the Maker of all things.

For a long time Pencroff and Harbert studied this country where their fate had flung them, but after such a quick look it was hard to imagine what the future held in store for them.

Then they started back, following the southern crest of the granite plateau, which was edged with a long, scalloped line of fantastic rocks that took on the strangest shapes. Several hundred birds lived there, nesting in holes in the stone. Harbert, jumping from rock to rock, sent a whole flock of them flying.

"Ah!" he cried. "Those aren't gulls of any kind!"

"Then what birds are they?" asked Pencroff. "Upon my word, they look like pigeons!"

"That's right, but they're wild pigeons — rock pigeons," answered Harbert. "I can tell them by the double black band on the wing, the white rump, and the ash-blue feathers. Now, if the rock pigeon is good to eat, its eggs must be excellent, and if these birds have left any in their nests at all!..."

"We won't give them time to hatch, except as an omelet!" Pencroff answered cheerfully.

"But what are you going to make your omelet in?" asked Harbert. "Your hat?"

"Well!" answered the sailor. "I'm not enough of a wizard for that. We'll have to settle for boiled eggs, my boy, and I'll take care of the hardest ones myself!"

Pencroff and the boy searched the crevices of the granite carefully, and sure enough, they found eggs in some of the hollows! A few dozen were gathered and wrapped up in the sailor's handkerchief. Then, since it was nearly time for high tide, Harbert and Pencroff began to make their way back down to the river.

When they reached the bend in the river it was one o'clock in the afternoon. The current was already turning. So they had to take advantage of the ebb to bring the timber raft down to the mouth. Pencroff had no intention of letting the raft drift off on the current with no one steering it, but he did not mean to climb aboard and steer it himself either. A sailor, though, is never at a loss when it comes to cables and ropes, and Pencroff quickly braided a rope several fathoms long out of dry creepers. This vegetable cable was tied to the back end of the raft, and the sailor held it in his hand while Harbert, pushing the raft off with a long pole, kept it out in the current.

The method worked perfectly. The enormous load of wood, which the sailor held back as he walked along the bank, followed the flow of the water. The bank was very steep, so there was no fear that the raft would run aground, and before two o'clock it arrived at the mouth, a few steps from the Chimneys.

Chapter 5: A Single Match

Fitting out the Chimneys — The all-important question of fire — The box of matches — A search on the beach — The reporter and Nab return — A single match! — The crackling hearth — The first supper — The first night on land

As soon as the timber raft had been unloaded, Pencroff's first concern was to make the Chimneys fit to live in by blocking up the passages that let the wind blow through. Sand, stones, woven branches and wet earth sealed off tight the galleries of the "&" that lay open to the south winds, and shut off its upper loop. A single narrow, winding gut that opened on one side was left clear, to carry the smoke outside and give the fire a draft. In this way the Chimneys were divided into three or four rooms — if you can call them rooms, those gloomy dens that a wild animal would hardly have put up with. But they were dry, and you could stand upright in them, at least in the main room, which took up the center. Fine sand covered the floor, and all things considered they could make do with it until they found something better.

Harbert and Pencroff talked as they worked.

"Maybe our friends have found a better place than ours," Harbert said.

"Could be," the sailor answered, "but when in doubt, don't hold back! Better an extra string to your bow than no string at all!"

"Oh," Harbert said again, "if only they bring Mr. Smith back — if only they find him — then all we'll have left to do is thank heaven!"

"Yes!" Pencroff murmured. "He was a man, that one, a real one!"

"He was?" said Harbert. "Have you given up hope of ever seeing him again?"

"God forbid!" the sailor answered.

The work of fitting out the place was soon done, and Pencroff declared himself very pleased with it.

"Now," he said, "our friends can come back. They'll find shelter enough."

That left the hearth to build and the meal to make. A simple, easy job, really. Large flat stones were laid at the back of the first passage on the left, at the mouth of the narrow gut that had been kept open. Whatever heat the smoke did not carry outside would obviously be enough to keep the inside at a comfortable temperature. The supply of wood was stored in one of the rooms, and the sailor laid a few logs on the hearthstones, mixed in with kindling.

The sailor was busy at this when Harbert asked him whether he had any matches.

"Certainly," Pencroff answered, "and I'll add: luckily, because without matches or tinder we'd be in a real fix!"

"We could always make fire the way the islanders do, couldn't we," Harbert answered, "by rubbing two pieces of dry wood together?"

"Well! Try it, my boy, and we'll see if you manage anything besides wearing your arms out!"

"But it's a very simple method, and they use it all the time in the islands of the Pacific."

"I'm not saying they don't," Pencroff answered, "but the islanders must know the trick of it, or else they use a special kind of wood, because more than once I've tried to get a fire going that way and I've never once pulled it off! So I'll admit I prefer matches! Where are my matches?"

Pencroff felt in his jacket for the box that never left him, for he was a dedicated smoker. He did not find it. He went through his trouser pockets, and to his utter astonishment he found no box there either.

"Now that's stupid, worse than stupid!" he said, looking at Harbert. "That box must have dropped out of my pocket, and I've lost it! But you, Harbert, haven't you got anything — a flint and steel, anything at all that could make a fire?"

"No, Pencroff!"

The sailor went out, with the boy behind him, scratching his forehead hard.

On the sand, among the rocks, along the riverbank, the two of them searched with the greatest care, but it was no use. The box was made of copper and would never have escaped their eyes.

"Pencroff," Harbert asked, "didn't you throw that box out of the basket?"

"I made very sure not to," the sailor answered. "But when you've been shaken up the way we just were, a little thing like that can easily go missing. Why, even my pipe has deserted me! Blasted box! Where can it be?"

"Well, the tide's going out," said Harbert. "Let's run to the place where we came ashore."

It was not very likely they would find the box, which the waves must have rolled among the pebbles at high tide, but it was worth taking the chance into account. Harbert and Pencroff went quickly to the spot where they had landed the day before, some two hundred paces from the Chimneys.

There, among the pebbles and in the hollows of the rocks, they searched every inch. Nothing. If the box had fallen there, the waves must have carried it off. As the sea went out, the sailor poked into every crack in the rocks and found nothing. Under the circumstances it was a serious loss, and for the moment one that could not be made good.

Pencroff did not hide how bitterly disappointed he was. His forehead was deeply furrowed. He did not say a word. Harbert tried to comfort him by pointing out that the matches would most likely have been soaked by the seawater and impossible to use anyway.

"No, my boy," the sailor answered. "They were in a copper box that shut tight! And now what are we going to do?"

"We'll find some way to get fire, I'm sure of it," said Harbert. "Mr. Smith or Mr. Spilett won't be caught short the way we are!"

"Yes," Pencroff answered, "but in the meantime we've got no fire, and our friends will come back to a sorry meal!"

"But," Harbert said quickly, "they can't possibly be without tinder or matches!"

"I doubt it," the sailor answered, shaking his head. "For one thing, Nab and Mr. Smith don't smoke, and I'm very much afraid Mr. Spilett held on to his notebook sooner than his box of matches!"

Harbert did not answer. Losing the box was obviously a misfortune. Still, the boy was confident they would get fire one way or another. Pencroff, who had more experience, did not see it that way, even though he was not a man to be put out by small troubles or by large ones. In any case, there was only one thing to do: wait for Nab and the reporter to come back. But he would have to give up the meal of hard-boiled eggs he had meant to make for them, and a diet of raw meat did not strike him as a pleasant prospect, either for them or for himself.

Before going back to the Chimneys, in case they should end up with no fire at all, the sailor and Harbert gathered another load of lithodomes, and then they silently took the road back to their lodging.

Pencroff kept his eyes fixed on the ground, still hunting for his vanished box. He even went back up the left bank of the river from its mouth to the bend where the raft had been moored. He returned to the plateau above, crisscrossed it in every direction, and searched the tall grass along the edge of the forest — all in vain.

It was five o'clock in the evening when he and Harbert came back to the Chimneys. Needless to say, the passages were searched down to their darkest corners, and in the end they had to give it up for good.

Toward six o'clock, just as the sun was disappearing behind the high ground to the west, Harbert, who was pacing up and down the beach, called out that Nab and Gédéon Spilett were coming back.

They were coming back alone! ... The boy felt an indescribable tightening of the heart. The sailor's forebodings had not been wrong. The engineer Cyrus Smith had not been found!

When the reporter arrived, he sat down on a rock without a word. Worn out, dying of hunger, he did not have the strength to speak!

As for Nab, his reddened eyes showed how much he had wept, and the fresh tears he could not hold back said all too plainly that he had lost all hope!

The reporter told the story of their search for Cyrus Smith. He and Nab had covered more than eight miles of the coast, and so had gone well beyond the place of the balloon's next-to-last fall — the fall after which the engineer and the dog Top had disappeared. The beach was deserted. No trace, no footprint. Not a pebble freshly turned over, not a sign on the sand, not one mark of a human foot along that whole stretch of shoreline. It was obvious that no inhabitant ever came to that part of the coast. The sea was as empty as the shore, and it was there, a few hundred feet off the coast, that the engineer had found his grave.

At that moment Nab stood up, and in a voice that showed how stubbornly hope held out in him, he cried:

"No! No! He isn't dead! No! It can't be! Him? Come on! Me — anybody else — maybe! But him? Never. He's a man who comes back from anything! ..."

Then, his strength leaving him:

"Oh, I can't go on!" he murmured.

Harbert ran to him.

"Nab," the boy said, "we'll find him! God will give him back to us! But for now, you're hungry! Eat — please, eat a little something!"

And as he said it he held out a few handfuls of shellfish to poor Nab — a thin, meager meal!

Nab had not eaten for many hours, but he refused. Without his master, Nab could not, or would not, go on living!

Gédéon Spilett, on the other hand, devoured the shellfish; then he lay down on the sand at the foot of a rock. He was exhausted, but calm.

Then Harbert went over to him and took his hand.

"Sir," he said, "we've found a shelter where you'll be better off than here. Night's coming. Come and rest! Tomorrow we'll see ..."

The reporter got up and, with the boy guiding him, made his way toward the Chimneys.

At that moment Pencroff came up to him and, in the most offhand tone in the world, asked whether he happened to have a match on him.

The reporter stopped, felt in his pockets, found nothing, and said:

"I had some, but I must have thrown everything out ..."

Then the sailor called Nab over, asked him the same question, and got the same answer.

"Damnation!" cried the sailor, unable to hold the word back.

The reporter heard him and came over to Pencroff.

"Not one match?" he said.

"Not one, and so no fire!"

"Oh!" cried Nab. "If he were here, my master, he'd know how to make you one!"

The four castaways stood motionless and looked at one another, not without alarm. It was Harbert who broke the silence first.

"Mr. Spilett," he said, "you're a smoker, you always carry matches! Maybe you didn't look properly? Look again! One single match is all we need!"

The reporter went through his pockets again — trousers, vest, coat — and at last, to Pencroff's great joy and to his own utter surprise, he felt a little stick of wood caught in the lining of his vest. His fingers had hold of the little stick through the cloth, but they could not get it out. Since it had to be a match, and only one, the whole point was not to scrape off its phosphorus tip.

"Will you let me do it?" the boy said to him.

And very deftly, without breaking it, he managed to work out that little stick of wood — that wretched, precious splinter that meant so much to these poor men! It was whole.

"A match!" cried Pencroff. "Why, it's as good as having a whole cargo of them!"

He took the match and, with his companions behind him, went back to the Chimneys.

This little stick of wood, which in inhabited countries people throw away so carelessly and which is worth nothing at all, had to be used here with the utmost care. The sailor made sure it was perfectly dry. Then, that done:

"We'll need some paper," he said.

"Here," answered Gédéon Spilett, who, after some hesitation, tore a page out of his notebook.
