Pencroff took the scrap of paper the reporter held out to him and crouched in front of the hearth. There, a few handfuls of dry grass, leaves and moss were placed under the bundles of sticks and arranged so that the air could move freely through them and set the dead wood quickly alight.

Then Pencroff folded the scrap of paper into a cone, as pipe smokers do in a high wind, and pushed it in among the moss. Next he picked up a slightly rough pebble and wiped it carefully, and, not without his heart pounding, he struck the match gently, holding his breath.

The first stroke did nothing. Pencroff had not pressed hard enough, for fear of scraping off the phosphorus.

"No, I can't do it," he said. "My hand's shaking ... The match would misfire ... I can't ... I won't! ..." And getting up, he handed the job to Harbert.

Certainly the boy had never in his life been so stirred. His heart was pounding. Prometheus going to steal fire from heaven can hardly have been more nervous! He did not hesitate, though, and struck the match quickly against the pebble. There was a little sputtering sound, and a small bluish flame sprang up, giving off a sharp, acrid smoke. Harbert gently turned the match over to feed the flame, then slid it into the paper cone. In a few seconds the paper caught, and the moss went up at once.

A few moments later the dry wood was crackling, and a cheerful blaze, fanned by the sailor's mighty breath, was growing in the middle of the darkness.

"At last!" cried Pencroff, getting to his feet. "I've never been so worked up in my life!"

There is no doubt that this fire looked fine on its hearth of flat stones. The smoke went out easily through the narrow flue, the chimney drew, and a pleasant warmth soon spread through the place.

As for the fire, they would have to take care never to let it go out again, and always to keep a few live embers banked under the ashes. But that was only a matter of care and attention, since there was no shortage of wood and the supply could always be renewed in good time.

Pencroff's first thought was to put the hearth to use by making a supper more nourishing than a plate of lithodomes. Harbert brought two dozen eggs. The reporter, propped up in a corner, watched these preparations without saying anything. Three questions strained his mind. Is Cyrus still alive? If he is alive, where can he be? If he survived his fall, how can it be that he has found no way to let them know he exists? As for Nab, he was wandering along the beach. He was nothing now but a body without a soul.

Pencroff, who knew fifty-two ways of cooking eggs, had no choice in the matter this time. He had to settle for burying them in the hot ashes and letting them harden slowly.

In a few minutes the cooking was done, and the sailor invited the reporter to take his share of the supper. Such was the castaways' first meal on that unknown coast. The hard-boiled eggs were excellent, and since an egg contains every element that human beings need for nourishment, these poor men felt much the better for them, and their strength came back.

Ah, if only one of them had not been missing from that meal! If all five of the prisoners who had escaped from Richmond had been there, under those heaped-up rocks, in front of that bright, crackling fire, on that dry sand, they might have had nothing but thanks to give to heaven! But the cleverest of them, and the most learned too, their undisputed leader, Cyrus Smith, was missing, alas — and his body had not even been granted a grave!

So passed that day, March 25. Night had fallen. Outside they could hear the wind whistling and the monotonous surf pounding the coast. The pebbles, pushed up and dragged back by the waves, rolled with a deafening roar.

The reporter had withdrawn to the back of a dark passage after jotting down a brief record of the day's events — the first sight of this new land, the disappearance of the engineer, the exploration of the coast, the business of the matches, and so on — and, with fatigue to help him, he managed to find some rest in sleep.

Harbert, for his part, soon fell asleep. As for the sailor, he spent the night beside the hearth sleeping with one eye open, and he did not spare the fuel.

Only one of the castaways did not rest in the Chimneys. It was Nab — inconsolable, despairing Nab — who, the whole night through, in spite of everything his companions said to persuade him to rest, wandered the beach calling for his master!

Chapter 6: The Castaways' Inventory

The castaways' inventory — Nothing — The burnt linen — An excursion into the forest — The flora of the evergreens — The jacamar gets away — Tracks of wild beasts — The couroucous — The grouse — A strange kind of fishing

The inventory of everything these castaways of the air possessed, thrown up on a coast that seemed to be uninhabited, will not take long to draw up.

They had nothing, apart from the clothes they had been wearing when disaster struck. One must mention, it is true, a notebook and a watch that Gédéon Spilett had kept, no doubt by oversight. But there was not a weapon, not a tool, not even a pocketknife. The passengers in the basket had thrown everything overboard to lighten the balloon.

The imaginary heroes of Daniel Defoe or of Wyss, who wrote The Swiss Family Robinson, and real castaways like Selkirk and Raynal, wrecked on Juan Fernández or in the Auckland Islands, were never so utterly destitute. Either they drew plentiful supplies from their stranded ship — seed, livestock, tools, ammunition — or else some piece of wreckage washed up on the shore that let them meet the first needs of life. They were never, at the start, completely unarmed in the face of nature. But here there was not a single instrument of any kind, not a single utensil. From nothing, they would have to arrive at everything!

And if only Cyrus Smith had been with them, if only the engineer could have put his practical knowledge and his inventive mind to work on their situation, perhaps all hope would not have been lost! Alas, they could no longer count on ever seeing Cyrus Smith again. The castaways had nothing to rely on but themselves, and that Providence which never abandons those whose faith is sincere.

But first of all, should they settle on this stretch of coast without trying to find out what continent it belonged to, whether it was inhabited, or whether it was only the shore of a desert island?

That was an important question, and one they needed to answer as soon as possible. On the answer would depend everything they did next. All the same, following Pencroff's advice, it seemed wise to wait a few days before setting out to explore. They had, in fact, to lay in food and find something more strengthening to eat than eggs and shellfish alone. The explorers might have to endure long, hard days with no shelter to rest their heads, and before anything else they had to get their strength back.

For the time being the Chimneys offered a good enough refuge. The fire was lit, and it would be easy to keep embers going. For the moment there was no shortage of shellfish and eggs among the rocks and on the beach. They would surely find some way to kill a few of the pigeons that flew by the hundreds along the crest of the plateau, even if it had to be with sticks or stones. Perhaps the trees of the nearby forest would give them fruit they could eat? And fresh water was right there. So it was agreed that they would stay at the Chimneys for a few days to get ready for an expedition, either along the coast or into the interior.

This plan suited Nab particularly well. As stubborn in his ideas as in his hunches, he was in no hurry to leave this part of the coast, the scene of the catastrophe. He did not believe — he refused to believe — that Cyrus Smith was lost. No, it did not seem possible to him that such a man could have come to so commonplace an end, carried off by a wave and drowned a few hundred paces from shore! As long as the sea had not thrown up the engineer's body, as long as he, Nab, had not seen his master's corpse with his own eyes and touched it with his own hands, he would not believe he was dead! And the idea took root deeper than ever in his stubborn heart. An illusion, perhaps, but an illusion that deserved respect, and the sailor had no wish to destroy it. For Pencroff there was no hope left: the engineer had truly perished in the waves. But with Nab there was no arguing. He was like the dog that cannot leave the spot where its master fell, and his grief was so great that he probably would not outlive him.

That morning, March 26, at first light, Nab had set off north along the coast again, back to the place where the sea had no doubt closed over the unfortunate Smith.

Breakfast that day consisted entirely of pigeon eggs and lithodomes. Harbert had found salt left by evaporation in the hollows of the rocks, and that mineral came in very handy.

When the meal was over, Pencroff asked the reporter whether he wanted to come with them into the forest, where he and Harbert were going to try their luck at hunting. But on second thought, someone had to stay behind to keep the fire going, and also in the very unlikely case that Nab needed help. So the reporter stayed.

"Off to the hunt, Harbert," said the sailor. "We'll find our ammunition along the way, and we'll cut our gun in the forest."

But just as they were leaving, Harbert pointed out that since they had no tinder, it might be wise to replace it with something else.

"With what?" asked Pencroff.

"Burnt linen," the boy answered. "In a pinch, it can do the job of tinder."

The sailor thought this very sensible advice. Its only drawback was that it meant sacrificing a piece of handkerchief. Still, it was worth it, and part of Pencroff's big checked handkerchief was soon reduced to a half-charred rag. This flammable stuff was stored in the central chamber, at the back of a little hollow in the rock, sheltered from all wind and damp.

It was now nine o'clock in the morning. The weather looked threatening, and the breeze was blowing from the southeast. Harbert and Pencroff rounded the corner of the Chimneys, not without a glance at the smoke curling up around a point of rock. Then they started up the left bank of the river.

When they reached the forest, Pencroff broke two stout branches off the first tree and turned them into clubs, and Harbert ground their tips to a point on a rock. Oh, what wouldn't he have given for a knife! Then the two hunters pushed on through the tall grass, following the bank. From the bend where the river turned toward the southwest, it narrowed little by little, and its banks formed a deep, steep-sided channel roofed over by the arching trees on either side. To keep from getting lost, Pencroff decided to follow the stream, which would always lead him back to where he had started. But the bank was not without its obstacles: here, trees whose supple branches bent down to the level of the current; there, creepers or thorns that had to be smashed through with a stick. Often Harbert would slip between the broken stumps as nimbly as a young cat and vanish into the undergrowth. But Pencroff would call him back at once and beg him not to wander off.

Meanwhile the sailor was paying close attention to the lay of the land and what it was like. On this left bank the ground was flat and rose very gradually toward the interior. In places it was damp, and then it took on a marshy look. You could sense a whole network of little trickles underneath, which must have been draining toward the river through some crack in the rock below. In places, too, a brook ran through the undergrowth, and it was easy to wade across. The opposite bank looked more rugged, and the valley, with the river running along its lowest line, showed its shape more clearly on that side. The hillside there, covered with trees rising in tiers, formed a screen that blocked the view. Walking on that right bank would have been hard, for the slopes dropped away steeply, and the trees, bent out over the water, held on only by the strength of their roots.

Needless to say, this forest, like the coast they had already covered, bore no trace of human beings. Pencroff noticed only the tracks of four-footed animals, fresh trails left by creatures whose species he could not make out. Quite certainly — and Harbert thought so too — some of them had been left by formidable wild beasts that they would no doubt have to reckon with. But nowhere was there the mark of an ax on a tree trunk, or the remains of a dead fire, or a human footprint. And perhaps they ought to be glad of that, for on this land in the middle of the Pacific, the presence of man might have been more to be feared than to be wished for.

Harbert and Pencroff, hardly talking, since the going was very rough, made only slow progress, and after an hour's walking they had covered barely a mile. So far the hunting had not paid off. A few birds were singing and fluttering among the branches, but they were very shy, as if man had instinctively taught them a well-founded fear. Among other birds, in a marshy part of the forest, Harbert pointed out one with a long, sharp beak that was built very much like a kingfisher. It differed from a kingfisher, though, in its rather coarse plumage, which had a metallic sheen.

"That must be a jacamar," said Harbert, trying to creep within good range of it.

"This would be a fine chance to taste jacamar," the sailor answered, "if that bird were in the mood to be roasted!"

At that moment a stone, thrown skillfully and hard by the boy, struck the bird where the wing joins the body. But the blow was not enough, for the jacamar ran off as fast as its legs would carry it and disappeared in an instant.

"What a clumsy fool I am!" cried Harbert.

"No, no, my boy!" the sailor answered. "That was a good throw, and plenty of people would have missed the bird altogether. Come on, don't be upset! We'll catch him another day!"

The exploration went on. The farther the hunters went, the more widely spaced and the more magnificent the trees became, but not one bore fruit they could eat. Pencroff looked in vain for some of those precious palm trees that serve so many purposes in daily life, and which have been found as far as the fortieth parallel in the northern hemisphere, but only as far as the thirty-fifth in the southern. This forest, however, was made up entirely of conifers: deodars, which Harbert had already recognized, Douglas firs like the ones that grow on the northwest coast of America, and splendid firs a hundred and fifty feet tall.

Just then a flock of small birds with pretty plumage and long, shimmering tails scattered among the branches, shedding their loosely attached feathers, which covered the ground with a fine down. Harbert picked up a few of the feathers and, after examining them, said:

"These are couroucous."

"I'd rather have a guinea fowl or a heath cock," answered Pencroff, "but anyway, are they good to eat?"

"They're good to eat, and their meat is actually very delicate," Harbert went on. "Besides, if I'm not mistaken, they're easy to get close to and knock down with a stick."

Slipping through the grass, the sailor and the boy reached the foot of a tree whose low branches were covered with the little birds. The couroucous were waiting there for the insects they feed on to fly past. You could see their feathered feet gripping tightly the middling shoots they were perched on.

The hunters then stood up and, swinging their sticks like scythes, mowed down whole rows of couroucous, which never thought of flying away and let themselves be knocked down like fools. A hundred of them already lay on the ground before the rest decided to escape.

"Good," said Pencroff. "Here's game made to measure for hunters like us! You could catch it by hand!"

The sailor strung the couroucous on a flexible switch, the way larks are strung for market, and the exploration went on. They could see that the stream curved slightly, so as to form a hook toward the south. But this detour probably did not go on for long, for the river must have had its source in the mountain and been fed by the melting of the snow that covered the sides of the central cone.

The particular purpose of this excursion, as we know, was to bring back to the residents of the Chimneys as much game as possible. It could not be said that this aim had been achieved so far. So the sailor kept up his search energetically, and grumbled whenever some animal, which he did not even have time to identify, bolted off through the tall grass. If only he had had the dog Top! But Top had disappeared at the same time as his master, and had probably perished with him!

Toward three o'clock in the afternoon, new flocks of birds were glimpsed through certain trees, pecking at their aromatic berries — junipers among them. Suddenly a real trumpet call rang through the forest. These strange, resounding fanfares came from the game birds known in the United States as grouse. Soon a few pairs came into view, with plumage mottled tawny and brown, and brown tails. Harbert could tell the males by the two pointed wings of feathers that stood up on their necks. Pencroff decided that it was absolutely essential to get hold of one of these birds, which were as big as a hen and whose meat is as good as a hazel grouse's. But it was difficult, for they would not let anyone near them. After several failed attempts, which did nothing but frighten the grouse, the sailor said to the boy:

"That settles it. Since we can't kill them on the wing, we'll have to try catching them with a line."

"Like a carp?" cried Harbert, very surprised at the suggestion.

"Like a carp," the sailor answered seriously.

In the grass Pencroff had found half a dozen grouse nests, each holding two or three eggs. He took great care not to touch these nests, since their owners were sure to come back to them. It was around them that he planned to set his lines — not snares, but real fishing lines with hooks. He led Harbert some distance from the nests, and there he prepared his peculiar tackle with all the care a disciple of Izaak Walton, the great writer on angling, would have brought to it. Harbert followed the work with an interest that is easy to understand, though he doubted it would succeed. The lines were made of thin creepers tied end to end, fifteen to twenty feet long. Big, very strong thorns with hooked points, taken from a bush of dwarf acacias, were tied to the ends of the creepers to serve as hooks. As for bait, fat red worms crawling on the ground did the job.

That done, Pencroff slipped through the grass, keeping cleverly out of sight, and laid the hooked ends of his lines near the grouse nests. Then he came back, took up the other ends, and hid with Harbert behind a big tree. Then both of them waited patiently. Harbert, it must be said, did not have much faith in the inventive Pencroff's success.

A good half hour went by, but, just as the sailor had predicted, several pairs of grouse came back to their nests. They hopped about, pecking at the ground, without the slightest suspicion that the hunters were there. The hunters, besides, had taken care to stay downwind of the birds.

There is no denying that at this moment the boy was intensely interested. He was holding his breath, and Pencroff, eyes wide, mouth open, lips pushed out as if he were about to taste a bite of grouse, was barely breathing at all.

Meanwhile the birds were strolling among the hooks without paying them much attention. Then Pencroff gave little tugs that jiggled the bait, as though the worms were still alive.

Without a doubt, the sailor felt a far stronger thrill at that moment than any angler does, since the angler cannot see his prey coming toward him through the water.

The tugs soon caught the birds' attention, and they began pecking at the hooks. Three grouse, very greedy no doubt, swallowed bait and hook together. Suddenly, with a sharp jerk, Pencroff set his hooks, and the beating of wings told him the birds were caught.

"Hurrah!" he shouted, rushing at the game, and he had it in hand in an instant.

Harbert had clapped his hands. It was the first time he had ever seen birds caught with a line. But the sailor, very modestly, assured him that this was not his first try, and that anyway the credit for the invention was not his.

"And in any case," he added, "in the situation we're in, we'd better expect to see plenty of other things like it!"

The grouse were tied together by the feet, and Pencroff, happy not to be going back empty-handed and seeing that the daylight was beginning to fade, thought it best to head for home.

The way back was plainly marked by the river; they had only to follow it downstream. And at about six o'clock, rather tired from their excursion, Harbert and Pencroff walked back into the Chimneys.

Chapter 7: Nab Has Not Come Back

Nab has not come back yet — The reporter's thoughts — Supper — A bad night in the making — The storm is terrible — They set out in the night — A fight against rain and wind — Eight miles from the first camp

Gédéon Spilett was standing motionless on the beach at that moment, his arms crossed, looking out to sea. In the east the horizon was melting into a great black cloud that was climbing swiftly toward the zenith. The wind was already strong, and it was freshening as the day declined. The whole sky had an ugly look, and the first signs of a gale were plain to see.

Harbert went into the Chimneys, and Pencroff walked over to the reporter, who was so deep in thought that he did not see him coming.

"We're in for a bad night, Mr. Spilett!" said the sailor. "Rain and wind enough to make the petrels happy — they're sea birds that love nothing better than a storm!"

The reporter turned around, saw Pencroff, and these were his first words:

"How far from the coast would you say the basket was when that wave hit it and carried off our companion?"

The sailor had not expected the question. He thought for a moment and answered:

"Two cable lengths, at the most."

"But what's a cable length?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"About a hundred and twenty fathoms, or six hundred feet."

"So," said the reporter, "Cyrus Smith disappeared twelve hundred feet from shore, at the most?"

"About that," answered Pencroff.

"And his dog too?"

"Him too."

"What surprises me," the reporter went on, "supposing our companion is dead, is that Top died as well, and that neither the dog's body nor his master's has washed up on the shore!"

"That's not surprising, with a sea as rough as that," answered the sailor. "Besides, the currents may have carried them farther along the coast."

"So it really is your opinion that our companion drowned?" the reporter asked once more.

"That's my opinion."

"Well, my own opinion," said Gédéon Spilett, "with all due respect to your experience, Pencroff, is that the twofold fact of Cyrus and Top vanishing completely, alive or dead, is something inexplicable and improbable."

"I'd like to think the way you do, Mr. Spilett," answered Pencroff. "Unfortunately, my mind's made up!"

With that, the sailor went back to the Chimneys. A good fire was crackling on the hearth. Harbert had just thrown an armful of dry wood onto it, and the flames cast great bursts of light into the dark parts of the passage.

Pencroff set to work on dinner at once. He thought it right to put something substantial on the menu, since they all needed to build their strength back up. The strings of couroucous were kept for the next day, but two grouse were plucked, and soon, skewered on a stick, the birds were roasting in front of a blazing fire.

At seven o'clock in the evening Nab had still not come back. His long absence could only make Pencroff anxious about him. The sailor had to fear that some accident had befallen him in this unknown land, or else that the poor fellow had done something desperate. But Harbert drew entirely different conclusions from Nab's absence. To his mind, if Nab had not come back, it was because something new had turned up that had led him to keep searching. And anything new could only be to Cyrus Smith's advantage. Why had Nab not returned, unless some hope was keeping him? Perhaps he had found some clue — a footprint, a scrap of wreckage — that had put him on the track. Perhaps at this very moment he was following a sure trail. Perhaps he was by his master's side...

That was how the boy reasoned. That was what he said. His companions let him talk. Only the reporter nodded his approval. But to Pencroff, the likely thing was that Nab had pushed his search along the shore farther than he had the day before, and simply could not have got back yet.

All the same, Harbert, stirred up by vague forebodings, said several times that he meant to go out and meet Nab. But Pencroff made him see that it would be a useless trip — that in this darkness and this dreadful weather he would never find Nab's tracks, and that it was better to wait. If Nab had not reappeared by the next day, Pencroff would not hesitate to go with Harbert and search for him.

Gédéon Spilett agreed with the sailor that they must not split up, and Harbert had to give up his plan; but two big tears fell from his eyes.

The reporter could not help throwing his arms around the generous boy.

The bad weather had now broken in earnest. A southeasterly gale was sweeping over the coast with unequaled violence. They could hear the sea, which was falling at that hour, roaring against the edge of the first line of rocks out beyond the shore. The rain, beaten into spray by the hurricane, lifted off like a liquid fog. It looked like rags of vapor trailing along the coast, where the shingle rattled violently, like cartloads of stones being dumped. The sand, whipped up by the wind, mixed with the downpour and made its onslaught unbearable. There was as much dust of rock in the air as dust of water. Between the mouth of the river and the face of the cliff, great eddies whirled, and the masses of air pouring out of that whirlpool, finding no other way out than the narrow valley at the bottom of which the river ran, rushed into it with irresistible force. So the smoke from the hearth, driven back down the narrow flue, kept blowing back into the passages, filling them and making them impossible to live in.

That was why, as soon as the grouse were cooked, Pencroff let the fire die down and kept only some embers buried under the ashes.

At eight o'clock Nab had still not reappeared. But by now it was reasonable to suppose that this frightful weather was all that had kept him from coming back, and that he must have taken shelter in some hollow to wait for the storm to end, or at least for daylight to return. As for going out to meet him, or trying to find him in such conditions, that was impossible.

The game made up the whole of supper. They ate the meat gladly, for it was excellent. Pencroff and Harbert, whose appetites had been sharpened by a long expedition, wolfed it down.

Then each of them went off to the corner where he had slept the night before, and Harbert soon fell asleep near the sailor, who had stretched out along the hearth.

Outside, as the night wore on, the storm grew to tremendous proportions. It was a gale to match the one that had carried the prisoners all the way from Richmond to this land in the Pacific. Storms like it are frequent at the time of the equinox, rich in disasters, and terrible above all over this wide open sea, which puts no obstacle in the way of their fury! So it is easy to understand that a coast facing east like this one — that is, straight into the blows of the hurricane, and taking them full on — was battered with a force no description can convey.

Very luckily, the heap of rocks that made up the Chimneys was solid. They were enormous blocks of granite, though a few of them, not quite balanced, seemed to tremble on their bases. Pencroff could feel it: with his hand pressed against the walls, he felt quick shudders running under it. Still, he kept telling himself, and rightly, that there was nothing to fear, and that his makeshift shelter would not collapse. All the same, he could hear stones, torn loose from the top of the plateau by the eddies of the wind, falling onto the beach. Some even rolled onto the upper part of the Chimneys, or shattered there when they came straight down. Twice the sailor got up and crawled to the mouth of the passage to look outside. But these small rockfalls were no real danger, and he went back to his place in front of the hearth, where the embers crackled under the ash.

In spite of the raging hurricane, the crash of the storm, the thunder of the tempest, Harbert slept soundly. In the end sleep took hold of Pencroff too, whose life at sea had used him to all such violence. Only Gédéon Spilett was kept awake by worry. He blamed himself for not having gone with Nab. As we have seen, he had not given up all hope. The forebodings that had stirred Harbert had never stopped stirring him as well. His thoughts were fixed on Nab. Why had Nab not come back? He tossed and turned on his bed of sand, paying hardly any attention to the battle of the elements outside. Now and then his eyes, heavy with exhaustion, closed for an instant, but some quick thought opened them again almost at once.

Meanwhile the night wore on. It might have been two o'clock in the morning when Pencroff, sound asleep by then, was shaken hard.

"What is it?" he cried, waking up and collecting his wits with the quickness peculiar to seafaring men.

The reporter was leaning over him and saying:

"Listen, Pencroff, listen!"

The sailor strained his ears and could make out no sound but the gusts.

"It's the wind," he said.

"No," answered Gédéon Spilett, listening again, "I thought I heard..."

"What?"

"A dog barking!"

"A dog!" cried Pencroff, leaping to his feet.

"Yes... barking..."

"That's impossible!" answered the sailor. "Anyway, how could you, with the storm roaring like that..."

"There... listen..." said the reporter.

Pencroff listened more closely, and in a moment of calm he did indeed think he heard distant barking.

"Well?..." said the reporter, gripping the sailor's hand.

"Yes... yes!..." answered Pencroff.

"It's Top! It's Top!..." cried Harbert, who had just woken up, and all three rushed for the mouth of the Chimneys.

They had a desperate struggle to get out. The wind kept driving them back. But at last they managed it, and they could stay on their feet only by bracing themselves against the rocks. They looked; they could not speak.

The darkness was total. Sea, sky and land were merged in one equal blackness. There did not seem to be a single atom of light anywhere in the air.

For several minutes the reporter and his two companions stayed like that, as if crushed by the wind, soaked by the rain, blinded by the sand. Then, in a lull in the storm, they heard the barking once more, and they could tell that it must be quite far off.

It could only be Top barking like that! But was he alone, or was someone with him? It was more likely that he was alone, for if Nab had been with him, Nab would have headed for the Chimneys as fast as he could.

The sailor squeezed the reporter's hand — he could not make himself heard — in a way that meant "Wait!" Then he went back into the passage.

A moment later he came out again with a burning bundle of sticks, flung it into the darkness, and gave a series of shrill whistles.

At this signal — one might have thought it was expected — barking answered from much nearer, and soon a dog dashed into the passage. Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett went back in after him.

An armful of dry wood was thrown on the coals. A bright blaze lit up the passage.

"It's Top!" cried Harbert.

It was Top, indeed — a magnificent Anglo-Norman hound, which had got from the crossing of those two breeds both speed of foot and keenness of scent, the two supreme qualities of a hunting dog.

It was the dog of the engineer Cyrus Smith.

But he was alone! Neither his master nor Nab was with him!

And yet how had his instinct been able to lead him to the Chimneys, a place he did not know? It seemed inexplicable, above all in the middle of that black night and in such a storm! But — a detail more inexplicable still — Top was neither tired nor worn out, nor even spattered with mud or sand!...

Harbert had drawn him close and was holding the dog's head between his hands. The dog let him, and rubbed his neck against the boy's hands.

"If the dog has turned up, the master will turn up too!" said the reporter.

"God grant it!" answered Harbert. "Let's go! Top will lead us!"

Pencroff did not raise a single objection. He could feel that Top's arrival might well prove his guesses wrong.

"Off we go!" he said.

Pencroff carefully covered the coals on the hearth. He laid a few pieces of wood under the ashes, so that there would be fire to come back to. Then, after taking the leftovers of supper, he plunged outside, preceded by the dog, who seemed to be urging him on with little barks, and followed by the reporter and the boy.

The storm was now at its most violent, perhaps even at its very peak. The moon, which was new — and so in conjunction with the sun — let not the faintest glimmer filter through the clouds. Keeping to a straight course was hard. The best thing was to trust to Top's instinct, and that is what they did. The reporter and the boy walked behind the dog, and the sailor brought up the rear. No talk would have been possible. The rain was not very heavy, since the hurricane's blast broke it into spray, but the hurricane itself was terrible.

One circumstance, though, worked very luckily in favor of the sailor and his two companions. The wind was blowing from the southeast, and so it was at their backs. The sand it hurled so violently, which would have been unbearable in their faces, struck them from behind, and as long as they did not turn around it could not trouble them enough to slow them down. In fact they often went faster than they meant to, and quickened their steps so as not to be knocked over. But an immense hope doubled their strength, and this time they were not walking up the shore at random. They had no doubt that Nab had found his master and had sent them the faithful dog. But was the engineer alive? Or was Nab summoning his companions only to pay their last respects to the body of the unfortunate Smith?

After passing the cut-off corner of the high ground, which they had been careful to keep well clear of, Harbert, the reporter and Pencroff stopped to catch their breath. The angle of the rock sheltered them from the wind, and they got their breath back after a quarter of an hour's march that had been more of a run.

Now they could hear one another and answer, and when the boy spoke the name of Cyrus Smith, Top gave a few short barks, as if he meant to say that his master was saved.

"Saved, isn't he?" Harbert kept repeating. "Saved, Top?"

And the dog barked as if in answer.

They set off again. It was about half past two in the morning. The sea was beginning to rise, and this tide, driven by the wind, was a spring tide — the high tide of new moon — and threatened to be very strong. The great waves thundered against the line of reefs and attacked it so violently that they were very probably sweeping right over the islet, which was completely invisible now. So that long breakwater no longer sheltered the coast, which lay wide open to the shocks of the open sea.

As soon as the sailor and his companions had left the shelter of the corner, the wind struck them again with tremendous fury. Bent over, backs to the blast, they walked very fast, following Top, who never hesitated over which way to go. They were heading north, with an endless crest of breakers on their right, crashing with a deafening roar, and on their left a dark country whose look it was impossible to make out. But they could feel that it must be fairly flat, because the hurricane now passed right over their heads without whirling back on them, as it had done when it struck the granite cliff.

By four o'clock in the morning they reckoned they had covered five miles. The clouds had lifted a little and no longer trailed along the ground. The wind, less wet now, blew in very sharp currents of air, drier and colder. Poorly protected by their clothes, Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett must have suffered cruelly, but not one complaint passed their lips. They were determined to follow Top wherever the intelligent animal chose to lead them.

Toward five o'clock day began to break. First, at the zenith, where the mists were thinner, a few grayish tints outlined the edges of the clouds, and soon, under an opaque band, a brighter streak sharply traced the horizon of the sea. The crests of the waves were touched with faint tawny gleams, and the foam turned white again. At the same time, on the left, the broken ground along the shore began to show in a blur, but it was still only gray on black.

At six o'clock in the morning it was full day. The clouds were racing along at great speed, fairly high up. The sailor and his companions were now about six miles from the Chimneys. They were following a very flat beach, bordered out to sea by a line of rocks of which only the tops showed above the water, since it was high tide. On the left the land, broken up by a few dunes bristling with thistles, had the rather wild look of a vast sandy region. The shoreline had few indentations, and the only barrier it offered the ocean was a fairly irregular chain of hummocks. Here and there one or two trees grimaced, bent over toward the west, their branches flung out in that direction. Far behind, to the southwest, curved the edge of the last forest.

At that moment Top showed unmistakable signs of excitement. He would run ahead, come back to the sailor, and seem to be urging him to hurry. The dog had now left the beach, and, driven by his remarkable instinct, without showing the least hesitation, he had gone in among the dunes.

They followed him. The country seemed completely deserted. Not a living creature stirred in it.

The belt of dunes was very wide, made up of hummocks and even of hills scattered about in the most haphazard way. It was like a little Switzerland of sand, and it took nothing short of a prodigious instinct to find the way through it.

Five minutes after leaving the beach, the reporter and his companions came to a kind of hollow dug into the back of a tall dune. There Top stopped and gave one clear bark. Spilett, Harbert and Pencroff went into this cave.

Nab was there, kneeling beside a body stretched out on a bed of grass...

The body was that of the engineer Cyrus Smith.

Chapter 8: Is Cyrus Smith Alive?

Is Cyrus Smith alive? — Nab's story — The footprints — A question with no answer — Cyrus Smith's first words — The footprints checked — The return to the Chimneys — Pencroff aghast!

Nab did not move. The sailor threw him just one word.

"Alive?" he cried.

Nab did not answer. Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff went pale. Harbert clasped his hands and stood frozen where he was. But it was plain that poor Nab, swallowed up in his grief, had neither seen his companions nor heard the sailor's words.

The reporter knelt beside the motionless body, opened the engineer's clothes, and laid his ear against his chest. A minute went by — it felt like a century! — while he tried to catch some beat of the heart.

Nab had straightened up a little and was staring without seeing. Despair could not have changed a man's face more. Nab was unrecognizable, worn out with fatigue, broken with grief. He believed his master was dead.

After a long and careful examination, Gédéon Spilett stood up.

"He's alive!" he said.

Pencroff knelt in his turn beside Cyrus Smith. His ear, too, caught a few heartbeats, and his lips felt a faint breath escaping from the engineer's lips.

At a word from the reporter, Harbert dashed outside to look for water. A hundred paces away he found a clear stream, obviously swollen by the rains of the day before, filtering through the sand. But there was nothing to carry the water in — not one shell in those dunes! The boy had to make do with soaking his handkerchief in the stream, and he ran back to the cave.

Luckily the wet handkerchief was all Gédéon Spilett needed, since he only wanted to moisten the engineer's lips. Those few drops of fresh water had an almost immediate effect. A sigh escaped from Cyrus Smith's chest, and he even seemed to be trying to say a few words.

"We'll save him!" said the reporter.

At those words Nab began to hope again. He undressed his master to see whether his body showed any wound. There were no bruises on the head, the chest or the limbs, not even a scrape — which was surprising, since Cyrus Smith's body must have been rolled about among the rocks. Even his hands were unmarked, and it was hard to explain how the engineer showed no trace of the struggle he must have gone through to get past the line of reefs.

But the explanation of this would come later. When Cyrus Smith could talk, he would tell them what had happened. For the moment the job was to bring him back to life, and rubbing him down would probably do it. So they rubbed him with the sailor's jacket. Warmed by this rough massage, the engineer moved his arm slightly, and his breathing began to settle into a steadier rhythm. He had been dying of exhaustion, and if the reporter and his companions had not arrived, that would certainly have been the end of Cyrus Smith.

"So you thought he was dead, your master?" the sailor asked Nab.

"Yes! Dead!" Nab answered. "And if Top hadn't found you, if you hadn't come, I would have buried my master and died beside him!"

You can see what a thread Cyrus Smith's life had hung by!

Then Nab told them what had happened. The day before, after leaving the Chimneys at dawn, he had gone up the coast heading north and reached the stretch of shore he had already searched.

There, without any hope, as he admitted, Nab had searched the shore, among the rocks and on the sand, for the slightest clue that might guide him. Above all he had examined the part of the beach that the high tide did not cover, because along its edge the rise and fall of the tide would have wiped out every trace. Nab no longer hoped to find his master alive. What he was looking for was a body — a body he wanted to bury with his own hands!

Nab had searched a long time, and all his efforts came to nothing. That deserted coast did not seem ever to have been visited by a human being. The shells that the sea could not reach — and there were millions of them above the high-tide line — lay untouched. Not one shell was crushed. Over a stretch of two or three hundred yards there was no sign of anyone having come ashore, either long ago or recently.

So Nab had decided to go on up the coast for a few miles. The currents might have carried a body to some point farther along. When a body is floating not far from a flat shore, it is very rare for the waves not to throw it up on the beach sooner or later. Nab knew that, and he wanted to see his master one last time.

"I walked along the coast for two more miles," he said. "I checked the whole line of reefs at low tide and the whole beach at high tide, and I'd given up hope of finding anything, when yesterday, around five o'clock in the evening, I noticed footprints in the sand."

"Footprints?" cried Pencroff.

"Yes!" answered Nab.

"And did these footprints start right at the reefs?" asked the reporter.

"No," Nab answered, "only at the high-tide line. Between the tide line and the reefs, the others must have been washed away."

"Go on, Nab," said Gédéon Spilett.

"When I saw those footprints, I went half out of my mind. They were very easy to make out, and they headed toward the dunes. I followed them for a quarter of a mile, running, but taking care not to step on them. Five minutes later, just as night was falling, I heard a dog barking. It was Top, and Top led me right here, to my master!"

Nab finished his story by telling them how he had grieved when he found that lifeless body. He had tried to catch some last sign of life in it! Now that he had found him dead, he wanted him alive! All his efforts had been useless! There was nothing left for him to do but pay his last respects to the man he loved so much!

Then Nab had thought of his companions. They would surely want to see the unfortunate man one last time! Top was there. Couldn't he rely on the cleverness of that faithful animal? Nab said the reporter's name several times over — of all the engineer's companions, he was the one Top knew best. Then he pointed south along the coast, and the dog dashed off in the direction he had been shown.

We know how Top got to the Chimneys all the same, guided by an instinct that could almost be called supernatural, since the animal had never been there before.

Nab's companions had listened to his story with the closest attention. To them there was something inexplicable in the fact that Cyrus Smith, after the struggle he must have gone through to escape the waves and cross the reefs, did not have so much as a scratch. And what was no easier to explain was how the engineer could have reached this cave, lost among the dunes more than a mile from the shore.

"So, Nab," said the reporter, "it wasn't you who carried your master here?"

"No, it wasn't me," Nab answered.

"It's pretty obvious Mr. Smith got here on his own," said Pencroff.

"Obvious, yes," remarked Gédéon Spilett, "but not believable!"

Only the engineer himself could explain it, and for that they would have to wait until he could speak again. Fortunately, life was already flowing back into him. The rubbing had got his blood circulating again. Cyrus Smith moved his arms once more, then his head, and once again a few words they could not understand escaped his lips.

Nab, bending over him, kept calling to him, but the engineer did not seem to hear, and his eyes stayed shut. Movement was the only sign of life in him. His senses had not yet come back.

Pencroff badly regretted having no fire, and nothing to make one with, because he had unfortunately forgotten to bring the burnt linen, which he could easily have lit by striking two pebbles together. As for the engineer's pockets, they were completely empty, except for his vest pocket, which held his watch. So they would have to carry Cyrus Smith to the Chimneys, and as soon as possible. On that, everyone agreed.

But the care they lavished on the engineer was to bring him round faster than they could have hoped. The water they moistened his lips with was reviving him little by little. Pencroff also had the idea of mixing the water with juice from the grouse meat he had brought along. Harbert ran down to the shore and came back with two big bivalve shells. The sailor made a sort of mixture in them and slipped it between the engineer's lips, and he seemed to drink it down eagerly.

Then his eyes opened. Nab and the reporter were bending over him.

"My master! My master!" cried Nab.

The engineer heard him. He recognized Nab and Spilett, then his two other companions, Harbert and the sailor, and his hand gave theirs a faint squeeze.

A few more words escaped his lips — words he had no doubt been saying before, and which showed what thoughts were tormenting his mind, even then. This time the words were understood.

"Island or continent?" he murmured.

"Ah!" cried Pencroff, who could not hold the exclamation back. "By all the devils, who cares, as long as you're alive, Mr. Cyrus! Island or continent? We'll find out later."

The engineer gave a slight nod and seemed to fall asleep.

They let him sleep, and the reporter immediately began making arrangements to carry the engineer back in the best possible way. Nab, Harbert and Pencroff left the cave and headed for a tall dune crowned with a few stunted trees. And as they went, the sailor could not stop himself from repeating:

"Island or continent! Thinking about that when he's got hardly a breath left in him! What a man!"

When they reached the top of the dune, Pencroff and his two companions, with no tools but their bare arms, stripped the main branches off a rather puny tree, a kind of maritime pine worn thin by the wind. Out of those branches they made a stretcher, which, once it was covered with leaves and grass, would let them carry the engineer.

It took them about forty minutes, and it was ten o'clock when the sailor, Nab and Harbert came back to Cyrus Smith, whom Gédéon Spilett had not left.

The engineer was just then waking from the sleep — or rather the stupor — in which they had found him. The color was coming back into his cheeks, which until then had been as pale as death. He raised himself a little, looked around him, and seemed to be asking where he was.

"Can you listen to me without tiring yourself, Cyrus?" said the reporter.

"Yes," answered the engineer.

"If you ask me," the sailor put in, "Mr. Smith will hear you even better if he has another go at this grouse jelly — because it is grouse, Mr. Cyrus," he added, holding out a little of the jelly, into which, this time, he had mixed a few shreds of meat.

Cyrus Smith chewed the bits of grouse, and what was left was shared among his three companions, who were suffering from hunger and found it a rather skimpy lunch.

"Good!" said the sailor. "There's food waiting for us at the Chimneys. Because you ought to know, Mr. Cyrus, that down there, to the south, we've got a house with rooms, beds and a fireplace, and in the pantry a few dozen birds that our Harbert calls couroucous. Your stretcher's ready, and as soon as you feel strong enough, we'll carry you home."

"Thank you, my friend," answered the engineer. "Another hour or two and we can go... And now, tell me, Spilett."

So the reporter told him what had happened. He told him everything Cyrus Smith could not have known: the balloon's last fall; the landing on this unknown land, which seemed deserted, whatever it turned out to be, island or continent; the discovery of the Chimneys; the search for the engineer; Nab's devotion; everything they owed to the intelligence of faithful Top; and so on.

"But," asked Cyrus Smith, his voice still weak, "you didn't pick me up on the beach, then?"

"No," answered the reporter.

"And it wasn't you who brought me to this cave?"

"No."

"How far is this cave from the reefs?"

"About half a mile," answered Pencroff. "And if you're amazed, Mr. Cyrus, we're no less surprised ourselves to find you here!"

"Indeed," answered the engineer, who was reviving little by little and taking an interest in these details, "indeed, that's very strange!"

"But," the sailor went on, "can you tell us what happened after that wave carried you off?"

Cyrus Smith gathered his memories. He knew very little. The wave had torn him out of the balloon's net. At first he had sunk several fathoms deep. When he came back up to the surface in the half darkness, he felt a living creature thrashing beside him. It was Top, who had leaped in to save him. Looking up, he could no longer see the balloon, which, relieved of his weight and the dog's, had shot away like an arrow. He found himself in the middle of the raging waves, at a distance from the coast that could not have been less than half a mile. He tried to fight the waves, swimming hard. Top held him up by his clothes. But a current as fast as lightning caught him and swept him north, and after half an hour of struggling he went under, dragging Top down with him into the depths. From that moment until the moment he had just found himself in his friends' arms, he remembered nothing at all.

"Still," Pencroff went on, "you must have been thrown up on the shore, and you must have had the strength to walk all the way here, since Nab found your footprints!"

"Yes... I must have..." answered the engineer, thinking it over. "And you didn't see any trace of human beings on this coast?"

"Not a trace," answered the reporter. "Besides, if by chance some rescuer had happened to be there at just the right moment, why would he have abandoned you after pulling you out of the waves?"

"You're right, my dear Spilett." Then, turning to his servant, the engineer added: "Tell me, Nab, it wasn't you who... you couldn't have had a moment's blackout... during which... No, that's absurd... Are any of those footprints still there?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"Yes, my master," answered Nab. "Right there at the entrance, on the back slope of this very dune, in a spot sheltered from the wind and rain. The others were wiped out by the storm."

"Pencroff," said Cyrus Smith, "would you take my shoes and see whether they fit those footprints exactly?"

The sailor did what the engineer asked. He and Harbert, guided by Nab, went to the place where the footprints were, while Cyrus Smith said to the reporter:

"Some inexplicable things have happened here!"

"Inexplicable indeed!" answered Gédéon Spilett.

"But let's not dwell on it now, my dear Spilett. We'll talk about it later."

A moment later the sailor, Nab and Harbert came back in.

There was no possible doubt. The engineer's shoes fitted the surviving footprints exactly. So it was Cyrus Smith who had left them in the sand.

"Well, then," he said, "it must have been me who had that hallucination, that blackout I was blaming on Nab! I must have walked like a sleepwalker, without knowing I was taking a step, and it must have been Top who led me here by instinct, after pulling me out of the waves... Come here, Top! Come, boy!"

The magnificent animal bounded up to his master, barking, and he was not short of pats and praise.

It will be agreed that there was no other explanation for the events that had led to Cyrus Smith's rescue, and that all the credit for the business belonged to Top.

Toward noon, when Pencroff asked Cyrus Smith whether he could be moved, Cyrus Smith's only answer was to stand up, with an effort that showed the most powerful willpower. But he had to lean on the sailor, or he would have fallen.

"Fine! Fine!" said Pencroff. "The stretcher for the engineer, please!"

The stretcher was brought. Its crosspieces had been covered with moss and long grass. They laid Cyrus Smith on it and set off toward the coast, Pencroff at one end of the poles, Nab at the other.

There were eight miles to cover, but since they could not go fast and might have to stop often, they would have to allow at least six hours to reach the Chimneys.

The wind was still violent, but fortunately it was no longer raining. Though he was lying down, the engineer propped himself on his elbow and studied the coast, especially the landward side, away from the sea. He did not speak, but he looked, and there is no doubt that the shape of that country — its rises and hollows, its forests, its different kinds of plants — was printed on his mind. After two hours on the way, however, fatigue won, and he fell asleep on the stretcher.

At half past five the little party reached the cut-off corner of the cliff, and a little later they stood in front of the Chimneys.

Everyone stopped, and the stretcher was set down on the sand. Cyrus Smith was sound asleep and did not wake.

Then, to his great surprise, Pencroff saw that the terrible storm of the day before had changed the look of the place. There had been some fairly big rockfalls. Large blocks of stone lay scattered on the beach, and a thick carpet of seaweed — wrack and algae — covered the whole shore. It was obvious that the sea had swept right over the islet and rolled all the way to the foot of the enormous granite rampart.

In front of the opening of the Chimneys the ground had been deeply gouged; the waves had battered it violently.

A kind of foreboding flashed through Pencroff's mind. He rushed into the passage.

Almost at once he came back out and stood frozen, staring at his companions...

The fire was out. The drowned ashes were nothing but mud. The burnt linen that was to serve as tinder was gone. The sea had pushed all the way to the back of the passages and turned everything upside down, wrecked everything, inside the Chimneys!

Chapter 9: Cyrus Is Here

Cyrus is here — Pencroff's attempts — Rubbing sticks — Island or continent? — The engineer's plans — Where in the Pacific Ocean? — Deep in the forest — The stone pine — A capybara hunt — A smoke of good omen

In a few words Gédéon Spilett, Harbert and Nab were told how things stood. This accident, which could have very serious consequences — at least, that was how Pencroff saw it — had different effects on the honest sailor's companions.

Nab, overjoyed at having found his master again, did not listen, or rather did not even want to bother himself with what Pencroff was saying.

Harbert, for his part, seemed to share the sailor's fears to some degree.

As for the reporter, he answered Pencroff's words quite simply:

"Upon my word, Pencroff, I couldn't care less!"

"But I'm telling you, we don't have a fire anymore!"

"Pooh!"

"And no way of lighting it again."

"Bah!"

"But Mr. Spilett..."

"Isn't Cyrus here?" answered the reporter. "Isn't our engineer alive? He'll find a way to make us a fire, all right!"

"And with what?"

"With nothing."

What could Pencroff have said to that? He would have said nothing, because deep down he shared the faith his companions had in Cyrus Smith. To them the engineer was a world in miniature, a compound of all human science and all human intelligence! They would rather be with Cyrus on a desert island than without Cyrus in the busiest industrial city in the Union. With him, they could want for nothing. With him, they could not lose hope. If someone had come and told these good people that a volcanic eruption was about to wipe out this land, that this land was about to sink into the depths of the Pacific, they would have answered, without turning a hair: "Cyrus is here! Ask Cyrus!"

In the meantime, though, the engineer had sunk back into an exhaustion brought on by being carried, and for the moment no one could call on his ingenuity. Supper was bound to be very thin. All the grouse meat had been eaten, and there was no way to cook any kind of game at all. Besides, the couroucous they had been keeping in reserve had disappeared. They would have to think of something.

First of all, Cyrus Smith was carried into the central passage. There they managed to make him a bed of seaweed and wrack that had stayed more or less dry. The deep sleep that had taken hold of him could only bring his strength back quickly — better, no doubt, than a big meal would have done.

Night had fallen, and with it the temperature dropped sharply, as the wind shifted round to the northeast. And since the sea had destroyed the walls Pencroff had built at certain points in the passages, drafts swept through, and the Chimneys became hardly fit to live in. So the engineer would have been in a rather bad way if his companions had not taken off their jackets and sailor's jerseys and carefully covered him with them.

Supper that evening was nothing but those inevitable lithodomes, which Harbert and Nab gathered in great quantities on the beach. To these shellfish, though, the boy added a certain amount of edible seaweed, which he collected on high rocks whose sides the sea could only wet at the time of the highest tides. This seaweed, which belonged to the family of the wracks, was a kind of sargassum. When it is dried it gives a jellylike substance that is fairly rich in nourishment. So the reporter and his companions, after swallowing a considerable quantity of lithodomes, sucked on this sargassum and found its taste quite bearable — and it must be said that along the coasts of Asia it makes up a good part of what the local people eat.

"All the same," said the sailor, "it's time Mr. Cyrus came to our rescue."

Meanwhile the cold grew bitter, and unfortunately there was no way to fight it.

The sailor, truly annoyed, tried every means he could think of to get a fire. Nab even helped him in the attempt. He had found some dry moss, and by striking two pebbles together he got sparks. But the moss was not flammable enough and did not catch. Besides, those sparks were only glowing bits of flint, and they did not have the body of the sparks that fly from the piece of steel in an ordinary flint and steel. So the attempt failed.

Next Pencroff, though he had no faith at all in the method, tried rubbing two pieces of dry wood together, the way the islanders do. Certainly, the motion he and Nab put into it, if it had all been turned into heat, as the new theories say it can be, would have been enough to boil a steamer's boiler! The result was nothing. The pieces of wood got warm, and that was all — and even then a good deal less warm than the workers themselves.

After an hour of work Pencroff was dripping with sweat, and he threw the pieces of wood down in disgust.

"When they get me to believe the islanders light fires that way," he said, "it'll be hot even in winter! I'd sooner set my arms on fire by rubbing them together!"

The sailor was wrong to deny the method. It is a well-established fact that such peoples set wood alight by rubbing it fast. But not every kind of wood will do for it, and then there is "the knack," as the saying goes, and Pencroff very probably did not have "the knack."

Pencroff's bad temper did not last long. Harbert had picked up the two pieces of wood the sailor had thrown away and was doing his best to rub them harder than ever. The sturdy sailor could not hold back a burst of laughter at the sight of the boy's efforts to succeed where he himself had failed.

"Rub, my boy, rub!" he said.

"I am rubbing," answered Harbert, laughing, "but all I'm trying to do is warm myself up in my turn instead of shivering, and soon I'll be as hot as you are, Pencroff!"

Which is what happened. Be that as it may, they had to give up getting a fire for that night. Gédéon Spilett repeated for the twentieth time that Cyrus Smith would not be stumped by so small a thing. And in the meantime he stretched out in one of the passages, on the bed of sand. Harbert, Nab and Pencroff did the same, while Top slept at his master's feet.

The next day, March 28, when the engineer woke up at about eight o'clock in the morning, he saw his companions beside him, waiting for him to wake, and, as on the day before, his first words were:

"Island or continent?"

As you can see, it was his one fixed idea.

"Well," answered Pencroff, "we don't know anything about that, Mr. Smith!"

"You still don't know?..."

"But we'll find out," Pencroff added, "once you've piloted us around this country."

"I think I'm up to trying," answered the engineer, who, without too much effort, got up and stood on his feet.

"Now that's good!" cried the sailor.

"What I was dying of was mostly exhaustion," answered Cyrus Smith. "My friends, a little food, and you won't be able to tell. You have a fire, don't you?"

This question did not get an answer right away. But after a few moments:

"Alas! We have no fire," said Pencroff, "or rather, Mr. Cyrus, we don't have one anymore!"

And the sailor told the story of what had happened the day before. He amused the engineer with the tale of their one and only match, and then his failed attempt to make fire the way the islanders do.

"We'll think of something," answered the engineer, "and if we can't find some substance like tinder..."

"Well?" asked the sailor.

"Well, we'll make matches."

"Chemical ones?"

"Chemical ones!"

"It's as simple as that!" cried the reporter, clapping the sailor on the shoulder.

The sailor did not think it was quite so simple, but he did not argue. They all went outside. The weather had turned fine again. A bright sun was rising over the horizon of the sea and sprinkling flecks of gold over the rough, prism-shaped faces of the enormous wall.

After a quick look around him, the engineer sat down on a block of rock. Harbert offered him a few handfuls of mussels and sargassum, saying:

"It's all we've got, Mr. Cyrus."

"Thank you, my boy," answered Cyrus Smith. "It will do — for this morning, at least."

And he ate this meager food with a good appetite, washing it down with a little fresh water, drawn from the river in a big shell.

His companions watched him without speaking. Then, after eating his fill as well as he could, Cyrus Smith folded his arms and said:

"So, my friends, you still don't know whether fate has thrown us onto a continent or onto an island?"

"No, Mr. Cyrus," answered the boy.

"We'll know tomorrow," the engineer went on. "Until then, there's nothing to be done."

"Yes, there is," Pencroff replied.

"What, then?"

"Fire," said the sailor, who had his fixed idea too.

"We'll make one, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith. "While you were carrying me yesterday, didn't I see a mountain to the west that towers over this country?"

"Yes," answered Gédéon Spilett, "a mountain that must be fairly high..."

"Good," the engineer went on. "Tomorrow we'll climb to its summit, and we'll see whether this land is an island or a continent. Until then, I say again, there's nothing to be done."

"Yes, there is — fire!" said the stubborn sailor once more.

"But we will make a fire!" Gédéon Spilett replied. "A little patience, Pencroff!"

The sailor looked at Gédéon Spilett in a way that seemed to say, "If it's up to you to make it, we won't be tasting a roast anytime soon!" But he held his tongue.

Cyrus Smith, meanwhile, had not answered. He seemed very little concerned with this question of fire. For a few moments he stayed lost in thought. Then he spoke again.

"My friends," he said, "our situation may be wretched, but in any case it is very simple. Either we're on a continent, and then, at the cost of more or less hard work, we'll reach some inhabited place; or else we're on an island. In that case, it's one of two things: if the island is inhabited, we'll see about getting out of our fix with the help of its inhabitants; if it's deserted, we'll see about getting out of our fix all by ourselves."

"Nothing could be simpler, that's certain," answered Pencroff.

"But continent or island," asked Gédéon Spilett, "where do you think this hurricane has thrown us, Cyrus?"

"I can't know exactly," answered the engineer, "but the odds favor a land in the Pacific. When we left Richmond, the wind was blowing from the northeast, and its very violence proves that its direction can't have changed. If it held that course, from northeast to southwest, we crossed the states of North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia, the Gulf of Mexico, Mexico itself at its narrow part, and then a portion of the Pacific Ocean. I put the distance the balloon traveled at no less than six or seven thousand miles, and if the wind shifted by even half a point of the compass, it must have carried us either to the Mendaña archipelago — the Marquesas — or to the Tuamotus, or even, if it blew faster than I suppose, as far as New Zealand. If that last guess is right, getting home will be easy. English or Maori, we'll always find someone to talk to. If, on the other hand, this coast belongs to some desert island in a Micronesian archipelago, perhaps we'll be able to see as much from the top of that cone that towers over the country — and then we'll set about settling here as if we were never going to leave!"

"Never!" cried the reporter. "You say 'never,' my dear Cyrus?"

"Better to assume the worst right away," answered the engineer, "and save only the best for a surprise."

"Well said!" Pencroff replied. "And let's hope too that this island, if it is one, won't lie right off the shipping lanes! That would be bad luck indeed!"

"We won't know where we stand until we've climbed the mountain, and that comes before anything else," answered the engineer.

"But tomorrow, Mr. Cyrus," asked Harbert, "will you be up to the strain of the climb?"

"I hope so," answered the engineer, "but on condition that Master Pencroff and you, my boy, prove to be clever and skillful hunters."

"Mr. Cyrus," answered the sailor, "since you mention game — if I were as sure of being able to roast it when I got back as I am of bringing it back..."

"Bring it back anyway, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith.

So it was agreed that the engineer and the reporter would spend the day at the Chimneys, so as to examine the shoreline and the plateau above. Meanwhile Nab, Harbert and the sailor would go back to the forest, renew the supply of wood, and lay hands on any creature with feathers or fur that came within their reach.

So they set off at about ten o'clock in the morning, Harbert confident, Nab cheerful, Pencroff muttering to himself:

"If I find a fire at home when I get back, it'll be because the thunder came in person to light it!"

All three climbed back up the bank, and when they reached the bend in the river, the sailor stopped and said to his two companions:

"Do we start as hunters or as woodcutters?"

"Hunters," answered Harbert. "Look, Top's already on the scent."

"Then let's hunt," the sailor went on. "We'll come back here afterward and lay in our wood."

That said, Harbert, Nab and Pencroff tore three sticks from the trunk of a young fir and followed Top, who was bounding through the tall grass.

This time, instead of following the course of the river, the hunters plunged more directly into the very heart of the forest. The trees were the same as before, most of them belonging to the pine family. In certain places, where they grew less crowded and stood apart in clumps, these pines reached a great size, and their growth seemed to show that this country lay at a higher latitude than the engineer supposed. A few clearings, bristling with stumps worn away by time, were covered with dead wood, and so made inexhaustible stores of fuel. Then, past the clearing, the undergrowth closed in again and became almost impossible to get through.

Finding the way among these thickets of trees, with no beaten path, was rather difficult. So every now and then the sailor marked his route by breaking a few branches in a way that would be easy to recognize. But perhaps he had been wrong not to go up along the stream, as he and Harbert had done on their first excursion, for after an hour's walk not a single head of game had shown itself. Top, running under the low branches, startled only birds that no one could get near. Even the couroucous were nowhere to be seen, and it was likely that the sailor would be forced to go back to that marshy part of the forest where he had made his lucky grouse fishing.

"Hey, Pencroff," said Nab in a slightly sarcastic tone, "if that's all the game you promised to bring back to my master, it won't take much of a fire to roast it!"

"Patience, Nab," answered the sailor. "It won't be game we're short of on the way back!"

"So you don't have faith in Mr. Smith?"

"I do."

"But you don't believe he'll make a fire?"

"I'll believe it when the wood's blazing in the hearth."

"It will blaze, because my master said so!"

"We'll see!"

The sun, meanwhile, had not yet reached the highest point of its course above the horizon. So the exploring went on, and it was usefully marked by Harbert's discovery of a tree whose fruit could be eaten. It was the stone pine, which produces an excellent nut, much prized in the temperate regions of America and Europe. These nuts were perfectly ripe, and Harbert pointed them out to his two companions, who feasted on them.

"Well," said Pencroff, "seaweed for bread, raw mussels for meat, and nuts for dessert — that's the dinner of people who haven't got a single match left in their pockets, all right!"

"We mustn't complain," answered Harbert.

"I'm not complaining, my boy," answered Pencroff. "I'm only saying again that meat is a little too scarce in this kind of meal!"

"Top's seen something!..." cried Nab, and he ran toward a thicket into which the dog had disappeared, barking. Mixed with Top's barking were some peculiar grunts.

The sailor and Harbert had followed Nab. If there was game in there, this was not the moment to argue about how they could cook it, but about how they could catch it.

The hunters had hardly entered the thicket when they saw Top struggling with an animal, which he was holding by one ear. This four-footed beast was a kind of pig about two and a half feet long, blackish brown but lighter on the belly, with hair that was coarse and fairly thin. Its toes, pressed hard against the ground just then, seemed to be joined by webs of skin.

Harbert thought he recognized the animal as a capybara — that is, one of the largest members of the order of rodents.

The capybara, however, was not fighting the dog. It was stupidly rolling its big eyes, which sat deep in a thick layer of fat. Perhaps it was seeing men for the first time.

Nab, meanwhile, had tightened his grip on his stick and was about to knock the rodent senseless, when it tore itself free of Top's teeth — Top kept only a scrap of its ear — let out a mighty grunt, rushed at Harbert, half knocked him over, and vanished into the woods.

"Ah, the scoundrel!" cried Pencroff.

At once all three had dashed off on Top's trail, and just as they were about to catch up with him, the animal disappeared under the water of a large pond, shaded by tall pines centuries old.

Nab, Harbert and Pencroff had stopped and stood motionless. Top had thrown himself into the water, but the capybara, hidden at the bottom of the pond, did not show itself again.

"Let's wait," said the boy, "because it'll soon come up to the surface to breathe."

"Won't it drown?" asked Nab.

"No," answered Harbert, "since it has webbed feet and it's almost an amphibian. But let's watch for it."

Top had stayed in the water, swimming. Pencroff and his two companions each took up a position at a different point on the bank, to cut off every escape for the capybara, which the dog was looking for as he swam about the surface of the pond.

Harbert was not mistaken. After a few minutes the animal came back up above the water. With one bound Top was on it, and kept it from diving again. A moment later the capybara, dragged to the bank, was knocked dead with a blow of Nab's stick.

"Hurrah!" cried Pencroff, who liked to use that cry of triumph. "Just one glowing coal, and this rodent will be gnawed right down to the bone!"

Pencroff hoisted the capybara onto his shoulder, and judging by the height of the sun that it must be about two o'clock, he gave the signal to head back.

Top's instinct was a great help to the hunters, who, thanks to the intelligent animal, were able to find the way they had already come. Half an hour later they reached the bend in the river.

Just as he had the first time, Pencroff quickly put together a timber raft — though, with no fire, it seemed a useless job to him — and, with the raft following the current, they made their way back toward the Chimneys.

But the sailor was not fifty paces from them when he stopped, let out another tremendous hurrah, and, stretching his hand toward the corner of the cliff, shouted:

"Harbert! Nab! Look!"

Smoke was escaping and swirling up above the rocks!

Chapter 10: The Engineer's Invention

An invention of the engineer's — The question that worries Cyrus Smith — Setting out for the mountain — The forest — Volcanic ground — The tragopans — The mouflons — The first plateau — Camp for the night — The summit of the cone

A few moments later the three hunters were standing before a crackling fire. Cyrus Smith and the reporter were there. Pencroff looked from one to the other without a word, his capybara in his hand.

"Well, yes, my good fellow," cried the reporter. "Fire, real fire, that's going to roast this magnificent game to perfection, and we'll be feasting on it before long!"

"But who lit it?" asked Pencroff.

"The sun!"

Gédéon Spilett's answer was exactly right. It was the sun that had supplied the heat Pencroff was marveling at. The sailor could not believe his eyes, and he was so dumbfounded that it did not even occur to him to question the engineer.

"So you had a lens, sir?" Harbert asked Cyrus Smith.

"No, my boy," he answered, "but I made one."

And he showed them the device that had served him as a lens. It was simply the two glasses he had taken off the reporter's watch and his own. He had filled the space between them with water and sealed their edges together with a little clay, and so he had made himself a real lens. Focusing the sun's rays on a bit of very dry moss, it had set the moss burning.

The sailor studied the device, then looked at the engineer without saying a word. But his look said a great deal! If Cyrus Smith was not a god to him, he was certainly more than a man. At last Pencroff found his voice again, and he cried:

"Write that down, Mr. Spilett, write that down on your paper!"

"It's written down," answered the reporter.

Then, with Nab's help, the sailor set up the spit, and the capybara, properly cleaned, was soon roasting like an ordinary suckling pig in front of a bright, crackling flame.

The Chimneys had become livable again, not only because the passages were warming up from the fire, but because the partitions of stones and sand had been rebuilt.

As you can see, the engineer and his companion had made good use of the day. Cyrus Smith had almost entirely recovered his strength, and he had tested it by climbing to the plateau above. From there his eye, trained to judge heights and distances, had rested for a long time on the cone whose peak he meant to reach the next day. The mountain, about six miles off to the northwest, seemed to him to stand three thousand five hundred feet above sea level. So an observer posted on its summit would be able to sweep the horizon for a radius of at least fifty miles. It was therefore likely that Cyrus Smith would easily settle the question of "continent or island," which he put, not without reason, ahead of every other.

They had a proper supper. The capybara meat was declared excellent. The sargassum and the stone-pine nuts rounded out the meal, during which the engineer said little. He was absorbed in the next day's plans.

Once or twice Pencroff put forward a few ideas about what ought to be done, but Cyrus Smith, who was clearly a methodical mind, merely shook his head.

"Tomorrow," he kept saying, "we'll know where we stand, and we'll act accordingly."

When the meal was over, fresh armfuls of wood were thrown on the fire, and the occupants of the Chimneys, faithful Top included, fell into a deep sleep. Nothing disturbed that peaceful night, and the next morning, March 29, they woke fresh and rested, ready to set out on the expedition that was to decide their fate.

Everything was ready for the start. What was left of the capybara could feed Cyrus Smith and his companions for another twenty-four hours. Besides, they fully expected to find more food along the way. Since the glasses had been put back on the engineer's and the reporter's watches, Pencroff burned a little more of the linen that was to serve as tinder. As for flint, there would be no shortage of it in ground of volcanic origin like this.

It was half past seven in the morning when the explorers, armed with sticks, left the Chimneys. On Pencroff's advice, it seemed best to take the road they had already traveled through the forest, even if they came back by another way. It was also the most direct route to the mountain. So they turned the southern corner and followed the left bank of the river, leaving it at the point where it bent toward the southwest. They found the path they had already beaten under the evergreens, and at nine o'clock Cyrus Smith and his companions reached the western edge of the forest.
