The ground, fairly level until then — marshy at first, then dry and sandy — now showed a gentle slope, rising from the shore toward the interior of the country. A few very shy animals had been glimpsed among the tall trees. Top was quick to flush them, but his master called him back at once, for this was no time to chase them. Later on, they would see. The engineer was not a man to be distracted from his one fixed idea. In fact, you would not have been wrong to say that he was not looking at the country at all, neither at its lay of the land nor at what grew and lived there. His only goal was the mountain he meant to climb, and he went straight for it.

At ten o'clock they halted for a few minutes. On leaving the forest, they had seen the whole system of the mountains spread before them. The mountain was made of two cones. The first, cut off flat at a height of about two thousand five hundred feet, was propped up by oddly shaped buttresses of rock, which seemed to branch out like the talons of an immense claw clamped down on the ground. Between these spurs lay as many narrow valleys, bristling with trees, whose last clumps climbed all the way up to the flat top of the first cone. The vegetation, however, seemed thinner on the side of the mountain that faced northeast, and there they could make out fairly deep streaks that must have been lava flows.

On the first cone sat a second one, slightly rounded at its top and tilted a little to one side. It looked like a huge round hat cocked over one ear. It seemed to be made of bare earth, pierced in many places by reddish rocks.

It was the summit of this second cone that they needed to reach, and the ridge of the spurs ought to offer the best route to it.

"We're on volcanic ground," Cyrus Smith had said, and his companions, following him, began to climb little by little along the back of one of the spurs. It wound its way up in a snaking line, which made it easier going, and ended at the first plateau.

The ground swelled in many places into lumps and blisters; volcanic forces had plainly thrown it into convulsions. Here and there lay stray boulders, plentiful fragments of basalt, pumice stones, and obsidian. In isolated clumps rose the same kind of conifers that, a few hundred feet lower, at the bottom of the narrow gorges, formed thick groves almost impenetrable to the sun.

During this first part of the climb, on the lower slopes, Harbert pointed out tracks that showed large animals had passed by recently — wild beasts, or something else.

"Those creatures may not hand their territory over to us without a fight," said Pencroff.

"Well," answered the reporter, who had already hunted tigers in India and lions in Africa, "we'll see about getting rid of them. But in the meantime, let's keep on our guard!"

All the while they were climbing, little by little. The way was long, made longer by detours and by obstacles that could not be crossed head-on. Sometimes, too, the ground suddenly dropped away, and they found themselves at the edge of deep crevasses that had to be gone around. Retracing their steps like this to find some passable track cost them time and effort. At noon, when the little band stopped for lunch at the foot of a large clump of firs, beside a small stream that went tumbling off in a cascade, they were still only halfway to the first plateau. From then on it seemed unlikely they would reach it before nightfall.

From that spot the sea horizon spread out more widely. But on the right their view was stopped by the sharp headland to the southeast, and they could not tell whether the coast turned back abruptly to join some land lying behind it. To the left, their line of sight gained a few miles to the north. But from the northwest onward, from where the explorers stood, it was cut off sharply by the ridge of a strangely shaped spur, which formed a kind of mighty buttress for the central cone. So they still could not guess the answer to the question Cyrus Smith wanted to settle.

At one o'clock they took up the climb again. They had to bear off toward the southwest and push once more into fairly thick undergrowth. There, under cover of the trees, several pairs of game birds of the pheasant family fluttered about. They were "tragopans," decorated with a fleshy wattle hanging down over the throat and with two thin, round horns set just behind the eyes. Among these pairs, each bird about the size of a rooster, the female was brown all over, while the male was resplendent in red plumage sprinkled with little white teardrops. Gédéon Spilett killed one of these tragopans with a stone thrown hard and true, and Pencroff, made ravenous by the open air, eyed it with more than a little longing.

After leaving this thicket, the climbers boosted one another up on their shoulders and scaled a very steep bank for a hundred feet. They reached a higher level, with few trees, where the ground began to look volcanic. Now they had to work back toward the east, zigzagging to make the slopes easier, for they had become very steep, and each of them had to choose carefully where he put his foot. Nab and Harbert led the way and Pencroff brought up the rear, with Cyrus and the reporter between them. The animals that lived on these heights — and there was no lack of tracks — had to belong to those sure-footed, nimble-backed breeds, the chamois or their Pyrenean cousins the izards. They saw a few of them, but that was not the name Pencroff gave them, for at one point he shouted:

"Sheep!"

Everyone had stopped fifty paces from half a dozen large animals with strong horns that curved back and flattened toward the tips, and with a woolly fleece hidden under long, silky, tawny hair.

These were not ordinary sheep, but a species widely found in the mountain regions of the temperate zones, which Harbert named as mouflons.

"Do they have legs of lamb and chops?" asked the sailor.

"Yes," answered Harbert.

"Well, then, they're sheep!" said Pencroff.

The animals stood motionless among the fragments of basalt and stared in astonishment, as though they were seeing two-legged humans for the first time. Then, their fear suddenly awakened, they vanished, bounding away over the rocks.

"So long!" Pencroff called after them, in a tone so comical that Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Harbert and Nab could not help laughing.

The climb went on. On some of the slopes they often noticed traces of lava, very oddly streaked. Little solfataras — vents that breathe out sulfurous steam — sometimes cut across the route the climbers were following, and they had to skirt around the edges. In a few places the sulfur had settled out as crystal crusts, amid the materials that usually come before an outpouring of lava: pozzolana, volcanic grit with irregular grains, heavily roasted, and whitish ash made of countless tiny crystals of feldspar.

As they drew near the first plateau, formed where the lower cone was cut off flat, the climb became very hard indeed. By about four o'clock they had passed the highest belt of trees. All that remained, here and there, were a few twisted, scrawny pines, which must have had a tough life to hold out against the great winds off the sea at that height. Luckily for the engineer and his companions, the weather was fine and the air still, for a strong breeze at an altitude of three thousand feet would have hampered their movements. The clearness of the air let them feel the purity of the sky overhead. A perfect calm reigned around them. They could no longer see the sun, which was now hidden by the vast screen of the upper cone. That screen blocked out the western half of the horizon, and its enormous shadow, stretching all the way to the shore, grew longer as the radiant sun sank on its daily course. A few vapors, more mist than cloud, were beginning to appear in the east, and the sun's rays tinted them with every color of the spectrum.

Only five hundred feet now separated the explorers from the plateau they wanted to reach to make camp for the night. But those five hundred feet grew into more than two miles because of the zigzags they had to make. The ground was practically giving way under their feet. The slopes were often so steep that they slid on the lava flows wherever the grooves, worn smooth by the weather, did not give them enough of a foothold. Evening was gradually coming on, and it was nearly night when Cyrus Smith and his companions, worn out by a seven-hour climb, arrived on the plateau of the first cone.

Now the business was to set up camp and get their strength back, first by eating supper and then by sleeping. This second level of the mountain rose from a base of rocks, and among them they easily found a sheltered spot. Fuel was not plentiful. Still, they could make a fire from the mosses and dry brush that bristled over parts of the plateau. While the sailor built his hearth on stones he set out for the purpose, Nab and Harbert busied themselves gathering fuel for it. They soon came back with their loads of brush. The flint and steel were struck, the burnt linen caught the sparks, and under Nab's breath a crackling fire grew up within a few moments in the shelter of the rocks.

This fire was meant only to fight off the rather cold night air. It was not used to cook the pheasant, which Nab was saving for the next day. The rest of the capybara and a few dozen stone-pine nuts made up the supper. It was not yet half past six, and everything was finished.

Cyrus Smith then had the idea of exploring, in the half-darkness, the wide circular shelf that held up the upper cone of the mountain. Before he took any rest, he wanted to know whether the base of that cone could be walked around, in case its sides proved too steep to climb all the way to the top. The question weighed on his mind, because it was possible that on the side toward which the hat tilted — that is, toward the north — the plateau would be impassable. And if the summit could not be reached on the one hand, and the base of the cone could not be circled on the other, there would be no way to examine the western part of the country, and the purpose of the climb would partly fail.

So the engineer, paying no attention to how tired he was, left Pencroff and Nab to arrange the sleeping quarters and Gédéon Spilett to write up the day's events, and began to follow the circular rim of the plateau, heading north. Harbert went with him.

The night was fine and still, and the darkness was not yet deep. Cyrus Smith and the boy walked side by side without speaking. In some places the plateau opened out wide in front of them, and they passed easily. In others, blocked by fallen rock, it left only a narrow trail where two people could not walk abreast. After twenty minutes of walking, Cyrus Smith and Harbert even had to stop. From that point on, the slopes of the two cones ran together. There was no longer any shoulder to separate the two parts of the mountain. Going around it on slopes that tilted at nearly seventy degrees became impossible.

But if the engineer and the boy had to give up following a circular path, they were given, in exchange, the chance to climb the cone directly.

For in front of them a deep gash opened in the mass of the mountain. It was the broken-out mouth of the upper crater — its spout, if you like — through which the molten matter had poured out in the days when the volcano was still active. Hardened lava and crusted cinders formed a kind of natural staircase, with broad, well-marked steps, which ought to make the way to the summit easier.

One glance was enough for Cyrus Smith to see how things lay, and without hesitating, with the boy behind him, he plunged into the enormous crevice in the gathering darkness.

There were still a thousand feet to climb. Would the inner slopes of the crater be passable? They would soon find out. The engineer would keep on climbing as long as nothing stopped him. Fortunately, these slopes, long and winding, made a wide spiral, like the thread of a screw, around the inside of the volcano, and that helped them gain height.

As for the volcano itself, there could be no doubt that it was completely extinct. Not a wisp of smoke escaped from its sides. Not a flame showed in its deep hollows. Not a rumble, not a murmur, not a tremor came out of that dark well, which perhaps sank all the way down to the bowels of the earth. Even the air inside the crater carried no trace of sulfurous fumes. This was more than a volcano asleep. It was a volcano dead and gone.

Cyrus Smith's attempt was bound to succeed. Little by little, as he and Harbert climbed the inner walls, they saw the crater widen above their heads. The circle of sky framed by the rim of the cone grew noticeably wider. With almost every step that Cyrus Smith and Harbert took, new stars came into view. The magnificent constellations of that southern sky were blazing. At the zenith shone the splendid Antares, in Scorpius, with its pure brilliance, and not far from it Beta Centauri, which is believed to be the star nearest the Earth. Then, as the crater opened out, there appeared Fomalhaut, in the Southern Fish, and the Southern Triangle, and at last, almost at the south pole of the heavens, the glittering Southern Cross, which takes the place of the North Star in the southern hemisphere.

It was nearly eight o'clock when Cyrus Smith and Harbert set foot on the upper crest of the mountain, at the summit of the cone.

By then it was completely dark, and their eyes could not see more than two miles in any direction. Did the sea surround this unknown land, or was this land joined, to the west, to some continent of the Pacific? It was still impossible to tell. Toward the west, a band of cloud lying sharply drawn along the horizon deepened the darkness, and the eye could not make out whether sky and water met there in one unbroken circle.

But at one point on that horizon a faint glow suddenly appeared, sinking slowly as the cloud rose toward the zenith.

It was the thin crescent of the moon, already about to set. But its light was enough to draw the line of the horizon clearly, now that it stood free of the cloud, and the engineer saw the moon's trembling image reflected for an instant on a surface of water.

Cyrus Smith took the boy's hand, and in a grave voice:

"An island!" he said, just as the crescent moon went out in the waves.

Chapter 11: Lincoln Island

At the top of the cone — Inside the crater — Sea all around — No land in sight — The coast from a bird's-eye view — Rivers and mountains — Is the island inhabited? — Christening the bays, gulfs, capes, rivers and so on — Lincoln Island

Half an hour later Cyrus Smith and Harbert were back at the camp. The engineer told his companions only that the land where chance had thrown them was an island, and that they would decide what to do in the morning. Then everyone settled down to sleep as best he could, and in that hole in the basalt, two thousand five hundred feet above the level of the sea, on a peaceful night, "the islanders" slept deeply.

The next day, March 30, after a quick breakfast made entirely of the roast tragopan, the engineer wanted to climb back up to the summit of the volcano. He meant to take a careful look at the island where he and his friends were imprisoned — imprisoned for life, perhaps, if it lay a long way from any other land, or if it was off the track of the ships that visit the island groups of the Pacific Ocean. This time his companions went with him on the new exploration. They too wanted to see this island, which they were going to ask to supply their every need.

It must have been about seven o'clock in the morning when Cyrus Smith, Harbert, Pencroff, Gédéon Spilett and Nab left the camp. None of them seemed worried about the position he was in. No doubt they had faith in themselves; but it should be pointed out that this faith did not rest on the same ground in Cyrus Smith as in his companions. The engineer was confident because he felt able to wring from this wild nature everything that his companions' lives and his own would need. And they feared nothing precisely because Cyrus Smith was with them. The difference will be understood. Pencroff above all, ever since the business of the fire that had been lit again, would not have despaired for a single moment even if he had found himself on a bare rock, as long as the engineer was on that rock with him.

"Bah!" he said. "We got out of Richmond without permission from the authorities! It would be the very devil if we couldn't manage, one of these days, to get away from a place where nobody's going to stop us!"

Cyrus Smith took the same path as the day before. They went around the cone by way of the plateau that formed a kind of shoulder on the mountain, as far as the mouth of the enormous crevice. The weather was magnificent. The sun was climbing in a clear sky, and its rays covered the whole eastern side of the mountain.

They reached the crater. It was just as the engineer had made it out in the dark: a vast funnel that widened steadily as it rose, to a height of a thousand feet above the plateau. Below the crevice, broad, thick streams of old lava wound down the sides of the mountain, marking the road that the erupted matter had taken down to the lower valleys that cut across the northern part of the island.

The inside of the crater sloped at no more than thirty-five to forty degrees, and it offered neither difficulties nor obstacles to the climb. They could see traces of very ancient lava there, which had probably poured out over the top of the cone before the crevice in the side opened a new way for it.

As for the volcanic chimney that connected the layers deep underground with the crater, no one could judge its depth by eye, because it disappeared into darkness. But as for whether the volcano was completely extinct, there was no doubt about that.

Before eight o'clock Cyrus Smith and his companions were gathered at the top of the crater, on a cone-shaped swelling that bulged up from its northern rim.

"The sea! Sea everywhere!" they cried, as if their lips could not hold back the word that made islanders of them.

The sea indeed — the immense ring of water all around them! Perhaps, in climbing back to the top of the cone, Cyrus Smith had hoped to discover some coast, some nearby island, that he had not been able to make out the evening before in the dark. But nothing appeared, all the way to the edge of the horizon — that is, for more than fifty miles in every direction. No land in sight. Not a sail. All that immensity was empty, and the island sat at the center of a circle that seemed to have no end.

For several minutes the engineer and his companions, silent and motionless, swept their eyes over every point of the ocean. They searched it to its farthest limits. But Pencroff, who had such marvelous powers of sight, saw nothing — and certainly, if any land had risen above the horizon, even if it had shown only as a faint wisp of haze, the sailor would have recognized it beyond any doubt, for nature had set a pair of real telescopes under those eyebrows of his!

From the ocean their eyes turned back to the island, which they looked down on in its entirety, and the first question was asked by Gédéon Spilett, in these words:

"How big can this island be?"

Truly, it did not look very large in the middle of that immense ocean.

Cyrus Smith thought for a few moments. He studied the outline of the island carefully, taking into account the height at which he stood. Then:

"My friends," he said, "I don't think I'm wrong in saying that the island's coastline runs to more than a hundred miles."

"And so its area...?"

"That's hard to judge," the engineer replied, "because the coast is too irregularly cut up."

If Cyrus Smith's estimate was right, the island was very nearly the size of Malta or Zante in the Mediterranean. But it was at once much more irregular and less rich in capes, headlands, points, bays, coves and inlets. Its shape, which was truly strange, caught the eye, and when Gédéon Spilett, at the engineer's suggestion, had sketched its outline, they found that it looked like some fantastic animal — a sort of monstrous pteropod, one of those sea creatures that swim on winglike flaps, lying asleep on the surface of the Pacific.

Here, in fact, is the exact shape of the island, which it is important to describe. The reporter at once drew up a map of it, accurate enough for their needs.

The eastern part of the coast — the part where the castaways had come ashore — was cut back in a broad curve and edged a vast bay, which ended to the southeast in a sharp cape that a point of land had hidden from Pencroff on his first exploration. To the northeast two more capes closed off the bay, and between them ran a narrow gulf that looked like the half-open jaws of some fearsome shark.

From northeast to northwest the coast curved around like the flattened skull of a wild beast, then rose again into a sort of hump that gave no very definite outline to that part of the island, at whose center stood the volcanic mountain.

From there the shore ran fairly evenly north and south. Two-thirds of the way along this stretch it was cut by a narrow inlet, and from that point it ended in a long tail, like the tail of a gigantic alligator.

This tail formed a true peninsula, which stretched more than thirty miles out to sea, counting from the southeast cape of the island already mentioned. It curved around to form a wide-open bay, broadly exposed to the sea, which the lower coast of this so strangely shaped land traced out.

At its narrowest — that is, between the Chimneys and the inlet seen on the west coast at the same latitude — the island measured only ten miles across. But its greatest length, from the jaws in the northeast to the tip of the tail in the southwest, was no less than thirty miles.

As for the interior, its general look was this. The whole southern part, from the mountain down to the shore, was thickly wooded; the northern part was dry and sandy. Between the volcano and the east coast, Cyrus Smith and his companions were quite surprised to see a lake framed by a border of green trees, which they had never suspected was there. Seen from that height, the lake seemed to be at the same level as the sea. But after thinking it over, the engineer explained to his companions that this little sheet of water must lie three hundred feet up, because the plateau that held it was simply a continuation of the one along the coast.

"So it's a freshwater lake?" asked Pencroff.

"It must be," replied the engineer, "because it has to be fed by the water that runs down off the mountain."

"I can see a little river flowing into it," said Harbert, pointing to a narrow stream whose source had to lie somewhere in the foothills to the west.

"So there is," Cyrus Smith replied. "And since that stream feeds the lake, there's probably an outlet somewhere on the side toward the sea, where the overflow escapes. We'll see about that on our way back."

This small, winding stream and the river they already knew made up the island's whole system of waters — at least as far as the explorers could see. Still, under the masses of trees that turned two-thirds of the island into one immense forest, other streams might well be running down to the sea. One even had to suppose so, the region looked so fertile and so rich in the most magnificent specimens of temperate-zone plant life. In the northern part, on the other hand, there was no sign of running water. There might be standing water in the marshy part to the northeast, but that was all. Altogether it was dunes, sand, and a very marked barrenness that stood out sharply against the richness of the soil over the greater part of the island.

The volcano did not stand in the middle of the island. On the contrary, it rose in the northwest region and seemed to mark the border between the two zones. To the southwest, south and southeast, the lower slopes of its foothills disappeared under masses of greenery. To the north, on the other hand, one could follow their branching ridges until they died away in the sandy plains. It was on this side, too, that in the days of eruptions the outpourings had forced their way through, and a broad causeway of lava stretched all the way to the narrow jaws that formed the gulf in the northeast.

Cyrus Smith and his friends stayed an hour like this at the top of the mountain. The island spread out beneath them like a relief map in its different colors: green for the forests, yellow for the sands, blue for the waters. They took it in as a whole. Only the ground hidden under the immense greenery, the floors of the shady valleys, and the insides of the narrow gorges cut into the foot of the volcano escaped their search.

There remained one serious question to settle, a question that was bound to weigh heavily on the castaways' future.

Was the island inhabited?

It was the reporter who asked it, and after the careful examination they had just made of every region of the island, it seemed that the answer could already be no.

Nowhere could they see the work of a human hand. Not a cluster of huts, not a single lonely cabin, not a fishing station on the shore. No smoke rose into the air to betray the presence of man. It was true that some thirty miles separated the watchers from the farthest points — from that tail stretching out to the southwest — and it would have been difficult, even for Pencroff's eyes, to make out a dwelling there. Nor could they lift the curtain of greenery that covered three-quarters of the island and see whether or not it sheltered some village. But as a rule, islanders who live on these small specks of land risen out of the Pacific tend to live along the shore, and the shore seemed to be completely deserted.

Until they had explored it more fully, then, they could take it that the island was uninhabited.

But was it visited, at least from time to time, by the natives of neighboring islands? That question was hard to answer. No land appeared within about fifty miles. But fifty miles can easily be crossed, whether by Malay proas or by the great canoes of the Polynesians. So everything depended on where the island lay — on whether it was isolated in the Pacific or close to some group of islands. Would Cyrus Smith, with no instruments, manage later on to work out its position in latitude and longitude? That would be difficult. While they were in doubt, it was only sensible to take certain precautions against a possible landing by natives from nearby.

The exploration of the island was finished. Its shape had been worked out, its heights measured, its size calculated, its rivers and mountains surveyed. The lie of the forests and the plains had been roughly set down on the reporter's map. All that remained was to go back down the slopes of the mountain and to explore the land from three points of view: its mineral, its plant, and its animal resources.

But before giving his companions the signal to leave, Cyrus Smith spoke to them in his calm, grave voice.

"Here, my friends, is the narrow corner of the earth where the hand of the Almighty has thrown us. This is where we're going to live — for a long time, perhaps. Perhaps, too, some unexpected help will reach us, if a ship happens to pass by chance... I say by chance, because this island is of little importance. It doesn't even offer a harbor where ships could put in, and I'm afraid it lies outside the routes ships usually follow — that is, too far south for the vessels that sail among the island groups of the Pacific, and too far north for those that round Cape Horn on their way to Australia. I don't want to hide anything about our situation from you..."

"And you're right, my dear Cyrus," the reporter replied quickly. "You're dealing with men. They trust you, and you can count on them. Isn't that so, my friends?"

"I'll obey you in everything, Mr. Cyrus," said Harbert, seizing the engineer's hand.

"My master — always and everywhere!" cried Nab.

"As for me," said the sailor, "may I lose my name if I ever shirk the work! And if you're willing, Mr. Smith, we'll make this island into a little America! We'll build towns on it, we'll lay railroads, we'll put up telegraphs, and one fine day, when it's well transformed, well fitted out, well civilized, we'll go and offer it to the government of the Union! Only I ask one thing."

"What's that?" asked the reporter.

"That we stop thinking of ourselves as castaways, and think of ourselves as colonists who've come here to colonize!"

Cyrus Smith could not help smiling, and the sailor's motion was adopted. Then he thanked his companions and added that he was counting on their energy and on the help of Heaven.

"Well then! Off to the Chimneys!" cried Pencroff.

"One moment, my friends," replied the engineer. "I think it would be a good idea to give a name to this island, and to the capes, the headlands and the rivers we can see in front of us."

"A very good idea," said the reporter. "It will make any directions we have to give or follow a lot simpler in the future."

"Right," the sailor went on. "It's already something to be able to say where you're going and where you've come from. At least it feels like you're somewhere."

"The Chimneys, for instance," said Harbert.

"Exactly!" replied Pencroff. "That name was handier already, and it came to me all by itself. Shall we keep the name of the Chimneys for our first camp, Mr. Cyrus?"

"Yes, Pencroff, since that's what you christened it."

"Good. As for the others, that'll be easy," the sailor went on, warming to it. "Let's give them names the way the Robinsons did in those stories Harbert's read me more than once: 'Providence Bay,' 'Sperm Whale Point,' 'Cape Disappointed Hope'...!"

"Or rather the names of Mr. Smith," replied Harbert, "and Mr. Spilett, and Nab...!"

"My name!" cried Nab, with a dazzling grin.

"Why not?" said Pencroff. "'Port Nab' would sound very well! And 'Cape Gédéon'..."

"I'd rather have names taken from our own country," replied the reporter, "names that would remind us of America."

"Yes, for the main ones," said Cyrus Smith then. "For the bays and the seas, I'm all for it. If we give this vast bay to the east the name Union Bay, for example, and this wide indentation to the south the name Washington Bay, and the mountain we're standing on the name Mount Franklin, and that lake spread out below us the name Lake Grant — nothing could be better, my friends. Those names will remind us of our country and of the great citizens who have honored it. But for the rivers, the gulfs, the capes and the headlands we can see from the top of this mountain, let's choose names that call up their particular shapes instead. They'll stick better in our minds, and they'll be more practical too. The shape of the island is strange enough that we won't have any trouble thinking up names that fit the picture. As for the streams we don't know yet, the different parts of the forest that we'll explore later, and the coves we discover from here on, we'll christen them as they come along. What do you think, my friends?"

The engineer's proposal was adopted unanimously by his companions. The island lay there before their eyes like an unfolded map, and all they had to do was put a name to each of its coves and points and each of its heights. Gédéon Spilett would write them down as they went, and the island's geography would be fixed once and for all.

First of all, the two bays and the mountain were named Union Bay, Washington Bay and Mount Franklin, as the engineer had proposed.

"Now," said the reporter, "for that peninsula that juts out from the southwest of the island, I propose the name Serpentine Peninsula, and for the curled-up tail at the end of it, Reptile End — because it really is a reptile's tail."

"Adopted," said the engineer.

"Now," said Harbert, "the other end of the island, that gulf that looks so oddly like a pair of open jaws — let's call it Shark Gulf."

"Well found!" cried Pencroff. "And we'll finish the picture by calling the two sides of the jaws Mandible Cape."

"But there are two capes," the reporter pointed out.

"Well then," replied Pencroff, "we'll have North Mandible Cape and South Mandible Cape."

"They're written down," replied Gédéon Spilett.

"That leaves the point at the southeast end of the island to name," said Pencroff.

"You mean the end of Union Bay?" replied Harbert.

"Claw Cape!" Nab cried at once. He too wanted to be godfather to some piece of his new domain.

And truly Nab had found an excellent name, for that cape really did look like the powerful claw of the fantastic animal that this so strangely outlined island represented.

Pencroff was delighted with the way things were going, and their imaginations, a little overexcited by now, soon produced the following:

For the river that supplied the colonists with drinking water, and near which the balloon had thrown them, the name of the Mercy — a real word of thanks to Providence.

For the islet where the castaways had first set foot, the name of Safety Islet.

For the plateau that crowned the high granite wall above the Chimneys, from which the eye could take in the whole vast bay, the name of Prospect Plateau.

And finally, for the whole mass of impenetrable woods that covered Serpentine Peninsula, the name of the Far West forests.

That completed the naming of the parts of the island that could be seen and were known. Later on it would be filled out as new discoveries were made.

As for the island's orientation, the engineer had worked it out roughly from the height and position of the sun, which put Union Bay and the whole of Prospect Plateau to the east. But the next day, by taking the exact times of sunrise and sunset, and noting the sun's position at the moment exactly halfway between the two, he meant to fix the island's true north precisely. For since the island lay in the Southern Hemisphere, the sun at the precise moment of its highest point in the sky passed to the north, not to the south, as it seems to do in its apparent motion for places in the Northern Hemisphere.

So everything was done, and the colonists had only to go back down Mount Franklin and return to the Chimneys, when Pencroff suddenly cried out:

"Well! What a pack of scatterbrains we are!"

"Why's that?" asked Gédéon Spilett, who had closed his notebook and was getting up to leave.

"What about our island? What! We forgot to christen it!"

Harbert was about to propose giving it the engineer's name, and all his companions would have applauded, when Cyrus Smith said simply:

"Let's name it after a great citizen, my friends, the man who is fighting right now to defend the unity of the American republic! Let's call it Lincoln Island!"

Three hurrahs were the answer to the engineer's proposal.

And that evening, before they fell asleep, the new colonists talked about their faraway country. They spoke of the terrible war that was soaking it in blood. They could not doubt that the South would soon be beaten, and that the cause of the North, the cause of justice, would triumph — thanks to Grant, thanks to Lincoln!

Now, this was March 30, 1865, and they little knew that sixteen days later a dreadful crime would be committed in Washington, and that on Good Friday Abraham Lincoln would fall to the bullet of a fanatic.

Chapter 12: Setting the Watches

Setting the watches — Pencroff is satisfied — A suspicious smoke — The course of Red Creek — The plants of Lincoln Island — The animals — Mountain pheasants — The kangaroo chase — The agouti — Lake Grant — Back to the Chimneys

The colonists of Lincoln Island took one last look around them. They walked the circuit of the crater along its narrow rim, and half an hour later they were back down on the first plateau, at the place where they had camped for the night.

Pencroff decided it was time for lunch, and that brought up the question of setting the two watches, Cyrus Smith's and the reporter's.

Gédéon Spilett's watch, as we know, had been spared by the seawater, since the reporter had been thrown up on the sand at the very start, out of reach of the waves. It was an excellently made instrument, a true pocket chronometer, and Gédéon Spilett had never once forgotten to wind it carefully every day.

The engineer's watch, on the other hand, had of course stopped during the time Cyrus Smith had spent in the dunes.

So the engineer wound it, and, judging from the height of the sun that it must be about nine o'clock in the morning, he set his watch to that hour.

Gédéon Spilett was about to do the same when the engineer stopped him with a hand and said:

"No, my dear Spilett, wait. You've kept Richmond time, haven't you?"

"Yes, Cyrus."

"So your watch is set to the meridian of that city — a meridian that's very nearly the same as Washington's?"

"Of course."

"Well, then, keep it that way. Just wind it very carefully every day, but don't touch the hands. It may be useful to us."

"What good will that do?" thought the sailor.

They ate, and ate so well that the store of game and almonds was completely used up. But Pencroff was not the least bit worried. They would stock up again along the way. Top, whose share had been a very meager one, would surely find some new game under cover of the thickets. Besides, the sailor was thinking of simply asking the engineer to make some gunpowder and one or two hunting guns, and he imagined that this would present no difficulty at all.

As they left the plateau, Cyrus Smith proposed to his companions that they take a new route back to the Chimneys. He wanted to get a look at Lake Grant, so magnificently framed by its border of trees. So they followed the crest of one of the spurs of the mountain, between which the creek that fed the lake probably had its source. As they talked, the colonists were already using nothing but the names they had just chosen, and that made it remarkably easier to share their ideas. Harbert and Pencroff — the one young, the other a bit of a child himself — were delighted with them, and as they walked the sailor said:

"Ha! Harbert! Look how well it works! We can't possibly get lost now, my boy, because whether we take the road by Lake Grant or cut through the Far West forests to the Mercy, we're bound to come out on Prospect Plateau, and so at Union Bay!"

It had been agreed that the colonists, without marching in a tight group, would not stray too far from one another. It was quite certain that some dangerous animals lived in the island's thick forests, and it was wise to stay on guard. Most of the time Pencroff, Harbert, and Nab walked in front, with Top ahead of them nosing into every corner. The reporter and the engineer went along together: Gédéon Spilett ready to note down any incident, the engineer silent most of the time, stepping off his path only to pick up now one thing, now another — some mineral or plant substance — which he put in his pocket without a word of comment.

"What the devil does he keep picking up?" Pencroff muttered. "I can look all I like, and I don't see a thing worth bending over for!"

Toward ten o'clock the little band was coming down the last slopes of Mount Franklin. So far the ground was dotted only with bushes and a few scattered trees. They were walking on yellowish, scorched earth, which formed a plain about a mile long in front of the edge of the woods. Big blocks of basalt lay strewn across the plain, which was very rough and broken in places — basalt of the kind that, according to Bischof's experiments, needed three hundred and fifty million years to cool. Still, there was no trace of lava, which had poured out mostly down the northern slopes.

Cyrus Smith expected, then, to reach the course of the creek without incident. By his reckoning it ought to wind along under the trees at the edge of the plain. Just then he saw Harbert running back in a hurry, while Nab and the sailor ducked out of sight behind the rocks.

"What is it, my boy?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"Smoke," answered Harbert. "We saw smoke rising between the rocks, a hundred paces from us."

"Men, here?" exclaimed the reporter.

"Let's not show ourselves until we know who we're dealing with," answered Cyrus Smith. "If there are natives on this island, I'd rather fear them than hope for them. Where's Top?"

"Top's up ahead."

"And he isn't barking?"

"No."

"That's odd. All the same, let's try to call him back."

In a few moments the engineer, Gédéon Spilett, and Harbert had joined their two companions, and like them they hid behind some broken chunks of basalt.

From there they could see, very clearly, a column of smoke swirling as it rose into the air — smoke of a very distinctive yellowish color.

Top, called back by a soft whistle from his master, returned, and his master, signaling to his companions to wait for him, slipped off between the rocks.

The colonists waited without moving, a little anxious to learn the result of this scouting, when a call from Cyrus Smith brought them running. They joined him at once, and the first thing that struck them was the unpleasant smell that filled the air.

That smell, easy to recognize, had been enough to tell the engineer what the smoke was — the smoke that must have worried him at first, and not without reason.

"This fire," he said, "or rather this smoke, is nature's doing and nobody else's. It's nothing but a sulfur spring, which will let us give our sore throats a proper treatment."

"Fine!" cried Pencroff. "What a shame I haven't got a cold!"

The colonists then made their way toward the spot the smoke was coming from. There they found a sodium-sulfur spring, flowing quite abundantly between the rocks. Its waters, once they had absorbed oxygen from the air, gave off a strong smell of hydrogen sulfide — the rotten-egg gas.

Cyrus Smith dipped his hand in and found the water oily to the touch. He tasted it and judged that it had a slightly sweetish flavor. As for its temperature, he put it at ninety-five degrees Fahrenheit. And when Harbert asked him what he based this estimate on, he said:

"Quite simply, my boy, on the fact that when I put my hand into this water, I felt no sensation of cold or of heat. So it's at the same temperature as the human body, which is about ninety-five degrees."

Then, since the sulfur spring offered nothing they could use for the moment, the colonists headed for the dense edge of the forest, which began a few hundred paces away.

There, just as they had guessed, the stream ran its lively, clear waters between high banks of red earth, whose color showed the presence of iron oxide. That color at once gave the stream its name: Red Creek.

It was really only a wide brook, deep and clear, formed by the waters coming off the mountain. Half river, half torrent — here flowing quietly over the sand, there roaring over the tops of rocks or plunging down in a cascade — it ran toward the lake for a mile and a half, varying between thirty and forty feet wide. Its water was fresh, which suggested that the lake's water must be fresh too. That was a lucky thing, in case they found on its shores a better place to live than the Chimneys.

As for the trees that shaded the banks of the creek a few hundred feet downstream, most of them belonged to species that are plentiful in the temperate zone of Australia or Tasmania, and no longer to the conifers that bristled over the part of the island already explored, a few miles from Prospect Plateau. At this time of year — the beginning of April, which in this hemisphere corresponds to October, that is, to the start of autumn — they had not yet lost their leaves. Most of them were casuarinas and eucalyptus trees, some of which would yield, the following spring, a sugary manna just like the manna of the East. Clumps of Australian cedars rose here and there in the clearings, which were covered in the tall grass known as "tussock" in New Holland, as Australia was then called. But the coconut palm, so plentiful in the archipelagos of the Pacific, seemed to be missing from the island, whose latitude was doubtless too high.

"What a pity!" said Harbert. "Such a useful tree, with such wonderful nuts!"

As for birds, they swarmed among the rather sparse branches of the eucalyptus and the casuarinas, which left them plenty of room to spread their wings. Black, white, and gray cockatoos; parrots and parakeets in plumage shaded with every color; "kings," a brilliant green and crowned with red; blue lories; "blue mountains" — they seemed to be seen only through a prism, and they fluttered about in a deafening chatter.

All of a sudden a strange concert of clashing voices rang out from the middle of a thicket. One after another, the colonists heard birdsong, the cries of four-footed animals, and a sort of clicking of the tongue that they might have thought came from the lips of a native. Nab and Harbert had rushed toward the bush, forgetting the most basic rules of caution. Very luckily there was no dangerous wild beast there, and no hostile native either — only half a dozen of those mocking, singing birds which they recognized as "mountain pheasants." A few well-aimed blows with a stick brought the imitation show to an end, and provided an excellent piece of game for that evening's dinner.

Harbert also pointed out some magnificent pigeons with bronze-colored wings, some topped with a superb crest, others draped in green like their cousins at Port Macquarie in Australia. But it was impossible to get at them, any more than at the crows and magpies that flew off in flocks. A single shot of birdshot would have brought down these birds by the dozen, but the hunters were still reduced to stones for throwing weapons and sticks for hand weapons, and those primitive tools fell a long way short.

Just how far short became even clearer when a troop of four-footed animals went bounding off over the thickets — hopping, leaping, making jumps of thirty feet, regular flying mammals — so nimbly and so high that you might have thought they were jumping from tree to tree like squirrels.

"Kangaroos!" cried Harbert.

"And can you eat them?" replied Pencroff.

"Stewed," answered the reporter, "they're as good as the finest venison!..."

Gédéon Spilett had not finished that exciting sentence before the sailor, followed by Nab and Harbert, was off on the kangaroos' trail. Cyrus Smith called them back, in vain. But it was in vain, too, that the hunters were going to chase this springy game, which bounced along like a rubber ball. After five minutes of running they were out of breath, and the troop was vanishing into the brush. Top had had no more luck than his masters.

"Mr. Cyrus," said Pencroff, once the engineer and the reporter had caught up with him, "Mr. Cyrus, you can see we absolutely have to make guns. Is that going to be possible?"

"Perhaps," the engineer answered. "But we'll start by making bows and arrows, and I have no doubt you'll get to be as skillful with them as the Australian hunters."

"Bows and arrows!" said Pencroff, with a scornful face. "That's for children!"

"Don't be so proud, friend Pencroff," the reporter answered. "For centuries bows and arrows were enough to drench the world in blood. Gunpowder only dates from yesterday, and war is as old as the human race — unfortunately!"

"Upon my word, that's true, Mr. Spilett," replied the sailor, "and I always talk too fast. You'll have to forgive me!"

Meanwhile Harbert, wrapped up in his favorite science, natural history, came back to the kangaroos.

"Anyway," he said, "those were the hardest kind to catch. They were giants with long gray fur. But if I'm not mistaken there are also black kangaroos and red kangaroos, rock kangaroos, and rat kangaroos, which are easier to get hold of. People count about a dozen species..."

"Harbert," the sailor replied solemnly, "as far as I'm concerned there's only one species of kangaroo — the kangaroo-on-a-spit — and that's exactly the one we'll be missing tonight!"

Nobody could help laughing at Master Pencroff's new system of classification. The good sailor made no secret of his regret at being reduced to singing pheasants for dinner. But fortune was about to smile on him once again.

Top, in fact, knew very well that his own interests were at stake, and he went ferreting about everywhere with an instinct sharpened by a ferocious appetite. It was even likely that if any game fell into his jaws there would not be much of it left for the hunters, and that Top was hunting on his own account just then. But Nab was keeping an eye on him, and a good thing too.

Toward three o'clock the dog disappeared into the brushwood, and soon some low growls told them that he was grappling with some animal.

Nab dashed in, and sure enough he found Top greedily devouring a four-footed creature which ten seconds later it would have been impossible to identify inside Top's stomach. But very luckily the dog had come upon a whole nest of them. He had made a triple catch, and two other rodents — for the animals in question belonged to that order — lay strangled on the ground.

So Nab came back in triumph, holding one of the rodents in each hand. They were bigger than a hare. Their yellow coats were mixed with greenish spots, and their tails were only stubs.

Citizens of the Union could not hesitate over the proper name for these rodents. They were "maras," a kind of agouti, a little bigger than their relatives in the tropical countries — true American rabbits, with long ears, and with jaws armed on each side with five molars, which is exactly what sets them apart from the agoutis.

"Hurrah!" cried Pencroff. "The roast has arrived! And now we can go home!"

The march, interrupted for a moment, began again. Red Creek still rolled its clear waters along under a vault of casuarinas, banksias, and gigantic gum trees. Superb lily plants rose as high as twenty feet. Other tree-like species, unknown to the young naturalist, leaned out over the stream, which they could hear murmuring beneath these green arbors.

Meanwhile the stream was growing noticeably wider, and Cyrus Smith was inclined to think they would soon reach its mouth. And indeed, as they came out of a thick stand of fine trees, there it was all at once.

The explorers had arrived on the western shore of Lake Grant. The place was well worth looking at. This sheet of water, about seven miles around and covering two hundred and fifty acres, lay in a border of many kinds of trees. To the east, through a curtain of greenery lifted here and there as if to frame a picture, a sparkling horizon of sea appeared. To the north the lake traced a gently curving inward line, which contrasted with the sharp outline of its lower tip. Large numbers of water birds frequented the shores of this little Ontario, whose namesake's "Thousand Islands" were represented by a single rock sticking up out of the water a few hundred feet from the southern shore. On it lived several pairs of kingfishers, all together, perched on some stone, grave and motionless, watching for fish to go by — then darting, diving with a shrill cry, and coming up again with their prey in their beaks. Elsewhere, on the shores and on the islet, strutted wild ducks, pelicans, moorhens, red-bills, and philedons, which are equipped with a tongue shaped like a paintbrush, and one or two specimens of those splendid lyrebirds whose tails spread out like the graceful arms of a lyre.

As for the water of the lake, it was fresh and clear, a little dark, and from certain bubblings, and from the rings that spread out and crossed one another on its surface, there could be no doubt that it was full of fish.

"It's really beautiful, this lake!" said Gédéon Spilett. "A person could live on its shores!"

"A person will!" answered Cyrus Smith.

The colonists, wanting now to go back to the Chimneys by the shortest way, went down to the corner formed at the south where the lake's shores met. They forced their way, not without trouble, through thickets and brushwood that no human hand had ever yet pushed aside, and in this way they headed for the shore, so as to come out at the northern end of Prospect Plateau. They covered two miles in that direction, and then, past the last curtain of trees, the plateau appeared, carpeted with thick grass, and beyond it the endless sea.

To get back to the Chimneys, they had only to cross the plateau on a slant for a mile and then go down to the elbow formed by the first bend of the Mercy. But the engineer wanted to find out how, and where, the lake's overflow escaped, and so the exploration was stretched out under the trees for a mile and a half to the north. It was likely, in fact, that there was a spillway somewhere, probably through a gap in the granite. The lake, after all, was nothing but an immense basin that had slowly filled up with the flow of the creek, and its overflow had to be draining away to the sea by some waterfall or other. If that was so, the engineer thought it might be possible to put that waterfall to use and borrow its power, which at present was going to waste and doing no one any good. So they kept following the shores of Lake Grant, climbing up the plateau. But after going another mile in that direction, Cyrus Smith had still not found the spillway, which nevertheless had to exist.

It was half past four by then. Dinner had to be got ready, and that meant the colonists had to go home. So the little band turned back, and by the left bank of the Mercy, Cyrus Smith and his companions reached the Chimneys.

There the fire was lit, and Nab and Pencroff, the colony's natural cooks, briskly grilled the agoutis, and everyone did them full justice.

When the meal was over, just as each of them was about to settle down to sleep, Cyrus Smith pulled out of his pocket some small samples of different kinds of minerals, and said only this:

"My friends, this is iron ore, this is pyrite, this is clay, this is lime, this is coal. That is what nature gives us, and that is nature's share of the common work! Tomorrow, ours!"

Chapter 13: What They Found on Top

What they found on Top — Making bows and arrows — A brickworks — The pottery kiln — Various cooking pots — The first stew — Mugwort — The Southern Cross — An important astronomical observation

"Well, Mr. Cyrus, where do we start?" Pencroff asked the engineer the next morning.

"At the beginning," answered Cyrus Smith.

And in fact it was at the very "beginning" that these colonists were going to be forced to start. They did not even have the tools needed to make tools. They were not even in the position of nature, which, "having time, saves effort." Time was exactly what they lacked, since they had to provide at once for the needs of daily life. Thanks to the experience of the human race they had nothing to invent, but at least they had everything to make. Their iron and their steel were still only ore, their pottery was still only clay, and their linen and their clothes were still only raw fiber.

It must be said, though, that these colonists were "men" in the finest and strongest sense of the word. The engineer could not have had more intelligent companions to help him, or more devoted and eager ones. He had questioned them. He knew what each of them could do.

Gédéon Spilett, a reporter of great talent, who had learned everything so that he could talk about everything, would contribute a great deal, with his head and with his hands, to the colonizing of the island. He would shrink from no task, and as a passionate hunter he would now make a trade of what until then had been only a pleasure.

Harbert, a fine boy, already remarkably well schooled in the natural sciences, was going to be a real asset to the common cause.

Nab was devotion itself. Skillful, intelligent, tireless, strong, with an iron constitution, he knew something of blacksmith's work and could only be extremely useful to the colony.

As for Pencroff, he had been a sailor on every ocean, a carpenter in the Brooklyn shipyards, a tailor's assistant aboard navy ships, and a gardener and a farmhand during his shore leaves, and so on. Like all seamen, he was fit for anything and knew how to do everything.

It would truly have been hard to bring together five men better fitted to struggle against fate, or more certain of winning.

"At the beginning," Cyrus Smith had said. And the beginning the engineer meant was building a piece of equipment that could be used to transform natural materials. Everyone knows the part that heat plays in such transformations. Fuel, whether wood or coal, could be used at once. So the task was to build a kiln to burn it in.

"What will the kiln be for?" asked Pencroff.

"For making the pottery we need," answered Cyrus Smith.

"And what will we make the kiln out of?"

"Bricks."

"And the bricks?"

"Clay. Let's go, my friends. To save ourselves hauling things back and forth, we'll set up our workshop right where the materials are. Nab will bring provisions, and there'll be no shortage of fire for cooking food."

"No," the reporter answered, "but what if there's a shortage of food, for lack of anything to hunt with?"

"Ah! If only we had a knife!" cried the sailor.

"Well?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"Well! I'd make a bow and arrows in no time, and there'd be plenty of game in the pantry!"

"Yes, a knife, a sharp blade..." said the engineer, as though he were talking to himself.

At that moment his eyes fell on Top, who was running back and forth along the shore.

Suddenly Cyrus Smith's face lit up.

"Top, here!" he said.

The dog came running at his master's call. The engineer took Top's head in his hands, unfastened the collar the animal wore around his neck, and broke it in two, saying:

"There are two knives, Pencroff!"

The sailor answered with two cheers. Top's collar was made of a thin strip of tempered steel. All they had to do was grind it first on a sandstone to bring the edge to a bare, sharp angle, and then take off the wire edge, the rough burr the grinding leaves, on a finer sandstone. Rock of that gritty kind was plentiful on the beach, and two hours later the colony's tool kit consisted of two sharp blades, which it had been easy to fit into sturdy handles.

The winning of this first tool was hailed as a triumph. And a precious winning it was, and it came at just the right moment.

They set off. Cyrus Smith meant to go back to the western shore of the lake, where the day before he had noticed the clayey soil he had brought a sample of. So they followed the bank of the Mercy, crossed Prospect Plateau, and after a walk of five miles at most they came to a clearing two hundred paces from Lake Grant.

On the way, Harbert had found a tree whose branches the Indians of South America use to make their bows. It was the "crejimba," a member of the palm family that bears no edible fruit. They cut long, straight branches, stripped them of leaves, and trimmed them, leaving them thicker in the middle and thinner at the ends. Now all that remained was to find a plant fit to make the bowstring. They found it in a species of the mallow family, an "Hibiscus heterophyllus," which supplied fibers so remarkably tough they could have been compared to animal sinews. In this way Pencroff got himself bows of considerable power, and the only thing they still lacked was arrows. The shafts were easy to make from straight, stiff branches without knots. But the head that had to tip them, something that could take the place of iron, was not going to be so easy to come by. Pencroff told himself, though, that since he had done his share of the work, luck would do the rest.

The colonists had arrived at the patch of ground they had explored the day before. It was made of the potter's clay that is used to make bricks and tiles, so it was very well suited to the job they had in hand. The work itself presented no difficulty. They only had to temper the clay with sand, so that it would not be too sticky, mold the bricks, and bake them in the heat of a wood fire.

Usually bricks are pressed into molds, but the engineer was satisfied to make them by hand. The whole day, and the next one, went into this work. The clay was soaked with water, then worked and kneaded with the feet and fists of the workmen, and then divided into blocks of equal size. A practiced workman can turn out as many as ten thousand bricks in twelve hours without a machine. But in their two days of work the five brickmakers of Lincoln Island made no more than three thousand. These were laid out side by side until they were completely dry and ready to be fired, which would be in three or four days.

It was on April 2 that Cyrus Smith set about fixing the island's orientation — finding exactly where north lay.

The evening before, he had noted the exact time at which the sun disappeared below the horizon, allowing for the refraction of the air, which makes the sun seem higher than it is. That morning he noted just as exactly the time at which it reappeared. Between that sunset and that sunrise, twelve hours and twenty-four minutes had passed. So six hours and twelve minutes after it rose, the sun, on that day, would cross the meridian exactly, and the point in the sky it occupied at that moment would be north. (At that time of year, and in that latitude, the sun was rising at 5:33 in the morning and setting at 6:17 in the evening.)

At the appointed time Cyrus took a sighting on that point. He lined up two trees with the sun, to serve him as markers, and in this way he obtained a fixed north-south line for all his later work.

During the two days before the bricks were fired, everyone was busy laying in fuel. Branches were cut all around the clearing, and they gathered up all the dead wood that had fallen under the trees. This did not happen without a little hunting in the neighborhood, all the more since Pencroff now had a few dozen arrows tipped with very sharp points. It was Top who had supplied those points, by bringing back a porcupine. As game it was fairly poor, but it was undeniably valuable for the quills that bristled all over it. These quills were fixed firmly to the ends of the arrows, and feathers from cockatoos were fitted to the other ends to make them fly true. The reporter and Harbert soon became very skillful archers. And so game of every kind, furred and feathered, poured into the Chimneys: capybaras, pigeons, agoutis, heath cocks, and more. Most of these animals were killed in the part of the forest on the left bank of the Mercy, which they named Jacamar Wood, in memory of the bird Pencroff and Harbert had chased on their first exploration.

This game was eaten fresh, but they saved the capybara hams. They seasoned them with fragrant leaves and then smoked them over a fire of green wood. Still, this very nourishing food was always roast after roast, and the diners would have been happy to hear a simple stew bubbling on the hearth. But for that they had to wait until the pot was made — which meant waiting until the kiln was built.

During these outings, which never went more than a short distance from the brickworks, the hunters found signs that large animals had passed by recently, animals armed with powerful claws, though they could not tell what species they were. So Cyrus Smith urged them to be extremely careful, because it was likely that the forest sheltered some dangerous wild beasts.

He was right to do it. One day, in fact, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert caught sight of an animal that looked like a jaguar. Luckily the beast did not attack them, because they might not have got away without some serious wound. But Gédéon Spilett promised himself that as soon as he had a real weapon — one of those guns Pencroff kept asking for — he would wage relentless war on the wild beasts and rid the island of them.

During those few days nothing was done to make the Chimneys more comfortable, since the engineer expected to discover, or if need be to build, a better place to live. They were content to spread a fresh bed of moss and dry leaves over the sand of the passages, and on these rather primitive beds the exhausted workers slept the sleep of the just.

They also worked out how many days had passed on Lincoln Island since the colonists had landed there, and from then on they kept a regular count. On April 5, which was a Wednesday, it had been twelve days since the wind had thrown the castaways onto this coast.

On April 6, at dawn, the engineer and his companions gathered in the clearing at the spot where the bricks were to be fired. Naturally this operation had to be done in the open air and not in kilns. Or rather, the pile of bricks would itself be one enormous kiln that would bake itself. The fuel, made of carefully prepared bundles of brushwood, was laid out on the ground, and around it they built several courses of dried bricks, which soon formed a great cube, with vents left in its outer walls to let the fire draw. This work took the whole day, and only in the evening did they set fire to the brushwood.

That night nobody went to bed, and they watched carefully to make sure the fire did not die down.

The firing lasted forty-eight hours and was a complete success. Then the smoking mass had to be left to cool. In the meantime Nab and Pencroff, guided by Cyrus Smith, hauled several loads of calcium carbonate — that is, limestone, a very common stone, which was plentiful north of the lake — on a hurdle made of woven branches. When these stones were broken down by heat, they gave a quicklime that was very rich, that swelled up a great deal when it was slaked with water, and that was in the end as pure as if it had been made by burning chalk or marble. Mixed with sand, which keeps the paste from shrinking as it hardens, this lime made an excellent mortar.

The result of all this work was that on April 9 the engineer had a good quantity of lime ready to use, and a few thousand bricks.

So, without losing a moment, they began building a kiln for firing the various kinds of pottery they needed for everyday household use. They managed it without much trouble. Five days later the kiln was loaded with coal from the open-air seam the engineer had discovered near the mouth of Red Creek, and the first smoke was pouring out of a chimney some twenty feet high. The clearing had been turned into a factory, and Pencroff was not far from believing that every product of modern industry was about to come out of that kiln.

In the meantime, what the colonists made first was a plain, coarse pottery, but one very well suited for cooking. The raw material was the very clay of the ground, to which Cyrus Smith had them add a little lime and some quartz. This paste was in fact real "pipe clay," the white clay that tobacco pipes are made from. Out of it they made pots; cups, molded over pebbles of suitable shapes; plates; big jars and tubs to hold water; and so on. These objects were clumsy and lopsided. But once they had been fired at a high temperature, the kitchen of the Chimneys found itself supplied with a number of utensils as precious as if they had been made of the finest porcelain clay.

It must be mentioned here that Pencroff, eager to find out whether this clay, prepared in this way, deserved its name of "pipe clay," made himself a few rather rough pipes. He thought they were charming, but alas, there was no tobacco to put in them! And it has to be said that this was a great hardship for Pencroff.

"But the tobacco will come, like everything else!" he kept saying, in his bursts of absolute confidence.

This work lasted until April 15, and it will be understood that the time was conscientiously spent. The colonists, turned potters, did nothing but make pottery. When it suited Cyrus Smith to turn them into blacksmiths, they would be blacksmiths. But since the next day was a Sunday, and Easter Sunday at that, they all agreed to keep it holy by resting. These Americans were religious men, who carefully observed the teachings of the Bible, and the situation they had been placed in could only deepen their trust in the Maker of all things.

On the evening of April 15, then, they went back to the Chimneys for good. The rest of the pottery was carried along with them, and the kiln was let go out until it was needed for something new. The return was marked by a lucky event: the engineer discovered something that could take the place of tinder. Everyone knows that tinder, that spongy, velvety flesh, comes from a certain mushroom, a bracket fungus of the genus Polyporus. Properly prepared, it catches fire extremely easily, especially if it has first been soaked in gunpowder or boiled in a solution of potassium nitrate or potassium chlorate. But until then they had not found any of those fungi, nor even any of the morels that can stand in for them. That day, though, the engineer recognized a certain plant belonging to the genus Artemisia, the mugworts, whose chief species include wormwood, southernwood, tarragon, genepi, and others. He pulled up several clumps, and holding them out to the sailor, he said:

"Here, Pencroff, this will make you happy."

Pencroff looked closely at the plant, which was covered with long, silky hairs, and whose leaves were coated in a cottony down.

"Eh! What's this, Mr. Cyrus?" asked Pencroff. "Good heavens! Is it tobacco?"

"No," answered Cyrus Smith. "It's artemisia — Chinese mugwort to the scientists — and for us it's going to be tinder."

And in fact this mugwort, once properly dried, did give them a substance that caught fire very easily, especially later on, when the engineer had soaked it in potassium nitrate, of which the island had several beds — and potassium nitrate is nothing other than saltpeter.

That evening all the colonists gathered in the central chamber and ate a proper supper. Nab had made an agouti stew and a seasoned capybara ham, and with them they had the boiled tubers of "Caladium macrorhizum," a kind of herbaceous plant of the arum family, which in the tropics would have grown into the shape of a tree. These rootstocks tasted excellent and were very nourishing, much like the substance sold in England under the name of "Portland sago," and up to a point they could take the place of bread, which the colonists of Lincoln Island still did not have.

When supper was over, before turning in for the night, Cyrus Smith and his companions went out to take the air on the beach. It was eight o'clock in the evening. The night promised to be magnificent. The moon, which had been full five days before, had not yet risen, but the horizon was already silvering with those soft, pale tints that might be called the moon's dawn. At the southern zenith the constellations that circle the pole were shining in all their splendor, and among them all the Southern Cross, which the engineer had greeted a few days before from the top of Mount Franklin.

Cyrus Smith watched that splendid constellation for some time. It carries two stars of the first magnitude at its top and its foot, a star of the second magnitude on its left arm, and one of the third magnitude on its right.

Then, after some thought, he asked the boy:

"Harbert, isn't today April 15?"

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus," answered Harbert.

"Well, unless I'm mistaken, tomorrow will be one of the four days of the year when true time and mean time are the same. That means, my boy, that tomorrow, to within a few seconds, the sun will cross the meridian exactly at noon by the clocks. So if the weather's fine, I think I'll be able to get the island's longitude to within a few degrees."

"Without instruments? Without a sextant?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"Yes," the engineer went on. "And since the night is clear, I'm going to try this very evening to get our latitude, by working out the height of the Southern Cross — that is, of the south pole — above the horizon. You understand, my friends, that before we take on any serious work of settling in, it isn't enough to have found out that this land is an island. We have to find out, as nearly as we can, how far it lies from the American continent, or from the Australian continent, or from the main island groups of the Pacific."

"Right," said the reporter. "Instead of building a house, it might be in our interest to build a boat, if we happen to be only a hundred miles or so from an inhabited coast."

"That's why," Cyrus Smith continued, "I'm going to try tonight to get the latitude of Lincoln Island, and tomorrow at noon I'll try to work out its longitude."

If the engineer had had a sextant — an instrument that uses mirrors to measure the angle between two distant objects with great precision — the operation would have presented no difficulty at all. That evening, from the height of the pole, and the next day, from the sun's passage across the meridian, he would have had the island's coordinates. But since he had no such instrument, he had to make up for it.

So Cyrus Smith went back into the Chimneys. By the light of the fire he whittled two small flat rulers and joined them together at one end, so as to make a kind of pair of compasses whose legs could be spread apart or brought together. The joint was held by a strong acacia thorn, taken from the dead wood of the woodpile.

When this instrument was finished, the engineer went back to the beach. But he had to take the height of the pole above a sharply drawn horizon — that is, a sea horizon — and Claw Cape hid the horizon to the south from him, so he had to look for a better place to observe from. The best would obviously have been the stretch of coast facing directly south, but to get there he would have had to cross the Mercy, which was deep at that point, and that was a problem.

Cyrus Smith therefore decided to make his observation from Prospect Plateau, and to allow for its height above sea level — a height he planned to work out the next day by a simple method of elementary geometry.

So the colonists made their way up onto the plateau, climbing along the left bank of the Mercy, and took their places on the edge that ran from northwest to southeast — that is, on the line of oddly jagged rocks that bordered the river.

This part of the plateau stood some fifty feet higher than the heights on the right bank, which sloped down two ways, to the tip of Claw Cape and to the island's southern coast. So nothing blocked the view, which took in half the horizon, from the cape all the way to Reptile End. To the south, that horizon, lit from below by the first glow of the moon, stood out sharply against the sky and could be sighted on with fair precision.

At that moment the Southern Cross appeared to the observer upside down, with the star Alpha marking its foot, the end nearer the south pole.

This constellation does not lie as close to the south pole as the North Star does to the north pole. Alpha is about twenty-seven degrees from it. But Cyrus Smith knew this and meant to allow for that distance in his calculation. He also took care to observe it at the moment when it was crossing the meridian below the pole, which would make his work simpler.

So Cyrus Smith aimed one leg of his wooden compasses at the sea horizon and the other at Alpha, as he would have aimed the telescopes of a repeating circle, and the opening between the two legs gave him the angle that separated Alpha from the horizon. To fix the angle so that it could not change, he pinned the two little boards of his instrument with thorns onto a third one laid across them, so that the spread between them was held firm.

Once that was done, all that remained was to work out the angle he had obtained, correcting the observation to sea level so as to allow for the dip of the horizon — the way a horizon seen from a height lies a little below the true level — and that meant measuring the height of the plateau. The value of this angle would then give the height of Alpha above the horizon, and from it the height of the pole above the horizon — in other words, the island's latitude, since the latitude of any point on the globe is always equal to the height of the pole above that point's horizon.

These calculations were put off until the next day, and by ten o'clock everyone was sound asleep.

Chapter 14: Measuring the Granite Wall

Measuring the granite wall — An application of the theorem of similar triangles — The latitude of the island — An excursion to the north — An oyster bed — Plans for the future — The sun crosses the meridian — The coordinates of Lincoln Island

The next day, April 16 — Easter Sunday — the colonists came out of the Chimneys at first light and set about washing their linen and cleaning their clothes. The engineer meant to make soap as soon as he could get hold of the raw materials soap-making calls for: soda or potash, and fat or oil. The all-important question of renewing their wardrobe would also be dealt with in its own time and place. In any case, their clothes would easily last another six months, because they were sturdy and could stand up to the wear and tear of manual work. But everything would depend on where the island lay in relation to inhabited lands. That was what would be settled this very day, if the weather allowed.

And the sun, rising over a clear horizon, promised a magnificent day, one of those beautiful autumn days that are like the warm season's last goodbye.

So the task was to complete the data from the evening before by measuring the height of Prospect Plateau above sea level.

"Don't you need an instrument like the one you used yesterday?" Harbert asked the engineer.

"No, my boy," he answered. "We're going to go about it another way, and one that's very nearly as precise."

Harbert, who loved to learn about everything, followed the engineer, who walked away from the foot of the granite wall and down to the edge of the beach. Meanwhile, Pencroff, Nab, and the reporter busied themselves with various jobs.

Cyrus Smith had brought along a sort of straight pole, about twelve feet long, which he had measured as exactly as he could by comparing it with his own height, which he knew to within a twelfth of an inch. Harbert carried a plumb line that Cyrus Smith had given him — simply a stone tied to the end of a flexible fiber.

When he was about twenty feet from the water's edge and about five hundred feet from the granite wall, which rose straight up, Cyrus Smith drove the pole two feet into the sand. Wedging it carefully, and checking it with the plumb line, he managed to stand it exactly upright — at right angles to the level of the horizon.

That done, he stepped back as far as he needed to so that, lying flat on the sand, he could send his line of sight from his eye past the top of the pole and the crest of the wall at the same time, just grazing both. Then he marked that spot carefully with a peg.

Then he turned to Harbert.

"Do you know the first principles of geometry?" he asked.

"A little, Mr. Cyrus," answered Harbert, who didn't want to claim too much.

"You remember the properties of two similar triangles?"

"Yes," said Harbert. "Their corresponding sides are proportional."

"Well, my boy, I've just built two similar triangles, both of them right triangles. The first, the smaller one, has for its sides the upright pole and the distance from the peg to the foot of the pole, and my line of sight for its hypotenuse. The second has for its sides the upright wall, whose height is what we want to measure, and the distance from the peg to the foot of that wall, and once again my line of sight for its hypotenuse — which happens to be the first triangle's hypotenuse, extended."
