"Oh, Mr. Cyrus, I see!" cried Harbert. "Just as the distance from the peg to the pole is in proportion to the distance from the peg to the foot of the wall, the height of the pole is in the same proportion to the height of the wall."

"Exactly, Harbert," the engineer answered. "Once we've measured those first two distances, since we know the height of the pole, we'll only have one proportion to work out. That will give us the height of the wall and save us the trouble of measuring it directly."

The two horizontal distances were taken, using the pole itself as the measuring rod. Its length above the sand was exactly ten feet.

The first distance, between the peg and the point where the pole was driven into the sand, was fifteen feet.

The second distance, between the peg and the foot of the wall, was five hundred feet.

With these measurements finished, Cyrus Smith and the boy went back to the Chimneys.

There the engineer took a flat stone he had brought back from one of his earlier excursions, a kind of slate on which it was easy to scratch figures with a sharp shell. And he set out the following proportion — 15 is to 500 as 10 is to x:

    15 : 500 :: 10 : x
    500 x 10 = 5000
    5000 / 15 = 333.33

From which it was established that the granite wall was three hundred and thirty-three feet high.

Cyrus Smith then picked up the instrument he had made the evening before, whose two little boards, by the spread between them, gave him the angular distance of the star Alpha above the horizon. He measured the opening of that angle very exactly on a circle that he divided into three hundred and sixty equal parts. Now, this angle — once he had added the twenty-seven degrees that separate Alpha from the south pole, and corrected the observation to sea level for the height of the plateau it had been made from — came to fifty-three degrees. Subtract those fifty-three degrees from ninety degrees — the distance from the pole to the equator — and thirty-seven degrees were left. So Cyrus Smith concluded that Lincoln Island lay on the thirty-seventh degree of south latitude; or, allowing for an error of five degrees, given how rough his methods were, that it must lie somewhere between the thirty-fifth and the fortieth parallels.

There remained the longitude, to complete the island's coordinates. The engineer would try to find it that very day at noon — that is, at the moment when the sun crossed the meridian.

It was decided that this Sunday would be spent on a walk, or rather on an exploration of the part of the island lying between the north end of the lake and Shark Gulf, and that, if the weather allowed, they would push the survey on as far as the northern side of South Mandible Cape. They would have lunch in the dunes and not come back until evening.

At half past eight in the morning the little troop was walking along the edge of the channel. On the other side, on Safety Islet, a great many birds were strolling about with a solemn air. They were diving birds of the penguin kind, easy to recognize by their unpleasant cry, which sounds like a donkey's bray. Pencroff considered them only from the point of view of eating, and he learned, not without some satisfaction, that their flesh, though blackish, is quite edible.

They could also see large amphibious animals crawling on the sand — seals, no doubt — which seemed to have chosen the islet as their refuge. There was little point in considering these as food, because their oily flesh is disgusting. Still, Cyrus Smith watched them closely, and, without explaining what he had in mind, he told his companions that very soon they would pay the islet a visit.

The shore the colonists were following was strewn with countless shells, some of which would have delighted any collector of mollusks. Among others there were pheasant shells, lamp shells, trigonias, and so on. But something far more useful was a huge oyster bed, uncovered at low tide, which Nab spotted among the rocks about four miles from the Chimneys.

"Nab hasn't wasted his day!" cried Pencroff, looking at the bed of oysters stretching out from the shore.

"It's a lucky find, all right," said the reporter. "And if it's true, as they say, that every oyster produces fifty to sixty thousand eggs a year, we'll have an inexhaustible supply there."

"Only I don't think oysters are very nourishing," said Harbert.

"No," answered Cyrus Smith. "An oyster contains very little nitrogenous matter — the stuff that builds up the body — and a man who lived on nothing else would need no fewer than fifteen or sixteen dozen a day."

"Fine!" said Pencroff. "We can swallow dozens and dozens of dozens before we use up the bed. How about taking a few for lunch?"

And without waiting for an answer to his proposal, knowing perfectly well that it was approved in advance, the sailor and Nab pried loose a good quantity of the shellfish. They put them in a sort of net made of hibiscus fibers that Nab had put together, which already held the meal's menu. Then they went on up the coast between the dunes and the sea.

Every now and then Cyrus Smith looked at his watch, so as to be ready in time for the observation of the sun, which had to be made at exactly noon.

This whole part of the island was very barren, all the way to the point that closed off Union Bay, the one that had been named South Mandible Cape. There was nothing to see there but sand and shells, mixed with fragments of lava. A few seabirds haunted this desolate coast — gulls, great albatrosses, and wild ducks too, which quite rightly roused Pencroff's appetite. He tried to bring some down with his arrows, but without success, because they hardly ever settled, and he would have had to hit them on the wing.

Which led the sailor to say to the engineer once again:

"You see, Mr. Cyrus, as long as we don't have a hunting gun or two, our equipment's going to leave something to be desired!"

"No doubt, Pencroff," the reporter answered, "but that's entirely up to you! Get us iron for the barrels, steel for the locks, saltpeter, charcoal, and sulfur for the powder, mercury and nitric acid for the fulminate that sets off the charge, and lead for the bullets, and Cyrus will make us first-class guns."

"Oh," answered the engineer, "we'll no doubt be able to find all those substances on the island, but a firearm is a delicate instrument, and it calls for tools of great precision. Well, we'll see later on."

"Why," cried Pencroff, "why did we have to throw overboard all those weapons we had in the basket with us, and our tools, right down to our pocketknives!"

"But if we hadn't thrown them out, Pencroff, the balloon would have thrown us into the bottom of the sea!" said Harbert.

"That's true enough, what you say, my boy!" answered the sailor.

Then, moving on to another idea:

"But now that I think of it," he added, "how flabbergasted Jonathan Forster and his friends must have been the next morning, when they found the place empty and the machine flown away!"

"What they might have thought is the least of my worries!" said the reporter.

"All the same, it was my idea!" said Pencroff, looking pleased with himself.

"A fine idea, Pencroff," answered Gédéon Spilett with a laugh, "and it's put us where we are!"

"I'd rather be here than in the hands of the Southerners!" cried the sailor. "Especially since Mr. Cyrus was kind enough to come and join us!"

"So would I, honestly!" replied the reporter. "Besides, what are we missing? Nothing!"

"Except... everything!" answered Pencroff, bursting out laughing and shaking his broad shoulders. "But one of these days we'll find a way to get out of here!"

"And sooner perhaps than you imagine, my friends," the engineer said then, "if Lincoln Island is only a moderate distance from an inhabited archipelago or a continent. Within an hour we'll know. I don't have a map of the Pacific, but I remember its southern part very clearly. The latitude I got yesterday puts Lincoln Island level with New Zealand to the west and with the coast of Chile to the east. But between those two lands the distance is at least six thousand miles. So what's left is to decide what point the island occupies in that wide stretch of sea, and that's what the longitude will give us in a little while — closely enough, I hope."

"Aren't the Tuamotus the islands nearest to us in latitude?" asked Harbert.

"Yes," answered the engineer, "but they're more than twelve hundred miles away from us."

"And over that way?" asked Nab, who was following the conversation with the greatest interest, and his hand pointed south.

"Over that way, nothing," answered Pencroff.

"Nothing, indeed," the engineer added.

"Well, Cyrus," asked the reporter, "what if Lincoln Island turns out to be only two or three hundred miles from New Zealand or Chile?..."

"Well," answered the engineer, "instead of building a house, we'll build a boat, and Master Pencroff will take charge of sailing her..."

"Why, of course, Mr. Cyrus," cried the sailor, "I'm all ready to become a captain — as soon as you've found a way to build a boat good enough to go to sea!"

"We'll do it, if it's necessary!" answered Cyrus Smith.

But while these men talked — men who truly had doubts about nothing — the hour was drawing near when the observation was to be made. How would Cyrus Smith go about recording the moment the sun crossed the island's meridian, without any instrument at all? That was something Harbert could not guess.

The observers were now six miles from the Chimneys, not far from the part of the dunes where the engineer had been found after his mysterious rescue. They halted at that spot and got everything ready for lunch, since it was half past eleven. Harbert went to fetch fresh water from the stream that ran close by, and he brought it back in a jug Nab had brought along.

While these preparations went on, Cyrus Smith set everything up for his astronomical observation. He chose a perfectly clear spot on the beach that the sea, as it went out, had leveled perfectly smooth. This layer of very fine sand was as flat as a mirror, without a single grain sticking up above the rest. Actually, it didn't matter whether this layer was level or not, and it mattered no more whether the stick, six feet tall, that was planted in it stood exactly upright. On the contrary, the engineer even tilted it toward the south — that is, away from the sun. For we must not forget that the colonists of Lincoln Island, precisely because the island lay in the Southern Hemisphere, saw the radiant sun trace its daily arc above the northern horizon, not above the southern one.

Harbert understood then how the engineer meant to record the sun's culmination — that is, its passage across the island's meridian, or, in other words, local noon. He would do it by means of the shadow the stick cast on the sand, a method that, lacking any instrument, would give him a close enough approximation for the result he wanted.

For the moment when this shadow reached its shortest length would be exactly noon, and it would be enough to follow the tip of the shadow to catch the instant when, after growing steadily shorter, it began to lengthen again. By tilting his stick away from the sun, Cyrus Smith made the shadow longer, and so its changes would be easier to see. After all, the bigger the hand of a dial, the more easily you can follow the movement of its tip. And the stick's shadow was nothing but the hand of a dial.

When he judged that the moment had come, Cyrus Smith knelt on the sand, and, with little wooden markers that he pushed into the sand, he began to mark off the shadow's successive shortenings. His companions, bending over him, followed the operation with the keenest interest.

The reporter held his chronometer in his hand, ready to note the time it showed when the shadow was at its shortest. What's more, since Cyrus Smith was working on April 16 — one of the days when true time and mean time are the same — the time given by Gédéon Spilett would be the true time in Washington at that moment, which would simplify the calculation.

Meanwhile the sun moved slowly on. The stick's shadow shrank little by little, and when it seemed to Cyrus Smith that it was starting to grow again:

"What time is it?" he asked.

"One minute past five," Gédéon Spilett answered at once.

All that was left was to do the arithmetic. Nothing could be easier. There was, as you can see, a difference of five hours, in round numbers, between the meridian of Washington and the meridian of Lincoln Island — that is, it was noon on Lincoln Island when it was already five in the afternoon in Washington. Now, the sun, in its apparent motion around the earth, travels one degree every four minutes, or fifteen degrees an hour. Fifteen degrees multiplied by five hours gave seventy-five degrees.

So, since Washington lies at 77° 3′ 11″ — call it seventy-seven degrees — counted from the meridian of Greenwich, which the Americans, along with the English, take as the starting point for longitude, it followed that the island lay seventy-seven degrees plus seventy-five degrees west of the meridian of Greenwich — that is, at one hundred and fifty-two degrees west longitude.

Cyrus Smith announced this result to his companions. And allowing for errors in the observations, as he had done with the latitude, he felt he could state that Lincoln Island lay between the thirty-fifth and the thirty-seventh parallels, and between the one hundred and fiftieth and the one hundred and fifty-fifth meridians west of Greenwich.

The margin he allowed for errors of observation was, as you can see, five degrees either way. At sixty miles to the degree, that could mean an error of three hundred miles in latitude or in longitude from the true position.

But this error would make no difference to the decision they had to make. It was perfectly obvious that Lincoln Island lay so far from any land or island group that no one could risk crossing that distance in a simple, fragile boat.

In fact, his reckoning put it at least twelve hundred miles from Tahiti and the islands of the Tuamotus, more than eighteen hundred miles from New Zealand, and more than four thousand five hundred miles from the American coast!

And when Cyrus Smith searched his memory, he could not recall that any island at all occupied, in that part of the Pacific, the position assigned to Lincoln Island.

Chapter 15: Iron and Steel

Wintering on the island is settled once and for all — The metallurgical question — Exploring Safety Islet — The seal hunt — An echidna captured — The koula — What is called the Catalan method — Making iron — How steel is obtained

The next morning, April 17, the sailor's first words were for Gédéon Spilett.

"Well, sir," he asked, "what are we going to be today?"

"Whatever Cyrus pleases," the reporter answered.

And so the engineer's companions, who until then had been brickmakers and potters, were about to become metalworkers.

The day before, after lunch, they had carried their exploration as far as the tip of Mandible Cape, nearly seven miles from the Chimneys. There the long line of dunes came to an end, and the ground took on a volcanic look. There were no more high walls of rock like those at Prospect Plateau. Instead, a strange, ragged border framed the narrow gulf between the two capes, and it was made of minerals the volcano had once spewed out. Having reached the point, the colonists had turned back, and they got home to the Chimneys as night was falling. But they did not go to sleep until they had settled, once and for all, whether or not they should think of leaving Lincoln Island.

The twelve hundred miles that lay between the island and the Pomotou Archipelago were a great distance. A small boat would not have been enough to cross it, especially with the bad season coming on. Pencroff had said so flatly. Besides, building even a simple boat was hard work, even with the right tools, and the colonists had no tools at all. They would have to begin by making hammers, axes, adzes, saws, augers, planes and so on, and that would take time. So it was decided that they would spend the winter on Lincoln Island, and that they would look for a more comfortable home than the Chimneys to live in through the winter months.

First of all, they had to put to use the iron ore that the engineer had spotted in a few deposits in the northwest part of the island, and turn that ore into iron or into steel.

As a rule, the ground does not hold metals in a pure state. Most of them are found combined with oxygen or with sulfur. As it happened, of the two samples Cyrus Smith had brought back, one was magnetic iron ore, not a carbonate, and the other was pyrite — in other words, iron sulfide. So it was the first, the iron oxide, that had to be reduced with charcoal or coal — that is, stripped of its oxygen — to get the iron pure. This reduction is done by heating the ore to a high temperature in the presence of the coal. There are two ways of going about it. One is the quick, easy "Catalan method," which has the advantage of turning the ore straight into iron in a single operation. The other is the blast-furnace method, which first turns the ore into cast iron, and then turns the cast iron into iron by taking out of it the three or four percent of carbon combined with it.

Now, what did Cyrus Smith need? Iron, not cast iron, and he had to find the quickest method of reduction. What was more, the ore he had collected was very pure and very rich in itself. It was the kind of magnetic oxide that turns up in shapeless dark-gray masses, gives a black powder when it is ground, crystallizes in regular octahedrons — eight-sided crystals — supplies natural magnets, and is used in Europe to make the finest grades of iron, which Sweden and Norway have in such abundance. Not far from this deposit lay the coal beds the colonists had already been working. That made it very easy to treat the ore, since everything needed for the job was close at hand. It is exactly this that makes the mines of the United Kingdom so prodigiously rich: there the coal that smelts the metal is dug out of the same ground, at the same time, as the ore itself.

"So, Mr. Cyrus," Pencroff said to him, "we're going to work the iron ore?"

"Yes, my friend," the engineer answered, "and to do that — which won't displease you — we'll begin with a seal hunt on the islet."

"A seal hunt!" cried the sailor, turning to Gédéon Spilett. "So it takes seals to make iron?"

"If Cyrus says so!" the reporter answered.

But the engineer had already left the Chimneys, and Pencroff got ready for the seal hunt without getting any further explanation.

Soon Cyrus Smith, Harbert, Gédéon Spilett, Nab and the sailor were gathered on the beach at a spot where the channel left a kind of ford at low tide. The tide was at the very bottom of the ebb, and the hunters were able to cross the channel without getting wet above the knee.

So this was the first time Cyrus Smith had set foot on the islet, and the second time for his companions, since it was there that the balloon had first thrown them down. As they came ashore, a few hundred auks looked at them with innocent eyes. The colonists, armed with sticks, could easily have killed them, but they never thought of carrying out a slaughter that would have been doubly pointless — the more so because it mattered not to frighten the seals, which were lying on the sand a few cable lengths away. They also spared certain perfectly harmless penguins, whose wings had shrunk to stumps and lay flat like flippers, covered with feathers that looked like scales.

So the colonists moved carefully toward the northern point, walking over ground pocked with little hollows, each of them the nest of some water bird. Toward the end of the islet they could see big black spots swimming at the surface of the water. They looked like the tops of reefs on the move.

These were the seals they had come to capture. They had to let them come ashore first. With their narrow hips, their short, close-set fur and their spindle-shaped bodies, seals are excellent swimmers and hard to catch in the sea, while on land their short webbed feet let them do no more than crawl, and not quickly.

Pencroff knew the habits of these animals, and he advised waiting until they had stretched out on the sand in the sunshine, which would soon put them into a deep sleep. Then they would maneuver to cut off their retreat and strike them on the nose.

So the hunters hid behind the rocks along the shore and waited in silence.

An hour went by before the seals came out to play on the sand. There were half a dozen of them. Pencroff and Harbert then slipped away to go around the point of the islet, so as to come up behind the animals and cut off their retreat. Meanwhile Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett and Nab crawled along the rocks and crept toward what was about to become the field of battle.

All of a sudden the sailor's tall figure rose to its full height. Pencroff gave a shout. The engineer and his two companions threw themselves as fast as they could between the sea and the seals. Two of the animals, struck hard, were left dead on the sand, but the others managed to get back to the sea and swim off.

"The seals you ordered, Mr. Cyrus!" said the sailor, walking up to the engineer.

"Good," Cyrus Smith answered. "We'll make forge bellows out of them!"

"Forge bellows!" cried Pencroff. "Well! There's a couple of lucky seals for you!"

It was in fact a blowing machine — a bellows, which the treatment of the ore required — that the engineer meant to make from the skins of these animals. They were of middling size, no more than six feet long, and their heads looked like dogs' heads.

Since there was no point in loading themselves down with the considerable weight of two whole seals, Nab and Pencroff decided to skin them on the spot, while Cyrus Smith and the reporter finished exploring the islet.

The sailor and Nab managed the job skillfully, and three hours later Cyrus Smith had two sealskins at his disposal. He meant to use them just as they were, without tanning them at all.

The colonists had to wait for the tide to go down again, and then they crossed the channel and went home to the Chimneys.

It was no small job to stretch those skins over wooden frames that would hold them open, and to sew them up with fibers so that they could store air without leaking too much. They had to try again several times. Cyrus Smith had nothing to work with but the two steel blades from Top's collar. Even so, he was so skillful, and his companions helped him so intelligently, that three days later the little colony's equipment had grown by one blowing machine. Its job was to drive air into the middle of the ore while it was being heated — a condition the operation could not succeed without.

It was on April 20, first thing in the morning, that what the reporter called in his notes "the metallurgical period" began. The engineer, as we know, had made up his mind to do the work right at the deposits of coal and ore. By his observations, these lay at the foot of the northeast spurs of Mount Franklin, which meant six miles away. So there was no question of coming back to the Chimneys every day, and it was agreed that the little colony would camp in a hut of branches, so that the important operation could be watched over night and day.

With this plan settled, they set out first thing in the morning. Nab and Pencroff dragged the blowing machine on a hurdle — a sledge of woven branches — along with a supply of vegetable and animal food, which they could top up along the way anyway.

The route they took ran through Jacamar Wood, which they crossed on a slant from southeast to northwest, through its thickest part. They had to cut a path, and that path was later to become the most direct road between Prospect Plateau and Mount Franklin. The trees, all of kinds they had already identified, were magnificent. Harbert pointed out some new ones, among them dragon trees, which Pencroff called "stuck-up leeks" — because, for all their height, they belonged to the same lily family as the onion, the chive, the shallot and the asparagus. These dragon trees could supply woody roots that are excellent cooked and that, when left to ferment a certain way, make a very pleasant liquor. They laid in a supply.

This march through the woods was long. It took the whole day, but it gave them a chance to observe the animals and plants. Top, who was more particularly in charge of the animals, ran through the grass and the brush and flushed every kind of game without distinction. Harbert and Gédéon Spilett killed two kangaroos with arrows, and also an animal that looked a great deal like both a hedgehog and an anteater: like the first, because it rolled itself into a ball and bristled with spines; like the second, because it had digging claws, a long thin snout ending in a bird's beak, and a tongue it could shoot out, covered with little barbs that held on to insects. It was an echidna.

"And when he's in the stewpot," Pencroff naturally remarked, "what will he taste like?"

"Like an excellent piece of beef," Harbert answered.

"We won't ask any more of him than that," the sailor answered.

During this outing they caught sight of a few wild boars, which made no attempt to attack the little party. It did not seem likely that they would meet any dangerous beasts — until, in a thick patch of brush, the reporter thought he saw, a few paces away, in the lowest branches of a tree, an animal he took for a bear. He calmly started to sketch it. Very luckily for Gédéon Spilett, the animal in question did not belong to that formidable family of flat-footed walkers the bears belong to. It was only a "koula," better known as a "sloth." It was the size of a big dog, with bristly fur of a dirty color and feet armed with strong claws, which let it climb trees and live on their leaves. Once the creature's identity had been checked — and nobody disturbed it in its business — Gédéon Spilett crossed out "bear" in the caption of his sketch, wrote "koula" in its place, and they went on their way.

At five in the evening Cyrus Smith gave the signal to halt. He was now outside the forest, where the mighty spurs that propped up Mount Franklin on its eastern side began. A few hundred paces off ran Red Creek, so drinking water was close by.

The camp was set up at once. In less than an hour, at the edge of the forest, among the trees, a hut of branches woven through with creepers and plastered with clay offered a good enough shelter. The geological search was put off until the next day. Supper was made ready, a good fire blazed in front of the hut, the spit turned, and by eight o'clock, while one of the colonists stayed awake to keep the fire going in case some dangerous animal came prowling around, the others were sound asleep.

The next day, April 21, Cyrus Smith, with Harbert, went to look for the very old rock formations where he had already found his sample of ore. He came on the deposit right at the surface, almost at the source of the creek, at the foot of the side of one of those northeast spurs. This ore, very rich in iron and set in a gangue — the waste rock around it — that melted easily, was perfectly suited to the method of reduction the engineer meant to use: the Catalan method, but in the simplified form used in Corsica.

The Catalan method proper calls for building furnaces and crucibles, where the ore and the charcoal, laid in alternate layers, are transformed and reduced. But Cyrus Smith intended to save himself all that construction. He simply wanted to build a cube-shaped heap of ore and coal and drive the wind from his bellows into the middle of it. This was no doubt the process used by Tubal-cain, the Bible's first worker in metals, and by the first metalworkers of the inhabited world. And what had worked for the grandsons of Adam, and what still gave good results in countries rich in ore and fuel, could hardly fail in the circumstances the colonists of Lincoln Island found themselves in.

Like the ore, the coal was gathered without trouble, close by and right on the surface. First they broke the ore into small pieces and cleaned the dirt off their surfaces by hand. Then coal and ore were stacked in a heap, in layer after layer — just as a charcoal burner stacks the wood he wants to turn into charcoal. That way, with the air blown in by the bellows, the coal would turn first into carbonic acid and then into carbon monoxide, and the carbon monoxide would reduce the iron oxide — that is, take its oxygen away.

That is how the engineer went about it. The sealskin bellows, fitted at its end with a pipe of fireclay that had been made beforehand in the pottery kiln, was set up next to the heap of ore. It was worked by a mechanism made of frames, fiber ropes and counterweights, and it drove a steady supply of air into the heap. This air raised the temperature, and it also played its part in the chemical change that was to yield pure iron.

The operation was hard. It took all the colonists' patience and all their ingenuity to carry it through, but in the end it succeeded. The final result was a bloom of iron — a lump of spongy metal — which had to be shingled and worked, that is, forged under the hammer, to drive out the melted gangue. Obviously these makeshift blacksmiths had no first hammer to start with. But after all, they were in the same position as the very first metalworker, and they did what he must have done.

The first bloom, fixed onto a stick for a handle, served as a hammer for forging the second on a granite anvil, and in this way they managed to get a metal that was rough but usable.

At last, after a great deal of effort and a great deal of weariness, by April 25 several bars of iron had been forged, and they were being turned into tools — crowbars, pincers, picks, mattocks and so on — which Pencroff and Nab declared to be real jewels.

But it was not as plain iron that this metal could be of most service. It was above all as steel. Now, steel is a combination of iron and carbon, and it is made in one of two ways: either from cast iron, by taking out the carbon it has too much of, or from iron, by adding the carbon it lacks. The first kind, made by decarburizing cast iron, gives natural or puddled steel. The second, made by carburizing iron, gives cementation steel.

So it was this second kind that Cyrus Smith had reason to try to make, since what he had was pure iron. He succeeded by heating the metal with powdered charcoal in a crucible made of fireclay.

Then he worked this steel, which can be shaped by hammering both hot and cold, under the hammer. Nab and Pencroff, skillfully guided, made axe heads. Heated red-hot and plunged suddenly into cold water, these took an excellent temper.

Other tools were made the same way — roughly shaped, it goes without saying: plane blades, axes, hatchets, strips of steel that were to be turned into saws, carpenter's chisels, and then the iron heads for mattocks, shovels and picks, hammers, nails and so on.

At last, on May 5, the first metallurgical period was over. The blacksmiths went home to the Chimneys, and new work would soon entitle them to take on yet another title.

Chapter 16: A Fight Under the Water

The question of a home comes up again — Pencroff's flights of fancy — An exploration north of the lake — The northern edge of the plateau — The snakes — The far end of the lake — Top uneasy — Top swimming — A fight under the water

It was now May 6, which corresponds to November 6 in the lands of the northern hemisphere. For some days the sky had been growing misty, and it was important to make certain arrangements with the winter in mind. The temperature, however, had not yet dropped noticeably, and a thermometer brought to Lincoln Island would still have shown an average of fifty to fifty-four degrees Fahrenheit. That average should not surprise anyone. Lincoln Island, very probably lying somewhere between the thirty-fifth and fortieth parallels, had to be subject, in the southern hemisphere, to the same climate as Sicily or Greece in the northern. But just as Greece and Sicily have spells of fierce cold that bring snow and ice, so Lincoln Island would no doubt suffer, at the very depth of winter, certain drops in temperature that it would be wise to guard against.

In any case, even if the cold was not yet a threat, the rainy season was close. On this isolated island, out in the middle of the Pacific Ocean and exposed to every kind of weather the open sea could throw at it, bad weather was bound to be frequent, and probably terrible.

So the question of a home more comfortable than the Chimneys had to be thought over seriously and settled quickly.

Pencroff, naturally, had a certain fondness for the shelter he had discovered himself. But he understood perfectly well that they had to look for another. The sea had already paid the Chimneys a visit, under circumstances the reader will remember, and they could not risk another accident like that one.

"Besides," added Cyrus Smith, who was talking these things over with his companions that day, "we have some precautions to take."

"Why?" said the reporter. "The island isn't inhabited."

"Probably not," answered the engineer, "although we haven't explored all of it yet. But even if there's no human being here, I'm afraid dangerous animals may be plentiful. So we ought to put ourselves out of reach of a possible attack, and stop making one of us stay up every night to keep a fire going. And then, my friends, we have to plan for everything. We're in a part of the Pacific that's often visited by Malay pirates..."

"What?" said Harbert. "This far from any land?"

"Yes, my boy," answered the engineer. "Those pirates are bold sailors as well as dangerous criminals, and we have to take our measures accordingly."

"Well then," answered Pencroff, "we'll fortify ourselves against wild beasts on two legs and on four. But, Mr. Cyrus, wouldn't it make sense to explore every part of the island before we start on anything?"

"That would be better," added Gédéon Spilett. "Who knows? We might find one of those caves on the opposite coast that we looked for on this one and never found."

"That's true," answered the engineer, "but you're forgetting, my friends, that we ought to settle near running water, and from the top of Mount Franklin we didn't see a single stream or river toward the west. Here, on the other hand, we're right between the Mercy and Lake Grant, and that's a considerable advantage we mustn't throw away. What's more, this coast faces east, so it isn't exposed the way the other one is to the trade winds, which blow from the northwest in this hemisphere."

"Then, Mr. Cyrus," answered the sailor, "let's build a house on the shore of the lake. We aren't short of bricks or tools now. We've been brickmakers, potters, smelters, and blacksmiths. We can certainly manage to be masons too, devil take it!"

"Yes, my friend, but before we decide, we have to look around. A home that nature had built for us at her own expense would save us a great deal of work, and it would probably give us an even safer refuge, because it would be as well defended against enemies from inside the island as against enemies from outside."

"True enough, Cyrus," answered the reporter, "but we've already examined that whole granite mass along the coast, and there isn't a hole in it, not even a crack!"

"No, not one!" added Pencroff. "Ah! If only we could have dug ourselves a home in that wall, high enough up to be out of reach — now that would have suited us! I can see it from here: five or six rooms on the face that looks out to sea..."

"With windows to let the light in!" said Harbert, laughing.

"And a staircase to get up to them!" added Nab.

"You're laughing," cried the sailor, "and why, I'd like to know? What's impossible about what I'm proposing? Don't we have picks and mattocks? Won't Mr. Cyrus know how to make gunpowder for blasting? Isn't that right, Mr. Cyrus — you'll make gunpowder the day we need it?"

Cyrus Smith had listened to the enthusiastic Pencroff as he spun out his somewhat fanciful plans. Attacking that mass of granite, even with blasting charges, would be a Herculean labor, and it really was a pity that nature had not done the hardest part of the job for them. But the engineer's only answer to the sailor was to suggest that they examine the wall more carefully, from the mouth of the river to the corner where it ended in the north.

So out they went, and the exploration was carried out, over a stretch of about two miles, with the greatest care. But nowhere did the smooth, straight wall show a single hollow of any kind. The nests of the rock pigeons that fluttered about its top turned out to be nothing more than holes bored into the very crest, along the jagged upper edge of the granite.

It was an unfortunate state of affairs, and as for attacking the mass with picks or gunpowder to hollow out a big enough space, that was not to be thought of. As chance would have it, on that whole stretch of the coast Pencroff had found the only shelter fit to live in for the time being — that is, the Chimneys, which they now had to give up after all.

When the exploration was finished, the colonists found themselves at the northern corner of the wall, where it ended in long slopes that ran down and died away on the beach. From there all the way to its western limit, the wall was nothing more than a kind of embankment: a thick mass of stones, earth and sand, bound together by plants, shrubs and grass, and sloping at an angle of only forty-five degrees. Here and there the granite still broke through and jutted out in sharp points from this sort of cliff. Clumps of trees rose in tiers up its slopes, and a fairly thick growth of grass carpeted it. But the vegetation went no farther than that, and a long sandy plain, starting at the foot of the embankment, stretched all the way to the shore.

Cyrus Smith thought, not without reason, that it must be on this side that the lake's overflow spilled out in a waterfall. After all, the surplus water that Red Creek poured in had to escape somewhere. Yet the engineer had not yet found that spot on any part of the shore they had already explored — that is, from the mouth of the creek in the west to Prospect Plateau.

So the engineer suggested to his companions that they climb the slope they were looking at and return to the Chimneys by the heights, exploring the northern and eastern shores of the lake on the way.

The suggestion was accepted, and within a few minutes Harbert and Nab had reached the plateau above. Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff followed at a steadier pace.

Two hundred feet away, through the leaves, the lovely sheet of water was glittering in the sunlight. The landscape was charming there. The trees, their leaves turning yellow, were grouped in the most wonderful way, a real feast for the eyes. A few huge old trunks, felled by age, stood out with their blackish bark against the green carpet that covered the ground. A whole world of noisy cockatoos chattered there — living prisms in motion — hopping from one branch to the next. It was as if the light could only reach the ground broken into its colors by that strange canopy.

Instead of heading straight for the north shore of the lake, the colonists went around the edge of the plateau so as to reach the mouth of the creek on its left bank. It was a detour of a mile and a half at most. The walk was easy, because the trees were widely spaced and left a free passage between them. They could tell that the fertile zone stopped at this boundary, and the vegetation here was less vigorous than in all the land between the creek and the Mercy.

Cyrus Smith and his companions walked with a certain caution over this ground that was new to them. Bows, arrows, and sticks tipped with sharp iron points were their only weapons. No wild beast showed itself, however, and it was likely that such animals kept rather to the thick forests of the south. But the colonists had the unpleasant surprise of seeing Top stop short in front of a large snake, fourteen or fifteen feet long. Nab killed it with a blow of his stick. Cyrus Smith examined the reptile and declared that it was not venomous, since it belonged to the species of diamond snakes that the Aboriginal people of New South Wales eat. But there might well be others whose bite was deadly, such as the deaf adders with forked tails that rear up under your foot, or those winged snakes with two little ear-flaps that let them launch themselves with tremendous speed. Once his first surprise was over, Top went hunting the reptiles so furiously that they feared for him, and his master kept calling him back.

They soon reached the mouth of Red Creek, where it emptied into the lake. On the opposite bank the explorers recognized the spot they had already visited on their way down from Mount Franklin. Cyrus Smith noted that the creek carried a fairly large flow of water. Somewhere, therefore, nature had to have provided an outlet for the lake's overflow. That outlet was what they had to find, for it surely formed a waterfall, and it might be possible to put its mechanical power to use.

So the colonists, walking as they pleased but without straying too far from one another, began to make their way around the shore of the lake, which dropped off very steeply. The water seemed to be teeming with fish, and Pencroff promised himself he would make some fishing tackle to take advantage of it.

First they had to round the sharp northeastern point. One might have supposed that the water drained away there, since the end of the lake came almost up to the edge of the plateau. But that was not so, and the colonists went on exploring the shore, which, after a slight curve, ran back down parallel to the coast.

On this side the bank was less wooded, but a few clumps of trees scattered here and there added to the beauty of the landscape. Lake Grant now lay before them in all its extent, and not a breath of wind ruffled its surface. Top, beating through the brush, flushed flocks of various birds, which Gédéon Spilett and Harbert greeted with their arrows. One of them was even neatly hit by the boy and fell among some marsh grass. Top rushed to it and brought back a handsome swimming bird, slate-colored, with a short beak, a large plate on its forehead, toes widened by a scalloped fringe, and wings edged with a thin white border. It was a coot, about the size of a big partridge, one of the group called macrodactyls, the "long-toed" birds that form the link between the order of wading birds and the order of web-footed ones. Poor game, all in all, and the taste was bound to leave something to be desired. But Top would no doubt be less fussy than his masters, and it was agreed that the coot would be his supper.

The colonists were now following the eastern shore of the lake, and they would soon reach the part they had already surveyed. The engineer was very much surprised, because he could see no sign of the overflow draining away anywhere. The reporter and the sailor were talking with him, and he made no secret of his astonishment.

At that moment Top, who had been perfectly calm until then, began to show signs of agitation. The intelligent animal ran back and forth along the bank, stopped suddenly, and stared at the water with one paw raised, as though he were pointing at some invisible game. Then he barked furiously, as if casting about for a scent, and suddenly fell silent.

At first neither Cyrus Smith nor his companions had paid any attention to Top's behavior. But soon the dog's barking became so frequent that the engineer grew concerned.

"What is it, Top?" he asked.

The dog bounded several times toward his master, clearly and genuinely uneasy, and then dashed back to the bank. Then, all at once, he plunged into the lake.

"Here, Top!" shouted Cyrus Smith, who did not want to let his dog venture into those suspicious waters.

"What on earth is going on down there?" asked Pencroff, studying the surface of the lake.

"Top must have smelled some amphibious animal," answered Harbert.

"An alligator, I suppose?" said the reporter.

"I don't think so," answered Cyrus Smith. "Alligators are found only in lower latitudes."

Top, meanwhile, had come back at his master's call and returned to the bank. But he could not settle down. He kept leaping about in the tall grass, and, guided by his instinct, he seemed to be following some invisible creature that was gliding along under the water, skimming close to the shore. Yet the water was calm, and not a ripple disturbed its surface. Several times the colonists stopped on the bank and watched closely. Nothing appeared. There was some mystery here.

The engineer was greatly intrigued.

"Let's finish this exploration," he said.

Half an hour later they had all reached the southeastern corner of the lake and were back on Prospect Plateau itself. At this point the survey of the lake's shores had to be considered complete — and yet the engineer had not been able to discover where or how the water drained away.

"All the same, that outlet exists," he kept repeating, "and since it isn't on the outside, it must be cut through the inside of the granite mass along the coast!"

"But why does it matter so much to you to find out, my dear Cyrus?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"It matters a good deal," answered the engineer, "because if the water flows out through the rock, there may be some cavity inside it that would be easy to make livable once we had turned the water aside."

"But isn't it possible, Mr. Cyrus," said Harbert, "that the water drains out through the bottom of the lake itself and reaches the sea by an underground channel?"

"That may well be," answered the engineer, "and if it is, we'll have to build our house ourselves, since nature hasn't paid the first costs of construction."

So the colonists were getting ready to cross the plateau and go back to the Chimneys, for it was five o'clock in the evening, when Top showed fresh signs of agitation. He barked furiously, and before his master could stop him, he rushed into the lake a second time.

Everyone ran to the bank. The dog was already more than twenty feet out, and Cyrus Smith was urgently calling him back, when an enormous head rose out of the water, which did not seem to be deep at that spot.

Harbert recognized at once the kind of amphibious animal that head belonged to — conical, with big eyes, and adorned with whiskers of long, silky hairs.

"A manatee!" he cried.

It was not a manatee, but a specimen of the species, classed in the order of cetaceans, that goes by the name of "dugong," for its nostrils opened on the upper part of its snout.

The enormous animal had lunged at the dog, who tried in vain to escape by turning back toward the bank. His master could do nothing to save him, and before it had even occurred to Gédéon Spilett or Harbert to string their bows, Top, seized by the dugong, vanished beneath the water.

Nab, his iron-tipped spear in his hand, was ready to throw himself in to the dog's rescue, determined to take on the formidable animal even in its own element.

"No, Nab," said the engineer, holding back his brave servant.

Meanwhile a struggle was going on under the water — an inexplicable struggle, since in such conditions Top obviously could not hold out; a struggle that had to be terrible, as they could see from the churning of the surface; a struggle, in short, that could only end in the dog's death! But suddenly, in the middle of a ring of foam, Top appeared again. Hurled into the air by some unknown force, he rose ten feet above the surface of the lake, fell back into the wildly churning water, and soon made it back to the bank without any serious wounds, miraculously saved.

Cyrus Smith and his companions stared without understanding. And here was something even more inexplicable! It looked as though the fight was still going on under the water. No doubt the dugong, attacked by some powerful animal after it had let go of the dog, was now fighting for its own life.

But it did not last long. The water turned red with blood, and the dugong's body, rising out of a scarlet slick that spread far and wide, soon ran aground on a little beach at the southern corner of the lake.

The colonists ran to the spot. The dugong was dead. It was an enormous animal, fifteen or sixteen feet long, and it must have weighed three or four thousand pounds. In its neck gaped a wound that seemed to have been made with a sharp blade.

What amphibious creature could have destroyed the formidable dugong with that terrible blow? No one could have said. And, deeply troubled by the incident, Cyrus Smith and his companions went back to the Chimneys.

Chapter 17: The New Waterfall

A visit to the lake — The telltale current — Cyrus Smith's plans — The dugong fat — What to do with pyritic shale — Iron sulfate — How glycerin is made — Soap — Saltpeter — Sulfuric acid — Nitric acid — The new waterfall

The next day, May 7, Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett left Nab to make breakfast and climbed up to Prospect Plateau, while Harbert and Pencroff went up the river to lay in a fresh supply of wood.

The engineer and the reporter soon reached the little beach at the southern tip of the lake where the amphibian had been left stranded. Flocks of birds had already swooped down on that great mass of flesh, and they had to drive them off with stones, because Cyrus Smith wanted to keep the dugong's fat and use it for the needs of the colony. As for the animal's meat, it could not fail to make excellent food, since in certain parts of Malaysia it is kept specially for the tables of the local princes. But that was Nab's business.

At that moment Cyrus Smith had other things on his mind. The incident of the day before had not faded from his thoughts, and it went on troubling him. He would have liked to get to the bottom of that underwater fight, and to know what cousin of the mastodons, or what other sea monster, had given the dugong such a strange wound.

So there he stood on the shore of the lake, watching, observing. But nothing showed itself beneath the calm water, which sparkled in the first rays of the sun.

At the little beach where the dugong's body lay, the water was shallow. But from there on the bottom of the lake sloped gradually downward, and in the middle it was probably very deep. The lake could be thought of as a wide basin that had been filled by the waters of Red Creek.

"Well, Cyrus," said the reporter, "I don't see anything suspicious about this water, do you?"

"No, my dear Spilett," answered the engineer, "and I really don't know how to explain what happened yesterday!"

"I admit," Gédéon Spilett went on, "that the wound on that amphibian is strange, to say the least. And I can't explain either how Top came to be thrown out of the water so violently. You'd really think a powerful arm had flung him out like that, and that the same arm, holding a dagger, had then killed the dugong!"

"Yes," answered the engineer, who had become thoughtful. "There's something here I can't understand. But do you understand any better, my dear Spilett, how I myself was saved — how I could have been pulled out of the waves and carried to the dunes? No, you don't, do you? That's why I sense some mystery here, one we'll no doubt uncover someday. So let's keep watching, but let's not dwell on these odd incidents in front of our companions. Let's keep our observations to ourselves and get on with our work."

As we know, the engineer had not yet been able to find where the lake's overflow escaped. But since he had seen no sign that it ever flooded its banks, there had to be a spillway somewhere. And now, as it happened, Cyrus Smith was rather surprised to notice a fairly strong current that could be felt at that very spot. He threw in a few small pieces of wood and saw that they drifted toward the southern corner. He followed the current, walking along the bank, and came to the southernmost point of the lake.

There the water seemed to sink a little, as though it were suddenly vanishing into some crack in the ground.

Cyrus Smith listened, putting his ear down to the level of the lake, and he heard, quite distinctly, the sound of an underground waterfall.

"That's where it is," he said, getting up again. "That's where the water drains out. That's where, no doubt, it runs through a channel cut in the mass of granite to reach the sea — through some hollows we might be able to put to good use! Well, I'm going to find out!"

The engineer cut a long branch and stripped it of its leaves. By pushing it down into the water at the corner where the two banks met, he found that there was a wide hole opening just one foot below the surface. This hole was the mouth of the spillway they had searched for in vain until then. The current there was so strong that the branch was torn out of the engineer's hands and disappeared.

"There's no doubt about it now," Cyrus Smith said again. "That's the mouth of the spillway, and I'm going to uncover it."

"How?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"By lowering the level of the lake by three feet."

"And how will you lower it?"

"By opening another outlet for the water, a bigger one than this."

"Where, Cyrus?"

"On the part of the shore that comes closest to the coast."

"But that shore is granite!" the reporter pointed out.

"Well then," answered Cyrus Smith, "I'll blow up the granite, and the water, as it rushes out, will drop far enough to uncover this opening..."

"And it'll make a waterfall as it pours down onto the beach," the reporter added.

"A waterfall we'll put to use!" answered Cyrus. "Come on, come on!"

The engineer hurried his companion along, and the reporter's trust in Cyrus Smith was so complete that he did not doubt for a moment that the plan would succeed. And yet — that granite shore — how could they open it? Without gunpowder, and with crude tools, how could they break up that rock? Wasn't the engineer about to throw himself into a task beyond his strength?

When Cyrus Smith and the reporter got back to the Chimneys, they found Harbert and Pencroff busy unloading their timber raft.

"The woodcutters are just about done, Mr. Cyrus," said the sailor with a laugh, "and when you need masons..."

"Not masons — chemists," answered the engineer.

"Yes," added the reporter, "we're going to blow up the island..."

"Blow up the island!" cried Pencroff.

"Part of it, at least!" Gédéon Spilett replied.

"Listen to me, my friends," said the engineer.

And he told them what he had found. In his view, there had to be a hollow of some size inside the mass of granite that held up Prospect Plateau, and he meant to get into it. To do that, they first had to clear the opening through which the water was rushing, and that meant lowering the level of the lake by giving the water a wider way out. Hence the need to make an explosive substance that could cut a deep breach at another point on the shore. That was what Cyrus Smith was going to attempt, using the minerals that nature had put within his reach.

There is no need to say how eagerly they all, and Pencroff above all, greeted this plan. Using drastic measures, tearing open the granite, creating a waterfall — that suited the sailor perfectly! And he would be a chemist just as readily as he had been a mason or a bootmaker, since the engineer needed chemists. He would be anything anybody wanted — "even a teacher of dancing and good manners," he told Nab — if that were ever needed.

Nab and Pencroff were given the first job: removing the dugong's fat and preserving its meat, which was meant for the table. They set off at once, without even asking for any more explanation. Their trust in the engineer was absolute.

A few moments after they left, Cyrus Smith, Harbert, and Gédéon Spilett, dragging the hurdle behind them, went up the river toward the coal seam. There they would find plenty of that pyritic shale — slate-like rock full of iron pyrite — which does indeed turn up in the most recent of the rock layers geologists then called "transition" formations, and of which Cyrus Smith had already brought back a sample.

The whole day was spent hauling a good amount of this pyrite-bearing rock to the Chimneys. By evening they had several tons of it.

The next day, May 8, the engineer began his chemistry. This pyritic shale is made up mainly of carbon, silica, alumina, and iron sulfide, with the iron sulfide in excess. The task was to separate out the iron sulfide and turn it into iron sulfate as quickly as possible. Once they had the sulfate, they would extract sulfuric acid from it.

That was in fact the goal. Sulfuric acid is one of the most widely used of all chemical agents — so much so that a nation's industrial importance can be measured by how much of it the nation consumes. Later on this acid would be enormously useful to the colonists for making candles, tanning hides, and so on. But for the moment the engineer had another use in mind for it.

Behind the Chimneys, Cyrus Smith chose a spot and had the ground carefully leveled. On this ground he laid a heap of branches and chopped wood. On top of it went pieces of the pyritic shale, propped up against one another like the stones of an arch. Then the whole thing was covered with a thin layer of pyrite that had first been broken down to the size of walnuts.

When that was done, they set fire to the wood. Its heat passed to the shale, and the shale caught fire too, since it contained carbon and sulfur. Then fresh layers of crushed pyrite were added, built up into an enormous mound. They left a few vents in it, and covered its outside with earth and grass, just as if they were making charcoal by slowly burning a stack of wood.

Then they let the change take place. It would take no less than ten to twelve days for the iron sulfide to turn into iron sulfate, and the alumina into aluminum sulfate. Both of these substances dissolve in water. The rest — the silica, the burnt carbon, and the ashes — do not.

While this chemical work went on, Cyrus Smith had other jobs done. They put more than zeal into it. It was something close to fury.

Nab and Pencroff had removed the dugong's fat and collected it in big earthenware jars. From this fat the engineer wanted to separate one of its ingredients, glycerin, by saponifying it — that is, by turning it into soap. To get that result, all he had to do was treat it with soda or with lime. Either substance would attack the fat and form a soap, and in doing so would set the glycerin free — and glycerin was exactly what the engineer was after. He had no shortage of lime, as we know. But treating the fat with lime would give only lime soaps, which do not dissolve in water and so are useless. Treating it with soda, on the other hand, would give a soap that did dissolve, one that would come in handy for washing and cleaning around the house. So, being a practical man, Cyrus Smith naturally tried to get soda. Was that difficult? No, because the shore was thick with seaweed and sea plants: glasswort, ice plants, and all the rockweeds and other brown seaweeds that make up kelp and wrack. So they gathered a great quantity of these plants. First they dried them, then they burned them in pits in the open air. The fire was kept going for several days, so that the heat would climb high enough to melt the ashes. The result of all that burning was a solid, grayish mass, long known by the name of "natural soda."

With that in hand, the engineer treated the fat with the soda. This gave him, on one side, a soap that dissolved in water, and on the other, that neutral substance, glycerin.

But that was not all. With an eye to what he meant to prepare later, Cyrus Smith still needed another substance: potassium nitrate, better known as niter, or saltpeter.

Cyrus Smith could have made this substance by treating potassium carbonate — which is easy to extract from the ashes of plants — with nitric acid. But he had no nitric acid, and nitric acid was precisely what he wanted to end up with. So it was a vicious circle, one he could never have broken out of. Very luckily, this time nature was going to hand him the saltpeter, and all he would have to do was pick it up. Harbert found a bed of it in the north of the island, at the foot of Mount Franklin, and all that remained was to purify it.

These various jobs took about eight days. So they were finished before the iron sulfide had finished turning into iron sulfate. In the days that followed, the colonists had time to make fireproof pottery out of potter's clay and to build a brick furnace of a special design, which would be used to distill the iron sulfate once they had it. All this was finished around May 18, at about the same time the chemical change was complete. Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Nab, and Pencroff, skillfully guided by the engineer, had become the handiest workmen in the world. Besides, of all teachers, necessity is the one people listen to most and the one who teaches best.

When the pile of pyrite had been completely burned down, what was left — iron sulfate, aluminum sulfate, silica, leftover carbon, and ashes — was put into a basin full of water. They stirred this mixture, let it settle, and then poured off the liquid. That gave them a clear liquid with the iron sulfate and aluminum sulfate dissolved in it, while the other materials stayed behind as solids, since they do not dissolve. Finally, once part of this liquid had evaporated, crystals of iron sulfate formed and settled out. The mother liquor — that is, the liquid that had not evaporated, which held the aluminum sulfate — was thrown away.

So Cyrus Smith now had a fairly large quantity of these iron sulfate crystals, and the next task was to get sulfuric acid out of them.

In industry, making sulfuric acid takes a costly installation. You need large factories, special equipment, platinum apparatus, and chambers lined with lead, which the acid cannot eat through, where the transformation takes place, and so on. The engineer had none of this equipment. But he knew that in Bohemia in particular, sulfuric acid is made by simpler methods, which even have the advantage of producing it at a higher concentration. That is how the acid known as Nordhausen acid is made.

To get his sulfuric acid, Cyrus Smith now had only one operation left to perform: to heat the iron sulfate crystals strongly in a closed vessel, so that the sulfuric acid would distill off as vapor. That vapor, when it condensed, would then give him the acid.

This was the job the fireproof pottery was for — the crystals were placed inside it — and the furnace, whose heat would distill the sulfuric acid. The operation was carried out perfectly, and on May 20, twelve days after he had begun, the engineer was the owner of the agent he expected to use later in so many different ways.

Now, why did he want this agent? Quite simply to produce nitric acid. And that was easy, since saltpeter, attacked by sulfuric acid, gave him exactly that acid by distillation.

But in the end, what was he going to use this nitric acid for? His companions still did not know, because he had not yet said the last word about his work.

The engineer was nearing his goal, though, and one last operation gave him the substance that had demanded all these preparations.

He took some nitric acid and brought it together with the glycerin, which he had first concentrated by evaporating it in a water bath — a pot set inside a larger pot of hot water. And even without using a freezing mixture to keep it cold, he obtained several pints of an oily, yellowish liquid.

Cyrus Smith had done this last operation alone, off by himself, far from the Chimneys, because there was a danger of explosion. When he brought a flask of the liquid back to his friends, all he said was:

"Here's nitroglycerin!"

It was indeed that terrible product, whose explosive power is perhaps ten times that of ordinary gunpowder, and which has already caused so many accidents! Since a way has been found to turn it into dynamite, though — that is, to mix it with a solid substance, clay or sugar, porous enough to hold it — the dangerous liquid has been used more safely. But dynamite was not yet known at the time when the colonists were at work on Lincoln Island.

"And this stuff is what's going to blow up our rocks?" said Pencroff, looking rather doubtful.

"Yes, my friend," answered the engineer. "And this nitroglycerin will have all the more effect because the granite is extremely hard and will put up that much more resistance to being blown apart."

"And when do we get to see it, Mr. Cyrus?"

"Tomorrow, as soon as we've dug a blasting hole," answered the engineer.

The next day — May 21 — at dawn, the miners went to a point of land that formed the eastern shore of Lake Grant, only five hundred paces from the coast. At that spot the plateau lay lower than the surface of the lake, and the water was held back only by its frame of granite. So it was obvious that if they broke this frame, the water would escape through the gap and form a stream. That stream would run down the sloping surface of the plateau and then plunge over onto the beach. As a result, the level of the whole lake would drop, and the mouth of the spillway would be uncovered — which was the final goal.

So it was the frame they had to break. Under the engineer's direction, Pencroff, armed with a pickax that he swung with skill and strength, attacked the outer face of the granite. The hole they had to drill started from a horizontal ledge on the shore, and it had to slant downward so as to reach a level well below the surface of the lake. That way, when the explosion pushed the rocks apart, the water would be able to pour out freely and drop far enough.

The work took a long time, because the engineer wanted a tremendous effect and meant to put no less than ten liters of nitroglycerin into the blast. But Pencroff, taking turns with Nab, did so well that by four o'clock in the afternoon the blasting hole was finished.

That left the question of how to set off the explosive. Normally nitroglycerin is fired by means of fulminate caps, which explode and so set off the main charge. It takes a shock to make it explode; if it is simply lit, it will burn without blowing up.

Cyrus Smith could certainly have made a cap. In place of fulminate, he could easily have made something like guncotton, since he had nitric acid on hand. Packed into a cartridge and pushed down into the nitroglycerin, this substance would have exploded when lit by a fuse and set off the blast.

But Cyrus Smith knew that nitroglycerin has the property of detonating when it is struck. So he decided to make use of this property, ready to try another method if this one failed.

The fact is that the blow of a hammer on a few drops of nitroglycerin spread on the surface of a hard stone is enough to set off an explosion. But whoever was there to strike the hammer blow would be a victim of the explosion. So Cyrus Smith came up with this idea. Above the blasting hole he set up a post, and from it, on a plant fiber, he hung a lump of iron weighing several pounds. A second long fiber, first soaked in sulfur, was tied by one end to the middle of the first, while its other end trailed along the ground for a distance of several feet from the hole. When this second fiber was lit, it would burn until the flame reached the first. The first fiber would catch fire in its turn and break, and the lump of iron would come crashing down onto the nitroglycerin.

So this apparatus was set up. Then the engineer sent his companions away, filled the blasting hole until the nitroglycerin came right up level with its mouth, and sprinkled a few drops of it on the surface of the rock, just under the hanging lump of iron.

That done, Cyrus Smith took the end of the sulfur-soaked fiber and lit it. Then he left the spot and went back to join his companions at the Chimneys.

The fiber was supposed to burn for twenty-five minutes, and sure enough, twenty-five minutes later, an explosion went off that no words could describe. The whole island seemed to shake on its foundations. A spray of stones shot up into the air as if a volcano had spewed it out. The blast of displaced air was so violent that the rocks of the Chimneys swayed. The colonists, though they were more than two miles from the blast, were knocked flat on the ground.

They got up again, climbed back up to the plateau, and ran toward the spot where the explosion must have torn open the lake's bank...

A triple hurrah burst from their chests! The granite frame had been split wide open! A rapid stream of water was pouring out of it. It raced foaming across the plateau, reached the edge, and plunged three hundred feet down onto the beach!

Chapter 18: Through the Granite

Pencroff doubts nothing anymore — The lake's old spillway — A descent underground — The road through the granite — Top has vanished — The central cavern — The lower well — Mystery — With blows of the pick — The return

Cyrus Smith's plan had succeeded. But, as was his habit, he showed no sign of satisfaction; he stood motionless, lips pressed together, eyes fixed. Harbert was overjoyed. Nab was leaping with delight. Pencroff wagged his big head and muttered:

"Well, well, our engineer sure knows his business!"

And indeed the nitroglycerin had done its work with tremendous force. The breach blown in the lake was so large that the volume of water now pouring out through this new spillway was at least three times what had flowed through the old one. The result had to be that, a short while after the operation, the level of the lake would have dropped by at least two feet.

The colonists went back to the Chimneys to fetch picks, iron-tipped spears, fiber ropes, a flint and steel, and some tinder; then they returned to the plateau. Top went with them.

On the way, the sailor could not keep from saying to the engineer:

"But do you realize, Mr. Cyrus, that with that charming liquid you've made, a person could blow up our whole island?"

"No doubt about it — the island, the continents, and the earth itself," replied Cyrus Smith. "It's only a question of quantity."

"Then couldn't you use this nitroglycerin to load firearms?" asked the sailor.

"No, Pencroff, because it's too violent a substance — it would shatter the gun. But it would be easy to make guncotton, or even ordinary gunpowder, since we have nitric acid, saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal. Unfortunately, it's the guns we don't have."

"Oh, Mr. Cyrus," replied the sailor, "with a little goodwill...!"

There was no doubt about it: Pencroff had struck the word "impossible" out of the dictionary of Lincoln Island.

When they reached Prospect Plateau, the colonists headed straight for the point of the lake near which the mouth of the old spillway opened. By now it ought to be uncovered. And since the water would no longer be rushing into it, the spillway should have become passable, and it would no doubt be easy to find out how it was laid out inside.

In a few moments the colonists had reached the lower corner of the lake, and one glance was enough to tell them that they had got the result they wanted.

There, in the granite wall of the lake and now above the level of the water, appeared the opening they had searched for so long. A narrow ledge, laid bare by the falling water, made it possible to reach it. The opening was about twenty feet wide but only two feet high. It looked like a storm drain in the edge of a sidewalk. So it could not have given the colonists an easy way in; but Nab and Pencroff took up their picks, and in less than an hour they had made it high enough.

The engineer then came closer and saw that, in its upper part, the walls of the spillway sloped at no more than thirty to thirty-five degrees. That meant they could be walked, and as long as the slope did not get steeper it would be easy to climb down them all the way to sea level. And if, as was very likely, some vast hollow existed inside the granite mass, they might find a way to put it to use.

"Well, Mr. Cyrus, what's stopping us?" asked the sailor, impatient to venture into the narrow passage. "You see Top's already gone ahead of us!"

"Fine," replied the engineer. "But we need to be able to see. Nab, go cut some resinous branches."

Nab and Harbert ran to the shores of the lake, which were shaded by pines and other evergreens, and soon came back with branches, which they made up into torches. The torches were lit from the flint and steel, and then, with Cyrus Smith in the lead, the colonists started down the dark tunnel that the lake's overflow had filled not long before.

Contrary to what one might have expected, the tunnel grew wider as it went, so that almost at once the explorers could stand upright as they descended. The granite walls, worn smooth by the water over endless ages, were slippery, and they had to watch out for falls. So the colonists had tied themselves to one another with a rope, the way mountain climbers do. Luckily, some ledges in the granite formed real steps and made the descent less dangerous. Droplets still hanging from the rock glittered in rainbow colors here and there in the torchlight, and one might have thought the walls were covered with countless stalactites. The engineer studied this black granite. He could not see a single layer in it, not a single crack. The mass was solid and extremely fine-grained. So this tunnel dated from the very birth of the island. It was not the water that had hollowed it out little by little. Pluto, the god of the fires underground, and not Neptune, the god of the sea, had bored it with his own hand, and on the wall they could still make out the traces of volcanic action that the scouring of the water had not been able to wipe away entirely.

The colonists went down very slowly. They could not help feeling a certain emotion at venturing like this into the depths of the rock, where human beings had obviously never been before. They did not talk, but they were thinking, and more than one of them must have had the thought that some octopus or other gigantic cephalopod might be living in the hollows inside, since they were connected with the sea. So they had to go forward with a certain caution.

Besides, Top was at the head of the little troop, and they could rely on the dog's keen instincts. He would not fail to give the alarm if there was need.

After they had gone down about a hundred feet, along a rather winding route, Cyrus Smith, who was in front, stopped, and his companions caught up with him. The spot where they had halted was hollowed out to form a cave of modest size. Drops of water were falling from its roof, but they were not seeping through the rock. They were simply the last traces left by the torrent that had roared through this hollow for so long. The air was slightly damp but gave off no foul or poisonous smell.

"Well, my dear Cyrus?" said Gédéon Spilett. "Here's a retreat that nobody knows about, well hidden down in these depths — but when all's said and done, it's not fit to live in."

"Why not fit to live in?" asked the sailor.

"Because it's too small and too dark."

"Can't we make it bigger, dig it out, cut openings in it for daylight and air?" replied Pencroff, who no longer doubted anything.

"Let's go on," replied Cyrus Smith. "Let's go on with our exploring. Maybe lower down nature will have spared us that work."

"We're only a third of the way down so far," Harbert pointed out.

"About a third," replied Cyrus Smith, "since we've come down roughly a hundred feet from the opening, and it isn't impossible that a hundred feet lower..."

"Where's Top?" asked Nab, interrupting his master.

They searched the cave. The dog was not there.

"He's probably gone on ahead," said Pencroff.

"Let's catch up with him," replied Cyrus Smith.

They took up the descent again. The engineer carefully watched every turn the spillway took, and despite its many windings he could keep track fairly easily of its general direction, which was toward the sea.

The colonists had gone down roughly another fifty feet, measured straight down, when their attention was caught by faraway sounds coming up from deep inside the rock. They stopped and listened. Carried along the passage the way a voice travels through a speaking tube, the sounds reached their ears clearly.

"That's Top barking!" cried Harbert.

"Yes," replied Pencroff, "and our good dog's barking like mad!"

"We have our iron-tipped spears," said Cyrus Smith. "Let's be on our guard — and forward!"

"This is getting more and more interesting," Gédéon Spilett murmured into the sailor's ear, and the sailor nodded.

Cyrus Smith and his companions rushed down to help the dog. Top's barking grew louder and louder. There was a strange fury in his jerky, broken yelps. Was he locked in a fight with some animal whose lair he had disturbed? It is fair to say that the colonists, without a thought for the danger they were exposing themselves to, were now in the grip of an irresistible curiosity. They were no longer climbing down the passage; they were practically sliding down its wall. And in a few minutes, sixty feet lower, they had caught up with Top.

There the passage opened into a vast and magnificent cavern. There Top was running back and forth, barking furiously. Pencroff and Nab shook their torches and flung great flashes of light across every jutting point of the granite, while Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, and Harbert stood with their spears raised, ready for anything.

The enormous cavern was empty. The colonists went over it in every direction. There was nothing — not an animal, not a living creature! And yet Top kept on barking. Neither petting nor threats could make him stop.

"There must be an exit somewhere that the lake water drained out through to the sea," said the engineer.

"Right," replied Pencroff, "and let's be careful not to fall into a hole."

"Go on, Top, go on!" cried Cyrus Smith.

The dog, roused by his master's words, ran toward the far end of the cavern, and there his barking doubled.

They followed him, and by the light of the torches they saw the mouth of a real well opening in the granite. This was surely where the water that had once run through the rock used to escape. And this time it was no longer a slanting passage that could be climbed down, but a straight vertical shaft that it would have been impossible to venture into.

They held their torches out over the opening. They could see nothing. Cyrus Smith broke off a burning branch and threw it into the abyss. The blazing resin, which shone all the brighter for the speed of its fall, lit up the inside of the well, but still nothing appeared. Then the flame went out with a faint hiss that showed it had reached a layer of water — that is, sea level.

By timing how long the fall took, the engineer was able to estimate the depth of the well, which turned out to be about ninety feet.

So the floor of the cavern lay ninety feet above sea level.

"Here's our home," said Cyrus Smith.

"But something was living in it," replied Gédéon Spilett, whose curiosity was not satisfied.

"Well, whatever it was, amphibian or something else, it has escaped through this exit," replied the engineer, "and left the place to us."

"All the same," added the sailor, "I'd have liked to be Top a quarter of an hour ago, because he didn't bark like that for no reason!"

Cyrus Smith was looking at his dog, and any of his companions who had come close to him would have heard him murmur these words:
