"Yes, I really do think Top knows more than we do about a good many things!"

Meanwhile, the colonists' wishes had for the most part come true. Chance, helped along by their leader's marvelous shrewdness, had served them well. Here, at their disposal, they had a vast cavern. They could not yet judge its size by the feeble light of the torches, but it would certainly be easy to divide it into rooms with brick partitions and to fit it out, if not as a house, then at least as a roomy apartment. The water had left it and could never come back. The place was theirs.

Two difficulties remained: first, how to bring light into a hollow carved out of solid rock; second, how to make it easier to get in and out. As for light, there was no point in thinking of letting it in from above, since an enormous thickness of granite roofed the cavern over. But perhaps they could cut through the front wall, the one that faced the sea. During the descent Cyrus Smith had judged fairly closely how steep the spillway was, and so how long; and that gave him good reason to believe that the front part of the wall could not be very thick. If they could get light that way, they would get access that way too, since it was just as easy to cut a door as windows, and to set up a ladder on the outside.

Cyrus Smith shared his ideas with his companions.

"Then let's get to work, Mr. Cyrus!" replied Pencroff. "I've got my pick, and I'll find a way to make daylight through that wall. Where do I hit it?"

"Here," replied the engineer, pointing out to the sturdy sailor a fairly deep recess in the wall, which ought to make it thinner at that spot.

Pencroff attacked the granite, and for half an hour, by the light of the torches, he sent chips flying all around him. The rock threw off sparks under his pick. Nab took over from him, and then Gédéon Spilett after Nab.

The work had been going on for two hours already, and they were beginning to fear that at this spot the wall might be thicker than the pick was long, when, at one last blow struck by Gédéon Spilett, the tool went right through the wall and fell outside.

"Hurrah! And hurrah again!" cried Pencroff.

At that point the wall was only three feet thick.

Cyrus Smith came and put his eye to the opening, which was eighty feet above the ground. Before him stretched the edge of the shore, the islet, and beyond it the boundless sea.

The hole was fairly wide, because the rock around it had crumbled a good deal, and through it the light came pouring in and flooded this splendid cavern with a magical effect! On its left side it was no more than thirty feet high and thirty feet wide, over a length of a hundred feet. But on its right side, by contrast, it was enormous, and its vault curved up to a height of more than eighty feet. Here and there, granite pillars, set irregularly, held up the springing of the arches, like those in the nave of a cathedral. Resting on side piers of a sort — here flattening into low round arches, there soaring up on pointed Gothic ribs, vanishing into dark bays whose fanciful arches could just be glimpsed in the shadows, and richly adorned with jutting knobs of rock that hung down like so many pendants — the vault offered a picturesque mixture of everything that Byzantine, Romanesque, and Gothic architecture have ever produced under the hand of man. And yet here it was only the work of nature! Nature alone had hollowed out this fairy-tale Alhambra in a mass of granite!

The colonists were struck dumb with wonder. Where they had expected to find nothing but a cramped hollow, they had found a kind of marvelous palace, and Nab had taken off his hat, as if he had been carried into a temple!

Cries of admiration burst from every mouth. Their hurrahs rang out and went echoing on and on until they died away in the depths of the dark naves.

"Ah, my friends!" cried Cyrus Smith. "Once we've let plenty of light into the inside of this rock, once we've laid out our bedrooms, our storerooms, and our kitchen and pantries in its left-hand part, we'll still have this splendid cavern left over, and we'll make it our study and our museum!"

"And what will we call it?" asked Harbert.

"Granite House," replied Cyrus Smith — a name his companions greeted with another round of hurrahs.

By now the torches were almost completely burned down, and since, to get back, they would have to climb up the passage to the top of the plateau, it was decided to put off until the next day the work of fitting out their new home.

Before leaving, Cyrus Smith came and leaned once more over the dark well that dropped straight down to sea level. He listened closely. There was no sound at all — not even the sound of the water, which the swell must sometimes stir down in those depths. Another flaming piece of resin was thrown down. The walls of the well lit up for a moment, but this time, no more than the first time, nothing suspicious came to light. If some sea monster had been caught by surprise when the water drained away, it had by now made its way back to the open sea through the underground channel that ran on beneath the beach — the channel the lake's overflow had followed before a new exit was opened for it.

Still, the engineer stood motionless, ears straining, eyes fixed on the depths, and did not say a single word.

At last the sailor came up to him and touched his arm.

"Mr. Smith?" he said.

"What is it, my friend?" replied the engineer, as if he were coming back from the land of dreams.

"The torches are about to go out."

"Let's go!" replied Cyrus Smith.

The little troop left the cavern and began its climb up through the dark spillway. Top brought up the rear, still letting out strange growls. The climb was hard going. The colonists stopped for a few moments at the upper cave, which made a kind of landing halfway up this long granite staircase. Then they started climbing again.

Soon they could feel fresher air. The droplets, dried up by evaporation, no longer glittered on the walls. The smoky light of the torches was growing paler. Nab's went out, and if they did not want to find themselves in deep darkness, they had to hurry.

So hurry they did, and a little before four o'clock, just as the sailor's torch went out in its turn, Cyrus Smith and his companions came out through the mouth of the spillway.

Chapter 19: Granite House

Cyrus Smith's plan — The front of Granite House — The rope ladder — Pencroff's dreams — The aromatic herbs — A natural warren — Bringing water to the new home — The view from the windows of Granite House

The next day, May 22, work began on fitting out the new home. The colonists were impatient, in fact, to trade their cramped shelter in the Chimneys for this vast, healthy retreat, hollowed out of the solid rock and safe from both the sea and the sky. The Chimneys were not to be abandoned entirely, though. The engineer meant to turn them into a workshop for the heavy jobs.

Cyrus Smith's first concern was to find out exactly where on the cliff the front of Granite House lay. He went down to the beach at the foot of the enormous wall. The pick that had slipped from the reporter's hands must have fallen straight down, so all they had to do was find the pick, and they would know the spot where the hole had been broken through the granite.

The pick was easily found. And sure enough, a hole opened in a straight vertical line above the place where it had stuck in the sand, about eighty feet above the beach. A few rock pigeons were already flying in and out through that narrow opening. It really seemed as if Granite House had been discovered for their sake!

The engineer intended to divide the right-hand portion of the cavern into several rooms, opening off an entrance corridor, and to light it with five windows and a door cut through the face of the cliff. Pencroff was fine with the five windows, but he could not see the use of the door, since the old spillway gave them a natural staircase by which they could always get into Granite House easily.

"My friend," Cyrus Smith answered him, "if it's easy for us to reach our home through the spillway, it will be just as easy for others. On the contrary, I plan to block the spillway at its mouth and seal it up tight. If necessary, I'll even hide the entrance completely by building a dam and raising the level of the lake."

"Then how will we get in?" asked the sailor.

"By a ladder on the outside," replied Cyrus Smith. "A rope ladder. Once it's pulled up, no one will be able to reach our home."

"But why all these precautions?" said Pencroff. "So far the animals haven't seemed all that dangerous. And as for natives, there aren't any on our island!"

"Are you quite sure of that, Pencroff?" asked the engineer, looking straight at the sailor.

"Well, obviously we won't be sure until we've explored every part of it," Pencroff answered.

"Exactly," said Cyrus Smith, "because so far we know only a small part of it. But in any case, even if we have no enemies inside the island, they may come from outside it. These waters of the Pacific are bad waters. So let's take our precautions against anything that might happen."

Cyrus Smith was talking sense, and Pencroff, without raising any further objection, got ready to carry out his orders.

So the front of Granite House was to be lit by five windows and a door, serving what made up the "apartment," properly speaking, and also by one wide bay and a row of small round windows that would let light pour into that marvelous nave, which was to serve as the great hall. This front, eighty feet above the ground, faced east, and the rising sun greeted it with its first rays. It stretched along the section of the cliff wall that lay between the projecting corner over the mouth of the Mercy and a line drawn straight up from the heap of rocks that formed the Chimneys. That meant the bad winds — the ones from the northeast — struck it only at a slant, because the very angle of that projecting corner sheltered it. Besides, until the window frames could be made, the engineer planned to close the openings with thick shutters that would let through neither wind nor rain, and that he could disguise if he needed to.

The first job, then, was to hollow out these openings. Working that hard rock with a pick would have been too slow, and Cyrus Smith, as we know, was a man for big methods. He still had a certain amount of nitroglycerin on hand, and he put it to good use. The explosive's effect was properly confined, and under its force the granite broke open at the very places the engineer had chosen. Then pick and mattock finished shaping the pointed Gothic arches of the five windows, the big bay, the round windows, and the door. They trimmed and squared the frames, whose outlines came out rather fanciful, and a few days after the work began, Granite House was flooded with the light of the eastern sky, which reached into its most hidden depths.

Under the plan Cyrus Smith had settled on, the apartment was to be divided into five compartments, all looking out over the sea. On the right came an entrance hall served by a door, where the ladder would end. Next came a first room, thirty feet wide, which would be the kitchen; then a dining room forty feet wide; then a bedroom just as wide; and finally a "guest room," which Pencroff had insisted on, and which lay next to the great hall.

These rooms — or rather this row of rooms that made up the apartment of Granite House — were not meant to fill the whole depth of the cavern. A corridor was to run behind them, between the rooms and a long storeroom, where the tools, the provisions, and the reserves would all find plenty of space. Everything gathered on the island, plant or animal, would keep there in excellent condition, completely protected from damp. There was no shortage of room, and every item could be stored in proper order. On top of that, the colonists still had the small cave above the great cavern, which would serve as the attic of their new house.

With the plan settled, all that remained was to carry it out. So the miners turned brickmakers once again, and the bricks were brought over and stacked at the foot of Granite House.

Until now Cyrus Smith and his companions had been able to get into the cavern only by way of the old spillway. To do that, they first had to climb to Prospect Plateau by a roundabout path along the riverbank, then go down two hundred feet through the tunnel, and climb back up just as far whenever they wanted to return to the plateau. All that cost a lot of time and a great deal of effort. So Cyrus Smith decided to get on at once with making a strong rope ladder, which, once it was pulled up, would make the entrance to Granite House absolutely impossible to reach.

This ladder was made with enormous care. Its two side ropes were braided from the fibers of the kurrajong, twisted together with a hand-turned winch, and they were as strong as a heavy cable. As for the rungs, they came from a kind of red cedar whose branches were light but tough. Pencroff did the work, and he did it like a master.

Other ropes were made from plant fibers too, and a rough block and tackle was rigged at the door. That way the bricks could easily be hoisted up to the level of Granite House. Moving the materials became much simpler, and the work on the inside began right away. There was plenty of lime, and several thousand bricks lay ready for use. They had no trouble putting up the framework for the partitions — a very simple one, as it happened — and in a very short time the apartment was divided into rooms and a storeroom, just as planned.

All this work went quickly under the direction of the engineer, who handled the hammer and the trowel himself. No kind of manual labor was foreign to Cyrus Smith, and in this way he set an example for companions who were intelligent and eager. They worked with confidence, even cheerfully. Pencroff always had a joke ready — carpenter one moment, ropemaker the next, mason after that — and he spread his good humor through their whole little world. His faith in the engineer was absolute. Nothing could have shaken it. He believed Smith could take on anything and succeed at everything. The question of clothes and shoes — a serious question, certainly — the question of light through the winter nights, the farming of the fertile parts of the island, the transformation of this wild plant life into cultivated crops: all of it looked easy to him, with Cyrus Smith's help, and all of it would be done in its own good time. He dreamed of rivers turned into canals to carry the wealth of the soil, of quarries and mines to be opened, of machines for every kind of industry, of railroads — yes, railroads! — whose network would surely cover Lincoln Island one day.

The engineer let Pencroff talk. He did not trim back a single one of that good-hearted man's exaggerations. He knew how catching confidence is. He even smiled to hear him, and he said nothing of the worries the future sometimes gave him. For in this part of the Pacific, far from the shipping lanes, he had reason to fear that help might never come. The colonists would have to rely on themselves, on themselves alone, because Lincoln Island lay so far from any other land that to venture out in a boat — and any boat they built would be a makeshift one — would be a serious and dangerous business.

"But," as the sailor said, "they stood a hundred cubits above the Robinsons of the old days, who had to work a miracle for every single thing."

And in fact, they "knew." And the man who "knows" succeeds where others would merely scrape by, and would inevitably die.

During all this work Harbert distinguished himself. He was intelligent and active, quick to understand and good at carrying things out, and Cyrus Smith grew more and more attached to the boy. Harbert, for his part, felt a warm and respectful friendship for the engineer. Pencroff could see perfectly well the close bond forming between the two of them, but he was not the least bit jealous.

Nab was Nab. He was what he would always be: courage, eagerness, devotion, and self-forgetfulness in person. He had the same faith in his master as Pencroff did, but he showed it less noisily. Whenever the sailor got carried away with enthusiasm, Nab always looked as though he were answering, "But what could be more natural?" He and Pencroff were very fond of each other, and they had soon dropped all formality between them.

As for Gédéon Spilett, he did his share of the common work, and he was not the clumsiest of them, either — which never stopped surprising the sailor a little. A "journalist" who was clever not just at understanding everything, but at doing everything!

The ladder was finally put in place on May 28. It had no fewer than a hundred rungs over the eighty feet of sheer height it covered. Luckily Cyrus Smith had been able to divide it into two sections by taking advantage of an overhang in the wall that jutted out about forty feet above the ground. This ledge, carefully leveled with the pick, became a kind of landing. The first ladder was fastened to it, which cut the ladder's swing in half, and a rope made it possible to haul that lower ladder up to the level of Granite House. As for the second ladder, it was made fast both at its lower end, which rested on the ledge, and at its upper end, which was tied to the door itself. That made the climb a good deal easier. Besides, Cyrus Smith meant to install a hydraulic elevator later on, which would spare the inhabitants of Granite House all that effort and lost time.

The colonists quickly got used to the ladder. They were nimble and skillful, and Pencroff, as a sailor used to running up the ratlines of a ship's rigging, was able to give them lessons. But he had to give lessons to Top as well. The poor dog, with his four paws, was not built for this kind of exercise. Pencroff, however, was such a devoted teacher that Top ended up making his climbs quite respectably, and he was soon going up the ladder the way his fellow dogs do every day in the circus. How proud the sailor was of his pupil, words cannot say. Still, more than once, Pencroff carried him up on his back, and Top never complained about that.

It should be pointed out here that during all this work — and it was pushed hard, since the bad season was coming — the food question had not been neglected. Every day the reporter and Harbert, who had now definitely become the colony's suppliers, spent a few hours hunting. So far they had worked only Jacamar Wood, on the left bank of the river, because without a bridge or a boat no one had crossed the Mercy yet. All those immense forests that had been given the name of the Far West forests were still unexplored. That important expedition was being saved for the first fine days of the coming spring. But Jacamar Wood had game enough. Kangaroos and wild boars were plentiful there, and the hunters' iron-tipped spears, bow, and arrows did wonders. What was more, near the southwest corner of the lagoon, Harbert discovered a natural warren — a sort of slightly damp meadow covered with willows and aromatic herbs that perfumed the air: thyme, wild thyme, basil, savory, all the fragrant plants of the mint family that rabbits are so fond of.

The reporter remarked that, since the table was so clearly laid for rabbits, it would be surprising if the rabbits failed to show up, and the two hunters explored this warren carefully. In any case, it grew useful plants in abundance, and a naturalist would have found plenty of specimens of the plant kingdom to study there. Harbert gathered a good quantity of shoots of basil, rosemary, lemon balm, betony, and others, which have various medicinal properties: some good for the chest, some astringent, some for bringing down fevers, others for easing cramps or rheumatism. And when Pencroff later asked what all this harvest of herbs was for:

"To take care of us," the boy answered, "to treat us when we're sick."

"Why would we get sick, when there aren't any doctors on the island?" Pencroff replied, perfectly seriously.

There was no answer to that. But the boy gathered his harvest all the same, and it was very well received at Granite House — all the more because, along with these medicinal plants, he was able to bring in a good amount of bee balm, Monarda didyma, the plant known in North America as "Oswego tea," which makes an excellent drink.

At last, that day, by searching hard, the two hunters came upon the actual site of the warren. The ground there was riddled with holes like a colander.

"Burrows!" cried Harbert.

"Yes," the reporter replied, "I can see them."

"But is anybody living in them?"

"That's the question."

The question was soon answered. Almost at once, hundreds of little animals that looked like rabbits went scattering in every direction, so fast that even Top could not have outrun them. Hunters and dog ran their hardest, but the rodents got away from them with ease. The reporter, however, was determined not to leave the spot before he had caught at least half a dozen of these animals. He wanted to stock the larder with them first, and later on they could tame any they caught. With a few snares set at the mouths of the burrows, the operation could not fail. But at that moment they had no snares, and nothing to make them with. So they had to resign themselves to visiting every hole, poking around in it with a stick, and doing by sheer patience what they could not do any other way.

At last, after an hour of digging around, four of the rodents were caught in their holes. They were rabbits quite like their European cousins, commonly known as "American rabbits."

So the day's catch was carried back to Granite House, and it appeared at supper that evening. The residents of that warren were not to be sneezed at, for they were delicious. Here was a precious resource for the colony, and one that looked as if it would never run out.

On May 31 the partitions were finished. All that was left was to furnish the rooms, which would be the work of the long winter days. A fireplace was built in the first room, which served as the kitchen. The pipe that was to carry the smoke outside gave the makeshift stove-fitters some trouble. Cyrus Smith thought it simplest to make it out of brick clay. Since there could be no question of running it out through the plateau above, they drilled a hole in the granite over the kitchen window, and the pipe, slanting upward, ended at that hole, like the pipe of a sheet-iron stove. Perhaps — very likely, in fact — the chimney would smoke whenever the strong east winds blew straight against the front of the cliff. But those winds were rare, and anyway Master Nab, the cook, was not so particular.

When this work inside was done, the engineer turned to blocking the mouth of the old spillway where it opened onto the lake, so as to shut off any way in by that route. Blocks of rock were rolled into the opening and firmly cemented. Cyrus Smith did not yet carry out the plan he had made to drown that opening under the waters of the lake by raising them back to their old level with a dam. For now he was content to hide the blockage with grasses, shrubs, and brush, planted in the cracks between the rocks, which the coming spring would make grow thick and wild.

He did, however, use the spillway to bring a thin stream of the lake's fresh water all the way down to their new home. A small channel cut below the surface of the lake did the job, and this branch of a pure, never-failing source delivered twenty-five to thirty gallons a day. So Granite House would never be short of water.

At last everything was finished — and none too soon, for the bad season was coming on. Thick shutters could close the windows in the front of the cliff until the engineer had time to make window glass.

Gédéon Spilett had very artistically arranged plants of all kinds in the projections of the rock around the windows, along with long, trailing grasses, so that the openings were framed in picturesque greenery that looked charming.

The inhabitants of this solid, healthy, and safe home could only be delighted with their work. From the windows their gaze could roam over a boundless horizon, closed off to the north by the two Mandible Capes and to the south by Claw Cape. All of Union Bay spread out magnificently before them. Yes, these good colonists had every reason to be satisfied, and Pencroff was not stingy in his praise of what he jokingly called "his apartment on the fifth floor above the mezzanine!"

Chapter 20: The Rainy Season

The rainy season — The question of clothing — A seal hunt — Making candles — Work inside Granite House — The two little bridges — Back from a visit to the oyster bed — What Harbert finds in his pocket

Winter truly began with the month of June, which in this hemisphere corresponds to December in the northern one. It opened with showers and squalls that followed one another without a break. The residents of Granite House could now appreciate the advantages of a home that no bad weather could touch. The shelter of the Chimneys would have been far too poor a refuge against the hardships of a winter, and there was reason to fear that the high tides, driven by winds from the open sea, might break into it again. Cyrus Smith even took a few precautions against that possibility, to protect as well as he could the forge and the furnaces that were set up there.

All through June, the time went into all sorts of work, which left room for both hunting and fishing, and the pantry's stores could be kept amply supplied. As soon as he had the leisure, Pencroff meant to set up traps, from which he expected great things. He had already made snares out of woody fibers, and not a day went by without the warren supplying its share of rodents. Nab spent nearly all his time salting or smoking meat, which kept him in excellent preserved provisions.

The question of clothing now came up for very serious discussion. The colonists had no clothes but the ones they had been wearing when the balloon threw them onto the island. Those clothes were warm and sturdy. They had taken the greatest care of them, and of their underclothes too, and they kept everything perfectly clean. But all of it would soon need replacing. Besides, if the winter turned out to be harsh, the colonists would suffer badly from the cold.

On this point, Cyrus Smith's ingenuity had come up short. He had had to see to the most urgent things first, to build the home and make sure of the food supply, and the cold might catch him before the question of clothing was solved. So they would just have to resign themselves to getting through this first winter without complaining too much. When the fine season came, they would go hunting in earnest for the mouflons whose presence had been noticed during the exploration of Mount Franklin, and once the wool was gathered, the engineer would surely know how to make warm, sturdy cloth out of it... How? He would think about that.

"Well, we'll just have to toast our shins by the fire in Granite House!" said Pencroff. "There's fuel everywhere, and no reason to go easy on it."

"Besides," said Gédéon Spilett, "Lincoln Island doesn't lie in a very high latitude, and the winters here probably aren't severe. Didn't you tell us, Cyrus, that this thirty-fifth parallel corresponds to the latitude of Spain in the other hemisphere?"

"Certainly," answered the engineer, "but some winters are very cold in Spain! Snow and ice, nothing missing, and Lincoln Island may be tested just as hard. Still, this is an island, and being an island, I hope its temperature will be milder."

"Why is that, Mr. Cyrus?" asked Harbert.

"Because the sea, my boy, can be thought of as an immense reservoir in which the heat of summer is stored up. When winter comes, the sea gives that heat back, and so the regions near the oceans enjoy a moderate average temperature — not as hot in summer, but not as cold in winter."

"We'll see," said Pencroff. "Personally, I don't intend to worry about how cold it will or won't be. What's certain is that the days are already short and the evenings long. Suppose we took up the question of lighting?"

"Nothing could be easier," said Cyrus Smith.

"To take up?" asked the sailor.

"To solve."

"And when do we start?"

"Tomorrow, with a seal hunt."

"To make tallow candles?"

"Tallow? For shame, Pencroff! Proper candles — stearin candles."

That was indeed the engineer's plan, and it was a workable one, since he had lime and sulfuric acid, and the amphibians on the islet would furnish the fat he needed to make them.

It was June 4. It was Pentecost Sunday, and everyone agreed to keep the holiday. All work stopped, and prayers rose toward heaven. But these prayers were now prayers of thanks. The colonists of Lincoln Island were no longer the wretched castaways who had been flung onto the islet. They no longer asked; they gave thanks.

The next day, June 5, in rather uncertain weather, they set out for the islet. Once again they had to wait for low tide to wade across the channel, and on that subject it was agreed that they would build a boat of some sort, however rough, which would make getting back and forth easier and would also let them travel up the Mercy during the great exploration of the island's southwest, which had been put off until the first fine days.

The seals were plentiful, and the hunters, armed with their iron-tipped spears, easily killed half a dozen. Nab and Pencroff skinned them and carried back to Granite House only their fat and their skins, the skins being meant for making sturdy shoes.

The result of this hunt was as follows: about three hundred pounds of fat, all of which was to go into making candles.

The process was extremely simple, and if it did not give perfect results, the candles were at least usable. Even if Cyrus Smith had had nothing but sulfuric acid at his disposal, he could have heated that acid with the neutral fat — in this case the seal fat — and separated out the glycerin. Then, from the new compound, he could easily have separated the olein, the margarin, and the stearin by using boiling water. But to keep the operation simple, he chose to saponify the fat with lime. In this way he obtained a lime soap, which sulfuric acid easily broke down: the acid made the lime settle out as calcium sulfate and set the fatty acids free.

Of these three acids — oleic, margaric, and stearic — the first, being liquid, was squeezed out under enough pressure. The other two together made up the very substance that would be molded into candles.

The whole operation took no more than twenty-four hours. After several trials, the wicks were made of plant fibers, and when they were dipped in the melted substance, they produced genuine stearin candles, molded by hand, which lacked nothing but bleaching and polishing. They did not, of course, have the advantage of wicks soaked in boric acid, which turn to glass little by little as they burn and so are consumed completely. But Cyrus Smith made a fine pair of snuffers, and these candles were greatly appreciated during the long evenings at Granite House.

All that month there was no shortage of work inside the new home. The joiners had plenty to do. The tools, which were very rough, were improved. More were added to them, too.

Among other things, scissors were made, and the colonists could at last cut their hair, and if not shave their beards, at least trim them as they pleased. Harbert had none, and Nab hardly any, but their companions were bristling with enough of it to justify making the scissors.

Making a handsaw — the kind called a panel saw — cost endless trouble, but in the end they had a tool that, worked hard enough, could cut through the fibers of wood. So they made tables, seats, and cupboards to furnish the main rooms, and bed frames whose only bedding was mattresses of eelgrass. The kitchen, with its shelves holding the earthenware utensils, its brick stove, and its stone sink for the washing up, looked very fine, and Nab went about his business there with great solemnity, as if he were working in a chemist's laboratory.

But the joiners soon had to give way to the carpenters. The new spillway, blasted open with explosives, made it necessary to build two little bridges, one on Prospect Plateau and the other down on the beach itself. Now, in fact, both the plateau and the beach were cut straight across by a stream that had to be crossed by anyone who wanted to reach the north of the island. To avoid it, the colonists would have had to make a long detour, going west until they were beyond the springs of Red Creek. The simplest thing, then, was to put two little bridges across, one on the plateau and one on the beach, each twenty to twenty-five feet long, whose entire framework was just a few tree trunks squared off with the ax. It took only a few days. Once the bridges were in place, Nab and Pencroff used them to go as far as the oyster bed that had been found off the dunes. They pulled along with them a sort of rough cart, which replaced the old hurdle, since that had really been too awkward, and they brought back a few thousand oysters. These quickly took to their new home among the rocks at the mouth of the Mercy, which made so many natural oyster pens. The oysters were of excellent quality, and the colonists ate them almost every day.

As you can see, Lincoln Island, although its inhabitants had explored only a very small part of it, already supplied almost all their needs. And it was likely that, searched down to its most hidden corners — all across the wooded country stretching from the Mercy to Reptile End — it would pour out new treasures.

Only one hardship still weighed on the colonists of Lincoln Island. They had no lack of meat, the nitrogen-rich food, nor of the vegetable foods that ought to balance it. The woody roots of the dragon trees, left to ferment, gave them a sour drink, a sort of beer far better than plain water. They had even made sugar, without sugarcane or beets, by collecting the sap that flows from "Acer saccharinum," a kind of maple, of the family Aceraceae, that thrives in every temperate zone, and of which the island had a great many. They made a very pleasant tea from the bee balm brought back from the warren. And they had plenty of salt, the only mineral that is part of the human diet... But they had no bread.

Perhaps, later on, the colonists could replace that food with some substitute, sago-palm flour or the starch of the breadfruit tree. And it was possible, in fact, that the southern forests might count some of those precious trees among their species, but so far none had been found.

Yet in this matter Providence was to come straight to the colonists' aid — in an infinitesimal amount, it is true, but still: Cyrus Smith, with all his intelligence and all his ingenuity, could never have produced what Harbert found one day, by the purest chance, in the lining of his jacket, which he was busy mending.

That day — it was pouring rain — the colonists were gathered in the great hall of Granite House when the boy suddenly cried out:

"Look, Mr. Cyrus! A grain of wheat!"

And he showed his companions a grain, one single grain, which had slipped from his torn pocket into the lining of his jacket.

The grain was there because Harbert, back in Richmond, had been in the habit of feeding some wood pigeons that Pencroff had given him.

"A grain of wheat?" the engineer said quickly.

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus, but just one, only one!"

"Well, my boy," cried Pencroff with a smile, "that gets us a long way, I must say! What could we possibly do with one grain of wheat?"

"We'll make bread out of it," answered Cyrus Smith.

"Bread, cakes, pies!" retorted the sailor. "Come on! The bread this grain of wheat gives us won't choke us anytime soon!"

Harbert, attaching very little importance to his discovery, was about to throw the grain away, but Cyrus Smith took it, examined it, saw that it was in good condition, and, looking the sailor straight in the eye, asked him calmly:

"Pencroff, do you know how many ears a grain of wheat can produce?"

"One, I suppose!" answered the sailor, surprised by the question.

"Ten, Pencroff. And do you know how many grains an ear carries?"

"No, I can't say I do."

"Eighty on average," said Cyrus Smith. "So if we plant this grain, at the first harvest we'll reap eight hundred grains. Those will produce six hundred and forty thousand at the second harvest, five hundred and twelve million at the third, and at the fourth more than four hundred billion grains. That's the proportion."

Cyrus Smith's companions listened without answering. The figures stunned them. And yet they were exact.

"Yes, my friends," the engineer went on. "Such are the arithmetical progressions of fruitful nature. And even so, what is this multiplication of the grain of wheat, whose ear carries only eight hundred grains, compared with the poppy plants that bear thirty-two thousand seeds, or the tobacco plants that produce three hundred and sixty thousand? Within a few years, if it weren't for the many causes of destruction that hold their fertility in check, those plants would overrun the whole earth."

But the engineer had not finished his little cross-examination.

"And now, Pencroff," he went on, "do you know how many bushels four hundred billion grains make?"

"No," answered the sailor, "but what I do know is that I'm nothing but a dunce!"

"Well, it would come to more than three million, at a hundred and thirty thousand grains to the bushel, Pencroff."

"Three million!" cried Pencroff.

"Three million."

"In four years?"

"In four years," answered Cyrus Smith, "and even in two, if, as I hope, we can get two harvests a year in this latitude."

To that, as was his habit, Pencroff could think of no reply but a tremendous hurrah.

"So, Harbert," the engineer added, "you've made a discovery of the greatest importance to us. Everything, my friends, everything can be of use to us in the situation we're in. Please don't forget it."

"No, Mr. Cyrus, no, we won't forget it," answered Pencroff. "And if I ever find one of those tobacco seeds that multiply by three hundred and sixty thousand, I promise you I won't throw it to the wind! And now, do you know what we have left to do?"

"We have to plant this grain," answered Harbert.

"Yes," added Gédéon Spilett, "and with all the respect it deserves, because it carries our future harvests inside it."

"If only it grows!" cried the sailor.

"It will grow," answered Cyrus Smith.

It was June 20. So the time was right for sowing that single, precious grain of wheat. At first there was talk of planting it in a pot. But on reflection they decided to trust nature more boldly and give it to the earth. That was done the very same day, and there is no need to add that every precaution was taken to make the operation succeed.

The weather having cleared a little, the colonists climbed to the heights above Granite House. There, on the plateau, they chose a spot well sheltered from the wind, where the noonday sun would pour down all its warmth. The spot was cleared, carefully weeded, and even dug over to drive out any insects or worms. They laid down a bed of good soil improved with a little lime. They put a fence around it. Then the grain was pressed down into the moist bed.

Didn't it seem as if these colonists were laying the cornerstone of a building? It reminded Pencroff of the day he had struck his one and only match, and of all the care he had taken over that operation. But this time the matter was more serious. For the castaways would always have managed to get fire, by one means or another, but no human power could ever give them back this grain of wheat if, by bad luck, it should die!

Chapter 21: A Few Degrees Below Zero

A few degrees below zero — Exploring the marshy southeast — The culpeos — A view of the sea — A conversation about the future of the Pacific Ocean — The ceaseless work of the infusoria — What will become of the globe — The hunt — Shelduck Marsh

From that moment on, not a single day went by without Pencroff paying a visit to what he called, in all seriousness, his "wheat field." And woe to any insect that ventured into it! It could expect no mercy.

Toward the end of June, after endless rains, the weather turned decidedly cold. On the 29th a Fahrenheit thermometer would certainly have read no more than twenty degrees.

The next day, June 30, which corresponds to December 31 in the northern year, was a Friday. Nab remarked that the year was ending on an unlucky day. But Pencroff answered that, naturally, the next one would begin on a lucky one, which was better.

In any case, it began with a very sharp cold. Chunks of ice piled up at the mouth of the Mercy, and before long the lake froze over from end to end.

The supply of fuel had to be renewed several times. Pencroff had not waited for the river to freeze before bringing enormous timber rafts down to where they were needed. The current was a tireless engine, and it was put to work carrying driftwood until the cold came and chained it up. To the fuel the forest provided so generously, the colonists also added several cartloads of coal, which had to be fetched from the foot of the spurs of Mount Franklin. The powerful heat of the coal was warmly appreciated when the temperature fell, on July 4, to eight degrees Fahrenheit. A second fireplace had been built in the dining room, and there they all worked together.

During this cold spell Cyrus Smith had every reason to congratulate himself on having brought a small stream of Lake Grant's water down to Granite House. The water was drawn from below the frozen surface and led through the old spillway, so it stayed liquid. It arrived in an inside reservoir, which had been dug out at the corner of the back storeroom, and the overflow ran away down the well to the sea.

About this time, the weather being extremely dry, the colonists, dressed as warmly as they could manage, decided to spend a day exploring the part of the island that lay to the southeast, between the Mercy and Claw Cape. It was a vast stretch of marshland, and there might be good hunting there, since water birds were bound to swarm in it.

They reckoned on eight or nine miles out and as many back, so the day would be well used. And since it also meant exploring an unknown part of the island, the whole colony had to take part. So on July 5, at six in the morning, with dawn barely breaking, Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Nab and Pencroff left Granite House, armed with spears, snares, bows and arrows and carrying enough provisions, with Top frisking ahead of them.

They took the shortest way, and the shortest way was to cross the Mercy on the ice that was then choking it.

"But," the reporter rightly observed, "this is no substitute for a real bridge!"

And so the building of a "real" bridge was added to the list of jobs to be done.

It was the first time the colonists had set foot on the right bank of the Mercy and ventured among those tall, magnificent conifers, now covered in snow.

But they had not gone half a mile when a whole family of four-footed animals burst out of a thick clump of brush where they had made their home. Top's barking had put them to flight.

"Oh! They look like foxes!" cried Harbert, as he watched the whole band clear out as fast as they could go.

They were foxes, as it happened, but very large ones, and they made a sort of barking sound that seemed to astonish Top himself. He stopped short in his chase and gave the swift animals time to disappear.

The dog had a right to be surprised, since he knew no natural history. But by their barking these foxes, reddish gray in coat, with black tails ending in a white tuft, had given away who they were. Harbert gave them their true name without a moment's hesitation: "culpeos." Culpeos are often found in Chile, in the Falklands, and all along the American coasts that lie between the thirtieth and fortieth parallels. Harbert was very sorry that Top had not managed to catch one of these carnivores.

"Can you eat them?" asked Pencroff, who never looked at the island's wildlife from more than one particular point of view.

"No," answered Harbert, "but zoologists still haven't settled whether the pupil of these foxes' eyes is made for day or for night, or whether they ought to be classed with the dogs proper."

Cyrus Smith could not help smiling at the boy's remark, which showed a serious mind. As for the sailor, once these foxes could not be classed in the edible genus, he did not care what they were. All the same, he pointed out that when a poultry yard was set up at Granite House, it would be wise to take a few precautions against probable visits from these four-legged robbers. Nobody disagreed.

After rounding Jetsam Point, the colonists came upon a long beach washed by the open sea. It was then eight o'clock in the morning. The sky was perfectly clear, as it often is in long spells of hard cold. But Cyrus Smith and his companions, warmed by their walk, did not feel the sting of the air too sharply. Besides, there was no wind, and that makes a deep drop in temperature far easier to bear. A brilliant sun, which gave no warmth at all, was just rising out of the ocean, and its enormous disk hung swaying on the horizon. The sea lay smooth and blue, like a Mediterranean bay under a clear sky. Claw Cape, curved like a scimitar, tapered to a sharp point some four miles off to the southeast. To the left, the edge of the marsh ended abruptly at a little point of land that the sun's rays were now outlining in a line of fire. Certainly, in this part of Union Bay, with nothing to shelter it from the open sea, not even a sandbank, ships beaten by the east winds would have found no refuge at all. From the calm of the sea, which no shoals disturbed, from its even color, unspotted by any yellowish tinge, and above all from the absence of any reef, you could tell that this coast dropped off steeply and that the ocean covered deep abysses here. Behind them, to the west, the first lines of trees of the Far West forests rose, but four miles away. You might almost have thought you were on the desolate coast of some island in the Antarctic, overrun by ice. The colonists halted there for lunch. They lit a fire of brushwood and dried wrack, and Nab prepared a lunch of cold meat, adding a few cups of Oswego tea.

As they ate, they looked around them. This part of Lincoln Island really was barren, a sharp contrast to the whole western region. That led the reporter to remark that if chance had first thrown the castaways onto this beach, they would have formed a dismal idea of their future domain.

"I don't think we could even have reached it," the engineer answered, "because the sea here is deep, and it didn't offer us a single rock to take refuge on. In front of Granite House, at least, there were sandbanks and an islet, and they multiplied our chances of being saved. Here there's nothing but the abyss!"

"It's rather odd," observed Gédéon Spilett, "that an island this small should have such varied ground. Logically, that kind of diversity belongs only to continents of a certain size. You'd really think that the western part of Lincoln Island, so rich and fertile, was washed by the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico, while its northern and southeastern shores stretched along some kind of Arctic sea."

"You're right, my dear Spilett," Cyrus Smith replied. "I've noticed it too. I find this island strange, in its shape as much as in its nature. It's like a summary of every aspect a continent can show, and I wouldn't be surprised if it had once been a continent."

"What! A continent in the middle of the Pacific?" cried Pencroff.

"Why not?" answered Cyrus Smith. "Why shouldn't Australia, New Ireland, everything the English geographers call Australasia, together with the archipelagos of the Pacific, once have formed a sixth part of the world, as important as Europe or Asia, as Africa or the two Americas? My mind has no trouble accepting that all the islands rising out of this vast ocean are nothing but the peaks of a continent now sunk beneath it, a continent that stood above the waters in prehistoric times."

"Like Atlantis long ago," said Harbert.

"Yes, my boy... if it ever existed, that is."

"And Lincoln Island would have been part of that continent?" asked Pencroff.

"Probably," answered Cyrus Smith, "and that would go a long way toward explaining the variety of things we see growing on it."

"And the large number of animals that still live here," Harbert added.

"Yes, my boy," the engineer replied, "and you've just handed me a new argument in support of my theory. From what we've seen, it's certain that there are a great many animals on the island, and, what's stranger, that the species are extremely varied. There's a reason for that, and in my view it's that Lincoln Island may once have been part of some vast continent that has slowly sunk beneath the Pacific."

"Then one fine day," Pencroff retorted, not seeming entirely convinced, "what's left of that old continent may disappear in its turn, and there'll be nothing at all between America and Asia?"

"Not so," answered Cyrus Smith. "There'll be the new continents that billions upon billions of tiny animals are working to build at this very moment."

"And who are these bricklayers?" asked Pencroff.

"The coral infusoria," answered Cyrus Smith. "Those microscopic creatures, by their unending labor, built Clermont-Tonnerre Island, the atolls, and the many other coral islands of the Pacific Ocean. It takes forty-seven million of them to weigh a single grain, and yet, out of the sea salts they absorb and the solid elements in the water that they take in, these tiny animals produce limestone. And that limestone forms enormous undersea foundations as hard and solid as granite. Long ago, in the first ages of creation, nature used fire, and produced the land by thrusting it up from below. But now she has handed the job over to microscopic animals, because the power of that fire inside the globe has plainly grown weaker, as the great number of volcanoes now extinct on the earth's surface shows. And I really do believe that, as century follows century and infusoria follow infusoria, this Pacific may one day turn into a vast continent, which new generations will settle and civilize in their turn."

"That'll take a while!" said Pencroff.

"Nature has time on her side," the engineer replied.

"But what's the use of new continents?" asked Harbert. "It seems to me that the habitable lands we have now are enough for humanity. And nature never does anything useless."

"Nothing useless, it's true," the engineer went on. "But here's one way the need for new continents in the future might be explained, and in exactly this tropical zone where the coral islands lie. At least, the explanation seems plausible to me."

"We're listening, Mr. Cyrus," Harbert answered.

"Here's what I think. Scientists generally agree that one day our globe will come to an end, or rather that animal and plant life will no longer be possible on it, because of the intense cooling it will undergo. Where they disagree is on the cause of that cooling. Some think it will come from the drop in the sun's temperature after millions of years. Others think it will come from the gradual dying out of the fires inside our globe, which have more influence on it than people generally suppose. I hold with the second theory myself, and I base it on this fact: the moon is truly a cooled-off body, which can no longer support life, even though the sun goes on pouring the same amount of heat onto its surface. So if the moon has cooled, it's because the inner fires to which it owed its origin, like every other body in the starry universe, have gone out completely. In any case, whatever the cause, our globe will cool one day, but the cooling will happen only little by little. And what will follow? The temperate zones, at some more or less distant time, will be no more habitable than the polar regions are now. So the populations of men, like the herds and flocks of animals, will flow back toward the latitudes that get the sun's most direct heat. An immense migration will take place. Europe, Central Asia, North America will gradually be abandoned, just like Australasia and the lower parts of South America. The plant life will follow the human migration. The flora will retreat toward the equator at the same time as the fauna. The central parts of South America and Africa will become the inhabited continents above all others. The Sami and the Samoyeds will find the climate of the polar sea on the shores of the Mediterranean. Who can tell us that, by then, the equatorial regions won't be too small to hold and feed the whole human race? So why shouldn't far-seeing nature, to give a refuge to that whole migration of plants and animals, be laying the foundations of a new continent under the equator even now, and why shouldn't she have given the infusoria the job of building it? I've often thought about all these things, my friends, and I seriously believe that the face of our globe will one day be completely transformed. As new continents rise, the seas will cover the old ones, and in centuries to come, new Columbuses will set out to discover the islands of Chimborazo, of the Himalayas or of Mont Blanc, all that is left of a drowned America, Asia and Europe. And then, finally, these new continents will in their turn become uninhabitable themselves. The heat will die out, like the heat of a body the soul has just left, and life will disappear from the globe, if not for good, then at least for a time. Perhaps then our sphere will rest, will renew itself in death, to rise again one day in higher conditions! But all that, my friends, is the secret of the Maker of all things, and, starting from the work of the infusoria, I've let myself be carried a little too far, perhaps, in prying into the secrets of the future."

"My dear Cyrus," Gédéon Spilett replied, "to me these theories are prophecies, and one day they'll come true."

"That's God's secret," said the engineer.

"That's all very well," said Pencroff, who had been listening with both ears, "but will you tell me, Mr. Cyrus, whether Lincoln Island was built by your infusoria?"

"No," answered Cyrus Smith. "It's purely volcanic in origin."

"Then it'll disappear one day?"

"Probably."

"I certainly hope we won't be on it then."

"No, don't worry, Pencroff. We won't be on it, because we have no wish to die here, and we may manage to get ourselves off it in the end."

"Meanwhile," answered Gédéon Spilett, "let's settle in as if it were for eternity. Never do anything by halves."

That ended the conversation. Lunch was over. The exploration began again, and the colonists reached the edge of the marshy region.

It was a true marsh, and it stretched all the way to the rounded coast at the southeastern end of the island, covering perhaps twenty square miles. The ground was a silt of clay and silica, mixed with a great deal of rotting plant matter. Pond algae, rushes, sedges and bulrushes covered it, with here and there a few patches of grass as thick as a heavy carpet. Frozen pools sparkled in many places in the sunlight. Neither the rains nor any river swollen by a sudden flood could have formed these reserves of water. The natural conclusion was that the marsh was fed by water seeping up through the ground, and so it was. There was even reason to fear that in the hot season the air here would fill with the foul vapors that breed marsh fevers.

Above the water plants, over the surface of the still water, fluttered a whole world of birds. A marsh hunter, or a professional shooting from a blind, could not have wasted a single shot here. Wild ducks, pintails, teal and snipe lived there in flocks, and these birds, not at all shy, let people come close to them easily.

A single charge of birdshot would certainly have brought down a few dozen of them, so tightly packed were their ranks. The colonists had to make do with arrows. The result was smaller, but the silent arrow had the advantage of not frightening the birds, which the bang of a gun would have scattered to every corner of the marsh. So this time the hunters settled for a dozen ducks, white-bodied with a cinnamon band around them, green heads, black, white and russet wings and flattened bills, which Harbert recognized as "shelducks." Top helped skillfully in catching them, and their name was given to this marshy part of the island: Shelduck Marsh. So the colonists had a plentiful reserve of water game there. When the time came, it would only be a matter of using it properly, and it was likely that several species of these birds could be, if not tamed, at least settled in the neighborhood of the lake, which would put them more directly within reach of the people who meant to eat them.

At about five in the evening Cyrus Smith and his companions started back for home. They crossed Shelduck Marsh and recrossed the Mercy on the bridge of ice.

By eight o'clock that evening they were all back at Granite House.

Chapter 22: The Mysterious Well

The traps — The foxes — The peccaries — The wind swings round to the northwest — A snowstorm — The basket makers — The hardest cold of the winter — Crystallizing the maple sugar — The mysterious well — The planned exploration — The lead pellet

The bitter cold lasted until August 15, though it never went below the lowest Fahrenheit reading they had seen so far. When the air was still, the low temperature was easy enough to bear. But when the north wind blew, it was hard going for people who were not properly dressed. Pencroff even got to the point of wishing that Lincoln Island had given shelter to a few families of bears, instead of these foxes and seals, whose fur left a lot to be desired.

"Bears," he would say, "are generally well dressed, and I'd ask nothing better than to borrow the warm coats they wear, just for the winter."

"But maybe," Nab answered with a laugh, "those bears wouldn't agree to give you their coats, Pencroff. They aren't Saint Martins, those beasts — they don't go cutting their cloaks in half for whoever's cold!"

"We'd make them, Nab, we'd make them," Pencroff replied, in a thoroughly commanding tone.

But those formidable meat-eaters did not exist on the island — or at least they had not shown themselves so far.

All the same, Harbert, Pencroff, and the reporter set about building traps on Prospect Plateau and along the edges of the forest. In the sailor's opinion any animal at all would be a fine catch, and whatever rodents or meat-eaters were the first to try out the new traps would be welcome at Granite House.

The traps were extremely simple, by the way. They were pits dug in the ground, with a ceiling of branches and grass over the top to hide the opening, and at the bottom some bait whose smell might draw the animals in. That was all. It should be said, though, that they had not been dug just anywhere, but in particular spots where a greater number of tracks showed that four-footed animals passed often. The traps were checked every day, and three times in those first days they found specimens of the culpeos that had already been seen on the right bank of the Mercy.

"Well, now! Is there nothing but foxes in this country?" cried Pencroff, the third time he pulled one of these animals out of the pit, where it was sitting looking thoroughly sheepish. "Beasts that aren't good for anything!"

"Oh, but they are," said Gédéon Spilett. "They're good for something!"

"And what's that?"

"For bait, to catch other animals with!"

The reporter was right, and from then on the traps were baited with the carcasses of these foxes.

The sailor had also made snares out of kurrajong fiber, and the snares brought in more than the traps did. Hardly a day went by without some rabbit from the warren letting itself get caught. It was always rabbit, but Nab knew how to vary his sauces, and the diners never thought of complaining.

Once or twice, however, in the second week of August, the traps gave the hunters animals other than culpeos, and more useful ones. They were some of the wild boars that had already been reported north of the lake. Pencroff did not need to ask whether these beasts were good to eat. That was plain enough from how much they looked like the pigs of America or Europe.

"But these aren't pigs, Pencroff," Harbert told him. "I'm warning you."

"My boy," answered the sailor, leaning over the trap and pulling out one of these representatives of the pig family by the little appendage that served it for a tail, "let me go on believing they're pigs!"

"Why?"

"Because it makes me happy!"

"So you're really fond of pork, Pencroff?"

"I'm very fond of pork," the sailor answered, "especially the feet. And if a pig had eight of them instead of four, I'd like it twice as much!"

As for the animals in question, they were peccaries, belonging to one of the four genera that make up the family. They were even of the species called "tajaçu," the collared peccary, recognizable by its dark color and by the lack of the long canine teeth that arm the mouths of its relatives. Peccaries usually live in herds, and it was likely that they were plentiful in the wooded parts of the island. In any case they were edible from head to foot, and Pencroff asked nothing more of them.

Toward August 15 the weather changed suddenly when the wind swung round to the northwest. The temperature rose a few degrees, and the moisture that had built up in the air soon came down as snow. The whole island was covered with a white layer and showed itself to its inhabitants in a new light. The snow fell heavily for several days, and it was soon two feet deep.

Before long the wind freshened with extreme violence, and from high up in Granite House they could hear the sea roaring over the reefs. At certain corners the air swirled in quick eddies, and the snow, caught up in them, formed tall spinning columns, like those waterspouts at sea that twirl on their bases and that ships fire their cannon at to break them up. Still, the hurricane was coming from the northwest, so it struck the island from behind, and the way Granite House faced protected it from a direct assault. But in the middle of that blizzard, as terrible as if it had been raging over some polar country, neither Cyrus Smith nor his companions could venture outside, however much they wanted to, and they stayed shut in for five days, from August 20 to 25. They could hear the storm roaring in Jacamar Wood, which was bound to suffer for it. Many trees would no doubt be torn up by the roots, but Pencroff consoled himself with the thought that he would not have the trouble of chopping them down.

"The wind's turned woodcutter — let it get on with it," he kept saying.

And anyway, there would have been no way to stop it.

How the residents of Granite House must have thanked Heaven, then, for providing them with this solid, unshakable retreat! Cyrus Smith certainly deserved his fair share of the thanks. But after all, it was nature that had hollowed out this huge cavern, and he had only discovered it. In there, all of them were safe, and the blows of the storm could not reach them. If they had built a house of brick and wood on Prospect Plateau, it would certainly not have stood up to the fury of this hurricane. As for the Chimneys, just from the crash of the breakers, which they could hear so loudly, it was clear that the place must be utterly uninhabitable, because the sea, sweeping over the islet, must be pounding it furiously. But here in Granite House, in the heart of this mass of rock that neither water nor air could get a grip on, there was nothing to fear.

During those few days of confinement the colonists did not sit idle. There was no shortage of wood, already sawn into planks, in the storeroom, and little by little they finished the furniture, tables and chairs, solid ones for sure, since no one had spared the material. These pieces were a bit heavy, and they hardly lived up to the old name for furniture — "movables" — which makes being easy to shift the whole point. But they were the pride of Nab and Pencroff, who would not have traded them for pieces by Boulle, the great cabinetmaker of the French kings.

Then the carpenters became basket makers, and they did not do badly at this new craft either. Near the point that the lake thrust out to the north, they had discovered a rich willow bed where purple osiers grew in large numbers. Before the rainy season Pencroff and Harbert had harvested these useful shrubs, and their stems, now well sorted, could be put to good use. The first attempts were shapeless. But thanks to the skill and intelligence of the workers — talking it over among themselves, remembering models they had seen, trying to outdo one another — baskets and hampers of various sizes soon added to the colony's equipment. The storeroom was stocked with them, and Nab put away his harvests of rootstocks, stone-pine nuts, and dragon-tree roots in special hampers of their own.

During the last week of August the weather changed once again. The temperature dropped a little and the storm died down. The colonists rushed outside. There were easily two feet of snow on the beach, but the surface of the snow had hardened, and they could walk on it without too much trouble. Cyrus Smith and his companions climbed up to Prospect Plateau.

What a change! The woods, which they had left green — especially the nearby part, where conifers grew thickest — had now vanished under a single color. Everything was white, from the summit of Mount Franklin down to the shore: the forests, the meadow, the lake, the river, the beaches. The water of the Mercy ran under a vault of ice, which broke up with a crash at every rise and fall of the tide. Numerous birds were fluttering over the frozen surface of the lake: ducks and snipe, pintails and guillemots. There were thousands of them. The rocks between which the waterfall poured over the edge of the plateau bristled with ice. You would have said the water was gushing from a monstrous gargoyle, carved with all the fancy of a Renaissance artist. As for judging how much damage the hurricane had done to the forest, that was not yet possible. They would have to wait until the immense white layer had melted away.

Gédéon Spilett, Pencroff, and Harbert did not miss this chance to go and check their traps. It was not easy to find them under the snow that covered them. They even had to be careful not to tumble into one or another of them, which would have been dangerous and humiliating at the same time: to be caught in your own trap! But in the end they avoided that embarrassment and found the traps completely intact. No animal had fallen into them, and yet there were many tracks all around, among them certain very sharply printed claw marks. Harbert did not hesitate to declare that some meat-eater of the cat family had passed that way, which bore out the engineer's opinion that there were dangerous wild beasts on Lincoln Island. No doubt these beasts usually lived in the dense forests of the Far West, but, driven by hunger, they had ventured as far as Prospect Plateau. Perhaps they could smell the residents of Granite House?

"So what exactly are these cats of yours?" asked Pencroff.

"They're tigers," Harbert answered.

"I thought those animals were only found in hot countries?"

"In the New World," the boy answered, "they've been seen everywhere from Mexico to the Pampas of Buenos Aires. And since Lincoln Island lies at about the same latitude as the provinces of the River Plate, it isn't surprising that there should be a few tigers here."

"All right, we'll keep watch," Pencroff answered.

Meanwhile the snow eventually disappeared as the temperature rose again. Rain began to fall, and its dissolving action wiped the white layer away. In spite of the bad weather, the colonists restocked their reserves of everything: stone-pine nuts, dragon-tree roots, rootstocks, and maple sap on the vegetable side; rabbits from the warren, agoutis, and kangaroos on the animal side. That called for a few trips into the forest, and they found that a good number of trees had been brought down by the last hurricane. The sailor and Nab even pushed on with the cart as far as the coal seam, to bring back a few tons of fuel. On the way they saw that the chimney of the pottery kiln had been badly damaged by the wind and had lost a good six feet at least from its top.

Along with the coal, the supply of firewood at Granite House was renewed too, and they took advantage of the Mercy's current, which was running free again, to float several rafts of timber down. The period of hard cold might not be over yet.

They had also paid a visit to the Chimneys, and the colonists could only congratulate themselves on not having lived there during the storm. The sea had left unmistakable marks of its ravages. Heaved up by the winds from offshore, it had leaped over the islet and violently attacked the passages, which were now half filled with sand, and thick layers of seaweed covered the rocks. While Nab, Harbert, and Pencroff were hunting or bringing in more fuel, Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett busied themselves clearing out the Chimneys. They found the forge and the furnaces more or less intact, protected as they had been, right from the start, by the sand piled up over them.

It was not for nothing that the fuel supply had been built up again. The colonists were not yet done with the hard cold. In the Northern Hemisphere, as everyone knows, February is the month best known for great drops in temperature. It was bound to be the same in the Southern Hemisphere, and the end of August, which is North America's February, did not escape this law of climate.

Around the 25th, after another round of snow and rain, the wind jumped to the southeast, and all of a sudden the cold became extremely sharp. By the engineer's estimate, the mercury in a Fahrenheit thermometer would have read no less than eight degrees below zero. This fierce cold, made still more painful by a biting wind, held for several days. The colonists had to shut themselves up in Granite House once again. Since every opening in the front of the cliff had to be sealed up tight, leaving only the bare minimum for fresh air to get in, they went through a great many candles. To save them, the colonists often lit the place only by the flames of the fireplaces, where no one stinted on fuel. Several times one or another of them went down to the beach, among the chunks of ice that the rising tide piled up there at every high water. But they soon climbed back up to Granite House, and it was not without trouble and pain that their hands held on to the rungs of the ladder. In that fierce cold, the rungs burned their fingers.

Once again they had to find ways to fill the idle hours that this confinement forced on the residents of Granite House. So Cyrus Smith took on a job that could be done behind closed doors.

As we know, the only sugar the colonists had was the liquid they drew from the maple by cutting deep notches in the tree. All they had to do was collect this sap in containers, and they used it as it was for all sorts of cooking, all the more readily because, as it aged, the sap tended to turn white and take on the thickness of syrup.

But they could do better than that, and one day Cyrus Smith announced to his companions that they were about to turn into sugar refiners.

"Refiners!" said Pencroff. "That's a pretty hot trade, isn't it?"

"Very hot!" answered the engineer.

"Then it's just right for the season!" the sailor shot back.

The word "refining" should not bring to mind those factories full of complicated machinery and crowds of workers. No! To crystallize this sap, all they had to do was purify it by an extremely easy process. It was put on the fire in big earthenware pots and simply allowed to boil down for a while, and soon a scum rose to the surface. As soon as it began to thicken, Nab took care to stir it with a wooden spatula, which would speed up the evaporation and at the same time keep it from taking on a burnt taste.

After a few hours of boiling over a good fire — which did as much good to the workers as to the stuff they were working on — the sap had turned into a thick syrup. This syrup was poured into clay molds, which had been made beforehand and fired in the kitchen stove itself, and which had been given all sorts of shapes. The next day the syrup had cooled and set into loaves and tablets. It was sugar — a little reddish in color, but almost transparent, and with a perfect taste.

The cold went on until the middle of September, and the prisoners of Granite House were beginning to find their captivity very long. Almost every day they tried a few outings, which could not last long. So they worked constantly at fitting out their home, and they talked as they worked. Cyrus Smith taught his companions about everything, and above all he explained the practical uses of science to them. The colonists had no library at their disposal. But the engineer was a book always ready, always open to the page each one needed — a book that answered all their questions, and that they leafed through often. So the time went by, and these good people did not seem to fear the future at all.

All the same, it was time for this confinement to end. They were all eager to see, if not the fine season, then at least the end of this unbearable cold. If only they had been dressed well enough to brave it, what trips they would have made, to the dunes, or to Shelduck Marsh! The game must have been easy to get close to, and the hunting would certainly have been rewarding. But Cyrus Smith insisted that no one should put his health at risk, because he needed every pair of hands, and his advice was followed.

But it must be said that the most impatient of all at this imprisonment — after Pencroff, at any rate — was Top. The faithful dog felt very cramped in Granite House. He kept going back and forth from one room to the next, and in his own way he showed how bored he was at being cooped up.

Cyrus Smith often noticed that whenever Top went near the dark well that connected with the sea, the one whose opening was at the back of the storeroom, he would give strange growls. Top would circle around this hole, which had been covered over with a wooden lid. Sometimes he even tried to slip his paws under the lid, as if he wanted to lift it. Then he would yelp in a peculiar way, a way that showed both anger and uneasiness.

The engineer watched this performance several times. What could there be in that pit to make such an impression on the intelligent animal? The well ran down to the sea, that much was certain. Did it branch off, then, into narrow tunnels running through the framework of the island? Did it connect with other caverns inside? Did some sea monster come, now and then, to breathe at the bottom of the well? The engineer did not know what to think, and he could not stop himself from dreaming up strange possibilities. Used as he was to traveling far into the realm of scientific fact, he could not forgive himself for letting himself be drawn into the realm of the strange, almost of the supernatural. But how else could he explain why Top — one of those sensible dogs that have never wasted their time barking at the moon — kept stubbornly probing that pit with his nose and his ears, if nothing was happening down there that ought to rouse his uneasiness? Top's behavior puzzled Cyrus Smith more than seemed reasonable to admit, even to himself.

In any case, the engineer shared his impressions only with Gédéon Spilett. He saw no point in letting his companions in on the thoughts that kept coming to him in spite of himself, over what was perhaps nothing more than a whim of Top's.

At last the cold ended. There were rains, squalls mixed with snow, sudden showers of sleet and hail, gusts of wind — but this foul weather did not last. The ice had melted and the snow was gone. The beach, the plateau, the banks of the Mercy, and the forest could all be used again. The return of spring delighted the residents of Granite House, and soon they were spending only the hours of sleep and meals inside.

They hunted a great deal in the second half of September, which led Pencroff to demand, more insistently than ever, the firearms that he claimed Cyrus Smith had promised him. The engineer knew very well that without special tools it would be almost impossible for him to make a gun that would be of any real use, so he kept putting the job off until later. Besides, he pointed out, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett had become skilled archers. All sorts of excellent animals — agoutis, kangaroos, capybaras, pigeons, bustards, wild ducks, snipe, in short every kind of game, furred or feathered — were falling to their arrows, and so they could afford to wait. But the stubborn sailor would not hear of it, and he would give the engineer no rest until his wish was granted. Gédéon Spilett, for that matter, backed Pencroff up.

"If the island has fierce animals on it, as we have some reason to suspect," he said, "we have to think about fighting them and wiping them out. A time may come when that's our first duty."

But at that point it was not the question of firearms that was on Cyrus Smith's mind. It was the question of clothing. The clothes the colonists wore had lasted through the winter, but they would not hold out until the next one. Hides from meat-eating animals or wool from grazing ones — that was what they had to get, at any cost. And since there was no shortage of mouflons, the thing to do was to find a way to gather a flock of them, which would be raised for the colony's needs. A pen for the domestic animals, a poultry yard fitted out for the birds — in short, a kind of farm to be set up at some spot on the island: those would be the two important projects to carry out during the fine season.

So, with these future settlements in view, it was becoming urgent to make a thorough reconnaissance of the whole unknown part of Lincoln Island — that is, under the tall forests that stretched along the right bank of the Mercy, from its mouth to the tip of Serpentine Peninsula, as well as along the whole of the west coast. But they needed settled weather, and another month would have to go by before the exploration could usefully be undertaken.

So they were waiting with a certain impatience, when something happened that made the colonists still more eager to visit every corner of their domain.

It was October 24. That day Pencroff had gone to check the traps, which he always kept properly baited. In one of them he found three animals that were sure to be welcome in the pantry. They were a female peccary and her two young.

So Pencroff came back to Granite House delighted with his catch, and, as always, the sailor made a great show of his hunting.

"Come on! We're going to have a fine meal, Mr. Cyrus!" he cried. "And you too, Mr. Spilett, you'll be eating some of this!"

"I'm quite willing to eat some," the reporter answered. "But what is it I'll be eating?"

"Suckling pig."

"Oh, really? Suckling pig, Pencroff? To hear you talk, I thought you were bringing back a partridge stuffed with truffles!"

"What?" cried Pencroff. "Are you turning up your nose at suckling pig, by any chance?"

"No," answered Gédéon Spilett, without showing any enthusiasm, "as long as we don't overdo it..."
