"All right, all right, Mr. Journalist," the sailor shot back — he did not like to hear his hunting run down. "So you're getting fussy, are you? And seven months ago, when we landed on the island, you'd have been only too happy to come across game like this!..."

"There you go, there you go," the reporter answered. "Man is never perfect, and never satisfied."

"Well," Pencroff went on, "I hope Nab will outdo himself. Look! These two little peccaries aren't even three months old! They'll be as tender as quail! Come on, Nab, come with me! I'll keep an eye on the cooking myself."

And the sailor, with Nab following him, made for the kitchen and buried himself in his culinary labors.

They let him do it his own way. So he and Nab prepared a magnificent meal: the two little peccaries, a kangaroo soup, a smoked ham, stone-pine nuts, dragon-tree drink, Oswego tea — everything they had that was best, in short. But among all the dishes, the place of honor was to go to the delicious peccaries, braised in their own juices.

At five o'clock dinner was served in the dining room of Granite House. The kangaroo soup was steaming on the table. Everyone found it excellent.

After the soup came the peccaries, which Pencroff insisted on carving himself, and he served each of the diners an enormous helping.

These suckling pigs were truly delicious, and Pencroff was devouring his share with tremendous gusto, when all at once a cry and an oath escaped him.

"What is it?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"It's... it's... I've just broken a tooth!" answered the sailor.

"Well, now! Are there pebbles in your peccaries, then?" said Gédéon Spilett.

"Must be," answered Pencroff, taking out of his mouth the object that had just cost him a molar!...

It was not a pebble...

It was a lead pellet.

Part Two: The Marooned Man

Chapter 1: The Lead Pellet

About the lead pellet — Building a canoe — The hunts — At the top of a kauri — Nothing to show that man is here — A catch by Nab and Harbert — A turtle turned over — A turtle gone — Cyrus Smith's explanation

It was seven months to the day since the passengers of the balloon had been thrown onto Lincoln Island. In all that time, however hard they had searched, not one human being had shown himself to them. Never had a wisp of smoke betrayed the presence of man anywhere on the island. Never had any work of human hands shown that someone had passed that way, whether long ago or lately. Not only did the island seem to be uninhabited; there was every reason to believe it had never been inhabited at all. And now that whole scaffolding of deductions was collapsing in front of a single pellet of metal found in the body of a harmless little animal!

For that lead had come out of a firearm, and who but a human being could have fired it?

When Pencroff set the pellet down on the table, his companions stared at it in deep astonishment. All the consequences of this incident, enormous for all its apparent smallness, had suddenly seized their minds. The sudden appearance of some supernatural being could not have struck them more sharply.

Cyrus Smith did not hesitate. He began at once to lay out the theories that so surprising and unexpected a fact was bound to raise. He picked up the pellet, turned it this way and that, and felt it between his thumb and forefinger. Then:

"You're sure," he asked Pencroff, "that the peccary this pellet wounded was barely three months old?"

"Barely, Mr. Cyrus," answered Pencroff. "It was still nursing at its mother when I found it in the pit."

"Well, then," said the engineer, "that proves, all by itself, that a gun has been fired on Lincoln Island within the last three months at most."

"And that a lead pellet hit this little animal," added Gédéon Spilett, "though not fatally."

"There's no doubt about it," Cyrus Smith went on, "and here are the consequences we ought to draw from it. Either the island was inhabited before we came, or men have landed on it within the last three months at most. Did those men come here on purpose or by accident? Did they put in to shore, or were they shipwrecked? That question can only be cleared up later. As for who they are — Europeans or Malays, enemies or friends to men like us — we have nothing at all to guess by. And whether they're still on the island or have left it, we don't know that either. But these questions concern us too closely for us to stay in doubt about them any longer."

"No! A hundred times no! A thousand times no!" cried the sailor, getting up from the table. "There are no other men on Lincoln Island but us! Hang it all, the island isn't big, and if anybody lived on it, we'd have caught sight of a few of them by now!"

"It would certainly be very surprising if we hadn't," said Harbert.

"But it would be a great deal more surprising, I should think," observed the reporter, "if this peccary had been born with a lead pellet inside it!"

"Unless," said Nab seriously, "Pencroff had..."

"Listen to him, Nab!" Pencroff shot back. "So for the last five or six months I've been carrying a lead pellet around in my jaw without noticing it! And where would it have been hiding?" the sailor added, opening his mouth to show off the splendid thirty-two teeth that filled it. "Take a good look, Nab, and if you find one hollow tooth in that set, you have my permission to pull out half a dozen!"

"Nab's theory can't be accepted, that's true," answered Cyrus Smith, who for all the seriousness of his thoughts could not hold back a smile. "It's certain that a gun has been fired on the island within the last three months at most. But I'm inclined to think that whoever landed on this coast has been here only a very short time, or else only stopped and went on. Because if the island had been inhabited when we were surveying it from the top of Mount Franklin, we would have seen them or they would have seen us. So most likely some castaways were thrown up somewhere on the coast by a storm only a few weeks ago. Whatever the truth is, we need to be certain about it."

"I think we ought to act carefully," said the reporter.

"I agree," answered Cyrus Smith, "because unfortunately there's reason to fear that it's Malay pirates who have landed on the island!"

"Mr. Cyrus," asked the sailor, "wouldn't it be a good idea, before we go out exploring, to build a boat that would let us go up the river, or around the coast if need be? We mustn't let ourselves be caught unprepared."

"That's a good idea, Pencroff," answered the engineer, "but we can't wait. It would take at least a month to build a boat..."

"A real boat, yes," the sailor answered. "But we don't need anything fit to go to sea. In five days at most I'll guarantee to build a canoe good enough to travel on the Mercy."

"In five days?" cried Nab. "Make a boat?"

"Yes, Nab, a boat the way the Indians make them."

"Out of wood?" asked Nab, not looking very convinced.

"Out of wood," answered Pencroff, "or rather out of bark. I'll say it again, Mr. Cyrus: in five days the job can be done!"

"Five days it is, then!" answered the engineer.

"But until then we'd better keep a sharp watch!" said Harbert.

"A very sharp watch, my friends," answered Cyrus Smith. "And I'll ask you to keep your hunting trips to the neighborhood of Granite House."

Dinner ended less cheerfully than Pencroff had hoped.

So the island was inhabited, or had been, by someone besides the colonists. Since the incident of the lead pellet, that was now a fact beyond dispute, and a discovery like that could only cause the colonists serious alarm.

Before going to bed, Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett talked these things over for a long time. They wondered whether, by any chance, this incident might have some connection with the unexplained circumstances of the engineer's rescue, and with the other strange details that had struck them more than once already. In the end, though, after arguing the question both ways, Cyrus Smith said:

"To sum it up, would you like to know what I think, my dear Spilett?"

"Yes, Cyrus."

"Well, here it is. However carefully we explore the island, we won't find anything!"

The very next day Pencroff set to work. The point was not to build a proper boat with ribs and planking, but simply a flat-bottomed craft that would float, which would be excellent for traveling on the Mercy, especially up near its sources, where the water would be shallow. Pieces of bark sewn one to another would be enough to make the light little vessel, and if natural obstacles meant it had to be carried overland, it would be neither heavy nor awkward. Pencroff planned to join the strips of bark with riveted nails, and to make sure, by fitting them tightly together, that the craft would be perfectly watertight.

So they had to choose trees whose bark was supple and tough enough to lend itself to the work. Now, as it happened, the last storm had brought down a number of Douglas firs, which were perfectly suited to this kind of construction. Some of these firs were lying on the ground, and all that remained was to strip off the bark. But that turned out to be the hardest part, given how poor the colonists' tools were. Still, in the end they managed it.

While the sailor, with the engineer's help, was busy at this without losing an hour, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert were not idle either. They had made themselves the colony's providers. The reporter never tired of admiring the boy, who had become remarkably skillful with the bow and the spear. Harbert also showed great daring, together with a good deal of that coolness one might rightly call "the reasoning side of bravery." The two hunting companions, heeding Cyrus Smith's advice, no longer went more than two miles from Granite House in any direction. But the lower slopes of the forest supplied plenty of agoutis, capybaras, kangaroos, peccaries and so on. And though the traps were not bringing in much now that the cold had ended, the warren at least was giving its usual share, which would have been enough to feed the whole colony of Lincoln Island.

Often, during these hunts, Harbert talked with Gédéon Spilett about the incident of the lead pellet and the conclusions the engineer had drawn from it. One day — it was October 26 — he said to him:

"But, Mr. Spilett, don't you think it's very strange that if some castaways have landed on this island, they still haven't shown themselves anywhere near Granite House?"

"Very surprising, if they're still here," answered the reporter, "but not surprising at all if they're gone!"

"So you think those people have already left the island?" Harbert went on.

"It's more than likely, my boy. If they had stayed for long, and above all if they were still here, something would have given them away sooner or later."

"But if they were able to leave again," the boy pointed out, "then they weren't castaways?"

"No, Harbert. Or at least they were what I'd call temporary castaways. It's quite possible that a gale threw them onto the island without wrecking their boat, and that once the gale had passed they put to sea again."

"One thing has to be said," Harbert remarked. "Mr. Smith has always seemed more afraid of finding human beings on our island than eager to."

"That's true," answered the reporter. "He doesn't see who could be sailing these seas except the Malays, and those gentlemen are nasty scoundrels, best avoided."

"It isn't impossible, Mr. Spilett," Harbert went on, "that one of these days we'll come across some traces of their landing, and then perhaps we'll know for certain?"

"I won't say no, my boy. An abandoned camp, a dead fire, could put us on the trail, and that's what we'll be looking for on our next expedition."

On the day the two hunters had this talk, they were in a part of the forest near the Mercy that was remarkable for its magnificent trees. Among others, there rose up there, nearly two hundred feet above the ground, a few of those superb conifers that the Maori people of New Zealand call "kauris."

"I have an idea, Mr. Spilett," said Harbert. "If I climbed to the top of one of these kauris, maybe I could look out over the country for quite a long way around?"

"It's a good idea," answered the reporter, "but can you climb all the way to the top of those giants?"

"I can at least try," answered Harbert.

The boy, nimble and skillful, sprang up onto the lowest branches, which were arranged so as to make the kauri fairly easy to climb, and in a few minutes he had reached its crown, which rose clear of the immense plain of green formed by the rounded treetops of the forest.

From that high point the eye could range over the whole southern part of the island, from Claw Cape in the southeast to Reptile End in the southwest. To the northwest stood Mount Franklin, which blocked out a good quarter of the horizon.

But from the top of his lookout Harbert could survey exactly the part of the island that was still unknown, the part that might have sheltered, or might be sheltering still, the strangers whose presence they suspected.

The boy looked with the closest attention. At sea, first of all, there was nothing in sight. Not a sail, either on the horizon or in the waters close to the island. Still, since the mass of trees hid the shoreline, it was possible that a ship — especially one that had lost its masts — had come in very close to land and so could not be seen by Harbert.

In the middle of the Far West forests there was nothing either. The forest made an impenetrable dome several square miles across, without a clearing, without a gap. It was not even possible to follow the course of the Mercy, or to make out the spot on the mountain where it had its source. Perhaps other creeks ran toward the west, but there was nothing to show it.

But even if every sign of a camp escaped Harbert, might he not catch some smoke in the air that would betray the presence of man? The air was clear, and the faintest wisp of vapor would have stood out sharply against the sky.

For a moment Harbert thought he saw a thin thread of smoke rising in the west, but a more careful look showed him he was mistaken. He looked with the greatest care, and his eyesight was excellent... No, there was definitely nothing there.

Harbert climbed back down to the foot of the kauri, and the two hunters returned to Granite House. There Cyrus Smith listened to the boy's account, shook his head, and said nothing. It was quite clear that no one could settle the question until the island had been explored from end to end.

Two days later — October 28 — another incident took place, and its explanation, too, would leave something to be desired.

While roaming along the beach two miles from Granite House, Harbert and Nab were lucky enough to capture a magnificent specimen of the order of chelonians, the turtles. It was a green turtle, of the genus Mydas, and its shell gave off wonderful green gleams.

Harbert had spotted the turtle as it was slipping between the rocks to reach the sea.

"Over here, Nab! Over here!" he shouted.

Nab came running.

"What a beautiful animal!" said Nab. "But how are we going to catch it?"

"Nothing could be easier, Nab," answered Harbert. "We'll turn this turtle over on its back, and then it won't be able to get away. Take your spear and do what I do."

Sensing danger, the reptile had drawn itself in between its upper shell and its under-shell. Neither its head nor its legs could be seen any longer, and it lay as still as a rock.

Harbert and Nab then worked their poles in under the animal's breastbone, and by heaving together they managed, not without trouble, to turn it over on its back. The turtle was three feet long and must have weighed at least four hundred pounds.

"Good!" cried Nab. "That's going to make friend Pencroff happy!"

And indeed friend Pencroff could hardly fail to be happy, because the flesh of these turtles, which feed on eelgrass, is extremely tasty. At that moment all that could still be seen of this one was its head — small and flat, but greatly widened at the back by large hollows at the temples, hidden under an arch of bone.

"And now what are we going to do with our game?" said Nab. "We can't drag it all the way to Granite House!"

"Let's leave it here, since it can't turn itself back over," answered Harbert, "and we'll come back for it with the cart."

"All right."

All the same, to be extra careful, Harbert took the trouble — which Nab thought unnecessary — to wedge the animal in place with big stones. After that the two hunters went back to Granite House along the beach, which the tide, low just then, had laid wide open. Harbert, who wanted to surprise Pencroff, said nothing to him about the "superb specimen of the chelonians" he had left turned over on the sand. But two hours later, when he and Nab came back with the cart to the place where they had left it, the "superb specimen of the chelonians" was no longer there.

Nab and Harbert first looked at each other, then looked all around them. Yet this was certainly the spot where the turtle had been left. The boy even found the stones he had used, so he was sure he was not mistaken.

"Well, how about that!" said Nab. "So these creatures can turn themselves back over?"

"It looks that way," answered Harbert, who could make no sense of it at all and was staring at the stones scattered on the sand.

"Well, Pencroff won't be pleased, that's for sure!"

"And Mr. Smith may have a hard time explaining how it disappeared!" thought Harbert.

"All right," said Nab, who wanted to hide their misadventure, "we just won't mention it."

"On the contrary, Nab, we have to mention it," answered Harbert.

And the two of them took up the cart they had brought for nothing and went back to Granite House.

When he reached the work yard, where the engineer and the sailor were working together, Harbert told them what had happened.

"Ah! You clumsy pair!" cried the sailor. "To let at least fifty bowls of soup get away!"

"But Pencroff," Nab retorted, "it's not our fault the creature ran off, because I'm telling you we'd turned it over!"

"Then you didn't turn it over enough!" the incorrigible sailor shot back with a grin.

"Not enough!" cried Harbert.

And he told how he had taken care to wedge the turtle in place with stones.

"Then it's a miracle!" Pencroff replied.

"I thought, Mr. Cyrus," said Harbert, "that turtles couldn't get back on their feet once they'd been turned on their backs — especially big ones?"

"That's true, my boy," answered Cyrus Smith.

"Then how could it have happened...?"

"How far from the sea had you left the turtle?" asked the engineer, who had stopped his work and was thinking the incident over.

"About fifteen feet, at most," answered Harbert.

"And the tide was low at the time?"

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus."

"Well, then," answered the engineer, "what the turtle couldn't do on the sand, it may have been able to do in the water. It must have turned itself over when the rising tide reached it, and then calmly made its way back out to sea."

"Oh! What clumsy fools we are!" cried Nab.

"That's exactly what I had the honor of telling you!" answered Pencroff.

Cyrus Smith had given this explanation, and it was a reasonable one, no doubt. But was he really convinced that it was the right one? One would not dare to say so.

Chapter 2: The Chest on the Beach

First trial of the canoe — Wreckage on the shore — The tow — Jetsam Point — Inventory of the chest: tools, weapons, instruments, clothing, books, utensils — What Pencroff misses — The Gospel — A verse from the holy book

By October 29 the bark canoe was entirely finished. Pencroff had kept his promise, and in five days a sort of canoe had been built, its hull ribbed with flexible rods of crejimba wood. A bench in the stern, a second bench amidships to hold the sides apart, a third bench in the bow, a gunwale to carry the tholepins for two oars, and a sculling oar for steering made up the whole of the little boat, which was twelve feet long and weighed under two hundred pounds. As for the launching, it was extremely simple. The light canoe was carried down onto the sand at the water's edge in front of Granite House, and the rising tide lifted it. Pencroff jumped straight in, worked it along with the sculling oar, and was able to confirm that it was entirely fit for the use they meant to make of it.

"Hurrah!" cried the sailor, who did not scorn to celebrate his own triumph that way. "With this you could go all the way around..."

"The world?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"No, the island. A few stones for ballast, a mast up in the bow, and a scrap of sail that Mr. Smith will make us one of these days, and we'll go a long way! Well, Mr. Cyrus, and you, Mr. Spilett, and you, Harbert, and you, Nab, aren't you coming to try out our new ship? What the devil! We've got to see whether she can carry all five of us!"

It was, in fact, a test worth making. With a stroke of the sculling oar Pencroff brought the boat back to the shore through a narrow passage between the rocks, and it was agreed that they would try out the canoe that very day by following the shore as far as the first point, where the rocks of the south ended.

Just as they were getting in, Nab exclaimed:

"But your ship's taking on quite a bit of water, Pencroff!"

"That's nothing, Nab," replied the sailor. "The wood has to swell tight! In two days you won't see a drop, and our canoe will have no more water in her belly than a drunkard has in his stomach. All aboard!"

So they all got in, and Pencroff pushed off. The weather was magnificent, and the sea as calm as if its waters had been held within the narrow shores of a lake. The canoe could face it as safely as if it had been going up the quiet current of the Mercy.

Nab took one of the two oars and Harbert the other, while Pencroff stayed in the stern to steer with the sculling oar.

The sailor first crossed the channel and ran close along the southern tip of the islet. A light breeze was blowing from the south. There was no swell, either in the channel or out at sea. A few long undulations, which the canoe hardly felt because it was heavily loaded, swelled the surface of the sea at regular intervals. They went out about half a mile from the coast, far enough to take in the whole sweep of Mount Franklin.

Then Pencroff came about and headed back toward the mouth of the river. The canoe now followed the shore, which curved round to the farthest point of land and hid the whole low, marshy plain of Shelduck Marsh.

Measured around the curve of the coast, that point was about three miles from the Mercy. The colonists decided to go as far as its tip and to round it only far enough to get a quick look at the coast as far as Claw Cape.

So the boat followed the shoreline two cable lengths out at most, steering clear of the reefs scattered all along that stretch of coast, which the rising tide was beginning to cover. The cliff kept getting lower from the river mouth to the point. It was a heap of granite blocks flung about at random, very different from the great wall that formed Prospect Plateau, and extremely wild to look at. It was as though an enormous cartload of rocks had been dumped there. Not a scrap of vegetation grew on that sharp spur, which ran out two miles in front of the forest, and the point looked rather like a giant's arm reaching out of a green sleeve.

Driven by its two oars, the boat moved along easily. Gédéon Spilett, a pencil in one hand and his notebook in the other, sketched the coast in broad strokes. Nab, Pencroff, and Harbert chatted as they looked over this part of their domain, which was new to them, and as the canoe went farther south the two Mandible Capes seemed to shift their places and close Union Bay in more tightly.

As for Cyrus Smith, he did not talk. He watched. And from the wariness in his eyes it always seemed as though he were studying some strange country.

Meanwhile, after three quarters of an hour on the water, the canoe had nearly reached the tip of the point, and Pencroff was getting ready to round it, when Harbert stood up and pointed to a black spot.

"What's that I see over there on the beach?" he said.

Every eye turned toward the place he pointed to.

"There's something there, all right," said the reporter. "It looks like a piece of wreckage half buried in the sand."

"Ah!" cried Pencroff. "I see what it is!"

"What?" asked Nab.

"Barrels! Barrels — and they may be full!" answered the sailor.

"To the shore, Pencroff!" said Cyrus Smith.

A few strokes of the oars, and the canoe grounded at the head of a little cove. Its passengers jumped out onto the beach.

Pencroff had not been mistaken. Two barrels lay there, half sunk in the sand, but still firmly lashed to a large chest. Held up by them, the chest had floated along until it ran aground on the shore.

"So there's been a shipwreck somewhere near the island?" asked Harbert.

"Obviously," replied Gédéon Spilett.

"But what's in this chest?" cried Pencroff, with an impatience that was only natural. "What's in this chest? It's shut tight, and nothing to break the lid open with! Well, then, we'll do it with stones..."

And the sailor, lifting a heavy rock, was about to smash in one side of the chest when the engineer stopped him.

"Pencroff," he said, "can you hold back your impatience for just one hour?"

"But, Mr. Cyrus, think of it! Maybe everything we're missing is in there!"

"We'll find out, Pencroff," replied the engineer. "But take my word for it, don't smash this chest. It may be useful to us. Let's take it to Granite House, where we can open it more easily without breaking it. It's all fitted out for the trip. Since it floated this far, it will surely float as far as the mouth of the river."

"You're right, Mr. Cyrus, and I was wrong," replied the sailor. "But a man isn't always master of himself!"

The engineer's advice was sound. For one thing, the canoe could not have held whatever the chest probably contained. It must be heavy, since it had needed two empty barrels to "buoy it up," as sailors say. So it was better to tow it just as it was to the shore below Granite House.

And now, where had this wreckage come from? That was an important question. Cyrus Smith and his companions looked carefully all around them and walked along the shore for several hundred paces. No other debris turned up. They searched the sea as well. Harbert and Nab climbed a tall rock, but the horizon was empty. Nothing in sight — neither a disabled ship nor a vessel under sail.

Still, there had been a shipwreck. There was no doubt about that. Could this incident be connected with the incident of the lead pellet? Had strangers perhaps landed somewhere else on the island? Could they still be there? But the colonists naturally reflected that these strangers could not be Malay pirates, because the wreckage had obviously come from either America or Europe.

They all went back to the chest. It measured five feet long by three feet wide. It was made of oak, very carefully closed, and covered with a thick hide held in place with copper nails. The two big casks, tightly sealed but clearly empty from the sound they gave when struck, were bound to its sides with stout ropes, tied in knots that Pencroff easily recognized as "sailor's knots." The chest seemed to be perfectly preserved, which was explained by the fact that it had run aground on a sandy beach and not on reefs. Looking it over carefully, one could even be sure that it had not been in the sea for long, and that it had only recently arrived on this shore. No water seemed to have got inside, and the things it held must be undamaged.

It was clear that the chest had been thrown overboard from a disabled ship running toward the island. In the hope that it would reach the coast, where they could find it again later, some of the people on board had taken the precaution of lightening it with a float.

"We'll tow this wreckage to Granite House," said the engineer, "and we'll make an inventory of what's in it. Then, if we find any survivors of this shipwreck on the island — supposing there was one — we'll give it back to its owners. If we don't find anyone..."

"We'll keep it for ourselves!" cried Pencroff. "But, for God's sake, what on earth can be in there?"

The tide was already starting to reach the wreckage, which would certainly float at high water. One of the ropes holding the barrels was partly unwound and used as a towline to tie the float to the boat. Then Pencroff and Nab dug away the sand with their oars to make it easier to move the chest. Soon the boat, towing the chest behind it, began to round the point, which was given the name Jetsam Point. The tow was heavy, and the barrels were barely enough to hold the chest above the water. So the sailor feared at every moment that it would break loose and sink to the bottom. Fortunately his fears did not come true, and an hour and a half after setting out — it had taken all that time to cover the three miles — the canoe came alongside the shore in front of Granite House.

Canoe and wreckage were then hauled up onto the sand, and since the sea was already going out, they were soon left high and dry. Nab had gone to fetch tools to force the chest open while damaging it as little as possible, and they set about the inventory. Pencroff made no attempt to hide that he was extremely excited.

The sailor began by untying the two barrels, which were in very good shape and could be put to use, it goes without saying. Then the locks were forced with a crowbar, and the lid fell open at once.

A second casing, of zinc, lined the inside of the chest. Plainly it had been arranged so that the things it held would be safe from damp under any circumstances.

"Ah!" cried Nab. "What if it's canned food in there!"

"I certainly hope not," replied the reporter.

"If only there were..." said the sailor under his breath.

"Were what?" asked Nab, who had heard him.

"Nothing!"

The zinc casing was cut open across its whole width and folded back over the sides of the chest, and little by little all sorts of very different things were taken out and set down on the sand. At each new object Pencroff let out new hurrahs, Harbert clapped his hands, and Nab danced for joy. There were books in there that would have driven Harbert wild with delight, and cooking utensils that Nab would have covered with kisses!

All in all, the colonists had every reason to be extremely pleased, for the chest held tools, weapons, instruments, clothing, and books. Here is the exact list, as Gédéon Spilett entered it in his notebook:

    Tools:        3 knives with several blades
                  2 woodcutter's axes
                  2 carpenter's hatchets
                  3 planes
                  2 adzes
                  1 twibill (a double-bladed mortising axe)
                  6 cold chisels
                  2 files
                  3 hammers
                  3 gimlets
                  2 augers
                  10 bags of nails and screws
                  3 saws of different sizes
                  2 boxes of needles
    Weapons:      2 flintlock guns
                  2 percussion-cap guns
                  2 center-fire carbines
                  5 cutlasses
                  4 boarding sabers
                  2 kegs of gunpowder, holding twenty-five pounds each
                  12 boxes of percussion caps
    Instruments:  1 sextant
                  1 pair of binoculars
                  1 telescope
                  1 case of drawing compasses
                  1 pocket compass
                  1 Fahrenheit thermometer
                  1 aneroid barometer
                  1 box holding a complete photographic outfit: lens,
                    plates, chemicals, etc.
    Clothing:     2 dozen shirts of an unusual fabric that looked like
                    wool but was plainly of vegetable origin
                  3 dozen stockings of the same fabric
    Utensils:     1 iron kettle
                  6 tin-lined copper saucepans
                  3 iron platters
                  10 sets of aluminum forks and spoons
                  2 teakettles
                  1 small portable stove
                  6 table knives
    Books:        1 Bible with the Old and New Testaments
                  1 atlas
                  1 dictionary of the various Polynesian languages
                  1 dictionary of natural science, in six volumes
                  3 reams of blank paper
                  2 ledgers with blank pages

"You have to admit," said the reporter, once the inventory was finished, "that the owner of this chest was a practical man! Tools, weapons, instruments, clothes, utensils, books — nothing's missing! You'd really think he'd been expecting to be shipwrecked and had got ready for it ahead of time!"

"Nothing's missing, indeed," murmured Cyrus Smith thoughtfully.

"And one thing's certain," added Harbert. "The ship that carried this chest and its owner wasn't a Malay pirate!"

"Unless," said Pencroff, "the owner had been taken prisoner by pirates..."

"That won't do," replied the reporter. "It's more likely that an American or European ship was driven into these waters, and that some passengers, wanting to save at least the bare necessities, packed this chest this way and threw it into the sea."

"Do you think so, Mr. Cyrus?" asked Harbert.

"Yes, my boy," replied the engineer. "That could be how it happened. It's possible that at the moment of a shipwreck, or in expectation of one, someone gathered various essential things into this chest, hoping to find them again somewhere on the coast..."

"Even the photography box!" the sailor remarked, looking rather unconvinced.

"As for that apparatus," replied Cyrus Smith, "I don't really see the use of it. A fuller supply of clothing or more ammunition would have served us better — or any other castaways, for that matter!"

"But isn't there some mark on these instruments, these tools, these books — some address — that could tell us where they came from?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

That remained to be seen. So every object was carefully examined, especially the books, the instruments, and the weapons. Contrary to the usual practice, neither the weapons nor the instruments bore a maker's mark. Besides, they were in perfect condition and did not seem ever to have been used. The same was true of the tools and the utensils: everything was new. That proved, in short, that these things had not been grabbed at random and tossed into the chest. On the contrary, they had been chosen with forethought and packed with care. The second casing of metal pointed the same way. It had kept them safe from all damp, and it could never have been soldered in a moment of haste.

As for the dictionaries of natural science and of the Polynesian languages, both were in English, but neither carried a publisher's name or a date of publication.

The same went for the Bible, printed in English — a quarto volume, remarkable as a piece of printing, which seemed to have been leafed through often.

As for the atlas, it was a magnificent work, with maps of the whole world and several maps of the globe drawn on Mercator's projection. Its place names were in French — but it too carried neither a date of publication nor a publisher's name.

So there was nothing on any of these things to show where they had come from, and therefore nothing to suggest the nationality of the ship that must have passed through these waters not long before. But wherever the chest had come from, it made the colonists of Lincoln Island rich. Until then they had made everything themselves by transforming the raw products of nature, and they had pulled through by their own intelligence. But didn't it seem as though Providence had wanted to reward them by sending them, just now, these products of human industry? And so, with one accord, they lifted up their thanks to Heaven.

Still, one of them was not entirely satisfied. That was Pencroff. It appeared that the chest did not contain something he cared about enormously. As the objects came out of it, his hurrahs grew fainter and fainter, and once the inventory was done he was heard to mutter:

"That's all fine and good, but you'll see — there won't be anything in this box for me!"

Which led Nab to say to him:

"Well now, friend Pencroff, what were you expecting?"

"Half a pound of tobacco!" Pencroff replied in all seriousness. "Then my happiness would have been complete!"

Nobody could help laughing at the sailor's remark.

But one consequence of finding the wreckage was that a serious exploration of the island was now more necessary than ever. So it was agreed that the next day, at first light, they would set out up the Mercy and make their way to the west coast. If any castaways had landed somewhere on that coast, they might well be without any resources, and help had to be brought to them without delay.

During the rest of that day the various objects were carried up to Granite House and arranged in an orderly way in the great hall.

That day — October 29 — happened to be a Sunday, and before going to bed Harbert asked the engineer whether he would read them some passage from the Gospel.

"Gladly," replied Cyrus Smith.

He took up the holy book and was about to open it when Pencroff stopped him.

"Mr. Cyrus," he said, "I'm superstitious. Open it at random and read us the first verse your eyes fall on. We'll see if it fits our situation."

Cyrus Smith smiled at the sailor's notion, and to humor him he opened the Gospel exactly where a bookmark lay between the pages.

At once his eyes were caught by a red cross, made in pencil, that had been placed beside verse 8 of chapter 7 of the Gospel of Saint Matthew.

And he read the verse, which went like this:

    Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds.

Chapter 3: The Fever Trees

The departure — The rising tide — Elms and nettle trees — Various plants — The jacamar — What the forest looked like — The giant eucalyptus trees — Why they are called "fever trees" — Troops of monkeys — The waterfall — Camp for the night

The next day, October 30, everything was ready for the planned exploration, which recent events had made so urgent. Things had in fact turned out in such a way that the colonists of Lincoln Island could imagine they were no longer the ones in need of rescue, but the ones who might be able to bring it.

So it was agreed that they would go up the Mercy as far as the river's current allowed a boat to travel. That way a large part of the journey would be made without effort, and the explorers could carry their provisions and their weapons to a point well into the west of the island.

They had had to think, after all, not only about the things they were taking but also about the things that luck might allow them to bring back to Granite House. If there had been a shipwreck on the coast, as everything suggested, there would be no shortage of wreckage, and it would be well worth salvaging. With that in mind, the cart would no doubt have suited better than the fragile canoe. But the cart was heavy and clumsy and had to be pulled by hand, which made it much less practical. That led Pencroff to express his regret that the chest had not contained, along with "his half-pound of tobacco," a pair of those sturdy New Jersey horses, which would have been extremely useful to the colony!

The provisions, already loaded by Nab, consisted of preserved meat and a few gallons of beer and fermented liquor — enough to keep them going for three days, the longest time Cyrus Smith meant to give the exploration. Besides, they counted on restocking along the way if they needed to, and Nab took good care not to forget the little portable stove.

For tools, the colonists took the two woodsman's axes, which would serve to cut a path through the thick forest. For instruments, they took the spyglass and the pocket compass.

For weapons, they chose the two flintlock guns. On this island these were more useful than the percussion-cap guns would have been, because a flintlock needs only flints, which are easy to replace, while the others need percussion caps, and frequent use would soon have exhausted the supply. All the same, they also took one of the carbines and a few cartridges. As for the gunpowder, of which the barrels held about fifty pounds, they had to bring a certain amount, but the engineer was counting on making an explosive substance that would let them spare it. To the firearms they added the five cutlasses, well sheathed in leather. Equipped like that, the colonists could venture into the vast forest with a fair chance of getting themselves out of any trouble.

There is no need to add that Pencroff, Harbert, and Nab, armed this way, had nothing left to wish for — even though Cyrus Smith had made them promise not to fire a single shot unless they had to.

At six o'clock in the morning the canoe was pushed into the water. Everyone climbed aboard, Top included, and they headed for the mouth of the Mercy.

The tide had been coming in for only half an hour. That meant there were still a few hours of flood tide, and they had to make the most of them, because later the ebb would make it hard to go upriver. The tide was already running strongly, since the moon would be full in three days, and the canoe, which only had to be kept in the current, moved quickly between the two high banks without any need for the oars to speed it along.

In a few minutes the explorers reached the bend in the Mercy — the very angle where, seven months earlier, Pencroff had put together his first timber raft.

After that rather sharp angle the river curved round and turned southwest, and its course ran on in the shade of tall evergreen conifers.

The banks of the Mercy were magnificent. Cyrus Smith and his companions could only admire, without reservation, those beautiful effects that nature achieves so easily with water and trees. As they went on, the kinds of trees in the forest changed. On the right bank rose tier upon tier of splendid members of the elm family — true elms, those precious trees that builders prize so highly, because their wood keeps for a long time under water. Then came many clusters from the same family, among them nettle trees, whose kernel yields a very useful oil. Farther on, Harbert noticed some plants of the lardizabala family, whose supple branches, soaked in water, make excellent rope, and two or three trunks of the ebony family, a beautiful black streaked with wandering veins.

Every now and then, at places where it was easy to land, the canoe stopped. Then Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, and Pencroff, guns in hand and with Top running ahead, beat the bank. Quite apart from the game, they might come across some useful plant that was not to be sneezed at — and the young naturalist got exactly what he had hoped for. He discovered a kind of wild spinach from the goosefoot family, and many specimens of the mustard family belonging to the cabbage genus, which could certainly be "civilized" by transplanting them: there was watercress, horseradish, and turnips, and finally some little branching stems, slightly hairy, about three feet high, that bore seeds of an almost brown color.

"Do you know what that plant is?" Harbert asked the sailor.

"Tobacco!" cried Pencroff, who had obviously never seen his favorite plant anywhere but in the bowl of his pipe.

"No, Pencroff!" answered Harbert. "That's not tobacco, it's mustard."

"Mustard it is, then!" answered the sailor. "But if by any chance a tobacco plant should turn up, my boy, kindly don't turn your nose up at it."

"We'll find some one day!" said Gédéon Spilett.

"Really?" cried Pencroff. "Well, on that day I honestly don't know what our island will still be missing!"

These various plants were carefully dug up by the roots and carried to the canoe. Cyrus Smith had not left it; he was still absorbed in his own thoughts.

The reporter, Harbert, and Pencroff went ashore several times in this way, sometimes on the right bank of the Mercy, sometimes on the left. The left bank was less steep, the right bank more heavily wooded. By consulting his pocket compass, the engineer was able to establish that from the first bend the river ran roughly southwest to northeast, in a nearly straight line, for a distance of about three miles. But it seemed likely that its course changed farther on, and that the Mercy climbed toward the northwest, toward the foothills of Mount Franklin, which must feed it with their waters.

During one of these excursions, Gédéon Spilett managed to catch two pairs of live birds of the chicken family. They had long, slender beaks, long necks, and short wings, and no tail to speak of. Harbert, rightly, named them "tinamous," and it was decided that they would be the first residents of the future poultry yard.

So far, though, the guns had not spoken. The first shot to ring out in that forest of the Far West was set off by the appearance of a handsome bird that looked, in its build, very much like a kingfisher.

"I know that one!" cried Pencroff — and it is fair to say that his gun went off almost in spite of him.

"What do you know?" asked the reporter.

"The bird that got away from us on our first trip, the one we named this part of the forest after."

"A jacamar!" cried Harbert.

It was indeed a jacamar, a beautiful bird whose rather coarse plumage has a metallic sheen. A few pellets of shot had brought it down, and Top carried it back to the canoe, along with a dozen "touraco-lories," climbing birds about the size of a pigeon, painted all over in green, with part of their wings crimson and an upright crest edged with a white border. The honor of that fine shot went to the boy, and he was rather proud of it. The lories made better eating than the jacamar, whose flesh is a little tough, but it would have been hard to persuade Pencroff that he had not killed the king of edible birds.

It was ten o'clock in the morning when the canoe reached a second bend of the Mercy, about five miles from its mouth. They stopped there for lunch, and the halt, in the shelter of tall, beautiful trees, lasted half an hour.

The river was still sixty to seventy feet wide, and its bed five to six feet deep. The engineer had noticed that many tributaries swelled its flow, but they were only small streams, too shallow for any boat. As for the forest — whether you called it Jacamar Wood or the Far West forests — it stretched as far as the eye could see. Nowhere, neither under the tall timber nor among the trees along the banks of the Mercy, was there any sign that human beings had been there. The explorers could not find a single suspicious trace. It was obvious that no woodsman's ax had ever notched these trees, that no pioneer's knife had ever cut these creepers stretched from trunk to trunk among the dense undergrowth and the long grass. If some castaways had landed on the island, they had not yet left the shore, and it was not under this thick cover that they should look for the survivors of the shipwreck they suspected.

So the engineer showed a certain haste to reach the west coast of Lincoln Island, which by his reckoning was at least five miles away. They set off again by water. Although, in its present direction, the Mercy seemed to run not toward the coast but rather toward Mount Franklin, it was decided that they would keep using the canoe as long as there was enough water under its keel to float it. That would spare them a great deal of effort and save time as well, because otherwise they would have had to hack a path with the axes through the thick brush.

But soon the flood tide gave out altogether — either because the tide was going down, as it was in fact due to at that hour, or because it was no longer felt this far from the mouth of the Mercy. So they had to get out the oars. Nab and Harbert took their places on the thwart, Pencroff took the steering oar at the stern, and they went on up the river.

The forest now seemed to be thinning out on the Far West side. The trees there stood farther apart and were often quite alone. But precisely because they were spaced out, they had more of the free, clean air that moved around them, and they were magnificent.

What splendid examples of the plant life of that latitude! Their presence alone would have been enough for a botanist to name, without a moment's hesitation, the parallel that Lincoln Island lay on!

"Eucalyptus!" Harbert had cried out.

And that is what they were — those superb trees, the last giants of the zone just beyond the tropics, the cousins of the eucalyptus of Australia and New Zealand, both of which lie in the same latitude as Lincoln Island. Some of them rose to a height of two hundred feet. Their trunks measured twenty feet around at the base, and their bark, furrowed with networks of fragrant resin, was as much as five inches thick. Nothing could be more marvelous — or stranger — than these enormous members of the myrtle family, whose leaves turned their edges to the light and let the sun's rays reach all the way to the ground!

At the foot of these eucalyptus trees, fresh grass carpeted the ground, and out of the tufts burst flocks of little birds that shone in the shafts of light like winged jewels.

"Now those are trees!" cried Nab. "But are they good for anything?"

"Pooh!" answered Pencroff. "Giant plants must be like giant people. They're not much good for anything except showing off at fairs!"

"I think you're mistaken, Pencroff," Gédéon Spilett answered. "Eucalyptus wood is starting to be used to great advantage in fine furniture-making."

"And I'll add," said the boy, "that eucalyptus trees belong to a family with plenty of useful members. There's the guava tree, which gives guavas; the clove tree, which produces cloves; the pomegranate, which bears pomegranates; the Eugenia cauliflora, whose fruit makes a passable wine; the ugni myrtle, which contains an excellent alcoholic liquor; the caryophyllus myrtle, whose bark makes a highly valued cinnamon; the Eugenia pimenta, which is where Jamaica pepper comes from; the common myrtle, whose berries can stand in for pepper; the Eucalyptus robusta, which produces an excellent kind of manna; the Eucalyptus gunei, whose sap turns into beer when it ferments; and finally all those trees known as 'trees of life' or 'ironwood,' which belong to this same myrtle family — and it has forty-six genera and thirteen hundred species!"

They let the boy go on, and he rattled off his little botany lesson with great enthusiasm. Cyrus Smith listened with a smile, and Pencroff with a pride beyond words.

"Fine, Harbert," Pencroff answered, "but I'd be willing to swear that none of those useful specimens you just listed are giants like these!"

"That's true, Pencroff."

"So that backs up what I said," the sailor replied. "Giants are good for nothing!"

"That's where you're wrong, Pencroff," the engineer put in, "and it so happens that these very giant eucalyptus trees sheltering us are good for something."

"And what's that?"

"For making the country they grow in healthier. Do you know what they call them in Australia and New Zealand?"

"No, Mr. Cyrus."

"They call them 'fever trees.'"

"Because they give you fever?"

"No — because they prevent it!"

"Good. I'll make a note of that," said the reporter.

"Note it down, then, my dear Spilett, because it seems to be proved that the presence of eucalyptus trees is enough to neutralize the poisonous vapors of marshes. This natural safeguard has been tried in certain regions of southern Europe and North Africa where the soil was thoroughly unhealthy, and the health of the people who live there has gradually improved. No more recurring fevers in the areas covered by forests of these trees. The fact is now beyond doubt, and it's a lucky thing for us, the colonists of Lincoln Island."

"Ah! What an island! What a blessed island!" cried Pencroff. "I'm telling you, it doesn't lack a thing... Except..."

"That will come, Pencroff, it will turn up," answered the engineer. "But let's get back on the river and push on as far as it will carry our canoe!"

So the exploration went on for at least two more miles through country covered with eucalyptus, which towered over all the other woods in that part of the island. The area they covered stretched beyond the reach of sight on both sides of the Mercy, whose rather winding bed now ran deep between high green banks. The channel was often choked with tall weeds and even with sharp rocks, which made the going quite hard. The oars were hampered, and Pencroff had to push the boat along with a pole. They could also feel the bottom rising little by little, and the moment was not far off when the canoe would have to stop for lack of water. The sun was already sinking toward the horizon and throwing the trees' enormous shadows across the ground. Cyrus Smith, seeing that he could not reach the west coast of the island that day, decided to camp at the very spot where lack of water would force them to stop. He reckoned he must still be five or six miles from the coast, and that distance was too great to attempt crossing at night through these unknown woods.

So they kept the boat moving through the forest without a rest. Little by little the forest grew thicker again, and it seemed more inhabited as well — for, unless the sailor's eyes deceived him, he thought he saw troops of monkeys running through the underbrush. Sometimes two or three of these animals even stopped a short distance from the canoe and stared at the colonists without showing the slightest fear, as if, seeing human beings for the first time, they had not yet learned to dread them. It would have been easy to shoot these four-handed creatures, but Cyrus Smith would not allow a pointless slaughter, though the hot-headed Pencroff was a little tempted by it. And it was the prudent choice besides, because these monkeys were strong and extremely agile and could be dangerous. It was better not to provoke them with an attack that served no purpose at all.

It is true that the sailor looked at monkeys from a purely culinary point of view, and in fact these animals, which eat nothing but plants, make excellent game. But since there was plenty of food, there was no reason to waste ammunition for nothing.

Toward four o'clock, going up the Mercy became very difficult, because its course was clogged with water plants and rocks. The banks rose higher and higher, and the riverbed was already cutting its way between the first foothills of Mount Franklin. So its sources could not be far off, since they were fed by all the waters of the mountain's southern slopes.

"Within a quarter of an hour we'll have to stop, Mr. Cyrus," said the sailor.

"Well, then, we'll stop, Pencroff, and set up a camp for the night."

"How far can we be from Granite House?" asked Harbert.

"About seven miles," the engineer answered, "though that takes into account the windings of the river, which have carried us to the northwest."

"Are we going on?" asked the reporter.

"Yes, for as long as we can," answered Cyrus Smith. "Tomorrow, at daybreak, we'll leave the canoe. In two hours, I hope, we'll cover the distance that separates us from the coast, and we'll have almost the whole day to explore the shore."

"Onward!" answered Pencroff.

But soon the canoe scraped the pebbly bottom of the river, which was by then no more than twenty feet wide. A thick arch of greenery curved over its bed and wrapped it in half-darkness. They could also hear the fairly loud sound of falling water, which told them that a natural dam lay a few hundred paces upstream.

And sure enough, at a last bend in the river, a waterfall appeared through the trees. The canoe struck the bottom, and a few moments later it was tied to a trunk near the right bank.

It was about five o'clock. The last rays of the sun were slipping under the thick branches and striking the little waterfall at a slant, so that its damp spray glittered with all the colors of the rainbow. Beyond it, the bed of the Mercy disappeared into the thickets, where it was fed by some hidden spring. The various streams that flowed into it along the way made it a real river farther down, but here it was no more than a clear, shallow brook.

They camped on that very spot, which was charming. The colonists went ashore, and a fire was lit under a clump of broad nettle trees, in whose branches Cyrus Smith and his companions could, if they had to, have found a refuge for the night.

Supper was soon devoured, because everyone was hungry, and after that nobody thought of anything but sleep. But as night fell, a few roars of a suspicious kind were heard, so the fire was built up for the night, to protect the sleepers with its crackling flames. Nab and Pencroff even kept watch in turn and did not spare the fuel. Perhaps they were not mistaken when they thought they saw the shadows of animals prowling around the camp, either in the underbrush or among the branches. But the night passed without incident, and the next day, October 31, at five o'clock in the morning, everyone was up and ready to set off.

Chapter 4: A Forest for a Coastline

Heading for the coast — Troops of monkeys — A new stream — Why the tide does not reach it — A forest for a coastline — Reptile End — Gédéon Spilett makes Harbert envious — The bamboo fireworks

At six o'clock in the morning, after a first breakfast, the colonists set off again, meaning to reach the west coast of the island by the shortest way. How long would it take them to get there? Cyrus Smith had said two hours, but that obviously depended on what kind of obstacles they met. This part of the Far West looked crammed with trees, like an immense thicket made up of every possible kind of wood. So they would probably have to clear a path through grass, brush and creepers, and walk with an ax in hand — and with a gun, too, no doubt, judging by the cries of wild beasts they had heard in the night.

The exact position of the camp could be fixed by the position of Mount Franklin. Since the volcano rose to the north at a distance of less than three miles, all they had to do was strike out in a straight line to the southwest to reach the west coast.

They set off, after carefully making sure the canoe was well moored. Pencroff and Nab carried provisions that would feed the little party for at least two days. There was no more talk of hunting. The engineer even urged his companions to avoid any unnecessary shot, so as not to give away their presence anywhere near the shore.

The first blows of the ax fell in the brush, among clumps of mastic shrubs, a little above the waterfall, and Cyrus Smith, compass in hand, pointed out the way.

The forest here was made up of trees most of which they had already identified around the lake and Prospect Plateau. There were deodars, Douglas firs, casuarinas, gum trees, eucalyptus, dragon trees, hibiscus, cedars and other kinds, mostly of middling size, because there were so many of them that they had stunted one another's growth. So the colonists could move only slowly along this road, which they were cutting as they walked, and which the engineer had in mind to link up later with the road to Red Creek.

Since leaving the camp, the colonists had been going down the low slopes that made up the island's mountain system, over very dry ground. But its lush growth hinted either at a network of water running underground or at some stream flowing nearby. All the same, Cyrus Smith did not remember seeing any watercourse but Red Creek and the Mercy on his expedition to the crater.

During the first hours of the trip they saw troops of monkeys again, which seemed utterly astonished at the sight of these men, whose appearance was new to them. Gédéon Spilett jokingly asked whether these agile, sturdy four-handed creatures might not take him and his companions for degenerate brothers! And frankly, mere pedestrians, hampered by the brush at every step, tangled in creepers, blocked by tree trunks, did not cut much of a figure next to those supple animals, which leaped from branch to branch and let nothing stop them. The monkeys were numerous, but, very fortunately, they showed no sign of hostility.

They also saw a few wild boars, some agoutis, some kangaroos and other rodents, and two or three koulas, which Pencroff would gladly have treated to a few loads of shot.

"But hunting season isn't open," he said. "So frisk around, my friends, jump and fly in peace! We'll have a word or two with you on the way back!"

At half past nine in the morning, the road, which ran straight to the southwest, was suddenly cut off by an unknown stream, thirty to forty feet wide. Its swift current, driven by the slope of its bed and broken by a great many rocks, rushed along with a harsh roar. This creek was deep and clear, but it would have been completely impossible to navigate.

"We're cut off!" cried Nab.

"No," answered Harbert, "it's only a brook, and we'll manage to swim across it."

"What for?" answered Cyrus Smith. "This creek obviously runs to the sea. Let's stay on its left bank and follow it, and I'll be very surprised if it doesn't take us to the coast in no time. Let's go!"

"Just a moment," said the reporter. "What about this creek's name, my friends? Let's not leave our geography incomplete."

"Right!" said Pencroff.

"Name it, my boy," said the engineer, turning to the boy.

"Wouldn't it be better to wait until we've followed it all the way to its mouth?" Harbert pointed out.

"Very well," answered Cyrus Smith. "Then let's follow it without stopping."

"One moment more!" said Pencroff.

"What is it?" asked the reporter.

"If hunting is forbidden, fishing is allowed, I suppose," said the sailor.

"We have no time to lose," answered the engineer.

"Oh! Five minutes!" Pencroff replied. "All I ask is five minutes, in the interest of our lunch!"

And Pencroff lay down on the bank, plunged his arms into the running water, and soon sent a few dozen fine crayfish flying out from among the rocks, where they were swarming.

"Now that's going to be good!" cried Nab, coming to help the sailor.

"Didn't I tell you? Except for tobacco, there's everything on this island!" Pencroff murmured with a sigh.

It took less than five minutes to make a miraculous catch, because the creek was teeming with crayfish. These crustaceans had cobalt-blue shells and a beak armed with a little tooth. They filled a bag with them, and set off again.

Once they were following the bank of this new stream, the colonists walked more easily and more quickly. Besides, its banks were untouched by any human footprint. From time to time they spotted tracks left by large animals that came regularly to drink at the stream, but nothing more. It was not in this part of the Far West, then, that the peccary had taken the lead pellet that had cost Pencroff a molar.

Meanwhile, looking at that swift current racing off toward the sea, Cyrus Smith began to suspect that he and his companions were much farther from the west coast than they thought. In fact, at that hour the tide was rising along the shore, and it ought to have pushed back the creek's current if its mouth had been only a few miles off. But no such thing was happening, and the water kept flowing along the natural slope of its bed. The engineer must have been very surprised, and he kept checking his compass to make sure that some bend in the stream was not leading him back into the heart of the Far West.

Little by little, however, the creek grew wider and its waters less turbulent. The trees on its right bank were as crowded as those on its left, and the eye could not see past them. But those wooded masses were certainly empty of people, because Top was not barking, and the clever animal would not have failed to signal any stranger in the neighborhood of the stream.

At half past ten, to Cyrus Smith's great surprise, Harbert, who had gone a little way ahead, suddenly stopped and shouted:

"The sea!"

And a few moments later the colonists, halted at the edge of the forest, saw the western shore of the island spread out before their eyes.

But what a contrast between this coast and the east coast, where chance had first thrown them! No more granite wall, no reef offshore, not even a sandy beach. The forest made the shore, and its last trees, lashed by the waves, leaned out over the water. It was not a shore of the kind nature usually makes, either by spreading out wide carpets of sand or by piling up rocks. It was a wonderful border made of the most beautiful trees in the world. The bank stood high enough to overlook the level of the highest tides, and over all that rich soil, which rested on a base of granite, the splendid forest trees seemed as firmly rooted as the ones massed in the island's interior.

The colonists were standing at the notch of a small, insignificant cove, which could not have held even two or three fishing boats, and which served as the outlet of the new creek. But — a curious arrangement — instead of running into the sea down a gently sloping mouth, its waters fell from a height of more than forty feet. That explained why the rising tide had not made itself felt anywhere up the creek. In fact, the tides of the Pacific, even at their very highest, could never reach the level of the river, whose bed formed a sort of upper reach, like the stretch of a canal above a lock. Millions of years, no doubt, would still go by before the water wore away that granite sill and carved out a mouth a boat could use. So, by common consent, they gave the stream the name of Fall River.

Beyond it, to the north, the forest border went on for about two miles. Then the trees grew sparser, and beyond them a line of very picturesque heights stood out, running almost straight north and south. In the other direction, along the whole stretch of shore between Fall River and Reptile End, there was nothing but masses of woods, magnificent trees, some upright, some leaning, whose roots were bathed by the long swell of the sea. And it was in that direction — that is, along the whole of the Serpentine Peninsula — that the exploration had to go on, because that part of the shore offered places of refuge that the other, bare and wild, would obviously have refused to castaways of any kind.

The weather was fine and clear. From the top of a cliff, where Nab and Pencroff set out lunch, the eye could see a long way. The horizon was perfectly sharp, and there was not a sail out at sea. Along the whole shore, as far as the eye could reach, not a ship, not even a piece of wreckage. But the engineer would not consider the question settled until he had explored the coast all the way to the very tip of the Serpentine Peninsula.

Lunch was quickly dispatched, and at half past eleven Cyrus Smith gave the signal to leave. Instead of traveling along the crest of a cliff or over a sandy beach, the colonists had to keep under cover of the trees in order to follow the shore.

The distance from the mouth of Fall River to Reptile End was about twelve miles. On a walkable beach, without hurrying, the colonists could have covered that distance in four hours. But it took them twice as long to reach their goal, because the trees they had to get around, the brush they had to cut, the creepers they had to break, kept stopping them, and so many detours made their road much longer.

For that matter, there was nothing on this shore to show that a ship had been wrecked there recently. It is true, as Gédéon Spilett pointed out, that the sea could have carried everything away, and that just because no trace of a wreck could be found anymore, they should not conclude that no ship had been thrown ashore on this part of Lincoln Island.

The reporter's reasoning was sound. Besides, the incident of the lead pellet proved beyond any doubt that a gun had been fired on the island within the last three months at most.

It was already five o'clock, and the tip of the Serpentine Peninsula was still two miles from where the colonists were. Clearly, once Cyrus Smith and his companions reached Reptile End, they would not have time to get back before sunset to the camp they had set up near the sources of the Mercy. So they would have to spend the night on the promontory itself. But they had plenty of provisions, and that was lucky, because furred game no longer showed itself along this strip of forest, which was only a shoreline, after all. Birds, on the other hand, swarmed there — jacamars, couroucous, tragopans, grouse, lories, parrots, cockatoos, pheasants, pigeons and a hundred others. Not a tree without a nest, not a nest that was not full of beating wings!

At about seven o'clock in the evening, worn out with fatigue, the colonists reached Reptile End, a sort of scroll strangely carved out against the sea. Here the shore forest of the peninsula ended, and along the whole southern stretch the coast took on the usual look of a coast again, with its rocks, its reefs and its beaches. So it was possible that a disabled ship had run aground on this part of the island. But night was coming on, and the exploration had to be put off until the next day.

Pencroff and Harbert at once hurried off to look for a good spot to make camp. The last trees of the Far West forest came to an end at this point, and among them the boy recognized thick clumps of bamboo.

"Good!" he said. "Now that's a valuable find."

"Valuable?" answered Pencroff.

"Of course," Harbert went on. "I won't tell you, Pencroff, that bamboo bark, cut into flexible strips, is used for making baskets and hampers; that the bark, pulped and soaked, is used for making Chinese paper; that the stems, depending on how thick they are, give you canes, pipe stems and water pipes; that big bamboos make excellent building material, light and strong and never attacked by insects. I won't even add that if you saw bamboo stems between the joints, and keep part of the crosswise wall that forms the joint as a bottom, you get strong, handy containers that the Chinese use a great deal! No! None of that would satisfy you. But..."

"But...?"

"But I'll tell you, in case you didn't know, that in India people eat bamboo like asparagus."

"Thirty-foot asparagus!" cried the sailor. "And is it good?"

"Excellent," answered Harbert. "Only it isn't the thirty-foot stems people eat. It's the young bamboo shoots."

"Perfect, my boy, perfect!" answered Pencroff.

"I'll also add that the pith of the new stems, pickled in vinegar, makes a much-prized relish."

"Better and better, Harbert."

"And finally, that between their joints bamboos ooze a sweet liquid you can make into a very pleasant drink."

"Is that all?" asked the sailor.

"That's all!"

"And you can't smoke it, by any chance?"

"You can't smoke it, my poor Pencroff!"

Harbert and the sailor did not have to look long for a good place to spend the night. The rocks of the shore were deeply split — the sea must batter them violently when the southwest winds blew — and they held hollows where the colonists could sleep sheltered from the weather. But just as the two of them were about to go into one of these caves, a tremendous roaring stopped them in their tracks.

"Back!" cried Pencroff. "We've got nothing but birdshot in our guns, and animals that roar like that wouldn't care any more about it than about a grain of salt!"

And the sailor, seizing Harbert by the arm, dragged him behind the shelter of the rocks, just as a magnificent animal appeared at the mouth of the cave.

It was a jaguar, at least as large as its Asian relatives — that is, it measured more than five feet from the tip of its head to the root of its tail. Its tawny coat was set off by several rows of black spots, regularly ringed like eyes, which stood out against the white fur of its belly. Harbert recognized it as that ferocious rival of the tiger, far more formidable than the cougar, which is only the rival of the wolf!

The jaguar came forward and looked around, its fur bristling, its eyes blazing, as if this were not the first time it had smelled a man.

Just then the reporter was coming around the high rocks. Harbert, thinking he had not seen the jaguar, was about to rush toward him. But Gédéon Spilett signaled to him with his hand and kept on walking. This was not his first tiger. He came up to within ten paces of the animal and stood still, his carbine at his shoulder, without a single muscle twitching.

The jaguar gathered itself and sprang at the hunter. But at the very moment it leaped, a bullet struck it between the eyes, and it dropped dead.

Harbert and Pencroff rushed over to the jaguar. Nab and Cyrus Smith came running from their side, and for a few moments they all stood looking at the animal stretched out on the ground. Its magnificent skin would be an ornament for the great hall of Granite House.

"Oh, Mr. Spilett! How I admire you, and how I envy you!" cried Harbert, in a burst of enthusiasm that was only natural.

"Come now, my boy," answered the reporter, "you'd have done the same."

"Me! With nerves like that...!"

"Just imagine, Harbert, that a jaguar is a hare, and you'll shoot it as calmly as you please."

"There you are!" answered Pencroff. "Nothing more to it than that!"

"And now," said Gédéon Spilett, "since this jaguar has left its den, my friends, I don't see why we shouldn't move into it for the night."

"But others might come back!" said Pencroff.

"It'll be enough to light a fire at the mouth of the cave," said the reporter, "and they won't risk crossing the threshold."

"To the jaguars' house, then!" answered the sailor, dragging the animal's body along behind him.

The colonists headed for the abandoned den, and there, while Nab skinned the jaguar, his companions piled a great heap of dry wood at the entrance, which the forest supplied in plenty.

But Cyrus Smith, having noticed the clump of bamboo, went and cut a good quantity of it and mixed it in with the fuel for the fire.

That done, they settled into the cave, whose sandy floor was strewn with bones. The guns were loaded, just in case of a sudden attack. They had supper, and then, when it was time to rest, they set fire to the woodpile at the mouth of the cave.

At once a regular volley of bangs burst out into the air! It was the bamboo, caught by the flames, going off like firecrackers! That racket alone would have been enough to terrify the boldest wild beasts!

And this way of making loud explosions was not the engineer's invention. According to Marco Polo, the Tartars have used it successfully for many centuries to drive the fearsome wild beasts of Central Asia away from their camps.

Chapter 5: Wreckage in the Air

A proposal to come back by the southern shore — The lay of the coast — Searching for the supposed shipwreck — Wreckage in the air — Discovery of a little natural harbor — Midnight on the banks of the Mercy — A boat adrift

Cyrus Smith and his companions slept like innocent marmots in the cave the jaguar had so politely left at their disposal.

At sunrise they were all on the shore, at the very tip of the promontory, and once again their eyes went to the horizon, which they could see around two-thirds of its circle. One last time the engineer was able to make sure that no sail and no hull of a wrecked ship could be seen on the sea, and the spyglass could not pick out a single suspicious spot.

There was nothing on the shore either, at least along the straight stretch that made up the south coast of the promontory for three miles. Beyond that, a bend in the land hid the rest of the coast, and even from the tip of Serpentine Peninsula they could not see Claw Cape, which was hidden behind high rocks.

That left the southern shore of the island still to explore. So should they set about exploring it right away, and give this day, November 2, to the job?

That had not been part of the original plan. When they left the canoe at the sources of the Mercy, it had been agreed that after looking over the west coast they would come back for it and return to Granite House by way of the river. At the time Cyrus Smith had believed that the western shore might offer shelter either to a ship in distress or to a vessel on an ordinary voyage. But since that coast had no landing place at all, they would have to look on the south side of the island for what they had not been able to find on the west.

It was Gédéon Spilett who proposed carrying the exploration on, so that the question of the supposed shipwreck could be settled once and for all, and he asked how far Claw Cape might be from the tip of the peninsula.

"About thirty miles," the engineer answered, "if we allow for the curves of the coast."

"Thirty miles!" said Gédéon Spilett. "That'll be a hard day's march. All the same, I think we ought to go back to Granite House along the southern shore."

"But from Claw Cape to Granite House," Harbert pointed out, "it's at least another ten miles."

"Call it forty miles altogether," answered the reporter, "and let's not hesitate to do them. At least we'll get a look at that unknown shore, and we won't have to start this exploration over again."

"Quite right," said Pencroff. "But what about the canoe?"

"The canoe stayed by itself at the sources of the Mercy for one day," answered Gédéon Spilett. "It can very well stay there for two! So far we can hardly say the island is overrun with thieves!"

"All the same," said the sailor, "when I remember that business with the turtle, I don't have any more confidence than I need to."

"The turtle! The turtle!" answered the reporter. "Don't you know it was the sea that turned it back over?"

"Who knows?" murmured the engineer.

"But..." said Nab.

Nab plainly had something to say, because he kept opening his mouth to speak and then not speaking.

"What is it you want to say, Nab?" the engineer asked him.

"If we go back along the shore as far as Claw Cape," answered Nab, "then once we've rounded the cape, we'll be blocked..."

"By the Mercy! That's right," answered Harbert, "and we won't have a bridge or a boat to get across it!"

"Oh, Mr. Cyrus," answered Pencroff, "with a few floating logs, we won't have any trouble getting over that river!"

"Never mind," said Gédéon Spilett, "it'll be useful to build a bridge if we want an easy way into the Far West."

"A bridge!" cried Pencroff. "Well, isn't Mr. Smith an engineer by trade? He'll build us a bridge whenever we want a bridge! As for getting you over to the other bank of the Mercy tonight, and without wetting a thread of your clothes, leave that to me. We've still got a day's food, which is all we need, and anyway the game may not let us down today the way it did yesterday. Let's go!"

The reporter's proposal, backed very warmly by the sailor, won everyone's approval, because each of them wanted to be done with his doubts, and if they came back by way of Claw Cape, the exploration would be complete. But there was not an hour to lose. A stage of forty miles was a long one, and they could not count on reaching Granite House before nightfall.

So at six o'clock in the morning the little troop set off. In case of unpleasant encounters with animals on two legs or on four, the guns were loaded with ball, and Top, who was to lead the way, was ordered to scour the edge of the forest.

From the tip of the promontory that formed the tail of the peninsula, the coast curved around for a distance of five miles. They covered it quickly, and the most painstaking search turned up no trace whatever of any landing, old or recent — no wreckage, no remains of a camp, no ashes of a dead fire, not a single footprint!
