When the colonists reached the corner where the curve ended and the coast turned northeast to form Washington Bay, they could take in the whole length of the island's southern shore at a glance. Twenty-five miles off, the coast ended at Claw Cape, which showed only faintly in the morning haze, and which a mirage lifted up so that it seemed to hang between land and water. Between the place where the colonists stood and the far end of the great bay, the shore was made up first of a wide, very smooth, very flat beach, with a fringe of trees behind it. After that the coastline grew very ragged and thrust sharp points out into the sea. And last of all a jumble of blackish rocks piled up in picturesque disorder all the way to Claw Cape.

That was the lay of this part of the island, which the explorers were seeing for the first time and which they took in at a glance after stopping for a moment.

"A ship that ran aground here," said Pencroff, "would be lost, no question about it. Sandbanks reaching far out from shore, and beyond them, reefs! Bad waters!"

"But at least there'd be something left of the ship," the reporter pointed out.

"There'd be pieces of timber left on the reefs, and nothing on the sand," answered the sailor.

"Why's that?"

"Because that sand is even more dangerous than the rocks. It swallows up everything that's thrown onto it, and a few days are enough for the hull of a ship of several hundred tons to disappear into it completely!"

"So, Pencroff," asked the engineer, "if a ship had been lost on those banks, it wouldn't be surprising if there were no trace of it left now?"

"No, Mr. Smith, not given time, or a storm. Still, even then it would be surprising if bits of the masts or a few spars hadn't been thrown up on the shore, out of reach of the sea."

"Then let's go on with our search," answered Cyrus Smith.

At one o'clock in the afternoon the colonists reached the far end of Washington Bay. By then they had covered twenty miles.

They stopped for lunch.

Here began an uneven coast, oddly jagged and lined by a long string of the reefs that took over from the sandbanks. The tide was slack just then, but it would soon go out and lay them bare. They could see the smooth swells of the sea breaking on the heads of the rocks and spreading out in long fringes of foam. From this point on to Claw Cape the beach was narrow, squeezed between the edge of the reefs and the edge of the forest.

So the going was about to get harder, because countless fallen rocks cluttered the shore. The granite wall, too, kept rising higher and higher, and of the trees that crowned it farther back they could see only the green tops, which not a breath of wind was stirring.

After half an hour's rest the colonists set off again, and their eyes did not leave a single spot of the reefs or the beach unexamined. Pencroff and Nab even ventured out among the rocks whenever something caught their eye. But wreckage there was none — they had been fooled by some odd shape in the rocks. They did see, though, that edible shellfish were plentiful on this beach. But it could not be put to good use until there was some link between the two banks of the Mercy, and until they had better means of carrying things.

So nothing that had to do with the supposed shipwreck appeared on this shore. And yet anything of any size — the hull of a ship, for instance — would have been visible by now, or its wreckage would have been carried ashore, as the chest had been, and the chest had been found less than twenty miles away. But there was nothing.

Toward three o'clock Cyrus Smith and his companions came to a narrow, well-sheltered cove with no stream flowing into it. It made a real little natural harbor, invisible from the open sea, and it was reached by a narrow channel that wound between the reefs.

At the back of this cove, some violent upheaval had torn open the rocky rim of the shore, and a cutting, hollowed out in a gentle slope, led up to the plateau above. That spot could not be more than ten miles from Claw Cape, and so it must lie four miles in a straight line from Prospect Plateau.

Gédéon Spilett suggested to his companions that they stop here. They agreed, because the walk had sharpened everyone's appetite, and though it was not yet dinnertime, nobody said no to a bite of venison to keep him going. This snack would let them hold out until supper at Granite House.

A few minutes later the colonists, seated at the foot of a magnificent clump of maritime pines, were devouring the provisions Nab had taken out of his knapsack.

The spot stood fifty to sixty feet above sea level. So the view from it reached a good way: passing over the last rocks of the cape, it ran on until it lost itself in Union Bay. But neither the islet nor Prospect Plateau could be seen, nor could they have been at that moment, because the rise of the ground and the screen of tall trees cut off the northern horizon abruptly.

Needless to say, wide as the stretch of sea was that the explorers could take in, and though the engineer's spyglass swept point by point around the whole circle where sky and water met, not a ship was sighted.

In the same way the spyglass was moved with the same care over the whole part of the coast that still remained to be explored, from the beach out to the reefs, and no wreckage appeared in the field of the instrument.

"Well," said Gédéon Spilett, "we'll have to make up our minds to it, and console ourselves with the thought that nobody's going to come and dispute our possession of Lincoln Island!"

"But what about that lead pellet?" said Harbert. "It wasn't imaginary, I suppose!"

"A thousand devils, no!" cried Pencroff, thinking of his missing molar.

"Then what are we to conclude?" asked the reporter.

"This," answered the engineer. "That three months ago at the most, a ship, willingly or not, put in here..."

"What! You'd accept, Cyrus, that it sank without leaving any trace?" cried the reporter.

"No, my dear Spilett. But notice this: if it's certain that a human being set foot on this island, it seems no less certain that he has left it now."

"Then if I understand you, Mr. Cyrus," said Harbert, "the ship has gone away again?..."

"Obviously."

"And we've lost a chance of getting home, and lost it for good?" said Nab.

"For good, I'm afraid."

"Well! Since the chance is lost, let's go," said Pencroff, who was already homesick for Granite House.

But he had barely stood up when Top's barking rang out loudly, and the dog came out of the woods holding in his mouth a scrap of cloth smeared with mud.

Nab pulled the scrap out of the dog's mouth. It was a piece of strong canvas.

Top kept barking, and by running back and forth he seemed to be inviting his master to follow him into the forest.

"There's something in there that might just explain my lead pellet!" cried Pencroff.

"A castaway!" answered Harbert.

"Wounded, maybe!" said Nab.

"Or dead!" answered the reporter.

And they all rushed after the dog, in among the tall pines that formed the first screen of the forest. Just in case, Cyrus Smith and his companions had their weapons ready.

They had to go a good way into the woods, but to their great disappointment they still saw no footprints. The brush and the creepers were untouched, and they even had to cut through them with the ax, as they had done in the densest depths of the forest. So it was hard to believe that any human creature had passed this way before them. And yet Top went back and forth, not like a dog searching at random but like a creature with a will of its own, following an idea.

After seven or eight minutes of walking, Top stopped. The colonists had come to a kind of clearing, ringed with tall trees. They looked all around them and saw nothing, either under the brush or between the tree trunks.

"Well, what is it, Top?" said Cyrus Smith.

Top barked harder than ever, jumping up at the foot of a gigantic pine.

All of a sudden Pencroff cried out:

"Ah! Good! Ah! Perfect!"

"What is it?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"We've been looking for wreckage on the sea or on land!"

"Well?"

"Well, it's in the air!"

And the sailor pointed to a sort of great whitish rag caught at the top of the pine. Top had brought back a piece of it that had fallen to the ground.

"But that's not wreckage!" cried Gédéon Spilett.

"Beg your pardon, it is!" answered Pencroff.

"What? It's...?"

"It's all that's left of our airship — our balloon, run aground up there at the top of that tree!"

Pencroff was not mistaken, and he let out a magnificent hurrah, adding:

"Now there's good cloth! There's enough to keep us in linen for years! Enough to make handkerchiefs and shirts! Eh, Mr. Spilett, what do you say to an island where shirts grow on trees?"

It really was a lucky thing for the colonists of Lincoln Island that the balloon, after its last leap through the air, had come down again on the island, and that they had now had the luck to find it. Either they would keep the envelope as it was, if they ever wanted to try another escape through the air, or they would put to good use those several hundred yards of fine-quality cotton cloth, once the varnish had been taken off it. As you can easily imagine, everyone shared Pencroff's joy, and shared it heartily.

But the envelope had to be taken down from the tree it was hanging in and put somewhere safe, and that was no small job. Nab, Harbert and the sailor climbed to the top of the tree, and it took wonders of skill to free the enormous, empty balloon.

The operation lasted nearly two hours. And at the end of it, not only the envelope, with its valve, its springs and its brass fittings, but also the net — that is, a great quantity of ropes and cords — and the ring and the balloon's anchor were all on the ground. Apart from the tear, the envelope was in good condition; only the neck at its bottom had been ripped.

It was a fortune that had fallen from the sky.

"All the same, Mr. Cyrus," said the sailor, "if we ever decide to leave the island, it won't be by balloon, will it? Those airships don't go where you want them to, and we know something about that! Look here, if you take my advice, we'll build a good boat of twenty tons or so, and you'll let me cut a foresail and a jib out of this cloth. As for the rest, it'll do to clothe us!"

"We'll see, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith. "We'll see."

"Meanwhile we have to put all this somewhere safe," said Nab.

And indeed, there was no thinking of carrying this load of cloth, cords and ropes to Granite House, for it weighed a great deal. And until they had a proper vehicle to haul it in, it was important not to leave these riches any longer at the mercy of the first hurricane that came along. By pooling their efforts the colonists managed to drag the whole lot down to the shore, where they found a fairly large hollow in the rock that, thanks to the way it faced, neither wind nor rain nor sea could get into.

"We needed a cupboard, and we've got a cupboard," said Pencroff. "But since it doesn't lock, it would be wise to hide the opening. I don't say that because of thieves on two feet, but because of thieves on four!"

By six o'clock in the evening everything was stored away. They gave the little inlet that formed the cove the very fitting name of "Balloon Harbor," and then they took the road for Claw Cape again. Pencroff and the engineer talked over various projects that ought to be carried out as soon as possible. Before anything else they had to throw a bridge across the Mercy, so as to have an easy way through to the south of the island. Then a cart would come back for the balloon, because the canoe could never have carried it all. Then they would build a decked boat. Then Pencroff would rig her as a cutter, and they could set out on voyages of circumnavigation... around the island. Then, and so on.

Meanwhile night was coming on, and the sky was already dark when the colonists reached Jetsam Point, at the very spot where they had found the precious chest. But there, no more than anywhere else, was there anything to show that any shipwreck had taken place, and they had to come back to the conclusions Cyrus Smith had already put forward.

From Jetsam Point to Granite House there were still four miles to go, and they were quickly covered. But it was after midnight when the colonists, having followed the shore to the mouth of the Mercy, reached the first bend in the river.

There the riverbed was eighty feet wide, which was not easy to cross. But Pencroff had promised to overcome that difficulty, and now he was called on to make good.

It has to be admitted that the colonists were worn out. The stage had been long, and the episode of the balloon had done nothing to rest their legs and arms. So they were in a hurry to get back to Granite House to eat their supper and sleep, and if the bridge had been built, they would have been home in a quarter of an hour.

The night was very dark. So Pencroff got ready to keep his promise by making a sort of raft on which they could cross the Mercy. He and Nab, armed with axes, picked out two trees near the bank to make the raft from, and began chopping at them from the base.

Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett sat on the bank, waiting for the moment when they could help their companions, while Harbert walked back and forth without straying very far.

All at once the boy, who had gone a little way up the river, came running back, and pointing upstream along the Mercy:

"What's that drifting down there?" he cried.

Pencroff stopped work and made out a moving object that showed dimly in the dark.

"A boat!" he said.

They all came closer and saw, to their utter surprise, a small craft following the current.

"Boat ahoy!" the sailor shouted, out of an old professional habit, without stopping to think that it might have been better to keep quiet.

No answer. The boat kept drifting, and it was no more than ten paces off when the sailor cried:

"Why, it's our canoe! It's broken its mooring line and come down with the current! I must say, it's turning up at just the right time!"

"Our canoe?..." murmured the engineer.

Pencroff was right. It really was the canoe, whose mooring line had broken, no doubt, and which was coming back all by itself from the sources of the Mercy! So it was important to catch it as it went by, before the river's swift current carried it out past the mouth. Nab and Pencroff did exactly that, deftly, with a long pole.

The canoe came in to the bank. The engineer, stepping into it first, took hold of the mooring line and made sure by feeling it that the line really had been worn through by rubbing against the rocks.

"Now that," the reporter said to him in a low voice, "is what you might call a circumstance..."

"A strange one!" answered Cyrus Smith.

Strange or not, it was a lucky one! Harbert, the reporter, Nab and Pencroff got in after him. They had no doubt that the line had simply worn through. But the most astonishing part of the business was really that the canoe had arrived at the very moment when the colonists were there to catch it as it went by — because a quarter of an hour later it would have been lost at sea.

If this had been the age of genies, the incident would have given them every right to think that the island was haunted by some supernatural being who had put his powers at the service of the castaways!

A few strokes of the paddle brought the colonists to the mouth of the Mercy. The canoe was hauled up the beach close to the Chimneys, and they all made for the ladder of Granite House.

But at that moment Top barked angrily, and Nab, who was feeling for the first rung, let out a cry...

The ladder was gone.

Chapter 6: A New Servant

Pencroff hails — A night in the Chimneys — Harbert's arrow — Cyrus Smith's plan — An unexpected solution — What had happened at Granite House — How a new servant entered the colonists' service

Cyrus Smith had stopped short without a word. His companions searched in the darkness, both up the face of the cliff, in case the wind had shifted the ladder, and along the ground, in case it had come loose and fallen... But the ladder had completely disappeared. As for whether a gust had lifted it up to the first landing, halfway up the wall, there was no telling in that pitch-dark night.

"If this is a joke," cried Pencroff, "it's a bad one! To come home and find there's no staircase up to your bedroom — that's nothing for tired people to laugh at!"

Nab, for his part, was lost in exclamations!

"But there hasn't been any wind!" Harbert pointed out.

"I'm beginning to think there are some strange goings-on on Lincoln Island!" said Pencroff.

"Strange?" replied Gédéon Spilett. "Not at all, Pencroff. Nothing could be more natural. Somebody came while we were away, took possession of the place, and pulled up the ladder!"

"Somebody!" cried the sailor. "And who, then?..."

"Why, the hunter with the lead pellet," the reporter answered. "What good would he be if he didn't explain our misfortune?"

"Well, if there's somebody up there," said Pencroff with an oath, for he was beginning to lose patience, "I'm going to hail him, and he'd better answer!"

And in a voice like thunder, the sailor let out a long "Ahoy!" which the echoes threw back with force.

The colonists listened, and they thought they heard, somewhere up near Granite House, a kind of snickering whose source they could not make out. But no voice answered Pencroff's voice, and he repeated his vigorous call to no purpose.

There was truly enough here to astonish the most unconcerned men in the world, and the colonists could not be unconcerned men of that kind. In their situation every incident was serious, and certainly, in the seven months they had lived on the island, none had come along that was quite so surprising.

Be that as it may, forgetting how tired they were and gripped by the strangeness of the event, they stood at the foot of Granite House, not knowing what to think or what to do, asking one another questions that no one could answer, piling up theories each more impossible than the last. Nab was moaning, bitterly disappointed not to be able to get back into his kitchen — all the more because the provisions for the journey were used up and he had no way to replace them just then.

"My friends," Cyrus Smith said at last, "there's only one thing for us to do: wait for daylight, and then act according to circumstances. But to do our waiting, let's go to the Chimneys. There we'll have shelter, and if we can't have supper, at least we can sleep."

"But who's the cheeky fellow who played this trick on us?" Pencroff asked once again, unable to resign himself to the business.

Whoever the "cheeky fellow" might be, the only thing to do, as the engineer had said, was to go back to the Chimneys and wait there for day. Top, however, was ordered to stay under the windows of Granite House, and when Top was given an order, Top carried it out without any argument. So the good dog stayed at the foot of the wall while his master and his companions took refuge among the rocks.

To say that the colonists, worn out as they were, slept well on the sand of the Chimneys would be stretching the truth. Not only could they not help being very anxious to learn how serious this new incident was — whether it was the result of some accident whose natural causes would become plain by daylight, or, on the contrary, the work of a human being — but they were also very badly bedded down. In any case, one way or another, their home was occupied at this moment, and they could not get back into it.

And Granite House was more than their home; it was their storehouse. All the colony's equipment was there: weapons, instruments, tools, ammunition, food supplies, and so on. If all that were plundered, the colonists would have to start setting themselves up all over again, make their weapons and tools over again. A serious matter! So, giving in to their uneasiness, one or another of them kept going out every few minutes to see whether Top was standing a good watch. Cyrus Smith alone waited with his usual patience, though his stubborn reason was exasperated to find itself facing a fact that was utterly inexplicable, and he was indignant at the thought that around him, perhaps above him, some influence was at work to which he could not put a name. Gédéon Spilett entirely shared his view on this point, and the two of them talked it over several times, but in low voices — these inexplicable circumstances that defeated all their insight and all their experience. There was certainly a mystery on this island, and how were they to get to the bottom of it? Harbert, for his part, could not imagine what to think, and would have liked to question Cyrus Smith. As for Nab, he had ended by telling himself that none of this was his business, that it was his master's business, and if he had not been afraid of offending his companions, good Nab would have slept that night every bit as soundly as if he had been resting on his own bunk in Granite House!

Pencroff, finally, was the most furious of them all, and he was honestly and thoroughly angry.

"It's a prank," he kept saying, "a prank somebody's pulled on us! Well, I don't like pranks, I don't, and woe to the prankster if he falls into my hands!"

As soon as the first glimmer of day rose in the east, the colonists, suitably armed, went down to the shore at the edge of the reefs. Granite House faced the rising sun directly and would soon be lit up by the light of dawn, and in fact, before five o'clock, the windows, with their shutters closed, appeared through their curtains of leaves.

On that side everything was in order. But a cry burst from the colonists' chests when they saw that the door — which they had certainly shut before they left — stood wide open.

Someone had got into Granite House. There was no longer any doubt about it.

The upper ladder, which usually stretched from the landing to the door, was in its place. But the lower ladder had been pulled up and hauled all the way to the doorsill. It was more than obvious that the intruders had wanted to protect themselves against any surprise.

As for what kind of intruders they were and how many, there was no telling yet, since not one of them showed himself.

Pencroff hailed again.

No answer.

"The scoundrels!" cried the sailor. "Would you look at that — sleeping peacefully as if they owned the place! Ahoy there! Pirates, bandits, privateers, sons of John Bull!"

When Pencroff, as an American, had called somebody a "son of John Bull" — that is, an Englishman — he had climbed to the very summit of insult.

By now it was full day, and the front of Granite House lit up in the rays of the sun. But inside as well as out, everything was silent and calm.

The colonists had come to wondering whether Granite House was occupied or not. And yet the position of the ladder proved it plainly enough, and it was even certain that the occupants, whoever they might be, could not have got away! But how could they reach them?

Then Harbert had the idea of tying a cord to an arrow and shooting the arrow so that it would pass between the first rungs of the ladder, which were hanging over the doorsill. Then, by means of the cord, they could unroll the ladder down to the ground and restore communication between the ground and Granite House.

There was obviously nothing else to be done, and with a little skill the method ought to work. Very luckily, bows and arrows had been left in one of the passages of the Chimneys, where there were also a few dozen fathoms of light hibiscus cord. Pencroff unwound this cord and fastened the end of it to a well-feathered arrow. Then Harbert set the arrow to his bow and took aim, with extreme care, at the dangling end of the ladder.

Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Pencroff and Nab had stepped back, so as to watch what would happen at the windows of Granite House. The reporter, his carbine at his shoulder, had the door in his sights.

The bow sprang, the arrow whistled off, pulling the cord after it, and passed between the last two rungs.

The operation had worked.

At once Harbert seized the end of the cord. But just as he gave it a jerk to bring the ladder tumbling down, an arm darted out between the wall and the door, snatched the ladder, and pulled it back inside Granite House.

"You triple scoundrel!" cried the sailor. "If a bullet's what would make you happy, you won't have long to wait!"

"But who is it?" asked Nab.

"Who? Didn't you recognize him?..."

"No."

"Why, it's a monkey, a macaque, a capuchin, a she-ape, an orang, a baboon, a gorilla, a marmoset! Our home's been invaded by monkeys, and they climbed up the ladder while we were gone!"

And at that very moment, as if to prove the sailor right, three or four of the four-handed creatures appeared at the windows, whose shutters they had pushed open, and greeted the rightful owners of the place with a thousand contortions and grimaces.

"I knew it was nothing but a prank!" cried Pencroff. "But here's one of the pranksters who's going to pay for the rest!"

The sailor raised his gun to his shoulder, took quick aim at one of the monkeys, and fired. They all vanished, except one, which was mortally hit and came hurtling down onto the beach.

This monkey, a tall one, belonged to the highest order of the four-handed animals; there was no mistaking it. Whether it was a chimpanzee, an orang, a gorilla or a gibbon, it ranked among the anthropoids, the apes so named for their resemblance to human beings. Besides, Harbert declared that it was an orangutan, and we know that the boy knew his zoology.

"What a magnificent animal!" cried Nab.

"As magnificent as you like!" Pencroff replied. "But I still don't see how we're going to get back into our house!"

"Harbert's a good shot," said the reporter, "and his bow is right here! Let him try again..."

"Huh! These monkeys are sly!" cried Pencroff. "They won't come back to the windows, and we won't be able to kill them, and when I think of the damage they can do in the rooms, in the storeroom..."

"Patience," Cyrus Smith answered. "These animals can't hold us off for long!"

"I won't be sure of that till they're on the ground," the sailor replied. "And to start with, Mr. Smith, do you know how many dozen of these pranksters there are up there?"

It would have been hard to answer Pencroff. And as for repeating the boy's attempt, that was not easy, because the bottom end of the ladder had been pulled back inside the door, and when they hauled on the cord again, the cord broke and the ladder did not come down.

The situation was truly awkward. Pencroff was raging. The business had a certain comic side, which he, for his part, did not find funny at all. Obviously the colonists would get back into their home in the end and drive out the intruders. But when, and how? That was what they could not have said.

Two hours went by, during which the monkeys took care not to show themselves. But they were still there, and three or four times a muzzle or a paw slipped out through the door or the windows and was greeted with gunfire.

"Let's hide," the engineer said then. "Perhaps the monkeys will think we've gone and show themselves again. But Spilett and Harbert should lie in wait behind the rocks and fire at anything that appears."

The engineer's orders were carried out. While the reporter and the boy, the two best marksmen in the colony, took up positions within easy range but out of the monkeys' sight, Nab, Pencroff and Cyrus Smith climbed to the plateau and made for the forest to kill some game, for it was time for the midday meal and there was nothing left in the way of food.

At the end of half an hour the hunters came back with a few rock pigeons, which were roasted after a fashion. Not one monkey had shown itself again.

Gédéon Spilett and Harbert went to take their share of the meal while Top kept watch under the windows. Then, after eating, they went back to their posts.

Two hours later the situation had still not changed in the least. The four-handed creatures gave no further sign of life, and you might have believed they had disappeared. But what seemed most likely was that, frightened by the death of one of their number and terrified by the gunshots, they were lying low at the back of the rooms of Granite House, or even in the storeroom. And when the colonists thought of the riches that storeroom held, the patience the engineer had urged on them so strongly ended by turning into violent irritation — and frankly, there was every reason for it.

"This is really too stupid," the reporter said at last, "and there's truly no reason for it ever to end!"

"We've got to make those rascals clear out, though!" cried Pencroff. "We'd get the better of them easily enough, even if there were twenty of them, but to do that we've got to fight them hand to hand! Look here! Isn't there any way at all of getting at them?"

"Yes," replied the engineer, through whose mind an idea had just flashed.

"One?" said Pencroff. "Well, then it's the right one, since there aren't any others! What is it?"

"Let's try to get down into Granite House through the lake's old spillway," the engineer replied.

"Oh, by a thousand thousand devils!" cried the sailor. "And I never thought of that!"

It was, in fact, the only way to get inside Granite House, fight the gang and throw it out. The mouth of the spillway, it is true, was closed by a wall of cemented stones, which would have to be sacrificed; but they would only have to build it again. Luckily, Cyrus Smith had not yet carried out his plan of hiding that opening by drowning it under the waters of the lake, because then the operation would have taken a good deal of time.

It was already past noon when the colonists, well armed and carrying picks and mattocks, left the Chimneys, passed under the windows of Granite House after ordering Top to stay at his post, and got ready to go up the left bank of the Mercy to reach Prospect Plateau.

But they had not gone fifty paces in that direction when they heard the dog barking furiously. It was like a desperate summons.

They stopped.

"Run!" said Pencroff.

And they all went tearing back down the bank as fast as their legs would carry them.

When they reached the bend, they saw that the situation had changed.

The monkeys, seized by a sudden fright from some unknown cause, were trying to escape. Two or three were running and leaping from one window to another with the agility of circus clowns. They were not even trying to put the ladder back, though it would have been easy for them to climb down by it; in their terror, perhaps, they had forgotten that way of clearing out. Soon five or six were in a position to be shot at, and the colonists, aiming at their leisure, fired. Some, wounded or killed, fell back into the rooms, shrieking shrilly. Others, flung outward, were smashed in their fall, and a few moments later it was reasonable to suppose there was not a single four-handed creature left alive in Granite House.

"Hurrah!" cried Pencroff. "Hurrah! Hurrah!"

"Not so many hurrahs!" said Gédéon Spilett.

"Why not? They're all dead," replied the sailor.

"Agreed, but that doesn't give us a way of getting back into our house."

"Let's go to the spillway!" retorted Pencroff.

"Of course," said the engineer. "And yet it would have been better..."

At that moment, as if in answer to Cyrus Smith's remark, they saw the ladder slide over the doorsill, then unroll and drop all the way to the ground.

"Well, a thousand pipes! That's a good one!" cried the sailor, looking at Cyrus Smith.

"Too good!" murmured the engineer, and he was the first to spring onto the ladder.

"Look out, Mr. Cyrus!" cried Pencroff. "If there are still some of those apes..."

"We shall see," the engineer replied without stopping.

All his companions followed him, and in a minute they had reached the doorsill.

They searched everywhere. There was no one in the rooms, and no one in the storeroom, which the gang of four-handed raiders had left untouched.

"Well, now, what about the ladder?" cried the sailor. "Who's the gentleman who sent it back down to us?"

But just then a shriek rang out, and a big ape that had taken refuge in the passage burst into the great hall with Nab after it.

"Ah, the bandit!" cried Pencroff.

And ax in hand, he was about to split the animal's head open, when Cyrus Smith stopped him and said:

"Spare him, Pencroff."

"Show mercy to this hairy rascal?"

"Yes! He's the one who threw us the ladder!"

And the engineer said it in so peculiar a voice that it would have been hard to tell whether he was speaking seriously or not.

Nevertheless they threw themselves on the ape, which put up a brave fight before it was brought down and tied up.

"Phew!" cried Pencroff. "And what are we going to do with him now?"

"Make him a servant!" Harbert answered.

And in saying so the boy was not altogether joking, for he knew how much use can be made of this intelligent race of four-handed animals.

The colonists then came up to the ape and looked him over closely. He did indeed belong to that species of anthropoid ape whose facial angle — the slope of the face from brow to jaw — is not much smaller than a human being's. He was an orang, and as such he had neither the ferocity of the baboon, nor the thoughtlessness of the macaque, nor the uncleanliness of the marmoset, nor the impatience of the Barbary ape, nor the bad instincts of the dog-faced monkey. It is to this family of anthropoids that so many traits belong which show in these animals an almost human intelligence. Employed in households, they can wait at table, clean the rooms, look after the clothes, black the boots, handle a knife, spoon and fork skillfully, and even drink wine... every bit as well as the best servant who ever walked on two legs without feathers. We know that the great naturalist Buffon owned one of these apes, which served him for a long time as a faithful and devoted servant.

The one who now lay tied up in the great hall of Granite House was a great big devil, six feet tall, his body admirably proportioned, his chest broad, his head of medium size, his facial angle reaching sixty-five degrees, his skull rounded, his nose prominent, his skin covered with smooth, soft, glossy hair — in short, a perfect specimen of the anthropoids. His eyes, a little smaller than human eyes, sparkled with intelligent liveliness; his white teeth gleamed under his mustache, and he wore a little curly beard the color of hazelnuts.

"A handsome fellow!" said Pencroff. "If only we knew his language, we could talk to him!"

"So, my master, it's serious?" said Nab. "We're going to take him on as a servant?"

"Yes, Nab," the engineer answered with a smile. "But don't be jealous!"

"And I hope he'll make an excellent servant," added Harbert. "He looks young, so his education will be easy, and we won't have to use force to tame him, or pull out his canine teeth, the way people do in such cases! He can't help but become attached to masters who are kind to him."

"And kind we'll be," replied Pencroff, who had forgotten all his grudge against "the pranksters."

Then, going up to the orang:

"Well, my boy," he asked him, "how are we doing?"

The orang answered with a little grunt that did not suggest too bad a temper.

"So we'd like to join the colony?" asked the sailor. "We're going to enter the service of Mr. Cyrus Smith?"

Another approving grunt from the ape.

"And we'll be content with our board for wages?"

A third grunt, in the affirmative.

"His conversation is a little monotonous," Gédéon Spilett observed.

"Good!" retorted Pencroff. "The best servants are the ones who talk the least. And besides — no wages! Do you hear, my boy? To start with, we won't give you any wages, but we'll double them later on, if we're pleased with you!"

That was how the colony gained a new member, who was to do it more than one good turn. As for what he should be called, the sailor asked that, in memory of another ape he had once known, he be named Jupiter — Jup for short.

And that is how, without further ceremony, Master Jup was installed in Granite House.

Chapter 7: A Bridge over the Mercy

Plans to carry out — A bridge over the Mercy — Making an island of Prospect Plateau — The drawbridge — The wheat harvest — The stream — The little bridges — The poultry yard — The dovecote — The two onaggas — The cart in harness — A trip to Balloon Harbor

So the colonists of Lincoln Island had won back their home without having to go in by the old spillway, and that spared them a good deal of masonry work. It was lucky, really, that just as they were getting ready to do it, the band of monkeys had been seized by a terror as sudden as it was inexplicable, and that this terror had driven them out of Granite House. Had the animals somehow sensed that a serious attack was about to be made on them by another route? That was about the only way to explain their retreat.

During the last hours of the day the monkeys' bodies were carried into the woods and buried there. Then the colonists set to work repairing the disorder the intruders had left behind. It was disorder, not damage: the monkeys had turned the furniture of the rooms upside down, but at least they had broken nothing. Nab lit his stoves again, and the reserves in the pantry provided a solid meal, which everyone did full justice to.

Jup was not forgotten. He ate stone-pine nuts and rootstocks with a good appetite, and he found himself supplied with plenty of both. Pencroff had untied his arms, but he thought it wise to leave the hobbles on his legs until he could count on the ape having accepted his new life.

Then, before going to bed, Cyrus Smith and his companions sat around the table and talked over several projects that urgently needed doing.

The most important and the most pressing were two: building a bridge over the Mercy, so as to connect the southern part of the island with Granite House, and then setting up a corral to house the mouflons, or any other wool-bearing animals they ought to capture.

As anyone can see, both projects were aimed at the question of clothing, which was then the most serious one they faced. The bridge would make it easy to bring home the balloon's envelope, which would give them linen, and the corral would supply a harvest of wool, which would give them winter clothes.

As for the corral, Cyrus Smith meant to build it at the very sources of Red Creek, where the grazing animals would find pastures with plenty of fresh food. The road between Prospect Plateau and the sources had already been partly cleared, and with a better-built cart than the first one, hauling would be easier — especially if they managed to capture some animal that could pull it.

But while there was no harm in the corral being a long way from Granite House, the same could not be said of the poultry yard, which Nab now brought to the colonists' attention. The birds really did need to be within reach of the head cook, and no spot seemed better suited for the poultry yard than the stretch of the lakeshore next to the old spillway. Water birds would thrive there as well as the others, and the pair of tinamous caught on the last expedition would serve for a first try at taming.

The next day, November 3, the new work began with the building of the bridge, and every pair of hands was called on for this important job. Saws, axes, chisels, and hammers were loaded onto the colonists' shoulders, and, turned into carpenters, they went down to the beach.

There Pencroff had a thought.

"And what if, while we're away, Master Jup takes it into his head to pull up the ladder he was so kind as to send down to us yesterday?"

"Let's fasten down its lower end," Cyrus Smith answered.

This was done with two stakes driven firmly into the sand. Then the colonists went up the left bank of the Mercy and soon came to the bend the river made.

There they stopped, to see whether the bridge ought to be built at this point. The place seemed right.

From here to Balloon Harbor, which they had discovered the day before on the south coast, it was only three and a half miles, and from the bridge to the harbor it would be easy to clear a road a cart could travel, which would make it simple to go back and forth between Granite House and the south of the island.

Cyrus Smith now told his companions about a plan he had been turning over for some time — one that was very simple to carry out and very much worth doing. It was to cut Prospect Plateau off completely, so as to protect it from any attack by four-footed or four-handed creatures. That way Granite House, the Chimneys, the poultry yard, and the whole upper part of the plateau, which was meant for planting, would be safe from the raids of animals.

Nothing could be easier to carry out than this plan, and here is how the engineer meant to go about it.

The plateau was already defended on three sides by water, some of it man-made and some of it natural:

On the northwest, by the shore of Lake Grant, from the corner that rested against the mouth of the old spillway all the way to the cut made in the lake's east bank to let the water out.

On the north, from that cut down to the sea, by the new stream that had dug itself a bed across the plateau and the beach, above and below the waterfall. And to make that stream impassable to animals, all they had to do was dig its bed deeper.

Along the whole eastern edge, by the sea itself, from the mouth of that same stream to the mouth of the Mercy.

And finally on the south, from that river mouth up to the bend of the Mercy where the bridge was to be built.

That left only the western side of the plateau, between the bend of the river and the southern corner of the lake. It was less than a mile long, and it lay open to anything that came along. But nothing was easier than to dig a wide, deep ditch there. The lake would fill it, and the overflow would pour down through a second waterfall into the bed of the Mercy. The level of the lake would no doubt drop a little because of this new outlet for its water, but Cyrus Smith had made sure that Red Creek brought in enough water to allow his plan to go ahead.

"So you see," the engineer added, "Prospect Plateau will be a real island, surrounded by water on every side. It will connect with the rest of our domain only by the bridge we are about to put across the Mercy, by the two little bridges already built above and below the waterfall, and finally by two more little bridges still to be built — one over the ditch I'm proposing we dig, and the other on the left bank of the Mercy. Now, if this bridge and these little bridges can be raised whenever we like, Prospect Plateau will be safe from any surprise."

To make himself clearer, Cyrus Smith had drawn a map of the plateau, and his companions grasped the whole plan at once. They approved it unanimously, and Pencroff, brandishing his carpenter's ax, shouted:

"The bridge first!"

It was the most urgent job. Trees were chosen, felled, stripped of their branches, and sawed up into joists, thick planks, and boards. The bridge was to be fixed in the section that rested on the right bank of the Mercy, and movable in the section that joined the left bank, so that this part could be raised by means of counterweights, the way certain bridges over canal locks are.

As anyone will understand, it was a large piece of work, and although it was skillfully managed, it did take a certain amount of time, because the Mercy was about eighty feet wide. They had to drive piles into the riverbed to hold up the fixed deck of the bridge, and they had to set up a pile driver — a heavy weight hoisted and dropped again and again — to pound on the tops of the piles. These piles would form two arches, so that the bridge could bear heavy loads.

Very fortunately, they lacked nothing: not the tools for working wood, not the ironwork for strengthening it, not the ingenuity of a man who understood this kind of work wonderfully well, and not the zeal of his companions, who after seven months had naturally become very skillful with their hands. And it must be said that Gédéon Spilett was not the clumsiest of them. He competed in skill with the sailor himself, who "would never have expected so much from a mere journalist!"

The building of the bridge over the Mercy took three weeks, and they were very busy weeks. The colonists ate their midday meal right at the work site, and since the weather was magnificent then, they went back to Granite House only for supper.

During this time it was clear that Master Jup was settling in easily and growing used to his new masters, whom he still watched with an extremely curious eye. All the same, as a precaution, Pencroff did not yet give him complete freedom of movement. He wanted to wait, and rightly, until the edges of the plateau had been made impossible to cross by the planned works. Top and Jup got along splendidly and liked to play together, but Jup did everything with great seriousness.

On November 20 the bridge was finished. Its movable section, balanced by counterweights, swung up easily, and only a slight effort was needed to raise it. Between its hinge and the last crossbeam, where it came to rest when it was lowered again, there was a gap of twenty feet — wide enough that no animal could jump across it.

Next came the question of going to fetch the balloon's envelope, which the colonists were eager to put somewhere completely safe. But to carry it, they would have to take a cart all the way to Balloon Harbor, and that meant clearing a road through the dense thickets of the Far West. That would take a certain amount of time. So Nab and Pencroff first went ahead to scout as far as the harbor, and when they found that the "stock of cloth" was not suffering in the least in the cave where it had been stored, it was decided that the work on Prospect Plateau would go on without a break.

"That," Pencroff pointed out, "will let us set up our poultry yard under better conditions, since we won't have to be afraid of visits from foxes or attacks from any other pests."

"Not to mention," Nab added, "that we'll be able to clear the plateau, and plant wild plants there..."

"And get our second wheat field ready!" the sailor cried triumphantly.

The fact was that the first wheat field, sown with a single grain, had done wonderfully well, thanks to Pencroff's care. It had produced the ten ears the engineer had predicted, and since each ear held eighty grains, the colony now found itself the owner of eight hundred grains — in six months — which promised two harvests every year.

These eight hundred grains, less about fifty kept back to be safe, were therefore to be sown in a new field, and with no less care than the single grain had been.

The field was prepared and then surrounded by a strong palisade, tall and sharp-pointed, which four-footed animals would have had a very hard time getting over. As for the birds, they were kept away by screeching whirligigs and frightful scarecrows, products of Pencroff's fanciful imagination. The seven hundred and fifty grains were then laid in small, very regular furrows, and nature had to do the rest.

On November 21 Cyrus Smith began laying out the ditch that was to close off the plateau on the west, from the southern corner of Lake Grant to the bend of the Mercy. There were two or three feet of topsoil there, and granite underneath. So they had to make nitroglycerin all over again, and the nitroglycerin did its usual work. In less than two weeks a ditch twelve feet wide and six deep had been dug in the hard ground of the plateau. By the same means a new cut was made in the rocky rim of the lake, and the water rushed into this new bed, forming a little stream that was given the name "Glycerin Creek." It became a tributary of the Mercy. Just as the engineer had said, the level of the lake dropped, but by an amount you could barely see. Finally, to complete the enclosure, the bed of the stream on the beach was made much wider, and the sand was held back by a double palisade.

By the end of the first half of December this work was completely finished. Prospect Plateau — an irregular sort of pentagon about four miles around, with a belt of water all the way round it — was now entirely safe from any attack.

During that month of December the heat was intense. Even so, the colonists would not stop carrying out their plans, and since setting up the poultry yard had become urgent, they went ahead and set it up.

It goes without saying that once the plateau was completely closed off, Master Jup had been set free. He never left his masters now and showed no wish at all to escape. He was a gentle animal, yet very strong, and astonishingly agile. Ah! When it came to climbing the ladder of Granite House, nobody could have competed with him. He was already being put to some kinds of work: he hauled loads of wood and carted away the stones that had been dug out of the bed of Glycerin Creek.

"He's not a mason yet, but he's already a 'monkey'!" Harbert said jokingly. He was referring to the nickname "monkey" that French masons give their apprentices. And if ever a name was deserved, it was this one!

The poultry yard took up an area of two hundred square yards, chosen on the southeast shore of the lake. It was surrounded by a palisade, and various shelters were built for the animals that were to live in it. These were huts of branches, divided into compartments, and they were soon simply waiting for their guests.

The first were the pair of tinamous, which before long produced a large brood of young. They were joined by half a dozen ducks that lived along the shores of the lake. Some of these belonged to that Chinese species whose wings open like a fan, and whose brilliant, vivid plumage rivals that of the golden pheasant. A few days later Harbert caught a pair of gallinaceous birds — game birds of the chicken family — with rounded tails made of long feathers: magnificent "alectors," which soon became tame. As for the pelicans, the kingfishers, and the moorhens, they came of their own accord to the shore by the poultry yard. And this whole little world, after a few quarrels, cooing, squawking, and clucking, ended up getting along, and it multiplied at a rate that was reassuring for the colony's future food supply.

Cyrus Smith, wanting to round out the work, also built a dovecote in one corner of the poultry yard. In it they housed a dozen of the pigeons that haunted the high rocks of the plateau. These birds easily got into the habit of coming back to their new home every evening, and they showed more of a tendency to be domesticated than their relatives the wood pigeons, which in any case breed only in the wild.

At last the time had come to use the balloon's envelope for making linen. As for keeping it in its present form and risking a hot-air balloon to leave the island, over a sea that was practically without limits — that would have been thinkable only for people who lacked everything, and Cyrus Smith, a practical mind, could not consider it.

So the job was to bring the envelope back to Granite House, and the colonists set about making their heavy cart lighter and easier to handle. But while they did not lack a vehicle, they still had to find something to pull it! Wasn't there some native grazing animal on the island that could take the place of a horse, a donkey, an ox, or a cow? That was the question.

"Honestly," Pencroff said, "a draft animal would be very useful to us, until Mr. Cyrus is good enough to build us a steam wagon, or even a locomotive — because one day, for sure, we'll have a railroad from Granite House to Balloon Harbor, with a branch line up Mount Franklin!"

And the honest sailor believed what he was saying! Oh, imagination, when faith gets mixed up in it!

But, not to exaggerate, a simple four-footed animal that could be put in harness would have suited Pencroff perfectly well. And since Providence had a soft spot for him, it did not keep him waiting long.

One day, December 23, they heard Nab shouting and Top barking, each trying to outdo the other. The colonists, who were busy at the Chimneys, came running at once, afraid that something unpleasant had happened.

What did they see? Two handsome, good-sized animals, which had wandered carelessly onto the plateau, since the little bridges had not been closed. They looked like two horses, or at least two donkeys, a male and a female. They were finely built, with pale yellowish-gray coats, white legs and tails, and black stripes across the head, neck, and body. They were walking calmly forward without showing the least alarm, and they looked with bright eyes at these men, whom they could not yet recognize as their masters.

"They're onaggas!" Harbert cried. "Animals halfway between the zebra and the quagga!"

"Why not donkeys?" asked Nab.

"Because they don't have long ears, and their shape is more graceful!"

"Donkeys or horses," Pencroff shot back, "they're 'engines,' as Mr. Smith would say, and as such they're worth catching!"

Without frightening the two animals, the sailor slipped through the grass to the little bridge over Glycerin Creek and swung it up, and the onaggas were prisoners.

Now, should they be seized by force and made to submit to domestication? No. It was decided that for a few days they would be left to come and go freely on the plateau, where there was plenty of grass, and the engineer immediately had a stable built near the poultry yard, where the onaggas would find good bedding and shelter for the night.

So this magnificent pair was left entirely free to move about, and the colonists even avoided frightening them by coming too close. Several times, though, the onaggas seemed to feel a need to leave this plateau, which was too cramped for animals used to wide-open spaces and deep forests. Then they could be seen following the belt of water that stood in their way as a barrier they could not cross, letting out a few shrill brays, then galloping off through the grass. And when they had calmed down, they would stand for hours on end gazing at those great woods that were closed to them forever!

Meanwhile, harness and traces had been made out of plant fibers, and a few days after the onaggas were captured, not only was the cart ready to be hitched up, but a straight road — or rather a cutting — had been made through the Far West forest from the bend of the Mercy to Balloon Harbor. So the cart could now be driven there, and it was toward the end of December that they tried out the onaggas for the first time.

Pencroff had already coaxed the animals enough that they would come and eat out of his hand, and they let people come near them without any trouble. But once they were in harness they reared, and it was very hard to hold them. All the same, they would soon get used to this new work, because the onagga, less rebellious than the zebra, is often put to harness in the mountainous parts of southern Africa, and it has even been acclimatized in Europe, in relatively cold regions.

That day the whole colony, except Pencroff, who walked at the head of his animals, climbed into the cart and took the road to Balloon Harbor. It goes without saying that they were jolted about on that barely roughed-out road. But the cart arrived without mishap, and that same day they were able to load the envelope and the balloon's various riggings onto it.

At eight o'clock in the evening the cart, having crossed back over the bridge over the Mercy, came down the left bank of the river and stopped on the beach. The onaggas were unhitched and led back to their stable, and Pencroff, before falling asleep, let out a sigh of satisfaction so loud that it echoed through Granite House.

Chapter 8: Guncotton

Linen — Sealskin shoes — Making guncotton — Various sowings — Fishing — Turtle eggs — Master Jup's progress — The corral — Hunting mouflons — New riches, plant and animal — Memories of the homeland far away

The first week of January was given over to making the linen the colony needed. The needles found in the chest went to work between fingers that were strong, if not delicate, and it is safe to say that whatever was sewn stayed sewn.

There was no shortage of thread, thanks to Cyrus Smith's idea of reusing the thread that had already served to stitch together the strips of the balloon. Gédéon Spilett and Harbert unpicked those long strips with admirable patience, because Pencroff had been forced to give up the job, which drove him to distraction. But once it came to sewing, he had no equal. Everybody knows, after all, that sailors have a remarkable gift for the seamstress's trade.

Next, the cloth that had made up the balloon's envelope was scoured with soda and potash, obtained by burning plants, so that the cotton, freed of its varnish, got back its natural softness and stretch. Then it was left out in the open air, which bleached it, until it turned a perfect white.

In this way they made a few dozen shirts and socks — the socks not knitted, of course, but cut and sewn from cloth. What a pleasure it was for the colonists to put on clean white linen at last — very rough linen, no doubt, but they were past worrying about such small things — and to sleep between sheets, which turned the bunks of Granite House into thoroughly respectable beds.

It was also around this time that they made shoes of sealskin, which arrived just in time to replace the shoes and boots they had brought from America. It is safe to say that these new shoes were wide and long, and never pinched the walkers' feet!

As the year 1866 began, the heat held on and on, but the hunting in the woods never let up. Agoutis, peccaries, capybaras, kangaroos, game with fur and game with feathers were positively swarming, and Gédéon Spilett and Harbert were by now too good as shots ever to waste a single shot.

Cyrus Smith kept urging them to go easy on the ammunition, and he took steps to replace the powder and shot found in the chest, which he wanted to keep in reserve for the future. After all, did he know where chance might someday throw him and his companions, if they ever left their domain? They had to be ready for every need the unknown might bring, and so they had to save their ammunition by putting other materials, easy to replace, in its place.

To replace lead, of which Cyrus Smith had found no trace on the island, he used iron shot, which was easy to make, and did so without much loss. Since these pellets were not as heavy as lead pellets, he had to make them bigger, and each charge held fewer of them, but the hunters' skill made up for the difference. As for gunpowder, Cyrus Smith could have made it, since he had saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal on hand. But making it calls for extreme care, and without special equipment it is hard to turn out powder of good quality.

So Cyrus Smith preferred to make pyroxylin — that is, guncotton — a substance in which cotton is not essential, because cotton goes into it only as cellulose. Now, cellulose is nothing other than the basic tissue of plants, and it is found in an almost pure state not only in cotton but in the textile fibers of hemp and flax, in paper, in old linen, in the pith of the elder, and so on. And it so happened that elders grew in abundance on the island, near the mouth of Red Creek. The colonists were already using the berries of these shrubs, which belong to the honeysuckle family, in place of coffee.

So all they had to do was gather this elder pith — the cellulose. As for the other material needed to make guncotton, it was nothing but fuming nitric acid. And Cyrus Smith, who had sulfuric acid at his disposal, had already been able to produce nitric acid easily by treating the saltpeter that nature had provided.

So he decided to make guncotton and use it, though he recognized that it had some fairly serious drawbacks: its effect was very uneven; it was far too flammable, since it catches fire at three hundred and thirty-eight degrees Fahrenheit instead of four hundred and sixty-four; and it burned so instantaneously that it could damage firearms. On the other hand, guncotton had these advantages: dampness did not spoil it, it did not foul the barrels of the guns, and its propelling force was four times that of ordinary gunpowder.

To make guncotton, you need only plunge cellulose into fuming nitric acid for a quarter of an hour, then wash it in plenty of water and let it dry. As you see, nothing could be simpler.

Cyrus Smith had only ordinary nitric acid on hand, not the fuming or monohydrated kind — that is, the acid that gives off whitish vapors when it meets damp air. But by using ordinary nitric acid in its place, mixed in the proportion of three volumes to five volumes of concentrated sulfuric acid, the engineer was bound to get the same result — and he got it. So the island's hunters soon had a perfectly prepared substance at their disposal, which, used with discretion, gave excellent results.

Around this time the colonists cleared three acres of Prospect Plateau, and the rest was kept as meadow to feed the onaggas. Several excursions were made into Jacamar Wood and the Far West forests, and they brought back a real harvest of wild vegetables — spinach, cress, horseradish, turnips — which careful cultivation would soon improve, and which were going to balance the high-protein diet that the colonists of Lincoln Island had lived on until then. They also hauled in sizable loads of wood and coal. Every excursion was at the same time a chance to improve the roads, whose surface was gradually being packed down under the wheels of the cart.

The warren still supplied its share of rabbits to the pantries of Granite House. Since it lay a little outside the point where Glycerin Creek began, its residents could not get onto the protected plateau, and so they could not ravage the new plantings there. As for the oyster bed, laid out among the rocks of the beach and frequently restocked, it gave them excellent shellfish every day. Besides that, the fishing, whether in the lake or in the current of the Mercy, soon paid off, because Pencroff had set out bottom lines armed with iron hooks. On these they often caught fine trout, and certain extremely tasty fish whose silvery sides were sprinkled with little yellowish spots. And so Master Nab, who was in charge of the cooking, could vary the menu of every meal very pleasantly. Only bread was still missing from the colonists' table, and, as has been said, it was a privation they truly felt.

Around this time they also hunted sea turtles, which came to the beaches of Mandible Cape. There the sand was covered with little bumps, each one holding perfectly round eggs with hard white shells, whose albumen has the property of not setting when cooked, as the white of a bird's egg does. The sun took care of hatching them, and there were naturally a great many of them, since each turtle can lay as many as two hundred and fifty a year.

"A regular field of eggs," Gédéon Spilett remarked, "and all we have to do is harvest them."

But they did not settle for the produce; they went after the producers too, and that hunt let them bring back to Granite House a dozen of these chelonians, which are truly excellent eating. Turtle soup, spiced up with aromatic herbs and set off with a few crucifers, often won Master Nab, who made it, the praise he deserved.

One more lucky event should be mentioned here, which let them lay in new stores for the winter. Salmon came in schools and ventured into the Mercy, swimming up it for several miles. It was the season when the females, going in search of suitable places to spawn, went ahead of the males and made a great commotion as they passed through the fresh water. A thousand or so of these fish, some as long as two and a half feet, poured into the river this way, and it was enough to build a few weirs to hold a great many of them back. In this way they caught several hundred, which were salted and stored away for the time when winter would freeze the streams and make all fishing impossible.

It was at this time that the very intelligent Jup was promoted to the post of valet. He had been dressed in a jacket, short breeches of white canvas, and an apron whose pockets were his delight, because he stuffed his hands into them and would not let anyone come rummaging in them. The clever orangutan had been wonderfully trained by Nab, and Nab and the ape seemed to understand each other when they talked together. Jup, besides, had a real fondness for Nab, and Nab returned it. Unless someone needed his services, whether to haul wood or to climb to the top of some tree, Jup spent most of his time in the kitchen and tried to imitate Nab in everything he saw him do. The teacher, for his part, showed great patience and even an extreme zeal in instructing his pupil, and the pupil showed a remarkable intelligence in profiting from the lessons his teacher gave him.

So you can imagine how delighted the diners of Granite House were one day when Master Jup, napkin over his arm, came in without any warning to wait on them at table. Skillful and attentive, he performed his service perfectly, changing the plates, bringing in the dishes, pouring the drinks, all with a gravity that amused the colonists no end and sent Pencroff into raptures.

"Jup, some soup!"

"Jup, a little agouti!"

"Jup, a plate!"

"Jup! Good Jup! Honest Jup!"

That was all you could hear, and Jup, never once flustered, answered every call and kept an eye on everything. And he nodded his intelligent head when Pencroff, repeating his joke from the first day, told him:

"Jup, there's no doubt about it — we'll have to double your wages!"

Needless to say, by now the orangutan was completely at home in Granite House, and he often went with his masters into the forest without ever showing the least wish to run away. You should have seen him then, walking along in the funniest way, with a cane that Pencroff had made him, which he carried on his shoulder like a gun! If they needed a fruit picked from the top of a tree, how fast he was up there! If the wheel of the cart got stuck in the mud, with what strength Jup set it back on its way with a single heave of his shoulder!

"What a fellow!" Pencroff often exclaimed. "If he were as wicked as he is good, there'd be no handling him!"

It was toward the end of January that the colonists undertook some major works in the central part of the island. It had been decided to build a corral near the sources of Red Creek, at the foot of Mount Franklin. It would hold the ruminants, which would have been a nuisance at Granite House — and above all the mouflons, which were to supply wool for making winter clothes.

Every morning the colony — sometimes all of it, more often only Cyrus Smith, Harbert and Pencroff — went out to the sources of the creek. With the onaggas helping, it was now nothing more than a five-mile outing under a dome of greenery, along the newly cut road, which came to be called "the Corral Road."

There a large site had been chosen, on the far side of the mountain's southern shoulder. It was a meadow dotted with clumps of trees, lying at the very foot of a spur that closed it in on one side. A little stream, born on the spur's slopes, ran diagonally across the meadow, watering it, and then lost itself in Red Creek. The grass was fresh, and the trees growing here and there let the air move freely over the ground. So all they had to do was surround the meadow with a palisade running in a curve, with each end resting against the spur, high enough that not even the most agile animals could jump it. This enclosure could hold a hundred or so horned animals, mouflons or wild goats, along with the young that would be born later on.

So the engineer laid out the boundary of the corral, and they had to set about felling the trees needed to build the palisade. But since cutting the road had already cost a good number of trunks, they hauled those over, and these supplied about a hundred stakes, which were planted firmly in the ground.

In the front of the palisade they left a fairly wide opening, closed by a double gate made of stout planks and meant to be strengthened by bars on the outside.

Building this corral took no less than three weeks, because besides the work on the palisade, Cyrus Smith put up large plank sheds where the ruminants could take shelter. Besides, these structures had to be built extremely solidly, because mouflons are powerful animals, and their first fits of violence were something to fear. The stakes, sharpened at the top and hardened there in the fire, had been tied together with bolted crossbars, and at intervals props secured the strength of the whole.

With the corral finished, the next step was a great roundup at the foot of Mount Franklin, in the middle of the pastures where the ruminants grazed. This took place on February 7, on a beautiful summer day, and everyone took part. The two onaggas, already fairly well broken and ridden by Gédéon Spilett and Harbert, were a great help on this occasion.

The whole maneuver consisted of driving the mouflons and goats inward by gradually tightening the circle of beaters around them. So Cyrus Smith, Pencroff, Nab and Jup took up positions at various points in the woods, while the two riders and Top galloped around the corral within a radius of half a mile.

There were plenty of mouflons in this part of the island. These handsome animals, as big as deer, with horns stronger than a ram's and a grayish fleece mixed with long hairs, looked like argalis.

What an exhausting day of hunting it was! So much coming and going, so much running back and forth, so much shouting! Of the hundred or so mouflons that were driven in, more than two-thirds slipped past the beaters. But in the end some thirty of these ruminants and about ten wild goats, pushed little by little toward the corral, whose open gate seemed to offer them a way out, rushed into it and could be shut in.

All in all, the result was satisfying, and the colonists had nothing to complain about. Most of the mouflons were females, some of which would soon give birth. So it was certain that the flock would thrive, and that before long they would have plenty not only of wool but of hides as well.

That evening the hunters came back to Granite House worn out. Even so, they went back to visit the corral the very next day. The prisoners had certainly tried to knock down the palisade, but they had not managed it, and they soon settled down.

Nothing of any importance happened during that month of February. The daily work went on methodically, and while the roads to the corral and to Balloon Harbor were being improved, a third was begun, which ran from the enclosure toward the west coast. The part of Lincoln Island still unknown was the great forest that covered Serpentine Peninsula, where the wild beasts took refuge — and Gédéon Spilett fully intended to rid his domain of them.

Before the cold season came back, the most careful attention was also given to cultivating the wild plants that had been transplanted from the forest to Prospect Plateau. Harbert hardly ever came back from an excursion without bringing some useful plants. One day it was specimens of the chicory tribe, whose very seed could be pressed to yield an excellent oil; another day it was a common sorrel, whose properties against scurvy were not to be scorned; then some of those precious tubers that have been grown in South America since time immemorial — potatoes, of which more than two hundred kinds are known today. The vegetable garden, now well tended, well watered and well protected from the birds, was divided into little square beds where lettuces, purple potatoes, sorrel, turnips, horseradish and other crucifers were growing. The soil of the plateau was wonderfully fertile, and they could hope for abundant harvests.

There was no lack of drinks either, and as long as they did not demand wine, even the fussiest had no reason to complain. To the Oswego tea that the bee balm supplied, and the fermented drink made from the roots of the dragon tree, Cyrus Smith had added real beer. He brewed it from the young shoots of the black spruce, Abies nigra, which, once boiled and fermented, gave that pleasant and particularly healthful drink the Anglo-Americans call spruce beer.

Toward the end of the summer the poultry yard held a fine pair of bustards of the houbara species, known by a sort of cape of feathers; a dozen shovelers, whose upper bill was extended on each side by a flap of skin; and some magnificent roosters, black in the comb, the wattles and the skin, like the roosters of Mozambique, which strutted about on the shore of the lake.

So everything was succeeding, thanks to the energy of these brave and intelligent men. Providence did a great deal for them, no doubt; but true to the great rule that Heaven helps those who help themselves, they helped themselves first, and Heaven came to their aid afterward.

After those hot summer days, in the evening, when the work was done and the sea breeze was rising, they liked to sit at the edge of Prospect Plateau, under a sort of veranda covered with climbing plants that Nab had put up with his own hands. There they talked, they taught one another, they made plans, and the sailor's hearty good humor kept cheering up this little world, in which the most perfect harmony had never stopped reigning.

They talked about home, too, about their dear, great America. How was the Civil War going? It obviously could not have dragged on! Richmond had surely fallen quickly into General Grant's hands! The capture of the Confederate capital must have been the last act of that deadly struggle! By now the North had triumphed for the good cause. Oh, how welcome a newspaper would have been to the exiles of Lincoln Island! For eleven months now, all contact between them and the rest of humankind had been cut off, and soon, on March 24, would come the anniversary of the day the balloon had flung them onto this unknown coast! They had been nothing but castaways then, not even knowing whether they could hold on to their miserable lives against the elements! And now, thanks to their leader's knowledge, thanks to their own intelligence, they were real colonists, equipped with weapons, tools and instruments, who had learned to turn the animals, the plants and the minerals of the island — the three kingdoms of nature — to their own use!

Yes! They often talked about all these things, and they still made many plans for the future!

As for Cyrus Smith, silent most of the time, he listened to his companions more often than he spoke. Now and then he smiled at some remark of Harbert's or some sally of Pencroff's, but always and everywhere he was thinking about those inexplicable events, that strange riddle whose secret still escaped him!

Chapter 9: The Hydraulic Elevator

Bad weather — The hydraulic elevator — Making window glass and glassware — The bread tree — Frequent visits to the corral — The flock grows — A question from the reporter — The exact position of Lincoln Island — Pencroff's proposal

The weather changed during the first week of March. There had been a full moon at the start of the month, and the heat was still fierce. The air felt charged with electricity, and a spell of stormy weather, longer or shorter, was truly to be feared.

And sure enough, on the 2nd, thunder rumbled with tremendous violence. The wind was blowing from the east, and hail struck full on the front of Granite House, rattling against it like a volley of grapeshot. They had to shut the door and the window shutters tight, or everything inside the rooms would have been flooded.

When Pencroff saw those hailstones coming down, some of them as big as a pigeon's egg, he had only one thought: his wheat field was in the gravest danger.

He ran straight to his field, where the ears were already beginning to lift their little green heads, and he managed to protect his crop by spreading a big sheet of canvas over it. He was stoned in its place, but he did not complain.

This bad weather lasted a week, and all that time the thunder never stopped rolling in the depths of the sky. Between two storms you could still hear it growling dully somewhere beyond the horizon; then it would start again with fresh fury. The sky was streaked with lightning, and bolts struck several trees on the island, among them an enormous pine that stood near the lake at the edge of the forest. Two or three times, too, the lightning hit the beach, melting the sand and turning it to glass. When the engineer found these fulgurites — tubes of sand fused by lightning — they led him to think it might be possible to fit the windows with thick, strong panes of glass that could stand up to wind, rain and hail.

With no urgent work to do outdoors, the colonists made use of the bad weather to work inside Granite House, which was being fitted out more fully and more comfortably day by day. The engineer set up a lathe, which let him turn a few utensils for washing or for the kitchen, and above all buttons, which they had been sorely missing. A rack had been put up for the guns, which were kept with the greatest care, and the shelves and cupboards left nothing to be desired. They sawed, they planed, they filed, they turned, and all through that stretch of bad weather nothing could be heard but the squeal of tools and the hum of the lathe, answering the rumble of the thunder.

Master Jup had not been forgotten. He had a room of his own near the main storeroom, a sort of cabin with a bunk always full of good bedding, which suited him perfectly.

"With good old Jup there's never any back talk," Pencroff often said, "never a rude answer! What a servant, Nab! What a servant!"

"My pupil," Nab would answer, "and soon my equal!"

"Your superior, you mean," the sailor would shoot back, laughing, "because you talk, Nab, and he doesn't!"

It goes without saying that Jup now knew his duties thoroughly. He beat the clothes, he turned the spit, he swept the rooms, he waited at table, he stacked the firewood, and — a detail that delighted Pencroff — he never went to bed without first coming to tuck the worthy sailor in.

As for the health of the members of the colony, two-legged or two-handed, four-handed or four-legged, it left nothing to be desired. Living this open-air life, on this healthy soil, in this temperate zone, working with head and hands, they could not believe that sickness would ever touch them.

And indeed they were all marvelously well. Harbert had already grown two inches in a year. His face was taking shape and becoming more manly, and he promised to be a young man as fine in body as in character. Besides, he used every spare moment his manual work left him to learn. He read the few books that had been found in the chest, and beyond the practical lessons that came out of the very necessities of their situation, he had in the engineer a teacher for the sciences and in the reporter a teacher for languages, and both were glad to round out his education.

The engineer's fixed idea was to pass on to the boy everything he knew, to teach him by example as much as by word, and Harbert made the most of his teacher's lessons.

"If I die," Cyrus Smith thought, "he will take my place!"

The storm ended around March 9, but the sky stayed covered with clouds for the whole of that last month of summer. The atmosphere, violently shaken by all those electrical upheavals, could not get back its former clearness, and there was rain and fog almost every day, apart from three or four fine days that allowed all kinds of excursions.
