Around this time the female onagga gave birth to a foal, a female like her mother, which thrived wonderfully. At the corral, likewise, the flock of mouflons increased, and several lambs were already bleating in the sheds, to the great delight of Nab and Harbert, who each had a favorite among the newborns.

They also tried domesticating the peccaries, and the experiment was a complete success. A sty was built near the poultry yard, and it soon held several young ones well on the way to becoming civilized — that is, to getting fat under Nab's care. Master Jup, whose job was to bring them their daily food — dishwater, kitchen scraps and so on — did his task conscientiously. Now and then, it is true, he amused himself at the expense of his little boarders by pulling their tails. But that was mischief, not malice: those little curly tails amused him like a toy, and his instincts were a child's.

One day that March, Pencroff, chatting with the engineer, reminded Cyrus Smith of a promise he had not yet had time to keep.

"You talked about a contraption that would do away with the long ladders at Granite House, Mr. Cyrus," he said. "Aren't you going to put it in someday?"

"You mean a sort of elevator?" answered Cyrus Smith.

"Let's call it an elevator, if you like," the sailor replied. "The name doesn't matter, as long as it takes us up to our house without wearing us out."

"Nothing could be easier, Pencroff. But is it really worth it?"

"Certainly, Mr. Cyrus. Now that we've given ourselves what we need, let's think a bit about comfort. For people it'll be a luxury, if you like; but for things it's a necessity! It's no fun climbing a long ladder when you're carrying a heavy load!"

"Well then, Pencroff, we'll try to make you happy," said Cyrus Smith.

"But you haven't got an engine to work it."

"We'll make one."

"A steam engine?"

"No, a water engine."

And in fact a natural force was right there at the engineer's disposal to drive his machine, and he could put it to use without much trouble.

All he had to do was increase the flow of the small branch channel taken off the lake, which supplied water to the inside of Granite House. The opening left among the stones and grass at the upper end of the old spillway was made bigger, which produced a strong fall of water at the bottom of the passage, and the overflow from it drained away down the inner well. Beneath this fall the engineer installed a drum fitted with paddles. Outside, it was linked to a wheel wound with a strong cable that carried a large basket. In this way, by means of a long rope that hung down to the ground and could be used to engage or disengage the water engine, a person could ride up in the basket all the way to the door of Granite House.

It was on March 17 that the elevator worked for the first time, to everyone's satisfaction. From then on all loads — wood, coal, provisions, and the colonists themselves — were hoisted up by this very simple system. It replaced the primitive ladder, which nobody thought of missing. Top showed himself particularly delighted with the improvement. He did not have, and could not have, Master Jup's knack for climbing rungs, and many a time he had had to make the ascent to Granite House on Nab's back, or even on the orangutan's.

Around this time, too, Cyrus Smith tried making glass, and first he had to adapt the old pottery kiln for this new purpose. That presented some fairly serious difficulties. But after several failed attempts he finally managed to set up a glassworks, which Gédéon Spilett and Harbert, the engineer's natural assistants, did not leave for several days.

As for the substances that go into glass, they are simply sand, chalk and soda (either the carbonate or the sulfate). Now, the shore supplied the sand; the lime supplied the chalk; the sea plants supplied the soda; the pyrites supplied the sulfuric acid; and the ground supplied the coal to heat the kiln to the necessary temperature. So Cyrus Smith had everything he needed to begin.

The tool that was hardest to make was the glassblower's "pipe": an iron tube five or six feet long, used to gather up on one of its ends the material that is kept in a molten state. But Pencroff managed to make this pipe by rolling a long, thin strip of iron the way a gun barrel is rolled, and it was soon ready for work.

On March 28 the kiln was fired up hot. A hundred parts of sand, thirty-five of chalk and forty of sulfate of soda, mixed with two or three parts of powdered charcoal, made up the batch, which was put into crucibles of fireclay. When the high heat of the kiln had turned it liquid, or rather into a thick paste, Cyrus Smith "gathered" a certain amount of this paste on the end of the pipe. He turned it over and over on a metal plate set out beforehand, so as to give it the right shape for blowing. Then he handed the pipe to Harbert and told him to blow into the other end.

"Like blowing soap bubbles?" the boy asked.

"Exactly," answered the engineer.

And Harbert, puffing out his cheeks, blew so long and so well into the pipe, taking care to keep turning it all the while, that his breath swelled the glassy mass. More molten material was added to the first, and soon the result was a bubble a foot across. Then Cyrus Smith took the pipe back from Harbert and, swinging it to and fro like a pendulum, drew the soft bubble out until it took the shape of a cylinder with cone-shaped ends.

So the blowing had produced a glass cylinder closed off by two rounded caps, like halves of a ball. These were easily cut off with a sharp iron dipped in cold water. Then, by the same method, the cylinder was split along its length. After a second heating had made it soft again, it was spread out on a plate and flattened with a wooden roller.

The first pane was made, and all they had to do was repeat the operation fifty times to have fifty panes. So the windows of Granite House were soon fitted with sheets of glass — not very clear, perhaps, but transparent enough.

As for glassware, tumblers and bottles, that was child's play. Besides, they took them just as they came off the end of the pipe. Pencroff had asked for the privilege of "blowing" in his turn, and he loved it. But he blew so hard that his products took on the most comical shapes, and he admired every one of them.

During one of the excursions made at this time, a new tree was discovered whose products added still more to the colony's food supply.

Cyrus Smith and Harbert, out hunting, had gone one day into the Far West forests, on the left bank of the Mercy, and as always the boy was asking the engineer a thousand questions, which he answered gladly. But hunting is like every other occupation here below: when you don't bring the proper zeal to it, there are plenty of reasons why you won't succeed. Now Cyrus Smith was no hunter, and on top of that, Harbert was talking chemistry and physics that day. So a good many kangaroos, capybaras and agoutis passed well within range and still got away from the boy's gun. As a result, the day was already well along and the two hunters were in a fair way to having made the trip for nothing, when Harbert stopped short and gave a shout of joy.

"Oh, Mr. Cyrus! Do you see that tree?"

And he pointed to what was a shrub rather than a tree, for it had only a single stem, covered in scaly bark, which bore leaves streaked with little parallel veins.

"And what is this tree that looks like a little palm?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"It's a Cycas revoluta — there's a picture of it in our dictionary of natural history!"

"But I don't see any fruit on this shrub."

"No, Mr. Cyrus," answered Harbert, "but its trunk holds a flour that nature gives us ready-ground."

"So it's the bread tree?"

"Yes! The bread tree."

"Well, my boy," said the engineer, "that's a precious discovery while we wait for our wheat harvest. Let's get to work — and heaven grant you're not mistaken!"

Harbert was not mistaken. He broke open the stem of a cycad. It was made of a glandular tissue and held a quantity of floury pith, crossed by bundles of woody fiber, which were separated by rings of the same material arranged one inside another. Mixed with this starch was a slimy juice with an unpleasant taste, but it would be easy to drive it out by pressing. This cellular substance made a real flour of superior quality, extremely nourishing — so much so that the laws of Japan once forbade its export.

Cyrus Smith and Harbert studied the part of the Far West where these cycads grew, took landmarks, and went back to Granite House, where they announced their discovery.

The next day the colonists went out to harvest, and Pencroff, more and more enthusiastic about his island, said to the engineer:

"Mr. Cyrus, do you believe there are castaway islands?"

"What do you mean by that, Pencroff?"

"Why, I mean islands made specially so that people can be shipwrecked on them properly, where poor devils can always manage to get by!"

"That's possible," said the engineer with a smile.

"It's certain, sir," answered Pencroff, "and it's just as certain that Lincoln Island is one of them!"

They came back to Granite House with an ample harvest of cycad stems. The engineer built a press to squeeze out the slimy juice mixed with the starch, and he got a good quantity of flour, which Nab's hands turned into cakes and puddings. It was not yet real wheat bread, but they were almost there.

At this time, too, the onagga, the goats and the ewes at the corral gave all the milk the colony needed every day. So the cart — or rather a sort of light two-wheeled trap that had replaced it — made frequent trips to the corral. And when it was Pencroff's turn to make the rounds, he took Jup along and let him drive, which Jup did with his usual intelligence, cracking his whip.

So everything was thriving, at the corral as well as at Granite House, and truly the colonists, apart from being far from their homeland, had nothing to complain about. Indeed, they had grown so used to this life, so at home on this island, that they could not have left its welcoming soil without regret!

And yet, so deeply is love of country rooted in the human heart that if some ship had unexpectedly come in sight of the island, the colonists would have signaled to it, drawn it in, and gone!... Meanwhile they lived this happy life, and they feared rather than wished for anything that might come along to interrupt it.

But who can boast of ever having pinned fortune down, and of being safe from her reverses?

Be that as it may, this Lincoln Island, where the colonists had now been living for more than a year, was often the subject of their conversation, and one day a remark was made that would later lead to serious consequences.

It was April 1, a Sunday — Easter Day — which Cyrus Smith and his companions had kept holy with rest and prayer. The day had been beautiful, as a day in October might be in the northern hemisphere.

Toward evening, after dinner, they were all gathered on the veranda at the edge of Prospect Plateau, watching night rise over the horizon. Nab had served a few cups of the infusion of elderberry seeds that stood in for coffee. They were talking about the island and its isolated position in the Pacific when Gédéon Spilett happened to say:

"My dear Cyrus, since you've had that sextant we found in the chest, have you taken our island's position again?"

"No," answered the engineer.

"But it might be a good idea to do it, with an instrument that's better than the one you used."

"What for?" said Pencroff. "The island's fine where it is!"

"No doubt," Gédéon Spilett went on, "but it may be that the flaws in your instruments affected the accuracy of your observations, and since it's easy to check them..."

"You're right, my dear Spilett," answered the engineer, "and I ought to have made that check sooner — although if I did make some mistake, it shouldn't be more than five degrees in longitude or latitude."

"Ah! Who knows?" the reporter went on. "Who knows whether we aren't a lot closer to an inhabited land than we think?"

"We'll know tomorrow," answered Cyrus Smith, "and if I hadn't had so much work that left me no free time, we'd know already."

"Good!" said Pencroff. "Mr. Cyrus is too good an observer to have gone wrong, and unless it's moved, the island is right where he put it!"

"We'll see."

So the next day the engineer used the sextant to make the observations needed to check the coordinates he had already obtained, and here is the result of his work.

His first observation had given him this position for Lincoln Island:

    Longitude west: from 150° to 155°
    Latitude south: from 30° to 35°

The second gave, exactly:

    Longitude west: 150° 30′
    Latitude south: 34° 57′

So, for all the imperfection of his instruments, Cyrus Smith had worked with such skill that his error had not gone beyond five degrees.

"Now," said Gédéon Spilett, "since we have an atlas as well as a sextant, let's see, my dear Cyrus, exactly where Lincoln Island sits in the Pacific."

Harbert went to get the atlas, which, as we know, had been published in France, so that its place names were in French.

The map of the Pacific was spread out, and the engineer, compasses in hand, got ready to fix the island's position on it.

Suddenly the compasses stopped in his hand, and he said:

"But there's already an island in this part of the Pacific!"

"An island?" cried Pencroff.

"Ours, surely?" said Gédéon Spilett.

"No," Cyrus Smith went on. "This island lies at 153° longitude and 37° 11′ latitude — that is, two and a half degrees farther west and two degrees farther south than Lincoln Island."

"And what island is it?" asked Harbert.

"Tabor Island."

"Is it a big island?"

"No, it's an islet lost in the Pacific, which perhaps nobody has ever visited!"

"Well, we'll visit it," said Pencroff.

"We will?"

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus. We'll build a decked boat, and I'll take charge of sailing her. How far are we from this Tabor Island?"

"About a hundred and fifty miles to the northeast," answered Cyrus Smith.

"A hundred and fifty miles! What's that?" answered Pencroff. "In forty-eight hours, with a good wind, it's done!"

"But what for?" asked the reporter.

"You never know. We'll have to see!"

And on that answer it was decided that a boat would be built, so that she could put to sea around next October, when the fine season came back.

Chapter 10: A Whale in Sight

Building the boat — The second wheat harvest — Hunting koulas — A new plant, more pleasant than useful — A whale in sight — The harpoon from the Vineyard — Cutting up the whale — What the whalebone was for — The end of May — Pencroff has nothing left to wish for

When Pencroff got an idea into his head, he gave himself no rest, and gave nobody else any, until it had been carried out. Now, he wanted to visit Tabor Island, and since a boat of some size was needed for the crossing, that boat had to be built.

Here is the plan the engineer settled on, in agreement with the sailor.

The boat would measure thirty-five feet along the keel and nine feet in the beam, which would make her a fast sailer if her bottom and her waterlines came out well. She should draw no more than six feet, enough depth in the water to keep her from drifting sideways off her course. She would be decked over her whole length, with two hatches opening into two cabins separated by a bulkhead. She would be rigged as a sloop, with a mainsail, a staysail, a square running sail, a topsail and a jib: a set of sails very easy to handle, quick to lower when a squall struck, and very good for sailing close to the wind. Finally, her hull would be carvel-built — that is, the planks would lie flush, edge to edge, instead of overlapping one another — and as for her frames, they would be bent into place hot, after the planking had been fitted over temporary molds.

What wood would they build her of? Elm or fir, both plentiful on the island? They decided on fir. It is a wood a little "splitty," as carpenters say, but it is easy to work, and it stands being soaked in water as well as elm does.

Once these details were settled, it was agreed that, since the fine season would not come back for another six months, Cyrus Smith and Pencroff would work on the boat by themselves. Gédéon Spilett and Harbert were to go on hunting, and neither Nab nor Master Jup, his assistant, would give up the household work that had fallen to them.

As soon as the trees were chosen, they were felled, cut into lengths and sawn into planks, the way pit sawyers would have done it. A week later a shipyard had been laid out in the recess between the Chimneys and the cliff, and a keel thirty-five feet long, with a sternpost at the after end and a stem at the forward end, lay stretched out on the sand.

Cyrus Smith had not gone blindly into this new job. He knew shipbuilding as he knew almost everything, and he had first worked out the shape of his boat on paper. Besides, he was well served by Pencroff, who had worked several years in a Brooklyn shipyard and knew the practical side of the trade. So it was only after strict calculation and careful thought that the temporary molds were set up on the keel.

Pencroff, as anyone will readily believe, was all on fire to see his new undertaking through, and he would not have left it for a moment.

Only one task had the privilege of tearing him away from his shipyard, and then for a single day. That was the second wheat harvest, which took place on April 15. It had done as well as the first and gave the yield of grain that had been predicted.

"Five bushels, Mr. Cyrus!" said Pencroff, after measuring his riches with the greatest care.

"Five bushels," answered the engineer, "and at a hundred and thirty thousand grains a bushel, that makes six hundred and fifty thousand grains."

"Well! This time we'll sow the lot," said the sailor, "except for a little reserve, all the same!"

"Yes, Pencroff, and if the next harvest gives a proportional yield, we'll have four thousand bushels."

"And we'll eat bread?"

"We'll eat bread."

"But we'll have to make a mill?"

"We'll make a mill."

So the third wheat field was incomparably larger than the first two, and the soil, prepared with the utmost care, received the precious seed. That done, Pencroff went back to his work.

Meanwhile Gédéon Spilett and Harbert went hunting in the surrounding country, and they ventured quite deep into the still unknown parts of the Far West, their guns loaded with ball, ready for any unpleasant encounter. It was a tangled mass of magnificent trees crowded against one another as though they were short of room. Exploring these great stands of timber was extremely difficult, and the reporter never risked it without taking the pocket compass, because the sun barely got through the thick branches and it would have been hard to find the way back. Game was naturally scarcer in such places, where it would not have had enough room to move freely. Still, three big plant-eaters were killed during the last two weeks of April. They were koulas, one of which the colonists had already seen north of the lake, and they let themselves be killed stupidly among the thick branches of the trees where they had taken refuge. Their skins were brought back to Granite House, and with the help of sulfuric acid they were put through a kind of tanning that made them usable.

On one of these excursions they also made a discovery, precious from another point of view altogether, and this one they owed to Gédéon Spilett.

It was April 30. The two hunters had pushed deep into the southwest of the Far West when the reporter, some fifty paces ahead of Harbert, came into a sort of clearing where the trees stood farther apart and let in a few rays of sun.

The first thing that struck Gédéon Spilett was the smell given off by certain plants with straight, round, branching stems, which bore their flowers in clusters and had very tiny seeds. The reporter pulled up one or two of these stems and went back to the boy.

"Look at this, Harbert. What is it?" he said.

"And where did you find this plant, Mr. Spilett?"

"Over there, in a clearing, where it grows in great quantities."

"Well, Mr. Spilett," said Harbert, "this is a find that gives you every right to Pencroff's gratitude!"

"So it's tobacco?"

"Yes, and if it isn't the finest quality, it's tobacco all the same!"

"Ah! Good old Pencroff! Won't he be happy! But he won't smoke the whole lot, hang it! He'll leave us our share!"

"Oh! I've got an idea, Mr. Spilett," answered Harbert. "Let's not say anything to Pencroff. We'll take the time to cure these leaves, and then one fine day we'll hand him a pipe all filled and ready!"

"Agreed, Harbert, and on that day our worthy companion won't have anything left in this world to wish for!"

The reporter and the boy gathered a good supply of the precious plant and went back to Granite House, where they smuggled it in "as contraband," with as many precautions as if Pencroff had been the strictest of customs officers.

Cyrus Smith and Nab were let in on the secret, and the sailor suspected nothing during the whole of the rather long time it took to dry the thin leaves, chop them, and roast them slightly on hot stones. That took two months; but all this handling could be done without Pencroff's knowing, because, busy as he was building the boat, he came up to Granite House only at rest time.

Once again, however, like it or not, his favorite work was interrupted on May 1 by a fishing adventure in which all the colonists had to take part.

For several days they had been able to watch an enormous animal swimming in the waters of Lincoln Island, two or three miles offshore. It was a whale of the largest size, which in all likelihood belonged to the southern species known as the "Cape whale."

"What a piece of luck it would be to catch her!" cried the sailor. "Ah! If we had a proper boat and a harpoon in good shape, I'd be saying, 'After that beast — she's worth the taking!'"

"Well, Pencroff," said Gédéon Spilett, "I'd have liked to see you handle a harpoon. It must be something to watch!"

"Very much something to watch, and not without danger," said the engineer. "But since we haven't the means to attack the animal, there's no point thinking about her."

"I'm surprised," said the reporter, "to see a whale in such a comparatively high latitude."

"Why's that, Mr. Spilett?" answered Harbert. "We're right in the part of the Pacific that English and American whalers call the 'Whale Field,' and it's here, between New Zealand and South America, that the whales of the southern hemisphere are found in the greatest numbers."

"Nothing truer," answered Pencroff, "and what surprises me is that we haven't seen more of them. After all, since we can't get near them, what does it matter!"

And Pencroff went back to his work, not without a sigh of regret. For in every sailor there is a fisherman, and if the pleasure of fishing goes up in direct proportion to the size of the fish, you can judge what a whaler feels in the presence of a whale!

And if it had only been the pleasure! But there was no hiding the fact that such a prize would have been very profitable to the colony, for the oil, the fat and the whalebone could all be put to a great many uses!

Now, it so happened that the whale they had sighted seemed unwilling to leave the waters around the island. So, from the windows of Granite House or from Prospect Plateau, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett when they were not out hunting, and Nab while he kept an eye on his stoves, never let go of the spyglass, and they followed every movement the animal made. The whale had come far into the wide expanse of Union Bay and was furrowing it at speed from Mandible Cape to Claw Cape, driven by her prodigiously powerful tail fin, which she bore down on to push herself forward in great surges, at a speed that sometimes reached twelve miles an hour. Sometimes, too, she came so close to the islet that they could make her out completely. It was indeed the southern right whale, which is entirely black, and whose head is flatter than that of the northern whales.

They could also see her shoot a cloud of vapor high into the air from her blowholes... or of water. For, odd as it may seem, naturalists and whalers still do not agree on the matter. Is it air or is it water that is forced out like that? The general view is that it is vapor, which condenses suddenly on meeting the cold air and falls back as rain.

All the same, the presence of this sea mammal was on the colonists' minds. It irritated Pencroff most of all and kept distracting him from his work. He ended up wanting that whale the way a child wants something it has been forbidden. At night he dreamed of her out loud, and certainly, if he had had any means of attacking her, if the boat had been fit to put to sea, he would not have hesitated to go after her.

But what the colonists could not do, chance did for them. On May 3, shouts from Nab, posted at his kitchen window, announced that the whale had run aground on the island's shore.

Harbert and Gédéon Spilett, who were just setting off to hunt, dropped their guns; Pencroff threw down his ax; Cyrus Smith and Nab joined their companions; and they all hurried toward the place where she had stranded.

She had run aground at high tide on the beach of Jetsam Point, three miles from Granite House. So it was likely that the whale would not be able to work herself free easily. In any case they had to hurry, so as to cut off her retreat if need be. They ran with picks and iron-tipped spears, crossed the bridge over the Mercy, went back down the right bank of the river, took the beach, and in less than twenty minutes the colonists stood beside the enormous animal, above which a whole world of birds was already swarming.

"What a monster!" cried Nab.

And the word was right, for it was a southern right whale eighty feet long, a giant of her kind, which could not have weighed less than a hundred and fifty thousand pounds!

Yet the monster, stranded as she was, did not stir, and did not thrash about trying to float herself off while the tide was still high.

The colonists soon had the explanation of why she lay so still, when at low tide they walked all the way around the animal.

She was dead, and a harpoon was sticking out of her left side.

"So there are whalers in our waters?" said Gédéon Spilett at once.

"Why do you say that?" asked the sailor.

"Because that harpoon is still there..."

"Eh, Mr. Spilett, that proves nothing," answered Pencroff. "Whales have been known to travel thousands of miles with a harpoon in their side, and if this one had been struck in the North Atlantic and come to die in the South Pacific, there'd be nothing surprising in it!"

"All the same..." said Gédéon Spilett, who was not satisfied by Pencroff's assurance.

"It's perfectly possible," answered Cyrus Smith, "but let's look at this harpoon. Perhaps, following a fairly common custom, the whalers engraved the name of their ship on it?"

And indeed, when Pencroff had pulled out the harpoon that was stuck in the animal's side, he read this inscription on it:

    Maria-Stella
    Vineyard.

"A ship from the Vineyard! A ship from my part of the world!" he cried. "The Maria-Stella! A fine whaler, upon my word! And one I know well! Ah, my friends, a ship from the Vineyard, a whaler from the Vineyard!"

And the sailor, brandishing the harpoon, kept repeating, not without emotion, that name so dear to his heart, the name of his native place!

But since they could hardly wait for the Maria-Stella to come and claim the animal she had harpooned, they decided to cut the whale up before she began to decompose. The birds of prey, which had been spying on this rich prize for several days, meant to take possession without further delay, and they had to be driven off with gunfire.

The whale was a female, and her udders yielded a large quantity of milk which, in the opinion of the naturalist Dieffenbach, could pass for cow's milk — and indeed it differs from it neither in taste, nor in color, nor in density.

Pencroff had once served aboard a whaling ship, and he was able to direct the cutting-up methodically. It was a rather unpleasant job, and it lasted three days, but not one of the colonists flinched from it — not even Gédéon Spilett, who, according to the sailor, would end up making "a very good castaway."

The blubber was cut into parallel slices two and a half feet thick, then divided into pieces that might weigh a thousand pounds each, and melted down in big earthenware vessels brought to the spot where the whale was being cut up — for they did not want to make the approaches to Prospect Plateau reek. In the melting it lost about a third of its weight. But there was blubber to spare: the tongue alone gave six thousand pounds of oil, and the lower lip four thousand. And besides this fat, which would keep them supplied with stearin and glycerin for a long time, there was the whalebone, which no doubt would find its uses too, even though nobody at Granite House carried an umbrella or wore a corset. The upper part of the whale's mouth was furnished, on both sides, with eight hundred horny plates, very springy, fibrous in texture, and fringed at their edges like two great combs whose teeth, six feet long, serve to strain out the thousands of tiny creatures, small fish and mollusks the whale lives on.

The job finished, to the great satisfaction of those who had done it, what was left of the animal was abandoned to the birds, which would make every last trace of it disappear, and the daily work at Granite House was taken up again.

Before going back to the shipyard, however, Cyrus Smith had the idea of making certain devices that greatly excited his companions' curiosity. He took a dozen strips of whalebone, cut each one into six equal pieces, and sharpened them at the ends.

"And those, Mr. Cyrus," asked Harbert, when the job was done, "what will they be good for...?"

"For killing wolves, foxes, and even jaguars," answered the engineer.

"Now?"

"No, this winter, when we have ice at our disposal."

"I don't understand..." answered Harbert.

"You will, my boy," answered the engineer. "This device isn't my invention. The Aleut hunters of Russian America use it a great deal. You see these strips of whalebone, my friends? Well, when it freezes, I'll bend them double and keep pouring water over them until each one is completely coated in a layer of ice that will hold it bent. Then I'll scatter them over the snow, after first hiding them under a layer of fat. Now, what will happen if a hungry animal swallows one of these baits? The heat of its stomach will melt the ice, and the whalebone will spring straight and pierce it with its sharpened ends."

"Now that's clever!" said Pencroff.

"And it will save powder and bullets," answered Cyrus Smith.

"It's better than traps!" added Nab.

"So let's wait for winter!"

"Let's wait for winter."

Meanwhile the building of the boat went forward, and toward the end of the month she was half planked. It could already be seen that her lines would be excellent for keeping the sea well.

Pencroff worked with unequaled energy, and it took his sturdy constitution to stand the strain. But his companions were secretly preparing a reward for all his trouble, and on May 31 he was to feel one of the greatest joys of his life.

That day, at the end of dinner, just as he was about to leave the table, Pencroff felt a hand come down on his shoulder.

It was the hand of Gédéon Spilett, who said to him:

"Just a moment, Master Pencroff! You don't walk out like that! What about the dessert you're forgetting?"

"Thank you, Mr. Spilett," answered the sailor, "but I'm going back to work."

"Well, then, a cup of coffee, my friend?"

"No more than that."

"A pipe, then?"

Pencroff had jumped to his feet, and his big, good-natured face went pale when he saw the reporter holding out a pipe all filled and ready, and Harbert holding out a glowing ember.

The sailor tried to say something and could not get a word out. But he seized the pipe and carried it to his lips; then, putting the ember to it, he drew five or six puffs, one after another.

A bluish, fragrant cloud spread out, and from the depths of that cloud came a voice in raptures, repeating:

"Tobacco! Real tobacco!"

"Yes, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith, "and excellent tobacco at that!"

"Oh, divine Providence! Holy Maker of all things!" cried the sailor. "Now there's nothing missing on our island!"

And Pencroff smoked, and smoked, and smoked!

"And who made this discovery?" he asked at last. "You, I suppose, Harbert?"

"No, Pencroff, it was Mr. Spilett."

"Mr. Spilett!" cried the sailor, crushing the reporter to his chest in a hug such as the reporter had never had to endure before.

"Oof! Pencroff," answered Gédéon Spilett, getting back his breath, which had been in some danger for a moment. "Save a share of your gratitude for Harbert, who recognized the plant, for Cyrus, who prepared it, and for Nab, who had a terrible time keeping the secret!"

"Well, my friends, I'll pay you back for this some day!" answered the sailor. "From now on, it's for life and death between us!"

Chapter 11: The Fuel of the Future

Winter — Fulling the wool — The mill — Pencroff's fixed idea — The whalebone — What an albatross can be used for — The fuel of the future — Top and Jup — Storms — Damage to the poultry yard — An excursion to the marsh — Cyrus Smith alone — Exploring the well

Meanwhile winter was arriving with the month of June, which is the December of the northern zones, and the great task of the season was making warm, sturdy clothes.

The mouflons in the corral had been sheared, so the colonists had their precious textile fiber. All that remained was to turn it into cloth.

It goes without saying that Cyrus Smith had no carding machines, no combing machines, no smoothing machines, no drawing frames, no twisting frames, no "spinning mule" or "self-acting" mule to spin the wool, and no loom to weave it. He had to go about it a simpler way, one that would save both spinning and weaving. And in fact he meant quite simply to make use of a property of wool fibers: when they are pressed together from every direction, they tangle up, and just by crisscrossing they form the fabric called felt. So felt could be made by simple fulling, that is, by pounding the wool. The process makes the fabric less supple, but it does a great deal to increase how well it holds in heat. And it so happened that the wool from the mouflons had very short fibers, which is just what makes for good felting.

The engineer, helped by his companions, Pencroff included (once again he had to leave his boat!), began with the preliminary work, whose purpose was to rid the wool of the oily, greasy substance it is soaked in, which is called suint. This degreasing was done in tubs full of water, heated to a temperature of a hundred and fifty-eight degrees Fahrenheit, and the wool soaked in them for twenty-four hours. After that it was washed thoroughly in baths of soda. Then, once the wool had been squeezed dry enough, it was ready to be fulled, that is, to be made into a strong fabric. It would be coarse, no doubt, and it would have had no value at all in a manufacturing center in Europe or America, but it was going to be prized very highly on "the markets of Lincoln Island."

Clearly this kind of fabric must have been known from the most ancient times, and in fact the first woolen fabrics ever made were made by the very process Cyrus Smith was about to use.

Where his training as an engineer served him best was in building the machine for fulling the wool. He cleverly took advantage of a mechanical power that had gone unused until then, the force of the waterfall on the beach, to drive a fulling mill.

Nothing could have been more primitive. A shaft fitted with cams, which lifted vertical pestles one after another and let them drop again; troughs to hold the wool, into which the pestles fell; a strong timber frame to hold and tie the whole system together: that was the machine in question. And that was what such machines had been for centuries, until someone had the idea of replacing the pestles with pressing rollers, so that the material was no longer beaten but truly rolled flat.

The operation, carefully directed by Cyrus Smith, was a complete success. The wool had first been soaked in a soapy solution. On the one hand this helped the fibers to slide, draw together, pack down and soften; on the other, it kept the beating from damaging them. The wool came out of the mill as a thick sheet of felt. The tiny ridges and rough scales that every wool fiber naturally carries had caught and tangled in one another so well that they made a fabric fit for clothes and blankets alike. Obviously it was not merino, or muslin, or Scotch cashmere, or worsted stuff, or rep, or China satin, or Orleans cloth, or alpaca, or broadcloth, or flannel! It was "Lincolnian felt," and Lincoln Island had one more industry.

So the colonists had good clothes and thick blankets, and they could watch the winter of 1866-67 approach without fear.

The real cold began to bite around June 20, and to his great regret Pencroff had to put off building the boat, which in any case was certain to be finished by the next spring.

The sailor's fixed idea was to make a voyage of exploration to Tabor Island. Cyrus Smith did not approve of the trip, which was pure curiosity, since there was obviously no help to be found on that bare, half-barren rock. A voyage of a hundred and fifty miles in a fairly small boat, across unknown seas, gave him a good deal of worry. Suppose the boat, once out at sea, found it impossible to reach Tabor and could not get back to Lincoln Island. What would become of her in the middle of the Pacific, an ocean so rich in disasters?

Cyrus Smith often talked over the plan with Pencroff, and he found in the sailor a rather odd stubbornness about making this voyage, a stubbornness that Pencroff himself may not have fully understood.

"After all," the engineer said to him one day, "I'll point out to you, my friend, that after singing the praises of Lincoln Island so often, after telling us so many times how sorry you'd be if you ever had to leave it, you're the first one who wants to go."

"Leave it for a few days, that's all," answered Pencroff, "just for a few days, Mr. Cyrus! Long enough to go and come back and see what that islet is!"

"But it can't be as good as Lincoln Island!"

"I'm sure of that already!"

"Then why take the risk?"

"To find out what's going on on Tabor Island!"

"But nothing's going on there! Nothing can be going on there!"

"Who knows?"

"And what if you're caught in a storm?"

"That's nothing to fear in the good season," answered Pencroff. "But, Mr. Cyrus, since we have to plan for everything, I'll ask your permission to take only Harbert with me on the voyage."

"Pencroff," said the engineer, putting his hand on the sailor's shoulder, "if anything happened to you and to that boy, whom chance has made our son, do you think we would ever get over it?"

"Mr. Cyrus," answered Pencroff with unshakable confidence, "we won't bring you that grief. Anyway, we'll talk about this voyage again when the time comes to make it. And then I imagine that when you've seen our boat well rigged and well fitted out, when you've watched how she behaves at sea, when we've sailed around our island — because we'll do that together — I imagine, I say, that you won't hesitate any longer to let me go! I won't hide it from you: she's going to be a masterpiece, that boat of yours!"

"At least say 'our boat,' Pencroff!" answered the engineer, disarmed for the moment.

There the conversation ended, to begin again later, without convincing either the sailor or the engineer.

The first snow fell toward the end of June. Before that, the corral had been well stocked with provisions and no longer needed daily visits, but it was decided that they would never let a week go by without going there.

The traps were set again, and the devices Cyrus Smith had made got their first trial. The curved strips of whalebone, locked in a sheath of ice and covered with a thick layer of fat, were laid at the edge of the forest, at the spot where animals usually passed on their way to the lake.

To the engineer's great satisfaction, this invention, borrowed from the Aleut hunters, worked perfectly. A dozen foxes, a few wild boars and even a jaguar were caught by it, and the animals were found dead, their stomachs pierced by the whalebone as it sprang straight.

Here belongs an experiment that deserves to be told, because it was the colonists' first attempt to communicate with their fellow men.

Gédéon Spilett had already thought several times of throwing a message into the sea, sealed in a bottle that the currents might carry to an inhabited coast, or else of entrusting it to pigeons. But how could anyone seriously hope that pigeons or bottles would cross the distance that separated the island from any land, which was twelve hundred miles? It would have been sheer folly.

But on June 30, not without trouble, they captured an albatross that a shot from Harbert's gun had slightly wounded in the foot. It was a magnificent bird of that family of great ocean fliers whose outspread wings measure ten feet from tip to tip, and which can cross seas as wide as the Pacific.

Harbert would have liked very much to keep the splendid bird. Its wound healed quickly, and he claimed he could tame it. But Gédéon Spilett made him understand that they could not pass up this chance to try to reach the lands of the Pacific by such a courier, and Harbert had to give in, for if the albatross had come from some inhabited region, it would surely go back there as soon as it was free.

Perhaps, deep down, Gédéon Spilett, in whom the newspaperman sometimes came back to the surface, was not sorry to launch, on the off chance, a gripping article telling the adventures of the colonists of Lincoln Island! What a triumph for the official reporter of the New York Herald, and for the issue that would carry the story, if it ever reached the desk of his editor, the Honorable John Bennett!

So Gédéon Spilett wrote a short account, which was put into a bag of strong gummed canvas, with an urgent request that whoever found it should forward it to the offices of the New York Herald. The little bag was tied around the albatross's neck, not its foot, because these birds have the habit of resting on the surface of the sea. Then this swift courier of the air was given its freedom, and it was not without some emotion that the colonists watched it vanish far off into the mists of the west.

"Where's he off to?" asked Pencroff.

"Toward New Zealand," answered Harbert.

"Bon voyage!" cried the sailor, who, for his part, did not expect much to come of this way of corresponding.

With the winter, the indoor work at Granite House had started up again: mending clothes, making all sorts of things, and among others the sails for the boat, which were cut from the balloon's inexhaustible envelope...

During the month of July the cold was severe, but they spared neither wood nor coal. Cyrus Smith had put a second fireplace into the great hall, and that was where they spent the long evenings. They talked while they worked, and read when their hands were idle, and the time passed profitably for everyone.

It was a real delight for the colonists when, in that room well lit with candles and well heated with coal, after a hearty dinner, with the elderberry coffee steaming in their cups and their pipes trailing plumes of fragrant smoke, they heard the storm roaring outside! Their comfort would have been complete, if comfort could ever be complete for people who are far from their fellow men and have no way of reaching them! They talked endlessly about their country, about the friends they had left behind, about the greatness of the American republic, whose influence could only grow. And Cyrus Smith, who had been deeply involved in the affairs of the Union, held his listeners spellbound with his stories, his insights and his predictions.

One day it happened that Gédéon Spilett was led to say to him:

"But really, my dear Cyrus, all this industrial and commercial activity that you predict will keep on growing — isn't it in danger of being stopped dead sooner or later?"

"Stopped! By what?"

"Why, by running out of coal, which has every right to be called the most precious of minerals!"

"Yes, the most precious, indeed," answered the engineer, "and it seems as though nature wanted to prove it, by making the diamond, which is nothing but pure carbon, crystallized."

"You don't mean, Mr. Cyrus," Pencroff put in, "that they'll burn diamonds instead of coal in the fireboxes of the boilers?"

"No, my friend," answered Cyrus Smith.

"All the same, I insist," Gédéon Spilett went on. "You don't deny that one day the coal will be entirely used up?"

"Oh, the coal deposits are still enormous, and the hundred thousand workers who dig ten million metric tons out of them every year are not close to exhausting them!"

"With the amount of coal being burned growing all the time," answered Gédéon Spilett, "we can foresee that those hundred thousand workers will soon be two hundred thousand, and that the output will double?"

"No doubt. But after the deposits in Europe, which new machines will soon let us mine more deeply, the coal mines of America and Australia will go on supplying industry for a long time yet."

"How long?" asked the reporter.

"Two hundred and fifty or three hundred years at least."

"That's reassuring for us," answered Pencroff, "but worrying for our great-grand-cousins!"

"They'll find something else," said Harbert.

"Let's hope so," answered Gédéon Spilett, "because without coal, no more machines, and without machines, no more railroads, no more steamships, no more factories, nothing that the progress of modern life demands!"

"But what will they find?" asked Pencroff. "Can you picture it, Mr. Cyrus?"

"More or less, my friend."

"And what will they burn instead of coal?"

"Water," answered Cyrus Smith.

"Water!" cried Pencroff. "Water to fire steamships and locomotives! Water to heat water!"

"Yes, but water broken down into the elements it is made of," answered Cyrus Smith, "and broken down, no doubt, by electricity, which by then will have become a powerful force that people know how to handle — for all the great discoveries, by some law nobody can explain, seem to arrive together and complete one another at the same moment. Yes, my friends, I believe that one day water will be used as fuel, and that hydrogen and oxygen, the two gases it is made of, used separately or together, will provide an inexhaustible source of heat and light, of an intensity that coal could never reach. One day the bunkers of steamships and the tenders of locomotives will be loaded, not with coal, but with these two gases, compressed, and they will burn in the fireboxes with enormous heating power. So there is nothing to fear. As long as this earth is inhabited, it will meet the needs of the people who live on it, and they will never lack light or heat, any more than they will lack the products of the vegetable, mineral or animal kingdoms. So I believe that when the coal deposits are exhausted, we will heat our engines and ourselves with water. Water will be the coal of the future."

"I'd like to see that," said the sailor.

"You were born too soon, Pencroff," answered Nab, and those were the only words he contributed to the discussion.

Still, it was not Nab's remark that ended the conversation, but Top's barking, which broke out again with that strange tone that had already troubled the engineer. At the same time Top began once more to circle around the opening of the well at the far end of the inside passage.

"What's Top barking like that about this time?" asked Pencroff.

"And why is Jup grunting that way?" added Harbert.

It was true: the orangutan had joined the dog and was showing unmistakable signs of agitation, and, a curious detail, the two animals seemed more uneasy than angry.

"It's obvious," said Gédéon Spilett, "that this well connects directly with the sea, and that some sea animal comes now and then to breathe at the bottom of it."

"That's obvious," answered the sailor, "and there's no other explanation to give... Come on, quiet, Top," Pencroff added, turning to the dog, "and you, Jup, off to your room!"

The ape and the dog fell silent. Jup went back to bed, but Top stayed in the great hall, and he went on growling under his breath for the rest of the evening.

Nobody spoke of the incident again, but it clouded the engineer's brow all the same.

For the rest of July there were spells of rain and spells of cold. The temperature did not drop as low as it had the winter before; at its coldest it went no lower than eight degrees Fahrenheit. But if this winter was less cold, it was at least more troubled by storms and gales. Once again the sea made violent attacks that more than once put the Chimneys in danger. You might have thought that a tidal wave, set off by some upheaval under the sea, was lifting these monstrous breakers and hurling them against the wall of Granite House.

When the colonists leaned out of their windows and watched those enormous masses of water breaking before their eyes, they could only admire the magnificent spectacle of the ocean's powerless fury. The waves bounced back in dazzling foam, the whole beach disappeared under the raging flood, and the cliff seemed to rise out of the sea itself, while the spray flew more than a hundred feet into the air.

During these storms it was hard to venture onto the island's roads, even dangerous, because trees came down often. Still, the colonists never let a week go by without visiting the corral. Luckily the enclosure, sheltered by the southeast shoulder of Mount Franklin, did not suffer much from the violence of the hurricane, which spared its trees, its sheds and its palisade. But the poultry yard, set up on Prospect Plateau and so directly exposed to the blasts of the east wind, took a good deal of damage. The dovecote lost its roof twice, and the fence was blown down as well. All of it would have to be rebuilt more solidly, because it was now clear that Lincoln Island lay in the worst waters of the Pacific. It truly seemed to be the center point of vast cyclones, which lashed it the way a whip lashes a spinning top. Only here it was the top that stood still, and the whip that went round.

During the first week of August the gusts died down little by little, and the air recovered a calm it had seemed to have lost forever. With the calm the temperature fell, the cold grew very sharp again, and the thermometer dropped to eight degrees below zero Fahrenheit.

On August 3 an excursion that had been planned for several days was made to the southeast of the island, toward Shelduck Marsh. The hunters were tempted by all the water birds that had set up their winter quarters there. Wild ducks, snipe, pintails, teal and grebes were plentiful, and it was decided that a day would be given to an expedition against these birds.

Not only Gédéon Spilett and Harbert but also Pencroff and Nab took part in the expedition. Cyrus Smith alone, pleading some work or other, did not join them and stayed at Granite House.

So the hunters took the road to Balloon Harbor to get to the marsh, after promising to be back by evening. Top and Jup went with them. As soon as they had crossed the bridge over the Mercy, the engineer raised it and went back, meaning to carry out a plan for which he wanted to be alone.

That plan was to make a thorough exploration of the inside well, whose opening was level with the passage of Granite House, and which connected with the sea, since it had once served as the channel for the waters of the lake.

Why did Top circle that opening so often? Why did he let out such strange barks when some kind of uneasiness drew him back to the well? Why did Jup join Top in a sort of shared anxiety? Did the well have other branches besides its straight connection down to the sea? Did it spread out toward other parts of the island? That was what Cyrus Smith wanted to know — and, to begin with, to be the only one to know. So he had made up his mind to try exploring the well while his companions were away, and now the chance had come.

It was easy to get down to the bottom of the well by using the rope ladder, which had not been in use since the elevator was put in and which was long enough. That is what the engineer did. He dragged the ladder to the hole, which was about six feet across, and after tying its upper end securely, he let it unroll down the shaft. Then, having lit a lantern, taken a revolver and stuck a cutlass in his belt, he started down the first rungs.

The wall was solid everywhere. But a few knobs of rock jutted out here and there, and by means of these projections it would really have been possible for some agile creature to climb up to the mouth of the well.

The engineer took note of that. But when he passed his lantern carefully over the projections, he found no mark, no chipped edge, nothing to suggest that they had ever been used for a climb, long ago or lately.

Cyrus Smith went deeper, lighting up every part of the wall.

He saw nothing suspicious.

When the engineer reached the last rungs, he felt the surface of the water, which was perfectly calm at that moment. Neither at the water's level nor anywhere else in the well was there any side passage that might branch off into the interior of the rock mass. The wall, when Cyrus Smith struck it with the handle of his cutlass, rang solid. It was compact granite, through which no living creature could force its way. To reach the bottom of the well and then climb to its opening, anything would have to come through that channel, always underwater, which linked it to the sea through the rocky ground beneath the beach — and that was possible only for sea animals. As for where the channel came out, at what point on the shore and how deep beneath the waves, there was no way to tell.

So Cyrus Smith, having finished his exploration, climbed back up, pulled up the ladder, covered the mouth of the well and went back to the great hall of Granite House, deep in thought, saying to himself:

"I saw nothing, and yet there is something there!"

Chapter 12: An Unexpected Document

Rigging the boat — An attack by culpeos — Jup wounded — Jup nursed — Jup cured — The boat finished — Pencroff's triumph — The Bonadventure — A first trial south of the island — An unexpected document

That same evening the hunters came home. They had had good hunting, and they were literally loaded down with game, carrying everything four men could carry.

Top had a string of pintails around his neck, and Jup had belts of snipe wound around his body.

"There, my master!" cried Nab. "There's something to keep us busy! Preserves, pâtés — we'll have a fine store of them! But somebody has to help me. I'm counting on you, Pencroff."

"No, Nab," the sailor answered. "The boat's rigging needs me, and you'll have to manage without me."

"What about you, Mr. Harbert?"

"I have to go to the corral tomorrow, Nab," the boy answered.

"Then it'll be you who helps me, Mr. Spilett?"

"To oblige you, Nab," the reporter answered. "But I warn you — if you let me in on your recipes, I'll publish them."

"As you please, Mr. Spilett," said Nab. "As you please!"

And that is how, the next day, Gédéon Spilett became Nab's assistant and was set up in his culinary laboratory. Before that, though, the engineer had told him the result of the exploration he had carried out the day before, and on that point the reporter shared Cyrus Smith's opinion: even though he had found nothing, there was still a secret waiting to be discovered!

The cold held on for another week, and the colonists did not leave Granite House except to look after the poultry yard. The whole dwelling was filled with the good smells given off by the expert operations of Nab and the reporter. Not all the game from the marsh hunt was turned into preserves, though. In that intense cold the meat kept perfectly, so wild ducks and the rest were eaten fresh, and they were declared superior to every other water bird in the known world.

During that week Pencroff, helped by Harbert, who handled a sailmaker's needle with skill, worked so hard that the boat's sails were finished. There was no shortage of hemp rope, thanks to the rigging that had been recovered along with the balloon's envelope. The cables and the cords of the net were all made of excellent line, and the sailor put it to good use. The sails were edged with strong bolt ropes — the ropes sewn around a sail's border to take the strain — and there was still enough left over to make the halyards, the shrouds, the sheets, and so on. As for the blocks, Cyrus Smith made the ones they needed on the lathe the sailor had set up, following Pencroff's advice. So it happened that the rigging was entirely ready long before the boat was finished. Pencroff even made a flag of blue, red, and white, its colors supplied by certain dye plants that were very plentiful on the island. Only, to the thirty-seven stars that stand for the thirty-seven states of the Union and shine on the blue corner of the American flag, the sailor had added a thirty-eighth: the star of "the State of Lincoln," because he already considered his island part of the great republic.

"And it is, at heart," he would say, "even if it isn't yet in fact!"

Meanwhile the flag was raised at the middle window of Granite House, and the colonists saluted it with three hurrahs.

By now the cold season was nearing its end, and it seemed that this second winter would pass without any serious incident, when, on the night of August 11, Prospect Plateau was threatened with complete devastation.

After a well-filled day the colonists were sound asleep when, at about four o'clock in the morning, they were suddenly wakened by Top's barking.

This time the dog was not barking near the mouth of the well, but at the threshold of the door, and he was throwing himself against it as if he wanted to break it down. Jup, for his part, was letting out shrill cries.

"Hey there, Top!" cried Nab, who was the first one awake.

But the dog went on barking even more furiously.

"What is it?" asked Cyrus Smith.

They all dressed in a hurry and rushed to the windows of the room and threw them open.

Before their eyes lay a sheet of snow that looked barely white in that very dark night. The colonists could see nothing, but they could hear strange barks bursting out of the darkness. It was obvious that the beach had been invaded by a number of animals that could not be made out.

"What is it?" cried Pencroff.

"Wolves, jaguars, or monkeys!" answered Nab.

"The devil! But they could get up onto the plateau!" said the reporter.

"And our poultry yard," cried Harbert, "and our plantations..."

"Which way did they get in?" asked Pencroff.

"They must have crossed the little bridge on the beach," the engineer answered. "One of us must have forgotten to close it."

"That's right," said Spilett. "I remember now — I left it down..."

"That was a fine piece of work, Mr. Spilett!" cried the sailor.

"What's done is done," Cyrus Smith answered. "Let's think about what has to be done now!"

Those were the questions and answers that flew back and forth between Cyrus Smith and his companions. It was certain that the little bridge had been crossed, that the beach had been invaded by animals, and that these animals, whatever they were, could reach Prospect Plateau by climbing along the left bank of the Mercy. So they had to get there first and fight them off, if need be.

"But what are these creatures?" someone asked a second time, just as the barking rang out louder.

The barking made Harbert start. He remembered having heard it before, during his first visit to the sources of Red Creek.

"They're culpeos — foxes!" he said.

"Forward!" cried the sailor.

And all of them, arming themselves with axes, carbines, and revolvers, crowded into the elevator's basket and set foot on the beach.

These culpeos are dangerous animals when there are a great many of them and hunger has made them savage. All the same, the colonists did not hesitate to throw themselves into the middle of the pack, and their first revolver shots, flashing quick bursts of light through the darkness, drove the leading attackers back.

What mattered above all was to keep these raiders from climbing up to Prospect Plateau. If they got there, the plantations and the poultry yard would be at their mercy, and immense damage — perhaps damage beyond repair, especially to the wheat field — would inevitably follow. But since the plateau could only be invaded by way of the left bank of the Mercy, it was enough to set up an impassable barrier against the culpeos on the narrow strip of bank between the river and the granite wall.

Everyone understood this, and at an order from Cyrus Smith they made for the spot he named, while the pack of culpeos leaped about in the dark.

So Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Pencroff, and Nab took up positions to form a line that nothing could get through. Top, his tremendous jaws wide open, stood out in front of the colonists, and behind him came Jup, armed with a knotty cudgel that he swung like a war club.

The night was extremely dark. Only in the flash of the shots — and every one of them had to count — could the attackers be seen. There must have been at least a hundred of them, and their eyes glowed like live coals.

"They mustn't get through!" cried Pencroff.

"They won't get through!" the engineer answered.

But if they did not get through, it was not for want of trying. The rear ranks pushed the front ones forward, and it was a ceaseless battle of revolver shots and ax blows. Many culpeo bodies must already have been strewn on the ground, but the pack did not seem to shrink. It was as if it were endlessly renewed by fresh arrivals over the little bridge on the beach.

Soon the colonists had to fight hand to hand, and they did not get away without a few wounds — slight ones, luckily. With one revolver shot Harbert had rid Nab of a culpeo that had just sprung onto his back like a wildcat. Top fought with real fury, leaping at the foxes' throats and strangling them outright. Jup, armed with his stick, laid about him like a madman, and it was no use trying to keep him in the rear. He must have had eyes that could pierce that darkness, because he was always where the fighting was thickest, and every now and then he let out a shrill whistle, which in him was the sign of tremendous glee. At one point he even pushed so far forward that, in the flash of a revolver shot, they could see him surrounded by five or six big culpeos, holding them off with rare coolness.

The fight was bound to end in the colonists' favor, but only after they had held out for two long hours! It was probably the first glimmers of dawn that decided the attackers to retreat. They bolted off to the north, back over the little bridge, which Nab ran to raise at once.

When the daylight was strong enough to light up the battlefield, the colonists counted some fifty bodies scattered across the beach.

"And Jup!" cried Pencroff. "Where's Jup?"

Jup had disappeared. His friend Nab called him, and for the first time Jup did not answer his friend's call.

Everyone set out to look for Jup, dreading to find him among the dead. They cleared the ground of the bodies, which were staining the snow with their blood, and Jup was found in the middle of a regular heap of culpeos. Their smashed jaws and broken backs showed that they had had to deal with the terrible cudgel of that fearless animal. Poor Jup was still holding the stump of his broken stick in his hand. But once he had lost his weapon, he had been overwhelmed by their numbers, and deep wounds furrowed his chest.

"He's alive!" cried Nab, bending over him.

"And we'll save him," the sailor answered. "We'll take care of him just as if he were one of us!"

It seemed as though Jup understood, for he leaned his head on Pencroff's shoulder as if to thank him. The sailor was wounded himself, but his wounds, like his companions', were trifling, since thanks to their firearms they had almost always been able to keep the attackers at a distance. So the orangutan was the only one in serious condition.

Carried by Nab and Pencroff, Jup was brought to the elevator, and barely a faint moan escaped his lips. They hoisted him gently up to Granite House. There he was laid on one of the mattresses taken from one of the bunks, and his wounds were washed with the greatest care. They did not seem to have reached any vital organ, but Jup had been badly weakened by loss of blood, and a fairly high fever set in.

So after his wounds were dressed they put him to bed and placed him on a strict diet — "just like a real person," said Nab — and they gave him a few cups of a cooling herbal tea, its ingredients supplied by Granite House's pharmacy of plants.

At first Jup's sleep was restless, but little by little his breathing became more regular, and they left him to rest in perfect quiet. From time to time Top came walking — on tiptoe, you might say — to visit his friend, and he seemed to approve of all the care being taken of him. One of Jup's hands hung over the edge of the bed, and Top licked it with a sorrowful air.

That same morning they buried the dead. The bodies were dragged to the Far West forest and buried deep.

This attack, which could have had such serious consequences, taught the colonists a lesson. From then on they never went to bed until one of them had made sure that all the bridges were raised and that no invasion was possible.

Meanwhile Jup, after giving them serious cause for worry for a few days, fought back hard against his illness. His constitution won out. The fever went down little by little, and Gédéon Spilett, who was something of a doctor, soon considered him out of danger. On August 16 Jup began to eat. Nab made him good little sweet dishes, which the patient savored with great relish, for if he had one endearing fault it was that he was a bit of a glutton, and Nab had never done a thing to cure him of it.

"What do you expect?" he would say to Gédéon Spilett, who sometimes scolded him for spoiling the ape. "The only pleasure poor Jup has is eating, and I'm only too happy to be able to repay him for his services this way!"

Ten days after taking to his bed, on August 21, Master Jup got up. His wounds had healed over, and it was plain that before long he would get back his usual agility and strength. Like every convalescent, he was seized with a ravenous hunger, and the reporter let him eat as much as he liked, trusting to the instinct that reasoning creatures so often lack and that would keep the orangutan from any excess. Nab was delighted to see his pupil's appetite coming back.

"Eat, my Jup," he would tell him, "and don't deny yourself a thing! You shed your blood for us, and the least I can do is help you make more!"

At last, on August 25, they heard Nab's voice calling his companions.

"Mr. Cyrus, Mr. Gédéon, Mr. Harbert, Pencroff — come here! Come here!"

The colonists, who were gathered in the great hall, got up at Nab's call. He was in the room set aside for Jup.

"What is it?" asked the reporter.

"Look!" Nab answered, with a huge burst of laughter.

And what did they see? Master Jup, sitting cross-legged in the doorway of Granite House, calmly and seriously smoking!

"My pipe!" cried Pencroff. "He's taken my pipe! Ah, my good Jup, I'm giving it to you! Smoke, my friend, smoke!"

And Jup solemnly puffed out thick clouds of tobacco smoke, which seemed to give him unequaled pleasure.

Cyrus Smith did not seem especially surprised by the incident, and he cited several cases of tame monkeys that had grown used to tobacco.

But from that day on, Master Jup had his own pipe — the sailor's former pipe — which was hung in his room beside his supply of tobacco. He filled it himself, he lit it with a glowing coal, and he seemed to be the happiest of all four-handed creatures. As you might expect, this shared taste only tightened the close bonds of friendship that already joined the worthy ape and the honest sailor.

"Maybe he's a man," Pencroff would sometimes say to Nab. "Would it surprise you if one day he started talking to us?"

"Goodness, no," Nab would answer. "What surprises me is that he doesn't talk. After all, the only thing he's missing is speech!"

"All the same, it would tickle me," the sailor went on, "if one fine day he said to me, 'How about we swap pipes, Pencroff?'"

"Yes," Nab answered. "What a pity he was born mute!"

With the month of September the winter was over for good, and work started up again in earnest.

The building of the boat moved quickly. Her outer planking was already all in place, and now they fitted her with frames on the inside, so as to tie every part of the hull together. The frames were made of timbers softened with steam, which bent to every curve the boat's lines called for.

Since there was no shortage of wood, Pencroff suggested to the engineer that they line the inside of the hull with a second, watertight layer of planking — what shipwrights call a ceiling — which would make the boat completely sound.

Cyrus Smith, not knowing what the future held in store, approved the sailor's idea of making their boat as strong as possible.

The ceiling and the deck were entirely finished around September 15. To caulk the seams they made oakum out of dried eelgrass, which was driven in with mallet blows between the planks of the hull, the ceiling, and the deck. Then the seams were coated with boiling tar, which the pines of the forest supplied in plenty.

The fitting out of the boat was as simple as could be. First she was ballasted with heavy pieces of granite, set in a bed of lime mortar, and they stowed about twelve thousand pounds of it. A floor was laid over this ballast, and the inside was divided into two cabins, each with a bench running along it that doubled as a storage chest. The foot of the mast was to serve as a prop for the partition between the two cabins, which were reached through two hatches opening onto the deck and fitted with hatch covers.

Pencroff had no trouble finding a suitable tree for the mast. He chose a young fir, good and straight and free of knots, which he only had to square off at the heel, where it would sit in its step, and round off at the top. The ironwork for the mast, the rudder, and the hull had been made at the forge in the Chimneys — roughly, but solidly. At last the yards, the topmast, the boom, the spars, the oars, and so on were all finished in the first week of October, and it was agreed that they would try the boat out in the waters around the island, to find out how she behaved at sea and how far they could trust her.

All this time the necessary work had not been neglected. The corral had been rearranged, since the flock of mouflons and goats now counted a number of young ones that had to be housed and fed. The colonists had kept up their visits to the oyster bed, to the warren, to the coal and iron deposits, and to certain parts of the Far West forests, which were full of game and had not yet been explored.

Some more native plants were discovered, too, and even if they were of no immediate use, they helped to vary the vegetable stores of Granite House. They were kinds of ice plant, some like the ones at the Cape of Good Hope, with fleshy leaves you could eat, and others producing seeds that held a sort of flour.

On October 10 the boat was launched. Pencroff was beaming. The operation went off perfectly. The boat, fully rigged, was pushed on rollers to the edge of the shore, where the rising tide took her, and she floated to the applause of the colonists — and especially of Pencroff, who showed no modesty whatever on this occasion. Besides, his pride was bound to outlast the boat's completion, since, having built her, he was now going to be called on to command her. The rank of captain was conferred on him with everyone's approval.

To satisfy Captain Pencroff, the first thing to do was give the boat a name. After several proposals had been argued over at length, the votes came together on Bonadventure, which was the honest sailor's baptismal name.

As soon as the rising tide had lifted the Bonadventure, they could see that she sat perfectly on her waterline and ought to sail well on every point of sailing.

In any case, she would be put to the test that very day, on an excursion off the coast. The weather was fine, the breeze fresh, and the sea easy, especially along the southern shore, since the wind had been blowing from the northwest for an hour already.

"All aboard! All aboard!" Captain Pencroff kept shouting.

But they had to have lunch before they left, and it even seemed wise to take provisions on board, in case the excursion stretched on into the evening.

Cyrus Smith was just as eager to try out this boat. The plans were his, though on the sailor's advice he had often changed parts of them. But he did not have the confidence in her that Pencroff showed, and since the sailor had not mentioned the voyage to Tabor Island again, Cyrus Smith even hoped he had given it up. He would have hated, in fact, to see two or three of his companions venture far out to sea in this boat, which was small, after all, and measured no more than fifteen tons.

At half past ten everyone was on board, even Jup, even Top. Nab and Harbert weighed the anchor, which was biting into the sand near the mouth of the Mercy. The mainsail was hoisted, the Lincolnian flag flew from the masthead, and the Bonadventure, steered by Pencroff, stood out to sea.

To get out of Union Bay they first had to run before the wind, and they could see that on that course the boat's speed was satisfactory.

After rounding Jetsam Point and Claw Cape, Pencroff had to sail close-hauled — as near into the wind as the boat would go — to run along the southern coast of the island. After a few tacks he observed that the Bonadventure could sail within about five points of the wind and held up well against drifting to leeward. She came about very well, having plenty of "way," as sailors say, and even gained ground as she turned.

The Bonadventure's passengers were truly delighted. They had a good boat here, one that could do them great service if the need arose, and in such fine weather, with such a steady breeze, the outing was a delight.

Pencroff stood out to sea three or four miles from the coast, abreast of Balloon Harbor. From there the island appeared in its full extent and in a new light: the varied panorama of its shoreline from Claw Cape to Reptile End; its forests in the foreground, where the conifers still stood out against the young leaves of the other trees, barely in bud; and Mount Franklin, towering over everything, its head still whitened with a little snow.

"How beautiful it is!" cried Harbert.

"Yes, our island is beautiful and good," Pencroff answered. "I love it the way I loved my poor mother! It took us in when we were poor and lacking everything, and what do these five children who dropped on it out of the sky lack now?"

"Nothing!" Nab answered. "Nothing, Captain!"

And the two good fellows gave three tremendous hurrahs in honor of their island!

Meanwhile Gédéon Spilett, leaning against the foot of the mast, was sketching the panorama spread out before his eyes.

Cyrus Smith watched in silence.

"Well, Mr. Cyrus," asked Pencroff, "what do you say about our boat?"

"She seems to handle well," the engineer answered.

"Good! And do you think now that she could make a voyage of some length?"

"What voyage, Pencroff?"

"To Tabor Island, for instance?"

"My friend," answered Cyrus Smith, "I believe that in an emergency we shouldn't hesitate to trust ourselves to the Bonadventure, even for a longer crossing. But, as you know, I would be sorry to see you leave for Tabor Island, since nothing obliges you to go there."

"A person likes to know his neighbors," Pencroff answered, digging in on his idea. "Tabor Island is our neighbor, and our only one! Good manners say we ought to go and pay it a visit, at least!"

"The devil!" said Gédéon Spilett. "Our friend Pencroff is a stickler for etiquette!"

"I'm not a stickler for anything at all," retorted the sailor. The engineer's opposition annoyed him a little, but he would not have wanted to cause him any pain.

"Remember, Pencroff," Cyrus Smith answered, "that you can't go to Tabor Island alone."

"One companion will be enough for me."

"Very well," answered the engineer. "So you're risking depriving the colony of Lincoln Island of two colonists out of five?"

"Out of six!" Pencroff answered. "You're forgetting Jup."

"Out of seven!" added Nab. "Top's worth as much as anybody!"

"There's no risk, Mr. Cyrus," Pencroff went on.

"That may be, Pencroff. But I'll say it again: it means exposing yourselves to danger for no need!"

The stubborn sailor made no reply and let the conversation drop, fully determined to take it up again. But he had no idea that an incident was about to come to his aid and turn what had been nothing but a whim — and a debatable one, after all — into a work of humanity.

After standing out to sea, the Bonadventure had just come back in toward the coast, heading for Balloon Harbor. It was important to check the channels that ran between the sandbanks and the reefs, and to mark them with buoys if necessary, since this little cove was to be the boat's home port.

They were now only half a mile from the coast, and they had had to beat their way in against the wind. The Bonadventure's speed was quite moderate at that point, because the breeze, partly blocked by the high ground, barely filled her sails. The sea, smooth as a mirror, rippled only when the cat's-paws passed fitfully across it.

Harbert had stationed himself in the bow, to point out the course to follow through the channels, when suddenly he cried:

"Luff, Pencroff, luff!"

"What's the matter?" answered the sailor, getting to his feet. "A rock?"

"No... wait," said Harbert. "I can't see well... luff a little more... good... bear off a bit..."

And as he said it Harbert, lying flat along the gunwale, plunged his arm quickly into the water and straightened up, saying:

"A bottle!"

He was holding a corked bottle in his hand, which he had just snatched from the water a few cable lengths from the coast.

Cyrus Smith took the bottle. Without saying a single word, he popped out the cork and drew out a damp piece of paper, on which these words could be read:

    Castaway... Tabor Island: 153° W. long. — 37° 11′ S. lat.

Chapter 13: Tabor Island

Departure decided — Hypotheses — Preparations — The three passengers — The first night — The second night — Tabor Island — Searching the beach — Searching the woods — Nobody — Animals — Plants — A dwelling — Deserted

"A castaway!" cried Pencroff. "Marooned a few hundred miles from us, on this Tabor Island! Ah, Mr. Cyrus, you won't stand in the way of my voyage now!"

"No, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith, "and you'll leave as soon as possible."

"Tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow."

The engineer was holding the paper he had pulled out of the bottle. He studied it for a few moments, then spoke again.

"From this document, my friends," he said, "and from the very way it's written, we can conclude two things right away.
