First, the castaway on Tabor Island is a man with a fairly advanced knowledge of seamanship, since he gives the island's latitude and longitude, and they agree with the ones we found, to within a single minute. Second, he's English or American, since the document is written in English."

"That's perfectly logical," answered Gédéon Spilett, "and the presence of this castaway explains how the chest came to wash up on our shores. There was a shipwreck, because there's a castaway. As for him, whoever he is, it's lucky for him that Pencroff had the idea of building this boat and trying her out today of all days. One day later, and this bottle might have smashed on the reefs."

"Yes," said Harbert, "it's a lucky chance that the Bonadventure passed that way just when the bottle was still floating!"

"And that doesn't strike you as odd?" Cyrus Smith asked Pencroff.

"It strikes me as lucky, that's all," answered the sailor. "Do you see anything extraordinary in it, Mr. Cyrus? That bottle had to end up somewhere, and why not here as well as anywhere else?"

"Perhaps you're right, Pencroff," answered the engineer, "and yet..."

"But," Harbert pointed out, "nothing proves that the bottle has been floating on the sea for a long time, does it?"

"Nothing," answered Gédéon Spilett, "and in fact the document looks as if it was written recently. What do you think, Cyrus?"

"That's hard to check, and anyway, we'll find out!" answered Cyrus Smith.

While they were talking, Pencroff had not been idle. He had put the boat about, and the Bonadventure, running on a broad reach with every sail drawing, was racing toward Claw Cape. Everyone was thinking about the castaway on Tabor Island. Was there still time to save him? It was a great event in the life of the colonists! They themselves were only castaways, but it was to be feared that another man had not been as fortunate as they had, and their duty was to hurry to the help of misfortune.

They rounded Claw Cape, and at about four o'clock the Bonadventure dropped anchor at the mouth of the Mercy.

That same evening the details of the new expedition were settled. It seemed best that Pencroff and Harbert, who both knew how to handle a boat, should make the voyage by themselves. If they left the next day, October 11, they could arrive sometime on the 13th, because with the wind that was blowing it would take no more than forty-eight hours to make the crossing of a hundred and fifty miles. Add one day on the island and three or four days to come back, and they could count on being home on Lincoln Island by the 17th. The weather was fine, the barometer was rising steadily, without any jumps, and the wind seemed well settled. Every chance, then, was on the side of these good men, whom a duty to their fellow man was about to carry far from their island.

So it had been agreed that Cyrus Smith, Nab and Gédéon Spilett would stay at Granite House. But a protest was raised. Gédéon Spilett, who had by no means forgotten his trade as a reporter for the New York Herald, declared that he would swim there rather than miss a chance like this, and so he was allowed to join the voyage.

The evening was spent carrying aboard the Bonadventure some bedding, utensils, weapons, ammunition, a compass, and provisions for about a week. The loading was quickly done, and the colonists went back up to Granite House.

The next morning at five o'clock they said their goodbyes, not without some emotion on both sides. Pencroff spread his sails to the wind and headed for Claw Cape, which he had to round before setting a direct course to the southwest.

The Bonadventure was already a quarter of a mile from the coast when her passengers saw two men on the heights of Granite House waving goodbye to them. It was Cyrus Smith and Nab.

"Our friends!" cried Gédéon Spilett. "This is our first separation in fifteen months!..."

Pencroff, the reporter and Harbert waved one last goodbye, and Granite House soon disappeared behind the high rocks of the cape.

For the first hours of the day the Bonadventure stayed in constant sight of the southern coast of Lincoln Island, which soon looked like nothing more than a green basket with Mount Franklin rising out of it. Distance had shrunk the heights, and from out here the island hardly looked like a place to tempt a ship in to land.

They passed Reptile End at about one o'clock, but ten miles out to sea. At that distance it was no longer possible to make out anything of the western coast, which stretched as far as the shoulders of Mount Franklin, and three hours later the whole of Lincoln Island had sunk below the horizon.

The Bonadventure behaved perfectly. She rose easily to the waves and made rapid headway. Pencroff had rigged his gaff topsail, and with every stitch of canvas set he held a dead straight course, checked by the compass.

From time to time Harbert took a turn at the helm, and the boy's hand was so steady that the sailor could not fault him for a single swerve off course.

Gédéon Spilett chatted with one and then the other, and lent a hand with the sails when needed. Captain Pencroff was entirely satisfied with his crew, and talked of nothing less than rewarding them with "a tot of wine every watch"!

In the evening the crescent moon, which would not reach its first quarter until the 16th, showed for a while in the twilight and soon went out. The night was dark but full of stars, and the next day promised to be fine again.

As a precaution, Pencroff took in the gaff topsail. He did not want to risk being caught by some sudden gust with canvas set at the masthead. It was perhaps too much caution for so calm a night, but Pencroff was a prudent seaman, and no one could have blamed him for it.

The reporter slept for part of the night. Pencroff and Harbert relieved each other at the helm every two hours. The sailor trusted Harbert as he trusted himself, and the boy's coolness and good sense justified that trust. Pencroff gave him the course the way a captain gives it to his helmsman, and Harbert did not let the Bonadventure stray from it by a hair.

The night passed well, and the day of October 12 went by under the same conditions. The southwesterly course was kept strictly all that day, and unless the Bonadventure was being carried along by some unknown current, she ought to make landfall right on Tabor Island.

As for the sea the boat was crossing, it was completely empty. Now and then some large bird, an albatross or a frigate bird, passed within gunshot, and Gédéon Spilett wondered whether it was to one of those powerful fliers that he had entrusted his last dispatch to the New York Herald. These birds were the only living things that seemed to visit this stretch of ocean between Tabor Island and Lincoln Island.

"And yet," Harbert remarked, "this is the time of year when the whalers usually head for the southern part of the Pacific. Honestly, I don't believe there's a lonelier sea than this one!"

"It's not as empty as all that!" answered Pencroff.

"What do you mean?" asked the reporter.

"Well, we're on it, aren't we! Do you take our boat for a piece of driftwood and the three of us for porpoises?"

And Pencroff laughed at his own joke.

By evening, going by dead reckoning, they could assume that the Bonadventure had covered a hundred and twenty miles since leaving Lincoln Island — that is, in thirty-six hours, which gave a speed of three and a third miles an hour. The breeze was light and dying down. Still, they could hope that at daybreak the next day, if the reckoning was right and the course had been true, they would sight Tabor Island.

So neither Gédéon Spilett, nor Harbert, nor Pencroff slept that night of October 12 to 13. Waiting for the morning, they could not help feeling deeply stirred. There were so many uncertainties in the venture they had undertaken! Were they near Tabor Island? Was the island still inhabited by the castaway they were coming to help? Who was this man? Wouldn't his arrival bring some trouble into their little colony, so united until now? And besides, would he agree to trade one prison for another? All these questions, which would surely be answered the next day, kept them awake, and at the first glimmer of dawn they turned their eyes to every point of the western horizon in turn.

"Land!" Pencroff shouted at about six o'clock in the morning.

And since it was unthinkable that Pencroff could be mistaken, it was obvious that land was there.

Imagine the joy of the Bonadventure's little crew! In a few hours they would be on the island's shore!

Tabor Island, a sort of low coast barely rising out of the waves, was no more than fifteen miles away. The Bonadventure's bow, which was pointing a little to the south of the island, was turned straight toward it, and as the sun climbed in the east, a few summits stood out here and there.

"It's only an islet, much less important than Lincoln Island," Harbert remarked, "and it was probably raised up from the sea floor, like ours."

At eleven in the morning the Bonadventure was only two miles off, and Pencroff, looking for a channel to bring her in, was moving forward only with extreme caution over these unknown waters.

By now they could take in the whole islet at a glance. Clumps of green gum trees stood out on it, along with a few other large trees of the same kinds that grew on Lincoln Island. But — a rather astonishing thing — not a wisp of smoke rose to show that the islet was inhabited, and not a signal could be seen anywhere along the shore!

And yet the document had been definite: there was a castaway, and that castaway should have been on the lookout!

Meanwhile the Bonadventure was threading her way through the rather tricky channels that the reefs left between them, and Pencroff watched every twist and turn of them with the closest attention. He had put Harbert at the helm and stationed himself in the bow, studying the water, ready to lower the sail, whose halyard he held in his hand. Gédéon Spilett swept the whole shoreline with the spyglass without seeing a thing.

At last, at about noon, the Bonadventure ran her stem up onto a sandy beach. The anchor was dropped, the sails lowered, and the little boat's crew went ashore.

And there was no doubt that this really was Tabor Island, since, according to the most recent charts, there was no other island in that part of the Pacific between New Zealand and the American coast.

The boat was moored securely, so that the ebbing tide could not carry her off. Then Pencroff and his two companions, well armed, went up the beach to reach a kind of cone, two hundred and fifty to three hundred feet high, that rose half a mile away.

"From the top of that hill," said Gédéon Spilett, "we should be able to get a general idea of the islet, and that will make our search easier."

"It's doing here," answered Harbert, "just what Mr. Cyrus did first thing on Lincoln Island, when he climbed Mount Franklin."

"Exactly," answered the reporter, "and it's the best way to go about it!"

Talking as they went, the explorers moved forward along the edge of a meadow that ran right up to the foot of the cone. Flocks of rock pigeons and terns, like the ones on Lincoln Island, flew up in front of them. In the woods that bordered the meadow on the left they heard brushwood rustling and glimpsed grass stirring, signs of very shy animals. But so far nothing showed that the islet was inhabited.

When they reached the foot of the cone, Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett climbed it in a few minutes and looked out to every point of the horizon.

They were indeed on an islet. It measured no more than six miles around, and its outline, with few capes or headlands jutting out and few coves or inlets cutting in, made a long oval. All around, the sea stretched to the edge of the sky, with nothing else at all. There was not a speck of land, not a sail in sight!

The islet was wooded all over, and it had none of the variety of Lincoln Island, which was barren and wild in one part and fertile and rich in the other. Here there was one even mass of green, with two or three low hills rising above it. A stream crossed the oval at a slant, flowing through a broad meadow and emptying into the sea on the western coast through a narrow mouth.

"It's a small estate," said Harbert.

"Yes," answered Pencroff, "it would have been a bit cramped for us!"

"And on top of that," answered the reporter, "it seems to be uninhabited."

"It does," answered Harbert. "Nothing here gives any sign of human beings."

"Let's go down," said Pencroff, "and look."

The sailor and his two companions went back to the shore, to the spot where they had left the Bonadventure. They had decided to go all the way around the islet on foot before venturing into the interior, so that not a single spot would escape their search.

The beach was easy to follow, and only in a few places was it cut by big rocks, which they could easily get around. The explorers headed south, scaring up large flocks of water birds and herds of seals, which threw themselves into the sea the moment they caught sight of the men, however far off.

"Those animals," the reporter pointed out, "aren't seeing human beings for the first time. They're afraid of them, so they know them."

An hour after setting out, the three of them had reached the southern tip of the islet, which ended in a sharp cape, and they turned north along the western coast. It was made of sand and rock as well, with thick woods behind.

Nowhere was there any trace of a dwelling, nowhere the print of a human foot, along the whole edge of the islet, which they had walked completely around after four hours.

It was extraordinary, to say the least, and they were bound to believe that Tabor Island was not inhabited, or was no longer. Perhaps, after all, the document was already several months or several years old, and in that case it was possible that the castaway had been taken home — or that he had died of hardship.

Pencroff, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert, trying out theories that were more or less likely, ate a quick dinner on board the Bonadventure, so that they could set off again and keep exploring until nightfall.

And so they did. At five in the afternoon they ventured into the woods.

Many animals fled at their approach — mainly, one could even say only, goats and pigs, which, as was easy to see, belonged to European breeds. No doubt some whaler had put them ashore on the island, where they had multiplied rapidly. Harbert promised himself that he would catch a pair or two alive to take back to Lincoln Island.

So there was no longer any doubt that men had visited this islet at some time or other. That became even clearer when, through the forest, they found trodden paths, tree trunks felled with an ax, and everywhere the mark of human work. But these trees, which were rotting away, had been cut down many years before. The ax cuts had grown a velvet of moss, and the grass grew long and thick across the paths, so that they were hard to make out.

"But," Gédéon Spilett pointed out, "that proves not only that men landed on this islet but that they lived on it for some time. Now, who were these men? How many of them were there? How many are left?"

"The document," said Harbert, "only mentions one castaway."

"Well, if he's still on the island," answered Pencroff, "there's no way we won't find him!"

So the exploration went on. The sailor and his companions naturally followed the path that cut diagonally across the islet, and so they came out beside the stream that ran down to the sea.

The animals of European stock and the bits of work done by human hands proved beyond question that people had come to this island before them. A number of specimens from the plant kingdom proved it no less. In some places, in the middle of clearings, it was plain that the ground had been planted with vegetables, probably quite a long time ago.

And what was Harbert's joy when he recognized potatoes, chicory, sorrel, carrots, cabbages and turnips! They had only to gather the seed to enrich the soil of Lincoln Island.

"Good! Fine!" answered Pencroff. "That'll suit Nab nicely, and us too. So even if we don't find the castaway, at least our voyage won't have been wasted, and God will have rewarded us!"

"No doubt," answered Gédéon Spilett. "But to judge by the state these plantings are in, I'm afraid the islet hasn't been inhabited for a long time."

"Yes," answered Harbert. "Anyone living here, whoever it was, would never have neglected such an important crop!"

"Right!" said Pencroff. "This castaway has gone!... That's what we have to suppose..."

"Then we have to accept that the document is already old?"

"Obviously."

"And that the bottle only reached Lincoln Island after floating on the sea for a long time?"

"Why not?" answered Pencroff. "But here comes the night," he added, "and I think we'd better stop searching for now."

"Let's go back on board, and we'll start again tomorrow," said the reporter.

That was the wisest course, and they were about to take it when Harbert pointed to a dark shapeless mass among the trees and cried:

"A house!"

At once all three of them made for the dwelling he had pointed out. In the last light of dusk they could see that it had been built of planks covered with thick tarred canvas.

The door was half shut. Pencroff pushed it open and strode quickly inside...

The house was empty!

Chapter 14: A Fire Lit in Time

An inventory — The night — A few letters — The search goes on — Plants and animals — Harbert in great danger — On board — Departure — Bad weather — A flash of instinct — Lost at sea — A fire lit in time

Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett had stood there silent in the darkness.

Pencroff called out in a loud voice.

No answer came.

So the sailor struck his flint and steel and lit a twig. For a moment its light showed a small room that seemed to be entirely deserted. At the far end was a rough fireplace holding a few cold ashes and an armful of dry wood. Pencroff tossed the burning twig onto it; the wood crackled and threw out a bright glow.

Now the sailor and his two companions could make out an unmade bed whose blankets, damp and yellowed, proved that it had not been slept in for a long time; in one corner of the fireplace, two kettles covered with rust and an overturned cooking pot; a cupboard with a few half-moldy sailor's clothes in it; on the table, a pewter plate and fork and a Bible eaten away by damp; in a corner, some tools — a shovel, a mattock, a pickax — and two hunting guns, one of them broken; on a plank that served as a shelf, a keg of gunpowder still untouched, a keg of shot and several boxes of percussion caps. And all of it lay under a thick coat of dust that had perhaps been gathering for many long years.

"There's nobody here," said the reporter.

"Nobody!" answered Pencroff.

"Nobody has lived in this room for a long time," Harbert observed.

"Yes, a very long time!" answered the reporter.

"Mr. Spilett," Pencroff said then, "instead of going back on board, I think we'd do better to spend the night in this house."

"You're right, Pencroff," answered Gédéon Spilett, "and if the owner comes back — well! Maybe he won't mind finding the place taken!"

"He won't come back!" said the sailor, shaking his head.

"You think he's left the island?" asked the reporter.

"If he'd left the island, he'd have taken his weapons and his tools with him," answered Pencroff. "You know what castaways think those things are worth — they're the last scraps saved from the wreck. No! No!" the sailor repeated, in a voice full of conviction. "No! He hasn't left the island! If he'd escaped in a boat he built himself, he'd have been even less likely to leave behind things he couldn't live without! No — he's on the island!"

"Alive?..." asked Harbert.

"Alive or dead. But if he's dead, I don't suppose he buried himself," answered Pencroff, "so at the very least we'll find his remains!"

So it was agreed that they would spend the night in the abandoned house, and a supply of wood stacked in one corner would keep it warm enough. With the door shut, Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett sat on a bench and stayed there, talking little but thinking a great deal. They were in a frame of mind to imagine anything and to expect anything, and they listened eagerly to every sound outside. If the door had suddenly opened and a man had stood before them, they would not have been very much surprised, in spite of everything about the place that spoke of long abandonment. Their hands were ready to clasp the hands of that man, that castaway, that unknown friend whom friends had come to find!

But no sound was heard, the door did not open, and the hours went by.

How long that night seemed to the sailor and his two companions! Only Harbert slept, for two hours, because at his age sleep is a necessity. All three of them were impatient to take up the previous day's exploration again and to search the islet down to its most hidden corners! Pencroff's conclusions were perfectly sound. Since the house was abandoned, and since the tools, the utensils and the weapons were still in it, it was almost certain that the man who had lived there had died. The right thing to do, then, was to look for his remains and at least give them a Christian burial.

Day came. Pencroff and his companions set about examining the house at once.

It had been built, truly, in a well-chosen spot, on the back slope of a little hill sheltered by five or six magnificent gum trees. In front of it, an ax had cleared a wide opening through the trees, so that the eye could travel out over the sea. A small lawn, surrounded by a wooden fence that was falling to pieces, led down to the shore, and on the left of it the mouth of the stream opened into the sea.

The house had been built of planks, and it was easy to see that those planks had come from the hull or the deck of a ship. So it was likely that a disabled vessel had been driven ashore on the island, that at least one man of her crew had been saved, and that this man, having tools at hand, had used the wreckage of the ship to build himself this dwelling.

That became plainer still when Gédéon Spilett, after walking all the way around the house, noticed on one of the planks — probably one of those that had formed the bulwarks of the wrecked ship — these letters, already half worn away:

    BR..TAN.A

"Britannia!" cried Pencroff, whom the reporter had called over. "That's a name plenty of ships have had, and I couldn't tell you whether this one was English or American!"

"It doesn't matter, Pencroff!"

"No, it doesn't matter," answered the sailor, "and the survivor of her crew, if he's still alive — we'll save him, whatever country he belongs to! But before we start exploring again, let's go back to the Bonadventure first!"

A kind of uneasiness about his boat had come over Pencroff. Suppose the islet was inhabited after all, and some inhabitant had taken possession of her... But he shrugged his shoulders at so unlikely an idea.

Still, the sailor was not sorry to go and have breakfast on board. The way was already marked out, and it was not long — barely a mile. So they set off again, searching the woods and thickets with their eyes as they went, while goats and pigs ran off through them by the hundreds.

Twenty minutes after leaving the house, Pencroff and his companions were back in sight of the eastern coast of the island and of the Bonadventure, held by her anchor, which had bitten deep into the sand.

Pencroff could not hold back a sigh of satisfaction. After all, that boat was his child, and it is a father's right to worry more often than he has reason to.

They went back on board and ate breakfast — a big enough one that they would not need dinner until very late. Then, the meal finished, the exploration began again and was carried out with the most painstaking care.

All things considered, it was very likely that the islet's one inhabitant had died. So it was a dead man, rather than a living one, whose traces Pencroff and his companions were trying to find! But their search was in vain. For half the day they combed the clumps of trees that covered the islet and found nothing. They had to admit at last that if the castaway was dead, no trace of his body was left now, and that some wild animal had no doubt devoured it down to the last bone.

"We'll leave tomorrow at daybreak," Pencroff said to his two companions. Around two o'clock in the afternoon the three of them had lain down in the shade of a clump of pines to rest for a few minutes.

"I think we can take the castaway's things with us without any qualms, can't we?" Harbert added.

"I think so too," answered Gédéon Spilett, "and these weapons and tools will round out the equipment of Granite House. Unless I'm mistaken, that's a sizable supply of powder and shot."

"Yes," answered Pencroff, "but let's not forget to catch a pair or two of these pigs. Lincoln Island hasn't got any..."

"Or to gather those seeds," Harbert added. "They'll give us every vegetable of the Old World and the New."

"Then perhaps it would be wise," said the reporter, "to stay one more day on Tabor Island, so we can collect everything that might be of use to us."

"No, Mr. Spilett," answered Pencroff, "and I'll ask you to leave first thing tomorrow, at daybreak. The wind looks to me as if it means to shift into the west, and after having a fair wind to come here, we'll have a fair wind to go home."

"Then let's not waste any time!" said Harbert, getting to his feet.

"Let's not waste any time," answered Pencroff. "You, Harbert, see to gathering those seeds — you know them better than we do. Meanwhile Mr. Spilett and I will go hunting the pigs, and even without Top, I'm pretty sure we'll manage to catch a few!"

So Harbert took the path that would lead him back toward the cultivated part of the islet, while the sailor and the reporter went straight into the forest.

A good many specimens of the pig family fled before them, and these remarkably nimble animals did not seem in any mood to let themselves be approached. Still, after half an hour's chase, the hunters had managed to seize a pair that had gone to ground in a dense thicket — when shouts rang out a few hundred paces to the north of the islet. Mixed with the shouts came horrible hoarse roars that had nothing human about them.

Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett straightened up, and the pigs took advantage of the movement to escape, just as the sailor was getting his ropes ready to tie them.

"That's Harbert's voice!" said the reporter.

"Run!" cried Pencroff.

And at once the sailor and Gédéon Spilett raced as fast as their legs would carry them toward the place the shouts were coming from.

They were right to hurry. At a turn in the path, near a clearing, they saw the boy thrown to the ground by a wild creature — a gigantic ape, no doubt — that was about to do him serious harm.

To hurl themselves on this monster, throw it down in its turn, tear Harbert away from it and then pin it firmly — for Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett it was the work of a moment. The sailor had the strength of a Hercules, and the reporter was very powerful too. In spite of the monster's struggles, it was tied up so securely that it could not make a single movement.

"You're not hurt, Harbert?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"No! No!"

"Oh! If that ape had hurt you!..." cried Pencroff.

"But it isn't an ape!" answered Harbert.

At these words, Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett took a good look at the strange being lying on the ground.

Truly, it was no ape! It was a human creature — it was a man! But what a man! A wild man, in all the horror of the word, and all the more appalling because he seemed to have sunk to the very lowest depth of brutishness!

Bristling hair; an untrimmed beard hanging down to his chest; a body almost naked except for a rag of blanket around his loins; fierce eyes; enormous hands with immensely long nails; skin as dark as mahogany; feet so hardened they might have been made of horn — such was the wretched creature that, in spite of everything, they had to call a man! Yet one really had the right to wonder whether there was still a soul in that body, or whether nothing but the crude instinct of the brute had survived in him!

"Are you quite sure that's a man, or that it ever was one?" Pencroff asked the reporter.

"Sadly, there's no doubt of it," the reporter answered.

"Then could he be the castaway?" said Harbert.

"Yes," answered Gédéon Spilett, "but the poor wretch has nothing human left in him!"

The reporter was right. It was clear that if the castaway had ever been a civilized being, solitude had turned him into a wild man — and worse, perhaps, into a true man of the woods. Hoarse sounds came from his throat, through teeth as sharp as a meat-eater's, made now for grinding nothing but raw flesh. His memory must have deserted him long ago, no doubt, and for a long time too he had no longer known how to use his tools or his weapons. He no longer knew how to make a fire! It could be seen that he was quick and supple, but that all his physical powers had developed at the expense of his mind and his moral nature!

Gédéon Spilett spoke to him. He did not seem to understand, or even to hear... And yet, looking him straight in the eyes, the reporter thought he could see that his reason was not entirely extinguished.

Meanwhile the prisoner was not struggling, and he made no attempt to break his bonds. Was he crushed by the presence of these men who had once been his own kind? Had he found, in some corner of his brain, a fleeting memory that was drawing him back toward humanity? If he had been set free, would he have tried to run away, or would he have stayed? No one knows — they did not put it to the test. And after studying the wretched man with the closest attention, Gédéon Spilett spoke.

"Whoever he is," he said, "whoever he was and whatever he may become, it's our duty to take him back with us to Lincoln Island!"

"Yes! Yes!" answered Harbert. "And maybe, with care, we can wake some spark of intelligence in him again!"

"The soul doesn't die," said the reporter, "and it would be a great thing to rescue this creature of God from the brute he's become!"

Pencroff shook his head doubtfully.

"We have to try, at any rate," the reporter answered him. "Our humanity demands it."

It was indeed their duty as civilized beings and as Christians. All three of them understood it, and they knew very well that Cyrus Smith would approve of what they had done.

"Do we leave him tied up?" asked the sailor.

"Maybe he'd walk if we untied his feet?" said Harbert.

"Let's try," answered Pencroff.

The ropes that hobbled the prisoner's feet were undone, but his arms stayed tightly bound. He stood up by himself and showed no sign of wanting to run away. His dry eyes darted sharp looks at the three men walking beside him, and nothing suggested that he remembered being one of their kind, or at least having once been one. A continuous hissing came from his lips, and he looked fierce, but he made no attempt to resist.

On the reporter's advice, the unfortunate man was taken back to his house. Perhaps the sight of the things that had belonged to him would make some impression on him! Perhaps a single spark would be enough to rekindle his darkened mind, to relight his extinguished soul!

The house was not far away. In a few minutes they had all reached it. But there the prisoner recognized nothing, and he seemed to have lost all awareness of everything!

What could they conclude from the depth of brutishness this miserable being had fallen to, except that his imprisonment on the islet must go back a long way, and that he had come there in his right mind, and solitude had reduced him to this state?

Then the reporter had the idea that the sight of fire might have some effect on him. In an instant one of those fine bright blazes that draw even animals to them lit up the hearth.

At first the sight of the flames seemed to hold the poor man's attention. But soon he drew back, and the light died out of his blank gaze.

Clearly there was nothing to be done, for the moment at least, except take him on board the Bonadventure. That was done, and there he stayed, under Pencroff's guard.

Harbert and Gédéon Spilett went back onto the islet to finish their work, and a few hours later they returned to the shore carrying the utensils and the weapons, a harvest of vegetable seeds, a few head of game and two pairs of pigs. Everything was loaded aboard, and the Bonadventure stood ready to weigh anchor as soon as the next morning's tide began to run.

The prisoner had been put in the forward cabin, where he stayed calm and silent, deaf and dumb at once.

Pencroff offered him something to eat, but he pushed away the cooked meat they held out to him, which no doubt no longer suited him. And sure enough, when the sailor showed him one of the ducks Harbert had shot, he threw himself on it with the greed of an animal and devoured it.

"You think he'll come back from this?" said Pencroff, shaking his head.

"Maybe," answered the reporter. "It isn't impossible that our care will end up having some effect on him, because it was solitude that made him what he is, and from now on he'll never be alone again!"

"The poor man must have been like this for a long time!" said Harbert.

"Maybe," answered Gédéon Spilett.

"How old could he be?" asked the boy.

"That's hard to say," answered the reporter, "because you can't see his features under that thick beard covering his face. But he isn't young anymore, and I'd guess he must be at least fifty."

"Did you notice, Mr. Spilett, how deeply his eyes are sunk under his brows?" asked the boy.

"Yes, Harbert, but I'd add that they're more human than you'd be tempted to believe from the look of the rest of him."

"Well, we'll see," answered Pencroff, "and I'm curious to hear what Mr. Smith makes of our wild man. We went looking for a human being, and it's a monster we're bringing back! Well, you do what you can!"

The night went by. Whether the prisoner slept or not, no one knows, but in any case, although he had been untied, he did not stir. He was like those wild animals that are stunned by the first hours of captivity, and whose rage comes back to them later.

At daybreak the next day — October 15 — the change of weather Pencroff had foreseen had come. The wind had backed into the northwest, and it favored the Bonadventure's return. But at the same time it was freshening, and that was bound to make the sailing harder.

At five o'clock in the morning the anchor was weighed. Pencroff took a reef in his mainsail and set his course east-northeast, so as to head straight for Lincoln Island.

The first day of the crossing passed without incident. The prisoner had stayed quiet in the forward cabin, and since he had once been a sailor, the motion of the sea seemed to have a kind of healthy effect on him. Was some memory of his old trade coming back to him, then? In any case, he kept still, more astonished than downcast.

The next day — October 16 — the wind freshened a great deal and swung still farther toward the north, which meant it blew from a direction less favorable to the Bonadventure, which went leaping over the waves. Pencroff soon found himself sailing close-hauled, and without saying anything about it he began to grow uneasy at the state of the sea, which was breaking violently over his boat's bow. Certainly, if the wind did not change, it would take him longer to reach Lincoln Island than it had taken to get to Tabor Island.

And in fact, by the morning of the 17th, the Bonadventure had been under way for forty-eight hours, and there was nothing to show that she was anywhere near the island. Besides, it was impossible to work out the distance they had covered by dead reckoning, since both her heading and her speed had been far too irregular.

Twenty-four hours later there was still no land in sight. By then the wind was blowing dead against them and the sea was atrocious. They had to work the boat's sails quickly, for the seas were breaking clean over her; they had to take in reefs and keep changing tack, beating to windward in short runs. It even happened, during the day of the 18th, that the Bonadventure was completely buried by a wave, and if her passengers had not taken the precaution beforehand of lashing themselves to the deck, they would have been swept away.

On that occasion Pencroff and his companions, hard at work clearing the boat, received help they had never expected — from the prisoner. He sprang up through the hatch as if his sailor's instinct had taken over, and with a mighty blow of a spar he smashed through the bulwarks so that the water filling the deck could drain away faster. Then, once the boat was clear, he went back down to his cabin without having said a single word.

Pencroff, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert, utterly astounded, had let him do it.

Still, their situation was bad, and the sailor had reason to believe he was lost on that immense sea, with no chance of finding his way again!

The night of the 18th to the 19th was dark and cold. Around eleven o'clock, however, the wind died down, the swell dropped, and the Bonadventure, tossed about less, picked up speed. She had, in any case, behaved wonderfully in the heavy sea.

Neither Pencroff nor Gédéon Spilett nor Harbert thought of taking even an hour's sleep. They kept watch with the utmost care, for one of two things was true: either Lincoln Island could not be far off, and they would sight it at daybreak, or else the Bonadventure had been carried off by currents and had drifted to leeward, and then it would be almost impossible to correct her course.

Pencroff, worried to the last degree, still did not despair, for his spirit was made of well-tempered stuff. Sitting at the tiller, he stubbornly tried to pierce the thick darkness that surrounded him.

Around two o'clock in the morning, he suddenly stood up.

"A fire! A fire!" he shouted.

And sure enough, a bright light had appeared twenty miles to the northeast. Lincoln Island was there, and that light, plainly lit by Cyrus Smith, was showing them the way.

Pencroff, who had been steering much too far to the north, changed course and headed for the fire, which shone above the horizon like a star of the first magnitude.

Chapter 15: A Few Tears

The return — Discussion — Cyrus Smith and the stranger — Balloon Harbor — The third harvest — A windmill — The first flour and the first bread — The engineer's devotion — A moving experiment — A few tears fall

The next day, October 20, at seven o'clock in the morning, after four days at sea, the Bonadventure ran gently aground on the beach at the mouth of the Mercy.

Cyrus Smith and Nab had grown very uneasy over the bad weather and their companions' long absence. They had climbed up to Prospect Plateau at first light, and at last they had sighted the boat that had taken so long to come back!

"Thank God! There they are!" Cyrus Smith had cried.

As for Nab, he had started dancing for joy, spinning round and round, clapping his hands and shouting, "Oh, my master!" — a pantomime more touching than the finest speech!

The engineer's first thought, as he counted the people he could see on the Bonadventure's deck, had been that Pencroff had not found the castaway of Tabor Island — or at least that the poor man had refused to leave his island and trade one prison for another.

And in fact Pencroff, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert were alone on the Bonadventure's deck.

When the boat came in, the engineer and Nab were waiting for her on the shore, and before the passengers had even jumped down onto the sand, Cyrus Smith was saying to them:

"We've been very worried that you were so late, my friends! Did something go wrong?"

"No," replied Gédéon Spilett. "Quite the opposite — everything went wonderfully. We'll tell you all about it."

"All the same," the engineer went on, "your search failed, since there are only three of you, just as when you left?"

"Beg your pardon, Mr. Cyrus," replied the sailor. "There are four of us!"

"You found the castaway?"

"Yes."

"And you brought him back?"

"Yes."

"Alive?"

"Yes."

"Where is he? Who is he?"

"He is," answered the reporter, "or rather he was, a man! That's all we can tell you, Cyrus!"

The engineer was told at once what had happened on the voyage. They described how the search had been carried out; how the islet's one dwelling had been abandoned long ago; and finally how they had captured a castaway who no longer seemed to belong to the human race.

"It's got to the point," Pencroff added, "where I don't know if we did right to bring him here."

"Of course you did right, Pencroff!" the engineer answered quickly.

"But the poor wretch has lost his reason, hasn't he?"

"Now, perhaps," replied Cyrus Smith. "But only a few months ago this unhappy man was a man like you and me. And who knows what would become of the last one of us left alive, after a long solitude on this island? Woe to the man who is alone, my friends! Isolation must destroy the reason quickly indeed, since you found the poor creature in such a state!"

"But, Mr. Cyrus," asked Harbert, "what makes you think the poor man has only sunk this low in the last few months?"

"Because the document we found had been written recently," answered the engineer, "and no one but the castaway could have written it."

"Unless," Gédéon Spilett pointed out, "it was written by a companion of his who has since died."

"That's impossible, my dear Spilett."

"Why?" asked the reporter.

"Because the document would have spoken of two castaways," replied Cyrus Smith, "and it speaks of only one."

Harbert told the story of the crossing in a few words, and he dwelt on one curious fact: the passing sort of resurrection that had taken place in the prisoner's mind when, for a moment, at the height of the storm, he had become a sailor again.

"Good, Harbert," replied the engineer. "You're right to attach great importance to that. This unfortunate man can't be incurable. It's despair that has made him what he is. But here he'll find his fellow men again, and since there's still a soul in him, we'll save that soul!"

So the castaway of Tabor Island was brought out of the cabin he occupied in the Bonadventure's bow, to the engineer's deep pity and Nab's great astonishment. The moment he was set ashore, he showed every intention of running away.

But Cyrus Smith came up to him and laid a hand on his shoulder with a gesture full of authority, and looked at him with infinite gentleness. At once the wretched man fell under a kind of instant spell. Little by little he grew calm; his eyes dropped, his head bowed, and he put up no more resistance.

"Poor marooned soul!" murmured the engineer.

Cyrus Smith had studied him closely. To judge by appearances, there was nothing human left in this miserable being. And yet Cyrus Smith, as the reporter had done before him, caught in his look something like an elusive glimmer of intelligence.

It was decided that the marooned man — or rather the stranger, for that was what his new companions called him from then on — would stay in one of the rooms of Granite House. He could not escape from there in any case. He let himself be led to it without any trouble, and with good care to help, they could perhaps hope that one day he would make one more companion for the colonists of Lincoln Island.

During lunch, which Nab had hurried along — the reporter, Harbert and Pencroff were dying of hunger — Cyrus Smith had them tell him in detail about everything that had happened on the voyage of exploration to the islet. He agreed with his friends that the stranger must be English or American. The name Britannia suggested as much, and besides, through that unkempt beard, under the thicket that served him for hair, the engineer believed he had made out the distinctive features of an Anglo-Saxon.

"But come to think of it," said Gédéon Spilett, turning to Harbert, "you never told us how you ran into this wild man. All we know is that he'd have strangled you if we hadn't had the luck to get there in time to help you!"

"Honestly," answered Harbert, "I'd be hard put to say what happened. I think I was busy gathering my plants when I heard a noise like an avalanche coming down out of a very tall tree. I barely had time to turn around... This poor man, who must have been crouching up in a tree, threw himself on me in less time than it takes me to tell you, and if it hadn't been for Mr. Spilett and Pencroff..."

"My boy!" said Cyrus Smith. "You ran a real risk there. But perhaps without it the poor creature would always have slipped away from your search, and we wouldn't have one more companion."

"So you hope to make a man of him again, Cyrus?" asked the reporter.

"Yes," replied the engineer.

When lunch was over, Cyrus Smith and his companions left Granite House and went back down to the beach. Then they unloaded the Bonadventure. The engineer examined the weapons and the tools, but he saw nothing that might allow him to establish the stranger's identity.

The pigs captured on the islet were judged likely to be a great asset to Lincoln Island, and they were taken to the sties, where they would surely settle in easily.

The two kegs of powder and shot, and the packets of percussion caps, were very well received. They even agreed to set up a small powder magazine, either outside Granite House or else in the upper cave, where there was no explosion to fear. All the same, they would go on using guncotton. It gave excellent results, so there was no reason to replace it with ordinary gunpowder.

When the boat had been unloaded:

"Mr. Cyrus," said Pencroff, "I think it would be wise to put our Bonadventure somewhere safe."

"Isn't she properly placed at the mouth of the Mercy?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"No, Mr. Cyrus," replied the sailor. "Half the time she's aground on the sand, and that strains her. She's a good boat, you see, and she behaved beautifully in that gale that hit us so hard on the way back."

"Couldn't we keep her afloat in the river itself?"

"We could, Mr. Cyrus, no doubt about it. But the river mouth gives her no shelter at all, and in an east wind I think the Bonadventure would take a terrible beating from the seas."

"Well, then, where do you want to put her, Pencroff?"

"At Balloon Harbor," replied the sailor. "That little cove, sheltered by the rocks, looks to me like just the harbor she needs."

"Isn't it a bit far?"

"Bah! It's not more than three miles from Granite House, and we've got a fine straight road to take us there!"

"Go ahead, Pencroff, and take your Bonadventure there," replied the engineer. "Still, I'd rather have her where we can keep a closer eye on her. When we have the time, we'll have to build her a little harbor of her own."

"Splendid!" cried Pencroff. "A harbor with a lighthouse, a breakwater and a dry dock! Honestly, Mr. Cyrus, with you everything's too easy!"

"Yes, my good Pencroff," replied the engineer, "but only on condition that you help me — because you do a good three-quarters of all our work!"

So Harbert and the sailor went back aboard the Bonadventure. The anchor was weighed, the sail hoisted, and the sea breeze carried her swiftly to Claw Cape. Two hours later she was riding on the calm waters of Balloon Harbor.

In the first days the stranger spent at Granite House, had he already given any reason to think that his wild nature had changed? Was a brighter light shining in the depths of that darkened mind? Was the soul, in short, coming back into the body? Yes, beyond any doubt — so much so that Cyrus Smith and the reporter wondered whether the poor man's reason had ever been completely snuffed out.

At first, used as he was to the open air and to the boundless freedom he had enjoyed on Tabor Island, the stranger had shown some fits of sullen rage, and they had to fear that he might hurl himself down onto the beach through one of the windows of Granite House. But little by little he calmed down, and they were able to leave him free to move about as he liked.

So there was reason to hope, and to hope a great deal. Already the stranger was forgetting the instincts of a beast of prey. He accepted food less brutish than what he had gorged himself on at the islet, and cooked meat no longer filled him with the disgust he had shown aboard the Bonadventure.

Cyrus Smith had taken advantage of a moment when he was asleep to cut his unkempt hair and beard, which had formed a kind of mane and given him such a wild look. He had also dressed him more decently, after taking away the scrap of cloth that had covered him. Thanks to this care, the stranger took on a human face again, and it even seemed that his eyes had grown gentler. Surely, when intelligence once lit it, this man's face must have had a sort of handsomeness.

Every day, Cyrus Smith made it his duty to spend a few hours in his company. He would come and work near him, busying himself with one thing and another, so as to catch his attention. A single flash, after all, might be enough to rekindle that soul; a single memory crossing that brain might be enough to call his reason back. They had seen it happen during the storm aboard the Bonadventure!

The engineer also made a point of talking out loud, so as to reach the depths of that numbed intelligence through the ears and the eyes at the same time. Sometimes one of his companions joined him, sometimes another, sometimes all of them. Most often they talked about things to do with the sea, which ought to move a sailor more than anything. At moments the stranger seemed to pay a vague kind of attention to what was being said, and the colonists soon became convinced that he partly understood them. Sometimes, even, his face wore an expression of deep pain — proof that he was suffering inside, for his features could not have been so misleading as that. But he did not speak, though more than once they might have thought a few words were about to escape his lips.

Be that as it may, the poor man was calm and sad! But was his calm only on the surface? Was his sadness only the result of being shut in? Nothing could be said for certain yet. He now saw only certain things, within a narrow field; he was constantly in contact with the colonists, and he was bound to grow used to them in the end; he had no desire left unsatisfied; he was better fed and better clothed. It was only natural that his physical nature should change little by little. But had a new life really entered into him? Or — to use a word that could fairly be applied to him — had he only been tamed, the way an animal is tamed by its master? That was an important question, and Cyrus Smith was eager to settle it. Yet he did not want to rush his patient! For to him the stranger was simply a patient! Would he ever be a convalescent?

And so how closely the engineer watched him, every moment! How he lay in wait for his soul, if one may put it that way! How ready he was to seize it!

The colonists followed every stage of the cure Cyrus Smith had undertaken with sincere emotion. They helped him, too, in this work of humanity, and all of them — except perhaps the doubting Pencroff — soon came to share his hope and his faith.

The stranger's calm was deep, as has been said, and he showed a kind of attachment to the engineer, whose influence he plainly felt. So Cyrus Smith decided to put him to the test by taking him into different surroundings: before the ocean his eyes had once been used to gazing on, at the edge of forests that must remind him of the ones where so many years of his life had been spent!

"But," said Gédéon Spilett, "can we hope that once he's set free he won't run away?"

"It's an experiment we have to try," answered the engineer.

"Ha!" said Pencroff. "Once that fellow has open space in front of him and gets a whiff of the fresh air, he'll be off as fast as his legs will carry him!"

"I don't think so," replied Cyrus Smith.

"Let's try it," said Gédéon Spilett.

"Let's try it," replied the engineer.

That day was October 30, which meant the castaway of Tabor Island had been a prisoner in Granite House for nine days. It was warm, and a fine sun was beating down on the island.

Cyrus Smith and Pencroff went to the stranger's room. They found him lying near the window, gazing at the sky.

"Come, my friend," the engineer said to him.

The stranger got up at once. His eyes fixed on Cyrus Smith, and he followed him, while the sailor walked behind, not very confident about how the experiment would turn out.

When they reached the door, Cyrus Smith and Pencroff had him take his place in the elevator, while Nab, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett waited for them at the foot of Granite House. The basket went down, and in a few moments they were all together on the beach.

The colonists moved a little way off from the stranger, so as to leave him some freedom.

He took a few steps toward the sea, and his eyes shone with an extraordinary eagerness, but he made no attempt at all to escape. He was watching the little waves that broke against the islet and came in to die on the sand.

"That's still only the sea," Gédéon Spilett remarked, "and it may not make him want to run off!"

"Yes," replied Cyrus Smith. "We need to take him up to the plateau, to the edge of the forest. There the experiment will tell us more."

"Anyway, he can't get away," Nab pointed out, "since the bridges are raised."

"Oh!" said Pencroff. "As if a man like that would let a little stream like Glycerin Creek stand in his way! He'd be across it in no time — in a single jump, even!"

"We'll see," was all Cyrus Smith answered, and his eyes never left his patient's.

The stranger was then led toward the mouth of the Mercy, and they all climbed up the left bank of the river and reached Prospect Plateau.

When he came to the spot where the first fine trees of the forest grew, their leaves stirring lightly in the breeze, the stranger seemed to drink in, intoxicated, the deep fragrance that filled the air, and a long sigh broke from his chest!

The colonists stayed back, ready to hold him if he made a move to escape!

And in fact the poor creature was on the point of leaping into the creek that separated him from the forest. For an instant his legs tensed like a spring... But almost at once he drew back into himself, he half sank to the ground, and a large tear rolled from his eyes!

"Ah!" cried Cyrus Smith. "So you've become a man again, since you're weeping!"

Chapter 16: Twelve Years on the Islet

A mystery to clear up — The stranger's first words — Twelve years on the islet! — Confessions that slip out — The disappearance — Cyrus Smith's confidence — Building a mill — The first bread — An act of devotion — Honest hands!

Yes! The poor wretch had wept! Some memory, no doubt, had passed through his mind, and, as Cyrus Smith put it, he had become a man again through his tears.

The colonists left him on the plateau for a while, and even moved a little way off, so that he would feel free. But he gave no thought at all to taking advantage of that freedom, and Cyrus Smith soon decided to bring him back to Granite House.

Two days after this scene, the stranger seemed to want to join little by little in the life they all shared. It was obvious that he heard and that he understood, but no less obvious that he was strangely stubborn about not speaking to the colonists. For one evening Pencroff, listening at the door of his room, heard these words escape his lips:

"No! Here! Me! Never!"

The sailor reported the words to his companions.

"There's some painful mystery here!" said Cyrus Smith.

The stranger had begun to use the farm tools, and he was working in the vegetable garden. When he stopped work, which happened often, he would stay as if withdrawn into himself; but on the engineer's advice the others respected the solitude he seemed to want to keep. If one of the colonists came near him, he drew back, and sobs heaved his chest, as if it were too full!

Was it remorse, then, that weighed on him so heavily? One might well think so, and one day Gédéon Spilett could not help making this remark:

"If he doesn't speak, I think it's because he would have things too serious to say!"

They had to be patient and wait.

A few days later, on November 3, the stranger was working on the plateau when he stopped and let his spade drop to the ground. Cyrus Smith, who was watching him from a short distance, saw tears running from his eyes once again. A kind of irresistible pity drew him over, and he touched the man's arm lightly.

"My friend?" he said.

The stranger's eyes tried to avoid his, and when Cyrus Smith tried to take his hand, he drew back sharply.

"My friend," said Cyrus Smith in a firmer voice, "look at me. I want you to!"

The stranger looked at the engineer and seemed to come under his power, like a mesmerized subject under the spell of his mesmerist. He wanted to run away. But then a kind of transformation came over his face. His eyes flashed like lightning. Words were struggling to break from his lips. He could not hold them back any longer!... At last he folded his arms, and then, in a hollow voice:

"Who are you?" he asked Cyrus Smith.

"Castaways like you," answered the engineer, who was deeply moved. "We've brought you here, among your fellow men."

"My fellow men!... I have none!"

"You're among friends..."

"Friends!... For me! Friends!" cried the stranger, hiding his head in his hands. "No... never... leave me alone! Leave me alone!"

Then he fled toward the side of the plateau that overlooked the sea, and there he stayed a long time without moving.

Cyrus Smith had rejoined his companions and was telling them what had just happened.

"Yes! There's a mystery in this man's life," said Gédéon Spilett, "and it seems the only road by which he has come back to humanity is remorse."

"I don't really know what kind of man we've brought back here," said the sailor. "He has secrets..."

"Which we'll respect," Cyrus Smith answered quickly. "If he has done some wrong, he has paid for it cruelly, and in our eyes he is forgiven."

For two hours the stranger stayed alone on the beach, plainly in the grip of memories that were bringing his whole past back to him — a dark past, no doubt — and the colonists, without letting him out of their sight, made no attempt to disturb his solitude.

After those two hours, however, he seemed to have come to a decision, and he came to find Cyrus Smith. His eyes were red from the tears he had shed, but he was no longer weeping. His whole face bore the mark of deep humility. He seemed fearful and ashamed, as though he were trying to make himself as small as possible, and his eyes stayed fixed on the ground.

"Sir," he said to Cyrus Smith, "you and your companions — are you English?"

"No," answered the engineer. "We're Americans."

"Ah!" said the stranger, and he murmured these words:

"I'd rather that!"

"And you, my friend?" asked the engineer.

"English," he answered hurriedly.

And as if those few words had cost him a great deal to say, he walked away from the shore and paced the beach from the waterfall to the mouth of the Mercy, in a state of extreme agitation.

Then, passing close to Harbert at one point, he stopped, and in a choked voice:

"What month?" he asked him.

"December," answered Harbert.

"What year?"

"1866."

"Twelve years! Twelve years!" he cried. Then he left the boy abruptly.

Harbert reported the questions and his answers to the colonists.

"That unhappy man," Gédéon Spilett observed, "had lost track of the months and the years!"

"Yes!" Harbert added. "And he had already been on the islet for twelve years when we found him there!"

"Twelve years!" answered Cyrus Smith. "Ah! Twelve years alone, after a life that was cursed, perhaps, could easily unsettle a man's reason!"

"I'm inclined to believe," Pencroff said then, "that this man didn't land on Tabor Island by shipwreck at all, but that he was left there as punishment for some crime."

"You must be right, Pencroff," replied the reporter, "and if that's so, it isn't impossible that the people who left him on the island will come back to fetch him one day!"

"And they won't find him anymore," said Harbert.

"But then," Pencroff went on, "we'd have to go back, and..."

"My friends," said Cyrus Smith, "let's not take up that question until we know where we stand. I believe this unhappy man has suffered, that he has paid hard for his wrongs, whatever they may be, and that the need to unburden himself is choking him. Let's not push him to tell us his story! He'll tell it to us, no doubt, and when we've heard it we'll see what course to take. Besides, only he can tell us whether he had something more than hope — whether he was certain of being taken home one day. But I doubt it!"

"And why?" asked the reporter.

"Because if he'd been sure of being rescued within a fixed time, he would have waited for the hour of his rescue and would not have thrown that document into the sea. No, it's more likely that he was condemned to die on that islet and was never to see his fellow men again!"

"But," the sailor observed, "there's one thing I can't explain."

"What's that?"

"If this man was abandoned on Tabor Island twelve years ago, we can easily suppose he'd already been for several years in the wild state we found him in!"

"That's likely," answered Cyrus Smith.

"So, as a consequence, it would be several years since he wrote that document!"

"No doubt... and yet the document looked as if it had been written recently!..."

"Besides, how can we believe that the bottle holding the document took several years to get from Tabor Island to Lincoln Island?"

"It isn't absolutely impossible," answered the reporter. "Couldn't it have been in the waters around the island for a long time already?"

"No," answered Pencroff, "because it was still floating. And we can't even suppose that after lying on the shore for some length of time it could have been carried off by the sea again, because it's all rocks along the south coast, and it would certainly have been smashed there!"

"That's true," answered Cyrus Smith, and he stood lost in thought.

"And then," the sailor added, "if the document was several years old, if it had been shut up in that bottle for several years, the damp would have spoiled it. But nothing of the kind — it was in a perfect state of preservation."

The sailor's observation was perfectly sound, and there was something incomprehensible here, for the document had seemed freshly written when the colonists found it in the bottle. What was more, it gave the position of Tabor Island precisely in latitude and longitude, and that implied that its author had a fairly thorough knowledge of hydrography — the science of charting the seas — which a simple sailor could not have had.

"Here again there is something inexplicable," said the engineer, "but let's not push our new companion to talk. When he wants to, my friends, we'll be ready to listen!"

During the days that followed, the stranger did not say a single word, and he did not once leave the bounds of the plateau. He worked the soil without losing an instant and without taking a moment's rest, but always apart from the others. At mealtimes he did not come up to Granite House, though he had been invited again and again, and he was content to eat a few raw vegetables. When night came he did not go back to the room that had been given to him, but stayed out there, under some clump of trees, or, when the weather was bad, huddled in some hollow in the rocks. He was still living, in other words, as he had in the days when the forests of Tabor Island were his only shelter. Since every effort to persuade him to change his way of life had failed, the colonists waited patiently. But the moment was finally coming when, driven by his conscience, irresistibly and almost against his will, he would let terrible confessions slip out.

On November 10, at about eight o'clock in the evening, just as darkness was beginning to fall, the stranger suddenly appeared in front of the colonists, who were gathered on the veranda. His eyes were shining strangely, and his whole person had taken on once more the wild look of the bad days.

Cyrus Smith and his companions were stunned to see that, in the grip of some terrible emotion, his teeth were chattering like a man in a fever. What was wrong with him? Was the sight of his fellow men unbearable to him? Had he had enough of this life among honest people? Was he homesick for his brutish state? They had to think so when they heard him pour out these broken sentences:

"Why am I here?... What right did you have to drag me away from my islet?... Can there be any bond between you and me?... Do you know who I am... what I've done... why I was out there... alone? And who told you I wasn't abandoned there... that I wasn't condemned to die there?... Do you know my past?... Do you know whether I haven't robbed, murdered... whether I'm not a wretch... a cursed creature... fit only to live like a wild beast... far from everyone... tell me... do you know?"

The colonists listened without interrupting the wretched man, from whom these half-confessions were escaping almost in spite of himself. Cyrus Smith tried to calm him by going up to him, but he drew back sharply.

"No! No!" he cried. "Just one word... Am I free?"

"You're free," answered the engineer.

"Then goodbye!" he cried, and he fled like a madman.

Nab, Pencroff and Harbert ran at once toward the edge of the woods... but they came back alone.

"We must let him go!" said Cyrus Smith.

"He'll never come back..." cried Pencroff.

"He'll come back," answered the engineer.

And many days went by after that; but Cyrus Smith — was it a kind of presentiment? — held stubbornly to the unshakable idea that the unhappy man would come back sooner or later.

"It's the last revolt of a rough nature," he would say, "one that remorse has touched, and that a new solitude would terrify."

Meanwhile work of every kind went on, both on Prospect Plateau and at the corral, where Cyrus Smith meant to build a farm. It goes without saying that the seeds Harbert had collected on Tabor Island had been carefully sown. The plateau was now one vast vegetable garden, well laid out and well tended, and it kept the colonists' arms busy. There was always work to do there. As the vegetables multiplied, the simple beds had had to be enlarged, and they were turning into real fields and taking the place of the meadows. But there was plenty of fodder in other parts of the island, and the onaggas need never fear being put on short rations. Besides, it was better to turn Prospect Plateau, defended by its deep belt of creeks, into a vegetable garden, and to move the meadows outside, since they had no need of protection against raids by the four-handed creatures and the four-footed ones.

On November 15 they brought in the third harvest. Here was a field that had grown in size in the eighteen months since the first grain of wheat was sown! The second crop, of six hundred thousand grains, yielded this time four thousand bushels — more than five hundred million grains! The colony was rich in wheat, for sowing ten bushels or so was enough to make sure of a harvest every year that would feed everyone, men and animals alike.

So the harvest was gathered in, and the last two weeks of November were given over to the work of breadmaking.

For they had the grain, but not the flour, and a mill had to be set up. Cyrus Smith could have used the second waterfall that poured down into the Mercy to drive his machinery, since the first was already busy working the hammers of the fulling mill. But after some discussion they decided to put up a simple windmill on the heights of Prospect Plateau. Building the one would be no harder than building the other, and they could be sure, besides, that there would be no lack of wind on that plateau, open as it was to the breezes off the sea.

"Not to mention," said Pencroff, "that a windmill will be more cheerful, and look fine in the landscape!"

So they set to work, choosing timber for the body of the mill and its machinery. Some big blocks of sandstone that lay at the north end of the lake could easily be made into millstones, and as for the sails, the inexhaustible envelope of the balloon would supply the canvas they needed.

Cyrus Smith drew up the plans, and they chose a site for the mill a little to the right of the poultry yard, near the lakeshore. The whole body of the mill was to rest on a pivot held in heavy timbers, so that it could turn, with all the machinery inside it, to face whichever way the wind asked.

The work went quickly. Nab and Pencroff had become very skillful carpenters and had only to follow the patterns the engineer gave them. And so a kind of cylindrical sentry box — a real pepper pot of a thing — topped with a pointed roof, soon rose on the chosen spot. The four frames that made up the sails had been firmly set into the windshaft — the main axle the sails turn — at a certain angle to it, and they were fastened with iron pins. As for the various parts of the machinery inside, they were made without any trouble: the casing to hold the two millstones, the stationary bedstone and the turning runner stone; the hopper, a sort of big square trough, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, which would let the grain fall onto the stones; the rocking spout that regulates the flow of grain, which its endless tick-tack has earned the nickname of "the chatterbox"; and finally the bolter, which sifts the flour and separates the bran from it. The tools were good, and the work was not very hard, for when all is said and done the working parts of a mill are very simple. It was only a question of time.

Everyone had worked on building the mill, and on December 1 it was finished.

As always, Pencroff was delighted with his work, and he had no doubt the machine was perfect.

"Now for a good wind," he said, "and we'll grind our first harvest in fine style!"

"A good wind, by all means," answered the engineer, "but not too much wind, Pencroff."

"Bah! Our mill will only turn the faster!"

"There's no need for it to turn so fast," replied Cyrus Smith. "We know from experience that a mill does the most work when the number of turns its sails make in a minute is six times the number of feet the wind travels in a second. With an average breeze, which moves twenty-four feet a second, the sails will make sixteen turns a minute, and that's all we need."

"Just right!" cried Harbert. "There's a nice breeze blowing from the northeast that will suit us perfectly!"

There was no reason to put off opening the mill, for the colonists were eager to taste the first piece of bread on Lincoln Island. So that very morning two or three bushels of wheat were ground, and the next day at breakfast a magnificent loaf — a little heavy, perhaps, though it had been raised with brewer's yeast — stood on the table at Granite House. Everyone bit into it with a will, and with what pleasure, you can easily imagine!

Still the stranger had not reappeared. Several times Gédéon Spilett and Harbert had searched the forest around Granite House without meeting him or finding any trace of him. They were seriously worried by this long disappearance. Certainly the former wild man of Tabor Island would have no trouble living in the Far West forests, so full of game. But wasn't there reason to fear that he would fall back into his old habits, and that this freedom would rekindle his wild instincts? Cyrus Smith, however, by some kind of presentiment no doubt, still kept saying that the runaway would come back.

"Yes, he'll come back!" he repeated, with a confidence his companions could not share. "When this unhappy man was on Tabor Island, he knew he was alone! Here, he knows his fellow men are waiting for him! Since he has half told us about his past life, this poor penitent, he'll come back to tell all of it, and on that day he'll be one of us!"

Events were about to prove Cyrus Smith right.

On December 3, Harbert had left Prospect Plateau and gone fishing on the southern shore of the lake. He was unarmed. Until then there had never been any need for precautions, since dangerous animals did not show themselves in that part of the island.

Meanwhile Pencroff and Nab were working in the poultry yard, while Cyrus Smith and the reporter were busy at the Chimneys making soda, since the supply of soap had run out.

Suddenly shouts ring out:

"Help! Help me!"

Cyrus Smith and the reporter were too far away to hear them. Pencroff and Nab, leaving the poultry yard in all haste, had rushed toward the lake.

But before them the stranger, whose presence in that place no one could have suspected, was crossing Glycerin Creek, which separated the plateau from the forest, and leaping onto the opposite bank.

There Harbert stood face to face with a formidable jaguar, like the one that had been killed at Reptile End. Taken completely by surprise, he was standing with his back against a tree, while the animal, crouched and gathered, was about to spring... But the stranger, with no weapon but a knife, hurled himself at the fearsome beast, which turned on this new adversary.

The fight was short. The stranger had tremendous strength and skill. He had seized the jaguar by the throat with a hand as powerful as a pair of shears, not caring whether the beast's claws dug into his flesh, and with the other hand he drove his knife into its heart.

The jaguar fell. The stranger pushed it aside with his foot and was about to run off just as the colonists arrived at the scene of the fight, when Harbert clung to him and cried:

"No! No! You won't go away!"

Cyrus Smith went toward the stranger, whose brows drew together as he saw him approach. Blood was running down his shoulder under his torn jacket, but he paid no attention to it.

"My friend," Cyrus Smith said to him, "we have just come into a debt of gratitude to you. You risked your life to save our boy!"

"My life!" murmured the stranger. "What's it worth? Less than nothing!"

"Are you hurt?"

"It doesn't matter."

"Will you give me your hand?"

And as Harbert tried to take hold of that hand, which had just saved him, the stranger folded his arms, his chest swelled, his eyes clouded over, and he seemed about to flee. But making a violent effort over himself, he said abruptly:

"Who are you? And what do you claim to be to me?"

It was the colonists' story that he was asking for in this way, and for the first time. Perhaps, once that story was told, he would tell his own?

In a few words Cyrus Smith told him everything that had happened since they left Richmond: how they had pulled through, and what resources they now had at their disposal.

The stranger listened with the closest attention.

Then the engineer told him who they all were — Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Pencroff, Nab, and himself — and he added that the greatest joy they had felt since they arrived on Lincoln Island was when they came back from the islet and could count one more companion among them.

At these words the man flushed, his head sank onto his chest, and his whole person showed how ashamed he was.

"And now that you know us," Cyrus Smith added, "will you give us your hand?"

"No," answered the stranger in a hollow voice. "No! You are honest men, you! And I!..."

Chapter 17: Abandoned on Tabor Island

Still keeping apart — The stranger's request — The farm set up at the corral — Twelve years ago! — The quartermaster of the Britannia — Abandoned on Tabor Island — Cyrus Smith's hand — The mysterious document

Those last words bore out what the colonists had sensed. There was some dark past in this unhappy man's life, atoned for perhaps in the eyes of men, but one his conscience had not yet absolved him of. In any case, the guilty man felt remorse, he repented, and his new friends would have shaken the hand they asked of him warmly — but he did not feel worthy to hold it out to honest people! Still, after the scene with the jaguar he did not go back to the forest, and from that day on he never again left the grounds of Granite House.

What was the mystery of this man's life? Would the stranger speak one day? Only the future would tell. In any case, they all agreed that his secret would never be asked of him, and that they would live with him as if they suspected nothing.

For some days, then, their life together went on as it had before. Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett worked side by side, chemists one day, physicists the next. The reporter left the engineer only to go hunting with Harbert, for it would not have been wise to let the boy roam the forest alone, and they had to stay on their guard. As for Nab and Pencroff — one day at the stables or the poultry yard, another at the corral, not to mention the work at Granite House — they were never short of things to do.

The stranger worked apart from the others. He had gone back to his usual way of living: he did not come to meals, he slept under the trees of the plateau, he never mixed with his companions. It really seemed as though the company of the men who had saved him was more than he could bear!

"But then," Pencroff would point out, "why did he ask other people for help? Why did he throw that document into the sea?"

"He'll tell us," Cyrus Smith always answered.

"When?"

"Sooner, perhaps, than you think, Pencroff."

And in fact the day of confession was near.

On December 10, a week after his return to Granite House, Cyrus Smith saw the stranger coming toward him. In a calm voice and a humble tone, the man said:

"Sir, I have something to ask of you."

"Go ahead," replied the engineer. "But first, let me ask you something."

At these words the stranger flushed and was on the point of turning away. Cyrus Smith understood what was going on in the guilty man's soul: no doubt he was afraid the engineer meant to question him about his past!

Cyrus Smith held him back with his hand.

"Comrade," he said, "we're not just your companions here. We're your friends. I wanted to tell you that. And now I'm listening."

The stranger passed his hand over his eyes. A kind of trembling had come over him, and for some moments he could not get a word out.

"Sir," he said at last, "I've come to ask you a favor."

"What is it?"

"Four or five miles from here, at the foot of the mountain, you have a corral for your livestock. Those animals need looking after. Will you let me live out there with them?"

For some moments Cyrus Smith looked at the unfortunate man with deep compassion. Then:

"My friend," he said, "the corral has nothing but stables, hardly fit for the animals..."

"It will be good enough for me, sir."

"My friend," Cyrus Smith went on, "we'll never stand in your way in anything. You'd like to live at the corral. Very well. You'll always be welcome at Granite House, of course. But since you want to live at the corral, we'll make the arrangements needed for you to be properly settled there."

"Any way at all, I'll be fine there."

"My friend," answered Cyrus Smith, who was leaning on that warm word on purpose, "you'll let us be the judges of what we ought to do about that!"

"Thank you, sir," the stranger answered, and he withdrew.

The engineer at once told his companions about the request that had been made to him, and they decided to build a wooden house at the corral and make it as comfortable as they could.

That very day the colonists went to the corral with the tools they would need, and before the week was out the house was ready to receive its occupant.
