It had been put up about twenty feet from the stables, and from there it would be easy to keep an eye on the flock of mouflons, which by then numbered more than eighty head. A few pieces of furniture were made — a bunk, a table, a bench, a cupboard, a chest — and weapons, ammunition and tools were carried out to the corral.

The stranger, for his part, had not gone to look at his new home. He had let the colonists work on it without him while he kept busy on the plateau, no doubt wanting to put the finishing touches to his own task. And in fact, thanks to him, all the fields had been plowed and were ready to be sown as soon as the time came.

The house at the corral was finished on December 20. The engineer told the stranger that his new home was ready for him, and the man replied that he would go and sleep there that very evening.

That evening the colonists were gathered in the great hall of Granite House. It was eight o'clock — the hour when their companion was to leave them. Not wanting to embarrass him by forcing on him, with their presence, a farewell that might have cost him dearly, they had left him alone and gone back up to Granite House.

They had been talking in the great hall for a few minutes when there came a light knock at the door. Almost at once the stranger came in, and without any preamble he said:

"Gentlemen, before I leave you, it's right that you should know my story. Here it is."

These simple words made a very deep impression on Cyrus Smith and his companions.

The engineer had risen to his feet.

"We ask nothing of you, my friend," he said. "It's your right to keep silent..."

"It's my duty to speak."

"Then sit down."

"I'll stay standing."

"We're ready to hear you," replied Cyrus Smith.

The stranger stood in a corner of the room, half sheltered by the shadows. He was bareheaded, his arms folded across his chest, and it was in that posture that, in a low, muffled voice, speaking like someone who is forcing himself to speak, he told the following story. His listeners did not interrupt him once.

"On December 20, 1854, a steam yacht, the Duncan, belonging to a Scottish laird, Lord Glenarvan, dropped anchor off Cape Bernouilli, on the west coast of Australia, at the latitude of the thirty-seventh parallel. On board the yacht were Lord Glenarvan, his wife, a major in the British army, a French geographer, a girl and a boy. These last two were the children of Captain Grant, whose ship, the Britannia, had been lost with all hands a year before. The Duncan was commanded by Captain John Mangles and manned by a crew of fifteen.

"This is why the yacht was off the coast of Australia at that time.

"Six months earlier, a bottle holding a document written in English, German and French had been found in the Irish Sea, picked up by the Duncan. The gist of the document was that there were still three survivors of the wreck of the Britannia — Captain Grant and two of his men — and that they had found refuge on a piece of land. The document gave its latitude, but the longitude had been washed out by the sea water and could no longer be read.

"That latitude was 37° 11′ south. So, with the longitude unknown, anyone who followed the thirty-seventh parallel across continents and seas was certain to reach the land where Captain Grant and his two companions were living.

"The British Admiralty hesitated to undertake the search, so Lord Glenarvan resolved to try everything to find the captain. Mary and Robert Grant had been put in touch with him. The Duncan was fitted out for a long voyage, and Lord Glenarvan's family and the captain's children wanted to take part in it. Leaving Glasgow, the Duncan headed into the Atlantic, rounded the Strait of Magellan, and sailed up the Pacific as far as Patagonia, where, by a first reading of the document, it could be supposed that Captain Grant was a prisoner of the native people.

"The Duncan landed her passengers on the west coast of Patagonia and sailed off to pick them up again on the east coast, at Cape Corrientes.

"Lord Glenarvan crossed Patagonia, following the thirty-seventh parallel, and, having found no trace of the captain, he took ship again on November 13 to carry on his search across the ocean.

"After visiting the islands of Tristan da Cunha and Amsterdam, which lay on his course, without success, the Duncan arrived, as I said, at Cape Bernouilli on the Australian coast on December 20, 1854.

"Lord Glenarvan meant to cross Australia as he had crossed America, and he went ashore. A few miles from the coast there was a farm belonging to an Irishman, who offered the travelers his hospitality. Lord Glenarvan told the Irishman the reasons that had brought him to those parts, and asked him whether he knew of an English three-master, the Britannia, being lost on the west coast of Australia within the last two years.

"The Irishman had never heard of any such wreck. But, to the great surprise of everyone there, one of the Irishman's farmhands broke in and said:

"'My lord, praise God and thank Him. If Captain Grant is still alive, he is alive on Australian soil.'

"'Who are you?' asked Lord Glenarvan.

"'A Scot like yourself, my lord,' the man answered, 'and I'm one of Captain Grant's companions — one of the castaways of the Britannia.'

"This man's name was Ayrton. He was indeed the quartermaster of the Britannia, as his papers showed. But he had been separated from Captain Grant at the moment the ship broke up on the reefs, and until then he had believed that his captain had died with the whole crew, and that he, Ayrton, was the only survivor of the Britannia.

"'Only,' he added, 'it wasn't on the west coast but on the east coast of Australia that the Britannia was lost. And if Captain Grant is still alive, as his document says, he's a prisoner of the Aboriginal people, and it's on the other coast that you have to look for him.'

"As he said this, the man's voice was frank and his gaze was steady. No one could doubt what he said. The Irishman, who had employed him for more than a year, vouched for him. Lord Glenarvan believed in the man's honesty, and on his advice he decided to cross Australia by following the thirty-seventh parallel. Lord Glenarvan, his wife, the two children, the major, the Frenchman, Captain Mangles and a few sailors would make up the little party, with Ayrton as their guide, while the Duncan, under the command of her first mate, Tom Austin, would go on to Melbourne and wait there for Lord Glenarvan's instructions.

"They set off on December 23, 1854.

"It is time to say that this Ayrton was a traitor. He had indeed been the quartermaster of the Britannia. But after quarrels with his captain he had tried to stir up the crew to mutiny and seize the ship, and on April 8, 1852, Captain Grant had put him ashore on the west coast of Australia and sailed off and left him there — which was no more than justice.

"So this wretch knew nothing of the wreck of the Britannia. He had only just learned of it from Glenarvan's account! Since he had been marooned, he had become, under the name of Ben Joyce, the leader of a gang of escaped convicts. And if he insisted so brazenly that the wreck had happened on the east coast, if he urged Lord Glenarvan to set off in that direction, it was because he hoped to separate him from his ship, seize the Duncan, and turn the yacht into a pirate ship of the Pacific."

Here the stranger broke off for a moment. His voice was trembling, but he went on in these words:

"The expedition set off and made its way across Australia. Naturally it was an unlucky one, since Ayrton — or Ben Joyce, whichever you like to call him — was leading it, with his band of convicts sometimes going on ahead of it, sometimes following behind, for they had been told of the blow that was to be struck.

"Meanwhile the Duncan had been sent to Melbourne for repairs. The thing, then, was to get Lord Glenarvan to order her to leave Melbourne and sail to the east coast of Australia, where it would be easy to seize her. Ayrton led the expedition fairly close to that coast, into the middle of vast forests where there was nothing at all to live on. Then he got himself a letter, which he had taken it upon himself to carry to the Duncan's first mate — a letter ordering the yacht to sail at once to the east coast, to Twofold Bay, a few days' journey from where the expedition had halted. That was where Ayrton had arranged to meet his accomplices.

"Just as the letter was about to be handed to him, the traitor was unmasked, and there was nothing left for him but to run. But that letter, which was to deliver the Duncan into his hands, he had to have at any cost. Ayrton managed to get hold of it, and two days later he reached Melbourne.

"Until then the criminal had succeeded in his vile plans. He would be able to bring the Duncan to Twofold Bay, where it would be easy for the convicts to take her, and once her crew had been massacred, Ben Joyce would be master of those seas... God was to stop him just as his evil designs were coming to their end.

"Ayrton reached Melbourne and handed the letter to the first mate, Tom Austin, who read it and set sail at once. But imagine Ayrton's disappointment and rage when, the day after they sailed, he learned that the mate was taking the ship not to the east coast of Australia, to Twofold Bay, but to the east coast of New Zealand! He tried to stop it. Austin showed him the letter!... And in fact, by a providential mistake on the part of the French geographer who had written that letter, the east coast of New Zealand was the destination it named.

"All of Ayrton's plans were falling apart! He tried to stir up a mutiny. They locked him up. And so he was carried off to the coast of New Zealand, with no idea anymore what would become of his accomplices, or what would become of Lord Glenarvan.

"The Duncan stayed cruising off that coast until March 3. That day Ayrton heard the boom of guns. It was the Duncan's carronades firing, and soon Lord Glenarvan and all his party came on board.

"Here is what had happened.

"After a thousand hardships and a thousand dangers, Lord Glenarvan had managed to finish his journey and reach the east coast of Australia, at Twofold Bay. No Duncan! He telegraphed to Melbourne. The answer came back: 'Duncan sailed on the 18th of this month for unknown destination.'

"Lord Glenarvan could think only one thing: that the honest yacht had fallen into the hands of Ben Joyce and had become a pirate ship!

"Even so, Lord Glenarvan would not give up. He was a fearless and generous man. He took passage on a merchant ship, had himself carried to the west coast of New Zealand, and crossed it along the thirty-seventh parallel without finding any trace of Captain Grant. But on the other coast, to his great surprise, and by the will of Heaven, he found the Duncan again, under the command of the first mate, who had been waiting for him for five weeks!

"It was March 3, 1855. Lord Glenarvan was aboard the Duncan, then, but so was Ayrton. He was brought before Lord Glenarvan, who wanted to get out of him everything the bandit might know about Captain Grant. Ayrton refused to speak. Lord Glenarvan then told him that at the first port they put in to, he would be handed over to the British authorities. Ayrton said nothing.

"The Duncan took up her course along the thirty-seventh parallel again. Meanwhile Lady Glenarvan set herself to break down the bandit's resistance. At last her influence won out, and Ayrton, in exchange for whatever he could tell, proposed that Lord Glenarvan maroon him on one of the islands of the Pacific instead of handing him over to the British authorities. Lord Glenarvan, determined to do anything to learn what had become of Captain Grant, agreed.

"Ayrton then told the whole story of his life, and it was established that he knew nothing at all after the day Captain Grant had put him ashore on the Australian coast.

"Nevertheless, Lord Glenarvan kept the promise he had made. The Duncan went on her way and came to Tabor Island. That was where Ayrton was to be left — and it was there too that, by a real miracle, they found Captain Grant and his two men, on that very thirty-seventh parallel. So the convict was to take their place on that deserted islet, and these are the words Lord Glenarvan spoke as Ayrton left the yacht:

"'Here, Ayrton, you will be far from any land, with no possible way of reaching other men. You will not be able to escape from this islet where the Duncan leaves you. You will be alone, under the eye of a God who reads the very depths of men's hearts. But you will not be lost, or forgotten, as Captain Grant was. Unworthy as you are to be remembered by men, men will remember you. I know where you are, Ayrton, and I know where to find you. I will never forget it!'

"And the Duncan set sail and was soon gone from sight.

"It was March 18, 1855.

"Ayrton was alone, but he had no shortage of ammunition, weapons, tools or seeds. At his disposal — his, the convict's — was the house built by honest Captain Grant. He had only to let himself live, and to atone in solitude for the crimes he had committed.

"Gentlemen, he repented. He was ashamed of his crimes, and he was very unhappy! He told himself that if men came back one day to look for him on that islet, he must be worthy of going back among them! How he suffered, the wretch! How he worked to remake himself by work! How he prayed to be made new by prayer!

"For two years, three years, it went on that way. But Ayrton, worn down by solitude, always watching for some ship to appear on the horizon of his island, always asking himself whether the time of his atonement would soon be over, suffered as no one has ever suffered! Ah, how hard that solitude is for a soul eaten away by remorse!

"But no doubt Heaven did not think him punished enough, the unhappy man, for little by little he felt himself becoming a wild man! Little by little he felt himself sinking to the level of a brute! He cannot tell you whether it was after two years of being abandoned or four, but in the end he became the wretched creature you found!

"I don't need to tell you, gentlemen, that Ayrton, or Ben Joyce, and I are one and the same!"

Cyrus Smith and his companions had risen to their feet when the story ended. It is hard to say how deeply they were moved! So much misery, so much pain and despair laid bare in front of them!

"Ayrton," Cyrus Smith said then, "you were a great criminal, but Heaven must surely find that you've atoned for your crimes! It has proved it by bringing you back among your fellow men. Ayrton, you are forgiven! And now, will you be our companion?"

Ayrton had stepped back.

"Here is my hand!" said the engineer.

Ayrton rushed to take the hand Cyrus Smith held out to him, and great tears ran from his eyes.

"Will you live with us?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"Mr. Smith, give me a little more time," Ayrton answered. "Let me stay alone in the house at the corral!"

"As you wish, Ayrton," replied Cyrus Smith.

Ayrton was about to leave when the engineer put one last question to him.

"One more word, my friend. If you meant to live alone, why did you throw into the sea the document that put us on your track?"

"A document?" answered Ayrton, who seemed not to know what he was being asked about.

"Yes, the document sealed in a bottle that we found, which gave the exact position of Tabor Island!"

Ayrton passed his hand across his forehead. Then, after thinking:

"I never threw any document into the sea!" he answered.

"Never?" cried Pencroff.

"Never!"

And Ayrton bowed, went back to the door, and was gone.

Chapter 18: The Electric Telegraph

Conversation — Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett — An idea of the engineer's — The electric telegraph — The wires — The battery — The alphabet — Fine weather — The colony prospers — Photography — A snow effect — Two years on Lincoln Island

"The poor man!" said Harbert. He had rushed to the door, but he came back after seeing Ayrton slide down the elevator rope and vanish into the darkness.

"He'll come back," said Cyrus Smith.

"Now look here, Mr. Cyrus," cried Pencroff, "what does this mean? What! It wasn't Ayrton who threw that bottle into the sea? Then who on earth was it?"

Certainly, if ever a question needed asking, it was that one!

"It was him," answered Nab. "Only, the poor man was already half out of his mind."

"Yes!" said Harbert. "He didn't know what he was doing anymore."

"That's the only way to explain it, my friends," Cyrus Smith answered quickly. "And now I understand how Ayrton could give the exact position of Tabor Island, since the very events that led up to his being abandoned there had taught it to him."

"All the same," Pencroff pointed out, "if he wasn't a brute yet when he wrote his document, and if it's seven or eight years since he threw it into the sea, how is it the paper wasn't spoiled by the damp?"

"That proves," answered Cyrus Smith, "that Ayrton lost his reason at a much more recent time than he believes."

"It must be so," answered Pencroff. "Otherwise the thing would be inexplicable."

"Inexplicable indeed," answered the engineer, who seemed unwilling to carry the conversation any further.

"But did Ayrton tell the truth?" asked the sailor.

"Yes," answered the reporter. "The story he told is true in every point. I remember very well that the newspapers reported Lord Glenarvan's attempt and the result he obtained."

"Ayrton told the truth," added Cyrus Smith. "Don't doubt it, Pencroff, because the truth was cruel enough to him. A man tells the truth when he accuses himself like that!"

The next day — December 21 — the colonists went down to the beach and climbed up to the plateau, but they found no Ayrton there. During the night Ayrton had gone off to his house at the corral, and the colonists judged it best not to trouble him with their company. Time would no doubt do what encouragement had not been able to do.

So Harbert, Pencroff and Nab went back to their usual occupations. As it happened, that same day the same work brought Cyrus Smith and the reporter together in the workshop at the Chimneys.

"Do you know, my dear Cyrus," said Gédéon Spilett, "that the explanation you gave yesterday about that bottle didn't satisfy me at all? How can anyone believe that the poor wretch could have written that document and thrown that bottle into the sea without keeping the slightest memory of it?"

"Which is why it wasn't he who threw it, my dear Spilett."

"Then you still believe..."

"I believe nothing, I know nothing!" Cyrus Smith answered, cutting the reporter off. "I'm content to file this incident among the ones I haven't been able to explain so far!"

"Really, Cyrus," said Gédéon Spilett, "these things are unbelievable! Your rescue, the chest stranded on the sand, Top's adventures, and now this bottle... Are we never going to get the answer to these riddles?"

"Yes!" the engineer answered sharply. "Yes, even if I have to search this island down to its very bowels!"

"Perhaps chance will give us the key to this mystery!"

"Chance, Spilett! I hardly believe in chance, any more than I believe in mysteries in this world. There's a cause for everything inexplicable that happens here, and I'll find that cause. But in the meantime, let's watch and work."

January came. The year 1867 was beginning. The summer work was pushed ahead steadily. In the days that followed, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett went over toward the corral and were able to see that Ayrton had taken possession of the home that had been prepared for him. He was looking after the large flock entrusted to his care, and he was going to spare his companions the trouble of coming to visit the corral every two or three days. All the same, so as not to leave Ayrton alone for too long, the colonists paid him visits fairly often.

Nor was it a matter of indifference — given certain suspicions that the engineer and Gédéon Spilett shared — that this part of the island should be kept under some sort of watch, and if anything happened, Ayrton would not fail to let the people at Granite House know.

Still, it was possible that something might happen suddenly and need to reach the engineer quickly. And quite apart from anything to do with the mystery of Lincoln Island, plenty of other things might happen that would call for the colonists to act at once: a ship passing in the offing within sight of the west coast, a wreck on the western approaches, a possible landing by pirates, and so on.

So Cyrus Smith decided to put the corral in instant communication with Granite House.

It was on January 10 that he told his companions about his plan.

"Now look here! How are you going to manage that, Mr. Cyrus?" asked Pencroff. "You aren't by any chance thinking of putting in a telegraph?"

"Exactly that," answered the engineer.

"Electric?" cried Harbert.

"Electric," answered Cyrus Smith. "We have everything we need to make a battery. The hardest part will be drawing out the iron wire, but with a drawplate I think we'll manage it."

"Well, after that," the sailor replied, "I'm not giving up hope of seeing us ride on a railroad one of these days!"

So they set to work, beginning with the hardest part — that is, making the wire — because if they failed at that, there would be no point in building the battery and the other equipment.

The iron of Lincoln Island, as we know, was of excellent quality, and so it was very well suited to being drawn out into wire. Cyrus Smith began by making a drawplate. This was a plate of steel pierced with cone-shaped holes of various sizes, which would bring the wire, one hole after another, down to the thinness he wanted. This piece of steel was tempered "to its full hardness," as metalworkers say, and then fixed immovably onto a frame driven solidly into the ground, only a few feet from the great waterfall, whose driving power the engineer was going to put to use once again.

That was where the fulling mill stood. It was not running at the time, but its main shaft, which turned with tremendous force, could be used to draw the wire by winding it around itself.

The operation was a delicate one and took a great deal of care. The iron was first prepared in long, thin rods whose ends had been filed down to a point. Each rod was pushed through the largest hole in the drawplate and pulled through by the main shaft, which wound it up over a length of twenty-five to thirty feet. Then it was unwound and fed in turn through the holes of smaller and smaller diameter! In the end the engineer had wires forty to fifty feet long, which could easily be joined together and strung across the five miles that separated the corral from the grounds of Granite House.

It took only a few days to finish this job. In fact, as soon as the machine was up and running, Cyrus Smith left his companions to work as wire-drawers and turned to making his battery.

What he needed, in this case, was a battery that would give a steady current. As everyone knows, the elements of modern batteries are usually made of retort carbon, zinc and copper. The engineer had no copper at all. In spite of all his searching, he had not found a trace of it on Lincoln Island, and he would have to do without. Retort carbon — that is, the hard graphite left in the retorts of gasworks after the hydrogen has been driven out of the coal — could have been produced, but it would have meant setting up special apparatus, which would have been a big job. As for zinc, you will remember that the chest found at Jetsam Point had been lined with a casing of that metal, which could not have been put to better use than this.

So Cyrus Smith, after thinking it over carefully, decided to build a very simple battery, close to the one Becquerel invented in 1820, in which zinc is the only metal used. As for the other substances, nitric acid and potash, he had all of them at hand.

Here, then, is how this battery was put together. Its effect was to come from the action of the acid and the potash on each other.

A number of glass bottles were made and filled with nitric acid. The engineer sealed each one with a stopper, and through the stopper ran a glass tube. The tube was closed at its lower end, which was meant to dip into the acid, by a plug of clay held in place with a piece of cloth. Into this tube, through its upper end, he then poured a solution of potash, which he had obtained beforehand by burning various plants to ash. In this way the acid and the potash could act on each other through the clay.

Next, Cyrus Smith took two strips of zinc. One was dipped into the nitric acid, the other into the potash solution. At once a current was set up, running from the strip in the bottle to the strip in the tube. When the two strips were connected by a metal wire, the strip in the tube became the positive pole of the apparatus and the strip in the bottle its negative pole. Each bottle, then, produced its own current, and all these currents together would be enough to bring about every effect needed for electric telegraphy.

Such was the ingenious and very simple apparatus that Cyrus Smith built — the apparatus that would let him set up telegraphic communication between Granite House and the corral.

It was on February 6 that they began planting the poles, fitted with glass insulators, that were to carry the wire along the Corral Road. A few days later the wire was strung, ready to carry the electric current at a speed of a hundred thousand kilometers a second, with the earth taking care of bringing it back to its starting point.

Two batteries had been made, one for Granite House and the other for the corral, because if the corral was to communicate with Granite House, it might be just as useful for Granite House to communicate with the corral.

As for the receiver and the transmitter, they were very simple. At both stations the wire was coiled around an electromagnet — that is, a piece of soft iron with a wire wound around it. When the connection was made between the two poles, the current set out from the positive pole, ran along the wire, passed through the electromagnet, which became a magnet for the time being, and returned through the ground to the negative pole. When the current was broken, the electromagnet stopped being a magnet at once. So all that was needed was to place a plate of soft iron in front of the electromagnet. While the current was flowing, the plate was pulled toward it; when the current was broken, the plate fell back. Once he had this movement of the plate, Cyrus Smith could very easily connect it to a needle set on a dial with the letters of the alphabet around its rim, and in that way the two stations could send messages to each other.

The whole thing was completely installed on February 12. That day Cyrus Smith sent the current through the wire, asked whether all was well at the corral, and a few moments later received a satisfactory reply from Ayrton.

Pencroff was beside himself with joy. Every morning and every evening he sent a telegram to the corral, and it never went unanswered.

This way of keeping in touch had two very real advantages. First, it let them make sure Ayrton was at the corral. Second, it kept him from being completely cut off. Besides, Cyrus Smith never let a week go by without going to see him, and Ayrton came to Granite House now and then, where he always found a warm welcome.

So the fine season went by in the usual work. The colony's resources, especially in vegetables and grain, grew from day to day, and the plants brought back from Tabor Island had done perfectly. Prospect Plateau looked very reassuring. The fourth wheat harvest had been splendid, and, as you can well imagine, nobody took it into his head to count whether the four hundred billion grains were all there at the harvest. Pencroff had had the idea of doing it, all the same. But Cyrus Smith told him that even if he managed to count three hundred grains a minute — that is, nine thousand an hour — it would take him about five thousand five hundred years to finish the job, and the good sailor decided he had better give it up.

The weather was magnificent, the temperature very hot during the day. But in the evening the sea breezes came in to cool the burning air and gave the people of Granite House fresh nights. There were a few thunderstorms, though. They did not last long, but they fell on Lincoln Island with extraordinary force. For several hours at a time the lightning never stopped setting the sky ablaze, and the thunder rolled without a pause.

By this time the little colony was extremely prosperous. The residents of the poultry yard were multiplying fast, and the colonists lived off the surplus, since it was becoming urgent to bring the population down to a more reasonable number. The pigs had already had young, and, as you can imagine, looking after these animals took up a large part of Nab's and Pencroff's time. The onaggas, which had produced two pretty foals, were ridden most often by Gédéon Spilett and Harbert, who had become an excellent rider under the reporter's coaching. They were also harnessed to the cart, to haul wood and coal to Granite House, or the various minerals the engineer was using.

Several reconnaissance trips were pushed, during this time, deep into the Far West forests. The explorers could venture there without fear of the heat, because the sun's rays barely got through the thick tangle of branches overhead. In this way they visited the whole left bank of the Mercy, which ran beside the road from the corral to the mouth of Fall River.

But on these excursions the colonists took care to be well armed, because they often met wild boars, very fierce and savage, which had to be fought in earnest.

During this season a fearful war was also waged on the jaguars. Gédéon Spilett had vowed a very special hatred against them, and his pupil Harbert backed him up well. Armed as they were, they hardly feared meeting one of these big cats. Harbert's daring was superb, and the reporter's coolness astonishing. And so some twenty magnificent skins already decorated the great hall of Granite House, and if things went on like this, the jaguars would soon be extinct on the island, which was exactly what the hunters were aiming for.

The engineer sometimes took part in the various reconnaissance trips into the unknown parts of the island, which he observed with close attention. In the thickest parts of those vast woods it was other tracks than animals' that he was looking for, but nothing suspicious ever met his eyes. Neither Top nor Jup, who went with him, gave any sign by the way they behaved that there was anything out of the ordinary. And yet, more than once again, the dog barked at the mouth of the well that the engineer had explored without result.

It was during this time that Gédéon Spilett, with Harbert's help, took several pictures of the most picturesque parts of the island, using the photographic outfit that had been found in the chest and had not been used until then.

The outfit, fitted with a powerful lens, was very complete. The substances needed for making photographs — collodion to prepare the glass plate, silver nitrate to make it sensitive to light, hyposulfate of soda to fix the image once it was taken, ammonium chloride to bathe the paper meant for the positive print, sodium acetate and gold chloride to soak that print in — nothing was missing. Even the papers were there, already treated with chloride. Before laying them in the frame on top of the negatives, all you had to do was soak them for a few minutes in silver nitrate diluted with water.

So in a short time the reporter and his assistant became skilled operators, and they got some quite fine prints of the scenery: the whole island, taken from Prospect Plateau, with Mount Franklin on the horizon; the mouth of the Mercy, so picturesquely framed by its high rocks; the clearing and the corral set against the first slopes of the mountain; the whole curious sweep of Claw Cape, of Jetsam Point, and so on.

The photographers did not forget to take portraits of everyone living on the island, without leaving anyone out.

"It fills the place up," said Pencroff.

And the sailor was delighted to see his likeness, faithfully reproduced, decorating the walls of Granite House, and he liked to stop in front of this exhibition just as he would have stopped at the finest shop windows on Broadway.

But, it must be said, the most successful portrait of all was beyond question Master Jup's. Master Jup had posed with a seriousness impossible to describe, and his picture was so lifelike it seemed about to speak!

"You'd think he was about to pull a face!" cried Pencroff.

And if Master Jup had not been pleased, he would have been very hard to please. But he was pleased, and he gazed at his picture with a sentimental air that let a slight touch of vanity show through.

The great heat of summer ended with the month of March. The weather was sometimes rainy, but the air was still warm. This month of March, which corresponds to September in northern latitudes, was not as fine as they might have hoped. Perhaps it meant an early, harsh winter.

One morning — the 21st — they might even have believed that the first snows had arrived. Harbert had gone early to one of the windows of Granite House, and he called out:

"Look! The islet's covered with snow!"

"Snow, at this time of year?" answered the reporter, who had joined the boy.

Their companions were soon beside them, and they could only agree on one thing: not only the islet but the whole beach at the foot of Granite House was covered with a white layer, spread evenly over the ground.

"It's snow all right!" said Pencroff.

"Or something very like it!" answered Nab.

"But the thermometer reads fifty-eight degrees!" Gédéon Spilett pointed out.

Cyrus Smith looked at the white sheet without giving an opinion, because he truly did not know how to explain this phenomenon, at that time of year and at such a temperature.

"A thousand devils!" cried Pencroff. "Our crops are going to freeze!"

And the sailor was getting ready to go down when the nimble Jup got ahead of him and slid all the way to the ground.

But the orangutan had not yet touched the ground when the enormous layer of snow rose up and scattered into the air in flakes so countless that they veiled the light of the sun for several minutes.

"Birds!" cried Harbert.

They were indeed flocks of seabirds with dazzling white plumage. They had come down by hundreds of thousands on the islet and the shore, and they vanished into the distance, leaving the colonists open-mouthed, as if they had watched a scene change in a fairy play, with summer taking the place of winter before their eyes. Unfortunately, the change had been so sudden that neither the reporter nor the boy managed to bring down one of these birds, and they could not tell what species they were.

A few days later it was March 26, and two years had passed since the castaways of the air had been thrown onto Lincoln Island!

Chapter 19: Memories of Home

Memories of home — The chances ahead — A plan to survey the island's coasts — Departure on April 16 — Serpentine Peninsula seen from the sea — The basalt of the west coast — Bad weather — Night falls — A new incident

Two years already! And for two years the colonists had had no contact with their fellow human beings! They had no news of the civilized world. They were lost on this island as completely as if they had been on some tiny asteroid of the solar system!

What was happening at home just then? The image of their country was always before their eyes — a country torn apart by civil war when they had left it, and one that the Southern rebellion was perhaps still drenching in blood! It was a great grief to them, and they often talked these things over, though never once doubting that the cause of the North must triumph, for the honor of the American Union.

In those two years not a single ship had passed within sight of the island — or at least not a single sail had been spotted. It was obvious that Lincoln Island lay outside the usual sea routes, and even that it was unknown — as the maps proved, besides — for even without a harbor, its fresh water ought to have drawn ships looking to refill their casks. But the sea around it was always empty, as far as the eye could reach, and the colonists could hardly count on anyone but themselves to get home.

There was, however, one chance of rescue, and that chance was discussed one day in the first week of April by the colonists, who had gathered in the great hall of Granite House.

They had, in fact, been talking about America, about the country where they were born and which they had so little hope of seeing again.

"There's no getting around it," said Gédéon Spilett. "We'll have only one way — just one — of leaving Lincoln Island, and that's to build a ship big enough to stay at sea for a few hundred miles. It seems to me that when you've built a sloop, you can perfectly well build a ship!"

"And when you've been to Tabor Island," Harbert added, "you can perfectly well go to the Tuamotus!"

"I don't say no," replied Pencroff, who always had the deciding voice on matters of the sea. "I don't say no — though going near and going far aren't quite the same thing! If our boat had been threatened by some nasty gale on the trip to Tabor Island, we knew there was a port not too far off one way or the other. But twelve hundred miles to cover is a good long stretch, and the nearest land is at least that far away!"

"If it came to it, Pencroff, wouldn't you try the venture?" asked the reporter.

"I'll try anything anyone likes, Mr. Spilett," the sailor answered, "and you know very well I'm not a man to back down!"

"Remember, too, that there's one more sailor among us now," Nab pointed out.

"Who's that?" asked Pencroff.

"Ayrton."

"That's true," said Harbert.

"If he'd agree to come!" Pencroff observed.

"Come now!" said the reporter. "Do you really think that if Lord Glenarvan's yacht had turned up at Tabor Island while Ayrton was still living there, he would have refused to leave?"

"You're forgetting, my friends," Cyrus Smith said then, "that Ayrton was no longer in his right mind during the last years he spent there. But that isn't the question. What we need to decide is whether we should count the Scottish ship's return among our chances of rescue. Now, Lord Glenarvan promised Ayrton he would come back for him on Tabor Island once he judged that his crimes had been sufficiently paid for, and I believe he will come back."

"Yes," said the reporter, "and I'd add that he'll come back soon, because it's been twelve years since Ayrton was marooned!"

"Well!" answered Pencroff. "I quite agree with you that the lord will come back, and soon too. But where will he put in? At Tabor Island, not at Lincoln Island."

"That's all the more certain," Harbert replied, "because Lincoln Island isn't even on the map."

"So, my friends," the engineer went on, "we must take the necessary steps to make sure that our presence, and Ayrton's, on Lincoln Island is made known on Tabor Island."

"Obviously," the reporter answered, "and nothing could be easier than to leave a notice in that hut which was the home of Captain Grant and of Ayrton — a notice giving our island's position, which Lord Glenarvan or his crew can't fail to find."

"It's a pity, in fact," the sailor observed, "that we forgot to take that precaution on our first trip to Tabor Island."

"And why would we have taken it?" Harbert replied. "We didn't know Ayrton's story at that point. We had no idea that someone was supposed to come looking for him one day, and by the time we did know the story, the season was too far along to let us go back to Tabor Island."

"Yes," said Cyrus Smith, "it was too late, and the crossing must wait until next spring."

"But what if the Scottish yacht comes before then?" said Pencroff.

"That's not likely," answered the engineer, "because Lord Glenarvan wouldn't choose the winter season to venture into these distant seas. Either he has already come back to Tabor Island since Ayrton has been with us — that is, in the last five months — and left again, or he won't come until later, and there will be time enough, as soon as the first fine days of October arrive, to go to Tabor Island and leave a notice there."

"You have to admit," said Nab, "it would be very bad luck if the Duncan had turned up in these seas only in the last few months!"

"I hope that isn't the case," replied Cyrus Smith, "and that Heaven hasn't taken away the best chance we have left!"

"I think," the reporter remarked, "that in any case we'll know where we stand once we've been back to Tabor Island, because if the Scots have returned there, they're bound to have left some traces of their visit."

"That's obvious," answered the engineer. "So then, my friends, since we have this chance of getting home, let us wait patiently, and if it's taken from us, we'll see then what we ought to do."

"In any case," said Pencroff, "it's understood that if we do leave Lincoln Island one way or another, it won't be because we're unhappy here!"

"No, Pencroff," answered the engineer. "It will be because here we are far from everything a man should hold dearest in the world — his family, his friends, the country where he was born!"

With matters settled that way, there was no more talk of building a ship big enough to risk the voyage, either north to the island groups or west to New Zealand, and they went about nothing but their usual tasks in preparation for a third winter at Granite House.

It was also decided, however, that before the bad weather came the boat would be used for a voyage around the island. The full survey of the coasts was not yet finished. The colonists had only a rough idea of the shoreline to the west and the north, from the mouth of Fall River all the way to the Mandible Capes, and no better idea of the narrow bay that cut in between those capes like the jaws of a shark.

The plan for this excursion was put forward by Pencroff, and Cyrus Smith gave it his full approval, because he wanted to see that whole part of his domain for himself.

The weather was changeable at the time, but the barometer was not making any sudden swings, so they could count on weather they could handle. As it happened, during the first week of April, after a sharp drop of the barometer, its rise again was announced by a strong wind from the west that lasted five or six days. Then the needle of the instrument settled again at a height of twenty-nine and nine-tenths inches, and conditions seemed right for the exploration.

The day of departure was set for April 16, and the Bonadventure, moored at Balloon Harbor, was stocked with supplies for a voyage that might last some time.

Cyrus Smith told Ayrton about the planned expedition and invited him to take part. But Ayrton preferred to stay on land, so it was decided that he would come to Granite House while his companions were away. Master Jup was to keep him company, and raised no objection whatever.

On the morning of April 16 all the colonists, with Top, were on board. The wind was blowing from the southwest, a fine breeze, and on leaving Balloon Harbor the Bonadventure had to tack back and forth to reach Reptile End. Of the ninety miles that made up the island's perimeter, the south coast accounted for some twenty, from the harbor to the headland. Hence the need to make those twenty miles sailing as close to the wind as she could, since the wind was dead ahead.

It took no less than the whole day to reach the headland, because when the boat left harbor she found only two more hours of ebb tide and then, against her, six hours of flood tide, which were very hard to make headway against. So night had fallen by the time they rounded the headland.

Pencroff then suggested to the engineer that they keep going at low speed, with two reefs in the sail. But Cyrus Smith preferred to anchor a few cable lengths offshore, so as to see this part of the coast again by daylight. It was even agreed that, since the point was a careful survey of the island's shoreline, they would not sail at night, and that when evening came they would drop anchor close to land, as long as the weather allowed.

So the night was spent at anchor in the lee of the headland, and since the wind had died down along with the mist, nothing broke the silence. The passengers, except the sailor, may have slept a little less well aboard the Bonadventure than they would have in their rooms at Granite House — but sleep they did.

The next day, April 17, Pencroff got under way at first light. On a broad reach, with the wind on the port side, he was able to run very close along the west coast.

The colonists knew this wooded and magnificent coast, since they had already walked along its edge, and yet it roused all their admiration once again. They hugged the land as closely as they could, slowing down so as to take everything in, and only taking care not to strike the tree trunks that floated here and there. Several times they even dropped anchor, and Gédéon Spilett took photographs of that superb shoreline.

Toward noon the Bonadventure reached the mouth of Fall River. Beyond it, on the right bank, the trees appeared again, but more thinly scattered, and three miles farther on they formed nothing but isolated clumps among the western spurs of the mountain, whose barren backbone stretched all the way to the shore.

What a contrast between the southern and the northern parts of this coast! The one was as wooded and green as the other was harsh and wild! It looked like one of those "iron coasts," as they are called in some countries, and its tortured structure seemed to show that a true crystallization had suddenly taken place in basalt that was still boiling in the geological ages. It was a terrible-looking heap, which would have struck terror into the colonists at the outset if chance had cast them up on this part of the island! When they were on the summit of Mount Franklin, they had not been able to make out how deeply sinister this shore looked, because they had seen it from too high above. But seen from the sea, this coastline had a strangeness to it whose equal could perhaps be found in no other corner of the world.

The Bonadventure passed along this coast, keeping half a mile off. It was easy to see that it was made of blocks of every size, from twenty feet to three hundred feet high, and of every shape: cylindrical like towers, prismatic like steeples, pyramidal like obelisks, conical like factory chimneys. An ice field in the polar seas could not have been piled up more fantastically in its sublime horror! Here, bridges flung from one rock to the next; there, arches set out like those of a cathedral nave, so deep the eye could not reach their end; in one place, broad hollows whose vaulted roofs looked like great monuments; in another, a real crowd of points, of little pyramids, of spires, more than any Gothic cathedral has ever had. All the whims of nature, more varied even than those of the imagination, shaped this grandiose shoreline, which ran on for eight or nine miles.

Cyrus Smith and his companions gazed at it with a surprise that came close to stupefaction. But if they were struck dumb, Top was not shy about letting out barks that were echoed back a thousand times by the basalt wall. The engineer even noticed that these barks had something odd about them, like the ones the dog gave at the mouth of the well in Granite House.

"Let's go in closer," he said.

And the Bonadventure came and skimmed as near as she could to the rocks of the shore. Perhaps there was some cave there that ought to be explored? But Cyrus Smith saw nothing — not a cavern, not a crevice that could have served as a hiding place for any creature at all, for the foot of the rocks was washed by the surf itself. Soon Top stopped barking, and the boat drew off again to a few cable lengths from the shore.

In the northwestern part of the island the shore became flat and sandy once more. A few scattered trees stood out above a low, marshy stretch of land that the colonists had glimpsed before, and, in violent contrast with the other, so lifeless coast, life now showed itself in myriads of water birds.

That evening the Bonadventure anchored in a slight inlet of the shore on the north side of the island, close to land, since the water was so deep there. The night passed peacefully, because the breeze died away, so to speak, with the last glimmers of daylight, and rose again only with the first tints of dawn.

As it was easy to get ashore that morning, the colony's official hunters — that is, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett — went off for a two-hour walk and came back with several strings of ducks and snipe. Top had done wonders, and not a single bird had been lost, thanks to his zeal and skill.

At eight in the morning the Bonadventure got under way and ran along very fast, heading north toward North Mandible Cape, for the wind was right behind her and the breeze was tending to freshen.

"Anyhow," said Pencroff, "I wouldn't be surprised if some westerly gale was brewing. Yesterday the sun set on a very red horizon, and this morning here are 'cats' tails,' which mean no good."

These cats' tails were wispy cirrus clouds scattered across the zenith, and they are never less than five thousand feet above sea level. They looked like light tufts of cotton wool, and their presence usually announces some coming disturbance in the elements.

"Well then," said Cyrus Smith, "let's carry as much sail as we can and go and look for shelter in Shark Gulf. I think the Bonadventure will be safe there."

"Exactly," Pencroff answered, "and besides, the north coast is nothing but dunes, not very interesting to look at."

"I wouldn't be sorry," the engineer added, "to spend not only the night but tomorrow as well in that bay. It deserves to be explored carefully."

"I think we'll be forced to, whether we like it or not," answered Pencroff, "because the horizon's starting to look threatening out to the west. Look how dirty it's getting!"

"In any case, we have a good wind to reach Mandible Cape," the reporter remarked.

"A very good wind," replied the sailor. "But to get into the gulf we'll have to tack, and I'd very much like to be able to see clearly in waters I don't know!"

"Waters that must be strewn with reefs," Harbert added, "if we judge by what we've seen on the south shore of Shark Gulf."

"Pencroff," Cyrus Smith said then, "do whatever you think best. We leave it to you."

"Don't worry, Mr. Cyrus," the sailor answered. "I won't take any risks I don't have to! I'd sooner have a knife in my belly than a rock in my Bonadventure's!"

What Pencroff called the belly was the part of his boat's hull that lay underwater, and he cared more about it than about his own skin!

"What time is it?" asked Pencroff.

"Ten o'clock," Gédéon Spilett answered.

"And how far do we have to go to the cape, Mr. Cyrus?"

"About fifteen miles," the engineer replied.

"That's a matter of two and a half hours," said the sailor, "and we'll be abreast of the cape between noon and one o'clock. Unfortunately, the tide will turn just then, and the ebb will be running out of the gulf. So I'm very much afraid it'll be hard to get in, with both wind and sea against us."

"All the more so because it's full moon today," Harbert observed, "and these April tides are very strong."

"Well, Pencroff," asked Cyrus Smith, "can't you anchor off the tip of the cape?"

"Anchor close to land, with bad weather on the way!" cried the sailor. "Are you serious, Mr. Cyrus? That would be running ourselves aground on purpose!"

"Then what will you do?"

"I'll try to stay out at sea until the flood tide — that is, until seven o'clock this evening — and if there's still a little daylight, I'll try to get into the gulf. If not, we'll stay out tacking back and forth all night, and go in tomorrow at sunrise."

"As I told you, Pencroff, we leave it to you," replied Cyrus Smith.

"Ah!" said Pencroff. "If only there were a lighthouse on this coast, it'd make things easier for sailors!"

"Yes," answered Harbert, "and this time we won't have an obliging engineer to light a fire to guide us into port!"

"Why, that's right, my dear Cyrus," said Gédéon Spilett. "We've never thanked you. But honestly, without that fire we could never have reached..."

"A fire...?" asked Cyrus Smith, greatly astonished at the reporter's words.

"What we mean, Mr. Cyrus," answered Pencroff, "is that we were in real trouble aboard the Bonadventure during the last hours before we got back, and we'd have passed the island on its leeward side if you hadn't taken the precaution of lighting a fire on the night of October 19 to 20, on the plateau above Granite House."

"Yes, yes!... That was a lucky idea I had!" the engineer replied.

"And this time," the sailor added, "unless Ayrton thinks of it, there'll be nobody to do us that little favor!"

"No! Nobody!" answered Cyrus Smith.

And a few moments later, finding himself alone with the reporter in the bow of the boat, the engineer leaned close to his ear and said:

"If there is one thing certain in this world, Spilett, it is that I never lit a fire on the night of October 19 to 20 — not on the plateau above Granite House, and not anywhere else on the island!"

Chapter 20: Shark Gulf

The night at sea — Shark Gulf — Confidences — Preparations for winter — The bad season comes early — Great cold — Work indoors — After six months — A photographic plate — An unexpected incident

Things turned out just as Pencroff had foreseen, for his hunches could not be wrong. The wind freshened, and from a good breeze it rose to a gale — that is, it reached a speed of forty to forty-five miles an hour, the kind of wind in which a ship at sea would have been down to close-reefed topsails, with her topgallant masts struck. Now, it was about six o'clock when the Bonadventure came abreast of the gulf, and at that moment the ebb was running, so it was impossible to get in. They had no choice but to stand off from the land, for even if he had wanted to, Pencroff could not have reached the mouth of the Mercy either. So he rigged his jib on the mast as a storm sail, and he waited, keeping her head toward the shore.

Very fortunately, though the wind was very strong, the sea, sheltered by the coast, did not build up much. So there was no need to dread the heavy seas that break aboard, which are a great danger to small boats. The Bonadventure would no doubt not have capsized, for she was well ballasted; but huge masses of water crashing onto her deck could have put her in danger if the hatches had given way. Pencroff, skilled sailor that he was, was ready for anything. Certainly he had enormous confidence in his boat, but he waited for daylight with a certain anxiety all the same.

During that night Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett had no chance to talk together, and yet the sentence the engineer had spoken into the reporter's ear was well worth one more discussion of that mysterious influence which seemed to rule over Lincoln Island. Gédéon Spilett could not stop thinking about this new and inexplicable incident, about this fire that had appeared on the coast of the island. He had really seen that fire! His companions, Harbert and Pencroff, had seen it just as he had! That fire had shown them where the island lay on that dark night, and they had never doubted that it was the engineer's hand that had lit it. And now here was Cyrus Smith declaring flatly that he had done nothing of the kind!

Gédéon Spilett promised himself that he would come back to this incident as soon as the Bonadventure was home again, and that he would urge Cyrus Smith to tell their companions about these strange events. Perhaps then they would decide to make, all together, a complete search of every part of Lincoln Island.

Be that as it may, no fire was lit that evening on those still-unknown shores that formed the entrance of the gulf, and the little boat went on standing off the land all night long.

When the first gleams of dawn began to show on the eastern horizon, the wind, which had eased a little, shifted two points and let Pencroff run more easily into the narrow entrance of the gulf. At about seven o'clock in the morning, the Bonadventure, having borne away toward North Mandible Cape, carefully entered the passage and ventured out onto those waters, which were shut in by the strangest frame of lava.

"Now there," said Pencroff, "is a stretch of sea that would make a wonderful anchorage, where whole fleets could maneuver at their ease!"

"What's especially curious," Cyrus Smith observed, "is that this gulf was formed by two flows of lava, thrown out by the volcano and piled up by one eruption after another. The result is that the gulf is completely sheltered on every side, and it's likely that even in the worst winds the sea in here is as calm as a lake."

"No doubt," the sailor went on, "since the only way the wind can get in is through that narrow gap between the two capes, and even then the north cape covers the south one, so it's very hard for a squall to get in. Honestly, our Bonadventure could stay in here from one end of the year to the other without even straining at her anchors!"

"It's a bit big for her!" the reporter pointed out.

"Ah, Mr. Spilett," replied the sailor, "I grant you it's too big for the Bonadventure. But if the fleets of the Union ever need a safe shelter in the Pacific, I don't believe they'll ever find a better anchorage than this one!"

"We're in the Shark's jaws," Nab remarked then, alluding to the shape of the gulf.

"Right inside its jaws, my good Nab!" replied Harbert. "But you're not afraid they'll snap shut on us, are you?"

"No, Mr. Harbert," replied Nab, "and yet I don't much like this gulf! It has a wicked look about it!"

"Well, now!" cried Pencroff. "Here's Nab running down my gulf, just when I'm thinking of making a present of it to America!"

"But are the waters deep, at least?" asked the engineer. "Because what's enough for the Bonadventure's keel wouldn't be enough for our ironclads."

"Easy to check," replied Pencroff.

And the sailor let down a long rope that served him as a sounding line, with a block of iron tied to the end of it. The line measured about fifty fathoms, and it ran out to the very end without touching bottom.

"There we are," said Pencroff. "Our ships can come in here! They won't run aground!"

"Indeed," said Cyrus Smith, "this gulf is a real abyss. But considering the volcanic origin of the island, it's not surprising that the sea floor should have hollows like this."

"It looks, too," Harbert observed, "as though these walls had been cut straight down. I really believe that at their foot, even with a line five or six times as long, Pencroff wouldn't find bottom."

"That's all very well," the reporter said then, "but I'll point out to Pencroff that his anchorage is missing one important thing!"

"And what's that, Mr. Spilett?"

"A gap, a cutting of some kind, that gives a way into the interior of the island. I can't see a single spot where anyone could set foot!"

And in fact the high lava walls, very steep, offered not one place along the whole edge of the gulf where a landing could be made. It was an impassable rampart, like the fjords of Norway, only more barren still. The Bonadventure, skimming so close along those high walls that she almost touched them, did not find even a ledge where her passengers could step ashore.

Pencroff consoled himself by saying that with the help of blasting they could easily break open that wall when it became necessary. And since there was plainly nothing to be done in this gulf, he steered his boat toward the narrow entrance and came out of it at about two o'clock in the afternoon.

"Phew!" said Nab, with a sigh of satisfaction.

You really would have said that good Nab did not feel at ease in those enormous jaws!

From Mandible Cape to the mouth of the Mercy it was hardly more than about eight miles. So they set a course for Granite House, and the Bonadventure, with the wind free in her sails, ran along the coast a mile out. The enormous lava rocks soon gave way to those fantastic dunes among which the engineer had been found in such a strange way, and which the seabirds haunted by the hundreds.

At about four o'clock, leaving the point of the islet to port, Pencroff entered the channel that separated it from the coast, and at five o'clock the Bonadventure's anchor bit into the sandy bottom at the mouth of the Mercy.

The colonists had left their home three days before. Ayrton was waiting for them on the beach, and Master Jup came joyfully to meet them, giving out hearty grunts of satisfaction.

So the whole of the island's coastline had now been explored, and no suspicious trace had been seen. If some mysterious being lived there, it could only be under cover of the impenetrable woods of Serpentine Peninsula, where the colonists had not yet carried their search.

Gédéon Spilett talked these things over with the engineer, and they agreed that they would draw their companions' attention to the strange character of certain incidents that had taken place on the island, the latest of which was one of the most inexplicable.

So Cyrus Smith, coming back to the business of a fire lit on the shore by an unknown hand, could not help asking the reporter for the twentieth time:

"But are you sure you really saw it? Wasn't it a partial eruption of the volcano, a meteor of some kind?"

"No, Cyrus," replied the reporter. "It was certainly a fire lit by a human hand. Besides, ask Pencroff and Harbert. They saw it just as I saw it myself, and they'll confirm what I say."

And so it came about that a few days later, on the evening of April 25, when all the colonists were gathered on Prospect Plateau, Cyrus Smith spoke up and said:

"My friends, I think I ought to call your attention to certain things that have happened on the island, and I'd very much like to have your opinion about them. These things are, so to speak, supernatural..."

"Supernatural!" cried the sailor, puffing out a cloud of tobacco smoke. "Could our island be supernatural?"

"No, Pencroff, but mysterious, certainly," replied the engineer, "unless you can explain to us what Spilett and I have not been able to understand so far."

"Go on, Mr. Cyrus," replied the sailor.

"Well, then," said the engineer, "have you understood how it could have happened that, after I fell into the sea, I was found a quarter of a mile inland, without being aware of having been moved?"

"Unless, while you were unconscious..." said Pencroff.

"That isn't possible," replied the engineer. "But let's go on. Have you understood how Top was able to find your shelter, five miles from the cave where I was lying?"

"The dog's instinct..." replied Harbert.

"A strange instinct!" the reporter pointed out. "Because in spite of the rain and wind that were raging that night, Top arrived at the Chimneys dry and without a speck of mud on him!"

"Let's go on," the engineer went on. "Have you understood how our dog was so strangely thrown up out of the water of the lake, after his fight with the dugong?"

"No! Not really, I admit," replied Pencroff. "And the wound the dugong had in its side, a wound that looked as if it had been made by a cutting blade, makes no more sense either."

"Let's go on again," Cyrus Smith resumed. "Have you understood, my friends, how that lead pellet came to be in the body of the young peccary? How that chest came ashore so luckily, without any trace of a shipwreck? How that bottle with the document in it turned up just when it did, on our first trip out to sea? How our canoe broke its mooring and came down the current of the Mercy to join us exactly when we needed it? How, after the invasion of the monkeys, the ladder was so conveniently sent back down from the heights of Granite House? And how, last of all, the document that Ayrton claims he never wrote fell into our hands?"

Cyrus Smith had just listed, without forgetting a single one, the strange events that had taken place on the island. Harbert, Pencroff and Nab looked at one another, not knowing what to answer, for the string of incidents, grouped together like this for the first time, could not fail to astonish them in the highest degree.

"Upon my word," Pencroff said at last, "you're right, Mr. Cyrus, and it's hard to explain those things!"

"Well, my friends," the engineer went on, "one last event has been added to those, and it's every bit as incomprehensible as the others!"

"What is it, Mr. Cyrus?" Harbert asked quickly.

"When you came back from Tabor Island, Pencroff," the engineer went on, "you say a fire appeared to you on Lincoln Island?"

"Certainly," replied the sailor.

"And you're quite sure you saw that fire?"

"As sure as I see you."

"You too, Harbert?"

"Oh, Mr. Cyrus!" cried Harbert. "That fire was shining like a star of the first magnitude!"

"But wasn't it a star?" the engineer insisted.

"No," replied Pencroff, "because the sky was covered with heavy clouds, and anyway a star wouldn't have been so low on the horizon. But Mr. Spilett saw it as well as we did, and he can confirm what we say!"

"I'll add," said the reporter, "that the fire was very bright, and that it threw out a sort of sheet of electric light."

"Yes! Yes! Exactly..." replied Harbert. "And it was certainly up on the heights of Granite House."

"Well, my friends," replied Cyrus Smith, "on that night of October 19 to 20, neither Nab nor I lit a fire on the coast."

"You didn't...?" cried Pencroff, so utterly astonished that he could not even finish his sentence.

"We never left Granite House," replied Cyrus Smith, "and if a fire appeared on the coast, it was some other hand than ours that lit it!"

Pencroff, Harbert and Nab were dumbfounded. There could have been no illusion: a fire really had struck their eyes during that night of October 19 to 20!

Yes! They had to admit it: a mystery existed! An inexplicable influence — clearly well disposed toward the colonists, but highly provoking to their curiosity — was making itself felt on Lincoln Island, and always, it seemed, at exactly the right moment. Was there, then, some being hidden in its deepest retreats? That was what they would have to find out, at any cost!

Cyrus Smith also reminded his companions of the odd behavior of Top and Jup when they used to prowl around the mouth of the well that connected Granite House with the sea, and he told them that he had explored that well without discovering anything suspicious. In the end, the conclusion of this conversation was a decision, taken by every member of the colony, to search the whole island from end to end as soon as the fine season returned.

But from that day on, Pencroff seemed troubled. This island, which he had made into his own personal property, no longer seemed to belong to him entirely. It seemed to him that he shared it with another master, to whom, like it or not, he felt himself subject. He and Nab often talked about these inexplicable things, and both of them, being much inclined by their very natures to believe in marvels, were not far from thinking that Lincoln Island was under the rule of some supernatural power.

Meanwhile the bad days had come with the month of May — the November of the northern latitudes. The winter looked likely to be hard and to come early. So the work of preparing for winter was taken in hand without delay.

Besides, the colonists were well prepared to meet this winter, however hard it might be. They had no shortage of felt clothing, and the mouflons, numerous by then, had supplied plenty of the wool needed to make that warm cloth.

It goes without saying that Ayrton had been given these comfortable clothes too. Cyrus Smith offered to let him come and spend the bad season at Granite House, where he would be better housed than at the corral, and Ayrton promised to do so as soon as the last jobs at the corral were finished. This he did around the middle of April. From then on Ayrton shared the common life and made himself useful at every opportunity; but always humble and sad, he never took part in his companions' pleasures!

For most of this third winter the colonists spent on Lincoln Island, they stayed shut up in Granite House. There were very great storms and terrible squalls that seemed to shake the rocks to their very foundations. Immense tidal surges threatened to sweep right over the island, and any ship anchored off its shores would certainly have been lost with all hands. Twice during one of these storms the Mercy rose so high that they feared the bridge and the little bridges would be carried away, and they even had to strengthen the ones on the beach, which vanished under the water whenever the sea beat against the shore.

You can well imagine that such gales, as violent as waterspouts and full of mingled rain and snow, did damage on Prospect Plateau. The mill and the poultry yard suffered particularly. The colonists often had to make urgent repairs there, or the lives of the birds would have been seriously threatened.

In these spells of really bad weather, a few pairs of jaguars and bands of monkeys would venture right up to the edge of the plateau, and there was always the fear that the nimblest and boldest of them, driven by hunger, would manage to get across the creek — which, besides, gave them an easy crossing when it was frozen. Crops and domestic animals would then have been destroyed without fail if not for a constant watch, and they often had to open fire to keep these dangerous visitors at a respectful distance. So the winterers never ran short of work, for besides the jobs outdoors there were always a thousand things to fit out and improve in Granite House.

There were also some fine hunts, made in the hard frosts on the vast Shelduck Marsh. Gédéon Spilett and Harbert, helped by Jup and Top, never wasted a shot among those myriads of ducks, snipe, teal, pintails and lapwings. Getting to that rich hunting ground was easy, too, either by going along the Balloon Harbor road after crossing the bridge over the Mercy, or by going around the rocks of Jetsam Point, and the hunters never went more than two or three miles from Granite House.

So the four months of winter passed — and they were truly harsh: June, July, August and September. But all in all, Granite House did not suffer too much from the bad weather. The same was true of the corral, which, being less exposed than the plateau and largely sheltered by Mount Franklin, caught only the tail ends of the gales, already broken by the forests and the high rocks of the coast. So the damage there was slight, and Ayrton's busy, skillful hands were enough to repair it quickly when, in the second half of October, he went back to spend a few days at the corral.

During this winter no new inexplicable incident occurred. Nothing strange happened, although Pencroff and Nab were on the lookout for the smallest events they might have been able to link to a mysterious cause. Even Top and Jup no longer prowled around the well, and gave no sign of uneasiness. So it seemed that the series of supernatural incidents had been interrupted, although they often talked about them during the evenings at Granite House, and it remained firmly agreed that the island would be searched down to its hardest-to-explore corners. But an event of the gravest kind, whose consequences might be disastrous, came along to turn Cyrus Smith and his companions away from their plans for a while.

It was October. The fine season was coming back fast. Nature was renewing herself under the rays of the sun, and amid the evergreen foliage of the conifers that lined the edge of the woods, the new leaves of the nettle trees, banksias and deodars were already appearing.

You will remember that Gédéon Spilett and Harbert had several times taken photographic views of Lincoln Island.

Now, on October 17, at about three o'clock in the afternoon, Harbert, tempted by the clearness of the sky, had the idea of photographing the whole of Union Bay, which lay facing Prospect Plateau, from Mandible Cape to Claw Cape.

The horizon stood out beautifully sharp, and the sea, gently rippling under a soft breeze, lay as still in the distance as the waters of a lake, flecked here and there with sparkles of light.

The camera had been set up at one of the windows of the great hall of Granite House, and so it looked down over the beach and the bay. Harbert went about it as he usually did, and once he had his negative on its glass plate, he went to fix it with the chemicals that were kept in a dark little closet of Granite House.

When he came back out into full daylight and examined it carefully, Harbert noticed on the plate a little, almost invisible dot that marked the sea horizon. He tried to make it disappear by washing it again and again, but he could not manage it.

"It's a flaw in the glass," he thought.

And then he was curious enough to examine this flaw with a strong lens, which he unscrewed from one of the telescopes.

But he had hardly looked when he let out a cry, and the plate nearly slipped from his hands.

Running at once to the room where Cyrus Smith was, he held out the plate and the lens to the engineer and pointed to the little spot.

Cyrus Smith examined the dot. Then, seizing his spyglass, he rushed to the window.

The spyglass swept slowly along the horizon and finally stopped on the suspicious point, and Cyrus Smith, lowering it, said only one word:

"A ship!"

And indeed, a ship was in sight of Lincoln Island!

Part Three: The Secret of the Island

Chapter 1: Ruin or Rescue?

Ruin or rescue? — Ayrton called back — An important discussion — It is not the Duncan — A suspicious ship — Precautions to take — The ship approaches — A cannon shot — The brig anchors in sight of the island — Night falls

For two and a half years the castaways of the balloon had been stranded on Lincoln Island, and in all that time no contact of any kind had been made between them and the rest of humankind. Once, the reporter had tried to get in touch with the inhabited world by entrusting a bird with a note that held the secret of their situation, but that was a chance no one could seriously count on. Only Ayrton, under the circumstances we know, had come to join the members of the little colony. And now, on this very day — October 17 — other men had suddenly appeared within sight of the island, on that sea which was always empty!

There could be no more doubt about it! A ship was out there! But would she pass by out at sea, or would she put in? Within a few hours the colonists would certainly know where they stood.

Cyrus Smith and Harbert had at once called Gédéon Spilett, Pencroff and Nab into the great hall of Granite House and told them what was happening. Pencroff snatched up the spyglass and swept the horizon quickly, then stopped on the point they showed him — the spot that had made the almost invisible speck on the photographic plate.

"A thousand devils! It's a ship, all right!" he said, in a voice that did not sound especially pleased.

"Is she coming toward us?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"No way of telling yet," answered Pencroff, "because only her masts show above the horizon. You can't see a scrap of her hull!"

"What should we do?" said the boy.

"Wait," answered Cyrus Smith.

And for a good long while the colonists stayed silent, given over to all the thoughts, all the emotions, all the fears, all the hopes that such an event could stir in them — the most serious thing that had happened since they had arrived on Lincoln Island.

Of course, the colonists were not in the position of those castaways left on some barren islet, who fight a cruel, stepmotherly nature for their miserable existence and are eaten up, every moment, by the longing to see inhabited lands again. Pencroff and Nab above all, who found themselves so happy and so rich at once, would not have left their island without regret. Besides, they had grown used to this new life, in the middle of this domain that their intelligence had, so to speak, civilized! But still — that ship meant news from the mainland, in any case. Perhaps it was a piece of their homeland coming out to meet them! She carried human beings like themselves, and anyone will understand how their hearts leaped at the sight of her!

Every so often Pencroff took up the spyglass again and stationed himself at the window. From there he studied the ship with the closest attention. She was twenty miles to the east, so the colonists still had no way at all to signal that they were there. A flag would not have been seen, a gunshot would not have been heard, a fire would not have been visible.

Still, it was certain that the island, with Mount Franklin towering over it, could not have escaped the eyes of the lookouts on board. But why would the ship land there? Wasn't it pure chance that had brought her into this part of the Pacific, where the charts showed no land at all except Tabor Island — and Tabor Island itself lay off the routes that ocean-going ships usually followed from the Polynesian archipelagos, New Zealand and the American coast?

The question everyone was asking himself was suddenly answered by Harbert.

"Could it be the Duncan?" he cried.

The Duncan, as no one will have forgotten, was the yacht of Lord Glenarvan, who had left Ayrton on the islet and who was supposed to come back for him one day. And the islet was not so far from Lincoln Island that a ship sailing for the one could not pass within sight of the other. Only a hundred and fifty miles of longitude separated them, and seventy-five miles of latitude.

"We must let Ayrton know," said Gédéon Spilett, "and send for him right away. He's the only one who can tell us if that's the Duncan."

Everyone agreed, and the reporter went to the telegraph that connected the corral with Granite House and sent this telegram:

"Come as fast as you can."

A few moments later the bell rang.

"I'm coming," Ayrton answered.

Then the colonists went on watching the ship.

"If it's the Duncan," said Harbert, "Ayrton will recognize her easily, since he sailed aboard her for a while."

"And if he does recognize her," added Pencroff, "it'll give him quite a shock!"

"Yes," answered Cyrus Smith, "but Ayrton is worthy now of going back aboard the Duncan, and heaven grant that it really is Lord Glenarvan's yacht, because any other ship would look suspicious to me! These seas have a bad reputation, and I'm always afraid our island will get a visit from Malay pirates."

"We'd defend it!" cried Harbert.

"No doubt, my boy," the engineer answered with a smile, "but it's better not to have to."

"Just one observation," said Gédéon Spilett. "Lincoln Island is unknown to sailors, since it isn't even marked on the most recent charts. Don't you think, Cyrus, that that's a reason for a ship that suddenly finds herself in sight of a new land to try to visit it rather than run away from it?"

"Certainly," answered Pencroff.

"I think so too," added the engineer. "You could even say that it's a captain's duty to report — and therefore to come and survey — any land or island not yet on the lists, and Lincoln Island is exactly that."

"Well, then," said Pencroff, "let's suppose this ship comes in and anchors there, a few cable lengths off our island. What do we do?"

The question, put so bluntly, at first got no answer. But Cyrus Smith, after thinking it over, replied in the calm tone that was usual with him:

"Here is what we'll do, my friends — what we ought to do.
