We'll make contact with the ship, we'll take passage aboard her, and we'll leave our island, after taking possession of it in the name of the States of the Union. Then we'll come back with everyone who wants to follow us, to colonize it for good and give the American republic a useful station in this part of the Pacific Ocean!"

"Hurrah!" cried Pencroff. "And that'll be no small present we'll be making our country! The colonizing is nearly finished already. Every part of the island has its name. There's a natural harbor, a watering place, roads, a telegraph line, a shipyard, a factory — and all that's left is to put Lincoln Island on the map!"

"But what if somebody takes it from us while we're away?" Gédéon Spilett pointed out.

"A thousand devils!" cried the sailor. "Then I'll stay here all by myself to guard it, and on Pencroff's word, nobody's going to steal it from me like a watch out of some gawker's pocket!"

For an hour it was impossible to say for certain whether the ship they had sighted was or was not heading for Lincoln Island. She had come nearer, though — but on what point of sail? That was something Pencroff could not make out. Still, since the wind was blowing from the northeast, it seemed likely that she was sailing on the starboard tack. Besides, the breeze was right for carrying her in toward the island's shores, and in so calm a sea she had no reason to be afraid of coming close, even though no soundings for those waters were marked on the chart.

At about four o'clock — an hour after he had been sent for — Ayrton arrived at Granite House. He came into the great hall, saying:

"At your service, gentlemen."

Cyrus Smith held out his hand to him, as he always did, and led him over to the window.

"Ayrton," he said, "we've asked you to come for a serious reason. There's a ship in sight of the island."

At first Ayrton went a little pale, and for a moment his eyes clouded. Then he leaned out of the window and swept the horizon, but he saw nothing.

"Take this spyglass," said Gédéon Spilett, "and look carefully, Ayrton, because this ship might be the Duncan, come into these seas to take you home."

"The Duncan!" Ayrton murmured. "Already!"

That last word slipped from Ayrton's lips as though in spite of himself, and he let his head fall into his hands.

So twelve years of abandonment on a desert islet did not seem to him atonement enough? Did the repentant man still not feel forgiven, either in his own eyes or in the eyes of others?

"No," he said, "no! It can't be the Duncan."

"Look, Ayrton," said the engineer then, "because it matters that we know ahead of time where we stand."

Ayrton took the glass and trained it in the direction they showed him. For several minutes he watched the horizon without moving, without saying a single word. Then:

"It's a ship, right enough," he said, "but I don't believe it's the Duncan."

"Why not?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"Because the Duncan is a steam yacht, and I can't see any trace of smoke, either above that ship or near her."

"Maybe she's just under sail," Pencroff pointed out. "The wind's good for the course she seems to be on, and she'd want to save her coal, being so far from any land."

"You may be right, Mr. Pencroff," answered Ayrton, "and she may have let her fires go out. So let's wait for her to come in toward the coast, and we'll soon know where we stand."

With that, Ayrton went and sat down in a corner of the great hall and stayed there in silence. The colonists went on discussing the unknown ship, but Ayrton took no part in the discussion.

They were all in a state of mind that would not have let them carry on with their work. Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff were strangely on edge, coming and going, unable to keep still. Harbert felt curiosity more than anything. Nab alone kept his usual calm. Wasn't his country wherever his master was? As for the engineer, he remained lost in thought, and deep down he dreaded the ship's arrival more than he wished for it.

Meanwhile the ship had come a little closer to the island. With the help of the spyglass they had been able to make out that she was an ocean-going vessel, and not one of the Malay proas that the pirates of the Pacific usually sail in. So there was reason to believe that the engineer's fears would not turn out to be justified, and that this ship's presence in the waters of Lincoln Island meant no danger to it. Pencroff, after studying her with minute attention, felt he could say for certain that she was rigged as a brig, and that she was running at a slant to the coast on the starboard tack, under her courses, her topsails and her topgallants. Ayrton confirmed it.

But if she kept on that way she would soon disappear behind the tip of Claw Cape, because she was heading southwest, and to watch her then they would have to go up onto the heights above Washington Bay, near Balloon Harbor. That was a nuisance, since it was already five o'clock in the afternoon, and twilight would soon make any observation very difficult.

"What do we do once night comes?" asked Gédéon Spilett. "Do we light a fire to signal that we're here on this coast?"

It was a serious question, and yet, whatever forebodings the engineer still had, it was settled in favor of the fire. During the night the ship might vanish, sail off for good — and once she was gone, would another ever come back into the waters of Lincoln Island? And who could foresee what the future held for the colonists?

"Yes," said the reporter, "we have to let this ship know, whatever she is, that the island is inhabited. If we let this chance slip, we'll be making regrets for ourselves later!"

So it was decided that Nab and Pencroff would go to Balloon Harbor, and that there, once night had fallen, they would light a big fire whose blaze would be sure to catch the attention of the brig's crew.

But just as Nab and the sailor were getting ready to leave Granite House, the ship changed course, bore away and headed straight for the island, making for Union Bay. She was a fast sailer, that brig, for she drew near quickly.

So Nab and Pencroff put off their departure, and the spyglass was handed to Ayrton so that he could say once and for all whether this ship was or was not the Duncan. The Scottish yacht was rigged as a brig too. The question, then, was whether a funnel rose between the two masts of the ship they were watching, which was now only ten miles away.

The horizon was still very clear. The check was easy, and Ayrton soon let the glass drop, saying:

"It isn't the Duncan! It couldn't have been!..."

Pencroff framed the brig in the field of the spyglass once more, and he saw that she was a vessel of three to four hundred tons, wonderfully slender, boldly masted, beautifully built for speed — she had to be a swift runner of the seas. But what nation did she belong to? That was hard to say.

"And yet," added the sailor, "there's a flag flying from her gaff, but I can't make out the colors."

"Within half an hour we'll know about that," answered the reporter. "Anyway, it's obvious that this ship's captain means to put in here, and so, if not today, then tomorrow at the latest, we'll be making his acquaintance."

"Never mind that!" said Pencroff. "It's better to know who you're dealing with, and I wouldn't mind knowing that fellow's colors!"

And all the while he talked, the sailor never took his eye from the glass.

The daylight was beginning to fade, and with it the wind from the sea was dropping too. The brig's flag, no longer stretched out, kept tangling in the halyards and grew harder and harder to see.

"That's not an American flag," Pencroff kept saying every now and then, "and not an English one either — you'd see the red easily — and not French or German colors, and not the white flag of Russia, and not the yellow of Spain... It looks as if it's all one color... Let's see... in these seas... what would we be most likely to meet?... The Chilean flag? But that's three colors... Brazilian? That's green... Japanese? That's black and yellow... whereas this one..."

At that moment a breeze spread out the unknown flag. Ayrton seized the spyglass the sailor had let drop, put it to his eye, and in a hollow voice:

"The black flag!" he cried.

And in fact a dark bunting was unfurling at the brig's gaff, and now there was every reason to regard her as a suspicious ship!

Had the engineer been right in his forebodings, then? Was this a pirate ship? Was she scouring these lower seas of the Pacific, in competition with the Malay proas that still infest them? What had she come looking for off the shores of Lincoln Island? Did she see in it an unknown, unheard-of land, just the place to hide stolen cargoes? Had she come to these coasts for a harbor of refuge in the winter months? Was the colonists' honest domain destined to turn into a vile den — a sort of capital of piracy in the Pacific?

All these ideas came into the colonists' minds by instinct. Besides, there could be no doubt what the color of the flag she flew was meant to signify. It was the flag of the sea raiders, all right! It was the one the Duncan would have been flying if the convicts had succeeded in their criminal plans!

They wasted no time in discussion.

"My friends," said Cyrus Smith, "perhaps this ship means only to look over the island's coastline. Perhaps her crew won't come ashore. That's one chance. Whatever happens, we must do everything we can to hide the fact that we're here. The windmill on Prospect Plateau is far too easy to spot. Ayrton and Nab, go and take its sails down. Let's also cover the windows of Granite House with thicker branches. Put out every fire. Let nothing at all betray that there are human beings on this island!"

"And our boat?" said Harbert.

"Oh," answered Pencroff, "she's sheltered in Balloon Harbor, and I defy those scoundrels to find her there!"

The engineer's orders were carried out at once. Nab and Ayrton went up onto the plateau and took the steps needed to hide every sign that anyone lived there. While they were busy with that job, their companions went to the edge of Jacamar Wood and brought back a great quantity of branches and creepers which, seen from a certain distance, would look like natural foliage and would screen the openings in the granite wall quite well. At the same time the ammunition and the weapons were laid out so that they could be used at a moment's notice in case of a sudden attack.

When all these precautions had been taken:

"My friends," said Cyrus Smith — and you could hear in his voice how moved he was — "if those villains try to seize Lincoln Island, we'll defend it, won't we?"

"Yes, Cyrus," answered the reporter, "and if we have to, we'll all die defending it!"

The engineer held out his hand to his companions, and they gripped it warmly.

Only Ayrton, who had stayed in his corner, had not joined the colonists. Perhaps he, the former convict, still felt unworthy!

Cyrus Smith understood what was going on in Ayrton's soul, and he went over to him.

"And you, Ayrton," he asked him, "what will you do?"

"My duty," answered Ayrton.

Then he went and took up his post by the window and fixed his gaze out through the leaves.

It was half past seven by then. The sun had gone down behind Granite House some twenty minutes before, and so the eastern horizon was slowly darkening. Meanwhile the brig kept on toward Union Bay. She was no more than eight miles off by then, and exactly abreast of Prospect Plateau, because after coming about off Claw Cape she had made a good deal of ground to the north, helped along by the current of the rising tide. You could even say that at that distance she had already entered the vast bay, since a straight line drawn from Claw Cape to Mandible Cape now lay to the west of her, off her starboard quarter.

Would the brig sail deep into the bay? That was the first question. Once inside, would she anchor there? That was the second. Or would she be content to look over the coastline and then head back out to sea without landing her crew? They would know within the hour. So the colonists had nothing to do but wait.

Cyrus Smith had watched the suspicious ship hoist the black flag with deep anxiety. Wasn't it a direct threat to the work that he and his companions had carried through so far? Had these pirates — for there could be no doubt the brig's sailors were that — been to the island before, since they had run up their colors on approaching it? Had they made some landing here in the past, which would explain certain things that had remained inexplicable until now? Was there, in some part of the island not yet explored, an accomplice ready to make contact with them?

Cyrus Smith had no answer to any of the questions he silently asked himself, but he felt that the colony's situation could only be very seriously endangered by the arrival of this brig.

All the same, he and his companions were determined to resist to the very last. Were these pirates many, and better armed than the colonists? That was what it would have been so important to know! But how to get near them?

Night had come. The new moon, lost in the glare of the sun, had gone down with it. Deep darkness wrapped the island and the sea. Heavy clouds, heaped up on the horizon, let no glimmer of light filter through. The wind had died away completely with the dusk. Not a leaf stirred on the trees, not a wave whispered on the shore. Of the ship nothing could be seen. All her lights were blacked out, and if she was still in sight of the island, there was no way even to tell where she lay.

"Eh! Who knows?" said Pencroff then. "Maybe that damned ship will sail off during the night, and we won't find her again at daybreak!"

As if in answer to the sailor's remark, a bright flash burst out at sea, and a cannon shot rang out.

The ship was still there, and she had guns on board.

Six seconds had passed between the flash and the sound.

So the brig was about a mile and a quarter from the coast.

And at the same moment they heard the sound of chains running and grinding through the hawseholes.

The ship had just dropped anchor in sight of Granite House!

Chapter 2: Six Against Fifty

Discussions — Forebodings — A proposal from Ayrton — It is accepted — Ayrton and Pencroff on Grant Islet — The convicts of Norfolk Island — Their plans — Ayrton's heroic attempt — His return — Six against fifty

There could be no more doubt about the pirates' intentions. They had dropped anchor a short distance from the island, and it was plain that the next day they meant to come ashore in their boats!

Cyrus Smith and his companions were ready to act, but however determined they were, they must not forget to be careful. Perhaps their presence could still be kept hidden, if the pirates were content to land on the shore without going up into the interior of the island. It was quite possible, after all, that they had no other plan than to take on fresh water at the watering place at the mouth of the Mercy, and it was not impossible that the bridge, a mile and a half upstream, and the fittings of the Chimneys might escape their notice.

But why had that flag been run up to the brig's gaff? Why that cannon shot? Pure bravado, no doubt — unless it was a sign that they were taking possession! Cyrus Smith now knew that the ship was formidably armed. And what did the colonists of Lincoln Island have to answer the pirates' cannon? A few guns, nothing more.

"All the same," Cyrus Smith pointed out, "here we're in a position no one can take. The enemy can't find the mouth of the old spillway now that it's hidden under reeds and grass, so there's no way for them to get into Granite House."

"But our plantings, our poultry yard, our corral — everything, everything!" cried Pencroff, stamping his foot. "They can lay it all waste, wreck it all in a few hours!"

"Everything, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith, "and we have no way of stopping them."

"Are there many of them? That's the question," said the reporter then. "If there are only a dozen, we'll know how to stop them. But forty, fifty, maybe more!..."

"Mr. Smith," said Ayrton, stepping up to the engineer, "will you give me permission for something?"

"For what, my friend?"

"To go out to that ship and find out how strong her crew is."

"But, Ayrton..." the engineer answered, hesitating, "you'd be risking your life..."

"Why not, sir?"

"That's more than your duty."

"I have more than my duty to do," answered Ayrton.

"You'd take the canoe out to the ship?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"No, sir. I'll swim. The canoe couldn't get through where a man can slip along just under the surface."

"Do you realize the brig is a mile and a quarter from the coast?" said Harbert.

"I'm a good swimmer, Mr. Harbert."

"It's risking your life, I tell you," the engineer said again.

"That doesn't matter," answered Ayrton. "Mr. Smith, I'm asking this of you as a favor. It may be a way for me to rise again in my own eyes!"

"Go, Ayrton," answered the engineer, who felt that a refusal would have hurt the former convict deeply — the convict who had become an honest man again.

"I'll come with you," said Pencroff.

"You don't trust me!" Ayrton answered sharply.

Then, more humbly:

"Alas!"

"No! No!" Cyrus Smith broke in warmly. "No, Ayrton! Pencroff doesn't distrust you! You've misunderstood him."

"That's right," answered the sailor. "What I'm proposing is to go with Ayrton as far as the islet, and no farther. It's possible — not likely, but possible — that one of those rascals has landed there, and if so, two men won't be too many to keep him from raising the alarm. I'll wait for Ayrton on the islet, and he'll go on to the ship alone, since that's what he offered to do."

With that settled, Ayrton got ready to go. His plan was daring, but it could succeed, thanks to the darkness of the night. Once he reached the ship, Ayrton could hang on to the bobstays under the bowsprit or to the chainplates where the shrouds were fastened along her side, and from there he could count the convicts and perhaps overhear what they meant to do.

Ayrton and Pencroff went down to the shore, followed by their companions. Ayrton undressed and rubbed himself with grease, so as to suffer less from the water, which was still cold. He might, after all, have to stay in it for several hours.

Meanwhile Pencroff and Nab had gone to fetch the canoe, which was moored a few hundred paces farther up, on the bank of the Mercy, and by the time they came back Ayrton was ready to leave.

A blanket was thrown over Ayrton's shoulders, and the colonists came up to shake his hand.

Ayrton got into the canoe with Pencroff.

It was half past ten at night when the two of them disappeared into the darkness. Their companions went back to the Chimneys to wait for them.

They crossed the channel easily, and the canoe came in to land on the far shore of the islet. They did this with some care, in case pirates were prowling about there. But after a good look around, it seemed certain that the islet was deserted. So Ayrton, with Pencroff behind him, crossed it at a quick pace, startling the birds that nested in the holes in the rocks. Then, without a moment's hesitation, he threw himself into the sea and swam noiselessly toward the ship, whose exact position was now marked by a few lights that had been lit not long before.

As for Pencroff, he crouched in a hollow in the rocks along the shore and waited for his companion to come back.

Meanwhile Ayrton swam with powerful strokes, gliding through the water without making even the faintest ripple. His head barely broke the surface, and his eyes were fixed on the dark mass of the brig, whose lights were reflected in the sea. He thought only of the duty he had promised to carry out, and gave no thought at all to the dangers he was running — not only on board the ship, but in these very waters, where sharks often came. The current was carrying him, and he was moving quickly away from the coast.

Half an hour later, without having been seen or heard, Ayrton slipped in under the surface, reached the ship, and caught hold of the bowsprit's bobstays with one hand. Then he got his breath back, and, pulling himself up by the chains, he managed to reach the very tip of the brig's head, the beak that juts out beneath the bowsprit. A few pairs of sailors' trousers were hanging there to dry. He pulled on a pair. Then, having wedged himself in firmly, he listened.

No one was asleep on board the brig. Quite the opposite. They were arguing, singing, laughing. And these were the remarks, mixed with oaths, that struck Ayrton most:

"Fine bargain we got in this brig!"

"She sails well, the Speedy! She lives up to her name!"

"The whole Norfolk navy can come chasing after her! Let 'em try!"

"Hurrah for her commander!"

"Hurrah for Bob Harvey!"

What Ayrton felt when he heard this scrap of conversation will be understood once it is known that in this Bob Harvey he had just recognized one of his old companions from Australia, a bold seaman who had taken up his own criminal schemes where Ayrton had left them off. Bob Harvey had seized this brig in the waters around Norfolk Island. She had been loaded with weapons, ammunition, utensils and tools of every kind, bound for one of the Sandwich Islands — what we now call Hawaii. His whole gang had gone aboard, and, pirates now after being convicts, these wretches were scouring the Pacific, destroying ships and massacring their crews, fiercer even than the Malay pirates!

The convicts were talking loudly, boasting of their exploits as they drank far more than they should, and this is what Ayrton was able to make out:

The Speedy's present crew was made up entirely of English prisoners who had escaped from Norfolk Island.

And here is what Norfolk Island is.

At latitude 29° 2′ south and longitude 165° 42′ east, to the east of Australia, lies a small island some fifteen miles around, overlooked by Mount Pitt, which rises eleven hundred feet above sea level. That is Norfolk Island, which has become the seat of a penal settlement where the most unmanageable convicts from the English prisons are penned up. There are five hundred of them there, held under iron discipline and the threat of terrible punishments, guarded by a hundred and fifty soldiers and a hundred and fifty officials under the orders of a governor. It would be hard to imagine a worse gathering of villains. Now and then — though it is rare — in spite of the extreme watch kept over them, a number of them manage to escape by seizing ships they take by surprise, and then they roam the island groups of Polynesia.

That is what this Bob Harvey and his companions had done. That is what Ayrton himself had once wanted to do. Bob Harvey had seized the brig Speedy while she lay at anchor in sight of Norfolk Island. Her crew had been massacred, and for a year now the ship, turned pirate vessel, had been beating about the seas of the Pacific under the command of Harvey — once a deep-sea merchant captain, now a sea robber, and a man Ayrton knew well!

Most of the convicts were gathered in the poop, the raised cabin at the stern of the ship, but a few were stretched out on the deck, talking loudly.

As the conversation went on amid shouting and drinking, Ayrton learned that it was pure chance that had brought the Speedy within sight of Lincoln Island.

Bob Harvey had never yet set foot on it. But, just as Cyrus Smith had guessed, when he came across this unknown land in his path, whose position no chart showed, he had made up his mind to look it over, and, if it suited him, to make it the brig's home port.

As for the black flag run up to the Speedy's gaff, and the cannon shot fired, the way warships fire a gun when they hoist their colors — that was pure pirates' bravado. It was not a signal, and as yet there was no connection of any kind between the escaped Norfolk convicts and Lincoln Island.

So the colonists' domain was threatened by an immense danger. Clearly the island — with its easy watering place, its little harbor, its resources of every kind that the colonists had put to such good use, and the hidden depths of Granite House — could only suit the convicts down to the ground. In their hands it would become an excellent hiding place, and, precisely because it was unknown, it would guarantee them safety and freedom from punishment, perhaps for a long time. Clearly, too, the colonists' lives would not be spared, and the first thing Bob Harvey and his accomplices would do would be to massacre them without mercy. So Cyrus Smith and his people did not even have the option of running away and hiding somewhere on the island, since the convicts meant to live there, and since, even if the Speedy left on some raid, a few of her crew would probably stay ashore to settle in. So they would have to fight. They would have to destroy these wretches to the last man — wretches unworthy of pity, against whom any means would be fair.

That was what Ayrton thought, and he knew very well that Cyrus Smith would see it the same way.

But was resistance possible — and, in the end, was victory? That depended on how the brig was armed and how many men she carried.

That was what Ayrton made up his mind to find out at any cost. An hour after he arrived, the bellowing had begun to die down, and a good many of the convicts were already sunk in a drunken sleep. So Ayrton did not hesitate to venture onto the Speedy's deck, which was now in deep darkness, since her lanterns had been put out.

He hauled himself up onto the beak, then made his way along the bowsprit to the brig's forecastle. Slipping between the convicts sprawled here and there, he went all the way around the ship, and found that the Speedy was armed with four cannon that must fire balls of eight to ten pounds. He even made sure, by feeling them, that they were breech-loaders. So these were modern guns, easy to handle and terrible in their effect.

As for the men lying on deck, there must have been about ten of them, but it was reasonable to suppose that others, many more, were asleep below. Besides, from listening to them, Ayrton had gathered that there were about fifty on board. That was a great many for the six colonists of Lincoln Island! But at least, thanks to Ayrton's devotion, Cyrus Smith would not be taken by surprise. He would know the strength of his enemies, and he would make his arrangements accordingly.

So all that was left for Ayrton was to go back and report to his companions on the mission he had taken on, and he got ready to make his way back to the bow of the brig so as to slip down into the sea.

But then, to this man who wanted — he had said so — to do more than his duty, there came a heroic thought. It meant sacrificing his life, but he would save the island and the colonists. Cyrus Smith plainly could not hold out against fifty bandits armed to the teeth, who would get the better of the colonists either by breaking into Granite House by force or by starving them out. And then he pictured his rescuers — the people who had made him a man again, and an honest man, the people to whom he owed everything — killed without pity, their work destroyed, their island turned into a pirates' den! He told himself that he, Ayrton, was when all was said and done the root cause of so much disaster, since his old companion Bob Harvey had only carried out Ayrton's own plans — and a feeling of horror seized his whole being. Then he was gripped by an irresistible urge to blow up the brig, and with her everyone she carried. Ayrton would die in the explosion, but he would have done his duty.

Ayrton did not hesitate. Getting to the powder magazine, which is always located at the stern of a ship, would be easy. A ship in that line of work could not be short of powder, and a single spark would be enough to destroy her in an instant.

Ayrton let himself down carefully to the lower deck, which was strewn with sleepers held heavy more by drink than by sleep. A lantern was burning at the foot of the mainmast, and around the mast hung a rack filled with firearms of every kind.

Ayrton took a revolver from the rack and made sure it was loaded and primed. He needed nothing more to carry out the work of destruction. So he crept toward the stern, so as to get beneath the brig's poop, where the magazine had to be.

But on that lower deck, which was almost pitch-dark, it was hard to crawl along without bumping into some convict who was not quite asleep. Then came curses and blows. More than once Ayrton had to stop and wait. But at last he reached the bulkhead that closed off the stern compartment, and he found the door that must open onto the magazine itself.

Ayrton had no choice but to force it, and he set to work. It was a hard job to do without noise, because it meant breaking a padlock. But under Ayrton's powerful hand the padlock snapped, and the door was open...

At that moment a hand came down on Ayrton's shoulder.

"What are you doing there?" a tall man demanded in a harsh voice, rising up out of the shadows and thrusting a lantern sharply into Ayrton's face.

Ayrton threw himself backward. In a quick flash of the lantern he had recognized his old accomplice, Bob Harvey. But Harvey could not recognize him, since he must have believed Ayrton dead long ago.

"What are you doing there?" said Bob Harvey, seizing Ayrton by the waistband of his trousers.

But Ayrton, without answering, shoved the convicts' leader violently away and tried to dash into the magazine. One revolver shot among those kegs of powder, and it would all have been over!...

"To me, boys!" Bob Harvey had shouted.

Two or three pirates, woken by his voice, had got to their feet, and, throwing themselves on Ayrton, they tried to wrestle him to the floor. The powerful Ayrton broke free of their grip. Two shots from his revolver rang out, and two convicts fell; but a knife thrust that he could not ward off slashed into the flesh of his shoulder.

Ayrton understood that he could no longer carry out his plan. Bob Harvey had shut the magazine door again, and there was a stir on the lower deck that meant the whole pirate crew was waking up. Ayrton had to save himself to fight at Cyrus Smith's side. There was nothing left for him but to run!

But was escape still possible? That was doubtful, though Ayrton was determined to try everything to get back to his companions.

He had four shots left. He fired two of them now. One, aimed at Bob Harvey, did not hit him — or at least not seriously — and Ayrton, taking advantage of a moment when his attackers fell back, rushed for the companion ladder that led up to the brig's deck. As he passed the lantern he smashed it with a blow from the butt of his revolver, and a deep darkness fell, which was bound to help his escape.

Two or three pirates, woken by the noise, were coming down the ladder at that very moment. A fifth shot from Ayrton's revolver sent one of them tumbling down the steps, and the others drew back, not understanding what was going on. In two bounds Ayrton was on the brig's deck, and three seconds later, after firing his revolver one last time into the face of a pirate who had just grabbed him by the neck, he swung over the bulwarks and threw himself into the sea.

Ayrton had not swum six strokes before bullets were crackling around him like hail.

What must Pencroff have felt, sheltering under a rock on the islet — and Cyrus Smith, the reporter, Harbert and Nab, huddled in the Chimneys — when they heard those shots go off on board the brig! They had rushed out onto the beach, and, guns at their shoulders, they stood ready to drive back any attack.

For them there could be no doubt at all! Ayrton had been caught by the pirates and murdered, and perhaps those wretches were going to take advantage of the night to make a landing on the island!

Half an hour went by in mortal dread. The shots had stopped, though, and neither Ayrton nor Pencroff came back. Had the islet been invaded, then? Shouldn't they hurry to help Ayrton and Pencroff? But how? The sea, high at that moment, made the channel impossible to cross. The canoe was not there! Imagine the terrible anxiety that took hold of Cyrus Smith and his companions!

At last, toward half past midnight, a canoe carrying two men came in to the beach. It was Ayrton, slightly wounded in the shoulder, and Pencroff, safe and sound, and their friends received them with open arms.

At once they all took shelter in the Chimneys. There Ayrton told them what had happened, and he did not hide the plan he had tried to carry out, to blow up the brig.

Every hand reached out to Ayrton, who did not hide how grave the situation was. The pirates were on their guard now. They knew Lincoln Island was inhabited. They would land only in force and well armed. They would spare nothing. If the colonists fell into their hands, they could expect no mercy!

"Well, then! We'll know how to die!" said the reporter.

"Let's go in and keep watch," answered the engineer.

"Have we got any chance of coming out of this, Mr. Cyrus?" asked the sailor.

"Yes, Pencroff."

"Hm! Six against fifty!"

"Yes! Six!... Not counting..."

"Who, then?" asked Pencroff.

Cyrus did not answer, but he pointed to the sky.

Chapter 3: The Fog Lifts

The fog lifts — The engineer's plan — Three posts — Ayrton and Pencroff — The first boat — Two more boats — On the islet — Six convicts ashore — The brig weighs anchor — The Speedy's cannonballs — A desperate situation — An unexpected ending

The night passed without incident. The colonists had stayed on the alert and had not left their post at the Chimneys. The pirates, for their part, did not seem to have made any attempt to land. Since the last shots fired at Ayrton, not a gunshot, not even a sound, had given away the brig's presence off the island. One might almost have believed that she had weighed anchor, thinking she had met too strong an enemy, and had sailed away from those waters.

But nothing of the kind had happened, and when dawn began to break the colonists could make out a shapeless mass in the morning mist. It was the Speedy.

"My friends," the engineer said then, "here is the plan I think we ought to follow before this fog has lifted completely. It hides us from the pirates' eyes, and we can act without drawing their attention. What matters most is to make the convicts believe that the island has a good many inhabitants, and that those inhabitants are therefore able to fight them off. So I propose that we split into three groups. The first will take up its post right here at the Chimneys, the second at the mouth of the Mercy. As for the third, I think it would be wise to put it on the islet, to prevent any attempt at a landing, or at least to delay it. We have two carbines and four guns between us. So every one of us will be armed, and since we have plenty of powder and bullets, we won't spare our shots. We have nothing to fear from the brig's guns, or even from her cannon. What could they do against these rocks? And since we won't be firing from the windows of Granite House, the pirates won't think of sending shells there, where they might do damage that could never be repaired. What we must fear is having to fight hand to hand, because the convicts have numbers on their side. So it's every landing we must try to stop — but without showing ourselves. Let's not be sparing with our ammunition, then. Let's shoot often, but let's shoot straight. Each of us has eight or ten enemies to kill, and he must kill them!"

Cyrus Smith had laid out the situation in plain figures, speaking all the while in the calmest of voices, as if he were directing a piece of work and not a battle. His companions approved the plan without saying a word. All that was left was for each man to reach his post before the mist had completely cleared.

Nab and Pencroff went straight up to Granite House and brought down enough ammunition. Gédéon Spilett and Ayrton, both of them excellent shots, were given the two precision carbines, which could carry nearly a mile. The four other guns were shared out among Cyrus Smith, Nab, Pencroff and Harbert.

This is how the posts were manned.

Cyrus Smith and Harbert stayed hidden at the Chimneys, and from there they commanded a fairly wide stretch of the beach at the foot of Granite House.

Gédéon Spilett and Nab went to crouch among the rocks at the mouth of the Mercy — the bridge and the little bridges had all been raised — so as to stop any boat from getting through and even any landing on the opposite bank.

As for Ayrton and Pencroff, they pushed the canoe into the water and got ready to cross the channel and occupy two separate posts on the islet. In this way, shots ringing out from four different points would make the convicts think that the island was both well populated and fiercely defended.

If a landing was made that they could not prevent, or even if they saw themselves about to be cut off by one of the brig's boats, Pencroff and Ayrton were to come back in the canoe, regain the shore, and hurry to whichever spot was most threatened.

Before going to their posts, the colonists shook hands one last time. Pencroff managed to master himself enough to hold back his feelings as he hugged Harbert, his boy!... and they parted.

A few moments later Cyrus Smith and Harbert on one side, and the reporter and Nab on the other, had vanished behind the rocks, and five minutes after that Ayrton and Pencroff, having crossed the channel without mishap, landed on the islet and hid themselves in the hollows of its eastern shore.

None of them could have been seen, for they themselves could still barely make out the brig in the fog.

It was half past six in the morning.

Soon the fog began to tear apart, little by little, in the upper layers of the air, and the tops of the brig's masts rose out of the vapor. For a few moments more, great rolls of mist tumbled over the surface of the sea. Then a breeze sprang up and quickly scattered the whole bank of fog.

The Speedy appeared in full view, riding at two anchors with her bow to the north and her port quarter turned toward the island. Just as Cyrus Smith had estimated, she lay no more than a mile and a quarter from the shore.

The sinister black flag flew from her gaff.

Through his spyglass the engineer could see that the four cannon that made up her armament had been trained on the island. They were obviously ready to fire at the first signal.

Yet the Speedy stayed silent. Some thirty pirates could be seen coming and going on deck. A few had climbed onto the poop. Two others, perched on the main topgallant crosstrees with long telescopes, were studying the island with the closest attention.

Bob Harvey and his crew, certainly, could have had only a very confused idea of what had happened aboard the brig during the night. That half-naked man who had forced the door of the powder room, whom they had fought, who had emptied his revolver at them six times, who had killed one of their number and wounded two others — had he escaped their bullets? Had he managed to swim back to the coast? Where had he come from? What had he come aboard to do? Had he really meant to blow up the brig, as Bob Harvey believed? All of this must have been fairly muddled in the convicts' minds. But one thing they could no longer doubt: the unknown island off which the Speedy had dropped anchor was inhabited, and there might be a whole colony there ready to defend it. And yet nobody showed himself, either on the beach or on the heights. The shore seemed utterly deserted. In any case there was no sign of any dwelling. Had the inhabitants fled into the interior, then?

That was what the pirate chief must have been asking himself, and no doubt, being a cautious man, he wanted to scout the ground before he committed his gang to it.

For an hour and a half no sign of an attack or a landing could be caught aboard the brig. Bob Harvey was plainly hesitating. Even his best telescopes, no doubt, had not let him make out a single one of the colonists crouching in the rocks. It was not even likely that his attention had been caught by the screen of green branches and creepers that hid the windows of Granite House and stood out against the bare rock wall. After all, how could he have imagined that a dwelling had been hollowed out of the granite mass at that height? From Claw Cape all the way to the Mandible Capes, along the whole sweep of Union Bay, nothing could have told him that the island was occupied, or even could be.

At eight o'clock, however, the colonists noticed a certain stir aboard the Speedy. Men were hauling on the tackles of the boat davits, and a boat was being lowered into the sea. Seven men climbed down into it. They were armed with guns. One of them took the tiller, four took the oars, and the other two, crouching in the bow ready to fire, studied the island. Their aim, no doubt, was to make a first reconnaissance, not to land — for in that case they would have come in greater numbers.

The pirates perched in the rigging as high as the topgallant crosstrees must have been able to see that an islet lay in front of the coast, separated from it by a channel about half a mile wide. But it soon became clear to Cyrus Smith, watching the course the boat was taking, that it would not try to enter the channel at first. It would come alongside the islet instead — a prudent step, and a sensible one.

Pencroff and Ayrton, each hidden on his own in a narrow cleft in the rocks, saw it coming straight at them, and they waited until it was well within range.

The boat came on with extreme caution. The oars dipped into the water only at long intervals. One could see, too, that one of the convicts in the bow was holding a sounding line and was trying to find the channel scoured out by the current of the Mercy. That showed that Bob Harvey meant to bring his brig as close to the coast as he could. Some thirty pirates, scattered through the shrouds, did not miss a single movement of the boat, and they were taking bearings on certain landmarks that would let them come in to shore without danger.

The boat was no more than two cable lengths from the islet when it stopped. The man at the tiller, standing up, was looking for the best place to bring it in.

In an instant two shots rang out. A little puff of smoke swirled above the rocks of the islet. The man at the tiller and the man with the sounding line fell over backward into the boat. Ayrton's and Pencroff's bullets had struck them both at the same moment.

Almost at once a louder explosion was heard. A bright jet of smoke burst from the brig's side, and a cannonball struck the top of the rocks that sheltered Ayrton and Pencroff and sent splinters of stone flying — but neither of the two marksmen had been hit.

Horrible curses had broken out in the boat, which immediately got under way again. The man at the tiller was replaced at once by one of his comrades, and the oars bit sharply into the water.

But instead of going back to the ship, as one might have expected, the boat ran along the shore of the islet so as to round its southern point. The pirates were rowing hard to get out of range of the bullets.

In this way they went on as far as five cable lengths from the hollow in the coastline that ends at Jetsam Point. Then, after swinging round it in a half circle, still covered by the brig's cannon, they headed for the mouth of the Mercy.

Their obvious intention was to get into the channel this way and take the colonists posted on the islet from behind, so that, however many of them there were, they would be caught between the fire of the boat and the fire of the brig, in a very bad position indeed.

A quarter of an hour went by while the boat moved on in that direction. Absolute silence; perfect stillness in the air and on the water.

Pencroff and Ayrton understood that they were in danger of being cut off, yet they had not left their post. Perhaps they did not want to show themselves to the attackers yet and expose themselves to the Speedy's cannon; perhaps they were counting on Nab and Gédéon Spilett, keeping watch at the mouth of the river, and on Cyrus Smith and Harbert, lying in wait among the rocks of the Chimneys.

Twenty minutes after the first shots, the boat was abreast of the Mercy, less than two cable lengths off. The tide was starting to come in with its usual violence, made fiercer by the narrowness of the strait, and the convicts felt themselves being swept toward the river. Only by hard rowing did they manage to keep to the middle of the channel. But as they passed well within range of the mouth of the Mercy, two bullets greeted them on their way, and two more of them were laid flat in the boat. Nab and Spilett had not missed.

At once the brig sent a second cannonball at the post that the gun smoke had given away, but it did nothing more than chip a few rocks.

By now the boat held only three men still fit to fight. Caught by the current, it shot through the channel like an arrow and passed in front of Cyrus Smith and Harbert, who held their fire, judging it not well within range. Then, rounding the northern point of the islet with the two oars it had left, it made its way back toward the brig.

So far the colonists had no cause for complaint. The game was going badly for their enemies. The pirates already counted four men badly wounded, perhaps dead. The colonists, on the other hand, were without a scratch and had not wasted a single bullet. If the pirates kept attacking them this way, if they tried another landing by boat, they could be destroyed one by one.

It is easy to see how well chosen the engineer's plan had been. The pirates might well believe they were up against a large and well-armed enemy, one they would not easily overcome.

Half an hour passed before the boat, which had to fight the current running out to sea, got back to the Speedy. Dreadful shouts rang out when it came alongside with the wounded, and three or four cannon shots were fired that could not possibly have hit anything.

But then other convicts, drunk with rage — and perhaps still drunk from the night before — threw themselves into the boat, a dozen of them.

A second boat was lowered into the sea as well, and eight men took their places in it. While the first headed straight for the islet to drive the colonists out, the second maneuvered to force its way into the mouth of the Mercy.

The situation was obviously becoming very dangerous for Pencroff and Ayrton, and they understood that they had to get back to the mainland.

Still, they waited until the first boat was well within range, and two well-aimed bullets threw its crew into disorder once again. Then Pencroff and Ayrton left their post, not without drawing a dozen shots, ran across the islet as fast as their legs would carry them, threw themselves into the canoe, crossed the channel just as the second boat was reaching the islet's southern point, and ran to take cover in the Chimneys.

They had hardly rejoined Cyrus Smith and Harbert when the islet was overrun, and the pirates from the first boat were searching it from end to end.

Almost at the same moment, new shots broke out at the post on the Mercy, which the second boat had swiftly come up to. Two of the eight men in it were fatally hit by Gédéon Spilett and Nab, and the boat itself, swept helplessly onto the reefs, was smashed to pieces there at the mouth of the Mercy. But the six survivors, holding their weapons above their heads to keep them out of the water, managed to get a footing on the right bank of the river. Then, seeing that they were too close to the post's fire, they ran off as fast as they could toward Jetsam Point, out of range of the bullets.

So this was where things now stood. On the islet were twelve convicts, several of them no doubt wounded, but with a boat still at their disposal. On the island were six who had landed, but who had no way of reaching Granite House, since they could not cross the river, whose bridges were raised.

"It's going well!" Pencroff had said as he rushed into the Chimneys. "It's going well, Mr. Cyrus! What do you think?"

"I think," replied the engineer, "that the fight is about to take a new shape. We can't suppose these convicts are stupid enough to keep it up on terms so bad for them!"

"They still won't get across the channel," said the sailor. "Ayrton's and Mr. Spilett's carbines are there to stop them. You know they carry more than a mile!"

"No doubt," Harbert answered, "but what could two carbines do against the brig's cannon?"

"Ha! The brig isn't in the channel yet, I should think!" Pencroff replied.

"And if she comes in?" said Cyrus Smith.

"She can't. She'd risk running aground and being wrecked!"

"She can," Ayrton answered then. "The convicts can use the high tide to come into the channel, even if it means going aground at low tide. And then, under the fire of their cannon, our posts won't be worth holding."

"By all the thousand devils of hell!" cried Pencroff. "It really looks as if the scoundrels are getting ready to weigh anchor!"

"Maybe we'll be forced to take refuge in Granite House?" Harbert suggested.

"Let's wait!" replied Cyrus Smith.

"But Nab and Mr. Spilett?..." said Pencroff.

"They'll know how to join us in good time. Be ready, Ayrton. It's your carbine and Spilett's that must do the talking now."

It was only too true! The Speedy was beginning to swing round on her anchor and was showing that she meant to move closer to the islet. The tide would go on rising for another hour and a half, and since the flood current had already slackened, it would be easy for the brig to maneuver. But as for entering the channel, Pencroff, against Ayrton's opinion, could not believe that she would dare to try it.

Meanwhile the pirates who held the islet had gradually moved over to its far shore, and now only the channel separated them from the land. Armed with nothing but guns, they could do no harm to the colonists hidden either at the Chimneys or at the mouth of the Mercy. But since they did not know the colonists had long-range carbines, they did not think they were in any danger themselves either. So they walked about the islet in the open and paced along its edge.

Their mistake did not last long. Ayrton's and Gédéon Spilett's carbines spoke up then, and no doubt said something unpleasant to two of those convicts, for the two men fell over backward.

It was a general rout. The ten others did not even take the time to pick up their wounded or dead companions. They rushed back to the other side of the islet, threw themselves into the boat that had brought them, and rowed hard back to the ship.

"Eight fewer!" Pencroff had cried. "Honestly, you'd think Mr. Spilett and Ayrton had agreed to work as a team!"

"Gentlemen," Ayrton answered as he reloaded his carbine, "this is about to get more serious. The brig is getting under way!"

"The anchor's up and down!..." cried Pencroff.

"Yes, and it's already breaking out."

And indeed they could clearly hear the clank of the pawl striking against the windlass as the brig's crew hove in. At first the Speedy had moved up over her anchor. Then, once it had been torn out of the bottom, she began to drift toward the land. The wind was blowing in from the sea. The jib and the fore-topsail were hoisted, and the ship drew closer and closer to the shore.

From both posts, the Mercy and the Chimneys, they watched her maneuver without giving any sign of life — but not without a certain anxiety. The colonists' situation would be a terrible one once they were exposed, at short range, to the fire of the brig's cannon, with no means of answering it to any purpose. How could they stop the pirates from landing then?

Cyrus Smith felt this keenly, and he was asking himself what could be done. Before long he would have to make a decision. But what decision? Shut themselves up in Granite House, let themselves be besieged there, and hold out for weeks — for months, even — since there was food in plenty? Good! But after that? The pirates would be masters of the island all the same, free to lay it waste as they pleased, and in time they would get the better of the prisoners of Granite House.

Still, one chance remained: that Bob Harvey would not risk his ship in the channel and would keep to the outside of the islet. Half a mile would still separate him from the coast, and at that distance his shots might not do too much harm.

"Never," Pencroff kept saying, "never will that Bob Harvey come into the channel — not if he's a good seaman! He knows perfectly well he'd be risking the brig if the sea turned the least bit rough! And what would become of him without his ship?"

Yet the brig had come close to the islet, and they could see that she was trying to reach its lower end. The breeze was light, and since the current had by then lost much of its strength, Bob Harvey was entirely free to maneuver as he pleased.

The course the boats had followed earlier had let him find the deep water, and he had boldly entered it. His plan was only too easy to understand. He meant to moor broadside on in front of the Chimneys and from there answer with shells and cannonballs the bullets that had so far been cutting down his crew.

Soon the Speedy reached the point of the islet. She rounded it easily. Then her spanker was filled, and the brig, hauling close to the wind, found herself abreast of the Mercy.

"The bandits! They're coming in!" cried Pencroff.

At that moment Cyrus Smith, Ayrton, the sailor and Harbert were joined by Nab and Gédéon Spilett.

The reporter and his companion had judged it best to abandon the post at the Mercy, from which they could do nothing more against the ship, and they had acted wisely. It was better that the colonists should be together at the moment when a decisive action was surely about to begin. Gédéon Spilett and Nab had made their way there by slipping along under cover of the rocks, though not without drawing a hail of bullets, none of which had hit them.

"Spilett! Nab!" the engineer had cried. "You're not hurt?"

"No!" answered the reporter. "Just a few bruises — ricochets! But that damned brig is coming into the channel!"

"Yes!" Pencroff answered. "And in less than ten minutes she'll be anchored in front of Granite House!"

"Do you have a plan, Cyrus?" asked the reporter.

"We must take refuge in Granite House while there's still time, and while the convicts can't see us."

"That's my opinion too," Gédéon Spilett answered. "But once we're shut in..."

"We'll be guided by circumstances," replied the engineer.

"Let's go, then, and quickly!" said the reporter.

"You don't want Ayrton and me to stay here, Mr. Cyrus?" asked the sailor.

"What good would that do, Pencroff?" replied Cyrus Smith. "No. Let's not split up!"

There was not a moment to lose. The colonists left the Chimneys. A small jutting angle of the cliff wall kept them out of sight of the brig, but two or three explosions and the crash of cannonballs on the rocks told them that the Speedy was now only a short distance away.

To rush into the elevator, hoist themselves up to the door of Granite House, where Top and Jup had been shut in since the day before, and dash into the great hall was the work of a moment.

It was not a moment too soon, for through the branches the colonists saw the Speedy, wreathed in smoke, gliding up the channel. They even had to stand aside from the windows, because the firing never stopped. The cannonballs from the four guns were pounding blindly both at the post on the Mercy, though no one was there now, and at the Chimneys. The rocks were shattered, and every shot was greeted with cheers.

Still, they could hope that Granite House would be spared, thanks to the precaution Cyrus Smith had taken of hiding its windows — when a cannonball grazed the doorway and came flying into the passage.

"Curse it! Have they found us?" cried Pencroff.

Perhaps the colonists had not been seen, but it was certain that Bob Harvey had seen fit to send a shot through the suspicious foliage that masked that part of the high wall. Soon he was firing harder than ever, for another cannonball tore through the curtain of leaves and laid bare a gaping opening in the granite.

The colonists' situation was desperate. Their refuge had been discovered. They had no way to block these projectiles or to shield the stone, whose splinters were flying around them like grapeshot. There was nothing left for them but to take refuge in the upper passage of Granite House and abandon their home to whatever destruction might come — when a dull roar was heard, followed by dreadful screams!

Cyrus Smith and his companions rushed to one of the windows...

The brig, lifted irresistibly on a kind of waterspout, had just split in two, and in less than ten seconds she had sunk with all her criminal crew!

Chapter 4: Salvage

The colonists on the beach — Ayrton and Pencroff at the salvage work — Talk over lunch — Pencroff's reasoning — A careful inspection of the brig's hull — The powder magazine intact — The new riches — The last of the wreckage — A piece of a broken cylinder

"They've blown up!" cried Harbert.

"Yes! Blown up as if Ayrton had set fire to the powder!" answered Pencroff, throwing himself into the elevator along with Nab and the boy.

"But what happened?" asked Gédéon Spilett, still stunned by this unexpected ending.

"Ah! This time we'll find out!..." the engineer answered quickly.

"Find out what?..."

"Later! Later! Come on, Spilett. What matters is that those pirates have been wiped out!"

And Cyrus Smith, drawing the reporter and Ayrton along with him, joined Pencroff, Nab and Harbert on the beach.

Nothing could be seen of the brig anymore, not even her masts. After being lifted up by that waterspout, she had fallen over on her side and sunk in that position, no doubt because some enormous leak had opened in her. But since the channel at that point was no more than twenty feet deep, it was certain that the sides of the sunken brig would show again at low tide.

A few pieces of wreckage were floating on the surface of the sea. There was a whole raft of spare masts and yards, chicken coops with their birds still alive, and crates and barrels that came bobbing up to the surface little by little after escaping through the hatches. But there was no debris drifting about — no planks from the deck, no planking from the hull — and that made the sudden sinking of the Speedy rather hard to explain.

Meanwhile the two masts, which had snapped a few feet above the deck where they passed through it, breaking their stays and shrouds as they went, soon rose to the surface of the channel with their sails, some spread and some furled. But they could not give the ebb time to carry off all these riches, and Ayrton and Pencroff jumped into the canoe, meaning to tie up all the floating wreckage either to the shore of the island or to the shore of the islet.

But just as they were about to push off, a thought from Gédéon Spilett stopped them.

"And the six convicts who landed on the right bank of the Mercy?" he said.

He was right. They must not forget that the six men whose boat had been smashed on the rocks had come ashore at Jetsam Point.

Everyone looked in that direction. None of the fugitives was in sight. Most likely, after watching the brig go down in the waters of the channel, they had fled into the interior of the island.

"We'll deal with them later," Cyrus Smith said then. "They may still be dangerous, because they're armed, but after all, it's six against six, so the odds are even. Let's see to the most urgent thing first."

Ayrton and Pencroff got into the canoe and rowed hard toward the wreckage.

The sea was at the slack just then, and very high, because the moon had been new for two days. So a good hour at least would have to pass before the hull of the brig came up out of the waters of the channel.

Ayrton and Pencroff had time to make fast the masts and spars with ropes, whose ends were carried to the beach below Granite House. There the colonists, pulling all together, managed to haul the wreckage ashore. Then the canoe picked up everything that was floating — chicken coops, barrels, crates — and it was all carried straight to the Chimneys.

A few bodies were floating too. Among them Ayrton recognized that of Bob Harvey, and he pointed it out to his companion, saying in a voice full of feeling:

"That's what I was, Pencroff!"

"But it's what you aren't anymore, my brave Ayrton!" answered the sailor.

It was rather strange that so few bodies were floating. They counted barely five or six, and the ebb was already starting to carry them out toward the open sea. Very probably the convicts, caught by the sudden sinking, had had no time to get away, and since the ship had gone over on her side, most of them had been trapped under the bulwarks. And so the outgoing tide, which was about to sweep the bodies of these wretched men out to sea, would spare the colonists the grim task of burying them in some corner of their island.

For two hours Cyrus Smith and his companions did nothing but haul the spars up onto the sand, unbend the sails from the yards, and spread them out to dry. The sails were perfectly undamaged. The colonists talked very little, so completely did the work absorb them — but what thoughts went through their minds! Owning this brig, or rather everything she held, was a fortune. A ship is like a small, complete world, and the colony's stock of equipment was about to grow by a great many useful things. It would be the chest found at Jetsam Point all over again, "on a grand scale."

"And besides," Pencroff was thinking, "why couldn't this brig be refloated? If she's got only a leak, well, a leak can be plugged, and a ship of three to four hundred tons — now that's a real ship next to our Bonadventure! You can go a long way in a ship like that! You can go wherever you like! Mr. Cyrus, Ayrton and I will have to look into it. It's worth the trouble!"

And indeed, if the brig was still fit to sail, the colonists' chances of getting home from Lincoln Island would be wonderfully improved. But to settle this important question they would have to wait until the tide was all the way out, so that every part of the brig's hull could be examined.

Once the wreckage was safe on the beach, Cyrus Smith and his companions allowed themselves a few moments for lunch. They were literally dying of hunger. Luckily the pantry was not far away, and Nab could pass for a ship's cook who got things on the table fast. So they ate beside the Chimneys, and during the meal, as you can well imagine, the only subject was the unexpected event that had saved the colony so miraculously.

"Miraculously is the word," Pencroff kept repeating, "because you have to admit those scoundrels blew up at exactly the right moment! Granite House was getting remarkably hard to live in!"

"And can you picture how it happened, Pencroff," asked the reporter, "and what could have set off that explosion on the brig?"

"Eh! Mr. Spilett, nothing simpler," answered Pencroff. "A pirate ship isn't run like a warship! Convicts aren't sailors! The brig's powder rooms must have been open, since they were firing at us nonstop, and it would only take one careless or clumsy fellow to blow the whole contraption sky-high!"

"Mr. Cyrus," said Harbert, "what surprises me is that the explosion didn't do more damage. The bang wasn't very loud, and when you come down to it, there's not much debris and not many planks torn off. It looks as if the ship sank rather than blew up."

"That surprises you, my boy?" asked the engineer.

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus."

"It surprises me too, Harbert," answered the engineer. "But when we inspect the brig's hull, we'll no doubt find the explanation."

"Now look here, Mr. Cyrus," said Pencroff, "you're not going to claim the Speedy simply sank like a ship that's run onto a reef?"

"Why not," Nab put in, "if there are rocks in the channel?"

"Come on, Nab," answered Pencroff. "You didn't have your eyes open at the right moment. An instant before she went down, the brig — I saw it perfectly well — rose up on an enormous wave and fell back, heeling over to port. Now if she'd only struck, she'd have sunk nice and quietly, like an honest ship going to the bottom."

"That's just it — she wasn't an honest ship!" answered Nab.

"Well, we'll see, Pencroff," said the engineer.

"We'll see," the sailor added, "but I'd bet my head there aren't any rocks in the channel. Come on, Mr. Cyrus, honestly — are you trying to tell me there's something marvelous about this business too?"

Cyrus Smith did not answer.

"In any case," said Gédéon Spilett, "collision or explosion, you'll grant, Pencroff, that it happened just in time!"

"Yes!... Yes!..." answered the sailor. "But that's not the question. I'm asking Mr. Smith if he sees anything supernatural in all this."

"I'm not saying either way, Pencroff," said the engineer. "That's all the answer I can give you."

That answer did not satisfy Pencroff in the least. He held to "an explosion," and nothing would shake him off it. He would never agree that there was some unknown reef in that channel, whose bed was fine sand like the beach itself, and which he had often crossed at low tide. Besides, at the moment the brig went down, the tide was high — which meant she had more than enough water under her to pass over, without touching, any rocks that did not show at low tide. Therefore there could not have been a collision. Therefore the ship had not struck. Therefore she had blown up.

And it must be admitted that the sailor's reasoning was not without a certain logic.

Toward half past one the colonists got into the canoe and went out to where the brig lay stranded. It was a pity that the brig's two boats could not have been saved. But one of them, as we know, had been smashed at the mouth of the Mercy and was completely useless, and the other had vanished when the brig went down and, no doubt crushed beneath her, had never come up again.

By now the hull of the Speedy was beginning to show above the water. The brig was lying worse than on her side. After snapping her masts under the weight of her ballast, which had shifted when she fell, she lay almost keel up. She had been truly turned over by that inexplicable but terrifying underwater force, which had at the same time shown itself by throwing up an enormous waterspout.

The colonists went all the way around the hull, and as the sea went down they were able to make out, if not the cause of the disaster, at least its effects.

In the bow, on both sides of the keel, seven or eight feet aft of the point where the stem begins, the brig's sides were horribly torn open along a length of at least twenty feet. There gaped two great holes that it would have been impossible to plug. Not only had the copper sheathing and the planking vanished — ground to powder, no doubt — but of the frames themselves, and of the iron bolts and wooden pegs that held them together, not a trace was left. All along the hull, right back to where it narrowed toward the stern, the strakes — the long rows of planking — were shredded and no longer held. The false keel had been torn away with an inexplicable violence, and the keel itself, ripped from the keelson — the inner timber that runs along on top of it — in several places, was broken along its whole length.

"A thousand devils!" cried Pencroff. "There's a ship that's going to be hard to refloat!"

"It will be impossible," said Ayrton.

"In any case," Gédéon Spilett pointed out to the sailor, "the explosion, if there was an explosion, has had some peculiar effects here! It has burst open the bottom of the ship's hull, instead of blowing off the deck and the upper works! These big holes look much more as if they'd been made by striking a reef than by a magazine blowing up!"

"There's no reef in the channel!" the sailor shot back. "I'll admit anything you like, except hitting a rock!"

"Let's try to get inside the brig," said the engineer. "Maybe we'll find out what to think about the cause of her destruction."

That was the best course to take, and besides, they needed to make an inventory of all the riches on board and arrange for getting everything out.

Getting inside the brig was easy now. The water was still dropping, and the underside of the deck — which, with the hull turned over, had now become the top — could be walked on. The ballast, made of heavy pigs of cast iron, had smashed through it in several places. They could hear the sea gurgling as it drained out through the cracks in the hull.

Cyrus Smith and his companions, axes in hand, made their way forward along the half-wrecked deck. Crates of every kind cluttered it, and since they had been in the water for only a very short time, perhaps their contents were not spoiled.

So they set about getting this whole cargo to a safe place. The tide would not come back for several hours, and those few hours were put to the most profitable use. Ayrton and Pencroff had rigged a block and tackle at the opening in the hull, and with it they hoisted out the barrels and crates. The canoe took them aboard and carried them straight to the beach. They took everything, without picking and choosing, leaving it until later to sort all these things out.

In any case, what the colonists could see at once, to their enormous satisfaction, was that the brig carried a very varied cargo — an assortment of goods of every sort: utensils, manufactured articles, tools, the kind of thing loaded by ships that trade from island to island across Polynesia. Most likely they would find a little of everything here, and you will agree that this was exactly what the colony on Lincoln Island needed.

All the same — and Cyrus Smith noticed it in silent astonishment — not only had the brig's hull, as has been said, suffered enormously from whatever blow had caused the disaster, but the inside of the ship was wrecked as well, especially toward the bow. Bulkheads and stanchions were shattered, as though some tremendous shell had burst inside the brig. The colonists could easily go from bow to stern once they had moved the crates, which were carried out one after another. These were not heavy bales, which would have been hard to shift, but ordinary packages, and in any case there was no telling anymore how they had been stowed.

The colonists then made their way to the stern of the brig, to the part that the poop deck used to cover. It was there, according to Ayrton, that they should look for the powder magazine. Since Cyrus Smith believed it had not exploded, it was possible that a few kegs could be saved, and that the powder, which is usually packed in metal casings, had not been harmed by the water.

And that, in fact, was what had happened. In the midst of a great quantity of shot and shells, they found about twenty kegs lined with copper, and these were carefully brought out. Pencroff saw with his own eyes that the destruction of the Speedy could not be put down to an explosion. The part of the hull where the magazine was located was exactly the part that had suffered least.

"Could be!" answered the stubborn sailor. "But as for a rock — there isn't any rock in the channel!"

"Then what happened?" asked Harbert.

"I have no idea," answered Pencroff. "Mr. Cyrus has no idea, and nobody has any idea, and nobody ever will!"

During all this searching, several hours had gone by, and the flood tide was starting to make itself felt. The salvage work had to be stopped. There was no fear, though, that the sea would carry the brig's carcass away. It was already sunk into the sand and held as firmly as if it had been moored with two anchors.

So they could safely wait for the next ebb to start work again. But as for the ship herself, she was certainly doomed, and they would even have to hurry to save the pieces of her hull, because before long it would disappear into the shifting sands of the channel.

It was five o'clock in the evening. The day had been a hard one for the workers. They ate with a hearty appetite, and however tired they were, after supper they could not resist the urge to look into the crates that made up the Speedy's cargo.

Most of them held ready-made clothes, which, as you can imagine, were very welcome. There was enough there to dress a whole colony — linen for every purpose, shoes for every foot.

"Now we're too rich!" Pencroff exclaimed. "But what are we going to do with all this?"

And every moment the jolly sailor burst out with another hurrah as he recognized kegs of tafia — a cheap rum made from sugarcane — hogsheads of tobacco, firearms and blades, bales of cotton, farming implements, tools for carpenters, joiners and blacksmiths, and boxes of seeds of every kind, which their short stay in the water had not harmed. Ah, two years earlier, how welcome all these things would have been! But even now, when these hardworking colonists had made their own tools, all these riches would find a use.

There was no shortage of room in the storerooms of Granite House, but that day there was no time to put everything away. They could not forget, though, that six survivors from the crew of the Speedy had set foot on the island, that they were very likely scoundrels of the first rank, and that the colonists would have to be on their guard against them. Even though the bridge over the Mercy and the little bridges had been raised, convicts like these were not the sort to let a river or a stream stop them, and driven by despair, such ruffians could be formidable.

They would see later what was best to do about them. Meanwhile, though, someone had to keep watch over the crates and packages piled up near the Chimneys, and the colonists took turns at it all night.

The night passed, however, without the convicts attempting any attack. Master Jup and Top, on guard at the foot of Granite House, would have given the alarm quickly enough.

The next three days, October 19, 20 and 21, were spent saving everything that might be of any value or any use at all, whether from the cargo or from the brig's rigging. At low tide they emptied the hold. At high tide they stored away what they had saved. A large part of the copper sheathing was stripped off the hull, which sank deeper into the sand every day. And before the sands could swallow up the heavy objects that had gone to the bottom, Ayrton and Pencroff dove down to the bed of the channel several times and found the brig's chains and anchors, the iron pigs of her ballast, and even her four cannons. They buoyed the cannons up with empty casks, and so managed to bring them ashore.

So you can see that the colony's arsenal had gained from the salvage no less than the pantries and storerooms of Granite House. Pencroff, always full of enthusiasm for his plans, was already talking about building a battery to command the channel and the mouth of the river. With four cannons, he promised, he would stop any fleet, "however powerful," from venturing into the waters of Lincoln Island!

In the meantime, when nothing was left of the brig but a useless shell, bad weather came along and finished destroying it. Cyrus Smith had meant to blow it up so as to collect the pieces along the shore, but a strong northeast wind and a heavy sea let him save his powder.

In fact, during the night of the 23rd to the 24th, the hull of the brig was completely broken up, and part of the wreckage washed up on the beach.

As for the ship's papers, it goes without saying that Cyrus Smith found no trace of them, even though he had carefully searched the cupboards in the poop. The pirates had obviously destroyed everything that had to do with either the captain or the owner of the Speedy, and since the name of her home port was not painted on her stern, there was nothing to suggest what country she came from. However, from certain lines of her bow, Ayrton and Pencroff seemed to think the brig must have been English-built.

A week after the disaster — or rather after the happy but inexplicable ending to which the colony owed its rescue — nothing more could be seen of the ship, even at low tide. Her remains had been scattered, and Granite House was rich with almost everything she had carried.

All the same, the mystery that hid her strange destruction would no doubt never have been cleared up if, on November 30, Nab, wandering along the beach, had not found a piece of a thick iron cylinder that showed traces of an explosion. The cylinder was twisted and torn along its edges, as if it had been subjected to the force of some explosive substance.

Nab brought this piece of metal to his master, who was busy just then with his companions in the workshop at the Chimneys.

Cyrus Smith examined the cylinder carefully. Then, turning to Pencroff:

"My friend," he said, "do you still insist that the Speedy didn't go down because she struck something?"

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus," answered the sailor. "You know as well as I do there aren't any rocks in the channel."

"But what if she had struck this piece of iron?" said the engineer, holding up the broken cylinder.

"What, this bit of pipe?" cried Pencroff, in a tone of complete disbelief.

"My friends," Cyrus Smith went on, "do you remember that before she sank, the brig rose up on the top of a regular waterspout?"

"Yes, Mr. Cyrus!" answered Harbert.

"Well, would you like to know what threw up that waterspout? This did," said the engineer, holding up the broken tube.

"This?" Pencroff shot back.

"Yes! This cylinder is all that's left of a torpedo — a mine, that is, laid under the water!"

"A torpedo!" cried the engineer's companions.

"And who put it there, this torpedo?" asked Pencroff, who would not give in.

"All I can tell you is that it wasn't me!" answered Cyrus Smith. "But it was there, and you've seen for yourselves how incomparably powerful it was!"

Chapter 5: Pencroff's Grand Theories

What the engineer affirms — Pencroff's grand theories — A battery in the air — The four shots — About the surviving convicts — Ayrton hesitates — Cyrus Smith's generous feelings — Pencroff gives in reluctantly

So everything was explained by the underwater explosion of that torpedo. Cyrus Smith, who had had occasion during the war for the Union to try out these terrible engines of destruction, could not be mistaken. It was the blast of that cylinder, packed with some explosive substance — nitroglycerin, picrate, or something of the same kind — that had thrown the water of the channel up like a waterspout and torn open the brig's bottom so that she sank on the spot. And that was why it had been impossible to refloat her: the damage to her hull had been so enormous. Against a torpedo that could have destroyed an ironclad frigate as easily as a little fishing boat, the Speedy had never stood a chance!

Yes! Everything was explained, everything... except what that torpedo had been doing in the waters of the channel!

"My friends," Cyrus Smith went on, "we can no longer doubt that some mysterious being is here — a castaway like us, perhaps, abandoned on our island. I say this so that Ayrton will know all the strange things that have happened over the past two years. Who is this unknown benefactor whose help, so fortunate for us, has shown itself on so many occasions? I can't imagine. What reason does he have for acting this way, for hiding himself after doing us so many services? I can't understand it. But his services are no less real for that, and they are the kind that only a man with prodigious power at his command could have done us. Ayrton is in his debt as much as we are.
