For if it was the stranger who saved me from the waves after the balloon fell, then it was obviously he who wrote the document, who put that bottle in the path of our boat in the channel, and who let us know where our companion was. I will add this: it was he who guided that chest, so well stocked with everything we lacked, and beached it at Jetsam Point; it was he who lit the fire on the heights of the island that let you make land; it was he who fired the lead pellet we found in the peccary's body; it was he who sank the torpedo in the channel that destroyed the brig. In a word, all those inexplicable facts we could never account for are owed to this mysterious being. So whoever he may be, castaway or exile on this island, we would be ungrateful if we thought ourselves released from all gratitude toward him. We have run up a debt, and I hope we will pay it one day."

"You're right to speak that way, my dear Cyrus," replied Gédéon Spilett. "Yes, there is someone, someone almost all-powerful, hidden somewhere on the island, whose influence has been remarkably useful to our colony. I'll add that this stranger seems to me to have means of action at his disposal that would border on the supernatural, if the supernatural could be accepted among the facts of practical life. Is it he who communicates with us in secret through the well of Granite House, and so knows all our plans? Is it he who held out that bottle to us when the canoe made her first trip out to sea? Is it he who threw Top out of the lake and killed the dugong? Is it he — as everything leads us to believe — who saved you from the waves, Cyrus, and in circumstances where anyone who was only a man could have done nothing? If it is, then he has a power that makes him master of the elements."

The reporter's remark was a fair one, and they all felt it.

"Yes," replied Cyrus Smith. "If the intervention of a human being is no longer in doubt, I agree that he has means of action at his disposal beyond those that humanity commands. There is a mystery still. But if we find the man, we'll find the answer to the mystery too. So the question is this: should we respect the incognito of this generous being, or should we do everything we can to reach him? What do you think?"

"What I think," replied Pencroff, "is that whoever he is, he's a good man, and he has my respect!"

"Fair enough," said Cyrus Smith, "but that's not an answer, Pencroff."

"My master," Nab said then, "I have an idea that we can look for this gentleman as long as we like, but we won't find him until he pleases."

"That's not a stupid thing to say, Nab," said Pencroff.

"I agree with Nab," said Gédéon Spilett, "but that's no reason not to try. Whether we find this mysterious being or not, we will at least have done our duty toward him."

"And you, my boy, give us your opinion," said the engineer, turning to Harbert.

"Oh!" cried Harbert, his eyes lighting up. "I'd like to thank him — the one who saved you first, and then saved the rest of us!"

"You and me both, my boy," Pencroff shot back, "and all of us! I'm not the curious sort, but I'd give one of my eyes to see that fellow face to face! I picture him handsome, tall, strong, with a fine beard and hair like rays of light, lying on the clouds with a big ball in his hand!"

"Why, Pencroff," replied Gédéon Spilett, "that's a portrait of God the Father you're painting for us!"

"Could be, Mr. Spilett," the sailor answered, "but that's how I imagine him!"

"And you, Ayrton?" asked the engineer.

"Mr. Smith," replied Ayrton, "I can hardly give you my opinion in this matter. Whatever you do will be well done. Whenever you want me to join your search, I'll be ready to follow you."

"Thank you, Ayrton," said Cyrus Smith, "but I'd like a more direct answer to the question I asked you. You are our companion. You have already risked yourself for us more than once, and like everyone here, you must be consulted when an important decision is to be made. So speak."

"Mr. Smith," replied Ayrton, "I think we must do everything we can to find this unknown benefactor. Perhaps he's alone? Perhaps he's suffering? Perhaps there's a life to be renewed? I too, as you said, have a debt of gratitude to pay him. It was he — it can only have been he — who came to Tabor Island, who found the wretch you knew there, who let you know there was an unhappy man to be saved!... So it's thanks to him that I became a man again. No, I will never forget it!"

"Then it's settled," said Cyrus Smith. "We'll begin our search as soon as possible. We won't leave one part of the island unexplored. We'll search it down to its most secret hiding places — and may our unknown friend forgive us, for the sake of our intentions!"

For several days the colonists were hard at work bringing in the hay and the harvest. Before carrying out their plan to explore the parts of the island still unknown, they wanted every essential job finished. This was also the season for gathering the various vegetables grown from the plants brought back from Tabor Island. So everything had to be stored, and fortunately there was no lack of room in Granite House, where they could have stored all the riches of the island. The colony's produce was kept there, methodically arranged and in a safe place — you can believe it — as secure from beasts as from men. There was no damp to fear in the middle of that thick mass of granite. Several of the natural hollows along the upper passage were enlarged or hollowed out, some with the pick, some by blasting, and Granite House became a general warehouse as well, holding the provisions, the ammunition, the spare tools and utensils — in a word, all the colony's equipment.

As for the cannons from the brig, they were handsome pieces of cast steel. At Pencroff's urging they were hoisted with tackles and cranes right up to the doorsill of Granite House. Gunports were cut between the windows, and soon the guns could be seen thrusting their gleaming muzzles out through the granite wall. From that height these pieces of artillery truly commanded the whole of Union Bay. It was a little Gibraltar, and any ship that anchored broadside to the shore off the islet would have been exposed, with no escape, to the fire of this battery in the air.

"Mr. Cyrus," Pencroff said one day — it was November 8 — "now that the guns are mounted, we really have to test their range."

"Do you think that would be useful?" replied the engineer.

"It's more than useful, it's necessary! Otherwise, how will we know how far we can send one of those fine cannonballs we've got such a stock of?"

"Let's try, then, Pencroff," replied the engineer. "But I think we should make the experiment using not ordinary gunpowder, since I want to keep our supply of that intact, but guncotton, which we'll never run short of."

"Can these cannons stand the blast of guncotton?" asked the reporter, who was no less eager than Pencroff to try out the artillery of Granite House.

"I think so. Besides," added the engineer, "we'll go about it carefully."

The engineer had good reason to think the cannons were of excellent make, and he knew what he was talking about. They were made of forged steel and loaded at the breech, so for that very reason they ought to stand a considerable charge, and therefore have an enormous range. For in practical terms, the path the shot travels should be as flat as possible, and that flatness can only be had if the projectile leaves the gun at a very high initial speed.

"Now," Cyrus Smith told his companions, "the initial speed depends on the amount of powder used. In making guns, the whole question comes down to using the strongest metal possible, and of all metals, steel is beyond question the one that holds up best. So I have reason to think our cannons will safely withstand the expanding gases of the guncotton and will give excellent results."

"We'll be a lot surer of that once we've tried it!" replied Pencroff.

It goes without saying that the four cannons were in perfect condition. Ever since they had been hauled out of the water, the sailor had made it his job to clean them conscientiously. How many hours he had spent rubbing them, greasing them, polishing them, cleaning the breech mechanism — the breechblock, the bolt, the clamping screw! And now the guns shone as brightly as if they had been aboard a frigate of the United States Navy.

So that day, in the presence of the whole colony, Master Jup and Top included, the four cannons were tested one after another. They were loaded with guncotton, allowing for its explosive power, which, as we have said, is four times that of ordinary gunpowder. The projectile they were to fire was cylindrical, with a conical nose.

Pencroff, holding the cord of the friction primer, stood ready to fire.

At a sign from Cyrus Smith, the shot went off. The ball, aimed out to sea, passed over the islet and vanished far offshore, at a distance that could not be judged with any accuracy.

The second cannon was trained on the farthest rocks of Jetsam Point, and the projectile struck a sharp-pointed stone nearly three miles from Granite House and blew it to pieces.

It was Harbert who had aimed the cannon and fired it, and he was very proud of his first attempt. Only Pencroff was prouder than he was! A shot like that — and the honor of it went to his dear boy!

The third projectile, fired this time at the dunes that formed the upper shore of Union Bay, struck the sand at a distance of at least four miles; then it ricocheted and was lost at sea in a cloud of spray.

For the fourth gun, Cyrus Smith increased the charge a little, to test its utmost range. Then, with everyone standing well aside in case it burst, the primer was fired by means of a long cord.

There was a violent explosion, but the gun held. The colonists rushed to the window and saw the projectile chip the rocks of Mandible Cape, nearly five miles from Granite House, and disappear into Shark Gulf.

"Well, Mr. Cyrus," cried Pencroff, whose hurrahs could have rivaled the explosions themselves, "what do you say about our battery? All the pirates of the Pacific can come and show themselves in front of Granite House! Not a single one of them will land now without our permission!"

"If you take my advice, Pencroff," replied the engineer, "it's better not to put that to the test."

"By the way," the sailor went on, "what about the six scoundrels prowling around the island? What are we going to do with them? Are we going to let them run loose through our forests, our fields, our meadows? They're real jaguars, those pirates, and it seems to me we shouldn't hesitate to treat them as such. What do you think, Ayrton?" Pencroff added, turning to his companion.

At first Ayrton hesitated to answer, and Cyrus Smith regretted that Pencroff had put the question to him so thoughtlessly. So he was deeply moved when Ayrton answered in a humble voice:

"I was one of those jaguars, Mr. Pencroff, and I have no right to speak..."

And he walked slowly away.

Pencroff had understood.

"What a blasted fool I am!" he cried. "Poor Ayrton! He has as much right to speak here as anybody!..."

"Yes," said Gédéon Spilett, "but his reserve does him credit, and we ought to respect the feeling he has about his unhappy past."

"Understood, Mr. Spilett," replied the sailor, "and you won't catch me at it again! I'd sooner swallow my tongue than hurt Ayrton's feelings! But let's get back to the question. It seems to me those bandits have no right to any pity, and we ought to rid the island of them as soon as we can."

"Is that really your opinion, Pencroff?" asked the engineer.

"Absolutely my opinion."

"And before hunting them down without mercy, you wouldn't wait until they had committed some fresh act of hostility against us?"

"So what they've already done isn't enough?" asked Pencroff, who could make no sense of all this hesitation.

"They may come to feel differently!" said Cyrus Smith. "And perhaps repent..."

"Repent — them!" cried the sailor, shrugging his shoulders.

"Pencroff, think of Ayrton!" Harbert said then, taking the sailor's hand. "He became an honest man again!"

Pencroff looked at his companions one after another. He would never have believed that his proposal could raise the slightest hesitation. His rough nature could not accept any compromise with the scoundrels who had landed on the island, the accomplices of Bob Harvey, the murderers of the Speedy's crew. He thought of them as wild beasts that had to be destroyed without hesitation and without remorse.

"Well, there it is!" he said. "Everybody's against me! You want to be generous with those villains! All right. Let's hope we don't live to regret it!"

"What danger are we in," said Harbert, "if we take care to stay on our guard?"

"Hmm!" said the reporter, who was not committing himself too far. "There are six of them, and well armed. If each of them lay in ambush in some corner and fired at one of us, they'd soon be masters of the colony!"

"Then why haven't they done it?" replied Harbert. "No doubt because it wasn't in their interest to. Besides, there are six of us too."

"Fine! Fine!" replied Pencroff, whom no argument could have convinced. "Let's leave those fine fellows to go about their little business, and not think about them anymore!"

"Come on, Pencroff," said Nab, "don't make yourself out to be so mean! If one of those poor wretches were here, right in front of you, within easy range of your gun, you wouldn't shoot him..."

"I'd shoot him like a mad dog, Nab," Pencroff replied coldly.

"Pencroff," the engineer said then, "you have often shown great respect for my advice. In this case, will you rely on me once again?"

"I'll do as you please, Mr. Smith," replied the sailor, who was not convinced in the least.

"Well then, let's wait, and attack only if we're attacked."

So that was how they decided to act toward the pirates, though Pencroff predicted nothing good from it. They would not attack them, but they would stay on their guard. After all, the island was large and fertile. If any feeling of honesty remained in the depths of their souls, those wretches might perhaps reform. Given the conditions they had to live in, wasn't it in their own best interest to make a new life for themselves? In any case, for humanity's sake if nothing else, they had to wait. The colonists might no longer be able to come and go as freely and trustingly as before. Until now they had only had wild beasts to guard against, and now six convicts, perhaps of the worst kind, were prowling about their island. It was serious, no doubt, and for less courageous people it would have meant the end of all their security.

No matter! For the present, the colonists were right and Pencroff was wrong. Would they be right in the future? Time would tell.

Chapter 6: Why the Wire Went Dead

Plans for an expedition — Ayrton at the corral — A visit to Balloon Harbor — Pencroff's remarks aboard the Bonadventure — A telegram sent to the corral — No answer from Ayrton — Setting out the next day — Why the wire no longer works — A gunshot

Meanwhile, the colonists' great concern was to carry out the complete exploration of the island that they had decided on. That exploration would now have two aims: first, to find the mysterious being whose existence could no longer be disputed; and at the same time, to find out what had become of the pirates — what hideout they had chosen, what sort of life they were leading, and what the colonists might have to fear from them.

Cyrus Smith wanted to set out without delay. But since the expedition would last several days, it had seemed sensible to load the cart with camping gear and various utensils that would make it easier to set up their stops along the way. Now, just then one of the onaggas had hurt its leg and could not be harnessed. It needed a few days' rest, and they decided they could put off their departure by a week, to November 20, without any harm done. In that latitude, the month of November corresponds to May in the northern regions. So it was the fine season. The sun was reaching the Tropic of Capricorn and giving the longest days of the year. The time would be ideal for the planned expedition — an expedition which, even if it did not achieve its main goal, could prove rich in discoveries, especially in the island's plants and animals, since Cyrus Smith meant to explore the dense Far West forests that stretched all the way to the tip of Serpentine Peninsula.

It was agreed that during the nine days before their departure they would put the finishing touches on the work on Prospect Plateau.

Ayrton, however, needed to go back to the corral, where the domestic animals required his care. So it was decided that he would spend two days there, and that he would not come back to Granite House until he had well stocked the stables.

Just as he was about to leave, Cyrus Smith asked him whether he would like one of them to go with him, pointing out that the island was less safe than it used to be.

Ayrton answered that there was no need: he could handle the work alone, and besides, he was not afraid of anything. If anything happened at the corral or in the neighborhood, he would warn the colonists at once by sending a telegram to Granite House.

So Ayrton left at dawn on the 9th, taking the cart, harnessed to a single onagga, and two hours later the electric bell announced that he had found everything in order at the corral.

During those two days, Cyrus Smith set about carrying out a project that was to put Granite House beyond the reach of any surprise attack for good. The idea was to hide completely the upper mouth of the old spillway, at the southern corner of Lake Grant. It was already walled up with masonry and half hidden under grass and plants. Nothing could have been easier, since all it took was to raise the level of the lake by two or three feet, and the opening would then be completely under water.

And to raise that level, all they had to do was build a dam across each of the two channels that had been cut from the lake — the ones that fed Glycerin Creek and the creek that ran to the great waterfall. The colonists were all called in to help with this work, and the two dams — which, after all, were no more than seven or eight feet wide and three feet high — were quickly put up out of blocks of stone, well cemented together.

When the job was finished, it would have been impossible to suspect that at that end of the lake there was an underground channel through which the lake's overflow had once poured out.

It goes without saying that the little side channel that kept Granite House's tank supplied and worked the elevator had been carefully preserved, so that they would never in any circumstances run short of water. Once the elevator was raised, this safe and comfortable retreat could defy any surprise or sudden attack.

This work had been dispatched quickly, and Pencroff, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert found time to make a quick trip out to Balloon Harbor. The sailor was very anxious to know whether the convicts had paid a visit to the little cove at the far end of which the Bonadventure lay at anchor.

"The thing is," he pointed out, "those gentlemen came ashore on the south coast, and if they followed the shoreline, I'm afraid they may have found the little harbor. And in that case I wouldn't give you half a dollar for our Bonadventure."

Pencroff's fears were not without some foundation, and a visit to Balloon Harbor seemed very much in order.

So the sailor and his companions set out in the afternoon of November 10, well armed. Pencroff, slipping two balls into each barrel of his gun so that everyone could see, kept shaking his head, which boded no good for anyone who came too close to him — "beast or man," as he said. Gédéon Spilett and Harbert took their guns too, and at about three o'clock all three of them left Granite House.

Nab went with them as far as the bend of the Mercy, and when they had crossed, he raised the bridge. It was agreed that a gunshot would announce the colonists' return, and that at that signal Nab would come back and reconnect the two banks of the river.

The little party went straight down the harbor road toward the south coast of the island. It was a distance of only three and a half miles, but Gédéon Spilett and his companions took two hours to cover it. That was because they searched the whole edge of the road, both on the side of the thick forest and on the side of Shelduck Marsh. They found no trace of the fugitives. No doubt, not yet knowing how many colonists there were or what means of defense they had, the convicts had made for the least accessible parts of the island.

When Pencroff reached Balloon Harbor, he was enormously pleased to see the Bonadventure riding quietly at anchor in the narrow inlet. And in fact, Balloon Harbor was so well hidden among those high rocks that no one could spot it from either the sea or the land — not unless they were right on top of it or right inside it.

"Well," said Pencroff, "those scoundrels haven't been here yet. Tall grass suits snakes better, and it's obviously in the Far West that we'll find them again."

"And a very lucky thing, too," Harbert added. "If they'd found the Bonadventure, they'd have seized her to get away, and that would have kept us from going back to Tabor Island any time soon."

"Indeed," the reporter answered. "It'll be important to take a document there telling where Lincoln Island lies and where Ayrton lives now, in case the Scottish yacht comes back to fetch him."

"Well, the Bonadventure's still right here, Mr. Spilett!" the sailor replied. "She and her crew are ready to sail at the first signal!"

"I think, Pencroff, that's something to do as soon as our expedition around the island is finished. After all, it's possible that this stranger — if we manage to find him — knows a great deal about both Lincoln Island and Tabor Island. Let's not forget that he's unquestionably the author of the document, and perhaps he knows what to expect about the yacht's return!"

"A thousand devils!" cried Pencroff. "Who on earth can he be? He knows us, this character, and we don't know him! If he's just a castaway, why is he hiding? We're decent people, I'd say, and nobody minds the company of decent people! Did he come here of his own free will? Can he leave the island if he feels like it? Is he still here? Is he gone?..."

As they talked, Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett had gone aboard and were walking around the deck of the Bonadventure. All of a sudden the sailor, who had been examining the bitt that the anchor cable was made fast to, cried out:

"Well, I'll be! Now that's a strong one!"

"What's the matter, Pencroff?" asked the reporter.

"The matter is, I didn't tie that knot!"

And Pencroff pointed to a rope that lashed the cable to the bitt itself, to keep it from slipping.

"What do you mean, you didn't?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"No! I'd swear to it. That's a reef knot, and I always tie two half hitches — a knot that never works loose."

"You must have made a mistake, Pencroff."

"I did not make a mistake!" the sailor declared. "You get that in your hands without thinking, and the hand doesn't make mistakes!"

"Then the convicts must have come aboard?" asked Harbert.

"I don't know about that," answered Pencroff, "but one thing's certain: somebody hauled up the Bonadventure's anchor and then dropped it again! And look here! Here's another proof. Somebody's paid out more of the anchor cable, and its chafing gear — the old canvas we wrap around the cable so it won't wear through where it runs out the hawsehole — isn't sitting at the hawsehole anymore. I'm telling you again, somebody has used our boat!"

"But if the convicts had used her, they'd either have plundered her or else they'd have escaped in her..."

"Escaped!... Where to?... Tabor Island?..." Pencroff shot back. "Do you really think they'd have risked it in a boat this small?"

"Besides, we'd have to assume they knew about the islet," the reporter answered.

"Be that as it may," said the sailor, "as sure as I'm Bonadventure Pencroff of the Vineyard, our Bonadventure has been sailing without us!"

The sailor was so positive that neither Gédéon Spilett nor Harbert could argue with what he said. It was clear that the boat had been moved, to some extent, since Pencroff had brought her back to Balloon Harbor. As far as the sailor was concerned, there was no doubt whatever that the anchor had been raised and then sent back down to the bottom. And why would anyone do those two things, unless the boat had been used for some expedition?

"But how could we have failed to see the Bonadventure sailing past the island?" the reporter pointed out. He was determined to raise every possible objection.

"Oh, Mr. Spilett," the sailor answered, "all you have to do is leave at night with a good breeze, and in two hours you're out of sight of the island!"

"All right," Gédéon Spilett went on. "I'll ask it again: what reason would the convicts have had to use the Bonadventure, and why, after using her, would they have brought her back to the harbor?"

"Oh, Mr. Spilett," the sailor answered, "let's just put it down among the inexplicable things and not think about it anymore! What mattered was that the Bonadventure should be here, and she is. The trouble is, if the convicts took her a second time, she might not turn up in her place again!"

"Then, Pencroff," said Harbert, "maybe it would be wise to bring the Bonadventure round to Granite House?"

"Yes and no," Pencroff answered. "Or rather, no. The mouth of the Mercy is a bad place for a boat, and the sea is rough there."

"But if we hauled her up on the sand, right to the foot of the Chimneys?..."

"Maybe... yes..." Pencroff answered. "Anyway, since we've got to leave Granite House for a fairly long expedition, I think the Bonadventure will be safer here while we're away, and we'd do well to leave her here until the island's been cleaned out of those rascals."

"I think so too," said the reporter. "At least if the weather turns bad she won't be exposed the way she would be at the mouth of the Mercy."

"But what if the convicts come to visit her again?" said Harbert.

"Well, my boy," Pencroff answered, "if they didn't find her here, they'd soon go looking for her over by Granite House, and while we're gone there'd be nothing to stop them taking her! So I think, like Mr. Spilett, that we ought to leave her at Balloon Harbor. But when we come back, if we haven't rid the island of those scoundrels, it'll be wise to bring our boat round to Granite House until she has no more nasty visits to fear."

"Agreed. Let's go!" said the reporter.

When Pencroff, Harbert and Gédéon Spilett got back to Granite House, they told the engineer what had happened, and he approved their plans for the present and for the future. He even promised the sailor that he would study the part of the channel lying between the islet and the coast, to see whether it might be possible to make an artificial harbor there by building dams. That way the Bonadventure would always be within reach, under the colonists' eyes, and under lock and key if need be.

That same evening they sent Ayrton a telegram asking him to bring back a couple of goats from the corral, which Nab wanted to get used to living in the meadows of the plateau. Oddly enough, Ayrton did not acknowledge the message the way he usually did. This rather surprised the engineer. But it could be that Ayrton was not at the corral just then, or even that he was already on his way back to Granite House. In fact, two days had gone by since he left, and it had been decided that he would be back on the evening of the 10th, or early on the morning of the 11th at the latest.

So the colonists waited for Ayrton to appear on the heights of Prospect Plateau. Nab and Harbert even kept watch near the bridge, so as to lower it as soon as their companion arrived.

But by ten o'clock that night there was still no sign of Ayrton. So they thought it best to send another telegram, asking for an immediate reply.

The bell at Granite House stayed silent.

Then the colonists grew very uneasy. What had happened? Was Ayrton no longer at the corral? Or if he was still there, was he no longer free to move? Should they go to the corral on such a dark night?

They talked it over. Some wanted to go, others to stay.

"But," said Harbert, "maybe there's been some accident to the telegraph, and it isn't working anymore?"

"That could be," said the reporter.

"Let's wait until tomorrow," answered Cyrus Smith. "It's possible, in fact, that Ayrton didn't receive our message, or even that we didn't receive his."

So they waited — not, as you can imagine, without a certain anxiety.

At the first light of day, on November 11, Cyrus Smith sent the electric current through the wire again, and got no answer.

He tried again. Same result.

"We're off to the corral!" he said.

"And well armed!" Pencroff added.

It was decided at once that Granite House would not be left on its own, and that Nab would stay there. After going with his companions as far as Glycerin Creek, he would raise the bridge, and then, hidden behind a tree, he would watch for their return or for Ayrton's.

If the pirates showed up and tried to force the crossing, he would try to stop them with his gun, and in the last resort he would take refuge in Granite House, where, once the elevator was raised, he would be safe.

Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Harbert and Pencroff were to go straight to the corral, and if they did not find Ayrton there, they would beat the woods all around it.

At six o'clock in the morning the engineer and his three companions had crossed Glycerin Creek, and Nab took up his post behind a low bank of earth, topped by a few tall dragon trees, on the left bank of the stream.

After leaving Prospect Plateau, the colonists immediately took the Corral Road. They carried their guns over their arms, ready to fire at the slightest sign of hostility. The two carbines and the two guns had been loaded with ball.

On either side of the road the undergrowth was thick and could easily have hidden criminals, who, thanks to their weapons, would have been truly dangerous.

The colonists walked quickly and in silence. Top went ahead of them, sometimes running along the road, sometimes making a little detour into the woods, but always silent and showing no sign of sensing anything unusual. And they could count on it that the faithful dog would not let himself be taken by surprise, and that he would bark at the slightest hint of danger.

As they followed the road, Cyrus Smith and his companions also followed the telegraph wire that linked the corral with Granite House. After walking about two miles, they had still not noticed any break in it. The poles were in good condition, the insulators intact, the wire evenly stretched. From that point on, however, the engineer noticed that the wire seemed less taut than before. And at last, when they reached pole No. 74, Harbert, who was out in front, stopped and shouted:

"The wire's broken!"

His companions hurried forward and reached the spot where the young man had stopped.

There the pole lay overturned across the road. So the break in the wire was confirmed, and it was obvious that messages from Granite House could not have reached the corral, nor messages from the corral Granite House.

"It wasn't the wind that knocked down this pole," Pencroff observed.

"No," answered Gédéon Spilett. "The earth has been dug out around its foot. It was pulled up by human hands."

"What's more, the wire's broken," Harbert added, pointing to the two ends of the iron wire, which had been violently snapped.

"Is the break fresh?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"Yes," answered Harbert. "It certainly hasn't been long since it was broken."

"To the corral! To the corral!" cried the sailor.

The colonists were now halfway between Granite House and the corral. That meant they still had two and a half miles to go. They broke into a run.

There was good reason to fear that something serious had happened at the corral. No doubt Ayrton might have sent a telegram that had never arrived, and that in itself was not what should worry his companions. But — and this was harder to explain — Ayrton, who had promised to come back the evening before, had not reappeared. And finally, it was not for nothing that all communication between the corral and Granite House had been cut. Who but the convicts had any reason to cut it?

So the colonists ran, their hearts tight with dread. They had grown truly attached to their new companion. Were they about to find him struck down by the very men whose leader he had once been?

Soon they came to the place where the road ran alongside the little stream, branching off Red Creek, that watered the corral's meadows. Here they slowed their pace, so as not to be out of breath at the moment when a fight might become necessary. Their guns were no longer at half-cock but fully cocked. Each man kept watch on one side of the forest. Top was letting out a few low growls, which did not bode well.

At last the palisade appeared through the trees. There was no sign of any damage. The gate was shut, as usual. A deep silence hung over the corral. Neither the usual bleating of the mouflons nor Ayrton's voice could be heard.

"Let's go in!" said Cyrus Smith.

And the engineer stepped forward, while his companions kept watch twenty paces behind him, ready to fire.

Cyrus Smith lifted the inside latch of the gate and was about to push one of its leaves open when Top barked furiously. A shot rang out above the palisade, and a cry of pain answered it.

Harbert, struck by a bullet, lay on the ground!

Chapter 7: A Sure and Faithful Messenger

The reporter and Pencroff in the corral — Harbert carried in — The sailor's despair — The reporter and the engineer confer — The treatment — Some hope returns — How to warn Nab? — A sure and faithful messenger — Nab's answer

At Harbert's cry, Pencroff had dropped his gun and rushed to him.

"They've killed him!" he cried. "My boy! They've killed him!"

Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett had run to Harbert. The reporter listened to find out whether the poor boy's heart was still beating.

"He's alive," he said. "But we've got to move him..."

"To Granite House? That's impossible!" answered the engineer.

"To the corral, then!" cried Pencroff.

"One moment," said Cyrus Smith.

And he dashed off to the left, to work his way around the palisade. There he found himself face to face with a convict, who took aim at him and put a bullet through his hat. A few seconds later, before the man even had time to fire his second shot, he fell, struck to the heart by Cyrus Smith's dagger, which was even surer than his gun.

Meanwhile Gédéon Spilett and the sailor hoisted themselves up at the corners of the palisade, swung their legs over the top, and jumped down inside. They knocked away the props that held the gate shut from within, rushed into the house, which was empty, and soon poor Harbert was lying on Ayrton's bed.

A few moments later Cyrus Smith was beside him.

When he saw Harbert lying there senseless, the sailor's grief was terrible. He sobbed, he wept, he wanted to dash his head against the wall. Neither the engineer nor the reporter could calm him. Their own emotion was choking them. They could not speak.

All the same, they did everything in their power to fight death for the poor boy who lay dying before their eyes. After all the adventures his life had been strewn with, Gédéon Spilett had some practical knowledge of everyday medicine. He knew a little about everything, and more than once he had found himself having to treat wounds made by a blade or by a gun. So, with Cyrus Smith's help, he set about giving Harbert the care his condition called for.

The first thing that struck the reporter was the deep stupor that held the boy, a stupor caused either by loss of blood or else by shock, if the bullet had hit a bone hard enough to jolt the whole body.

Harbert was extremely pale, and his pulse was so weak that Gédéon Spilett could feel it beat only at long intervals, as though it were about to stop. At the same time his senses and his mind seemed almost entirely gone. These were very grave symptoms.

They bared Harbert's chest, stanched the blood with handkerchiefs, and washed the chest with cold water.

The wound appeared: a bruised, torn wound where the bullet had struck. There was an oval hole in the chest between the third and fourth ribs. That was where the bullet had hit Harbert.

Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett then turned the poor boy over. He let out a moan so faint that it might have been his last breath.

A second wound was bleeding on Harbert's back, and the bullet that had struck him dropped out of it at once.

"Thank God!" said the reporter. "The bullet didn't stay in his body, and we won't have to take it out."

"But the heart?..." asked Cyrus Smith.

"The heart wasn't touched, or Harbert would be dead!"

"Dead!" cried Pencroff, with a roar.

The sailor had heard only the reporter's last words.

"No, Pencroff," Cyrus Smith answered. "No! He isn't dead. His pulse is still beating! He even moaned. But for your boy's own sake, calm down. We need to keep our heads. Don't make us lose them, my friend."

Pencroff fell silent, but a reaction set in, and great tears flooded down his face.

Meanwhile Gédéon Spilett was trying to gather his memories and go about things methodically. From what he had seen, he had no doubt that the bullet had gone in at the front and come out at the back. But what damage had it done on its way through? Which vital organs had it reached? That was something a professional surgeon could hardly have said at that moment, let alone the reporter.

Still, he knew one thing: he would have to keep the injured tissue from swelling up and choking itself with inflammation, and then fight the local inflammation and the fever that would follow such a wound — a wound that might well be fatal! And what dressings, what remedies against inflammation could he use? How could he head that inflammation off?

In any case, the important thing was to dress both wounds without delay. Gédéon Spilett did not think it necessary to start the blood flowing again by washing them in warm water and pressing their edges. The bleeding had been very heavy, and Harbert was already far too weak from the loss of blood.

So the reporter decided to do no more than wash the two wounds with cold water.

Harbert was laid on his left side, and they kept him in that position.

"He mustn't move," said Gédéon Spilett. "He's in the best position for the wounds in his back and chest to drain freely, and he needs absolute rest."

"What! We can't carry him to Granite House?" asked Pencroff.

"No, Pencroff," answered the reporter.

"Damnation!" cried the sailor, shaking his fist at the sky.

"Pencroff!" said Cyrus Smith.

Gédéon Spilett had gone back to examining the wounded boy with the greatest care. Harbert was still so dreadfully pale that the reporter felt shaken.

"Cyrus," he said, "I'm not a doctor... I'm terribly unsure what to do... You have to help me with your advice, your experience!..."

"Steady... my friend," answered the engineer, gripping the reporter's hand. "Judge it coolly... think of only one thing: we have to save Harbert!"

These words gave Gédéon Spilett back the self-command that a sharp sense of his responsibility had made him lose in a moment of discouragement. He sat down by the bed. Cyrus Smith stood. Pencroff had torn up his shirt and, without thinking, was picking it apart into lint for dressings.

Gédéon Spilett then explained to Cyrus Smith that, above all, he thought he ought to stop the bleeding — but not close the two wounds or try to make them heal over at once. There had been a puncture inside, and the pus must not be allowed to collect in the chest.

Cyrus Smith agreed completely, and it was decided that they would dress the two wounds without trying to close them by drawing their edges together. Fortunately, it did not seem that they would need to be opened up any further.

And now, did the colonists have anything that would work against the inflammation that was bound to come?

Yes! They had something, for nature has given it out generously. They had cold water — the most powerful soothing agent that can be used against inflamed wounds, the most effective remedy in serious cases, and one that every doctor has now adopted. Cold water has the further advantage of leaving the wound perfectly at rest and sparing it any premature dressing, a considerable advantage, since experience has shown that contact with the air does harm during the first few days.

Gédéon Spilett and Cyrus Smith reasoned it out this way, by plain common sense, and they acted as the best surgeon would have done. Linen compresses were laid on poor Harbert's two wounds, and these had to be kept constantly soaked in cold water.

The sailor had first of all lit a fire in the fireplace of the house, which was well stocked with the necessities of life. Maple sugar and medicinal plants — the very ones the boy had gathered on the banks of Lake Grant — let them make a few cooling herbal teas, and they got him to drink them without his knowing it. His fever was extremely high, and the whole day and the whole night went by without his regaining consciousness. Harbert's life hung by a thread, and that thread might snap at any moment.

The next day, November 12, Cyrus Smith and his companions began to have some hope. Harbert had come out of his long stupor. He opened his eyes. He recognized Cyrus Smith, the reporter, Pencroff. He said two or three words. He did not know what had happened. They told him, and Gédéon Spilett begged him to keep absolutely still, telling him that his life was not in danger and that his wounds would heal over in a few days. Besides, Harbert was in almost no pain, and the cold water they kept pouring over the wounds without a break was holding off all inflammation. The wounds were draining steadily, the fever showed no sign of rising, and there was reason to hope that this terrible wound would not end in disaster. Little by little the weight lifted from Pencroff's heart. He was like a Sister of Charity, like a mother at her child's bedside.

Harbert dozed off again, but his sleep seemed better now.

"Tell me again that you've got hope, Mr. Spilett!" said Pencroff. "Tell me again that you'll save Harbert!"

"Yes, we'll save him!" answered the reporter. "The wound is serious, and the bullet may even have gone through the lung, but a hole in that organ isn't fatal."

"God hear you!" Pencroff said again.

As can easily be imagined, in the twenty-four hours since they had come to the corral, the colonists had had no other thought than caring for Harbert. They had worried neither about the danger that might threaten them if the convicts came back nor about the precautions to take for the future.

But that day, while Pencroff watched at the sickbed, Cyrus Smith and the reporter talked over what ought to be done.

First of all, they went over the whole corral. There was no trace of Ayrton. Had the unfortunate man been dragged off by his former accomplices? Had they taken him by surprise in the corral? Had he fought and been killed in the fight? This last guess was only too likely. As he was climbing the palisade, Gédéon Spilett had clearly seen one of the convicts running away along the southern shoulder of Mount Franklin, with Top racing after him. It was one of the men whose boat had been smashed on the rocks at the mouth of the Mercy. Besides, the one Cyrus Smith had killed, whose body was found outside the palisade, was certainly one of Bob Harvey's gang.

As for the corral, it had not yet been damaged in any way. The gates were shut, and the animals had not been able to scatter into the forest. Nor was there any sign of a struggle, any damage, either to the house or to the palisade. Only the ammunition Ayrton had been supplied with had disappeared along with him.

"The poor man must have been taken by surprise," said Cyrus Smith, "and since he was a man who would defend himself, he must have been killed."

"Yes! That's what I'm afraid of!" answered the reporter. "And then, no doubt, the convicts settled in at the corral, where they found plenty of everything, and they ran off only when they saw us coming. It's obvious, too, that by then Ayrton, dead or alive, wasn't here anymore."

"We'll have to beat the forest," said the engineer, "and rid the island of these scoundrels. Pencroff's instincts weren't wrong when he wanted us to hunt them down like wild beasts. It would have spared us a great deal of misery!"

"Yes," answered the reporter, "but now we have the right to show no mercy!"

"In any case," said the engineer, "we're forced to wait a while and stay at the corral until Harbert can be carried safely to Granite House."

"But what about Nab?" asked the reporter.

"Nab is safe."

"And if he gets worried because we haven't come back, and risks coming here?"

"He mustn't come!" Cyrus Smith answered quickly. "He'd be murdered on the way!"

"But it's very likely he'll try to join us!"

"Ah! If the telegraph were still working, we could warn him! But that's impossible now! And we can't leave Pencroff and Harbert here alone!... All right, I'll go to Granite House by myself."

"No, no, Cyrus!" answered the reporter. "You mustn't put yourself in danger! Your courage wouldn't do any good. Those scoundrels are obviously watching the corral. They're lying in wait in the thick woods all around it, and if you left, we'd soon have two disasters to mourn instead of one!"

"But Nab?" the engineer kept saying. "He's had no news of us for twenty-four hours! He'll want to come!"

"And since he'll be even less on his guard than we would be ourselves," answered Gédéon Spilett, "they'll shoot him!..."

"Is there no way at all to warn him?"

While the engineer was thinking, his eyes fell on Top, who was going back and forth and seemed to be saying, "Well, what about me? Aren't I here?"

"Top!" cried Cyrus Smith.

The dog bounded up at his master's call.

"Yes, Top will go!" said the reporter, who had understood the engineer. "Top will get through where we couldn't! He'll take the news from the corral to Granite House, and he'll bring us back the news from Granite House!"

"Quick!" answered Cyrus Smith. "Quick!"

Gédéon Spilett had swiftly torn a page out of his notebook, and on it he wrote these lines:

    "Harbert wounded. We are at the corral. Be on your guard. Do not leave Granite House. Have the convicts shown themselves near you? Answer by Top."

This brief note held everything Nab needed to learn, and at the same time it asked him everything the colonists needed to know. It was folded and tied to Top's collar where it could not be missed.

"Top! Good dog," said the engineer, stroking him. "Nab, Top! Nab! Go! Go!"

Top leaped up at these words. He understood; he guessed what was being asked of him. He knew the Corral Road by heart. He could cover it in less than half an hour, and there was reason to hope that where neither Cyrus Smith nor the reporter could have ventured without danger, Top, running through the grass or along the edge of the woods, would get by unseen.

The engineer went to the gate of the corral and pushed open one of its two halves.

"Nab! Top, Nab!" the engineer said once more, stretching out his hand toward Granite House.

Top sprang outside and vanished almost at once.

"He'll get there!" said the reporter.

"Yes, and he'll come back, the faithful animal!"

"What time is it?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"Ten o'clock."

"He could be here in an hour. We'll watch for him."

The gate of the corral was shut again. The engineer and the reporter went back into the house. Harbert was sound asleep by then. Pencroff kept his compresses wet all the time.

Seeing that there was nothing more to be done for the moment, Gédéon Spilett busied himself with getting some food ready, while keeping a careful watch on the part of the palisade that backed onto the mountain's shoulder, where an attack might come from.

The colonists waited for Top's return, and not without anxiety. A little before eleven o'clock, Cyrus Smith and the reporter were standing behind the gate, carbines in hand, ready to open it at the first bark of their dog. They had no doubt that if Top had reached Granite House safely, Nab would have sent him straight back.

The two of them had been there for about ten minutes when a shot rang out, followed at once by a burst of barking.

The engineer opened the gate, saw a last wisp of smoke a hundred paces off in the woods, and fired in that direction.

Almost at the same moment Top bounded into the corral, and the gate was quickly shut again.

"Top! Top!" cried the engineer, taking the dog's big, good-natured head in his arms.

A note was tied to his neck, and Cyrus Smith read these words, written in Nab's large handwriting:

    "No pirates around Granite House. I won't budge. Poor Mr. Harbert!"

Chapter 8: The Convicts Near the Corral

The convicts near the corral — A temporary arrangement — Harbert's treatment continues — Pencroff's first rejoicings — Looking back at the past — What the future holds — Cyrus Smith's ideas on the subject

So the convicts were still there, spying on the corral, determined to kill the colonists one after another! There was nothing left to do but treat them as wild beasts. Yet great precautions had to be taken, because at that moment the wretches held every advantage of position. They could see without being seen. They could take their enemies by surprise with a sudden attack, and they could not be taken by surprise themselves.

Cyrus Smith therefore arranged things so that they could live at the corral, whose stores, besides, would last for a fairly long time. Ayrton's house had been furnished with everything needed for daily life, and the convicts, frightened off by the colonists' arrival, had not had time to plunder it. It was likely, as Gédéon Spilett pointed out, that things had happened this way. The six convicts, once landed on the island, had followed its southern coast. After going along both shores of Serpentine Peninsula, and being in no mood to venture into the Far West forests, they had reached the mouth of Fall River. From there they had gone up the right bank of the stream and come to the spurs of Mount Franklin, where it was natural that they should look for some hiding place among them, and they could not have been long in discovering the corral, which was empty at the time. There, very probably, they had settled in to wait for the moment to carry out their abominable plans. Ayrton's arrival had surprised them, but they had managed to seize the unfortunate man, and... what followed was easy enough to guess!

Now the convicts — down to five, it was true, but well armed — were prowling in the woods, and to venture in among the trees was to lay oneself open to their shots, with no way of either warding them off or seeing them coming.

"Wait! There's nothing else we can do!" Cyrus Smith kept repeating. "When Harbert is well again, we can organize a general sweep of the island and settle with these convicts. That will be the purpose of our great expedition, and at the same time..."

"...the search for our mysterious protector," added Gédéon Spilett, finishing the engineer's sentence. "Ah! You have to admit, my dear Cyrus, that this time his protection let us down — and at the very moment we needed it most!"

"Who knows?" answered the engineer.

"What do you mean?" asked the reporter.

"That we haven't come to the end of our troubles, my dear Spilett, and that this powerful intervention may yet have a chance to act. But that isn't the question now. Harbert's life comes before everything."

That was the colonists' most painful concern. Several days went by, and the poor boy's condition, fortunately, had not grown worse. Now, every day won from the illness counted for a great deal. The cold water, always kept at the right temperature, had entirely prevented the wounds from becoming inflamed. It even seemed to the reporter that this water, which was slightly sulfurous — the nearness of the volcano explained that — acted more directly to help the wounds heal over. There was much less pus, and thanks to the unceasing care that surrounded him, Harbert was coming back to life, and his fever was tending to fall. He was kept, besides, on a strict diet, and so his weakness was extreme, as it had to be. But he never lacked for herbal teas, and complete rest was doing him the greatest good.

Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff had become very skillful at dressing the young patient's wounds. Every scrap of linen in the house had been sacrificed. Harbert's wounds were covered with compresses and lint and bound neither too tightly nor too loosely, so as to help them heal without setting off any inflammation. The reporter brought extreme care to these dressings, knowing well how much they mattered, and he kept repeating to his companions what most doctors readily admit: that a well-made dressing is perhaps rarer to see than a well-done operation.

After ten days, on November 22, Harbert was noticeably better. He had begun to take a little food. The color was coming back into his cheeks, and his kind eyes smiled at his nurses. He chatted a little, in spite of the efforts of Pencroff, who talked the whole time himself to keep him from speaking and told him the most unlikely stories. Harbert had asked him about Ayrton, whom he was surprised not to see near him, thinking he must be at the corral. But the sailor, not wanting to distress Harbert, had simply answered that Ayrton had gone to join Nab and help defend Granite House.

"Ha!" he would say. "Those pirates! Those gentlemen have lost all right to any consideration! And Mr. Smith wanted to win them over with kindness! I'll send them some kindness, all right — good lead, the proper caliber!"

"And nobody's seen them since?" asked Harbert.

"No, my boy," answered the sailor, "but we'll find them again, and when you're well, we'll see whether those cowards who shoot people in the back will dare to attack us face to face!"

"I'm still very weak, my poor Pencroff!"

"Eh! Your strength will come back little by little! What's a bullet through the chest? A mere joke! I've seen plenty worse, and I'm none the worse for it!"

In short, things seemed to be going as well as they could, and as long as no complications set in, Harbert's recovery could be considered certain. But what would the colonists' situation have been if his condition had worsened — if, for example, the bullet had stayed lodged in his body, or if his arm or his leg had had to be amputated!

"No," Gédéon Spilett said more than once, "I've never thought of a thing like that without shuddering!"

"And yet, if you'd had to act," Cyrus Smith answered him one day, "you wouldn't have hesitated?"

"No, Cyrus!" said Gédéon Spilett. "But God be thanked for sparing us that!"

As in so many other situations, the colonists had called on that logic of plain common sense which had served them so often, and once again, thanks to their general knowledge, they had succeeded! But would the moment not come when all their science would fail them? They were alone on this island. Yet people complete one another by living in society; they need one another. Cyrus Smith knew that well, and sometimes he wondered whether some circumstance might not arise that they would be powerless to overcome!

It seemed to him, besides, that he and his companions, so fortunate until then, had entered an unlucky period. In the more than two and a half years since they had escaped from Richmond, one could say that everything had gone their way. The island had supplied them generously with minerals, plants and animals, and if nature had showered gifts on them without end, their science had known how to make use of what she offered. The material well-being of the colony was, so to speak, complete. More than that, on certain occasions an inexplicable influence had come to their aid!... But all of that could last only for a time!

In short, Cyrus Smith believed he could see their luck beginning to turn against them.

And indeed, the convicts' ship had appeared in the waters of the island, and if those pirates had been destroyed almost by a miracle, six of them, at least, had escaped the disaster. They had landed on the island, and the five who survived were all but impossible to catch. Ayrton had beyond any doubt been murdered by those wretches, who had firearms, and the very first time they used them, Harbert had fallen, struck almost to death. Were these, then, the first blows that hostile fortune was dealing the colonists? That was what Cyrus Smith asked himself! That was what he often repeated to the reporter. And it seemed to them, too, that the intervention which had been so strange, but so effective, and which had served them so well until now, was failing them at last. This mysterious being, whoever he might be, whose existence they could not deny — had he left the island, then? Had he died in his turn?

To these questions no answer was possible. But let no one imagine that Cyrus Smith and his companion, because they talked over such things, were the kind of men to despair! Far from it. They looked the situation in the face, they weighed the chances, they prepared themselves for whatever might happen, they stood firm and upright before the future, and if adversity was at last to strike them, it would find in them men ready to fight it.

Chapter 9: No News of Nab

No news of Nab — A proposal by Pencroff and the reporter that is not accepted — A few sorties by Gédéon Spilett — A scrap of cloth — A message — A hasty departure — Arrival at Prospect Plateau

The young patient's recovery was going steadily. Only one thing was left to wish for now: that his condition would allow them to take him back to Granite House. However well fitted out and well stocked the house at the corral might be, it could not offer the comfort of their healthy granite home. Besides, it was not as safe, and the people inside it, for all their watchfulness, were always under the threat of a shot from the convicts. Back there, on the other hand, in the middle of that impregnable, inaccessible mass of rock, they would have nothing to fear, and any attempt against them would be bound to fail. So they were waiting impatiently for the moment when Harbert could be moved without danger to his wound, and they had made up their minds to move him, even though getting through Jacamar Wood was very difficult.

They had no news of Nab, but they were not worried about him. The brave fellow, well entrenched deep inside Granite House, would not let himself be taken by surprise. Top had not been sent back to him. It had seemed pointless to expose the faithful dog to some gunshot that would have robbed the colonists of their most useful helper.

So they waited, but the colonists were in a hurry to be together again at Granite House. It pained the engineer to see his forces divided, because that was playing into the pirates' hands. Since Ayrton's disappearance there were only four of them against five, for Harbert could not be counted yet — and that was not the least of the worries of the brave boy, who understood very well the trouble he was causing!

The question of how to act against the convicts, as things stood, was talked through thoroughly on November 29 by Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff, at a moment when Harbert was dozing and could not hear them.

"My friends," said the reporter, after they had spoken of Nab and of the impossibility of getting in touch with him, "I agree with you that venturing out on the Corral Road would mean risking a bullet without being able to return it. But don't you think that what we ought to do now is go after those wretches openly and hunt them down?"

"That's just what I was thinking," answered Pencroff. "I don't suppose we've come to the point of being afraid of a bullet, and for my part, if Mr. Cyrus agrees, I'm ready to throw myself into the forest! What the devil! One man's as good as another!"

"But is he as good as five?" asked the engineer.

"I'll go with Pencroff," answered the reporter, "and the two of us, well armed, along with Top..."

"My dear Spilett, and you too, Pencroff," Cyrus Smith went on, "let's think this through coolly. If the convicts were holed up in one spot on the island, if we knew where that spot was, and if all we had to do was flush them out of it, I'd understand a direct attack. But isn't there reason to fear, on the contrary, that they'd be sure of firing the first shot?"

"Oh, Mr. Cyrus," cried Pencroff, "a bullet doesn't always reach its address!"

"The one that hit Harbert didn't go astray, Pencroff," answered the engineer. "Besides, notice that if the two of you left the corral, I'd be left here alone to defend it. Can you promise me that the convicts won't see you leave it, that they won't let you go deep into the forest and then attack the corral while you're gone, knowing there's no one here but a wounded boy and one man?"

"You're right, Mr. Cyrus," answered Pencroff, his chest swelling with a smothered anger. "You're right. They'll do anything to take back the corral, because they know it's well stocked! And on your own you couldn't hold out against them! Oh, if only we were at Granite House!"

"If we were at Granite House," answered the engineer, "things would be very different! There I wouldn't be afraid to leave Harbert with one of us, and the other three could go and search the island's forests. But we're at the corral, and the right thing is to stay here until we can all leave it together!"

There was no answer to Cyrus Smith's reasoning, and his companions knew it.

"If only Ayrton were still with us!" said Gédéon Spilett. "Poor man! His return to the society of men didn't last long!"

"If he's dead?..." Pencroff added, in a rather odd tone.

"So, Pencroff, you hope those scoundrels spared him?" asked Gédéon Spilett.

"Yes! If they had some reason to!"

"What! You'd suppose that Ayrton, finding his old accomplices again, forgetting everything he owes us..."

"Who knows?" answered the sailor, who did not put forward this ugly suggestion without hesitating.

"Pencroff," said Cyrus Smith, taking the sailor by the arm, "that's an unworthy thought, and you'd hurt me deeply if you kept on talking that way! I vouch for Ayrton's loyalty!"

"So do I," the reporter put in quickly.

"Yes... yes!... Mr. Cyrus... I'm wrong," answered Pencroff. "That was an unworthy thought I had there, and nothing justifies it! But what do you expect? My head's not quite my own anymore. Being shut up in this corral weighs on me something terrible, and I've never been so worked up in my life!"

"Be patient, Pencroff," answered the engineer. "How soon, my dear Spilett, do you think Harbert can be moved to Granite House?"

"That's hard to say, Cyrus," answered the reporter, "because one careless move could have fatal consequences. But still, his recovery is coming along steadily, and if his strength has come back a week from now — well, we'll see!"

A week! That put off the return to Granite House until the first days of December at the earliest.

By that time spring was already two months old. The weather was fine, and the heat was beginning to grow strong. The island's forests were in full leaf, and the time was coming when the usual harvests would have to be brought in. So their return to Prospect Plateau would be followed by a great deal of farm work, interrupted only by the expedition they had planned across the island.

You can see, then, how much harm this confinement at the corral was doing the colonists. But if they were forced to bow to necessity, they did not do it without impatience.

Once or twice the reporter ventured out onto the road and made a circuit around the palisade. Top went with him, and Gédéon Spilett, his carbine cocked, was ready for anything.

He had no bad encounters and found no suspicious tracks. His dog would have warned him of any danger, and since Top did not bark, it was fair to conclude that there was nothing to fear, at the moment at least, and that the convicts were busy in some other part of the island.

On his second sortie, however, on November 27, Gédéon Spilett, who had ventured a quarter of a mile into the woods south of the mountain, noticed that Top was onto something. The dog had dropped his casual manner. He was running back and forth, nosing through the grass and the brush, as if his sense of smell had told him of something suspicious.

Gédéon Spilett followed Top, egging him on and urging him with his voice, while keeping a sharp lookout, his carbine at his shoulder, and using the trees for cover. It was not likely that Top had scented a man, because in that case he would have announced it with half-held-back barks and a kind of muffled fury. And since he was not growling at all, the danger was neither near nor close at hand.

About five minutes went by like this, with Top nosing about and the reporter cautiously following, when all of a sudden the dog dashed into a thick bush and dragged out a scrap of cloth.

It was a piece of clothing, stained and torn, and Gédéon Spilett brought it straight back to the corral.

There the colonists examined it, and they recognized it as a piece of Ayrton's jacket, a piece of the felt that was made nowhere but in the workshop at Granite House.

"You see, Pencroff," Cyrus Smith pointed out, "the unlucky Ayrton put up a fight. The convicts dragged him off against his will! Do you still doubt his honesty?"

"No, Mr. Cyrus," answered the sailor, "and I got over that moment of distrust a long time ago! But it seems to me there's a conclusion to be drawn from this."

"What's that?" asked the reporter.

"That Ayrton wasn't killed at the corral! That they dragged him off alive, since he fought back! So maybe he's still alive!"

"Maybe so, indeed," answered the engineer, and he stayed lost in thought.

Here was a hope that Ayrton's companions could cling to. Until now they had had to believe that Ayrton, taken by surprise at the corral, had fallen to some bullet, just as Harbert had. But if the convicts had not killed him at once, if they had carried him off alive to some other part of the island, wasn't it possible that he was still their prisoner? Perhaps one of them had even recognized in Ayrton an old companion from Australia — Ben Joyce, the leader of the escaped convicts! And who knows whether they had not formed the impossible hope of winning Ayrton back to their side! He would have been so useful to them if they could have made a traitor of him!...

So this incident was taken as a good sign at the corral, and it no longer seemed impossible that they would find Ayrton again. For his part, if he was only a prisoner, Ayrton would no doubt do everything he could to escape from those bandits' hands, and he would be a powerful ally to the colonists!

"In any case," Gédéon Spilett pointed out, "if by good luck Ayrton manages to get away, he'll go straight to Granite House. He doesn't know about the attempt to murder Harbert, and so he can't imagine we're shut up here at the corral."

"Oh! I wish he were there, at Granite House!" cried Pencroff. "And us too! Because after all, even if those scoundrels can't do anything against our home, they can at least lay waste to the plateau — our plantations, our poultry yard!"

Pencroff had become a real farmer, attached heart and soul to his crops. But it must be said that Harbert was more impatient than any of them to get back to Granite House, because he knew how badly the colonists were needed there. And he was the one keeping them at the corral! So a single idea filled his mind: to leave the corral, to leave it no matter what! He believed he could stand being moved to Granite House. He insisted that his strength would come back faster in his own room, with the sea air and the view of the sea!

Several times he pressed Gédéon Spilett. But the reporter was afraid — and rightly — that Harbert's wounds, still badly healed, would open again on the way, and he did not give the order to leave.

Then something happened that led Cyrus Smith and his two friends to give in to the boy's wishes — and God knows what grief and remorse that decision might bring them!

It was November 29. It was seven o'clock in the morning. The three colonists were talking in Harbert's room when they heard Top barking loudly.

Cyrus Smith, Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett seized their guns, which were always loaded and ready to fire, and went out of the house.

Top had run to the foot of the palisade and was jumping and barking — but with pleasure, not anger.

"Someone's coming!"

"Yes!"

"It isn't an enemy!"

"Nab, maybe?"

"Or Ayrton?"

These words had barely passed between the engineer and his two companions when a body came leaping over the palisade and landed on the ground inside the corral.

It was Jup — Master Jup in person — and Top gave him a true friend's welcome!

"Jup!" cried Pencroff.

"Nab's sent him to us!" said the reporter.

"Then," answered the engineer, "he must have a note on him."

Pencroff rushed over to the orangutan. Clearly, if Nab had had something important to tell his master, he could not have used a surer or swifter messenger — one who could get through where neither the colonists nor perhaps even Top himself could have gone.

Cyrus Smith had not been mistaken. A little bag hung around Jup's neck, and in the bag was a note in Nab's hand.

Imagine the despair of Cyrus Smith and his companions when they read these words:

    "Friday, 6 a.m.
    Plateau overrun by the convicts!
    Nab."

They looked at one another without saying a word, and then they went back into the house. What were they to do? The convicts on Prospect Plateau — that meant disaster, devastation, ruin!

When Harbert saw the engineer, the reporter and Pencroff come back in, he understood that the situation had just taken a turn for the worse, and when he caught sight of Jup, he no longer doubted that some misfortune was threatening Granite House.

"Mr. Cyrus," he said, "I want to go. I can stand the trip! I want to go!"

Gédéon Spilett went over to Harbert. Then, after looking at him for a moment:

"Let's go, then!" he said.

The question of whether Harbert should be carried on a stretcher or in the cart that Ayrton had brought to the corral was quickly settled. The stretcher would have moved more gently for the wounded boy, but it needed two bearers, which meant two guns fewer for their defense if they were attacked on the way.

Couldn't they, on the other hand, use the cart and leave every pair of hands free? Was it really impossible to lay the mattresses Harbert was lying on inside it, and to go forward so carefully that he would be spared every jolt? It could be done.

The cart was brought round. Pencroff harnessed the onagga to it. Cyrus Smith and the reporter lifted Harbert's mattresses and laid them on the floor of the cart, between its two side rails.

The weather was fine. Bright rays of sunlight were slipping through the trees.

"Are the weapons ready?" asked Cyrus Smith.

They were. The engineer and Pencroff, each armed with a double-barreled gun, and Gédéon Spilett, holding his carbine, had only to set off.

"Are you comfortable, Harbert?" asked the engineer.

"Oh, Mr. Cyrus," answered the boy, "don't worry, I won't die on the way!"

As he said this, anyone could see that the poor boy was calling up all his energy, and that by a supreme effort of will he was holding on to a strength that was ready to go out.

The engineer felt his heart clench painfully. He still hesitated to give the signal to leave. But that would have driven Harbert to despair — perhaps killed him.

"Let's go!" said Cyrus Smith.

The gate of the corral was opened. Jup and Top, who knew when to keep quiet, rushed out ahead. The cart went out, the gate was shut again, and the onagga, led by Pencroff, moved forward at a slow walk.

It would certainly have been better to take some road other than the one that ran straight from the corral to Granite House, but the cart would have had great difficulty getting through the woods. So they had to follow that road, even though the convicts were bound to know it.

Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett walked on either side of the cart, ready to answer any attack. Still, it was not likely that the convicts had left Prospect Plateau yet. Nab's note had obviously been written and sent off the moment the convicts showed themselves there. Now, the note was dated six o'clock in the morning, and the nimble orangutan, used to coming to the corral often, had taken barely three quarters of an hour to cover the five miles that lay between it and Granite House. So the road ought to be safe for the moment, and if there was any shooting to be done, it would most likely be only as they drew near Granite House.

All the same, the colonists kept strictly on their guard. Top and Jup — Jup armed with his stick — now ranging ahead, now beating the woods along the sides of the road, gave no sign of danger.

The cart moved slowly forward, with Pencroff at its head. It had left the corral at half past seven. An hour later, four of the five miles had been covered without anything happening.

The road was as deserted as all that part of Jacamar Wood that stretched between the Mercy and the lake. There was no alarm of any kind. The thickets seemed as empty as on the day the colonists first landed on the island.

They were drawing near the plateau. One more mile, and they would see the little bridge over Glycerin Creek. Cyrus Smith had no doubt that this bridge would be down and in place — either because the convicts had come in that way, or because, after crossing one of the streams that closed off the plateau, they had taken the precaution of lowering it to leave themselves a way of retreat.

At last a gap in the last of the trees opened onto a view of the sea's horizon. But the cart kept on going, since none of its defenders could think of leaving it.

At that moment Pencroff stopped the onagga, and in a terrible voice he cried:

"Oh! The villains!"

And he pointed to a thick smoke swirling over the mill, the stables and the buildings of the poultry yard.

A man was moving about in the middle of that smoke.

It was Nab.

His companions gave a shout. He heard them and ran toward them...

The convicts had left the plateau about half an hour before, after laying it waste!

"And Mr. Harbert?" cried Nab.

Gédéon Spilett came back to the cart at that moment.

Harbert had lost consciousness!

Chapter 10: A Deadly Fever

Harbert carried to Granite House — Nab tells what happened — Cyrus Smith visits the plateau — Ruin and devastation — The colonists helpless against illness — Willow bark — A deadly fever — Top barks again!

The convicts, the dangers that threatened Granite House, the ruins that covered the plateau — none of it mattered anymore. Harbert's condition outweighed everything. Had the journey done him fatal harm by causing some injury inside? The reporter could not say, but he and his companions were in despair.

The cart was brought to the bend of the river. There a few branches, laid out in the shape of a stretcher, received the mattresses on which Harbert lay unconscious. Ten minutes later Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff were at the foot of the cliff, leaving Nab to take the cart back up to Prospect Plateau.

The elevator was set in motion, and soon Harbert was lying in his own bed in Granite House.

The care they lavished on him brought him back to life. He smiled for a moment when he found himself in his room again, but he could barely murmur a few words, he was so weak.

Gédéon Spilett examined his wounds. He was afraid they had reopened, since they had not fully healed... but they had not. Then where did this collapse come from? Why had Harbert's condition grown worse?

The boy then fell into a kind of feverish sleep, and the reporter and Pencroff stayed by his bed.

Meanwhile Cyrus Smith was telling Nab what had happened at the corral, and Nab was telling his master about the events that had just taken place on the plateau.

It was only the night before that the convicts had shown themselves at the edge of the forest, near Glycerin Creek. Nab, who was keeping watch near the poultry yard, had not hesitated to fire at one of the pirates as he was getting ready to cross the stream; but the night was fairly dark, and he could not tell whether he had hit the wretch. In any case, that had not been enough to drive the gang off, and Nab had only just had time to get back up to Granite House, where at least he was safe.

But what was he to do then? How could he prevent the destruction the convicts were threatening to wreak on the plateau? Did Nab have any way of warning his master? And besides, what situation were the people at the corral in themselves?

Cyrus Smith and his companions had left on November 11, and it was now the 29th. So for nineteen days Nab had had no news except what Top had brought him, and that news was disastrous: Ayrton gone, Harbert badly wounded, the engineer, the reporter and the sailor all but imprisoned in the corral!

What was he to do? poor Nab kept asking himself. For himself he had nothing to fear, since the convicts could not reach him in Granite House. But the buildings, the plantations, everything they had built up, all at the mercy of the pirates! Wouldn't it be right to leave it to Cyrus Smith to judge what had to be done, and at least to warn him of the danger that hung over him?

That was when Nab had the idea of using Jup and trusting him with a note. He knew how extremely intelligent the orangutan was; it had been put to the test many times. Jup understood the word "corral," which had often been spoken in front of him, and, as the reader will remember, he had often driven the cart there with Pencroff. Day had not yet broken. The nimble orangutan would know how to slip through those woods unseen — and in any case the convicts would take him for one of their natural inhabitants.

Nab did not hesitate. He wrote the note, he tied it around Jup's neck, he led the ape to the door of Granite House, let a long rope unroll from it all the way to the ground, and then, several times over, he repeated these words:

"Jup! Jup! Corral! Corral!"

The animal understood, seized the rope, slid quickly down to the beach and disappeared into the darkness, without stirring the convicts' attention in the least.

"You did well, Nab," Cyrus Smith answered, "but perhaps you'd have done even better not to warn us!"

And as he said this, Cyrus Smith was thinking of Harbert, whose recovery the journey seemed to have put in such grave danger.

Nab finished his story. The convicts had not shown themselves on the beach. Not knowing how many people lived on the island, they might suppose that Granite House was defended by a sizable force. They must have remembered that during the attack on the brig they had been met by a heavy fire from both the lower rocks and the upper ones, and no doubt they did not want to expose themselves to it. But Prospect Plateau lay open to them, and the guns of Granite House could not sweep it. So there they gave free rein to their instinct for plunder — looting, burning, doing harm for harm's sake — and they withdrew only half an hour before the colonists arrived, believing them still shut up in the corral.
