Nab had rushed out of his refuge. He had climbed back up onto the plateau, at the risk of catching a bullet, he had tried to put out the fire that was devouring the poultry-yard buildings, and he had fought the flames, but in vain, until the moment the cart appeared at the edge of the woods.

Such had been these grave events. The presence of the convicts was a permanent threat to the colonists of Lincoln Island, who had been so happy until then — and who could expect still greater misfortunes to come!

Gédéon Spilett stayed in Granite House with Harbert and Pencroff, while Cyrus Smith, with Nab beside him, went to judge for himself how great the disaster was.

It was lucky that the convicts had not come as far as the foot of Granite House. The workshops at the Chimneys would not have escaped destruction. But then again, that damage might have been easier to repair than the ruins piled up on Prospect Plateau!

Cyrus Smith and Nab made their way toward the Mercy and walked up its left bank without meeting any trace of the convicts' passage. On the other side of the river, in the thick of the woods, they saw no suspicious sign either.

Besides, in all probability, one of two things could be assumed. Either the convicts knew that the colonists had come back to Granite House — they might have seen them go by on the Corral Road — or else, after laying waste the plateau, they had plunged into Jacamar Wood, following the course of the Mercy, and knew nothing of the colonists' return.

In the first case, they would have gone back toward the corral, which was now undefended and held supplies that were precious to them.

In the second, they would have gone back to their camp to wait there for some chance to renew the attack.

So there would be good reason to strike first; but any undertaking meant to rid the island of them still depended on Harbert's condition. Cyrus Smith would need every one of his men, and no one could leave Granite House at that moment.

The engineer and Nab reached the plateau. It was a scene of desolation. The fields had been trampled. The ears of grain, which were just about to be harvested, lay on the ground. The other plantings had suffered no less. The kitchen garden was torn up. Fortunately Granite House held a reserve of seeds that would make it possible to repair the damage.

As for the mill, the poultry-yard buildings and the onaggas' stable, the fire had destroyed them all.

A few frightened animals were wandering across the plateau. The birds, which had taken refuge on the waters of the lake during the fire, were already coming back to their usual places and dabbling along the shore. Here everything would have to be done over again.

Cyrus Smith's face, paler than usual, showed an inner anger he was mastering only with difficulty, but he did not say a word. He took one last look at his ravaged fields and at the smoke still rising from the ruins, and then he went back to Granite House.

The days that followed were the saddest the colonists had yet spent on the island! Harbert was visibly growing weaker. It seemed that a more serious illness, the result of the deep upheaval his body had suffered, was threatening to break out, and Gédéon Spilett foresaw such a turn for the worse that he would be powerless to fight it!

And indeed Harbert lay in an almost continuous drowsiness, and a few signs of delirium began to show. Cooling herbal teas were the only remedies the colonists had. The fever was not yet very high, but soon it seemed bent on settling into regular attacks.

Gédéon Spilett recognized it on December 6. The poor boy's fingers, nose and ears turned extremely pale, and at first he was seized with light chills, with goose flesh, with shivering. His pulse was weak and irregular, his skin dry, his thirst intense. This stage was soon followed by a stage of heat: his face flushed, his skin reddened, his pulse quickened. Then came a heavy sweat, after which the fever seemed to drop. The attack had lasted about five hours.

Gédéon Spilett had not left Harbert's side. The boy now had an intermittent fever — that was only too certain — and this fever had to be cut short at all costs before it grew worse.

"And to cut it short," Gédéon Spilett said to Cyrus Smith, "we need a febrifuge — something that brings fever down."

"A febrifuge!" the engineer answered. "We have no cinchona bark and no quinine sulfate!"

"No," said Gédéon Spilett, "but there are willows on the shore of the lake, and willow bark can sometimes take the place of quinine."

"Then let's try it without losing a moment!" answered Cyrus Smith.

Willow bark, in fact, has rightly been regarded as a substitute for cinchona, like the horse chestnut, holly leaves, snakeroot and others. They obviously had to try it, even though it was not as good as cinchona, and they would have to use it in its natural state, since they had no means of extracting its alkaloid — that is, salicin.

Cyrus Smith went himself to cut a few pieces of bark from the trunk of a kind of black willow. He brought them back to Granite House, ground them to a powder, and that powder was given to Harbert that same evening.

The night passed without any serious incident. Harbert was somewhat delirious, but the fever did not come back in the night, and it did not come back the following day either.

Pencroff began to hope again. Gédéon Spilett said nothing. It might be that the attacks did not come every day — that the fever was tertian, in a word, returning every other day — and that it would come back the day after. So that day was awaited with the keenest anxiety.

It could be noticed, besides, that in the fever-free interval Harbert lay as if shattered, his head heavy and easily dizzy. And there was another symptom that frightened the reporter to the last degree: Harbert's liver was beginning to become congested, and soon a more violent delirium showed that his brain was being affected too.

Gédéon Spilett was appalled by this new complication. He took the engineer aside.

"It's a pernicious fever!" he told him.

"A pernicious fever!" cried Cyrus Smith. "You're mistaken, Spilett. A pernicious fever doesn't break out on its own. You have to have caught the germ of it!"

"I'm not mistaken," answered the reporter. "No doubt Harbert picked up that germ in the island's marshes, and that's enough. He's already had a first attack. If a second one comes, and if we can't prevent the third... he's lost!"

"But the willow bark?"

"It isn't enough," answered the reporter, "and a third attack of pernicious fever that isn't cut short with quinine is always fatal!"

Fortunately Pencroff had heard none of this conversation. It would have driven him mad.

It is easy to imagine the anxiety the engineer and the reporter went through during that day of December 7 and the night that followed.

Toward the middle of the day the second attack came. The crisis was terrible. Harbert felt that he was lost! He stretched out his arms to Cyrus Smith, to Spilett, to Pencroff! He did not want to die!... It was a heartbreaking scene. Pencroff had to be led away.

The attack lasted five hours. It was clear that Harbert would not survive a third.

The night was dreadful. In his delirium Harbert said things that broke his companions' hearts! He raved, he fought the convicts, he called for Ayrton! He pleaded with that mysterious being, that protector who had vanished now and whose image haunted him... then he fell back into a deep prostration that drained the life from him entirely... Several times Gédéon Spilett thought the poor boy was dead!

The next day, December 8, was nothing but one fainting spell after another. Harbert's wasted hands clutched at his sheets. They had given him fresh doses of the ground bark, but the reporter no longer expected anything from it.

"If we haven't given him a stronger febrifuge before tomorrow morning," said the reporter, "Harbert will be dead!"

Night came — the last night, no doubt, of this brave, good, intelligent boy, so far beyond his years, whom they all loved like their own son! The only remedy that existed against this terrible pernicious fever, the only specific that could defeat it, was not to be found on Lincoln Island!

During that night of December 8 to 9, Harbert was seized again by a more violent delirium. His liver was horribly congested, his brain was under attack, and by now it was impossible for him to recognize anyone.

Would he live until the morning, until that third attack that was bound to carry him off? It no longer seemed likely. His strength was exhausted, and between the crises he lay as if lifeless.

Toward three o'clock in the morning Harbert gave a terrifying cry. He seemed to writhe in a final convulsion. Nab, who was beside him, rushed in terror into the next room, where his companions were keeping watch!

At that moment Top barked in a strange way...

They all came back in at once and managed to hold down the dying boy, who was trying to throw himself out of bed, while Gédéon Spilett, taking his arm, felt his pulse slowly rising...

It was five o'clock in the morning. The rays of the rising sun were beginning to slip into the rooms of Granite House. A fine day was dawning, and that day would be poor Harbert's last!...

A ray of light slipped as far as the table that stood near the bed.

Suddenly Pencroff gave a cry and pointed to an object lying on that table...

It was a small oblong box, and on its lid were these words:

    Quinine Sulfate.

Chapter 11: An Inexplicable Mystery

An inexplicable mystery — Harbert's recovery — The parts of the island still to explore — Preparations for departure — The first day — The night — The second day — The kauris — The pair of cassowaries — Footprints in the forest

Gédéon Spilett took the box and opened it. Inside were about two hundred grains of a white powder. He touched a few specks of it to his lips. Its extreme bitterness could not deceive him. It was indeed the precious alkaloid of cinchona bark, the best febrifuge there is.

They had to give this powder to Harbert without a moment's hesitation. How it had come to be there could be argued about later.

"Coffee," said Gédéon Spilett.

A few moments later Nab brought a cup of the lukewarm brew. Gédéon Spilett stirred about eighteen grains of the quinine into it, and they managed to get Harbert to drink the mixture.

There was still time, for the third attack of the pernicious fever had not yet come!

And, if we may add it here, it was never going to come!

Besides, it must be said, every one of them had found hope again. The mysterious influence had made itself felt once more, and at the supreme moment, just when they had given up hope of it!...

After a few hours Harbert was resting more peacefully. Now the colonists could talk over what had happened. The unknown being's intervention was plainer than ever. But how had he managed to get inside Granite House during the night? It was absolutely inexplicable, and truly the way the "genie of the island" went about things was no less strange than the genie himself.

Throughout that day, roughly every three hours, Harbert was given a dose of the quinine sulfate.

By the very next day Harbert felt a certain improvement. He was certainly not cured. Intermittent fevers are apt to come back, often and dangerously. But he lacked no care. And then, the remedy was there — and no doubt the one who had brought it was not far off! In short, an immense hope came back into every heart.

That hope was not disappointed. Ten days later, on December 20, Harbert began his convalescence. He was still weak, and he had been put on a strict diet, but not a single attack had come back. And the obedient boy followed every order he was given so willingly! He wanted so badly to get well!

Pencroff was like a man who has been pulled up from the bottom of an abyss. He had fits of joy that came close to delirium. Once the hour of the third attack had gone by, he had hugged the reporter so hard he nearly smothered him. From then on he never called him anything but Dr. Spilett.

The real doctor remained to be found.

"We'll find him!" the sailor kept saying.

And certainly that man, whoever he might be, could expect a rough hug from the worthy Pencroff!

December came to an end, and with it the year 1867, in which the colonists of Lincoln Island had been so hard tried. They entered the year 1868 in magnificent weather — splendid heat, a tropical temperature, happily cooled by the sea breeze. Harbert was coming back to life. From his bed, set beside one of the windows of Granite House, he breathed in that healthy air, heavy with the smell of salt, and it gave him back his health. He was beginning to eat, and heaven knows what good little dishes, light and tasty, Nab cooked up for him!

"It was enough to make you wish you'd been dying!" said Pencroff.

During this whole period the convicts did not show themselves near Granite House a single time. Of Ayrton there was no news. The engineer and Harbert still kept some hope of finding him, but their companions no longer doubted that the unfortunate man had been killed. All the same, this uncertainty could not go on, and as soon as the boy was fit, the expedition would be undertaken — and its result was to be of great importance. But they would have to wait perhaps a month, because it would take the colony's full strength to get the better of the convicts.

Meanwhile Harbert was getting better and better. The congestion of the liver had cleared, and his wounds could be considered healed for good.

During that month of January important work was done on Prospect Plateau, but it consisted only of saving what could be saved of the ruined crops, wheat and vegetables alike. Seeds and plants were gathered up, so as to provide a new harvest in the coming season. As for rebuilding the poultry-yard sheds, the mill and the stables, Cyrus Smith preferred to wait. While he and his companions were out hunting the convicts, those villains might very well pay the plateau another visit, and it would not do to give them a reason to go back to their trade of plunderers and arsonists. Once the island had been cleared of these criminals, they would see about rebuilding.

The young convalescent had begun to get up in the second half of January — at first for one hour a day, then two, then three. His strength came back visibly, so vigorous was his constitution. He was eighteen by then. He was tall, and he promised to become a man of fine and noble bearing. From that time on his recovery, though it still called for some care — and Dr. Spilett was very strict — went steadily forward.

By the end of the month Harbert was already walking about Prospect Plateau and the beaches. A few sea baths that he took with Pencroff and Nab did him a world of good. Cyrus Smith thought he could already set the day of departure, and it was fixed for the coming February 15. The nights, very clear at that time of year, would favor the searches they meant to make over the whole island.

So the preparations for this exploration were begun, and they had to be thorough, because the colonists had sworn not to come back to Granite House until their double goal had been reached: on the one hand, to destroy the convicts and find Ayrton, if he was still alive; on the other, to discover the one who watched over the colony's fortunes so effectively.

Of Lincoln Island, the colonists knew thoroughly the whole east coast from Claw Cape to the Mandible Capes, the vast Shelduck Marsh, the surroundings of Lake Grant, Jacamar Wood between the Corral Road and the Mercy, the courses of the Mercy and Red Creek, and finally the spurs of Mount Franklin, among which the corral had been built.

They had explored, but only incompletely, the long shoreline of Washington Bay from Claw Cape to Reptile End, the strip of forest and marsh along the west coast, and those endless dunes that ended at the half-open jaws of Shark Gulf.

But they had not surveyed at all the broad wooded stretches that covered Serpentine Peninsula, the whole right bank of the Mercy, the left bank of Fall River, and the tangle of spurs and side valleys that held up three-quarters of the base of Mount Franklin to the west, north and east — where no doubt there were plenty of deep hiding places. That meant several thousand acres of the island had still escaped their investigations.

So it was decided that the expedition would cross the Far West, so as to take in the whole region lying on the right bank of the Mercy.

It might perhaps have been better to head first for the corral, where it was feared the convicts had taken refuge again, either to plunder it or to settle in. But either the corral had already been laid waste, and it was too late to prevent it, or the convicts had found it worth their while to dig in there, and there would always be time to go and drive them out of their hideout.

So, after some discussion, the first plan was kept, and the colonists resolved to make their way through the woods to Reptile End. They would cut their way with axes, and so lay out the first track of a road that would link Granite House with the tip of the peninsula, over a distance of sixteen or seventeen miles.

The cart was in perfect condition. The onaggas, well rested, could manage a long haul. Food, camping gear, the portable stove and various utensils were loaded onto the cart, along with weapons and ammunition chosen with care from Granite House's arsenal, so well stocked now. But they could not forget that the convicts might be roaming the woods, and that in the middle of those thick forests a shot was quickly fired — and quickly taken. So the little band of colonists had to stay together and not split up on any pretext.

It was also decided that no one would stay behind at Granite House. Even Top and Jup were to be part of the expedition. The inaccessible dwelling could guard itself.

February 14, the day before they left, was a Sunday. It was given over entirely to rest and made holy by the thanksgiving the colonists offered to the Creator. Harbert, completely cured but still a little weak, would have a place kept for him on the cart.

The next day, at daybreak, Cyrus Smith took the measures needed to keep Granite House safe from any invasion. The ladders that had once been used to climb up were carried to the Chimneys and buried deep in the sand, so that they could serve for the return — because the drum of the elevator was taken apart, and nothing was left of the machine. Pencroff stayed in Granite House last, to finish the job, and he came down by means of a doubled rope whose other end was held at the bottom. Once the rope had been pulled down to the ground, there was no longer any link at all between the upper landing and the beach.

The weather was magnificent.

"It's going to be a hot day!" said the reporter cheerfully.

"Bah! Dr. Spilett," answered Pencroff, "we'll be walking in the shade of the trees, and we won't even see the sun!"

"Let's go!" said the engineer.

The cart was waiting on the shore in front of the Chimneys. The reporter had insisted that Harbert ride in it, at least for the first few hours of the trip, and the boy had to obey his doctor's orders.

Nab went at the head of the onaggas. Cyrus Smith, the reporter and the sailor walked ahead. Top frisked about happily. Harbert had offered Jup a seat in his carriage, and Jup had accepted without any fuss. The moment of departure had come, and the little band set off.

The cart first rounded the corner at the river mouth. Then, after going a mile up the left bank of the Mercy, it crossed the bridge where the road to Balloon Harbor began. There the explorers left that road on their left and began to push in under the cover of the immense woods that made up the Far West.

For the first two miles the trees were widely spaced, and the cart could move about freely. Now and then they had to cut through a few creepers and thickets of brush, but nothing serious stopped the colonists' progress.

The thick branches overhead kept a cool shade on the ground. Deodars, Douglas firs, casuarinas, banksias, gum trees, dragon trees and other species they already knew followed one another as far as the eye could see. All the birds familiar on the island were there in full force — grouse, jacamars, pheasants, lories, and the whole chattering family of cockatoos, parakeets and parrots. Agoutis, kangaroos and capybaras darted through the grass, and all of it reminded the colonists of their first excursions when they had arrived on the island.

"All the same," Cyrus Smith pointed out, "I notice that these animals, four-footed and feathered alike, are shyer than they used to be. So these woods have been gone through recently by the convicts, and we're sure to find traces of them."

And indeed, in many places they could make out where a band of men had passed, more or less recently. Here, branches broken on the trees, perhaps to mark the way; there, the ashes of a dead fire, and footprints kept by patches of clayey ground. But all in all, nothing that looked like a permanent camp.

The engineer had told his companions not to hunt. Gunshots might have alerted the convicts, who were perhaps prowling the forest. Besides, the hunters would inevitably have been drawn some distance from the cart, and walking alone was strictly forbidden.

In the second part of the day, about six miles from Granite House, the going became rather hard. To get through certain thickets they had to fell trees and clear a path. Before going into these dense copses, Cyrus Smith took care to send Top and Jup in first, and they carried out their task conscientiously. When the dog and the orangutan came back without having raised any alarm, it meant there was nothing to fear, either from the convicts or from the wild beasts — two kinds of creature in the animal kingdom whose savage instincts put them on the same level.

On the evening of that first day the colonists camped about nine miles from Granite House, on the bank of a little tributary of the Mercy that they had not known existed. It must have belonged to the network of waters to which this soil owed its astonishing fertility.

They ate a hearty supper, for the colonists' appetites were very sharp, and measures were taken so that the night would pass without trouble. If the engineer had had to deal only with wild animals, jaguars or others, he would simply have lit fires around his camp, which would have been enough to protect it. But the convicts would have been drawn by those flames rather than kept off, and in that case it was better to wrap themselves in deep darkness.

The watch, besides, was strictly organized. Two of the colonists were to keep watch together, and it was agreed that they would be relieved by their comrades every two hours. Since Harbert, in spite of his protests, was let off guard duty, Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett on the one hand, and the engineer and Nab on the other, took turns standing guard at the approaches to the camp.

As it happened, there were barely a few hours of night. The darkness came more from the thickness of the branches than from the setting of the sun. The silence was hardly broken except by the hoarse howls of jaguars and the cackling of monkeys, which seemed to get on Master Jup's nerves in particular.

The night passed without incident, and the next day, February 16, the march through the forest resumed — slow rather than hard.

That day they could cover only six miles, because at every moment they had to hack out a road with the ax. Like true settlers, the colonists spared the tall, handsome trees — felling them would have cost them enormous effort anyway — and sacrificed the small ones. But the result was that the road did not run very straight and grew longer with many detours.

During that day Harbert discovered new species whose presence had not yet been noted on the island: tree ferns, their drooping fronds seeming to spill over like the water from a fountain basin, and carob trees, whose long pods the onaggas browsed greedily and which gave a sweet pulp with an excellent taste. There, too, the colonists came across magnificent kauris again, standing in groups, their cylindrical trunks, crowned with a cone of greenery, rising to a height of two hundred feet. These were indeed the royal trees of New Zealand, as famous as the cedars of Lebanon.

As for the animals, they showed no specimens other than those the hunters already knew. However, they caught a glimpse, without being able to get near them, of a pair of those large birds found only in Australia — a kind of cassowary called the emu — which stand five feet tall, have brown plumage, and belong to the order of wading birds. Top dashed after them as fast as his four legs would carry him, but the cassowaries easily left him behind, so prodigious was their speed.

As for the traces the convicts had left in the forest, a few more were found. Near a fire that seemed to have been put out recently, the colonists noticed footprints, and these were studied with the greatest attention. By measuring them one after another, length and breadth, they easily made out the tracks of five men's feet. The five convicts had clearly camped at this spot. But — and this was the whole point of so careful an examination! — they could not find a sixth footprint, which in that case would have been Ayrton's.

"Ayrton wasn't with them!" said Harbert.

"No," answered Pencroff, "and if he wasn't with them, it's because those villains had already killed him! But don't these scoundrels have a den, so we can go and hunt them down like tigers?"

"No," answered the reporter. "It's more likely they're wandering wherever chance takes them. It's in their interest to keep roaming like that until the moment they're masters of the island."

"Masters of the island!" cried the sailor. "Masters of the island!..." he repeated, and his voice was choked, as if an iron fist had seized him by the throat. Then, more calmly:

"Do you know, Mr. Cyrus," he said, "what bullet I've loaded into my gun?"

"No, Pencroff!"

"It's the bullet that went through Harbert's chest, and I promise you that one won't miss its mark!"

But that just revenge could not bring Ayrton back to life, and from this examination of the prints left on the ground they had, alas, to conclude that there was no longer any hope at all of ever seeing him again!

That evening the camp was set up fourteen miles from Granite House, and Cyrus Smith reckoned that it could not be more than five miles from Reptile End.

And in fact, the next day, they reached the tip of the peninsula, and the forest had been crossed from end to end. But not a single clue had led them to the hideout where the convicts had taken refuge — nor to the one, no less secret, that sheltered the mysterious stranger.

Chapter 12: A Lighted Window

Exploring Serpentine Peninsula — Camp at the mouth of Fall River — Six hundred paces from the corral — Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff scout ahead — Their return — Everyone forward! — An open gate — A lighted window — By the light of the moon

The next day, February 18, was given over to exploring the whole wooded stretch that made up the coast from Reptile End to Fall River. The colonists were able to search this forest thoroughly, since it was only three to four miles wide, lying as it did between the two shores of Serpentine Peninsula. The trees, with their great height and their thick spreading branches, bore witness to the power of the soil to make things grow, and here it was more astonishing than anywhere else on the island. It looked like a corner of the virgin forests of America or Central Africa, carried bodily into this temperate zone. All of which suggested that these magnificent trees found in the soil, damp in its upper layer but heated from within by volcanic fires, a warmth that could not belong to a temperate climate. The commonest kinds were exactly those kauris and eucalyptus trees, which grew here to gigantic size.

But the colonists had not come to admire these splendors of the plant world. They already knew that in this respect Lincoln Island would have deserved a place among the Canaries, whose first name was the Fortunate Isles. Now, alas, their island no longer belonged wholly to them. Others had taken possession of it; scoundrels were treading its soil, and they had to be destroyed to the last man.

On the west coast they found no further traces, however carefully they looked. No more footprints, no more broken branches on the trees, no more cold ashes, no more abandoned camps.

"That doesn't surprise me," Cyrus Smith told his companions. "The convicts landed somewhere near Jetsam Point, and they went straight into the Far West forests after crossing Shelduck Marsh. So they followed more or less the route we took when we left Granite House. That explains the traces we found in the woods. But once they reached the coast, the convicts saw clearly that they wouldn't find a decent hideout there, and that's when they headed back north and discovered the corral..."

"Where they may have gone back..." said Pencroff.

"I don't think so," answered the engineer, "because they must guess that our search will turn in that direction. For them the corral is only a place to get supplies, not a permanent camp."

"I agree with Cyrus," said the reporter. "In my opinion, it's among the spurs of Mount Franklin that the convicts will have looked for a den."

"Then straight to the corral, Mr. Cyrus!" cried Pencroff. "We've got to finish this, and so far we've wasted our time!"

"No, my friend," answered the engineer. "You're forgetting that we needed to know whether the Far West forests might hold some dwelling. Our exploration has a double purpose, Pencroff. If on the one hand we must punish crime, on the other we have a debt of gratitude to pay!"

"Well spoken, Mr. Cyrus," answered the sailor. "All the same, it's my belief we won't find that gentleman unless he wants us to!"

And really, Pencroff was only saying what they all thought. It was likely that the stranger's hiding place would prove no less mysterious than the stranger himself!

That evening the cart stopped at the mouth of Fall River. They set up camp for the night in the usual way and took the usual precautions. Harbert, once again the strong, healthy boy he had been before his illness, was making the most of this open-air life between the ocean breezes and the bracing air of the forests. His place was no longer in the cart but at the head of the caravan.

The next day, February 19, the colonists left the coast, where beyond the river's mouth basalt rocks of every shape were piled up so picturesquely, and went up the river along its left bank. The way had been partly cleared already by earlier trips made from the corral to the west coast. The colonists were now six miles from Mount Franklin.

The engineer's plan was this: to examine with great care the whole valley whose lowest line formed the bed of the river, and to approach the neighborhood of the corral cautiously. If the corral was occupied, they would take it by force. If it was not, they would dig in there and make it the base for operations whose goal would be the exploration of Mount Franklin.

The colonists approved this plan unanimously, and indeed they were impatient to have their island wholly back in their own hands!

So they made their way along the narrow valley that separated two of the mightiest spurs of Mount Franklin. The trees crowded the banks of the river but grew sparser toward the upper slopes of the volcano. It was hilly, rather broken ground, made for ambushes, and they ventured across it only with the greatest caution. Top and Jup went ahead as scouts, plunging to right and left into the thick undergrowth, each trying to outdo the other in cleverness and skill. But nothing showed that anyone had been along the banks of the stream lately; nothing announced that the convicts were there or anywhere near.

At about five in the evening the cart stopped roughly six hundred paces from the palisade. A half-circle curtain of tall trees still hid it from view.

The thing to do, then, was to scout the corral and find out whether it was occupied. To go there openly, in broad daylight, would be asking to be shot, if the convicts were lying in wait there at all — just as had happened to Harbert. It was better to wait until night had fallen.

Gédéon Spilett, however, wanted to look over the approaches to the corral without any more delay, and Pencroff, at the end of his patience, offered to go with him.

"No, my friends," answered the engineer. "Wait for nightfall. I won't let any of you expose himself in broad daylight."

"But, Mr. Cyrus..." the sailor replied, not much inclined to obey.

"I'm asking you, Pencroff," said the engineer.

"Have it your way!" answered the sailor, who found another outlet for his anger by treating the convicts to the roughest names in the whole seafaring vocabulary.

So the colonists stayed close to the cart and kept a careful watch on the nearby parts of the forest.

Three hours went by like that. The wind had dropped, and an absolute silence reigned under the great trees. The snap of the thinnest twig, a footstep on dry leaves, a body sliding through the grass, would all have been heard easily. Everything was quiet. Besides, Top, lying on the ground with his head stretched out on his paws, showed no sign of uneasiness.

At eight o'clock the evening seemed far enough along for the scouting to be done under good conditions. Gédéon Spilett said he was ready to go, with Pencroff. Cyrus Smith agreed. Top and Jup had to stay behind with the engineer, Harbert and Nab, because a bark or a cry at the wrong moment must not give the alarm.

"Don't take any rash chances," Cyrus Smith told the sailor and the reporter. "You're not there to take the corral, only to find out whether it's occupied or not."

"Agreed," answered Pencroff.

And the two of them set off.

Under the trees, because the foliage was so thick, a certain darkness already made it impossible to see anything more than thirty or forty feet away. The reporter and Pencroff moved forward with the most extreme care, stopping the moment any sound seemed suspicious to them.

They walked some distance apart, to make a smaller target for gunfire. And to tell the whole truth, they expected a shot to ring out at any moment.

Five minutes after leaving the cart, Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff reached the edge of the woods, facing the clearing at the far end of which the palisade rose.

They stopped. A little faint light still washed over the treeless meadow. Thirty paces away stood the gate of the corral, which seemed to be shut. Those thirty paces they would have to cross between the edge of the woods and the palisade were the danger zone, to borrow an expression from the science of gunnery. One or more bullets fired from the top of the palisade would have knocked down anyone who ventured into that zone.

Gédéon Spilett and the sailor were not men to hang back, but they knew that any recklessness on their part, though they would be its first victims, would fall afterward on their companions. If the two of them were killed, what would become of Cyrus Smith, Nab and Harbert?

But Pencroff, worked up at feeling himself so close to the corral, where he supposed the convicts had taken refuge, was about to push forward when the reporter held him back with a firm hand.

"In a few moments it'll be completely dark," Gédéon Spilett whispered in Pencroff's ear, "and that will be the time to act."

Pencroff, his hand clenched tight on the stock of his gun, held himself in and waited, grumbling.

Soon the last glimmers of twilight faded away entirely. The darkness, which seemed to pour out of the thick forest, flooded the clearing. Mount Franklin rose like an enormous screen against the western horizon, and night came on quickly, as it does in regions already fairly low in latitude. This was the moment.

Ever since they had taken up their post at the edge of the woods, the reporter and Pencroff had not taken their eyes off the palisade. The corral seemed to be completely deserted. The top of the palisade made a line a little blacker than the surrounding shadow, and nothing broke its sharp edge. Still, if the convicts were there, they would have had to post one of their number as a lookout, to protect themselves against any surprise.

Gédéon Spilett pressed his companion's hand, and the two of them crawled toward the corral, their guns ready to fire.

They reached the gate of the enclosure without a single streak of light cutting through the darkness.

Pencroff tried to push the gate, which, as he and the reporter had supposed, was shut. However, the sailor was able to make sure that the outside bars had not been put in place.

From this they could conclude that the convicts were in the corral at that moment, and that they had most likely made the gate fast from the inside so that it could not be forced.

Gédéon Spilett and Pencroff listened.

Not a sound inside the enclosure. The mouflons and the goats, no doubt asleep in their stables, did nothing at all to disturb the calm of the night.

Hearing nothing, the reporter and the sailor wondered whether they ought to climb the palisade and get into the corral. That would be going against Cyrus Smith's instructions.

True, the attempt might succeed — but it might fail, too. And if the convicts suspected nothing, if they knew nothing of the expedition launched against them, if in short there was at this moment a chance of taking them by surprise, ought they to throw that chance away by rashly venturing over the palisade?

The reporter thought not. He judged it sensible to wait until the colonists were all together before trying to get into the corral. One thing was certain: it was possible to get right up to the palisade without being seen, and the enclosure did not seem to be guarded. With that settled, all that remained was to go back to the cart and decide what to do.

Pencroff probably shared this view, for he raised no objection to following the reporter when the reporter fell back into the woods.

A few minutes later the engineer had been told how matters stood.

"Well," he said, after thinking it over, "I now have reason to believe that the convicts are not at the corral."

"We'll find out soon enough," answered Pencroff, "once we've climbed the palisade."

"To the corral, my friends!" said Cyrus Smith.

"Do we leave the cart in the woods?" asked Nab.

"No," answered the engineer. "It's our supply wagon for ammunition and food, and if need be it will serve us as a breastwork."

"Forward, then!" said Gédéon Spilett.

The cart came out of the woods and began to roll silently toward the palisade. The darkness was deep now, the silence as complete as when Pencroff and the reporter had crawled away over the ground. The thick grass smothered the sound of their footsteps entirely.

The colonists were ready to fire. Jup, on Pencroff's orders, kept to the rear. Nab held Top on a leash so that he would not dash ahead.

The clearing soon came into view. It was deserted. Without hesitating, the little band headed for the enclosure. In a short space of time they had crossed the danger zone. Not a shot had been fired. When the cart reached the palisade, it stopped. Nab stayed at the onaggas' heads to keep them still. The engineer, the reporter, Harbert and Pencroff then went toward the gate, to see whether it was barricaded on the inside...

One of the two halves of the gate was open!

"But what were you telling me?" asked the engineer, turning to the sailor and Gédéon Spilett.

The two of them were dumbfounded.

"On my soul," said Pencroff, "that gate was shut a little while ago!"

At that the colonists hesitated. Had the convicts been in the corral, then, at the very moment Pencroff and the reporter were scouting it? There could be no doubt of it, since the gate, which had been shut then, could only have been opened by them! Were they still inside, or had one of them just gone out?

All these questions leaped into everyone's mind at once, but how were they to answer them?

At that moment Harbert, who had gone a few steps inside the enclosure, drew back hastily and seized Cyrus Smith's hand.

"What is it?" asked the engineer.

"A light!"

"In the house?"

"Yes!"

All five of them moved up to the gate, and sure enough, through the panes of the window facing them, they saw a faint glimmer flickering.

Cyrus Smith made up his mind quickly.

"It's a unique chance," he told his companions, "to find the convicts shut up in that house, expecting nothing! They're ours! Forward!"

The colonists slipped into the enclosure, guns ready to raise to their shoulders. The cart had been left outside in the care of Jup and Top, who had been tied to it as a precaution.

Cyrus Smith, Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett on one side, Harbert and Nab on the other, moved along the palisade and looked over that part of the corral, which was completely dark and deserted.

In a few moments they were all near the house, in front of its door, which was shut.

Cyrus Smith signaled to his companions with his hand not to move, and he went up to the window, which was faintly lit by the light inside.

He looked into the single room that made up the ground floor of the house.

On the table a lantern was burning. Beside the table was the bed that Ayrton used to sleep in.

On the bed lay the body of a man.

Suddenly Cyrus Smith drew back, and in a stifled voice he cried:

"Ayrton!"

At once the door was burst in rather than opened, and the colonists rushed into the room.

Ayrton seemed to be asleep. His face showed that he had suffered long and cruelly. On his wrists and ankles there were broad bruises.

Cyrus Smith bent over him.

"Ayrton!" cried the engineer, gripping the arm of the man he had just found again in such unexpected circumstances.

At the sound of his name Ayrton opened his eyes, and, looking straight at Cyrus Smith, then at the others, he cried:

"You? You?"

"Ayrton! Ayrton!" Cyrus Smith repeated.

"Where am I?"

"In the house at the corral!"

"Alone?"

"Yes!"

"But they're coming back!" cried Ayrton. "Defend yourselves! Defend yourselves!"

And Ayrton fell back, exhausted.

"Spilett," the engineer said then, "we may be attacked at any moment. Bring the cart into the corral. Then barricade the gate, and all of you come back here."

Pencroff, Nab and the reporter hurried to carry out the engineer's orders. There was not a moment to lose. Perhaps the cart was already in the convicts' hands!

In an instant the reporter and his two companions had crossed the corral and reached the gate in the palisade, behind which they could hear Top growling low.

The engineer, leaving Ayrton for a moment, went out of the house, ready to shoot. Harbert was at his side. Both of them kept watch on the crest of the spur that overlooked the corral. If the convicts were lying in wait up there, they could pick the colonists off one after another.

At that moment the moon appeared in the east above the black curtain of the forest, and a white sheet of light spread across the inside of the enclosure. The whole corral lit up, with its clumps of trees, the little stream that watered it, and its broad carpet of grass. On the mountain side, the house and part of the palisade stood out white. On the opposite side, toward the gate, the enclosure remained dark.

Soon a black mass came into view. It was the cart, rolling into the circle of light, and Cyrus Smith could hear the sound of the gate as his companions shut it and made its two halves fast from the inside.

But at that moment Top, snapping his leash with a violent jerk, began to bark furiously and rushed toward the far end of the corral, to the right of the house.

"Look out, my friends! Take aim!..." shouted Cyrus Smith.

The colonists had shouldered their guns and were waiting for the moment to fire. Top was still barking, and Jup, running toward the dog, gave a series of shrill whistles.

The colonists followed him and came out on the bank of the little brook, shaded by tall trees.

And there, in the full light of the moon, what did they see?

Five bodies, stretched out on the bank!

They were the bodies of the convicts who, four months before, had landed on Lincoln Island!

Chapter 13: Ayrton's Story

Ayrton's story — The plans of his former accomplices — They settle in at the corral — Lincoln Island's dispenser of justice — The Bonadventure — Searching around Mount Franklin — The upper valleys — Rumblings underground — An answer from Pencroff — At the bottom of the crater — Home again

What had happened? Who had struck the convicts down? Could it have been Ayrton? No, since only a moment before he had been dreading their return!

But Ayrton was by then sunk in a deep sleep, and there was no longer any way to rouse him from it. After the few words he had spoken, a crushing torpor had taken hold of him, and he had fallen back on his bed without moving.

The colonists, a prey to a thousand confused thoughts and in a state of violent excitement, waited all through the night without leaving Ayrton's house and without going back to the place where the bodies of the convicts lay. As for the circumstances in which those men had met their deaths, Ayrton would most likely be unable to tell them anything, since he had not even known that he was in the house at the corral. But at least he would be able to tell them what had happened before that terrible execution.

The next day Ayrton came out of his torpor, and his companions warmly showed him all the joy they felt at seeing him again, more or less safe and sound, after a hundred and four days apart.

Ayrton then told them in a few words what had happened, or at least what he knew.

On the day after he arrived at the corral — November 10 of the year before — at nightfall, he had been taken by surprise by the convicts, who had climbed over the palisade. They tied him up and gagged him, and then he was carried off to a dark cave at the foot of Mount Franklin, where the convicts had taken refuge.

They had decided on his death, and the next day he was about to be killed when one of the convicts recognized him and called him by the name he had gone by in Australia. These wretches had been ready to murder Ayrton. They spared Ben Joyce!

But from that moment on, Ayrton was hounded day and night by his former accomplices. They wanted to win him back to their side, and they were counting on him to help them seize Granite House, to get inside that unreachable dwelling, and to make themselves masters of the island after murdering the colonists!

Ayrton refused. The former convict, repentant and forgiven, would sooner have died than betray his companions.

Bound, gagged, and watched every moment, Ayrton lived in that cave for four months.

The convicts, meanwhile, had found the corral not long after they landed on the island, and since then they had been living off its stores, though they did not live in it. On November 11, two of these bandits, caught off guard by the colonists' unexpected arrival, fired on Harbert, and one of them came back boasting that he had killed one of the island's inhabitants. But he came back alone. His companion, as we know, had fallen under Cyrus Smith's dagger.

Imagine Ayrton's anxiety and despair when he heard that news of Harbert's death! The colonists were only four now, and so, you might say, at the mercy of the convicts!

After that, and for the whole time the colonists stayed at the corral, held there by Harbert's illness, the pirates did not leave their cave. Even after they had plundered Prospect Plateau, they did not think it wise to abandon it.

The ill treatment they gave Ayrton grew worse then. His hands and feet still bore the bloody marks of the ropes that bound him day and night. At every moment he expected a death that it did not seem he could possibly escape.

So it went on until the third week of February. Still watching for a good opportunity, the convicts seldom left their hiding place, and made only a few hunting trips, either into the interior of the island or as far as the south coast. Ayrton had no more news of his friends, and he no longer hoped to see them again!

At last, weakened by ill treatment, the unhappy man fell into a deep prostration in which he could no longer see or hear anything. And so from that point on — that is, for the past two days — he could not even say what had happened.

"But, Mr. Smith," he added, "if I was a prisoner in that cave, how is it that I find myself back at the corral?"

"How is it that the convicts are lying out there dead, in the middle of the enclosure?" answered the engineer.

"Dead!" cried Ayrton, and weak as he was, he half raised himself.

His companions held him up. He wanted to get to his feet. They let him, and all of them went toward the little stream.

It was broad daylight.

There on the bank, in the very positions in which a death that must have been as sudden as a lightning stroke had caught them, lay the five bodies of the convicts!

Ayrton was stunned. Cyrus Smith and his companions watched him without saying a word.

At a sign from the engineer, Nab and Pencroff examined the bodies, which were already stiff with the cold.

They bore no visible trace of any wound.

But after looking them over carefully, Pencroff noticed on the forehead of one, on the chest of another, on the back of this one, on the shoulder of that one, a small red spot — a kind of bruise, barely visible, and impossible to account for.

"That's where they were struck!" said Cyrus Smith.

"But with what weapon?" cried the reporter.

"A weapon that strikes like lightning, and whose secret we don't have!"

"And who struck them down?" asked Pencroff.

"The island's dispenser of justice," answered Cyrus Smith. "The one who carried you here, Ayrton. The one whose influence has just made itself felt once again. The one who does for us everything we can't do for ourselves, and who then, once it's done, slips away from us."

"Then let's find him!" cried Pencroff.

"Yes, let's look for him," answered Cyrus Smith. "But the superior being who works such wonders — we'll find him only if he finally chooses to call us to him!"

This invisible protection, which reduced their own efforts to nothing, both irritated and touched the engineer. The relative inferiority it made plain was the kind that can wound a proud soul. A generosity that arranges things so as to dodge every mark of gratitude suggested a sort of disdain for the people it obliged, and in Cyrus Smith's eyes that spoiled, to some degree, the value of the kindness.

"Let's search," he went on, "and God grant that one day we may be allowed to prove to this haughty protector that he isn't dealing with ungrateful people! What wouldn't I give for us to be able to repay him, by doing him some great service in our turn, even at the cost of our lives!"

From that day on, this search was the one concern of the inhabitants of Lincoln Island. Everything drove them to find the answer to the riddle, and that answer could only be the name of a man gifted with a truly inexplicable and, in a way, superhuman power.

After a few moments the colonists went back into the house at the corral, where their care soon restored Ayrton's strength of mind and body.

Nab and Pencroff carried the convicts' bodies into the forest, some distance from the corral, and buried them deep.

Then Ayrton was told everything that had happened while he was held prisoner. He heard about Harbert's adventures, and about the whole series of trials the colonists had been through. As for them, they had given up hope of ever seeing Ayrton again, and had feared that the convicts had murdered him without mercy.

"And now," said Cyrus Smith, as he finished his account, "we still have a duty to carry out. Half our task is done. But if the convicts are no longer to be feared, it isn't to ourselves that we owe being masters of the island again."

"Well, then," answered Gédéon Spilett, "let's search the whole labyrinth of Mount Franklin's spurs! Let's not leave a single hollow, a single hole unexplored! Ah! If ever a reporter found himself face to face with a thrilling mystery, my friends, it's the one talking to you now!"

"And we won't go back to Granite House," said Harbert, "until we've found our benefactor."

"Yes!" said the engineer. "We'll do everything that's humanly possible... but I'll say it again — we'll find him only if he's willing to let us!"

"Do we stay at the corral?" asked Pencroff.

"Let's stay here," answered Cyrus Smith. "There are plenty of provisions, and we're right at the center of the circle we have to search. Besides, if need be, the cart can get to Granite House quickly."

"Good," answered the sailor. "Only, one remark."

"What's that?"

"The fine season's coming on, and we mustn't forget we have a crossing to make."

"A crossing?" said Gédéon Spilett.

"Yes! To Tabor Island," answered Pencroff. "We have to take a notice over there giving the position of our island, and saying that Ayrton is here now, in case the Scottish yacht comes back to pick him up. Who knows if it isn't already too late?"

"But, Pencroff," asked Ayrton, "how do you plan to make that crossing?"

"In the Bonadventure!"

"The Bonadventure!" cried Ayrton. "She doesn't exist anymore."

"My Bonadventure doesn't exist anymore!" roared Pencroff, leaping to his feet.

"No!" answered Ayrton. "The convicts found her in her little harbor barely a week ago. They put to sea, and..."

"And?" said Pencroff, his heart pounding.

"And with no Bob Harvey to handle her, they ran her onto the rocks, and the boat was smashed to pieces!"

"Oh, the wretches! The bandits! The low-down scoundrels!" cried Pencroff.

"Pencroff," said Harbert, taking the sailor's hand, "we'll build another Bonadventure — a bigger one! We have all the brig's ironwork and all her rigging to use!"

"But do you know," answered Pencroff, "that it takes five or six months at least to build a boat of thirty to forty tons?"

"We'll take our time," answered the reporter, "and we'll give up making the crossing to Tabor Island this year."

"What can you do, Pencroff? We have to resign ourselves," said the engineer. "And I hope this delay won't do us any harm."

"Oh, my Bonadventure! My poor Bonadventure!" cried Pencroff, truly heartbroken at the loss of the boat he had been so proud of.

The destruction of the Bonadventure was obviously a regrettable thing for the colonists, and they agreed that the loss would have to be made good as soon as possible. Once that was settled, their only concern was to carry through the exploration of the most hidden parts of the island.

The search began that very day, February 19, and went on for a whole week. The base of the mountain, between its spurs and their many branches, formed a labyrinth of valleys and side valleys laid out in the most haphazard way. It was obviously there, at the bottom of those narrow gorges, or perhaps even inside the mass of Mount Franklin itself, that the search ought to be pursued. No part of the island would have been better suited to hide a dwelling whose occupant wished to remain unknown. But the spurs were so tangled together that Cyrus Smith had to explore them with strict method.

The colonists first went over the whole valley that opened to the south of the volcano and collected the first waters of Fall River. It was there that Ayrton showed them the cave where the convicts had taken refuge and where he had been held prisoner until he was carried to the corral. The cave was exactly as Ayrton had left it. They found there a certain quantity of ammunition and food that the convicts had carried off, meaning to lay in a store of their own.

The whole valley that led to the cave, shaded by fine trees, mostly conifers, was explored with the greatest care. Then, after rounding the tip of the southwest spur, the colonists made their way into a narrower gorge that began at that very picturesque heap of basalt columns along the shore.

Here the trees were scarcer. Stone took the place of grass. Wild goats and mouflons skipped about among the rocks. This was where the barren part of the island began. They could already see that of the many valleys branching out at the foot of Mount Franklin, only three were wooded and rich in pasture like the valley of the corral, which bordered the valley of Fall River on the west and the valley of Red Creek on the east. Those two streams, which turned into rivers farther down by taking in a few tributaries, were formed from all the waters of the mountain, and so they were what made its southern part fertile. As for the Mercy, it was fed more directly by plentiful springs hidden under the cover of Jacamar Wood, and it was springs of the same kind, spilling out in a thousand little trickles, that watered the soil of Serpentine Peninsula.

Now, of these three valleys where there was no shortage of water, any one could have served as a retreat for some solitary man, who would have found everything there that he needed to live. But the colonists had already explored them, and nowhere had they found any sign of a human presence.

Was it, then, at the bottom of those barren gorges, among the rockfalls, in the rugged ravines of the north, between the lava flows, that the hiding place and its occupant would be found?

At its base, the northern part of Mount Franklin consisted of nothing but two valleys, broad, shallow, without a trace of green, strewn with stray boulders, streaked with long moraines, paved with lava, bulging here and there with great mineral swellings, and sprinkled with obsidian and labradorite. This part called for long and difficult exploration. A thousand hollows had been dug out there — not very comfortable, no doubt, but perfectly hidden and hard to get into. The colonists even went through dark tunnels that dated from the age when fire shaped the earth, still blackened by the fires that had passed through them long ago, and that ran deep into the mass of the mountain. They went along those dark galleries, carrying blazing torches of resin; they searched the smallest hollows and sounded the smallest depths. But everywhere there was silence and darkness. It did not seem that a human being had ever set foot in those ancient passages, or that any arm had ever moved a single one of those blocks. They lay just as the volcano had flung them up when the island rose above the waters.

And yet, though these underground vaults seemed to be entirely deserted, and though the darkness in them was complete, Cyrus Smith was forced to admit that complete silence did not reign there.

On reaching the far end of one of those dark hollows, which ran several hundred feet into the mountain, he was surprised to hear dull rumblings, made louder by the echoing rock.

Gédéon Spilett, who was with him, heard those distant murmurs too, and they pointed to a reawakening of the underground fires. Several times the two of them stopped to listen, and they agreed that some chemical reaction was working itself out in the depths of the earth.

"So the volcano isn't completely extinct?" said the reporter.

"It's possible," answered Cyrus Smith, "that since we explored the crater some change has taken place in the lower layers. Any volcano, even one that's thought to be extinct, can obviously light up again."

"But if Mount Franklin were getting ready to erupt," asked Gédéon Spilett, "wouldn't Lincoln Island be in danger?"

"I don't think so," answered the engineer. "The crater — that is, the safety valve — is there, and the overflow of vapors and lava will escape, as it used to, through its usual outlet."

"Unless the lava cuts itself a new way out toward the fertile parts of the island!"

"Why, my dear Spilett," answered Cyrus Smith, "why wouldn't it follow the road that's naturally laid out for it?"

"Well! Volcanoes are unpredictable!" answered the reporter.

"Notice," the engineer went on, "that the slope of the whole mass of Mount Franklin favors an outflow of material toward the valleys we're exploring right now. It would take an earthquake shifting the mountain's center of gravity for that outflow to change course."

"But an earthquake is always to be feared in conditions like these," Gédéon Spilett pointed out.

"Always," answered the engineer, "especially when the forces underground are beginning to wake, and the insides of the globe may have become blocked up after a long rest. So, my dear Spilett, an eruption would be a serious matter for us, and it would be far better if this volcano had no wish to wake up! But there's nothing we can do about it, is there? In any case, whatever happens, I don't believe our domain on Prospect Plateau can be seriously threatened. Between the plateau and the mountain the ground dips noticeably, and if the lava ever took the road toward the lake, it would be thrown off onto the dunes and the nearby parts of Shark Gulf."

"We haven't yet seen any smoke at the top of the mountain to suggest an eruption is coming," said Gédéon Spilett.

"No," answered Cyrus Smith. "Not a wisp of vapor is coming out of the crater — I was looking at its summit only yesterday. But it's possible that over time rocks, ashes, and hardened lava have piled up in the lower part of the volcanic chimney, and that the safety valve I spoke of is overloaded for the moment. Still, at the first serious push, every obstacle will be swept away, and you can be sure, my dear Spilett, that neither the island, which is the boiler, nor the volcano, which is the smokestack, will burst under the pressure of the gases. All the same, I repeat, it would be better if there were no eruption."

"And yet we aren't mistaken," the reporter went on. "We can definitely hear dull rumblings in the very depths of the volcano!"

"Indeed," answered the engineer, listening again with the closest attention, "there's no mistaking it... some reaction is taking place there, and we can't judge how great it is or how it will end."

When they came out, Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett rejoined their companions and told them how matters stood.

"Fine!" cried Pencroff. "So this volcano wants to get up to its tricks! Well, let it try! It'll find its master!..."

"Who's that?" asked Nab.

"Our genie, Nab, our genie! He'll gag its crater for it if it so much as looks like opening it!"

As you can see, the sailor's faith in his island's own private god was absolute. And certainly the hidden power that had shown itself so far through so many inexplicable acts seemed to have no limits. But it also knew how to escape the colonists' painstaking search, because in spite of all their efforts, in spite of the zeal — more than zeal, the stubbornness — they brought to their exploration, the strange hiding place could not be found.

From February 19 to 25, the circle of the search was widened to take in the whole northern region of Lincoln Island, and its most secret nooks were ransacked. The colonists went so far as to sound every rock wall, the way police officers tap the walls of a suspect house. The engineer even made a very exact survey of the mountain, and pushed his search down to the lowest foundations that supported it. In the same way it was explored up as high as the truncated cone that topped the first tier of rock, and then right up to the upper rim of that enormous hat at the bottom of which the crater opened.

They did more: they went down into the pit. It was still extinct, but rumblings could be distinctly heard in its depths. Yet not a puff of smoke, not a wisp of vapor, not the least warming of the rock walls pointed to an eruption to come. But neither there nor in any other part of Mount Franklin did the colonists find any trace of the one they were looking for.

Next, the search turned to the whole region of the dunes. They went carefully over the high lava walls of Shark Gulf, from bottom to top, though it was extremely hard even to get down to the level of the gulf itself. No one! Nothing!

In the end, those two words summed up so much fatigue spent for nothing, so much stubbornness that came to nothing, and there was a sort of anger in the disappointment of Cyrus Smith and his companions.

So they had to think about going back, since this search could not go on forever. The colonists had every right to believe now that the mysterious being did not live on the surface of the island, and then the wildest theories haunted their overexcited imaginations. Pencroff and Nab especially were no longer content with the strange, and let themselves be carried off into the world of the supernatural.

On February 25 the colonists returned to Granite House. By means of the double rope, which an arrow carried back up to the doorsill, they restored the link between their home and the ground below.

A month later, on the twenty-fifth day of March, they celebrated the third anniversary of their arrival on Lincoln Island!

Chapter 14: Three Years Have Passed

Three years have passed — The question of the new ship — What is decided — The colony prospers — The shipyard — The cold of the southern hemisphere — Pencroff resigns himself — Washing the linen — Mount Franklin

Three years had gone by since the prisoners of Richmond made their escape, and how often, in those three years, they had talked of their homeland, which was never far from their thoughts!

They had no doubt that the Civil War was over by now, and it seemed impossible to them that the just cause of the North had not won. But what had happened in that terrible war? How much blood had it cost? Which of their own friends had fallen in the struggle? That was what they often talked about, without yet glimpsing the day when they would be allowed to see their country again. To go back, if only for a few days; to tie the social bond with the inhabited world once more; to open a line of communication between their homeland and their island; and then to spend the longest and perhaps the best part of their lives in this colony they had founded, which would then belong to the mother country — was that, after all, a dream that could never come true?

But there were only two ways to make that dream come true. Either a ship would one day appear in the waters of Lincoln Island, or the colonists would build a vessel themselves, one strong enough to hold the sea as far as the nearest land.

"Unless," Pencroff would say, "our genie hands us the means of getting home himself!"

And truly, if someone had come and told Pencroff and Nab that a ship of three hundred tons was waiting for them in Shark Gulf or at Balloon Harbor, they would not even have made a gesture of surprise. Along those lines, they were ready for anything.

But Cyrus Smith, less trusting, advised them to come back down to earth. That was over the question of building a ship — a truly urgent job, since they needed to leave a notice on Tabor Island as soon as possible, telling where Ayrton was now living.

The Bonadventure was gone, and building a new ship would take six months at the very least. Now, winter was on its way, and the voyage could not be made before the following spring.

"So we have time to get ready for the fine season," said the engineer, who was talking these things over with Pencroff. "Now, my friend, since we have to build our boat over again, I think it would be better to make her considerably bigger. Whether the Scottish yacht will ever come to Tabor Island is very doubtful. She may even have come months ago and left again, after searching in vain for some trace of Ayrton. So wouldn't it be wise to build a ship that could carry us, if it came to that, either to the island groups of Polynesia or to New Zealand? What do you think?"

"I think, Mr. Cyrus," the sailor answered, "I think you're every bit as able to build a big ship as a little one. We're short of neither timber nor tools. It's only a question of time."

"And how many months would it take to build a ship of two hundred and fifty to three hundred tons?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"Seven or eight months at least," answered Pencroff. "But we mustn't forget that winter's coming, and in hard frost wood is difficult to work. So let's count on a few weeks of idleness, and if our ship is ready by next November we ought to think ourselves very lucky."

"Well," replied Cyrus Smith, "that would be exactly the right season to undertake a voyage of any length, whether to Tabor Island or to some land farther away."

"Just so, Mr. Cyrus," answered the sailor. "So draw up your plans. The workmen are ready, and I expect Ayrton can give us a good hand with it."

The colonists were consulted, and they approved the engineer's plan, which was, in truth, the best thing they could do. Building a ship of two to three hundred tons was a big undertaking, it is true, but the colonists had a confidence in themselves that many successes had already justified.

So Cyrus Smith set to work drawing the ship's plan and fixing her lines. Meanwhile his companions busied themselves felling and hauling the trees that were to supply the knees, the frames and the planking. It was the Far West forest that yielded the best kinds of oak and elm. They took advantage of the gap already cut during their last expedition to open a usable road, which took the name of the Far West Road, and the trees were carried to the Chimneys, where the shipyard was set up. As for the road itself, its course wandered somewhat whimsically, for it was more or less the choice of timber that laid it out; but it made a sizable part of Serpentine Peninsula easy to reach.

It was important to cut and saw the timber quickly, because it could not be used green; time had to be left to season and harden it. So the carpenters worked hard all through April, which was disturbed only by a few rather violent equinoctial gales. Master Jup helped them nimbly, either climbing to the top of a tree to fasten the felling ropes, or lending his sturdy shoulders to carry off the trimmed trunks.

All this timber was stacked under a large plank shed built beside the Chimneys, and there it waited for the moment it would be put to use.

April was quite fine, as October often is in the northern zone. At the same time, the farm work was pushed forward energetically, and soon every trace of the devastation had vanished from Prospect Plateau. The mill was rebuilt, and new buildings went up on the site of the poultry yard. It had seemed necessary to rebuild them on a larger scale, because the bird population was growing considerably. The stables now held five onaggas: four strong ones, well broken, that would let themselves be harnessed or ridden, and a little one just born. The colony's equipment had gained a plow, and the onaggas were put to plowing, just like real Yorkshire or Kentucky oxen. Each of the colonists took his share of the work, and nobody's hands sat idle. And what fine health these workers enjoyed, and what good humor they brought to their evenings in Granite House, making a thousand plans for the future!

It goes without saying that Ayrton shared the common life completely, and there was no longer any question of his going to live at the corral. Still, he remained sad and kept to himself, and joined in his companions' work more readily than in their pleasures. But he was a powerful worker on any job — strong, skillful, inventive, intelligent. He was respected and loved by everyone, and he could not have failed to know it.

The corral, however, was not abandoned. Every other day one of the colonists, driving the cart or riding one of the onaggas, went to look after the flock of mouflons and goats and brought back the milk that stocked Nab's pantry. These trips were also chances to hunt. So Harbert and Gédéon Spilett — with Top out in front — ran along the Corral Road more often than any of their companions, and with the excellent guns they now had at their disposal, the house was never short of game: capybaras, agoutis, kangaroos, wild boars and wild pigs for the large game; ducks, grouse, heath cocks, jacamars and snipe for the small. What came out of the warren, what came out of the oyster bed, a few turtles they caught, a new haul of those excellent salmon that once again came crowding into the waters of the Mercy, the vegetables from Prospect Plateau, the wild fruits of the forest — it was riches upon riches, and Nab, the head cook, could barely find room to store them all.

It goes without saying that the telegraph wire strung between the corral and Granite House had been repaired, and it was put to work whenever one or another of the colonists was at the corral and thought it necessary to spend the night there. Besides, the island was safe now, and no attack was to be feared — at least, not from men.

Still, what had happened once could happen again. A landing by pirates, or even by escaped convicts, was always to be feared. It was possible that companions of Bob Harvey's, accomplices still held on Norfolk Island, had been in on the secret of his plans and might be tempted to follow his example. So the colonists did not fail to watch the approaches to the island, and every day their spyglass swept the wide horizon that closed off Union Bay and Washington Bay. When they went to the corral, they studied the western part of the sea with no less care, and by climbing the mountain's shoulder they could take in a wide sweep of the western horizon.

Nothing suspicious appeared, but they still had to keep on their guard at all times.

So one evening the engineer told his friends about a plan he had formed for fortifying the corral. It seemed wise to him to raise its palisade and to flank it with a sort of blockhouse, in which, if it came to that, the colonists could hold out against an enemy band. Granite House had to be considered impregnable by its very position. The corral, then, with its buildings, its stores and the animals it held, would always be the target of any pirates, whoever they were, who landed on the island; and if the colonists were forced to shut themselves up there, they had to be able to hold out on equal terms.

That was a plan to be thought through, and in any case it had to be put off until the following spring.

Around May 15, the keel of the new ship lay stretched out in the shipyard, and soon the stem and the sternpost, mortised into each end of it, rose up from it almost vertically. This keel, made of good oak, was a hundred and ten feet long, which would allow the ship a beam of twenty-five feet at her widest point. But that was all the carpenters could manage before the cold and the bad weather arrived. During the following week they still managed to put the first frames of the stern in place; then the work had to stop.

During the last days of the month the weather was extremely bad. The wind blew from the east, sometimes with the violence of a hurricane. The engineer was somewhat worried about the shipyard's sheds — though he could not have put them anywhere else near Granite House — because the islet sheltered the shore only imperfectly against the fury of the open sea, and in great storms the waves broke straight against the foot of the granite wall.

But, very fortunately, these fears came to nothing. The wind backed instead toward the southeast, and in those conditions the shore below Granite House was completely sheltered by the jutting spur of Jetsam Point.

Pencroff and Ayrton, the two keenest builders of the new ship, kept at their work as long as they could. They were not men to be bothered by the wind twisting their hair or the rain soaking them to the bone, and a hammer blow is as good in foul weather as in fair. But when a very sharp cold followed that wet spell, the wood, whose fibers took on the hardness of iron, became extremely difficult to work, and around June 10 the building of the ship had to be given up for good.

Cyrus Smith and his companions had not failed to notice how harsh the winters of Lincoln Island were. The cold was comparable to what the states of New England feel, and they lie at about the same distance from the equator as the island. In the northern hemisphere — or at least in the part of it taken up by British North America and the northern United States — the cold is explained by the flatness of the lands that stretch toward the pole, where no rise in the ground stands in the way of the Arctic winds. But here, where Lincoln Island was concerned, that explanation could not hold.

"It's even been observed," Cyrus Smith told his companions one day, "that at the same latitude, islands and coastal regions suffer less from the cold than inland countries. I've often heard it said that the winters of Lombardy, for example, are harsher than those of Scotland, and that would be because the sea gives back in winter the heat it took in during the summer. So islands are in the best position to profit from that giving back."

"But then, Mr. Cyrus," asked Harbert, "why does Lincoln Island seem to escape the general rule?"

"That's hard to explain," replied the engineer. "Still, I'd be inclined to think that this oddity comes from the island's position in the southern hemisphere, which, as you know, my boy, is colder than the northern hemisphere."

"That's true," said Harbert, "and floating ice is found at lower latitudes in the south of the Pacific than in the north."

"So it is," said Pencroff, "and when I was in the whaling trade I saw icebergs as far up as off Cape Horn."

"Then perhaps," said Gédéon Spilett, "the hard cold that strikes Lincoln Island could be explained by ice floes or pack ice relatively close by."

"Your opinion is a very reasonable one, my dear Spilett," answered Cyrus Smith, "and it's clearly to the nearness of the pack ice that we owe our hard winters. But let me point out to you that a purely physical cause also makes the southern hemisphere colder than the northern. Since the sun is closer to this hemisphere during its summer, it is necessarily farther away during its winter. That explains why the temperature runs to extremes in both directions, and if we find the winters very cold on Lincoln Island, let's not forget that the summers here are very hot instead."

"But why, if you please, Mr. Smith," asked Pencroff, frowning, "why should our hemisphere, as you call it, get such a poor share? That isn't fair!"

"Friend Pencroff," answered the engineer, laughing, "fair or not, we have to put up with it, and here's where the peculiarity comes from. The earth doesn't travel around the sun in a circle, but in an ellipse, as the laws of mechanics require. The earth occupies one of the foci of the ellipse, and so at one point in its path the earth is at its apogee — that is, at its greatest distance from the sun — and at another point it's at its perigee — that is, at its shortest distance. Now, it so happens that it's precisely during the winter of the southern lands that the earth is at the point farthest from the sun, and therefore in just the conditions to make those regions suffer the greatest cold. There's nothing to be done about it, and men, Pencroff, however learned they may be, will never be able to change anything at all in the order of the heavens that God himself has set."

"And yet," Pencroff added, who showed a certain difficulty in resigning himself, "the world knows such a lot! What a big book you could make, Mr. Cyrus, out of everything people know!"

"And what a much bigger book out of everything they don't know," answered Cyrus Smith.

In any case, for one reason or another, June brought back the cold with its usual violence, and the colonists were confined to Granite House most of the time.
