Ah, how hard that confinement seemed to all of them, and perhaps to Gédéon Spilett most of all!

"You see," he said to Nab one day, "I'd sign over to you, before a notary, every inheritance that's ever coming to me, if you'd be a good enough fellow to go off somewhere — anywhere — and take out a subscription to a newspaper for me — any newspaper! There's no doubt about it: what my happiness misses most is knowing every morning what happened the day before, somewhere other than here!"

Nab had burst out laughing.

"My word," he had answered, "what keeps me busy is the day's work!"

The truth is that indoors and out, there was no shortage of work.

The colony of Lincoln Island had now reached the height of its prosperity, and three years of steady labor had made it what it was. The episode of the destroyed brig had been a fresh source of riches. To say nothing of her complete rigging, which would serve the ship on the stocks, the storerooms of Granite House were now crammed with utensils and tools of every kind, arms and ammunition, clothes and instruments. There had been no further need even to make coarse felt cloth. If the colonists had suffered from the cold during their first winter, now the bad season could come without their having to dread its hardships. There was plenty of linen as well, and it was looked after with extreme care. From sodium chloride, which is nothing other than sea salt, Cyrus Smith had easily extracted soda and chlorine. The soda, which was easy to turn into sodium carbonate, and the chlorine, from which he made chloride of lime and other chlorides, were put to various household uses, and in particular to bleaching the linen. Besides, they now did only four big washes a year, as families used to do in the old days; and it may be added that Pencroff and Gédéon Spilett — the reporter while he waited for the mailman to bring him his newspaper — proved to be first-class laundrymen.

So the winter months went by: June, July and August. They were very harsh, and the average of the thermometer readings came to no more than eight degrees Fahrenheit, lower than the temperature of the winter before. And what a good fire blazed all the time in the fireplaces of Granite House, whose smoke streaked the granite wall with long black stripes! They did not spare the fuel, which grew naturally a few steps away. Besides, the leftover timber cut for building the ship let them save on coal, which was harder to haul.

Men and animals were all in good health. Master Jup did show himself a bit sensitive to the cold, it must be admitted. It was perhaps his only fault, and he had to be made a good, well-padded dressing gown. But what a servant — skillful, eager, tireless, not nosy, not a chatterbox! He could rightly have been held up as a model to all his two-legged fellow servants in the Old World and the New.

"After all," Pencroff would say, "when you've got four hands at your service, the least you can do is your work properly!"

And indeed, the intelligent four-handed creature did it well!

During the seven months that passed after the last searches around the mountain, and during September, which brought back the fine days, there was no question of the genie of the island at all. His hand did not show itself on any occasion. True, it would have been useless, for nothing happened that put the colonists to any painful test.

Cyrus Smith even observed that if by chance some communication had ever been established through the mass of granite between the stranger and the residents of Granite House, and if Top's instinct had somehow sensed it, there was no more of it during this period. The dog's growling had stopped completely, and so had the orangutan's uneasiness. The two friends — for friends they were — no longer prowled around the mouth of the inner well; they did not bark, and they no longer whined in that strange way that had put the engineer on the alert from the very beginning. But could he be sure that this was the end of the riddle, and that he would never find its answer? Could he be certain that some turn of events would not come about again and bring the mysterious being back onto the scene? Who could tell what the future held in store?

At last the winter came to an end. But an event whose consequences might well prove serious occurred in the very first days that marked the return of spring.

On September 7, Cyrus Smith, looking at the summit of Mount Franklin, saw smoke curling above the crater, its first wisps rising into the air.

Chapter 15: The Volcano Wakes

The volcano wakes — The fine season — Work resumes — The evening of October 15 — A telegram — A question — An answer — Off to the corral — The note — The extra wire — The basalt coast — At high tide — At low tide — The cavern — A dazzling light

The engineer had called out to the colonists. They had stopped their work and stood looking in silence at the summit of Mount Franklin.

So the volcano had woken up, and the vapors had broken through the layer of mineral matter heaped up at the bottom of the crater. But would the underground fires bring on some violent eruption? That was a possibility no one could guard against.

And yet, even supposing there were an eruption, it was likely that Lincoln Island as a whole would not suffer from it. Outpourings of volcanic matter are not always disastrous. The island had already been through this ordeal once, as the lava flows that striped the northern slopes of the mountain bore witness. Besides, the shape of the crater, with the great notch broken out of its upper rim, ought to throw whatever it spewed out toward the side opposite the fertile parts of the island.

Still, the past did not necessarily promise anything about the future. At the summits of volcanoes, old craters often close and new ones open. It has happened in both the Old World and the New — at Etna, at Popocatépetl, at Orizaba — and on the eve of an eruption anything may be feared. All it would take, in short, was an earthquake — a thing that sometimes goes along with volcanic outpourings — to change the inner layout of the mountain and clear new paths for the white-hot lava.

Cyrus Smith explained all this to his companions, and without making the situation sound worse than it was, he laid out the arguments on both sides.

After all, there was nothing they could do about it. Granite House did not seem to be in any danger, unless an earthquake shook the ground itself. But the corral would have everything to fear if some new crater opened in the southern flanks of Mount Franklin.

From that day on, the vapors never stopped crowning the top of the mountain like a plume, and it was even possible to see that they were growing taller and thicker, though no flame mixed with their heavy coils. The activity was still confined to the lower part of the central chimney.

Meanwhile, with the fine weather, the work had started up again. They pushed on with building the ship as fast as they could, and Cyrus Smith used the waterfall on the beach to set up a water-powered sawmill, which cut the tree trunks into planks and beams much more quickly. The machinery was as simple as that of the rustic sawmills that run in Norway. One horizontal motion to push the log forward, one vertical motion to work the saw up and down — that was all he needed to produce, and the engineer managed it with a wheel, two cylinders and some pulleys, properly arranged.

Toward the end of September the skeleton of the ship, which was to be rigged as a schooner, stood on the stocks in the shipyard. The frames were almost all in place, and since they were held together by temporary battens, the lines of the vessel could already be judged. This schooner, sharp at the bow and very clean in her run aft, would obviously be fit for a fairly long voyage if it came to that. But laying the planking, the inner planking and the deck would still take a good deal of time. Very luckily, the ironwork of the old brig had been saved after the underwater explosion. Pencroff and Ayrton had pulled the bolts and a great quantity of copper nails out of the damaged planks and knees. That was so much work saved for the blacksmiths, but the carpenters had plenty to do.

The shipbuilding had to be broken off for a week for the harvest, the haymaking and the bringing in of the various crops that grew in abundance on Prospect Plateau. Once that job was done, every moment from then on went to finishing the schooner.

When night came, the workers were truly worn out. So as not to lose any time, they had changed their mealtimes: they ate dinner at noon and did not have supper until the daylight gave out. Then they went back up to Granite House and hurried off to bed.

Sometimes, though, when the talk turned to some interesting subject, it kept them up a little past bedtime. The colonists let themselves talk about the future, and they liked to discuss the changes a voyage of the schooner to the nearest inhabited lands would bring to their situation. But in the middle of all these plans, one thought always came first: that they would come back to Lincoln Island afterward. They would never abandon this colony, founded with so much toil and so much success, to which a link with America would give a new life.

Pencroff and Nab especially fully expected to end their days there.

"Harbert," the sailor would say, "you'll never abandon Lincoln Island, will you?"

"Never, Pencroff — especially if you make up your mind to stay here!"

"It's made up, my boy," Pencroff would answer. "I'll wait for you! You'll bring me back your wife and your children, and I'll turn your little ones into a fine pack of rascals!"

"It's a deal," Harbert would reply, laughing and blushing at the same time.

"And you, Mr. Cyrus," Pencroff would go on, carried away, "you'll always be governor of the island! Now look here, how many people can she feed? Ten thousand at least!"

They would talk on like that, letting Pencroff run on, and one thing leading to another, the reporter would end up founding a newspaper — the New Lincoln Herald!

Such is the human heart. The need to make a work that lasts, that will outlive him, is the sign of man's superiority over everything else that lives here below. It is what has founded his dominion, and it is what justifies that dominion throughout the world.

After that, who knows whether Jup and Top did not have their own little dreams of the future too?

Ayrton, silent, would tell himself that he wanted to see Lord Glenarvan again and show himself to everyone, redeemed.

One evening, October 15, the conversation, launched among all these speculations, had gone on longer than usual. It was nine o'clock at night. Long yawns, badly hidden, were already announcing bedtime, and Pencroff had just headed for his bed when the electric bell set up in the great hall suddenly rang.

Everyone was there: Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett, Harbert, Ayrton, Pencroff, Nab. So not one of the colonists was at the corral.

Cyrus Smith had stood up. His companions looked at one another, thinking they must have heard wrong.

"What does that mean?" cried Nab. "Is it the devil ringing?"

No one answered.

"The weather's stormy," Harbert pointed out. "Couldn't the electricity in the air..."

Harbert did not finish his sentence. The engineer, toward whom every eye had turned, was shaking his head.

"Let's wait," said Gédéon Spilett then. "If it's a signal, whoever is making it will make it again."

"But who do you think it could be?" cried Nab.

"Why," answered Pencroff, "the one who..."

The sailor's sentence was cut off by a fresh quivering of the hammer on the bell.

Cyrus Smith went over to the apparatus, sent the current along the wire, and dispatched this question to the corral:

    "What do you want?"

A few moments later the needle, moving around the alphabet dial, gave the occupants of Granite House this answer:

    "Come to the corral with all speed."

"At last!" cried Cyrus Smith.

Yes! At last! The mystery was going to be revealed! In the face of the overwhelming interest that was going to drive them to the corral, all the colonists' weariness vanished, all need of rest was gone. Without a word spoken, in a few moments they had left Granite House and were down on the beach. Only Jup and Top stayed behind. They could do without them.

The night was black. The moon, new that very day, had set along with the sun. As Harbert had pointed out, great storm clouds made a low, heavy vault overhead that blotted out every gleam of starlight. A few flashes of heat lightning, reflections of a distant storm, lit up the horizon.

It was possible that within a few hours the thunder would be crashing over the island itself. It was a threatening night.

But the darkness, however deep, could not stop people who knew the Corral Road as well as they did. They went up the left bank of the Mercy, reached the plateau, crossed the bridge over Glycerin Creek and pushed on through the forest.

They walked at a good pace, gripped by strong emotion. For them there was no doubt about it: they were at last going to learn the long-sought answer to the riddle, the name of that mysterious being who had entered so deeply into their lives, so generous in his influence, so powerful in his acts! Didn't this stranger have to be mixed up in their existence, didn't he have to know its smallest details, didn't he have to hear everything that was said in Granite House, to have always been able to act at exactly the right moment?

Each of them, lost in his thoughts, hurried on. Under that vault of trees the darkness was so thick that they could not even see the edge of the road. There was no sound in the forest, either. Beasts and birds, weighed down by the heaviness of the air, were still and silent. Not a breath stirred the leaves. Only the colonists' footsteps rang out in the dark on the hardened ground.

During the first quarter of an hour of the walk, the silence was broken only by this remark from Pencroff:

"We should have brought a lantern."

And by this reply from the engineer:

"We'll find one at the corral."

Cyrus Smith and his companions had left Granite House at twelve minutes past nine. At nine forty-seven they had covered three miles of the five that separated the mouth of the Mercy from the corral.

At that moment great whitish flashes of lightning were bursting over the island, cutting out the jagged shapes of the leaves in black. These intense flashes dazzled and blinded them. The storm obviously could not hold off much longer. Little by little the lightning came faster and brighter. Distant rumblings rolled through the depths of the sky. The air was stifling.

The colonists went on as though some irresistible force were pushing them forward.

At a quarter past nine a bright flash showed them the palisade, and they had not yet passed through the gate when the thunder broke with tremendous violence.

In an instant they had crossed the corral, and Cyrus Smith stood before the house.

It was possible that the stranger was in the house, since it was from the house itself that the telegram must have been sent. Yet no light shone in its window.

The engineer knocked at the door.

No answer.

Cyrus Smith opened the door, and the colonists went into the room, which was pitch dark.

Nab struck a light with his flint and steel, and a moment later the lantern was lit and carried into every corner of the room...

There was no one there. Everything was just as they had left it.

"Have we been taken in by an illusion?" murmured Cyrus Smith.

No! It wasn't possible! The telegram had plainly said:

    "Come to the corral with all speed."

They went over to the table set aside for working the line. Everything on it was in place — the battery and the box that held it, as well as the receiver and the transmitter.

"Who was the last one here?" asked the engineer.

"I was, Mr. Smith," answered Ayrton.

"And that was...?"

"Four days ago."

"Look — a note!" cried Harbert, pointing to a sheet of paper lying on the table.

On that paper these words were written, in English:

    "Follow the new wire."

"Let's go!" cried Cyrus Smith. He understood that the message had not been sent from the corral at all, but from the mysterious hiding place, which an extra wire, spliced onto the old one, connected directly with Granite House.

Nab took the lighted lantern, and they all left the corral.

The storm was now raging with tremendous violence. The gap between each flash of lightning and each clap of thunder was growing noticeably shorter. Soon the storm would be right over Mount Franklin and the whole island. By the glare of the flickering flashes they could see the summit of the volcano crowned with its plume of vapor.

In the part of the corral between the house and the palisade there was no telegraph line at all. But once he was through the gate, the engineer ran straight to the first pole, and by the light of a flash he saw a new wire hanging down from the insulator to the ground.

"There it is!" he said.

This wire lay along the ground, but along its whole length it was covered in an insulating substance, the way an undersea cable is, so that the current could travel freely through it. To judge by its direction, it seemed to make its way through the woods and the southern spurs of the mountain, and so it ran toward the west.

"Let's follow it!" said Cyrus Smith.

And now by the light of the lantern, now in the middle of the blazing lightning, the colonists set off along the path the wire laid out for them.

By then the rolling of the thunder was continuous, and so violent that no word could have been heard. Anyway, this was no time for talking, only for pressing on.

Cyrus Smith and his people first climbed the spur that rose between the valley of the corral and the valley of Fall River, and they crossed the river at its narrowest point. The wire, sometimes stretched over the low branches of the trees, sometimes running along the ground, guided them without fail.

The engineer had supposed that the wire might stop at the bottom of the valley, and that the unknown hiding place would be there.

Not at all. They had to climb the southwest spur and come down again onto that barren plateau which ended in the wall of strangely heaped-up basalt. Every so often one or another of the colonists bent down, felt the wire with his hand and corrected their course if need be. But there was no longer any doubt that the wire ran straight to the sea. There, no doubt, somewhere deep in the volcanic rock, lay the dwelling they had searched for in vain until now.

The sky was on fire. One flash did not wait for the next. Several struck the summit of the volcano and plunged into the crater through the thick smoke. At moments you might have thought the mountain was throwing out flames.

At a few minutes before ten the colonists reached the high edge that looked down over the ocean to the west. The wind had risen. The surf was roaring five hundred feet below.

Cyrus Smith worked out that he and his companions had covered a mile and a half since leaving the corral.

At this point the wire plunged in among the rocks, following the fairly steep slope of a narrow ravine that twisted every which way.

The colonists started down it, at the risk of setting off a slide of loosely balanced rocks and being hurled into the sea. The descent was extremely dangerous, but they took no account of the danger. They were no longer masters of themselves, and an irresistible pull drew them toward that mysterious spot, as a magnet draws iron.

So they went down that ravine almost without knowing it — a ravine that would have been all but impassable even in broad daylight. Stones rolled away and blazed like fiery meteors as they passed through the zones of light. Cyrus Smith was in the lead. Ayrton brought up the rear. Here they went step by step; there they slid on the smooth rock; then they picked themselves up and kept going.

At last the wire turned sharply and touched the rocks of the shore, a regular scattering of reefs that the high tides must pound. The colonists had reached the bottom of the basalt wall.

Here a narrow ledge ran level along the face, parallel to the sea. The wire followed it, and so did the colonists. They had not gone a hundred paces before the ledge, sloping gently downward, came right down to the level of the waves.

The engineer took hold of the wire and saw that it disappeared into the sea.

His companions, standing beside him, were dumbfounded.

A cry of disappointment, almost a cry of despair, burst from them! Were they going to have to throw themselves into the water and look for some undersea cavern? In the state of mental and physical overexcitement they were in, they would not have hesitated to do it.

A remark from the engineer stopped them.

Cyrus Smith led his companions under a hollow in the rocks, and there he said:

"Let's wait. The tide's high. At low tide the way will be open."

"But what makes you think...?" asked Pencroff.

"He wouldn't have called us if there were no way for us to reach him!"

Cyrus Smith had spoken with such conviction that no one raised an objection. And his reasoning was logical. They had to suppose that an opening, passable at low tide and blocked by the sea at that moment, lay at the foot of the wall.

That meant a wait of a few hours. So the colonists stayed huddled in silence under a kind of deep porch hollowed out of the rock. The rain was starting to fall by now, and soon the clouds, torn open by the lightning, were coming down in torrents. The echoes threw back the crash of the thunder and gave it a tremendous resonance.

The colonists' emotion was intense. A thousand strange, supernatural thoughts went through their minds, and they imagined some great, superhuman apparition — the only thing that could have lived up to the idea they had formed of the mysterious genie of the island.

At midnight Cyrus Smith took the lantern and went down to the level of the shore to look at how the rocks lay. The tide had already been going out for two hours.

The engineer had not been mistaken. The curve of a huge vault was beginning to show above the water. There the wire bent at a right angle and went in through that gaping mouth.

Cyrus Smith came back to his companions and said simply:

"In an hour the opening will be passable."

"So it does exist?" asked Pencroff.

"Did you doubt it?" answered Cyrus Smith.

"But this cave will be full of water up to a certain height," Harbert pointed out.

"Either the cave dries out completely," answered Cyrus Smith, "and in that case we'll walk through it, or it doesn't dry out, and some way of getting through it will be put at our disposal."

An hour went by. They all went down through the rain to the water's edge. In three hours the tide had dropped fifteen feet. The top of the arch stood at least eight feet above the water now. It was like the arch of a bridge, with the water flowing under it, flecked with foam.

Leaning over, the engineer saw a black object floating on the surface of the sea. He drew it toward him.

It was a boat, moored by a rope to some projection on the inside of the rock wall. It was made of bolted sheet iron. Two oars lay in the bottom, under the thwarts.

"Let's get in," said Cyrus Smith.

A moment later the colonists were in the boat. Nab and Ayrton took the oars, Pencroff the tiller. Cyrus Smith sat in the bow with the lantern set on the stem, lighting the way.

The roof was very low where the boat first passed under it, but then it rose sharply. Yet the darkness was too deep, and the lantern's light too weak, for them to make out how big the cave was — its width, its height, its depth. In the middle of this vault of basalt an imposing silence reigned. No sound from outside got in, and the crashes of the thunder could not pierce its thick walls.

There are, in a few parts of the globe, immense caverns of this kind, natural crypts of a sort that date from the geological ages of the earth. Some are invaded by the waters of the sea; others hold whole lakes inside them. Such is Fingal's Cave on the island of Staffa, one of the Hebrides; such are the caves of Morgat on the bay of Douarnenez in Brittany, the caves of Bonifacio in Corsica, and those of the Lysefjord in Norway; such is the immense Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, five hundred feet high and more than twenty miles long! In many places on the globe, nature has hollowed out these crypts and preserved them for man to marvel at.

As for the cave the colonists were now exploring — did it really reach all the way to the center of the island? For a quarter of an hour the boat had been moving forward, winding this way and that as the engineer called the turns to Pencroff in a few curt words, when all at once he gave the order:

"More to starboard!"

The boat changed course and at once ran along close to the right-hand wall. The engineer wanted, quite rightly, to make sure the wire was still running along that wall.

The wire was there, hooked onto the jutting rock.

"Go ahead!" said Cyrus Smith.

And the two oars, dipping into the black water, sent the boat on.

The boat went on for another quarter of an hour, and since the mouth of the cave it must have covered half a mile, when Cyrus Smith's voice was heard once more.

"Stop!" he said.

The boat stopped, and the colonists saw a brilliant light flooding the enormous crypt, hollowed out so deep in the bowels of the island.

Now they could look at this cavern, whose existence nothing had ever let them suspect.

A hundred feet up curved a vault, resting on shafts of basalt that all seemed to have been cast in the same mold. Irregular arches and fanciful ribs sprang from these columns, which nature had set up by the thousands in the earliest ages of the world's making. The basalt sections, fitted one into the other, stood forty to fifty feet high, and the water, calm despite the turmoil outside, lapped at their bases. The glare of the light the engineer had pointed out caught every edge of every prism and pricked it with points of fire. It seemed to shine right through the walls, as if they had been transparent, and it turned the least projection of the vault into a glittering polished gem.

By reflection, the water repeated all this brilliance on its surface, so that the boat seemed to float between two layers of sparkling light.

There was no mistaking the nature of the radiance pouring out from that bright center, whose sharp, straight rays broke against every angle and every rib of the crypt. This light came from an electric source; its white color gave away where it came from. It was the sun of this cavern, and it filled the whole of it.

At a sign from Cyrus Smith the oars dipped again, throwing up a perfect shower of sparkling gems, and the boat headed toward the source of the light, until it was soon no more than half a cable length away.

At this point the stretch of water was about three hundred and fifty feet wide, and beyond the dazzling center they could make out an enormous wall of basalt that closed off every way out on that side. So the cave had widened a great deal here, and the sea formed a little lake inside it. But the vault, the side walls, the wall at the far end, all those prisms, all those cylinders, all those cones were so bathed in the electric fluid that the glow seemed to be their own. You could have said of those stones, cut in facets like priceless diamonds, that they were sweating light!

In the middle of the lake a long, spindle-shaped object floated on the surface of the water, silent and motionless. The glow that came from it poured out of its sides, as if from two furnace mouths heated to a welding white heat. This machine, which looked like the body of an enormous whale, was about two hundred and fifty feet long and rose ten to twelve feet above the level of the sea.

The boat drew slowly nearer. In the bow, Cyrus Smith had risen to his feet. He was staring, gripped by violent agitation. Then, all at once, he seized the reporter's arm.

"But it's him! It can only be him!" he cried. "Him!..."

Then he dropped back onto his seat, murmuring a name that only Gédéon Spilett heard.

The reporter evidently knew that name, for it had an extraordinary effect on him, and he answered in a hollow voice:

"Him! An outlaw!"

"Him!" said Cyrus Smith.

At the engineer's order, the boat came up alongside this strange floating machine. It touched on the port quarter, where a beam of light streamed out through a thick pane of glass.

Cyrus Smith and his companions climbed onto the platform. A hatch stood open there. They all rushed through the opening.

At the bottom of the ladder a passageway ran inside, lit by electricity. At the end of the passageway was a door, which Cyrus Smith pushed open.

The colonists hurried through a richly decorated room that led into a library, where a luminous ceiling poured down a flood of light.

At the far end of the library was a wide door, also closed. The engineer opened it.

A vast salon, a kind of museum crammed with all the treasures of the mineral world, with works of art and marvels of industry, appeared before the colonists' eyes. They must have thought they had been carried off by magic into the world of dreams.

Stretched out on a rich divan they saw a man, who did not seem to notice they were there.

Then Cyrus Smith raised his voice, and to the utter amazement of his companions, he spoke these words:

"Captain Nemo, you asked for us? Here we are."

Chapter 16: Captain Nemo

Captain Nemo — His first words — The story of a hero of independence — His hatred of the invaders — His companions — Life beneath the sea — Alone — The Nautilus's last refuge at Lincoln Island — The mysterious genie of the island

At these words the man lying on the divan raised himself, and his face came into the full light: a magnificent head, a high forehead, a proud gaze, a white beard, and thick hair swept back from his brow.

He leaned with one hand on the back of the divan he had just left. His gaze was calm. It was plain that some slow illness had been wearing him down little by little, but his voice still sounded strong when he spoke, in English, in a tone of the utmost surprise:

"I have no name, sir."

"I know you!" answered Cyrus Smith.

Captain Nemo fixed a burning look on the engineer, as though he meant to annihilate him.

Then, sinking back onto the cushions of the divan, he murmured:

"What does it matter, after all? I am going to die!"

Cyrus Smith went up to Captain Nemo, and Gédéon Spilett took his hand, which he found burning hot. Ayrton, Pencroff, Harbert and Nab stood respectfully apart in a corner of that magnificent salon, whose air was charged with electricity.

But Captain Nemo at once drew his hand away, and with a gesture he asked the engineer and the reporter to sit down.

They all looked at him with real emotion. So here he was, the one they had called "the genie of the island," the powerful being whose help had come so effectively on so many occasions, the benefactor to whom they owed so great a debt of gratitude! Before their eyes they had only a man, where Pencroff and Nab had expected to find something close to a god — and that man was about to die!

But how did Cyrus Smith come to know Captain Nemo? And why had the captain started up so sharply on hearing that name, which he must have believed unknown to everyone?...

The captain had settled back on the divan and, propped on his arm, he was looking at the engineer, who sat beside him.

"You know the name I once bore, sir?" he asked.

"I know it," answered Cyrus Smith, "just as I know the name of this wonderful submarine machine..."

"The Nautilus?" said the captain, with half a smile.

"The Nautilus."

"But do you know... do you know who I am?"

"I know."

"And yet it has been thirty years since I had any communication with the inhabited world — thirty years that I have lived in the depths of the sea, the only place where I have found independence! Who, then, can have betrayed my secret?"

"A man who had never made you any promise, Captain Nemo, and who therefore cannot be accused of betrayal."

"That Frenchman whom chance threw aboard my ship sixteen years ago?"

"The same."

"Then that man and his two companions did not die in the Maelström, where the Nautilus had been caught?"

"They did not die. And a book has appeared, under the title Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, that contains your story."

"My story for a few months only, sir!" the captain answered sharply.

"That's true," Cyrus Smith went on, "but a few months of that strange life were enough to make you known..."

"As a great criminal, no doubt?" answered Captain Nemo, letting a haughty smile pass over his lips. "Yes — a rebel, an outlaw cast out from humanity, perhaps!"

The engineer did not answer.

"Well, sir?"

"It is not for me to judge Captain Nemo," answered Cyrus Smith, "at least as far as his past life is concerned. Like everyone else, I don't know what drove him to so strange an existence, and I cannot judge the effects without knowing the causes. But what I do know is that a kindly hand has been stretched out over us ever since we came to Lincoln Island. I know that every one of us owes his life to a being who is good, generous and powerful — and that this being, so powerful, so generous and so good, is you, Captain Nemo!"

"It is I," the captain answered simply.

The engineer and the reporter had risen. Their companions had drawn closer, and the gratitude that was overflowing their hearts was about to pour out in gestures and words...

Captain Nemo stopped them with a sign, and in a voice more moved than he would have wished, no doubt, he said:

"When you have heard me."

And in a few sentences, clear and hurried, the captain told them the whole of his life.

His story was brief, and yet he had to gather into himself all the strength he had left to tell it to the end. It was obvious that he was struggling against an extreme weakness. Several times Cyrus Smith urged him to rest a little, but he shook his head like a man to whom tomorrow no longer belongs, and when the reporter offered to tend him, he answered:

"It is useless. My hours are numbered."

Captain Nemo was an Indian, Prince Dakkar, the son of a rajah of the then independent territory of Bundelkhand, and nephew of the Indian hero Tipu Sultan. When the boy was ten years old, his father sent him to Europe to receive a complete education there — with the secret intention that one day he might fight on equal terms against the men he regarded as the oppressors of his country.

From the age of ten to thirty, Prince Dakkar, superbly gifted, great of heart and of mind, made himself master of everything. In the sciences, in literature and in the arts he carried his studies high and far.

Prince Dakkar traveled throughout Europe. His birth and his fortune made him sought after everywhere, but the attractions of society never drew him. Young and handsome, he remained serious and somber, devoured by a thirst for learning, with an implacable resentment riveted to his heart.

Prince Dakkar hated. He hated the one country where he had always refused to set foot, the one nation whose advances he rejected again and again: he hated England — and all the more because, on more than one point, he admired her.

For this Indian carried in himself all the fierce hatred of the conquered for the conqueror. The invader could find no forgiveness in the invaded. He was the son of one of those sovereigns whose servitude the United Kingdom had managed to secure only in name; a prince of the family of Tipu Sultan, raised on ideas of reclaiming what had been taken and of vengeance, bound by an inescapable love to his poetic land weighed down with English chains. He would never set foot on that accursed soil to which India owed its enslavement.

Prince Dakkar became an artist whom the wonders of art stirred nobly, a scientist to whom nothing in the higher sciences was foreign, a statesman schooled in the courts of Europe. To those who observed him only superficially, he may perhaps have passed for one of those cosmopolitans, curious to know but disdainful of acting — one of those wealthy travelers, proud and detached spirits, who wander the world endlessly and belong to no country.

It was nothing of the kind. This artist, this scientist, this man had remained Indian at heart, Indian in his longing for revenge, Indian in the hope he nourished of one day reclaiming his country's rights, driving out the foreigner and giving it back its independence.

And so Prince Dakkar returned to Bundelkhand in the year 1849. He married a noble Indian woman whose heart bled, as his did, for the misfortunes of their homeland. They had two children, whom he cherished. But happiness at home could not make him forget India's enslavement. He waited for his opportunity. It came.

The English yoke had perhaps pressed too heavily on the peoples of India. Prince Dakkar gave voice to the discontented. He poured into their minds all the hatred he felt for the foreigner. He traveled not only through the regions of the Indian peninsula that were still independent, but also through the lands directly under English rule. He reminded the people of the great days of Tipu Sultan, who had died a hero's death at Seringapatam defending his homeland.

In 1857 the great Sepoy Rebellion broke out. Prince Dakkar was its soul. He organized that immense uprising. He put his talents and his wealth at the service of the cause. He did not spare himself: he fought in the front rank; he risked his life like the humblest of those heroes who had risen to free their country; he was wounded ten times in twenty battles, and still had not found death when the last soldiers of independence fell beneath English bullets.

Never had British power in India been in such danger. And if, as they had hoped, the sepoys had found help from outside, the influence and the dominion of the United Kingdom in Asia might well have come to an end.

The name of Prince Dakkar was famous then. The hero who bore it did not hide; he fought in the open. A price was put on his head, and though no traitor could be found to hand it over, his father, his mother, his wife, his children paid for him, before he could even know of the dangers they were running because of him...

Right, once again, had fallen before might. But civilization never retreats, and it seems to borrow every right from necessity. The sepoys were defeated, and the land of the old rajahs fell back under England's tighter rule.

Prince Dakkar, who had not been able to die, went back into the mountains of Bundelkhand. There, alone from then on, seized by an immense disgust for everything that bore the name of man, filled with hatred and horror for the civilized world and wishing to flee it forever, he turned what was left of his fortune into money, gathered some twenty of his most faithful companions, and one day they all vanished.

Where, then, had Prince Dakkar gone to look for the independence that the inhabited earth refused him? Beneath the waters, in the depths of the sea, where no one could follow him.

The man of war gave way to the man of science. A deserted island in the Pacific served him as a shipyard, and there a submarine boat was built to his designs. Electricity, whose immeasurable mechanical power he had learned to harness by means that will one day be known, and which he drew from inexhaustible sources, was put to every use his floating machine required: it drove her, lit her and heated her. The sea, with its infinite treasures, its myriads of fish, its harvests of seaweed and sargassum, its enormous mammals — and not only everything that nature kept there but everything that men had lost there too — amply supplied the needs of the prince and his crew. And that fulfilled his dearest wish, since he wanted no more communication of any kind with the land. He named his submarine machine the Nautilus, he called himself Captain Nemo, and he disappeared beneath the seas.

For many years the captain roamed every ocean, from one pole to the other. A pariah from the inhabited world, he gathered admirable treasures in those unknown realms. The millions lost in Vigo Bay in 1702 by the Spanish galleons gave him an inexhaustible mine of wealth, which he always spent, anonymously, on behalf of peoples fighting for the independence of their countries — the Cretans in their rising among them.

At last, when he had had no communication with his fellow men for a long time, three men were thrown aboard his ship during the night of November 6, 1866: a French professor, his servant and a Canadian fisherman. These three men had been hurled into the sea by a collision between the Nautilus and the United States frigate Abraham Lincoln, which was hunting her.

Captain Nemo learned from this professor that the Nautilus — taken sometimes for a giant mammal of the whale family, sometimes for a submarine machine carrying a crew of pirates — was being pursued on every sea.

Captain Nemo could have given those three men back to the ocean, men whom chance had flung so suddenly across his mysterious existence. He did not. He kept them prisoner, and for seven months they were able to gaze on all the wonders of a voyage that went on for twenty thousand leagues under the sea.

One day, June 22, 1867, these three men, who knew nothing of Captain Nemo's past, managed to escape after seizing the Nautilus's dinghy. But since at that moment the Nautilus was being dragged toward the coast of Norway in the whirlpools of the Maelström, the captain was bound to believe that the fugitives had drowned in those terrifying eddies and met their death at the bottom of the abyss. So he did not know that the Frenchman and his two companions had been miraculously thrown up on the shore, that fishermen of the Lofoten Islands had taken them in, and that the professor, on his return to France, had published the book in which seven months of the Nautilus's strange and adventurous voyage were told and delivered up to public curiosity.

For a long time still, Captain Nemo went on living in the same way, roaming the seas. But little by little his companions died and went to rest in their coral cemetery at the bottom of the Pacific. The Nautilus grew empty, and at last Captain Nemo was left alone, the only one remaining of all those who had taken refuge with him in the depths of the ocean.

Captain Nemo was sixty years old by then. When he found himself alone, he managed to bring his Nautilus back to one of the undersea harbors he sometimes used as ports of call.

One of these harbors was hollowed out beneath Lincoln Island, and it was the one now sheltering the Nautilus.

The captain had been there for six years, no longer sailing, waiting for death — that is, for the moment when he would be reunited with his companions — when chance made him a witness to the fall of the balloon that was carrying the Southerners' prisoners. He was walking under the water in his diving suit, a few cable lengths from the island's shore, when the engineer was flung into the sea. A generous impulse carried the captain away... and he saved Cyrus Smith.

At first he meant to flee from these five castaways. But his harbor of refuge was closed. Because the basalt had been heaved up under the action of the volcano, he could no longer pass through the entrance to the crypt. Where there was still enough water for a light boat to cross the bar, there was no longer enough for the Nautilus, which drew a comparatively great depth of water.

So Captain Nemo stayed. Then he watched these men, thrown without resources onto a deserted island, but he did not want to be seen. Little by little, when he saw that they were honest and full of energy, bound to one another by a brotherly friendship, he took an interest in their efforts. Almost in spite of himself, he came to know all the secrets of their lives. With the diving suit it was easy for him to reach the bottom of the inner well of Granite House, and by climbing the projections of the rock up to its upper mouth he could hear the colonists talking over the past and studying the present and the future. From them he learned of America's immense effort against America itself, to abolish slavery. Yes! These were men worthy to reconcile Captain Nemo with the humanity they represented so honestly on the island!

Captain Nemo had saved Cyrus Smith. It was he, too, who brought the dog back to the Chimneys; who flung Top out of the waters of the lake; who ran aground at Jetsam Point the chest that held so many useful things for the colonists; who sent the canoe back down the current of the Mercy; who threw down the rope from the top of Granite House when the monkeys attacked; who made Ayrton's presence on Tabor Island known by means of the document sealed in the bottle; who blew up the brig with a torpedo laid at the bottom of the channel; who saved Harbert from certain death by bringing the quinine sulfate; and it was he, finally, who struck down the convicts with those electric bullets whose secret he alone possessed and which he used in his hunts beneath the sea. That explained so many incidents that must have seemed supernatural, and that all bore witness to the captain's generosity and power.

And yet this great misanthrope thirsted to do good. He still had useful advice to give the people he had protected. And besides, feeling his heart, restored to itself by the approach of death, beating once more, he summoned the colonists from Granite House, as the reader knows, by means of a wire with which he had connected the corral to the Nautilus, which was fitted with an alphabet dial... Perhaps he would not have done it had he known that Cyrus Smith knew enough of his story to greet him by the name of Nemo.

The captain had finished the story of his life. Then Cyrus Smith spoke. He recalled all the incidents that had had so beneficial an influence on the colony, and in his companions' name as well as his own he thanked the generous being to whom they owed so much.

But Captain Nemo had no thought of claiming any reward for the services he had rendered. One last thought was troubling his mind, and before he took the hand the engineer held out to him, he said:

"Now, sir — now that you know my life, judge it!"

In speaking this way, the captain was clearly alluding to a grave incident that the three strangers flung aboard his ship had witnessed — an incident the French professor would necessarily have told in his book, and which must have caused a terrible stir.

And indeed, a few days before the professor and his two companions escaped, the Nautilus, chased by a frigate in the North Atlantic, had hurled herself like a battering ram against that frigate and sunk her without mercy.

Cyrus Smith understood the allusion and made no reply.

"It was an English frigate, sir!" cried Captain Nemo, for a moment Prince Dakkar again. "An English frigate, do you hear me? She was attacking me! I was hemmed in, in a narrow, shallow bay!... I had to get through, and... I got through!"

Then, in a calmer voice, he added:

"I was in the right, and justice was on my side. Everywhere I have done the good I could — and the harm I had to do as well. Not all justice lies in forgiveness!"

A few moments of silence followed this answer, and Captain Nemo spoke the same words again:

"What do you think of me, gentlemen?"

Cyrus Smith held out his hand to the captain, and in answer to his question he said in a grave voice:

"Captain, your mistake was to believe that the past could be brought back to life, and you fought against necessary progress. It was one of those errors that some admire and others condemn, which God alone can judge, and which human reason must absolve. A man who goes wrong with an intention he believes to be good may be fought, but he does not lose our esteem. Your error is one that does not rule out admiration, and your name has nothing to fear from the judgment of history. History loves heroic follies, even while it condemns the consequences they bring."

Captain Nemo's chest heaved, and his hand reached toward the sky.

"Was I wrong? Was I right?" he murmured.

Cyrus Smith went on:

"All great deeds go back to God, for they come from Him! Captain Nemo, the honest men here, whom you have helped, will mourn you forever!"

Harbert had come close to the captain. He knelt, took his hand and kissed it.

A tear slid from the dying man's eyes.

"My child," he said, "may you be blessed!..."

Chapter 17: The Last Hours of Captain Nemo

The last hours of Captain Nemo — The wishes of a dying man — A keepsake for his friends of a day — Captain Nemo's coffin — Some advice to the colonists — The supreme moment — At the bottom of the sea

Day had come. Not a ray of it reached that deep crypt. The sea, at high tide just then, blocked its opening. But the artificial light that streamed out in long beams through the sides of the Nautilus had not weakened, and the sheet of water still glowed all around the floating vessel.

By now an extreme weariness had overwhelmed Captain Nemo, who had sunk back onto the divan. There could be no thought of carrying him to Granite House. He had made it plain that he wished to stay among these marvels of the Nautilus, which millions could not have bought, and there to wait for a death that could not be long in coming.

Through a fairly long collapse that left him almost unconscious, Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett watched the sick man's condition closely. It was plain that the captain was fading little by little. Strength was about to fail that body, once so powerful and now the frail shell of a soul about to escape. All the life left in him was gathered in his heart and his head.

The engineer and the reporter had consulted in low voices. Was there any care they could give this dying man? If they could not save him, could they at least prolong his life for a few days? He himself had said that there was no remedy, and he was waiting calmly for death, which he did not fear.

"There's nothing we can do," said Gédéon Spilett.

"But what's he dying of?" asked Pencroff.

"He's burning out," answered the reporter.

"Still," the sailor went on, "if we carried him out into the open air, into the full sun, maybe he'd revive?"

"No, Pencroff," answered the engineer, "there's nothing to try! Besides, Captain Nemo would never agree to leave his ship. He's lived aboard the Nautilus for thirty years, and it's aboard the Nautilus that he means to die."

Captain Nemo must have heard Cyrus Smith's answer, for he raised himself a little, and in a weaker voice, but one still perfectly clear, he said:

"You are right, sir. I must die here, and I wish to. And so I have a request to make of you."

Cyrus Smith and his companions had come closer to the divan, and they arranged its cushions so that the dying man was better supported.

Then they could see his gaze come to rest on all the marvels of that salon, lit by electric rays softened through the arabesques of a luminous ceiling. One after another he looked at the paintings that hung on the splendid tapestries of the walls, those masterpieces of the Italian, Flemish, French and Spanish masters; at the marble and bronze statuettes standing on their pedestals; at the magnificent organ set against the after bulkhead; then at the glass cases arranged around a central basin, in which the most wonderful products of the sea were on display — marine plants, zoophytes, strings of pearls beyond price. And at last his eyes stopped on the motto inscribed over the doorway of this museum, the motto of the Nautilus:

    Mobilis in Mobili.

It seemed as though he wanted to caress with his eyes, one last time, these masterpieces of art and nature to which he had limited his horizon through so many years spent in the depths of the seas!

Cyrus Smith had respected the silence Captain Nemo was keeping. He waited for the dying man to speak again.

After a few minutes, during which, no doubt, he saw his whole life pass before him once more, Captain Nemo turned toward the colonists and said to them:

"You believe, gentlemen, that you owe me some gratitude?..."

"Captain, we would give our lives to prolong yours!"

"Good," Captain Nemo went on, "good!... Promise me that you will carry out my last wishes, and I shall be repaid for everything I have done for you."

"We promise," answered Cyrus Smith.

And with that promise he bound his companions and himself alike.

"Gentlemen," the captain resumed, "tomorrow I shall be dead."

With a sign he stopped Harbert, who wanted to protest.

"Tomorrow I shall be dead, and I wish to have no other tomb than the Nautilus. She is my coffin — mine! All my friends rest at the bottom of the sea, and I wish to rest there too."

A deep silence met these words of Captain Nemo's.

"Listen to me carefully, gentlemen," he went on. "The Nautilus is imprisoned in this cave, whose entrance has been raised up. But if she cannot leave her prison, she can at least sink into the abyss beneath it and keep my mortal remains there."

The colonists listened to the dying man's words with reverence.

"Tomorrow, after my death, Mr. Smith," the captain went on, "you and your companions will leave the Nautilus, for all the riches she contains must disappear with me. Only one keepsake will remain to you of Prince Dakkar, whose story you now know. This casket... there... holds several millions' worth of diamonds — most of them mementos of the time when, as a father and a husband, I almost believed in happiness — and a collection of pearls gathered by my friends and me at the bottom of the sea. With this treasure you will be able, when the day comes, to do good things. In hands like yours and your companions', Mr. Smith, money cannot be a danger. So from up there I shall be a partner in your works, and I have no fear of them!"

After a few moments of rest, made necessary by his extreme weakness, Captain Nemo went on in these words:

"Tomorrow you will take this casket and leave this salon, closing its door behind you. Then you will climb back up onto the platform of the Nautilus, and you will close the hatch and fasten it down with its bolts."

"We will, Captain," answered Cyrus Smith.

"Good. You will then go aboard the boat that brought you here. But before you leave the Nautilus, go to the stern, and there open two large valves that are set at the waterline. The water will flow into the tanks, and the Nautilus will sink little by little beneath the surface, to come to rest at the bottom of the abyss."

And at a gesture from Cyrus Smith, the captain added:

"Have no fear! You will be burying only a dead man!"

Neither Cyrus Smith nor any of his companions would have thought it right to raise any objection with Captain Nemo. These were his last wishes he was handing on to them, and all they had to do was carry them out.

"I have your promise, gentlemen?" Captain Nemo added.

"You have it, Captain," answered the engineer.

The captain made a sign of thanks and asked the colonists to leave him alone for a few hours. Gédéon Spilett insisted on staying near him in case a crisis came on, but the dying man refused, saying:

"I shall live until tomorrow, sir!"

They all left the salon, passed through the library and the dining room, and came forward to the engine room, where the electrical apparatus was installed that supplied the Nautilus with mechanical power as well as heat and light.

The Nautilus was a masterpiece that held masterpieces, and the engineer was filled with wonder.

The colonists climbed up onto the platform, which rose seven or eight feet above the water. There they stretched out beside a thick lens-shaped pane of glass that closed off a kind of great eye, from which a sheaf of light was pouring. Behind this eye lay a hollowed-out cabin that held the wheels of the rudder, where the helmsman stood when he steered the Nautilus through the layers of the deep — layers that the electric rays must have lit up over a considerable distance.

At first Cyrus Smith and his companions stayed silent, for they were deeply moved by what they had just seen and what they had just heard. Their hearts ached when they thought that the man whose arm had come to their rescue so many times, this protector they would have known for barely a few hours, was on the eve of death!

Whatever judgment posterity might pass on the deeds of that existence — an existence, so to speak, beyond the human — Prince Dakkar would always remain one of those strange figures whose memory can never fade.

"There's a man for you!" said Pencroff. "Can you believe he lived like that, at the bottom of the ocean? And when I think that maybe he didn't find any more peace down there than anywhere else!"

"The Nautilus," Ayrton observed then, "might have let us leave Lincoln Island and reach some inhabited land."

"A thousand devils!" cried Pencroff. "I'm not the man who'd ever risk steering a boat like that. Sailing on the sea — fine! But under the sea — no!"

"I'd think," the reporter answered, "that handling an underwater machine like this Nautilus must be very easy, Pencroff, and that we'd soon get used to it. No storms, no collisions to fear. A few feet below the surface, the waters of the sea are as calm as a lake's."

"Could be!" the sailor shot back. "But I'd rather have a good stiff blow aboard a well-rigged ship. A boat is made to go on the water, not under it."

"My friends," the engineer answered, "there's no point — at least where the Nautilus is concerned — in arguing over this question of underwater ships. The Nautilus isn't ours, and we have no right to dispose of her. Nor could she be of any use to us in any case. Besides the fact that she can no longer get out of this cavern, whose entrance is now closed by the uplift of the basalt rocks, Captain Nemo wants her to go down with him after his death. His wish is explicit, and we will carry it out."

After a conversation that went on a while longer, Cyrus Smith and his companions went back down inside the Nautilus. There they took some food and then returned to the salon.

Captain Nemo had come out of the collapse that had overwhelmed him, and his eyes had regained their brilliance. Something like a smile could be seen forming on his lips.

The colonists went up to him.

"Gentlemen," the captain said to them, "you are brave men, honest and good. You have all given yourselves without reserve to the common work. I have often watched you. I have loved you — I love you!... Your hand, Mr. Smith!"

Cyrus Smith held out his hand to the captain, who pressed it warmly.

"That is good!" he murmured.

Then, going on:

"But that is enough talk of me! I have to talk to you of yourselves, and of Lincoln Island, where you have found refuge... You are thinking of leaving it?"

"To come back to it, Captain!" Pencroff answered quickly.

"Come back to it?... Indeed, Pencroff," the captain answered with a smile, "I know how much you love this island. It has been transformed by your efforts, and it is truly yours!"

"Our plan, Captain," Cyrus Smith said then, "would be to make a gift of it to the United States, and to found on it a port of call for our navy — one that would be very well placed in this part of the Pacific."

"You are thinking of your country, gentlemen," the captain answered. "You are working for its prosperity, for its glory. You are right. One's country!... That is where one must return! That is where one ought to die!... And I — I am dying far from everything I have loved!"

"Do you have any last wish to pass on?" the engineer asked quickly. "Any keepsake to give to the friends you may have left behind in those mountains of India?"

"No, Mr. Smith. I have no friends left! I am the last of my race... and I have been dead a long time to everyone I ever knew... But let us come back to you. Solitude, isolation, are sad things, beyond human strength... I am dying of having believed that a man could live alone!... So you must try everything to leave Lincoln Island and to see again the land where you were born. I know that those wretches destroyed the boat you had built..."

"We're building a ship," said Gédéon Spilett, "a ship big enough to carry us to the nearest lands. But if we do manage to leave, sooner or later we'll come back to Lincoln Island. Too many memories bind us to it for us ever to forget it!"

"It is here that we came to know Captain Nemo," said Cyrus Smith.

"It's only here that we'll find the whole memory of you!" Harbert added.

"And it is here that I shall rest in the eternal sleep, if..." the captain answered.

He hesitated, and instead of finishing his sentence he simply said:

"Mr. Smith, I would like to speak with you... with you alone!"

The engineer's companions, respecting the dying man's wish, withdrew.

Cyrus Smith stayed shut in with Captain Nemo for only a few minutes, and soon he called his friends back. But he told them nothing of the secret things the dying man had wished to confide to him.

Gédéon Spilett then watched the sick man with the closest attention. It was obvious that the captain was now held up by nothing but strength of spirit, which would soon be unable to fight back against his physical decline.

The day ended without any change appearing. The colonists did not leave the Nautilus for a moment. Night had come, though there was no way to tell it in that crypt.

Captain Nemo was not in pain, but he was sinking. His noble face, paled by the approach of death, was calm. From his lips there sometimes escaped words that could barely be made out, touching on various incidents of his strange existence. They could feel the life withdrawing little by little from that body, whose hands and feet were already cold.

Once or twice more he spoke to the colonists gathered beside him, and he smiled at them with that last smile that lasts on even into death.

At last, a little after midnight, Captain Nemo made one supreme movement, and he managed to cross his arms over his chest, as though he wished to die in that attitude.

By about one o'clock in the morning, all the life left in him had taken refuge in his eyes alone. A last fire shone in those eyes, from which so many flames had once flashed. Then, murmuring the words "God and country!", he gently breathed his last.

Cyrus Smith bent down and closed the eyes of the man who had been Prince Dakkar and who was now no longer even Captain Nemo.

Harbert and Pencroff were weeping. Ayrton wiped away a furtive tear. Nab was on his knees beside the reporter, turned to stone.

Cyrus Smith raised his hand above the dead man's head.

"May God have his soul!" he said, and, turning to his friends, he added:

"Let us pray for the one we have lost!"

.........................

A few hours later the colonists were keeping the promise they had made to the captain. They were carrying out the dead man's last wishes.

Cyrus Smith and his companions left the Nautilus, taking with them the one keepsake their benefactor had left them, that casket which held a hundred fortunes.

The marvelous salon, still flooded with light, had been carefully closed. Then the sheet-iron door of the hatch was bolted down, so that not a drop of water could get into the rooms of the Nautilus.

Then the colonists went down into the boat, which was moored alongside the submarine vessel.

The boat was brought round to the stern. There, at the waterline, were the two large valves that connected with the tanks used to make the vessel dive.

The valves were opened, the tanks filled, and the Nautilus, sinking little by little, disappeared beneath the surface.

But the colonists could still follow her down through the deep layers of water. Her powerful light lit up the clear water, while the crypt went dark again. Then that vast outpouring of electric radiance faded at last, and soon the Nautilus, now Captain Nemo's coffin, lay at rest at the bottom of the sea.

Chapter 18: The Dakkar Crypt

Each one's thoughts — The shipbuilding resumed — January 1, 1869 — A plume on the top of the volcano — First signs of an eruption — Ayrton and Cyrus Smith at the corral — Exploring the Dakkar Crypt — What Captain Nemo had told the engineer

At daybreak the colonists made their way back in silence to the mouth of the cavern, which they named "the Dakkar Crypt" in memory of Captain Nemo. The tide was low now, and they could pass easily under the arch, where the water was lapping at the foot of its basalt pillar.

The sheet-iron boat was left there, placed so that the waves could not get at it. As an extra precaution, Pencroff, Nab and Ayrton hauled it up onto the little beach that ran along one side of the crypt, in a spot where it was in no danger at all.

The storm had ended with the night. The last rolls of thunder were dying away in the west. It was no longer raining, but the sky was still heavy with clouds. All in all, this month of October, the beginning of the southern spring, was not getting off to a promising start, and the wind kept jumping from one point of the compass to another, so that no one could count on settled weather.

On leaving the Dakkar Crypt, Cyrus Smith and his companions had set off back along the Corral Road. As they went, Nab and Harbert took care to free the wire the captain had strung between the corral and the crypt, since it might be useful later on.

The colonists said little as they walked. The events of that night of October 15 to 16 had struck them very deeply. The stranger whose influence had protected them so well, the man their imagination had turned into a genie — Captain Nemo — was gone. He and his Nautilus lay buried at the bottom of an abyss. It seemed to each of them that they were more alone than before. They had grown used, so to speak, to counting on that powerful help which they no longer had, and neither Gédéon Spilett nor even Cyrus Smith himself escaped the feeling. And so they all kept a deep silence as they followed the Corral Road.

At about nine in the morning the colonists were back at Granite House.

It had been firmly agreed that the building of the ship would be pushed forward as hard as possible, and Cyrus Smith gave it more of his time and care than ever. No one knew what the future held. And it would be a real safeguard for the colonists to have at their disposal a solid vessel, one that could keep the sea even in heavy weather, and big enough to attempt a voyage of some length if need be. Even if, once the vessel was finished, the colonists did not yet decide to leave Lincoln Island and make for one of the Polynesian archipelagos of the Pacific or the coast of New Zealand, they must at the very least go to Tabor Island as soon as possible and leave there the notice about Ayrton. It was an essential precaution in case the Scottish yacht should come back to these seas, and nothing was to be neglected on that score.

So the work was taken up again. Cyrus Smith, Pencroff and Ayrton, helped by Nab, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert whenever some other urgent job did not call them away, worked without a break. The new vessel had to be ready in five months — that is, by the beginning of March — if they wanted to visit Tabor Island before the equinoctial gales made the crossing impossible. So the carpenters did not lose a moment. They did not, for that matter, have to worry about making any rigging, since the Speedy's had been saved whole. Above all else, then, it was the hull of the ship that had to be finished.

The end of the year 1868 slipped by amid this important work, almost to the exclusion of everything else. After two and a half months the frames had been set in place and the first planks of the hull fitted. It was already clear that the plans Cyrus Smith had drawn were excellent and that the ship would handle well at sea. Pencroff threw himself into the work with a devouring energy, and he did not hesitate to grumble whenever one or another of them laid down the carpenter's ax for the hunter's gun. All the same, the stores of Granite House had to be kept up, with the coming winter in mind. No matter. The good sailor was not happy when there were hands missing from the shipyard. On those occasions, grumbling all the while, he did the work of six men — out of sheer temper.

The whole summer season was a bad one. For some days at a time the heat was crushing, and the air, saturated with electricity, would discharge itself only in violent storms that churned up the layers of the atmosphere. Hardly a day went by without the distant rolling of thunder. It was like a low but never-ending murmur, the kind heard in the equatorial regions of the globe.

January 1, 1869, was even marked by a storm of extreme violence, and lightning struck the island several times. Big trees were hit by the electric fluid and shattered, among them one of the enormous nettle trees that shaded the poultry yard at the southern end of the lake. Did this display in the sky have any connection with what was going on in the bowels of the earth? Was there some kind of link between the disturbances in the air and the disturbances deep inside the globe? Cyrus Smith was inclined to think so, for as these storms grew, the volcanic symptoms grew stronger too.

It was on January 3 that Harbert, who had gone up to Prospect Plateau at dawn to saddle one of the onaggas, saw an enormous plume unrolling from the top of the volcano.

Harbert at once alerted the colonists, who came straight away to look at the summit of Mount Franklin.

"Hey!" cried Pencroff. "That's not steam this time! Looks to me like the giant isn't satisfied with breathing anymore — he's smoking!"

The sailor's image described exactly the change that had taken place at the mouth of the volcano. For three months already the crater had been giving off steam, sometimes more, sometimes less, but it had come only from the minerals boiling inside. This time the steam had given way to a thick smoke, rising in a grayish column more than three hundred feet wide at its base, which spread out like an immense mushroom seven or eight hundred feet above the top of the mountain.

"The chimney's on fire," said Gédéon Spilett.

"And we can't put it out!" answered Harbert.

"Somebody ought to sweep out volcanoes," Nab remarked, apparently in the most serious way in the world.

"Good, Nab!" cried Pencroff. "Will you be the one to take on that sweeping job?"

And Pencroff let out a great roar of laughter.

Cyrus Smith was watching closely the thick smoke that Mount Franklin was throwing up, and he was even listening hard, as though he hoped to catch some distant rumbling. Then he came back to his companions, from whom he had moved a little way apart.

"You're right, my friends. An important change has taken place — there's no point in hiding it from ourselves. The volcanic matter isn't just boiling anymore. It has caught fire, and we are very certainly threatened with an eruption before long!"

"Well then, Mr. Smith, we'll watch the eruption," cried Pencroff, "and we'll applaud it if it's a good one! I don't see anything there for us to worry about!"

"No, Pencroff," answered Cyrus Smith, "because the old path of the lava is still open, and the way the crater is shaped, it has always poured its lava out toward the north until now. And yet..."

"And yet, since there's nothing to be gained from an eruption, it would be better if it didn't happen," said the reporter.

"Who knows?" answered the sailor. "Maybe there's some useful, valuable stuff in that volcano that it'll be kind enough to spit up, and we'll put it to good use!"

Cyrus Smith shook his head like a man who expected nothing good from something that had developed so suddenly. He did not take the consequences of an eruption as lightly as Pencroff did. Even if the lava, because of the way the crater faced, did not directly threaten the wooded and cultivated parts of the island, other complications could arise. Eruptions, in fact, are quite often accompanied by earthquakes. And an island like Lincoln Island, made of such different materials — basalt on one side, granite on the other, lava to the north, loose soil to the south — materials that could not, therefore, be solidly bound to one another, would run the risk of being broken apart. So even if the outpouring of volcanic matter was no very serious danger, any movement in the earth's framework that shook the island could lead to extremely grave consequences.

"It seems to me," said Ayrton, who had lain down so as to put his ear to the ground, "it seems to me I can hear a dull rumbling, like a wagon loaded with iron bars."

The colonists listened with the closest attention and could tell that Ayrton was not mistaken. Now and then the rumbling was mixed with underground roars that swelled into a kind of "rinforzando," as musicians say, and then died slowly away, as though some violent wind had blown through the depths of the globe. But no actual explosion could be heard yet. So they could conclude that the steam and smoke were finding a free way out through the central chimney, and that, since the safety valve was wide enough, nothing would break apart and no explosion was to be feared.

"Now look here!" said Pencroff then. "Aren't we going back to work? Mount Franklin can smoke, bawl, groan, spit out fire and flames as much as it pleases — that's no reason to do nothing! Come on, Ayrton, Nab, Harbert, Mr. Cyrus, Mr. Spilett — today everybody has to lend a hand! We're going to fit the wales, and a dozen arms won't be too many. Within two months I want our new Bonadventure — because we'll keep that name for her, won't we? — floating on the waters of Balloon Harbor! So, not an hour to lose!"

All the colonists, whose arms Pencroff was calling for, went down to the shipyard and set about fitting the wales — the thick planks that run around a ship like a belt and bind the frames of her skeleton firmly together. It was heavy, hard work, and every one of them had to take part.

So they worked steadily all that day of January 3, without worrying about the volcano, which in any case could not be seen from the beach below Granite House. But once or twice great shadows, veiling the sun as it traveled its daily arc across an extremely clear sky, showed that a thick cloud of smoke was passing between its disk and the island. The wind, blowing in from the sea, was carrying all these vapors off to the west. Cyrus Smith and Gédéon Spilett noticed these passing darkenings perfectly well, and more than once they talked over the obvious progress the volcano was making, but the work did not stop. It was, besides, of the greatest importance from every point of view that the vessel should be finished as soon as possible. Whatever might happen, the colonists' safety would be all the better assured by it. Who knew whether this ship might not one day be their only refuge?

That evening, after supper, Cyrus Smith, Gédéon Spilett and Harbert climbed back up to Prospect Plateau. Night had already fallen, and the darkness should let them see whether flames, or red-hot matter thrown up by the volcano, were mixed with the steam and smoke piled up at the mouth of the crater.

"The crater's on fire!" cried Harbert, who, being nimbler than his companions, had reached the plateau first.

Mount Franklin, about six miles away, now looked like a gigantic torch, with a few sooty flames twisting at its top. So much smoke, so much cinder and perhaps ash was mixed with them that their glow, greatly dimmed, did not stand out sharply against the darkness of the night. But a kind of tawny light spread over the island and picked out, dimly, the wooded masses in the foreground. Immense whirling clouds darkened the heights of the sky, and through them a few stars twinkled.

"It's moving fast!" said the engineer.

"That's not surprising," answered the reporter. "The volcano has been waking up for some time already. You remember, Cyrus, that the first steam appeared at about the time we were searching the mountain's spurs for Captain Nemo's hiding place. That was around October 15, if I'm not mistaken?"

"Yes!" answered Harbert. "Two and a half months ago already!"

"So the underground fires have been smoldering for ten weeks," Gédéon Spilett went on, "and it's no wonder they're growing so violent now!"

"Don't you feel a kind of vibration in the ground?" asked Cyrus Smith.

"I do," answered Gédéon Spilett, "but from that to an earthquake..."

"I'm not saying we're threatened with an earthquake," answered Cyrus Smith, "and God keep us from one! No. These vibrations come from the seething of the central fire. The earth's crust is nothing more than the wall of a boiler, and you know that the wall of a boiler, under the pressure of the gases, vibrates like a sounding board. That's what is happening right now."

"What magnificent sprays of fire!" cried Harbert.

At that moment there burst from the crater a sort of fireworks display whose brilliance the steam could not dim. Thousands of glowing fragments and bright points of light were flung out in every direction. Some of them shot past the dome of smoke, pierced it in a swift streak, and left behind them a real dust of glowing sparks. This burst of fire was accompanied by explosion after explosion, like the ripping fire of a battery of machine guns.

After an hour on Prospect Plateau, Cyrus Smith, the reporter and the boy went back down to the beach and returned to Granite House. The engineer was thoughtful, even worried, so much so that Gédéon Spilett felt he should ask him whether he foresaw some danger close at hand, for which the eruption would be either the direct or the indirect cause.

"Yes and no," answered Cyrus Smith.

"All the same," the reporter went on, "the greatest disaster that could happen to us — wouldn't that be an earthquake that turned the island upside down? And I don't think that's to be feared, since the steam and the lava have found a free way out."

"And so," answered Cyrus Smith, "I'm not afraid of an earthquake in the usual sense of the word — the convulsions of the ground caused by the expansion of underground vapors. But other causes can bring about great disasters."

"Which ones, my dear Cyrus?"

"I don't quite know... I need to see... to go over the mountain... In a few days I'll be sure about it."

Gédéon Spilett did not press him, and soon, in spite of the volcano's explosions, which were growing louder and which the echoes of the island repeated, the occupants of Granite House were sound asleep.

Three days went by: January 4, 5 and 6. They kept working on the boat, and the engineer, without explaining himself any further, pushed the work along with all his might. Mount Franklin was now hooded in a dark, sinister-looking cloud, and along with its flames it was spewing out red-hot rocks, some of which fell back into the crater itself. That led Pencroff, who was determined to see only the funny side of the thing, to say:

"Look at that! The giant's playing cup-and-ball! The giant's juggling!"

And in fact the matter it spewed out was falling back into the abyss, and it did not seem that the lava, swollen by the pressure inside, had yet risen as high as the mouth of the crater. At any rate, the breach in the crater's rim to the northeast, which was partly visible, was not pouring any stream down the northern slope of the mountain.

And yet, however urgent the shipbuilding was, other tasks required the colonists' presence at various points on the island. First of all, someone had to go to the corral, where the flock of mouflons and goats was penned, and renew the animals' supply of fodder. So it was agreed that Ayrton would go there the next day, January 7.
